column2: KAMPALA LAW REPORTS - SUBJECT INDEX
SUBJECT MATTER
ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
Works Ltd Vs. 1.Departed Asians Property Custodian Board.
2. National Resistance Movement Secretariat.
Whether NRM secretariat is a legal entity that can sue and be
sued on its own.
Held: The NRM secretariat does not have an independent existence on
its own because it gets its vote from Government and was therefore an
arm of Government like the Resistance Councils.  The proper 2nd
defendant would have been the Attorney General.
No injunction can issue against Government.
Since there was another similar suit pending before the Magistrates'
court, the suit filed later in the High Court would be stayed.
Wyclief Kiggundu Kato Vs. Attorney General.
Appointment to and dismissal from public service - the nature of
the contract.
Held: A cause of action is fact or combination of facts which give rise to
a right of action.
The procedure to strike out a plaint is appropriate where it is obvious
that the plaint is insufficient for the relief sought, unmaintainable and
unarguable.
Persons are employed in the Public Service by the President under A
104(1) of the Constitution which gives him the unfettered prerogative to
dismiss and retire at pleasure, and in the public interest.
R.36 of the Public Service Commission Regulations empowers a
responsible officer, in this case the Permanent Secretary, to interdict
an officer.  The rule does not indicate any limitation on duration of the
interdiction.
The presentation was required for purposes of rr.45(1) (a) and (b), and
48 (2) which avail the officer an opportunity to be heard.  The plaintiff
denied himself the right to be heard by refusal to make the presentation.
The retirement of the plaintiff was proper, and the plaint did not disclose
a cause of action.
Uganda Engineering Corp. Ltd. Vs. Lugazi Town Council.
Local authority whether local authority can levy rates beyond its
rating area.
Held: The local authority could not levy rates beyond its rating area,
however, whether the appellant company was within or without the
ratable area was a question that would be proved by fresh evidence
and therefore a retrial would be order in the valuation.
A Government valuer has a statutory formula for rating hereditaments
and once the formula is known, it is incumbent on him to show how he
applied the particular formula to arrive at a given value.
Since this was first appeal fresh evidence would not be allowed and
therefore the production of maps to prove whether the appellant
company was within a ratable would not be allowed.
Ontario Ltd Vs. Crispus Kiyonga & ars.
Vicarious liability - whether government could be held liable for
the action of a rebel movement that subsequently assumes power.
Held: Revolutionary movements are not legal entities until they assume
power.
The Government was a wrong party to the suit because the movement
was non-existent in law prior to its assumption of power.  A non-existing
entity cannot be a party to a contract thereby bind government.
For a contract to be binding, it must be between persons existing at the
time the contract is made.  "The NRM interim Government" did not
exist in law at the time of the alleged contract.  Therefore there was no
valid concluded contract.
The NRM interim Government could not have acted as agent of the
Government because the Government was not capable of entering into
such a contract.  An act which cannot be done by the principal cannot
be done by him through an agent.
The contract was unenforceable for being illegal because it was made
to commit a crime against the established government of the day.
The alleged contract could not be said to have been ratified by
Government because the subsequent government was established by a
proclamation in legal notice No.1 of 1986, which did not act
retrospectively to legalize acts done by the Interim Government of NRM.
The contract was frustrated by impossibility of performance since by
subsequently assuming power the then "interim Government of NRM"
had now to act legally within the confines of the law; this thereby meant
that the contract could not be performed as envisaged by the parties.
Uganda Blanket Manufacturers (1973) Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Administrative field - dash whether  - a minister can wind up a
statutory organ without statutory provision.
Held: Decree 22 of 1974 provided that the Minister of Industry shall
control the management of the appellant company through the Board of
Directors, therefore for the Minister to purport to have wound up the
Board which was a statutory body so that he could control the
management of the company directly was illegal.  A statutory body can
only be wound up by a statutory provision.
An action to enforce the company's rights was properly commenced in
the company's name because a new group had assumed the control of
the company which was allowing it to be run on an ultra-vires basis.
And moreover neither the Ministry, nor the Board of Directors nor the
general meeting could have commenced these proceedings in the
circumstances.
The conduct of the Minister did not occasion the award of exemplary
damages because the Minister merely misconceived his task.
He thought he was operating a Government owned Company by virtue
of Decree 2 of 1974 and thought he was preserving Government property
and looking to the wider interests of the textile industry.
Attorney General Vs. Abdul Karim Ninyi.
Game control - whether importation of chimpanzees through lia,
a non-scheduled entry point - was lawful.
Held: All non-Ugandans Chimpanzees were defined in the 1959 Game
(Preservation and Control) Act as Pan Anthropopithecus and were
scheduled in the 11th schedule as species that were protected as
endangered species internationally and a valid permit from the Chief
Game Warden had not given the requisite permit.
Lia the entry through which the said chimpanzees were imported from
Zaire was not a scheduled entry point and notwithstanding evidence of
an established modus operandi by government officials of allowing
importation of the said animals through lia, the importation, the subject
of the appeal, was illegal.
The provisions of the Act did not schedule Lia as an approved entry
point for the importation of the said Chimpanzees and the conduct of the
government officials in establishing a modus operendi of using Lia for
proposes of importing into Uganda such animals could not estopped
the Attorney General from complaining of such conduct.
Since the Respondent had prayed for the value of the Chimpanzees at
the date of judgment and had further stated at the trial that the
Chimpanzees had no value as they were too old, no special damages
would have been awarded for the value of the animals.  Having stated
that he wanted the value as at the date of judgment the respondent
pre-clueded himself from asking for consequential damages, namely
damages based on the value at an earlier date than the date of
judgment.
Edward Fredrick Sempebwa Vs. Attorney General.
proclamation - whether statutory instrument or substantive
legislation.
Held: It was not settled whether the court that makes the reference of
matters to the Constitutional Court should as well act as the
constitutional Court to decide on the substantive matter thereby referred.
The view of the Court was that the Court is not necessarily the same
Court as the one that finally determines the Constitutional questions in
substance.
There is no laid down procedure as to how the questions framed by the
Court for reference may be brought before the Constitutional Court.
Neither of the respondents did not contest the method used, I.e., the
notice of motion however.
On or about the 26th day of January 1986 an armed group known as the
National Resistance Army entered Kampala the capital of Uganda and
by force of  arms took its control and seized the reigns of power.
Therefore, this amounted means, and that the proclamation (LN 2/86)
extra - Constitutional legal order, in accordance with which the validity
of laws in Uganda has to be determined.
The authorities that made the successful revolution set up conditions for
the basis of the new legal order, and spelt these conditions in Legal
Notice No.1 of 1996 and the saved provisions of the 1967 Constitution.
Once this was done, the authorities were precluded from departing from
these conditions and any subsequent legislation by them was to be in
conformity therewith, I.e. within this legislative framework.  Therefore
the validity or otherwise of Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 must be viewed
within the perimeters of the legal order already in place.
Since Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 was a proclamation and not a decree
promulgated by the National Resistance Council as required by Legal
Notice No.1 of 1986, and since the proclamation was not signed by the
President of Uganda but by the Chairman of the meant that the Legal
Notice was made not in accordance with the rules already laid down.
Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 would be declared invalid because it was not
made in accordance with the Legal Legislation framework put in place
by the revolution.  The Court's pronouncement of invalidation would be
necessary to avoid uncertainty in legislation and cause government to
follow the rule of law in exercising legislative powers and others and
moreover the declaration would not prejudice the security of the state,
and that the situation would easily be corrected retrospectively by the
state putting in place the right legislation in accordance with the law.
Shah's case set a precedent and defined a judgment debt/decree to be
properly protected by the constitution and this precedent would be
followed since the court in the instant, case is of co-ordinate jurisdiction
with the court in Shah's case which was a court of first instance on the
issue of judgment debt being property protected by the constitution and
the modern practice demands that a judge of first instance should as a
matter of judicial community follow the decision of another judge of
first instance unless he is convinced that the judgment was wrong.  The
view should apply to the instant case.
Since the applicant's judgment debt is properly protected by the
constitution, para 12(2) of Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 conflicted with and
infringed upon the constitutional rights of the applicant and consequently
that paragraph cannot be valid unless Article 8 (2) (c ) and 13 of the
constitution are repealed or modified by paragraph 13 does not
expressly repeal the said articles, let alone its being retrospective.  The
cardinal principles of Statutory Interpretation require that legislation that
infringes upon constitutional rights must expressly state so.
Sam Osingida & David Opolot by next friend Peter Ariong
Vs. Attorney General.
Law - public trustee- award of general damages to infants-maybe
paid to public trustee.
Held: Court took judicial notice of the state of insurgency in the area
and of the regulations.
The soldier was acting in the course of his duties and government was
vicariously liable.
To determine the quantum of lost dependence, the annual income of the
deceased which used to be spent on the infants would be multiplied by
the number of years that the dependency would have continued.  It
would have continued for 25 years.
Proved funeral expenses incurred by the deceased's brother as special
damages are allowed.
Award of exemplary damages was prohibited by S.33(2) of the Law
Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions Act).
Uganda National Examination Board Vs. Okello - Okello.
Government proceedings - whether the Uganda National Examine-
tion Board performed government functions and therefore the
Attorney General was the right - defendant.
Held: By virtue of its functions the applicant Uganda National
Examinations Board was a government department since it was an
independent body seeking to observe the Government overall objectives
in Education.  However by its very set up as a corporation sole, the
respondent litigant had a choice whether to sue the Board as an
emanation of the Government or as an independent body.  He chose the
Attorney General was not thereby governed by the Government
proceedings Act but by the Civil Procedure Act and Rules.  This meant
that the endorsement of the hearing Notice by the Attorney General's
registry clerk was sufficient evidence of service.  Therefore the Attorney
General was not prevented from attending court by sufficient cause and
therefore his application to restore the appeal would thereby be refused.
Bucket Farmers & General Marchan Dise Ltd Vs. Libyan
Arab Bank & Bank of Uganda.
Bank of Uganda - whether entitled to fix its own exchange rate
when dealing in foreign currency.
Held: Bank of Uganda was entitled to purchase the appellant's Kenya
currency at any of the two rates is sh. 3/70 or sh.86/80 as per its power
conferred on it by s.23 of the Bank of Uganda Acts foreign currency.
And s.20(2) (a) allowed the Bank got fix its exchange rate.
Christopher Sebuliba Vs. Treasury Officer of Account c/o
Attorney General.
Mandamus - whether writ may issue against the Treasury Officer
of Accounts to pay the applicant his decretal account.
Held: Failure to respect the order of the Court to pay was a delaying
tactic which was oppressive to the applicant citizen.  This was a proper
case for the issue of the writ of mandamus.
Siiva Nabugere Vs. Faalo s/o Sukura
Court inspection O.46 r7 -whether the high court - may
impeach a decision of the Grade III Magistrate passed
25 years ago.
Held: Court was not persuaded to interfere with a decision made in
1969 25 years ago without causing great inconvenience or even injustice
to those who were made to act upon it on the belief that it was a
correct decision.
Lalani William Vs. Alan Williamson & anor.
Approved schools- Destitute Child - whether court may
declare a child destitute without calling its parents .
Held: S.18(2) of the Approved School's Act defines a child who is in need
of care and protection.  However since the infants were found with their
father, and were in fact taken away from him, they could not be presumed
to be children needing care and protection under s.18(2) of the Act.
Moreover S.190(2) mandatorily requires that before a child can be found
to be in need of care and protection his known parents or guardians must
be afforded an opportunity to attend and be heard in court.  This
mandatory provision was not followed by the Ag. Judge and thereby his
order was not valid and be set aside.
When divorce proceedings are pending in court custody of children must
be left to the parent or guardian having the defacto custody during the
pendency of the proceedings unless court directs otherwise and it
should be only court to order that the children of the marriage may be
taken outside the jurisdiction of court without a court order but by merely
a letter from the Ag. Judge.  This was unlawful.
The paramount consideration in custody proceedings is the welfare of
the child.  The court invariably considers the conduct of the parents, their
wishes and their means.  Since the evidence that the Mother of the
infants was paranoid had not been rebutted, the custody of the children
should go to the father.
Jovda K.Patel Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority.
Certiorari - whether writ may issue against the respondent
quashing her assessment of the income tax of the applicant on
grounds that the assessment was not lawful.
Prohibition - whether writ may issue against the respondent
prohibiting her from receiving money from the applicable till there was
proper assessment of the applicants tax liability.
Held: The evidence on record shows that the income tax assessment
was based on the applicant's gross income when it levied on his income.
this allegation must be investigated at the hearing of the application for
the writs of certiorari and prohibition and therefore leave would be given
to the applicant to apply for the said writs.
Administrator General Vs. Uganda Posts Telecommunications
Mandamus - whether writ may issue when no leave for application
thereof has been sought - nor granted.
Summary administration - whether Administrator General may
summarily administer an estate whose value is known to be above
Held:  The application for mandamus was wrongly before court since no
leave for the application had first been sought by Chamber Summons as
required by R.3 (2) of the Law Reform (Misc.Prov.) (Rules of Court) Rules.
Even if the application was to be held to be properly before Court it was
misconceived because for the Administrator General to administer an
estate whose value is more than shs.20,ooo/= he must have letters of
Administration.  Unless the applicant produced such letters the
respondent was not obliged to surrender the death benefits of its
deceased employees in the applicant.
Lawrence Mussitwa K. Kyazze Vs. Eunice Busigye.
Attorney General proper defendant in a suit for recovery of land
where the defendant government officer is in possession.
Recovery of possession against government officer-whether order tenable.
Damages and mesne profits against government officer-whether order to
pay the same is tanable.
Held: Under Common Law rules of pleading and practice, in suits for
recovery of possession a person found in possession of the suit Land is
the proper defendant.  The appellant was the one in physical possession
and was properly sued.  It was upon him to claim indemnity from those
that put him in possession by serving upon them third party notice.
S.15 (1) (b) prohibits orders of recovery of Land against a government
officer such as the appellant, if the effect of the order would be the same
as an order against Government.  The appellant was in possession in
his official capacity as misconceived and a declaration of ownership by
the respondent would be substituted instead.
S. 15 91) (b) constituted a restriction on the rights of citizens and
would thereby be construed narrowly.  Accordingly to imply that order
for the payment of damages and mesne profits is veiled under what is
expressly prohibited under s.15 (1) (b) would not be tenable.  Therefore
these orders would not be interfered with.
Ronald Kayara Vs. Hassan Ali Ahmed.
Grant of lease by municipal council - whether equity and
constitutional guarantees are a fetter on the power - whether the
council acted ultra-vires.
Held: The plaintiff was not a beer licensee because the council by
conduct had let the plaintiff to believe that his renewal of his T.O.L was
permanent.  This meant that the plaintiff's license was coupled with a
proprietary interest which was protected by equity and the principle of
estoppel would operate to prevent revocation of a right which one party
has led the other to suppose it was permanent.  Moreover Art. 13 of the
Constitution disallowed expropriation of any ones proprietary interest
without compensation.  Therefore the municipal council acted ultra-vires
when they made a grant of a lease to the defendant on the plaintiff's
premises, he occupied under a T.O.L without due regard to compensation.
The law requires a higher standard of proof of fraud than in ordinary Civil
cases.  The learned trial judge, had he in the instant case applied the
requisite standard of proof to the facts it cannot be said that the evidence
would be sufficient to prove fraud.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself on the standard of proof of fraud and thereby arrived
at a wrong conclusion of a finding on fraud.
A third party Notice under O.1 r14 issues where the defendant claims to
be entitled to contribution or indemnity from the Third party.  In the
instant case the defendant never claimed anything from the municipal
council but it is only the plaintiff who claimed that the council had acted
ultra vires or arbitrarily.  Therefore it is the plaintiff under O.1 r3 CPR who
should have joined the council as a co-defendant.  Therefore the learned
trial judge misdirected himself to have held that it was the defendant to
apply for court's leave to issue a third party notice.
Wycliff Kiggundu Vs. Attorney General.
Public service - interdiction - whether this may be indefinite.
Held: Rejected the plaint under O.7 r11 (a) CPR must be primarily and
only the result of constructing the plaint as it stands and no other
extraneous matter must be considered.  The plaint must be found
defective such that if fails to disclose a cause of action.  In the instant
case the argument that the action was not maintainable at law was a
preliminary point of law and not a result of a defect in the plaint.
Therefore the preliminary point of law should have been set down for
hearing and the plaintiff's suit should have been dismissed if the court
found that his action not maintainable but his plaint should not have
been rejected.  The trial judge misdirected himself when he rejected the
plaintiff's plaint.
Regulation no 36 of the Public Service Regulations provides that a Public
Servant may be interdicted if proceedings for his dismissal are about to
be taken or if criminal proceedings are being instituted against him.
The gap between either of these proceedings and his interdiction must
be reasonably short.  Therefore the plaintiff had a maintainable cause of
action for a declaration and or damages for having been on interdiction
for more than 2 years.  The trial judge misdirected himself in rejecting
the plaintiff's plaint.
Again Regulation no.36 of the Public Service Regulations provides that a
public servant may be interdicted if proceedings for his dismissal are
about to be taken or Criminal Proceedings are being instituted against
him.  The plaintiff was interdicted upon the commencement of police
inquires against his conduct and not upon the determination of the
authorities to institute actual proceedings for dismissal or prosecution.
Therefore, his interdiction was commenced on an illegal basis.  The
plaintiff has a maintainable action for a declaration and or for damages
upon the unlawful interdiction.  The trial judge misdirected himself in
rejecting the plaintiff's plaint.
The trial judge misdirected himself when he held at the plaintiff's cause
of action was not maintainable at law due to the Presidential prerogative
under Art.104 of the Constitution to dismiss the plaintiff in public because
the plaintiff's action did not seek impeach the Presidential prerogative but
the conduct of the Public Service Commission which had acted outside
the law in interdicting him and advising the president to dismiss him in
Public interest.
Paul Kisekka Saku Vs. Seventh Day Adventist Church.
Prescribed Authority - public land - whether since prescribed
Authority was not defined, there was no need to give notice to
prescribed Authority to have a transfer of public land.
Held: Since the appellant's acquisition of the Kibanja did not constitute
a creation of a new customary interest on public land, the transfer of the
customary interest from Nandaula to the appellant was governed by
S.4(1) of the Land Reform Decree which requires that the transfer should
be proceeded by a three months notice of the intended transfer to the
prescribed authority.  Since there was no such notice, the transfer was
unlawful and void.
A.16 of the Land Reform Decree defines Prescribed Authority as
including the Uganda Land Commission.  This includes the Local chiefs
and the land committees.
Harriet Grace Bamale(through her next friend)Kituuma Magala
Vs.The Board of Government of Makerere College School.
Certiorari - whether school Board of Governors is amenable to
writ of certiorari - Education (Board of governors) Regulations
1991 - whether Boards of governors perform administrative,
judicial, or quasi judicial functions.
Held: For a body to be amenable to a writ of Certiorari, it must be
excising judicial or quasi judicial functions, I.e. arriving at its decisions
after hearing evidence between a proposal and an opposition.  The Board
of Governors for schools is regulated by the Education (Board of
Governors) Regulations 1991.  There is no procedure laid down in the
regulation for securing that a student is to have a right of hearing before
the Board.  The Board is not required to hold an inquiry, public or other-
wise, it is not required to receive evidence from any one.  There is
nothing to suggest that the Board has to act judicially.  The Board is a
pure administrative body carrying out administrative functions and
therefore it is not amenable to a writ of certiorari.
Lake Victoria Bottling Co. & 2 ors Vs. Crown Boilers Ltd.
Suits against government - whether the third party notice may
issue against government - whether government is in possession
of the information indicating the cause of liability.
Yosia Ofumbi Vs. Nagongera Farmers & anor.
Natural justice - whether breached where lease granted without
customary tenant being heard.
Held: There was undisputed evidence that the plaintiff used to grow
seasoned crops on one part of the suit and which thereby established
his usufructory rights.  S.24(1) of the Public Lands Act recognizes such
tenancy as customary tenancy.
Since the defendant had had a dispute over the suit land in the RC
Courts but went ahead and processed a title over the land through the
2nd defendant Land Commission without first suit solving the dispute,
means that the first defendant had knowledge of the existence of the
plaintiff's unregistered interest in the disputed land but knowingly and
wrongfully defeated the plaintiff's interest by registration and this
constituted fraud on the part of the 1st defendant.
The fact that the plaintiff had not been heard in defence of his customary
interest before the 1st defendant could take a lease of the disputed land,
constituted a breach of the principle of natural justice, the right to be
heard.  The plaintiff was therefore entitled to a redemacation of the
disputed land for the rectification of the register or he could elect to be
compensated.
Fancy Stores Ltd anor Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Government proceedings - statutory notice - failure to file statutory
notice, whether fatal.
Held: The defendant having denied the contents of paragraph 25 of the
plaint which alleged that service of the statutory notice had been done,
the service of the statutory notice was an issue.
The suit was barred by law because of non service of the statutory notice
as required by S.1(1) of the Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc./Prov.)
Act 1969 and the plaint must be rejected.
Hannington Wasswa &anor Vs. Maria Onyango Ochola&3ors.
Public officer - court broker - whether a court broker was a public
officer and therefore action against him was time barred by s.3 of
the Act.
Held: S.81(2) of the Civil Procedure Act only empowers the court of
appeal to perform only the duties conferred on the court of first instance,
the court of original jurisdiction. In the present case the Chief Magistrate's
court as court of first instance to order for the cancellation of a
certification of Title.  The appellate therefore had no jurisdiction to order
for the cancellation of the certificate of Title.
S.3 of the Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc.Prov) Act 20/69 requires
that any action brought against a public officer challenging any act done
in execution of his public duty, be brought within six months next after
the act being challenged.  Since a court broker was a public officer
executing a public duty, the action against him brought in 1982 was time
barred.
Even if it could be said that since the action brought against the court
broker was based on fraud, then time started running when the fraud
could have been discovered.  According to the facts of the case, the
alleged fraud must have been discovered by May 1981 and yet the first
motion on notice was brought in September 1982 which was definitely
out of time.
It was not proper to commence proceedings to challenge the alleged acts
of fraud by notice of motion because the standard of proof of fraud must
be high.  This therefore requires an ordinary suit where witnesses may
be cross examined.
A court broker is an agent of the court and not an agent of the parties.
Therefore it is necessary that the court broker should be sued separately.
Nazarali Hassanali Sayani Vs. Edward Mperese Nsubuga.
Delegation of duty - propriated properties (repossession and
Disposal) Regulations- whether letter of repossession signed by
minister of state for finance instead of the minister of finance is
defective.
Held: Since the plaintiff's land before the re-entry by the landlord, had not
been taken over or appropriated the plaintiff did not have a cause of action
under S.1(a), (b), ( c) of the Expropriated Properties Act.  His suit was
misconceived.  The re-entry was lawful and was not precluded by the Act
since the re-entry took place after the coming into force of the Act.
The letter of repossession was of no consequences since it was not
provided for in law.  The Expropriated Properties (Repossession and
Disposal Regulations) empowered only the Minister of Finance to issue a
Certificate of Repossession.  A letter of repossession by a Minister of
State for Finance was not provided for in law.
The defendant's proprietary interest could not be defeated because he
was a bonafide purchaser for value without notice of any defect in title.
He was protected by S.189 of the Registration of Titles Act.
Suit dismissed with costs.
MDG Khan Vs. Islamic University of Uganda.
Certiorari law reform (miscellaneous provisions) Rules S.74 - R1
rr5 and 8 (2) -quasi-judicial body-whether a statutory University is
a public body whether it acts quasi - judiciously while considering
appointments - whether is amenable to a writ of certiorari.
Held: The Islamic University of Uganda was a statutory public body.
However, its appointment committee did not sit as either a quasi-judicial
or judicial organ while considering appointments.  Therefore the
respondent was not emendable to a writ of certiorari.
application dismissed.
Wilson Nuwemugizi Vs. National Water & Sewerage Corp.
Public service standing orders-whether public services standing
should be applied to the situation because the regulations of the
corporation did not - adequately cover the circumstances of
retirement.
Held: The learned trial Judge misdirected himself on the evidence when he
held that the plaintiff/appellant had accepted voluntary retirement.  The
acceptance of the emoluments as suggested in the letter the defendant
did not mean that the plaintiff had accepted to retire voluntarily.  There
was evidence that the plaintiff wanted the contrary situation but the
Managing Director showed him that he could not change the decision of
the Board of the defendant.
Moreover, the terms of service of the defendant stipulated that where a
given situation was not adequately covered by the Terms of Service
Regulations, re-course should be had to the Government Standing Orders.
It happens that the terms of service of the defendant did not provide the
procedure for voluntary retirement and therefore resort must be had to the
Government Standing Orders, 1968 chapter one, regulation one, which
provides that an officer cannot voluntarily retire until he has applied for the
purpose and acceptance therefore given.  In the instant case the
appellant never applied for voluntary retirement.  Therefore the trial Judge
misdirected himself on the law when he held that the appellant had
voluntarily retired.
The defendant/respondent never pleaded in its Written Statement of
Defence that the plaintiff/appellant had had his contract of service
terminated.  However, the same was framed as an issue for trial and the
plaintiff never protested.  Evidence thereafter was led and the issue was
resolved on the evidence.  Therefore since the plaintiff never objected to
the issue being framed at all nor evidence being led to prove the issue the
irregularity of lack of pleading had been cured.  The learned trial Judge
was entitled to hold that the plaintiff's contract of employment had been
terminated.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Jan Mohamed Ltd Vs. Keniisa Senya.
Delegates non-Protest delegare-s.5 (I) expropriated properties Act
whether the minister responsible for finance could easily be the
minister but not his deputy or assistant.
Held: The literal interpretation of the "Minister responsible for Finance"
would absurdly lead to the conclusion that the Minister himself and not
his deputy or Minister of state should deal with the thousands of
applications from former owners of expropriated properties.  The meaning
therefore would be modified to avoid the absurdity and conclude that the
certificate of repossession was Finance.
The regulations made by the Minister for Finance under the power
conferred upon him by S.15 (a) (b) of the Expropriated Properties Act
prescribing the forms of application for repossession could not be strictly
interpreted as to deny the right granted by statute for repossession.
Therefore the objection that the repossession certificate did not satisfy the
prescribed form would be overruled since the right to repossess was
already granted by the statute.
Objection overruled.
In re Captain Mike Kmakeal Mwaka.
Habeas Corpus s.33 judicature Act -court martial jurisdiction s.80(1)
NRA statute - whether general court martial has no jurisdiction to
try the applicant as a court of first instance.
Habeas corpus-detention without trial in military prison-whether High Court
has jurisdiction to order a court martial to release the applicant on bail.
Held: S.80 (1) of the National Resistance Army Statute provides that the
General Court-Martial has jurisdiction original and appellate.  Therefore
the applicant was lawfully charged in and remanded by the General Court
Martial.
S.33 (1) Judicature Act provides that the High Court may issue a writ of
habeas corpus for the production of the applicant before it against the
person illegally detaining such person in order for the court to inquire into
the circumstances of the alleged illegal detention.  But where it is clear
that a person is remanded by a court with competent jurisdiction then the
applicant cannot be released.  In the instant case, the General Court-
Martial was court of competent jurisdiction which remanded the
applicant and court would therefore not release him.
The High Court has no jurisdiction over the proceedings of a court martial.
Therefore the High Court cannot order the General Court Martial to release
the applicant on bail.
Application dismissed.
Tom Byakatonda on behalf of Rushwa Growers Co-op Soc.
Vs. The Board of Directors Banyankole Kweterana Co-op union.
Mandamus and prohibition - Locus standi-whether applicant
society was directly affected by acts complained of-whether
applicant society had sufficient interest to protect -whether there
was no other remedy available at law.
Police discretion to investigate crime-Judicial intervention-whether court may
not interfere with police's discretion in the investigation of crime.
Held: First an applicant for a writ of mandamus must have been directly
affected by the decision of the respondent, he seeks to quash or annual.
In the instant case, though Byakatonda Bangirana were officials of the
applicant, the decisions allegedly taken by the Board of the respondent did
not directly affect applicant therefore the applicant Cooperative Society had
no locus to file this application.
Secondly, an application for a writ of mandamus must show that he had
sufficient interest to be protected by the violence of the unit.  In the instant
case the applicant society had no sufficient interest in the individual
grievances of its grounds.  Therefore the applicant society had no locus.
Thirdly an applicant for a unit of mandamus must show that there is not
other available remedy convenient apart from the application for the unit. In
the instant case the officials of the cooperative society the applicant since
they were individually aggrieved could have filed proceedings against the
registrar of cooperative societies as provided by the Cooperative Societies
Regulations 1992.  Therefore an alternative remedy provided by law existed.
Therefore, the applicant had no locus to file their proceedings.
Police have discretion in the way they carry out criminal investigations and
court cannot interfere in their investigations.
Application dismissed with costs.
Uganda Bankers (employers)Association Vs. National union
of Clerical, Commercial Professional & Technical Employers.
Writ of certiorari and prohibition error of law on face of record -
whether there was an error of law self evident on the record -
whether therefore the award of the industrial Court may be quashed
and award prohibited from taking effect.
Held: S.4 the Trade Disputes (Arbitration & Settlement) Act establishes
the Industrial court and provides for its composition.  It does not state
that the independent panelist must sit on all cases that arises before
the court.
The alleged error of law for purposes of certiorari, must be apparent on
the face on the record, must be self-evident.  The Court's regret that some
information was unavailable did not constitute an error of law apparent on
the face of the record because it is not the duty of court to look for
evidence.  Therefore the writs for certiorari and prohibition are refused.
Application dismissed with costs.
Stephen Byaruhanga Vs. Mbarara Municipal Council.
Certiorari and prohibition - jurisdiction whether orders of certiorari
and prohibition should issue to quash subordinate legislation -
whether Court has jurisdiction to grant orders of certiorari and
prohibition to quash subordinate legislation.
Held: In law, a counter offer operates as a rejection of the original offer.
A rejection of the original offer means that no contract is concluded since
there was no acceptance.  Since the respondent inter alia offered that the
applicants must pay the balance within one year and yet the applicants
counter offered to pay it within two years, it means that no contract was
concluded between the applicants and the respondent.
Certiorari is a prerogative with which will issue to quash a decision of
a tribunal exercising judicial or quasi judicial functions, which tribunal is
found to have acted ultra-vires its powers or its decision is vitiated by error
on the face of the record.  Prohibition issues to forbid some act or
decisions which would be ultra vires.  In the case instant the decision by
the respondent Municipal Council to rescind its decision to sell the
houses was legislative act, exercising its powers to make subordinate
legislation.  Therefore, the writs of certiorari and prohibition could not
apply to a decision which was purely legislative and not judicial or quasi
judicial.
H.M.B Kayondo S.C Vs. Attorney General.
Contract of service between the state and plaintiff - whether
established.
Held: In an application to strike out pleadings which do not disclose a
cause of action or defence, the court would only look at the pleadings
as filed by the parties to the action and no formal application is required.
That a preliminary objection could be raised even after the pleadings
were closed, since, if argued as a preliminary, could dispose of the suit.
That the Government Standing Orders do not constitute a contract
between the President as appointing authority and public officers and
therefore such public officers may not sue for breach of contract.
That the plaint failed to disclose a cause of action and that this
incurable and would be struck out.
W.W.Kaggwa & 16 others Vs. Yowana Kiwanuka & 2 ors.
Administration of Estates -Revocation of grant - whether application
therefore must be an ordinary suit under s.263 of the Succession Act.
Held: S.265 of the Succession Act provides that whenever there is a
contention in any case, it shall take the form of an ordinary suit.  This
provision however applies where an application for grant of probate or
letters of administration is contested by the caveat.  But in the instant
case the grant of probate was made already to the respondent.
Therefore s.265 of the Succession Act was not applicable but the
originating summons under O.34 r1, 2 CPR where the instant case
properly fitted.
Mugambwa G.W. Vs. Kisembo Muleju G.W.
Certiorari-whether certiorari may issue to quash decisions of High
Court.
Held: The High Court is not amenable to the writ to certiorari because it is
not an inferior tribunal.
S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act provides that the award of costs was at the
discretion of court and therefore the decision of the High Court not to award
costs was not an error on the face of the record.
S.15(3) Parliamentary Elections Statute 1996 provides that the orders of the
High Court on appeal in determining complaints emanating from the
Electoral Commission shall be final.  Therefore the refusal to award costs
was not appealable since the Court had in its discretion, exercised under
s.27(1) Civil Procedure Act, decided not to award any costs.  Therefore, the
respondent had no right of appeal.
Application allowed no order as to costs.
In re Mustapha Ramathan
Certiorari-time-whether application out of time.
Certiorari-other alternative remedies-whether writ not available
because other alternative legal remedies exist.
Prohibition-whether order preventive or corrective.
Held: S.34(b) Judicature Act requires an application for leave to file for a writ
of certiorari to be filed within 6 months from the date of the happening of the
act sought to be quashed. In the instant case the repossession order is
dated 6th October 1995 and yet the application is filed on 25th April,1996,
well beyond the statutory 6 months.  Therefore the application was out of
time since the provisions of the law are mandatory.
Where a statutory remedy by way of appeal is available then the prerogative
jurisdiction of the court cannot be invoked.  S.14 of the Expropriated
Properties Act 1982 provides that any person aggrieved by the order of the
minister in granting repossession may appeal to the High Court.  Therefore,
the instant application could not be entertained when another statutory
remedy was available.
The writ of prohibition is a preventive writ, by which court's prerogative
jurisdiction is invoked to prevent happening of an act complained of.  The
writ is not corrective.  In the instant case the application to prohibit the
Registrar of Titles from registering the third respondent as owner of the suit
property was misconceived since the registration already took place;
likewise, the application to prohibit the third misconceived, since upon
registration the third respondent took constructive possession.
Application dismissed.
Uganda Blanket Manufacturers Vs. Attorney General.
Mandamus, S.3 Law Reform (Misc.Prov.) Act-interest on costs-
whether Treasury Officer of Accounts may be ordered to pay
interest had neither been prayed for nor awarded in the suit.
Mandamus, S.3 Law Reform (Misc.Prov.)Act-decree-lack of a
decree ordering the judgment debtor (Attorney General) to pay
interest on costs-whether thereby to valid demand made on Treasury
Officer of Accounts to pay.
Held: No order for the payment of interest on costs was made by the judges
that presided over the appeal from which the present application arose.
Secondly no decree was extracted and served on the Treasury Officer of
Accounts ordering him to pay the applicant interest on costs.  Therefore,
there was no valid demand made on the Treasury Officer of Accounts, which
the said TOA had refused, necessitating the order of Mandamus.
Application refused with costs.
Rurangaranga Edward Vs. Mbarara Municipal Council & 2 ors
Municipal Council -Controlling Authority-leases-whether there was
no Controlling Authority to grant a valid lease, S.22 Public Lands
Act.
Held: The appellant to have applied for the suit land stating that there was
no building there on except stones and sand, repeating the same in court,
whereas there was an erected building already occupied, was evidence of
guilty knowledge and fraud.
The Local Administrations & Urban Authorities Decree 1971 dissolved all
District, Town and Municipal Councils and their functions were vested in a
committee appointed by the Minister by statutory order for a period of two
years.  The last such statutory order appointed the committee whose
existence expired on 13th September 1980, such that by May 1981 when
the committee purported to grant the suit lease to the appellant it had no
such power to do so.  Therefore the appellant did not obtain a valid lease
because the committee that purported to do so had expired.
It was inequitable for the 1st respondent to revoke the 2nd and 3rd
respondents' lease without adequate hearing, when the two respondents had
by letter explained that their failure to complete the building was due to the
onset of the 1979 Nyerere-Amin war, and the subsequent failure to find
building materials.  And moreover, the building had been substantially
completed excepting the water system, and a temporary occupation permit
had been given.
Though S.56 Registration of Titles Act provides that a registered proprietor
named in the certificate of title is conclusively the owner of the property,
S.69 of the same Act provides for those instances such as the present one
where the Registrar of Titles may upon proof of fraud or mistake, cancel
such certificate3 and re-issue the same in the name of the person deprived
of the land by the said fraud or mistake.  In the instant, it was not sufficient
for the appellant to wave the certificate of title to the court as ultimate proof
of ownership.  Therefore the learned trial judge was correct to go behind the
certificate of registration and to find that the respondents had been deprived
of their property by fraud, inspite of the existence of the certificate of title in
the names of the appellant.
The learned trial judge erred to have awarded damages as manse profits
against the appellant because the appellant was not a trespasser at the
time he occupied the suit property, it having been on a lease which had
been granted him by the 1st respondent.
Appeal dismissed except as regards the decree to pay manse profits.
Kobwome Mera Vs. Attorney General.
Mandamus, S.38 Judicature Statute 1996-application to compel
Treasury Officer of Accounts to pay judgment Debt-whether
application tenable.
Held: A writ of Mandamus is discretionary and not as of right.  The discretion
is exercised in favor of the applicant where the applicant has a clear legal
right and the corresponding statutory duty of the respondent and a clear
omission on the part of the respondent to carry out his statutory duty.  In the
instant case the failure of the failure of the respondent to carry out his
statutory duty for over 2 years by paying the applicant her decretal moneys
was such an instance where Court would exercise its discretion in using
the writ of Mandamus against the respondent.
Application allowed with cost.
Fire Masters Ltd Vs. Uganda Railways Corporation
Mandamus S.39 Judicature Statute-leave to apply order thereof-
whether application must be accompanied by affidavits and the
certificate of order sought to enforce.
Held: Failure to accompany the application for Mandamus with an affidavit
or affidavits verifying the facts of the application and failure to attach a
certificate of the order sought to be enforced made the application fatally
defective.
Application dismissed.
Mwesigye Enock Vs. Electoral Commission
Certiorari-Electoral Commission -whether acted in excess of its
powers under S.138(1) Local Government Act-whether-
ascertainment of results included power to cancel results.
Certiorari -judicial or quasi judicial authority -whether the only basis
for issuance of writ of certiorari against respondent.
Held: The position that obtained under the Common Law to the effect that
the prerogative writ of certiorari would only issue where the respondent had
exercised a judicial or quasi-judicial authority or function is no longer the
position of the law.  The power of obtaining an order of certiorari as not
limited to judicial Acts or orders in the strict sense.  That power extends to
Acts and orders of a competent statutory public authority, which has power
to impose a liability or give a decision, which determines the right of affected
parties.  In the instant case it was immaterial whether the respondent when
it cancelled the results the applicant was acting judicially, quasi judicially or
administratively.  The writ would issue if the respondent as a statutory body
acted in excess of its powers.
In S.138(1) Local Government Act, under which the respondent claims to
have derived its powers to cancel the results of the applicant, the word
"ascertain" the results relates only to the numerical correctness of the results
and not the validity of the electoral exercise.  The validity of the electoral
exercise can only be impugned by a competent court therefore the
respondent acted in exercise of its powers when it purported to impugn the
validity of the electoral excess long after the applicant had been declared
winner by the agents of the respondents from the results of the various
polling stations.
Application for certiorari allowed and the respondent's canceling the election
of the applicant quashed, with costs to the applicant.
ADMINISTRATION OF ESTATES
W.W. Kaggwa & 16 others Vs. Yowana Kiwanuka & 2 ors
Administration of estates-Revocation of grant-whether application
therefore must be an ordinary suit under s.265 of the Succession Act.
Held: S.265 of the Succession Act provides that whenever there is
contention in any case, it shall take the form of an ordinary suit.  This
provision however applies where an application for grant of probate or
letters of administration is contested by the caveat.  But in the instant
case the grant of probate was made already to the respondent.
Therefore S.265 of the Succession Act was not applicable but the
originating Summons under O.34 r.1, 2 CPR where the instant case
properly fitted.
BOSA & CO ADVOCATES VS. NASSANGA & ORS
Will - capacity to make a will-whether the testator was not of sound mind
when he made the will.
Will-undue influence whether testator made the will under undue influence.
Held: In deciding upon the capacity of a testator to make a Will it is the
soundness mind and not the particular state of the bodily health that is to
be considered.  In the instant case, the deceased's mental power could
have been reduced below the ordinary standard by his illness, yet he was
seized with the requisition intelligence to understand and appreciate the
testamentary act he had undertaken and accomplished.
Undue influence or duress is when the testator is induced to make
disposition, which he did, not really intend to make even where force is not
used or threatened.  When pressure of whatever nature is exerted on the
testator as to overpower his own volition without convincing his judgment.
The defendant had not proved that the testator's widow had brought such
pressure upon the testator.  It was not enough for them to show that the
widow had power to unduly press the testator.  It must positively be
shown that she exercised power or pressure.
Moreover the burden of proof of the existence of undue influence lay on
the party alleging the same.  The defendant had not discharged it.
Thirdly the defendant were supposed to have pleaded particulars of
respective acts of undue influence complained or, with necessary dates,
which they did not.  This is because undue influence must be positively
proved and not merely assumed.
Where the testator or those interested in the residue have been the cause
of the litigation, for instance where in the testator used words that were
difficult to understand and required construction by the courts for such
litigation will be paid out of the estate.  In the case before us, the
defendants that the testator's Will was made under undue influence, with-
out attempting reasonably to prove their allegations.  Therefore the two
defendants should be ordered to pay the costs of the whole action.
Suit allowed defendant to pay costs of suit.
Joyce Kasule Kweguya Vs. Apollo Matovu & 3 others
Succession-Will-whether deceased left will.
Will-intestacy - whether deceased though left a will he died intestate to
the extent of the property not devised or bequeathed in the will-whether will
never made specific devise or bequest-whether therefore the will did not
have probative value.
Held: Though the deceased died intestate, he died testate to the extent
that the will did not define the property it purported to devise to the
beneficiaries.
No trust was created because the will never defined the property the
subject of the trust. Since no trust was created the first defendant was
free to make a statutory declaration of the loss of the duplicate Certificate
of Title pursuant to S.67 Rat.  This section allowed any person to make a
statutory declaration.
Walter Mulyanti  Vs. Anne Mulyanti
Trust-Resulting Trust - whether a trust was created by the testator-whether
the trust failed due to lack of certainty as to the beneficial interest-whether
thereby a resulting trust formed.
Held: It is not enough for the Will to show the existence of the trust be
must clearly state its terms and the property to be affected must
ascertainable.  Since these factors were missing in the testator's will, no
trust was created.  Instead it was a resulting trust in favor of the testator
but since he was dead the property devolved on the intestates.
In Re Gurdas Ram Desor
Demise of executrix S.233(1) (d) - whether thereby grant of probate
becomes useless and inoperative and the testator becomes intestate.
Held: Failure by the applicant to have the alleged will and grant of probate
certified, as true copies of the original rendered the documents of no
probative value and the application on that ground would fail.
Further S.233(1) (d) which provides that probate may be annulled when it
has become useless and inoperative was not applicable to the situation
because in the case instant the executrix had already obtained the grant
of probate before her demise.  This therefore meant that upon her demise
the grant was part and parcel of her estate administrable by her testator
intestate, which was untenable in law as it amounted to disrespecting
the will of the deceased.
Application dismissed.
ABBASI MAGUNDA & ANOR VS. SULAIMAN SENOGA & ORS
Will - validity S.50(a) (b) Succession Act - whether Will not valid because
witnesses thereto did not at least to it in each other's presence.
Will-validity S.46(1) (3) (4) Succession Act whereto Will not valid because
testator was of unsound mind.
Law applicable - Sharia law-whether will not valid because testator was a
Muslim who should have not made a Will but relied on Sharia Islamic law of
succession.
contentions estates - Administrator General - S.198 Succession Act
whether though the deceased died testate, his estate should be
administered by Administrator General because it was too contentious.
Isaac Kasiba Lule Vs. Administrator General & another
Limitation Act S.21-whether suit for an order to redistribute estate of
intestate was not barred by limitation because filed within 12 years from the
date of distribution as required by S.21 of the Limitation Act.
Administrator General - Trustee-whether Administrator General was a
trustee as provided by S.20 of the Limitation Act.
Held: The present application was not subject S.20 Limitation Act because
the beneficiary applicant does not seek to recover from the trustee
Administrator General trust property but the application merely impugned
the scheme of distribution of the deceased's personal estate by the
administrator general.  Therefore the applicant's application was not time
barred.
To hold that the proceedings as commenced by counsel for the applicant
were a nullity because he lacked a practicing certificate would be to deny
the administration of substantive justice as required by the Constitution Art.
Preliminary objections overruled.
Ojiambo Gideon Vs. Barclays Bank of Uganda Ltd.
Succession Act S.25-intestate succession - whether testator is otherwise
intestate to the extent of the property unbequeathed in the will.
Held: Although S.25 of the Succession Act states that a person is
considered to have died intestate in respect of the property of which he has
not made a testamentary disposition capable of taking effect, the section
should be read together with SS.179 and 188 of the Succession Act which
vest in the executor or administrator all the property of the deceased person.
Letters of Administration have effect over all the property of the deceased,
means that a testator whose will has been proved and probate granted
cannot be said to have died intestate in respect of some of the property he
did not mention in the will.  Therefore the bank acted unlawfully in refusing
the applicant to deal with the deceased's account as per his will.
Application allowed with costs and respondent bank ordered to pay 10%
interest to the applicant from the date of refusal of the applicant to deal with
the deceased's account.
Administrator General Vs. Akello Joyce Otti & Anor.
Administrator General's powers - S.6 Administrator General's Act -whether
A.G's application for grant of the letters of administration takes precedence
over the next of kin of the intestate.
Held: S.6 of the Administrator General Act is provides that a widow or a
widower may apply for and obtain letters of Administration of her or his
deceased's spouse's estate without having sought a certificate of no
objection from the Administrator General (AG).  In the instant case, the
trial court was entitled to grant the letters of administration in preference to
the AG's application because the first respondent was the widow of the
intestate.
R.84(1) of the rules of the Supreme Court require that a Memorandum of
Appeal should set out interalia the nature of the order sought from the
appellate court.  The appellant's Memorandum of Appeal was defective for
failure to point out the nature of the order required from court. Therefore the
appeal would be dismissed.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Israel Kabwa Vs. Martin Banoba Musiga
Letters of Administration -lack thereof-whether therefore such a person has
no locus to institute a suit in respect of the intestate - whether because
respondent was heir he had locus in his own right to sue.
Held: A beneficiary of the estate of the intestate has locus to sue in own
name to protect the estate of the intestate for the own benefit without firs
having Letters of Administration.  Therefore the respondent being heir to the
estate of his father had locus to bring this suit without having first sought
Letters of Administration.
Moreover the belated grant of Letters of Administration validated all the
intermediate actions related to the estate including the filling of the suit.
The trial Judge was entitled to frame fraud as an issue and to decide the
same as proved against the appellant even though the respondent's
pleadings had given no particulars thereof because the respondents led
evidence at the trial to prove fraud without any objection from the appellant
and the appellant submitted on the same.  Therefore the appellant was
prejudiced by the Judge's approach.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Ibingira Monica Ntarumbana & 3 ors Vs. Muriel Baingana
& 3 others.
Application for letters of administration-certificate of no objection-
whether a requirement.
Held: The general rule is that costs follow the event.  However, court is
empowered with discretion under S.27 CPA when deciding whether a
loosing party may not pay costs, looking at the peculiar circumstances of
the case. In the instant case the parties are very close relatives and ordered
the defendants to pay costs would be failing to help process of
reconciliation amongst the parties.  Therefore, this was the proper case for
refu7sing to order the loosing party to pay the costs of the suit
It is ordered that each party meets its own costs.
Yiga Ezra Vs. Esinemu Mutiibwa & anor
Revocation of grant S.265 Succession Act-application therefore by
originating Summons-whether tenable.
Disposal of property under probate S.272 Succession Act-whether
respondents were guilty of doing acts detrimental to the estate.
Held: Where a party seeks to challenge the validity of a Will or impeach the
grant of  probate of a Will of letters of administration, that party raises
essentially contentious issues which ought to be resolved in an ordinary suit
in order to afford the parties the opportunity to prepare order to afford the
parties the opportunity to prepare adequately for the case.  In the present
application the applicant seeks the temporary surrender of the grant pending
the disposal of the Originating Summons.  However, since the success of
the originating summons was remote, the temporary surrender applied for
would be refused because there was no likelihood of the change of the
status quo.  The respondents were likely to continue as executors even after
the disposal of the Originating Summons.
Application dismissed with costs.
Ijumba Sulaiti Habib Haji & 3 ors Vs. Sanyu Safarani Hajati.
Will-validity-whether circumstances of execution of will suspicious.
Held: Where a Will is prepared and executed under circumstances which
raise suspicion it ought not be pronounced valid by court unless the party
seeking to rely on it proves that the testator knew and approved the contents
of the document.  In the instant case the material contradictions between
the plaintiff persons who attested the Will did not help to prove that the
testator knew the contents of the Will.  Since the Will cannot be pronounced
valid, the plaintiffs cannot be granted probate.
Case dismissed. Costs to be met by estate.  Order for joint grant of letters
of Administration for the defendant and plaintiffs.
Kara Suman Naresh Vs. Norattam Bhatia
Domicile-probate-whether High Court of Uganda has jurisdiction to
grant probate of a will made and executed by a person domiciled
outside Uganda at the time of her death -S.3 Probate Resealing
Act and S.5(2) Succession Act.
Held: S.5(2) of the Succession Act provides that succession to movable
property of a deceased person is regulated by the law of the country in which
he had his domicile at the time of his death.  In the instant case the High
Court of Uganda had no jurisdiction to entertain an application for probate
of a Will executed outside Uganda by a person domiciled outside Uganda at
the time of her demise.  Art 139(1) and S.16 of the Constitution and
Judicature Act respectively while conferring unlimited original jurisdiction in
civil matters, also requires that the jurisdiction should be exercised
according to law.  And the particular law, namely S.5(2) Succession Act
puts a fetter to the said unlimited original jurisdiction of the High Court.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Dharamsy Morarji & Sons Ltd Vs. Suman Naresh Kara.
Succession to shares in a company-whether succession was
contingent on the will and not on proved probate-whether executrix
of an unproved probate was nevertheless entitled as under the
will to the transmission of shares, S.2(a) Companies Act.
Held: S.187 of the Succession Act provides that no right of executor or
legatee is established unless a court of competent jurisdiction has granted
probate of the Will or letters of Administration.  Therefore since the High
Court refused to grant probate of the Will that established the respondent's
right to claim shares in the respondent company, the respondent's claim for
the shares could not succeed.
The appellant company being a private company that restricted the
transmission of shares, the single director who formed the quorum for the
meeting and subsequent resolution not to transmit the shares, was entitled
to refuse to transfer the shares to the respondent because the Articles of
Association gave the director a discretion to do so and no bad motive was
proved against the director.
The participation of two more persons in the meeting of the director where
the resolution not to transmit shares was reached, did not invalidate the
decision of the director since he alone formed the requisite quorum.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Musoke Sanyu Lwanga Vs. Sam Galiwango
Succession-unproved will S.187 Succession Act-whether will not
admissible in evidence.
Revocation of grant S.233(1)(2) Succession Act-application to
obtain grant of Letters of Administration stating that no will was
left whereas yes-whether ground to revoke letters of Administration.
Revocation of grant S233(1)(2) Succession Act-jurisdiction of
Chief Magistrate where estate is beyond Ugshs.100,000/=-whether
grant may be revoked.
Held: S.233(1),(2)(b)(c) Succession Act provides that a grant may be revoked
where it was obtained fraudulently by making a false statement.  In the
instant case there was ample evidence on record to show that the deceased
left a Will which fact the respondent was privy to.  By making a false
allegation to the effect that the deceased left no Will, which allegation was
the basis of the grant of Letters of Administration to the respondent, it
means that the grant was obtained by fraud and should be revoked.
S.187 Succession Act precludes a claimant to take benefit of the provisions
of an unproved Will but the section does render inadmissible in evidence a
Will that has not yet been proved by grant of probate.  Therefore the trial
court misdirected itself when it refused to admit in evidence the alleged Will
for purposes of proving its existence.
It is not necessary to appeal against an interlocutory ruling separate from
the final decision.  Therefore, it was not necessary for the appellant to have
pleaded against the trial judge's upholding of the objection to tender in
evidence the Will.  It was enough that this was incorporated in the
memorandum of appeal against the whole final decision of the trial court.
Therefore, the appeal against the introductory order could not be caught by
time before the final decision on the matter is made.
Under S.32 Judicature Act, the High Court has unlimited jurisdiction to inter
alia take any step to rectify any wrong findings on the face of the record
which comes to its attention.  In the instant case even if there was no
appeal against the grant of the lower court, the High Court could have
interfered against the grant on grounds that the grant was based on a
fraudulent misrepresentation of an essential fact and that the Chief
Magistrate had no jurisdiction to make a grant where the estate was above
Moreover, court countenance an illegality and leave it standing.
Appeal allowed.  Grounds to affirm decision dismissed.
Nuwagaba Joy Vs. Emmanuel Kakuramatsi
Letters of Administration -application by widow-whether grant may
be made to her because she is entitled to the biggest percentage
of the estate.
Held: Dowry is an essential aspect of a valid customary marriage.  However
the parents of the girl have the option to waive the payment of the dowry as
it was in this case.
Non registration of a customary marriage does not render it void because
S.19 of the Customary Marriages Registration Decree does not say so but
penalizes the parties to a fine of Ugandan shillings 500/= for failure to
register it.  Therefore, the failure of the intestate to register the marriage
before his demise did not render the marriage void.
Letters of Administration should be granted ordinarily to a person who has
the highest percentage of benefit from the estate.  In the case instant the
Widow/plaintiff together with her children were entitled to the biggest part of
the estate.  Moreover, Letters of Administration should ordinarily also be
granted to widow or widower as first choice.
Application for Letters of Administration granted to widow with costs against
the defendant.
Nalwanga Rehema Vs. Hadija Nassimbwa & anor
Letters of Administration - revocation thereof, S.233 Succession
Act -whether Letters of Administration may be revoked for being
obtained fraudulently.
Will, S.50(2) ( c) Succession Act-whether contents of the will
ground for invalidating the same.
Held: S. 233(1) Succession Act provides that a grant to Probate or Letters
of Administration may be annulled for just cause and just includes obtaining
a grant fraudulently by making a false statement concerning something
material to the court. In the instant case the defendants claimed that the
deceased left no Will and thereby obtained a grant to Letters of
Administration fraudulently by concealing the fact that the deceased left a
Will, which was something material influencing court's decision to grant the
Letters of Administration.
S.50(2) Succession Act provides the reasons for the validity of the Will.
And a Will is not invalid merely because it has named one person as
beneficiary of the estate as long as it is not alleged that any dependant was
left out of the Will.  Therefore there was a valid Will in Law and the
defendants were not entitled to over look it as if it did not exist.
Grant of Letters of Administration to the defendants annulled and the grant
made to the plaintiff.
ADVOCATES.
Christopher Kayokoke Vs. Amos Agaba & Joseph
Byamugisha and Baryaruha.
Professional Conduct - whether a party to the proceedings can
at the same time act as counsel.
Held: Since Dr. Byamugisha was defendant number 2 and was as a
result likely to give evidence in this suit, it would not be proper for
Dr. Byamugisha to act in person for the there 2 defendants as their
counsel.
The plaintiff had tow causes of action properly brought before court I.e.
a personal action by which he sought court's protection of his pecuniary
interest is the company a derivative action by which he sought court's
directors.  Therefore court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
The question of whether the plaintiff was estopped from complaining
against the manner of running the company because it was a long
established mode to which he himself was party, would be a question
to be determined at the trial.
Clouds 10 Ltd Vs. Standard Chartered Bank (u) Ltd.
Advocates Professional conduct -Non payment of fees to counsel-
whether thereby as of principle, counsel has no instructions.
Held: The Court is only entitle to grant an extension of time for sufficient
reason, which must be shown to the Court.  The Supreme Court would
not overrule the decision of a single judge exercising his discretion
unless it is exercised upon a wrong principle of the law or upon a
misdirection as to the facts so that the decision was entirely
unreasonable.  The Advocate had failed to show court sufficient reason
for his delay.
There was no rule in the Supreme Court Rules whereby the parties can
consent to the extension of time within which to file a notice or record
of appeal.
It is not correct that in all circumstances that an Advocate whose fees
had not been paid is an Advocate whose fees had not been paid is an
Advocate without instructions.
Yunusu Ismail t/a Bombo City Store Vs. Alex Kamukamu &
ors t/a O.K Bazaar.
Evidence of affidavit of counsel -whether counsel infringed regulation
8 of the Advocates (Professional Conduct) Regulation 1977 when
he deponed of matters substantive and contentious in the case.
Held: The entry of appearance by the defendants was effective because
as partners they were represented by the same counsel who stated in
court the names of the individual partners he was appearing for.
Since Kyeyune's affidavit stated that he had authority from the other
partners to swear the affidavit on their behalf and this had not been
contradicted contrary evidence and since the affidavit of Kyeyune also
showed that he was the managing Direction or the active partner of the
firm, Kyeyune's affidavit was proper.
The seventh ground of appeal would fail because it was too general and
unsustainable and offended against r.84 of the rules of Court of Appeal
which requires that a Memorandum of appeal should state concisely the
grounds of objection to the decision appealed against the specify the
points which are alleged to have been wrongly decided.
Professor Timothy Wangusa Vs. Edward Muloosi.
Advocate Remuneration and Taxation - Whether costs of the
petition could be included in thrown away costs.
Held: The costs of the petition from its commencement could not be
included in thrown away consequence of the non appearance of the
petitioner.
As long as the taxing officer acted judicially and not capriciously and
followed the proper principles in the taxation of costs, he should not be
divested of his wide discretion in the taxation and allowed
Ismail Dabul Vs. Mrs. Georgia Pankelakis.
Witness - advocates supposed to be witness not act as counsel.
Held: The case should be referred back to the High Court for retrial.
Theresa Okoth - Ofumbi & anor Vs. Haji Hamedali Ahmed
Respondent inferior - whether a solicitor was liable for the fraud of
his principal.
Held: The second appellant/advocate's part in the case would cover the
same ground as proving the fraud against the company and under O.1 r3
of CPR as per the pleadings the advocate had been properly joined as
defendant as it was him together with other defendants against whom
the right to relief, I.e. fraudulent breach of contract, had been claimed.
The advocate/appellant had specific instructions from the plaintiff
respondent to effect a transfer of the suit property in his favour.  instead
he neither effected the said transfer nor stopped or declined to act for
the defendant company when making the second sale of the same
property to the fourth defendant.
The director of a company had a fiduciary duty to act in utmost good
faith but the first appellant herein as director of the defendant company
that had fraudulently deprived the plaintiff/respondent company of its
property was not guilty of the breach of such fiduciary duty since this
duty is owed to the company above.  Secondly, the first appellant could
not be liable for the tortuous interference in the contract between the
plaintiff/respondent and the defendant company because this tort had
not been pleaded by the plaintiff/respondent.
East African Development Bank Vs. Papco Industries.
Appeal - whether the suit and appeal therefrom were one action
and the Advocate who represented the opposing party at the suit
can not represent the other party on the appeal.
Held: The was an appeal against the registrar's assessment of the
broker's fee.  It was neither an appeal against the registrar's taxation
of the judgment creditor's costs.  Therefore this appeal and the main
suit were not one and the same suit.  Therefore there is no reason why
an Advocate who represented a client in the court below cannot
represent the opposing party against a court broker in a case in which
the court broker seeks the payment of his costs.
suit for even an appeal against the Judgment in summon.
Kasozi Stephen & 3 others Vs. Peoples Transport Service Ltd.
Consent by counsel - whether counsel had authority to concede
liability on the part of his client.
Held: So long as counsel acting for the party in a case and his
instructions have not been terminated he has full control over the
conduct of the trial and has apparent authority to compromise all
matters connected with the action.
The plaintiffs did not show court that they were fare paying passengers.
Therefore, the defendant has no contractual relation with the plaintiffs.
This meant that the plaintiffs were mere trespassers and the defendant
had no duty of care towards them.
The doctor that made the report should have been called as a witness
failure to which made his report in admissible.
Olwora Alfred Vs. Uganda Central Co-operative Union Ltd.
Practicing certificate-whether practicing without a valid practicing
certificate between 1st January and March 1st disentitle the
advocate from recovery of costs.
Held: An Advocate that practices during the period of grace cannot
recover his costs through the courts but the papers he signs and files
are valid.
Lubega George Vs. Uganda Transport Co. Ltd.
Costs - whether counsel may pay costs personally for having filed
appeal without instructions.
Instructions to counsel - whether these may be delegated to another council.
Held: Counsel for the appellant would not be ordered to pay costs
personally for the dismissed appeal before he has been given the
opportunity of answering the complaint raised against him that he filed
the appeal without instructions.
The Advocates (Professional Conduct) Regulations 1977 require the
personal appearances of an advocate instructed to represent his chief in
contentious matters.  The rules allow such advocate to brief a partner
or assistant in the firm to appear on his behalf but counsel can only
brief another advocate outside his firm only with the permission of his
client.  Therefore it was unprofessional conduct on part of counsel for the
respondent to have briefed another advocate outside his firm without the
permission of his client with whom he had a retainer contract, and the
issue at hand being so contentions.  Moreover the briefing of another
counsel who worked with counsel for the opposite party was quiet
unprofessional.
Kasozi Steven & 2 ors Vs. People Transport Service.
Compromise by counsel whether Court may reject a compromise
by counsel.
Held: In cases involving disputes arising out of judiciary relationships,
the court must sanction the compromise arrived at by counsel or parties
involved.  The instant case was dispute arising out of a commercial
relationship between a transporter and passengers and it had not been
shown that counsel for the defendant/respondent had acted without
authority when he entered the compromise.  Therefore it was not open to
the trial court to reject the compromise.
The trial could not reject the compromise and go ahead and pass
judgment without calling for faster evidence from the defendant/
respondent who had not given any evidence.
The trial court not hold the plaintiff/appellants were trespassers when
this had not been an issue raised by the parties and no evidence had
been recorded therefore from the defence.
Kabogere Coffee Factory Ltd Vs. Haji Twaibu Kigongo.
Practice without a valid certificate - whether documents filed
thereby are incurably in -competent.
Held: The defects in the incompetent appeals were so judgmental that
they were incurable even by extension of time within which to appeal.
The fundamental defects concerned the inability of the Advocate without
a valid appeal.  This defect was incurable even by extension of time.
Therefore in this instance the tendency of an incurably incompetent
appeal was a bar to an application for extension of time.
The pending of an incompetent appeal was a bar to filing a fresh appeal.
Even if the applicants had succeeded on a number of grounds, since
they failed on the ground that disposed of the application in the award
costs to the respondents.
The learned single judge misdirected himself when he dismissed the
applications.  He would instead have had them struck out since they
were not decided to their merits as per r4 of the Rules of the Supreme Court.
Ntege Mayambala Vs. Mwanje Christopher.
Disciplinary proceedings before Law Council whether they are of a
Criminal nature and therefore requiring proof beyond reasonable
doubt.
Negligence -whether counsel has a duty of care to a party that is not his
client.
Held: Disciplinary proceedings before the Law Council were of a criminal
nature which meant that the burden of proof must be on the prosecution
and the proof must be proof beyond reasonable doubt.  This was an
aspect of the case which the prosecution or the committee overlooked
and thereby arrived at a wrong decision.
The Committee erred when they believed that the appellant as a
lawyer owed the complainant a duty to protect him when the complainant
was not his client in the transaction itself.
