The subsequent finding based on this belief that a lawyer acting for a
seller of land hand an obligation to a buyer to ensure that his client's
title was good right up to the moment of the transfer and that the breach
of that obligation would have the effect of rendering the lawyer personally
liable to the purchaser who was not his client was thereby wrong in law.
The appellant did not owe any duty of care to the complainant other than
they duty to draw up a sale agreement that would transfer whatever title
the seller had to the complainant.
G.W.Mulindwa Vs. J.J.Kisubika.
Negligence of counsel in non-appearance - whether
ground for setting a side dismissal of suit.
Held: The professional negligence of counsel leading to the suit being
dismissed under O.9 r.19 CPR, when the applicant plaintiff has engaged
another counsel, should not act as a bar to justice.  Therefore, for
purposes of justice court was empowered under s.101 of CPA to set
aside the dismissal.
Pyarali Abdulla & sons Vs. Fiba (u) Ltd.
Advocates Professional conduct -r.8 of the Advocates
(Professional Conduct) Regulations-whether affidavit was defective
for deponing to contentious matters.
Held: Where parties to the suit are available it is desirable that they
themselves swear the relevant affidavits.  However, in the instant case
counsel's affidavit was not defective since he swore to matters that were
within his own knowledge and were not contentious.
Developing the suit premises enhanced their value and it was not an
injury to the premises.
Since the applicants prior to the hearing to this application sought a
settlement, it could not be said that the applicants would suffer
irreparable damage since by so participating it meant that their injury,
as result of the temporary injunction, could be atoned in damages.
It was in the national interest that the construction of a unique building on
the suit premises, should continue, though national interest per se would
not be a ground to grant a temporary injunction.
The balance of convenience favoured the respondents since they had
gone too far in developing the suit premises.
Sengendo Blasio & anor Vs. Uganda.
Watching brief - whether counsel holding a watching brief may
interrupt the prosecutor.
Held: Although the charge sheet showed that the appellants had been
charged under S.257 (c ) the correct subsection should have been (b)
since the embezzlement with which they were charged concerned a
limited liability company.
Embezzlement is committed by an employee when he steals
property of the employer before the employer acquires either actual or
constructive possession of that property.  In the present case, the
property alleged to have been stolen was already in the custody of the
employer and therefore the offence of embezzlement was not committed.
The offence of theft was committed when the spares were taken out of the
shop even if they were intercepted at the gate but he issue is whether it
were the appellants who stole the spares.  The fraudulent intent was
indicated by the stranger who ran away when he was intercepted with the
spares.  His running away was evidence that he fraudulently intended to
deprive the owner of the property permanently.
An admission is a statement made by the accused, though not amounting
to a confession but contains gravely incriminating facts against the maker.
In the instant case the alleged apologies were not unequivocal as they
were open to different interpretations, one such interpretation being that
they were sorry for a theft to be committed against the company without
their preventing it.
When the trial Magistrate ruled out the possibility that PW3 was not a
credible witness in light of the contradictions in his evidence and should
have admitted his evidence with caution.
It is trial law that invariably circumstantial evidence must be narrowly
examined to avoid a possibility of a fabrication by ruling out co-existing
circumstances reasonably capable of explaining the situation, before
inferring the guilt of the accused.  In the instant case there were several
contradictions in the prosecution case which were not explained away
and his cast doubt on the guilt of the accused.  The circumstantial
evidence was not water tight.
Counsel holding a watching brief has no right to address court in
opposition to a prosecutor although as an officer of court he may inform
court on matters that can assist court while the interest of justice demand.
A trial magistrate has a discretion under S.98 of the Magistrates Court
Act to decide whether or not to recall a witness.  The trial magistrate was
entitled to refuse the recall of the witness and this did not indicate bias on
plot of the magistrate.
The inference of bias must be as to what a reasonable man would think
given the set of circumstances.  It the reasonable man would thing that
the Magistrate did favour one side unfairly at the expense of another than
bias is proved.  In the instant case there was no evidence of a real
likelihood of bias on the part of the Magistrate.
It is not a correct statement of the law that court is at liberty to cancel
bail at any stage.  Evidence in favour of cancellation of bail must be
evidence on oath and the court must decide judiciously that it is justified
in the present case the trial Magistrate erred when she cancelled the
accused's bail on mere speculative information from prosecution.
Appeal allowed.
G.M.Combained Ltd Vs. Uganda Development & 4 ors.
Professional conduct - Regulations 3,8 and 16 - whether breached.
Professional conduct-conflict of interest-whether counsel represented the
plaintiff in an earlier matter and would therefore have a conflict of interest
in the matter sub-judice while representing the defendants.
Held: It is true that submission from the bar may not negate what is
stated on oath.  Nevertheless the allegation by Professor Sempebwa to
the effect that his affidavit contained a typographical omission would be
believed because, it was the only logical conclusion when the whole of
his affidavit is read together with the evidence that court never found any
record where Sempebwa had acted for the plaintiff company.
The drawing of an agreement for a given set of parties by an advocate
does not necessarily turn the advocate into a witness in a subsequent
dispute, because, it is the parties to the agreement that are the most
relevant witness since it is them that know what they agreed upon and
why.  Therefore the fact that Sempebwa may have drawn an agreement
turn him into a witness and therefore would not be disqualified under r.8
of the Advocates (Professional Conduction) Regulations in the present
matter.
A party seeking to disqualified an advocates (Professional Conduct)
Regulations on grounds that the said advocate is seized with knowledge
by virtue of him having acted for his former client, must show which
specific facts are feared that might be used to the prejudice of the party
seeking the disqualification of the advocate.  In this the applicant advocate
had failed and therefore no disqualification of the said advocates would be
ordered. Application dismissed.
Mufumu William Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority.
Costs - payment of, costs by counsel - whether counsel may pay
costs personally for ill-advising the plaintiff to file an unsustainable
suit.
Held: S.12 of the Uganda Revenue Authority Statue provides that the
Uganda Revenue Authority Board shall be responsible for recruitment of
the Authority's staff.  The District Revenue Officer therefore had no
authority to recruit the plaintiff as an employee of the defendant.
Therefore the plaintiff was not recognized as an employee of the defendant
and his suit for damages for wrongful dismissal was unsustainable.
The facts of the case w3ere such that there was no reasonable cause why
the plaintiff had been advised to file the suit.  Therefore his counsel
would be personally liable for the payments of the costs.
Uganda Development Bank vs. Kasirye Byaruhanga & Co. Advocate
Advocates (Professional Conduct) Regulations r.8-whether proceedings
by an advocate who depones to contentious matters are void.
Held: Regulation 8 of the Advocates (Professional Conduct) Regulations
is not a primitive regulation and therefore it does not provide that an
affidavit deposing to contentious matters by counsel is thereby defective.
It simply provides that counsel must choose either to be witness in the
case or to be counsel but not both.  In the instant case, counsel for the
applicant deposed to matters that would not necessarily require him to
appear as a witness since the matter deposed to where on court record.
There, there was no need or authority to strike out the appellant's motion.
Appeal allowed.
Fr.Francis Payer Vs. Josephat Kawalya Mwebe & ors.
Affidavit by counsel on contentious matters whether affidavit by
counsel legally offensive.
Affidavit by counsel on contentious matters whether affidavit by counsel
legally offensive.
Held: A mere letter from the Deputy registrar is an administrative request
to stay execution but cannot amount to an order of court to stay
execution.  The plaintiff/respondent could have ignored it and gone ahead
to execute.
O.9 r9 and O.9 r24 CPR are in respect of two different situations.  Under
O.9 r 9 an application to set aside exparte judgment and Decree in
default appearance is brought when judgment has been entered by the
registrar, and hereunder, the court to which the application is brought
has wider discretion to allow or refuse the application than under O.9 r24
where court is limited only to being shown sufficient cause for non
appearance.  Therefore it was wrong in law to bring the application under
both rules simultaneously. However, it was not fatal to the case.
Rule 8 of the Advocates Professional Conduct) Regulations preclude
counsel from deposing to contentions matters in which he acts or
appears.  However, in the instant application, counsel's affidavit in reply
depond to matters already agreed by the opposite party and therefore
the matters were not contentious.
O.9 r9 under which the application was filed (inter alia), gives court wide
discretion in allowing or refusing applications to set aside exparte
judgment and decree entered in default, upon such terms as to costs as
the justice of the case demands.  In this application, it was apparent that
the defendants were in fact served with summons to enter appearance.
However justice required that the defendants who had shown an interest
in being heard should be given the opportunity as long as they be
penalized in costs.
Application allowed with costs to the respondent.
Mukwaya Vincent Vs. Herbert Katwere.
Lack of practicing certificate - whether therefore proceedings
illegal.
Held: Proceedings by an advocate, who has no practicing certificate outside
the grace period, are illegal and must be set aside.  A retrial is ordered.
Appeal allowed, a retrial ordered.
Kabunga Charles Vs. Christopher Baryaruha & 3 ors.
Affidavit by counsel - whether materially defective because
deponed to contentious matters r- 8 Advocates (professional
conduct) Regulations 1977.
Held: An Advocate is not allowed to depone to matters that are not purely
formal but contentious as par r.8 of the Advocates (Professional Conduct)
Regulations 1977.  When counsel deponed to the value of the land he was
deponing to a contentious matter since this was not a formal fact in his
knowledge.  Therefore his affidavit was materially defective and would not be
relied upon in court.
The procedure of originating summons applies to questions that arise
between the executors, administrators or trustees on one hand and creditor,
devisee or next of kin who sets up a claim on the other.  In the instant
case the applicant's claim does not fall in that category of questions
because the applicant is a person who has obtained judgment for the
recovery of interest in land against a registered proprietor under s.185 RTA.
The application by notice of motion was properly brought by notice of
motion.
A decree for the recovery of land is a decree in rem.  When the trial court
ordered the 1st respondent to redistribute the land to include the applicant
in the distribution, the second respondent, though not a party in the court
that issued the original decree, his interest had to be affected because he
derived title from the first unlawful distribution.
Application allowed.  Registrar to cancel the relevant certificates of title and
transfer the same to the applicant.
Obadi Enterprises Ltd Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority & anor.
Instruction fees - r-45 Advocates (Remuneration and taxation of
costs) Rules - whether breached.
Held:S.84 ( c) Civil Procedure Act empowers court to make an order of
Revision where it is shown that the lower court acted in exercise of its
jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity or injustice.  In this case the
taxation of costs was based on the amount claimed but not subsequently
awarded.  This lead to the excessive taxation of costs where the award was
Ush 1,500,000/= and the cost over 17 million. This did not represent fairness.
Therefore this was a clear case for Revision and the taxed bill of costs would
be set aside.
Application allowed and bill of costs set aside and respondent asked to
present a fresh bill of costs for taxation.
Kasiba Saac Lule Vs. Administrator General & anor.
Practicing without a valid certificate - whether nullification of the
proceedings would be justice as required by the constitution Art.
Held: The present application was not subject to S.20 Limitation Act
because the beneficiary applicant does not seek to recover from the trustee
Administrator General trust property but the application merely impugned
the scheme of distribution of the deceased's personal estate by the
administrator general.  Therefore the applicant's application was not time
barred.
To hold that the proceedings as commenced by counsel for the applicant
were a nullity because he lacked a practicing certificate would be to deny
the administration of substantive justice as required by the Constitution Art.
Preliminary objections overruled.
Semakula Abbey Vs. Eldad Bubarenzya.
Commissioner for oaths commissioning affidavit without a valid
practicing certificate - whether thereby affidavit defective.
Held: The allegation that the respective Commissioners for Oaths did not
have valid practicing certificates at the time they commissioned the affidavits
was not substantiated or proved either by an affidavit of counsel alleging the
same or by any other evidence.  Therefore, the Learned Chief Magistrate
was correct in law in not considering the same.
Costs are never taken into account in computing the sum in a decree.
therefore since the decretal award did not exceed Ush 5,000,000/= the
Learned Chief Magistrate did not exceed his jurisdiction.
The discrepancies in the affidavits of service as to their dates in which it
appeared that the dates of deponing preceded the dates of service were
clearly typographical errors, which could be ignored.  Therefore this did not
render the affidavits incurably defective.
However, the ambiguities and discrepancies in the process servers' affidavits
of service and reply tended to show that there was no effective service and
that is why the defendant did not appear to defend the suit.
Appeal allowed.
Mugabi Evarist Vs. Benedicto Tugumikiriza.
Professional conduct regulations 7(2) - failure to account for client's
money - whether accounting for client's money involved merely
telling client that certain amount on his behalf.
Professional conduct - complaint against advocate-whether only by person
having an interest in the matter.
Professional conduct-complaint against advocates - whether must be in
writing.
Held: Advocates (Disciplinary Committee) Procedure) Regulations 1, 1994
provides that any person who wishes to complain may do so in writing but
regulation 2 provides that the committee may consider a complaint which do
not comply with regulation 1.  Therefore the disciplinary committee was
entitled to act on the complaint of a person who had no interest in the
matter and to act on a complaint not in writing.
Appeal dismissed.
Shariff Osman Vs. Haji Haruna Mulangwa.
Representation - deed drafted by vendor's advocate - whether
ambiguity therefore to be resolved in favour of the purchaser.
Held: A vendor of real property retains a lien in the property for the unpaid
balance of the purchase money.  However, in the instant case the
agreement of the parties provided a specific time when the purchaser would
take possession.  Since the agreement was prepared by counsel for the
appellant the clause providing for taking possession would strictly be
construed against the vendor/appellant so that it is taken that delivery of
possession was not contingent upon completion of purchase price; since
upon payment of the deposit property passed to the purchaser.
The principle at Common Law is that in absence of a contrary intention time
is of essence of a contract even though the parties have not expressly
provided it.  In the case instant however, it took two years for the appellant/
vendor to claim to rescind the contract.  This was evidence that time of
payment of the purchase price was not of essence to the contract for failure
to the contract and therefore the respondent/purchaser was not in breach
of the contract for failure to pay the balance by the agreed date.
If the appellant/vendor had successfully rescinded the contract he would not
be entitled to keep the deposit.
The respondent/purchaser was not entitled to manse profits and general
damages because he had in ordinarily delayed in enforcing specific
performance.
Appeal dismissed except as to general damages.
Gulyetonda Jesse Vs. Henry Muganwa Kajura & 2 others.
Practicing without a valid practicing certificate whether therefore
documents thus filed are incurably defective.
Commissioner for Oaths - commissioning affidavit without a valid
practicing certificate-whether affidavit thus commissioned is
incurably defective.
Held: An advocate who neglects to renew his certificate does not get de-
registered but his name continues on the roll of advocates.  It would be an
injury to litigants to hold that the absence of a certificate had the effect of
invalidating all proceedings taken in the suit, whereas the litigants would
find it almost impossible to investigate the existence of the certificate before
handing down their instructions.  Therefore, lack of an advocate's practicing
certificate does not invalidate proceedings and the petition was validly
before court.
S.2(4) of the Commissioner for Oaths (Advocates Act) provides that where
an Advocate Commissioner for Oaths ceases to practice as an Advocate
then such commissioner shall cease to be commissioner for Oaths. Since
the Advocate who commissioned the affidavit had never been de-registered
as an Advocate, inspite of his lack of a practicing certificate he validly
continue to act as Commissioner for Oaths and the affidavit he
commissioned could not be impeached merely because of lack of a
practicing certificate.
R 5(6) of the Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules 1996
provides mandatorily that where a constituency to which a petition relates
is within a district registry of the High Court then the petition must be
presented in that District Registry.  In the instant case the presentation of
the petition at Kampala instead of Masindi where the relevant constituency
had its district registry, was fatal and on that account the petition was
incompetent.
Petition struck off the court record with costs for having been filed in wrong
registry.
Kyowola Eva Vs. Lakeri Naluwoza.
Instruction to institute suit- lack thereof - whether this was a
preliminary issue or was an issue after evidence was led.
Held: Court has inherent powers to strike out an action at any stage of the
proceedings where want of authority to institute the suit is proved.  In the
instant case since was of authority did not appear plainly at the stage of
proceedings when the issue was raised as a preliminary objection, the suit
would proceed to hearing.
Preliminary objection dismissed with no order as to costs.
Mugyenyi Ponsiano Vs. Jacob Asiimwe & 2 others.
Advocate commissioner for oaths-whether must have a valid
practicing Advocate's Certificate-whether practices under the
Commissioner for Oaths (Advocates) Act.
Held: Statutory Instruments comprise of only legal instruments that
constitute subordinate legislation.  A notification of election results by the
Electoral Commission is not a legislative but administrative act.  The
notification is not valid from the date it is made by the Electoral Commission
but on the date it is made by the Electoral Commission but on the date it is
published in the gazette.  Therefore s.17 instrument is valid from the date it
is published does not apply to a notification because a notification cannot
be published independently outside the gazette.  Therefore the proper date
of reckoning of the 30 days of filing the petition was from the date the
notification was published in the gazette on 5th July 1996 and therefore the
filed on 30th August was filed in time.
Once an Advocate has been appointed Commissioner for Oaths, he starts
acting under the Commissioner for Oaths (Advocates) Act.  This act does
not require a commissioner to have a valid practicing certificate.
Moreover, since the issue of an Advocate commissioning an affidavit without
a valid practicing certificate is not canvassed by written law then the
provisions of S.16 of the Judicature Statute apply to the effect that common
law must govern the situation as the law applicable.  Under common law
an Advocate practicing without a valid practicing certificate only loses the
legal opportunity to recover his costs but the documents executed by him
must remain valid.
Preliminary objections all overruled with costs.
Ngirabakunzi Kwera Stella Vs. Ntabgoba Jenninah & another.
Practicing certificate-advocate drafting election petition without
practicing certificate-whether "drafting" does not amount to practice-
whether thereby documents validly before court.
Held: S.65 of the Advocates act requires every document prepared by an
Advocate to be endorsed with the name and address of the drawer advocate
and failure to do so is an offence under S.66 of the same Act.  Therefore the
drawing of court documents by counsel without anticipation for reward, is
part of the practice prohibited by S.66 of the Advocates Act and such
documents are null and void.  Therefore, the petitioners petition was invalid
because it was drawn by counsel who had no practicing certificate.
Petition struck out with costs.
British India General Insurance Co. Ltd Vs. Dolatrai Solanki.
Instructions to institute proceedings by non existing company-
whether counsel personally liable for costs.
Held: The court can grant a stay of execution when satisfied that there is
good cause and that special circumstances exist to justify such a cause.
And the likelihood of success of the applicant's appeal and the consequent
fear of rendering an appeal likely to succeed, nugatory, consist of special
stay.  In the instant case the appeal was not likely to succeed because it
was instituted by an applicant who had no capacity to institute it.
A company can only authorize the commencement of legal proceedings in
its name by way of a resolution.  In the instant case there was no such
resolution and therefore, the counsel who purported to act on behalf of the
applicant who had not made any resolution to that effect, must be personally
liable for the costs arising from such proceedings where the Advocates is
apparently acting without instructions.
Application dismissed.
The Registered Trustees of Benedictine Fathers Vs. Hussein
Hassan & anor.
Compromise by counsel-S.61 Advocates Act-without authority of
party-whether compromise unenforceable.
Held: Where a party instructs counsel to represent him in an action, counsel
continues to act on behalf as his client without requiring fresh authority for
every step.  Therefore, the appellant's counsel was entitled to compromise
on behalf of his client and the appellant was bound thereto.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Prof. Syed Huq Vs. Islamic University in Uganda.
Practicing without a valid certificate S.14(1) Advocates Act. -
whether proceedings invalid.
Held: An Advocate that practice without a valid practicing certificate after the
grace period, practices illegally and is liable to prosecution as provided by
S.14(1) Advocates Act.  And all proceedings taken by such counsel and
documents signed by him are invalid, because to say otherwise would
amount to a perpetuation of an illegality.
However, in this case, the issue of the competence of the appeal could not
be raised as a preliminary objection without the leave of the court according
to the provisions of r101(b) RSC.  Therefore the lack of a practicing
certificate by counsel who extracted the decree, would not interfere with the
competence of the appeal.
Where two parties to a contract have agreed to contract, then there is a
contract which non of the parties may deny.  In the instant case the
respondent's WSD admitted that the appellant was appointed Rector by the
Governing Council of the respondent.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself when he held that the appointment was null and void
due to lack of quorum by the appointing council.
However, S.13 of the Employment Decree provides that a foreign contract of
employment shall not be enforced unless it has been approved or attested
in accordance with the Employment Decree.  In the instant case since the
appellant was not a Ugandan and the respondent was a corporation that
belonged to a foreign body, the contract the subject of the suit was a foreign
body, the contract and the contract was unenforceable due to lack of it
having been approved or attested in accordance with the Employment
Decree.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Kaggwa John Vs. J.B.M. Balikuddembe
Appeal against sentence of suspension from practice, S.21(1)
Advocates Act - stay of execution pending appeal, S.41(2)
Judicature Statute-whether court has no jurisdiction to entertain an
application from practice pending appeal.
Held: S.21(3) Advocates Act provides that once the Law Council Disciplinary
Committee passes its sentence, it cannot be stayed but can only appealed
and set aside or quashed by an appellate court.  Therefore this application
was misconceived.
Application dismissed with costs.
Bakunda Darlington Vs. Dr. Kinyatta & anor
Commissioner for Oaths without a valid Practicing Certificate S.2(1)
Commissioner for Oaths (Advocates) Act -whether commission
expires at the expiration of the Advocates Practicing Certificate.
Held: An Advocates who is commissioned under S.2 (1) Commissioner for
Oaths (Advocates) Act ceases to be a commissioner for oaths at the date
of the expire of his practicing certificate.  The learned trial Judge was
entitled to rule that the petition was incompetent because the accompanying
affidavit was a nullity, it having been sworn before a Commissioner whose
commission had expired.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Kwesigabo, Bamwine & Walubiri Advocates Vs. Nytil Picfare
Practicing certificate-recovery of costs-whether an advocate may
not recover costs for instructions he obtained when not certificated
even if he subsequently gets certificated before the completion of
the instructions.
Held: A lien is a kind of attachment and the value of the property to be
attached must be commensurate to the amount of the debt.  In instant case
the land title were the applicants sought to exercise alien was valued at
Ush. 400 million and yet the debt of Uhs 2.3 million was disproportionately
too small such that the attachment would be unjust and unconscionable.
The ground for review to the effect that there was an error apparent on the
record was not proved because no error was proved when the applicant
merely dated the items for which fees was claimed whereas in earlier bill of
costs no date was supplied.  This meant that the dictates of O.42 r1 were
not satisfied.
Where an advocate receives instructions to represent his client in a matter
when that advocate is not certificated his subsequent certificated ness does
not render the instructions lawful.
Application dismissed with costs.
Abdalla Faraj Vs. Ali Omar & Odimbe Advocates.
Negligence-failure by counsel to certify that he was the author of
the document which relates to the illiterate-whether thereby
counsel is liable in negligence for damages and costs.
Held: S.4 Illiterates Protection Act requires that the author of an agreement
where an illiterate is a party must certify on that document that he is author
thereof and appendage his full names and address after explaining the
contents of the document claiming that he was not party to the contents
thereof.  The Court can only resolve the contents in favour of the literate if
the literate fulfilled the requirements of S.4 of the Illiterates Protection Act.
It was not enough for the 2nd defendant as Advocate to subscribe his
signature as witness and his firms stamp.  He should have gone further to
certify explicitly that he was the author of the agreement, in which the 2nd
defendant failed.
The Advocate would pay 60% of the costs and damages.
Uhs 50m/= would be awarded as damages for deprivation of business.
Case allowed with costs.
Trade Investments (U) Ltd Vs. Magezi Ibale & Co. Advocates
Costs-taxation -whether instructions fees of Ush.20M/- excessive
where subject matter is about Ush.800M.
Cpsts whether Ush.500,000/= excessive as telephone costs.
Held: The proviso to the 6th schedule of the Advocates (Remuneration and
Taxation of Costs) Rules allows an Advocate to claim a higher figure than
provided in the schedule but only on condition that the presiding Judge/
arbitrator/Magistrate as the case may be has given a certificate of
complexity to the concerned counsel allowing him to therefore claim a higher
figure.  Therefore, the award of Ush. 20m/= as instruction fees was
excessive and arbitrary and would be set aide and substituted therefore the
award of Ush. 8.9m as provided by the rules in the 6th schedule since the
subject matter was valued about Ush. 800m/ but no certificate of complexity
had been obtained.
The award of Ush. 500,000/= as telephone costs would not be considered to
be arbitrary because the case spanned over two years and the respondent
Advocate had to keep in touch with his clients who were spread as far as
Dar-Es-Salaam.
Appeal allowed in part. Each party to bear own costs.
Uganda Bankers (Employers Association) Vs. National Union
of Clerical,Commercial,Professionals & Technical Employees
Taxation-Advocates (Remunerations and Taxation of costs)
applicable as at the date the order to pay costs was made or as
the date the costs were taxed.
Costs-taxation-Advocates (Remunerations and Taxation of costs)
Rules, 1982, r.34 & 35 taxation of costs in contentious matters-
where only figure provided in schedule can be allowed and higher
fee only with leave of trial court.
Held: The Remuneration Rules and the mode of assessing instruction fees
were matters of law, which the learned Judge was presumed to known and
had been argued before him when he sat in his appellant capacity.
Therefore, the learned Judge erred in holding that the appellants had not
stated the principles of taxation, which the taxing master as alleged to have
breached.
S.13 (2) Interpretation Decree provides that where a law is repealed, the
repeal does not affect a right, privilege, obligation or liability which had
accrued before the repeal came into effect.  In the present case the
appellant's liability to pay costs accrued on 17th August 1995 when the
order to pay costs was made against the appellant and not when the bill
was taxed on 31.3.96.  Therefore the law applicable was the Advocates
Remuneration and Taxation of Costs) Rules, 1982 which provided for a
minimum scale of Ush. 1500/- for arguing or defending a chamber summons
and not the Advocates (Remuneration and Taxation of Costs) (Amendment)
Rules, which came in force on 22/2/96, which provided for ush.75,000/- as
the minimum scale for  arguing or defending a chamber summons. Therefore
the learned Judge erred to have applied the later rules and therefore applied
the later rules and therefore applied wrong principles of taxation of costs.
Moreover, because no value had been given of the subject matter, it was
wrong for the learned Judge to speak of value of billions.  Of shillings.
Therefore he was influenced by wrong assessment of the instruction fees.
Proviso number one to the sixth schedule provides that where an advocate
claims that a given matter was specifically complicated and for that matter
was specifically complicated and for that matter wishes to claim as
instruction fees, a fee higher than provided in the scale, must first obtain a
certificate of complexity from the presiding Judge or Magistrate (trial or
appellate as the case may be).  In the instant case for the taxing master to
have allowed instruction fee to defend a chamber summons at Ush. 40m/-
from minimum scale provided of Ush. 15000/- required a certificate of
complexity from the presiding Judge the taxing master, without which, as it
was in the case instant no higher fee should have been allowed.
Appeal allowed with costs to the appellants.  Taxation to be done denovo
before another taxing master.
ARBITRATION
Associated architects Vs. Uganda Tea Authority
Application to remove arbitration-whether by notice of motion.
Bias-whether arbitrator may be removed for likelihood of bias.
Held: S.101 CPA was improperly invoked and the application was
thereby not properly before Court because it was not possible to invoke
court's inherent jurisdiction when there was a specific provision in place,
namely applications to remove an arbitrator are governed by r.16 of the
Arbitration Rules which provides that such applications must be by
Chamber Summons.
The allegations of likelihood of bias at this stage would not result in the
removal of the arbitrator since in the proceedings so far he had shown
no proved bias and moreover since the Arbitration Act s.14 provides that
an arbitrator could be removed on grounds of misconduct, the machinery
was open to the applicants once hey alleged and proved bias.
Shell (U) Ltd Vs. Agip (U) Ltd.
S.17-a step in the proceedings-whether proceedings in court may
not be stayed because defendant has taken a step in the
proceedings-whether notice of produce documents was a step in
the proceedings.
Opting out of arbitration agreement-whether parties had opted out
of arbitration agreement.
Held: A notice to produce documents under O.19 rr15 and 16, even if filed in
court does not amount to taking a step in the proceedings as provided under
S.17 of the Arbitration Act. A step in the proceedings must be an act
involving a court summons as under O.10 r18. In the present case the
notices to produce documents and to inspect the same was mere discourse
between counsel of both parties and did not amount to taking a step in
proceedings as envisaged by S.17 Arbitration Act.  Therefore the learned
trial judge erred in holding that the defendant/appellant had taken a step in
the proceedings when he filed the notice to produce documents and thus
and thus misdirected himself on that basis to refuse to grant a stay of the
proceedings.
A notice to confirm the decision of the trial court arises when party wishes
the appellate court to hold the same conclusion as the trial court on reasons
other than what the trial court gave, but arising from the evidence of facts
and law during the proceedings in the trial or lower court as the case may
be.  In the instant case counsel for the respondents wanted the appellate
court to hold that the trial judge could still have dismissed the appellant's
application on another ground directly arising from the evidence in that court,
that is, that the parties had opted out of the arbitration clause when they
chose to submit the dispute to the auditors.  However, there was no
evidence that the appointment of the auditors amounted to opting out of the
arbitration clause.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Oil Seeds (U) Ltd Vs. Uganda Development Bank
Whether award by arbitrator is final and not subject to court's
intervention unless secured by improper conduct, SS.11.12.
Arbitration Act.
Held: The court may remit or set aside an arbitrator's award in certain
circumstances in the interests of justice. SS.11 & 12 Arbitration Act provide
court with discretion in the interests of justice to set aside an arbitrator's
award or remit for reconsideration.  The learned judge erred in declining
jurisdiction.
Appeal allowed with costs.  Application for objection to arbitrator's award to
be rehearsed another judge.
BANKING
Karim Hirji Vs. M/S Pan African Insurance.
Letter of guarantee-whether the plaintiff opened a letter of
guarantee in favour of the defendant.
Held: After backing the offer with the letter of guarantee, the condition
annexed by the defendant it was necessary that the offer be
communicated to the defendant within the time fixed by the plaintiff to
accept it.  Therefore, since this time had elapsed there was no
complete contract between the parties, but only a bargain of a highly
conditional nature.
A banker's (letters of) guarantee is where the Banker gives financial
backing of a payment on first demand.  The plaintiff's banker testified
truthfully that he had to block up funds on the plaintiff's account for this
purpose.  Therefore, the plaintiff did indeed open letters of guarantee.
Evidence by an affidavit to prove an important point in a case, where the
other party had not been given a chance to reply should not be admitted
in court.
Esso Standard (u) Ltd Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank (u) Ltd.
Delay in collecting cheques and giving notice of dishonour to
customer whether breach of collecting bank's duty to customers.
Held: Delay in collecting cheques and giving notice of dishounor to a
customer is breach of duty by the bank, and the customer may recover
the amount of the cheques.
Responsibility for selling and banking the proceeds there from, the
accuracy of figures and payment, amounts to operating an account,
even as agent.
The private arrangement negated banking of the cheques, and the
defendant was on that account not liable for delay caused thereby.
Bukoto Farmers & General Merchandise Ltd Vs. Libyan
Arab Bank & Bank of Uganda.
Purchase external currency whether bank of Uganda was entitled
to deal in foreign currency at its own exchange rate.
Held: Bank of Uganda was entitled to purchase the appellant's Kenya
currency at any of the two rates I.e. sh.3/70 or sh.86/80 as per its
powers conferred on it by s.23 of the Bank of Uganda Acts foreign
currency.  And S.20 (2) (a) allowed the Bank to fix its exchange rate.
Edwin Otile Ojungu Vs. Acan llwete Co-op society Ltd &anor.
Securities- lien - whether the objection Bank could success
fully object to the attachment of a lorry over which the bank had
lien.
Held: The execution creditor must first pay off the objector bank's out-
standing loan so that he can validly seize and attack the lorry over which
the Bank had a lien, because goods pledged by the judgment debtor
as security for a loan cannot be lawfully seized.
Lac Vic Agro Industrial supplies Vs. Greenland Bank.
Cheques - conversion - whether collecting bank was liable in
conversion it collected them for payment for a customer other than
account payee.
Collecting Bank negligence S.82 Bills of Exchange Act-whether collecting
Bank was negligent when it collected and paid cheque to someone other
than Account payee-whether the paying banks were equally liable in
negligence.
Cheque-contributory negligence-whether plaintiff was contributory
negligent because it failed to keep a closer eye on the banking of its
cheques when the cheques were stolen.
Negligence by collecting bank-damages for loss suffered - quantum.
Held: The plaintiff's action was founded in conversion and the plaintiff ably
pleaded this and evidence was lead to reveal the ingredients of conversion.
S.82 of the Bills of Exchange Act only provided a defense for the
defendant in rebuttal to the allegation of conversion that the collecting
Bank acted in good faith and without negligence.  The defendant therefore
could not impeach the plaintiff's action merely by stating that the
plaintiff must have pleaded statutory negligence as per S.82 Bill of
Exchange Act.
It was not enough to allege that the similarities in names between the
plaintiff and the defendant's customer were confusing to any normal
person.  The defendant should have produced its employees as witnesses
to show how the normal person could get confused and yet the defendant
chose to call no witnesses.
S. 82 Bills of Exchange Act provides that a collecting bank that acts in
good faith, and without negligence cannot be found liable in conversion or
negligence.  However the burden of proof is on the collecting bank to
show that it acted in good faith and without negligence.  In the instant
case, when the defendant chose to call no witness or evidence meant
that it had failed to discharge this burden.
Generally speaking when an action is founded on negligence the defence
could be that the plaintiff was contributorily negligent.  However in the
instant case the plaintiff's action was in conversion and the defendant
would only be protected if it lead evidence to show that it acted in good
faith and without negligence.  The defence of contributory negligence is
precluded.
The quantum of damages for loss suffered is the face value of the cherub.
Kassim Mpanga Vs. Uganda.
Unsecured bank credits-causing financial loss c/s 258(1) PCA
whether a manager who advances unsecured credits to customers
contrary to bank policy of securing credits is guilty of causing
financial loss.
Held: The gist of the offence of causing financial loss is the term "loss".
A thing may be said to be lost after a reasonable time has elapsed to allow
diligent search and recovery and such diligent search has been made and
has been fruitless.  In the instant case, in respect of 29 accounts inspite of
diligent recovery efforts of several months, recovery was impossible.
Therefore the learned trial magistrate was correct to have found the accused
guilty of causing financial loss c/s 258(1) PCA because the loss was a
natural consequence of the unauthorized and unsecured credit.
Abuse of office is the doing of an act by an accused person's employers,
prejudicial to the interest, in abuse of authority of his office in the instant
case the accused acted arbitrarily by giving out the overdrafts unsecured
and without authority contrary to bank policy.  This act amounted to abuse
of office by the appellant.
S.259 PCA mandatory requires court to consequently impose an order of
compensation against an accused convicted of causing financial loss and
embezzlement.  The order of compensation must be impose specifically
count by count.  In the instant case the trial magistrate imposed a blanket
order and this was illegal.  However, a court of Appeal is empowered under
S.337(2) CPC to vary a judgment of the High Court on appeal.  Therefore
the order of compensation would be substituted for the order to apply to only
count one.
Appeal dismissed.  Order of compensation to apply to count one only.
Multi Constructors Ltd Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Securities - debenture - whether the discharge of the debenture to
the holding company was also discharge of the subsidiary.
Securities - Banking Act 1969 S.9(c ) (ii)-whether the defendant/respondent
debenture holder and mortgagee Bank was precluded from the purchasing a
security it itself-whether the purchase must be in hold.
Held: Since the appellant company still owed money to the respondent its
debenture could not be said to have been discharged.  Therefore the sale of
the suit property over which the respondent had a debenture was validly
done.
The receiver/managers once they were appointed became the agents of the
appellant and therefore when the receiver sold the suit property he did so as
the agent of the appellant.  The debenture terms and the law provided this.
s.9( c) (ii) of the banking Act allows a bank to buy its security in hold.  In
the instant case when the respondent bank bought the suit property it did
so in hold.  But the hold could not be forever, the property eventually could
be and was taken over by the bank lawfully.
Appeal dismissed.
Banax Ltd Vs. Gold Trust Bank Ltd.
Banking -Bank's refusal to operate a clients account in grounds
of irregularities - whether breach of contract.
Held: The defendant bank was not in breach of its contractual obligation
towards its customer and was justified to stop the operation of the
account.  The bank was supposed to operate the account if everything
was apparently regular, but everything was not regular in the instance
case since there was a conflict that had been brought to its notice.
Esso Standard (u) Ltd Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Duty of collecting bank - whether when the collecting bank
presented cheques 25 days after they were deposited, did not
act diligently and thereby was in breach of it's contractual duty to
it's customer.
Held: A drawer cannot recall cheques that he has drawn but can only
countermand payment by his bankers of the cheques.
The respondent Bank was vicariously responsible for whatever loss that
would be occasioned by their employee's fraudulent refusal to present
cheques deposited for payment in time.
A cheque is banked 25 days from the time it was banked for payment
was not presented within a reasonable time having regard to the fact
that the respondent and drawing bank were to be found in the same
location.
A cheque is banked when it is received and deposited at the collecting
bank and not when it is presented for payment at the drawing Bank.
The respondent bank's presentment of the cheques for payment 25
days after they were banked, failed to act diligently and was in breach
of its contractual duty to its customer.
The drawer was not discharged on the liability of the cheques merely
because the respondent delayed in presenting the cheques for payment
because even if had the cheques been presented in time there were no
sufficient funds to have the cheques paid.
Barclays Bank of Uganda Vs. Livingstone Katende Luutu.
Securities - whether bank may sell mortgagor's land without a
court order - whether court's jurisdiction is expressly ousted by
s.6 of the mortgage decree.
Held: The Bank did not require leave of court to realize its security since
by the terms of the mortgage the Mortgagor irrevocably expressly
consented to the Sale without recourse to court in event of failure to repay
the loan. This power conformed to s.9 of the mortgage Decree.
The trial judge erred when he held that s.9 of the mortgage Decree which
allowed the mortgagee to sell without recourse to court ousted the
jurisdiction of court and was thereby a violation of the principle of natural
justice which guaranteed the right to be heard.
The trial judge should have known that there can be no principle of
natural justice which outshines an express legislative provision such as
S.9 of the mortgage Decree.  The sale without recourse to court having
been agreed by the parties it was sanctioned by S.9 of the mortgage
Decree.
Major John Kazoora Vs. Uganda.
Crewing customer's account - whether this may constitute theft by
by the customer.
Held: S.86 (d) of the Magistrates' Court Act requires that the charge
sheet specifically names or describes the co-charged.  However by long
time practice it has become acceptable to mention in a charge that
some body unnamed and or undescribed is not joined because he is not
available to be joined.  Therefore, the non disclosure did not occasion
injustice to the appellant in as much as the charge sheet is not really
evidence.
Considering that ISO is an intelligence organization whose operations
have of necessity to be covert on the evidence of the prosecution, it
could not rule out the possibility that the sh.12 million was intended for
ISO purposes such as payment to Jane as an ISO agent.  The
prosecution had failed in their evidence to rule out beyond reasonable
doubt that the said money was not meant for an agent.  The trial Chief
Magistrate clearly erred in law and fact when he failed to scrutinize the
evidence of the prosecution.
Rule 10 of the Evidence (Statement to Police Officers) Rules does not
preclude an oral admission to a police officer of relevant rank provided
the suspect is properly cautioned.  However when the accused denied
having made the admission, the Chief Magistrate should have held a trial
within trial to determine whether the admission was really made by the
appellant.  The trial Chief Magistrate misdirected himself when he
accepted as made a confession the appellant had denied, without first
holding a trial within a trial.
The trial Chief Magistrate erred in law to have held that the debiting of
ISO account and Crediting of appellant's account on 25th January 1991
constituted theft because the money which is in the bank belongs to the
bank and therefore mere debiting and crediting does not constitute taking
or aspiration which is an element in the offence of theft.
Bank Ltd Vs. Gold Trust Bank Ltd.
Breach of contract - whether with it's customer by freezing it's
account - whether bank had notice of irregularity.
Damages for breach of contract-quantum
Held: The reorganization of the company was an internal matter and the
respondent bank should only have looked at the resolution which had
been duly registered with the registrar of companies.  Therefore, the
bank would not be said to have had notice of something irregular and
was thereby in breach of contract to freeze the appellant's account.
The plaintiff appellant must prove that it had suffered actual damage due
to its non-use of its account as a basis for the award of general damages.
This had not been the case and Shs.100,000/= would be awarded for
inconvenience suffered.
Lac Vic Agro Industrial Supplies Vs. Greenland Bank.
Cheques - conversion -whether collecting Bank was liable in
conversion of the plaintiff's cheques when it collected them for
payment for a customer other than account payee.
Multi Constructors Ltd Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Securities - debenture - whether the discharge of the debenture
also discharge of the debenture to the holding company was also
discharge of the subsidiary.
Kavuma F.W. Vs. Sembule Investments Bank
Bills of Exchange Act S.82-conversion of cheques-whether Bank
acted in good faith without negligence-whether defence of good
faith was not available because cheques were not proved crossed.
Held: A person is guilty of conversion who without lawful excuse, deprives
another of his goods by giving some other person a lawful title to them.
In the present case, the third party had only defective title to the cheques
as the true owner was the plaintiff.  The defendant dealt with the cheques in
a manner inconsistent with the rights of the plaintiff who was the true owner,
and are therefore prima facie, liable to him for the conversion of the cheques.
S.82(1)(2) Bills of Exchange Act protects a bank from liability in conversion
where the bank has acted in good faith and without negligence and the
cheque in question is a crossed cheque.  In the instant case though the
bank sought to rely on Section 82 Bills of Exchange Act for protection and
pleaded to have acted in good faith and without negligence, the bank did not
lead evidence to show that the cheques in question were crossed.
Secondly, the bank's failure to investigate the particulars of the customer
who purported to be the owner of the cheques was evidence in question
were crossed.
The plea that the plaintiff had ratified the act of the third party cannot stand.
A principal can only ratify the act of a person who is his agent.  In the
instant case the third party never acted for the plaintiff and never said so.
The plead that the plaintiff was a partner of the third party cannot stand
because even if it were true that the third party and the plaintiff were partners
a co-owner can commit conversion in respect of joint property.  However,
neither the third party nor the plaintiff claimed that they were partners.
The alleged indemnification of the defendant by the plaintiff when he agreed
to drop his complaint against the defendant cannot be said to have been
done voluntarily because, the plaintiff had had no legal counsel; the plaintiff
was desperate for accessing even the little balance to offset his debts, so
it was a corrupt bargain and it was unenforceable and moreover the
defendant never performed his part of the bargain.
The measure of damages for conversion of (a chattel) cheques is their face
value.  Therefore, the defendant would pay Ugshs.31 million to the plaintiff
the face value of the cheques.
Case allowed with costs against the defendant.
BANKRUPTCY
In re Teddy Seezi Cheeye
Receiving order-whether the responded had committed an act of
bankruptcy S.3(1) (g) Bankruptcy Act - whether receiving order
may be made under Ss.74,75,76 & 155 Bankruptcy Act.
Held: In a bankruptcy petition the two essential elements are, the proof of
the petitioner's debt and the proof of an act of bankruptcy.  In the present
case there was ample proof of the petitioner was not obliged to accept as
satisfaction of his debt the payment of the decretal amount into court, and
the applications for stay of execution and setting aside exparte judgment
had been dismissed and the decree remained unsatisfied.  Therefore the
respondent had committed an act of bankruptcy under s.3(1) (a) of the
Bankruptcy Act.
Receiving order granted.
CIVIL PROCEDURE
H.M.B.Kayondo S.C. Vs.  Attorney General.
Cause of action - whether existed.
Held: In an application to strike out pleadings which do not
disclose a cause of action or defence, the court would only look
at the pleadings as filed by the parties to the action and no formal
application is required.
(2) That a preliminary objection could be raised even after the
pleadings were closed, since, if argued as a preliminary could
dispose of the suit.
(3) That the Government Standing Orders do not constitute a
contract between the President as appointing authority and public
officers and therefore such public officers may not sue for breach
of contract.
(4) That the plaint failed to disclose a cause of action and that this
incurable and would be struck out.
Jayant Meena Madhavani Vs. Madhavani Muljibhai Pratabi.
Temporary injunction - violating temporary injunction-principles
upon which court may commit contemnor to civil prison.
Held: An injunction although discharged subsequently for one
reason or another must be obeyed while it lasts.
An injunction should not be used as an instrument of oppression as
the citizen's liberty was sacrosanct.  Therefore as long as there is
a reasonable alternative for ensuring the obedience of a court
order such alternative should be preferred where the contemnor
has not been very contemptuous and flagrantly disrespectful.
The social status of the contemnor was not relevant in deciding
whether such contemnor should be committed to a civil prison
because the law was no respect of persons however
distinguished.
Bikeway Kidney Vs. Gideon Kibande.
Jurisdiction of Grade 1 Magistrate (Pecuniary) whether Magistrate
Grade has powers to try suit whose pecuniary Jurisdiction is
above ten thousand shillings -whether Magistrate Grade 1 has
power to order eviction and entertain the suit as to ownership of
Registered Land, where subject matter is in excess of pecuniary
jurisdiction.
Held: The Civil Jurisdiction of Magistrate Courts is dealt with by
S.219 of the Magistrates Court Act as amended by Act 4/85.
By this statute a Magistrate Grade 1 is empowered to try any
suit where the subject matter in dispute does not exceed 10,000/=.
The learned trial Magistrate should never have entertained a claim
The statement that the learned Magistrate Grade 1 had power to
order eviction and also power to entertain a suit as to ownership of
the Registered Land was correct infact but the value of the subject
matter capable of clothing the Magistrate with the requisite
legality was lacking.
Banax Ltd Vs. Daniel Muliika.
Preliminary objection - Arbitration  - where arbitration proceeds
court action- whether there is no cause of action before arbitration
takes place.
Held: The plaintiff company had a separate existence from its
members and the former sought to enforce its rights in its
capacity as such.  The memorandum and Articles of Association
formed a contract between the members interest shareholder to
deal with the company in his private capacity and not as a
member and this was the case in the instant.
therefore the requirements of plaintiff company's Articles were
inapplicable.
Nawemba Sulaiman Vs. Byekwaso Magada.
Appeal - appeal instituted with notice of appeal instead of
memorandum of appeal - whether this was a fatal irregularity-
Appeal - named "misc. application" instead "misc. Appeal" -
whether this was irregular.
Held: Because the courts have to be moved to get the record of the
proceedings ready this may be done by way of notice of Appeal
or by an ordinary letter.  Therefore the action taken by counsel for
the appellant was quite proper in the circumstances and does not
way render the subsequent memo fled a nullity.
Marisa Lucas Vs. Uganda Breweries Ltd.
Application to set a side the dismissal of the suit for non-appearance
of plaintiff whether there was sufficient cause for non-appearance
of plaintiff 's counsel when suit was dismissed - whether applicant
guilty of inordinate delay.
Held: The statements in Counsel's affidavit were false in material
particular and must be rejected since the judge would definitely
have recorded the presence of the plaintiff if he was there.
It is trite law that where an affidavit is sworn based on information
the source of information must be disclosed.  The counsel swore
an affidavit based on information whose source was not disclosed.
The affidavit also contained hearsay evidence which was
inadmissible.
For an application of this nature to succeed the applicant must
satisfy court that there was sufficient cause for non-appearance
but counsel for the applicant had failed in this.
Another ground for refusing the application is that the plaintiff/
applicant is guilty of inordinate delay in bringing the application
and setting it down for hearing.
Walugogo Nangwe Vs. Walugogo Kaluna & anor.
Appeal - application for leave to appeal to the High Court against
ruling and order of Chief Magistrate - whether if the decision sought
to stand substantial  injustice will result - whether basis to allow
the application.
Held: Leave to appeal to the High Court was governed by S.232(1)
( c) of the MCA.  It can only be granted where the decision
intended to be appealed from involves a substantial question of law
or has caused or is likely to cause substantial miscarriage of
justice.  The instant case did not involve all or any of those
elements.
Muke Muhammad & ors Vs. M/s Shell (u) Ltd.
Defendant entering appearance but not filing without statement of
defence in time - whether there is sufficient cause justifying
defendant to file defence out of time.
Held: Where a defendant has entered appearance but fails to file
a defence and has a good defence on the merits the court should
normally exercise its discretion and allow him to be heard in the
matter penalize him severely in costs, unless he is trying to delay
the action by doing.  In the instant case counsel for the defendant
should have exercised more care than he did after he had returned
from the Peace Mission.  His application for leave to file defence
would be refused because there was unreasonable and inordinate
delay as well as negligence on his part.
Babizalirwa Francis Vs. Buyanja Tweheyo Co. Ltd.
Application for leave to appear and defend o.33 r.11 by defendant
whether may be granted out of time because plaintiff did not pay
Court fees for the head suit - whether application may be granted
because defendant has a triable issue in whether execution may
be stayed.
Held: In view of the general powers conferred upon court to enlarge
time by S.99 of the Civil Procedure Act, and of the fact that the
defendant's application disclosed a triable issue and no court fees
had been paid for filing plaint the application will be had despite
applicant's delay.
The general rule is that leave to defend should be given
unconditionally unless there is a good ground for thinking that the
defences put forward are no more than a sham.  The applicant
must satisfy court that he has a good defence sufficient to entitle
him to defend himself as was the case with the instant application.
The law is settled that no document is properly filed until fees have
been paid.  In the instant case, no fees were paid and since no
affidavit was filed in reply to this.  Therefore the suit was
improperly filed.
The improper filing of the suit has the effect of nullifying the
Judgment entered in favor of the plaintiff and should be set a
side, so should the subsequent orders of execution and
attachment of the defendant's property
Muwumba Kabire & anor Vs. H.H Abdi & sons Transporters Ltd.
Objection proceedings o.19rr 55,56+ 57-whether objector's property
wrongly attached where objector is shareholder in a company
which is the judgment debtor.
Held: Where an application is made for the attachment of any
moveable property belonging to a judgment - debtor, but not in his
possession, the decree-holder shall annex to application an
inventory of the property to be attached, containing a reasonably
accurate description the same.  In the instant case it was
improper not to specify the properties to be attached.
As regards the motor vehicle attached it is well established that
the property of the company is distinct from that of its members.
therefore the attachment of the objector's property was wrong.
A power of attorney is defined as an authority given by one to
another to act for him in his absence e.g. to convey land, sue etc.
The attorney like in the instant case does not necessarily have
to have any interest in the thing to be done or transaction to be
executed.
Agadi Did Vs. James Namakaso
Default in entry of appearance and failure to file written statement
of defence within set time or at after entry of interlocutory judgment.
Held: The defendant cannot be heard because he had filled no
defence.
That failure to file a defence raises a presumption or constructive
admission, of the claim made in the plaint.
The story told by the plaintiff in absence of a defence to contradict
it, must be accepted as the truth.
Yakuze Yoana Vs. Victoria Nakabembe.
Appeal - whether appeal filed out of time.
Held: Failure to have a court seal would render the appeal a nullity
since the memorandum of appeal without a court seal was would
not pass for a Court Document.
Failure to extract a formal Decree before filing the appeal was a
defect that would render the appeal incompetent.
Rajimpex Ltd Vs. National Textile Board, Nyanza Textiles Ind. Ltd.
Application to set a side exparte Judgment - whether reasonable
excuse for failure to enter appearance and merit in defence existed.
Held: The application had failed to show sufficient cause before
the court could exercise its discretion in the favour of the
applicant to set aside the ex-part judgment.
Since it was beyond contention that the goods the subject of the
debt were received and accepted and permission for their payment
received from Bank of Uganda, there was no merit in the defence.
The managing Director's letter acknowledging the debt revived
right of action.
Opika Opoka Vs. Muno Newspaper,& 2 others.
Pleadings - whether the written statement of defence does not
plead that the plaint does not disclose a cause of action whether
the same can be pleaded at the trial.
Held: Since the first and second objections were not raised in the WSD
they were new facts inconsistent with the pleadings and they constituted
a departure from the pleadings.
The publication of the printed matter to the public makes the publisher
(jointly with the author and printer) personally liable and therefore it was
not necessary for the plaint to plead that the publisher is vicariously
liable.
Gokaldas Laxilidas Tanna Vs. Sister Rose Muyinza.
Res Judicata - whether rule applies only against a person whom
judgment was given.
Held: Res judicata can only apply against a person whom judgment
has been given.  The order made against the defendant had nothing to
do with the Custodian Board as it was not claiming through the
defendant.
There was sufficient evidence to indicate that the applicant's legal right
would be affected by the granting of the relief claimed in the action and
therefore his presence was necessary to enable the court effectually
and completely to adjudicate on the issues in the case.
Therefore, the applicant may be added as a party upon his own
application.
Waddimba Joje William Vs. Zacchama K.S.Bukenya.
Evidence - when may fresh evidence be allowed by court.
Held: It is the primary duty of a court to decide on the truth of the facts
as is established by evidence and if need be by fresh evidence rather
than to decide it on the mode in which it is forensically conducted.
Therefore considering that the evidence sought to be adduced is of
independent witness court would agree with counsel for the Plaintiff's
submission that the evidence sought to be adduced is likely to be
beneficial to the parties and to court for justice to be done.
Amos Mugisa & sons Chemico Ind. Vs. Departed Asia & anor.
Injunction - whether an injunction can issue against government.
Held: the NRM Secretariat does not have an independent existence on
its own because it gets its vote from Government and was therefore an
arm of Government like the Resistance Councils.  The proper 2nd
defendant would have been the Attorney General.
No injunction can issue against Government.
Since there was another similar suit pending before the Magistrates'
Court, the suit filed later in the High Court would be stayed.
Matovu Bulaimu & ors Vs. The Attorney General & ors.
Government proceedings - whether an injunction can ensue
against eviction by government from public land.
Held: The application for an order that the plaintiffs remain on their
Bibanja until final disposal of the suit was on unsustainable orders for
recovery of land against Government.  The plaintiffs were entitled to an
order for compensation only, only for the development upon their
Bibanja.
Struggle (u) Ltd Vs. Pan African Insurance Co. Ltd.
Pleadings - facts not pleaded in the plaint whether could be raise
at the trial.
Held: The issue whether the defendant  company has ceased
to exist is not a fact in issue as it was not pleaded.  Therefore evidence
to prove its non-existence was not admissible.
Okidi Terensio Vs. Attorney General.
Suits against Government - whether the Government can be
vicariously liable.
Held: The plaintiff has not proved that he was arrested by the NRM
soldiers and has no complaint against the Police both at Busia and
Kampala or against any specific Government servant or agent.
There was no evidence adduced to lead court to  believe that there were
circumstances requiring the army to act as they ought under s.6 of the
Armed Force Act nor was there army evidence to show any criminal
offence which would have warranted the plaintiff's alleged, but not
produced police statement.
Government is not vicariously liable to the plaintiff since he has not
proved any case against its agents.
No damages have been proved against the Government suit dismissed
with costs to the defendant.
Opio Pule Vincent Vs. Attorney General
Limitation - whether a suit which is time barred by the provisions
of s.2 (1) (a) of civil procedure and limitation (miscellaneous
provisions) Act 20 1969 11 maintainable.
Held: It is an established law that a suit which in time barred by statute
must be rejected because is such a suit the judge is barred from
granting relief or remedy.
S.4 of the Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Provisions Act 20/69
however allows extension of limitation period in case of disability.  As
to what amounts to disability section 8(2) of this Act is not exhaustive
but inclusive infancy and unsoundness of mind given in that section
are merely examples of disability.
The plaintiff suffered paralysis of both upper limbs from 1987 until April
1989 following his arrest and torture by soldiers of the NRA.  This
(in my view) is a disability which falls under S.8 (2) (a) of the Civil
Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Provision) Act 20/69. The justifies
extension of time under s.4 of the Act.  Limitation period in such a case
starts to run when the disability ceased.
Oryema Boniface Vs. U.M.S.C
Application to stay execution of exparte decree until the
application seeking to set a side that exparte judgment is heard
and finalized - application brought under S.101 CPA -whether
such an application can succeed.
Held: Parties to a dispute cannot ordinarily invoke the inherent
jurisdiction of the court under s.101 of the CPA if there is a remedy
provided elsewhere which meets the necessity of the case.  In the
instant case the situation was catered for by O.19 r.26 of the CPR,
which provision does not refer only to distinct suits but includes
pending applications to set aside the exparte judgment, as was instant
case.
Bunjo Amos Vs. Barclays Bank of Uganda Ltd.
Temporary injunction to restrain selling of mortgagor's property
pending disposal of suit - whether grounds given for the application
are good in law.
Held: The application for a temporary injunction would be allowed
because the applicant would suffer irreparable damage if his dwelling
house was sold before the expiry of the agreed 24 months, and
The applicant would be more greatly inconvenienced than the defendant
bank if the property in question is auctioned prematurely, and
The applicant has a probability of succeeding in the main suit where he
seeks a declaration that the purported fore closure is premature and
unlawful.
Notay Engineering Industries(1981) Ltd. Vs. Superior
construction & Engineering Ltd.
Application to set a side exparte decree by notice of motion -
whether the notice of motion did not disclose the ground upon
which the application was made -whether this was a fatal defect.
Held: Since the notice of motion stated that the grounds of the
application sufficiently appeared in the affidavit filed with the notice
of motion, by that reference, the contents of the affidavit filed in support
of the application were incorporated in the notice of motion.
Barironda Y. Vs. Bitakweise Joen and another.
Notice of motion - not stating grounds of application - whether
defective.
Held: By reference the contents of the affidavit annexed to or in support
of the application were incorporated in the notice of motion.
When the affidavit is read as a whole and some paragraphs or implied.
The omission to state the already implied or apparent source of
information is minor discrepancy which does not point to a deliberate
lie, cannot therefore invalidate, the affidavit.
Law Development Centre Vs. Edward Mugalu & anor.
Procedure for applying to the High Court to exercise its supervisory
jurisdiction over Magistrates Courts - whether by notice of motion.
Held: It is sufficient that any aggrieved party writes to the Registrar
High Court drawing his attention to the irregularity by a subordinate
court and requests that the matter be brought before a judge.
The Chief Magistrate's order to the applicant to pay a sum of
sh.300.000/= on his own motion, being security for costs was neither
unjust nor irregular because Order 39 rule 9 empowers the High Court
in its own discretion, at any time, after an appeal is lodged to demand
from the appellant security for the costs of the appeal and section
231 of the MCA proscribes the Civil Procedure Rules as the procedure
to be followed by the Chief Magistrates Courts and Magistrates Grade
1, and proceedings for revision are analogous to the proceedings for
appeals.
Bulenzi Moses Vs. Wandera Cornie Mufta.
Application to set a side decree, execution and exparte judgment
to give defendant leave to appear and defend.
Held: Service upon a wife of defendant who was known to have traveled
abroad was not effective service upon the defendant.
Order 49 rule 3 requires that when a given act is supposed to be done
at a given date, which date happens to be Sunday or other Holiday
such act should be done on the date when the office next opens.
In the instant case, the day when the office next opened was a Monday
24th December but order 47 rule 4 states that period between the 24th
December and 15 January, unless court otherwise directs, shall not be
recorded  upon doing any act.  Therefore entering a judgment in default
on 4th January 1991 was an act null and void.
Kakire Joyce and Another Vs. Charles Mpanga Kaggwa.
Wrong date from the actual date of probate relied upon - whether
this was an incurable fundamental error.
through the Uganda law did not provide for an instance of
surrendering probate before it was revoked, it was a Lacuna made
possible by the fact that a human legislator could not provide for every
possible human failure.  Therefore court was empowered by the
Judicature Act in such circumstances to look at the provisions of the
Common Law.  And the common law provides that once process issued
to the defendant to an action of probate, the defendant or plaintiff,
whoever has the grant must surrender it to the Registrar.
The misquotation of the date was clearly a pure error there being no
other document to which that date might refer and therefore the court
was prepared to accept as fact that the Probate being referred to was
that dated 30/4/1987.
Ann Application for A Writ of Habeas corpus ad Sub
juciendum by Mpiso Fred.
Attachment of property to compel respondent to obey the order of
habeas courpus - whether necessary.
Held: Since the charge sheet showed that the applicant was charged
with desertion on dates when he was in Military custody smacked of
bad faith and showed that the motive of the charge was bad.
Since the Court Martial before which the applicant was supposed to
appear was under dissolution it would be unconstitutional for the
applicant to continue under detention indefinitely.
Mayanja Norah & others Vs. Habre International Trading Co.
Stay of execution -application for a final order for stay of execution
application can stand.
Held: Although Court has inherent jurisdiction to stay execution apart
from the specific powers given under legislation, properly made ex-
parte.The applicant had not disclosed those exceptional circumstances.
Therefore only an interim stay order can be passed pending the
disposal of the application to stay without notice to the decree holder.
A final order, staying execution should not be made without such notice.
Oryema Boniface Vs. Uganda Supreme Council.
Change of advocate - consent to file WSD out of time by an
advocate without instructions - whether such consent is valid.
Held: Since judgment was entered in favour of the plaintiff under O.9 r 6
of the Civil Procedure Rules and since such judgment was not contested
and set aside, the interlocutory judgment upheld the plaintiff's claim
to the compensation for his house hold property detained and for
wrongful eviction.
Special damages shall be computed by a factor of 3/5 of the value of
the detained goods at the current prices of the new such pieces.
An Advocate without instructions cannot consent to filing a WSD out
of time and this also meant that there was no WSD filed.
M/s R.M.L Technical Services Ltd. Vs. National Enterprises
Corporation.
Interim injunction - whether it could issue against a sale in
execution of a Decree.
Held: A sale is wrongful when it is neither authorized nor justified by
writ of execution or by judgment under which it is issued, or when the
warrant is issued maliciously and without reasonable or probable cause
and this was not the case.
M/s Ayigihugu & Co. Advocates Vs. Munyankindi Muteeri M
Parties to suits - whether done of special powers to a suit.
Held: Since the plaintiff was a done of powers of Attorney he did not
have a cause of action and therefore he could not institute a suit in his
own name. He was an agent and he could only sue in the name of the
principal. Therefore the plaintiff should be struck out.
Karim Hirji Vs. M/s Pan African Insurance Co.
Affidavit - whether evidence by affidavit may be admissible where
there is no affidavit in reply.
Held: After backing the offer with the letter of guarantee, the condition
annexed by he defendant it was necessary that the offer be
communicated to the defendant within the time fixed by the plaintiff
to accept it.  Therefore, since this time had elapsed there was no
complete contract between the parties, but only a bargain of a highly
conditional nature.
A banker's (letters of ) guarantee is where the Banker, gives financial
backing of a payment on first demand.  The plaintiff's banker testified
truthfully that he had to block up funds on the plaintiff did indeed open
letters of guarantee.
Evidence by an affidavit to prove an important point in a case, where the
other party has not been given a chance to reply should not be
admitted in court.
Gomil (U) Ltd Vs. Latex (U) Ltd.
Jurisdiction of Registrars - whether a High Court Registrar on
District Registrar can entertain interlocutory application such as
application to grant an interim injunction.
Held: Since there are no words in O.46 r.3 which can be regarded as
limiting the interlocutory applications with which a Registrar may deal
to those which are necessarily incidental to the preparation of a suit
for trial, and since s.2 of the Civil Procedure Act defines Registrar
to include a District Registrar, a High Court Registrar has the
Registrar has he necessary jurisdiction to make orders on interlocutory
applications including the granting an interim injunction.
Under O.46 r.6 a Registrar is deemed a Civil Court and this enables
the Registrar to avail himself of the advantage of the Civil Procedure
Rules which are normally utilized by the Courts in exercising their
jurisdiction in interlocutory applications including powers to dispense
with hearing notice to the party to the dispute when deemed necessary
like in the instant case.
Brown George Turyamureeba Vs. Attorney General
Application by plaintiff to recover vehicle which was seized by
NRA soldiers. Whether plaintiff is lawful owner of the suit vehicle.
Held: In the light of the overwhelming evidence the plaintiff is lawful
owner of the suit vehicle.
The evidence overwhelming supports the conclusion that the vehicle
was seized by NRA officers.
The NRA officers were acting in the course of their employment.
The normal measure of damages is the market value of the goods
where the goods are not ordered to be returned to the plaintiff.
Plaintiffs and their advocates have the burden to prove special damages
strictly.
Exemplary damages may be awarded where there has been wanton or
oppressive and high handed conduct by the defendant in respect of
which there must be punishment as a deterrent to others who may act
in a similar manner.
Dr.E.Kigenya Vs. Margaret Naiga.
Estoppel - whether the plaintiff who did not demand interest on the
principal was estopped from demanding the same at the trial.
Held: There was no evidence on record to show that the plaintiff had
offered not to claim interest by a certain date, on which offer the
defendant had acted.  Therefore the question of estoppel did not arise.
