Further, Counsel was supposed to plead the circumstances that would
establish the existence of estoppel, in the written statement of defence
as required by O.6 r1. For counsel to adduce evidence of estoppel
which was not established by pleadings constituted departure and should
not be allowed therefore, the defendant should pay interest as she had
failed to prove that the plaintiff had offered to waive his right to interest.
The plaintiff was entitled to bring this suit because the defendant
refused to pay.  Therefore, the plaintiff was entitled to costs since he
had been necessitated to bring this suit.
Nile Bank Ltd Vs. Gomba Machinery &General Equipment Ltd.
Execution - an order sought under 019 r 34(1) CPR for a warrant
of a judgment against the managing director of the judgment
debtor/company personally - whether the rule is applicable.
Held: Whether or not Mr. Gombya, the Managing Director was the
proper  judgment debtor, the correct mode of executing a decree
arresting the judgment debtor would be made Under S.39 (d) of the
Civil Procedure Act and Order 19 r.8 (2) (I) (m) but not under 19 r.34(1).
Rules 34(1) of Order 19 is applicable as an alternative mode of
execution where there has been an application properly made for the
arrest of a judgment debtor under section 39(d) and O.19 r 8 (2) (I) (iii)
when the court may, instead of issuing a warrant of arrest for the
judgment debtor, issue a notice calling upon him to civil prison.  Further
Rule 34 (7) of Order 19 cannot be invoked by the judgment debtor.
The rule is explicitly within the discretion of the court and this is explicitly
indicated in form 11 of Appendix D to Civil Procedure Rules at page
13/2.  The notice is issued and signed by the Judge.
As far as Lifting of veil for the purpose of enabling the judgment Creditor/
Applicant to recover its decretal sum from the Managing Director
instead of recovering it from the J/d company, this would probably be
done if the applicant, J/c in his affidavit proved that the defendant
company was as it was described in Jones Vs. Lipman (1962) 1 WLR
832 at page 838, the creature of the Managing Director, a device and
sham, a mask which he held before his face in an attempt to avoid
recognition by the eye of equity.
Haji Sula Sendegeya Vs. Masaka Cooperative Union.
Pleadings - plaintiff not pleading how he came to own the suit
vehicle where he is not the registered proprietor, whether this was
fatal.
Held: The plaintiff failed to plead the facts by which he could establish
his proprietary right over the suit vehicle as required by O.6 r.6 which
requires that the plaintiff should be entitled to only the relief in regard to
that which he alleges in the pleadings and proves. This failure rendered
the plaint bad in law.
The amendment would be allowed since court had such powers to allow
either party to amend his pleadings at any stage of the proceedings,
when it is just to do so and necessary for deciding the real issues in
dispute between the parties.  Since the real issue between the parties
was which of them was liable for the accident and quantum of damages,
the plaintiff should be allowed to set out the facts establishing his
ownership of the vehicle.
Ramanbahi J.Patel Vs. Madhvani International Ltd.
Setting a side exparte judgment on counter claim in default of
filing a reply - whether ground that counsel was under mistaken
belief that a reply was necessary sufficient to warrant the
setting a side.
Held: In order to set aside the exparte judgment the applicant must
show that he has a prima-facie defence and satisfy court that there is a
reasonable explanation why the experte judgment was entered against
him.  Since if the counterclaim of the plaintiff is already, which claim
presents some triable issues and since no hardships would be suffered
by the respondent as it can be compensated by costs, the judgment
would be set aside.
Imerida Nandaula Vs. Ugandev Bank Ltd
Civil Procedure: Stay of execution - property of the defendant bank
attached in execution of a decree-whether execution may be stayed.
The applicant Bank sought execution against it stayed.  The respondent/
plaintiff had obtained judgment, decree, her costs taxed and a warrant
of attachment, against the applicant/defendant bank, all on the same
day, exparte, in the lower court, which court also rejected an application
for setting aside the exparte judgment.
Charles Okia Vs. Uganda Consolidated Properties Ltd.
Third party notice - Directions - not mandatory to seek direction of
court.
Held: It is not mandatory to seek the directions of court.
Without seeking directions, however, it would be difficult for court to
assess the amount due from the third party, and the cause of action
against that third party would be obscure, and he could be struck off.
Yowana Ariko Vs. Firipo Malinga.
Consolidation/stay of suits - plaintiff in second suit - real contest
between the plaintiffs - seconds suit's defendant was the
plaintiff in the first suit - whether proper to consolidate and
proceed on plaint of first suit.
Held: The proper order should have been to say C.S.201/81 and proceed
with C.S.202/81 since the real contest was between the parties in the
latter suit.
Dr. Joshua Emmanuel Tegule & ors Vs. Uganda Medical
Practitioners and dental Surgeons Council.
Appeal - Rules prescribing procedure not made - whether court
can entertain the appeal.
M/s Unidrom Ltd Vs. M/s Kawesi & Co.
Security for costs - plaintiff a foreign company without property
or investments in Uganda - whether this is ground for ordering
security for costs.
Held: An order will issue if the foreign company has no property or
investments in Uganda.
Security for costs is to be by bond to the satisfaction of the Registrar.
Wycliffe Kiggundu - Kato Vs. Attorney General
Cause of Action -Plaint -rejection of plaint for non-disclosure of
cause of action.
Held: A cause of action is a fact or combination of facts which give rise
to a right of action.
The procedure to strike out a plaint is appropriate where it is obvious
that the plaint is insufficient for the relief sought, unmaintainable and
unarguable.
Persons are employed in the Public Service by the President under A
104(1) of the Constitution which gives him the unfettered prerogative to
dismiss and retire at pleasure, and in the public interest.
R. 36 of the Public Service Commission Regulations empowers a
responsible officer, in this case the Permanent Secretary, to interdict an
officer.  The rule does not indicate any limitation on duration of the
interdiction.
The presentation was required for purposes of rr.45(1) (a) and (b) 48(2)
which avail the officer an opportunity to be heard.  The plaintiff denied
himself the right to be hard by refusal to make the presentation.
Ben Byabashaija & anor Vs. Attorney General.
Written statement of defence - whether defendant can call
evidence where his written statement of defence was merely a
general denial without raising any defence.
Held: Evidence by a photocopy would be admitted since the original
was in the possession of the defendant.  It was therefore not necessary
either to annex the document on the plaint nor to list it.
The defendant would not be given leave to call evidence since in his
written statement of defence there was no specific denial.
The defendant's amended written statement of defence was improperly
filed since it was filed late after six months which required either leave
of court or consent by the plaintiff.
Special damages are not awardable when not pleaded.
Damages awardable are assessed at the market value at the date of
judgment, of the properties confiscated.
Sh. 50,000 general damages for each plaintiff to be awarded for detinue.
Ugma Engineering Corp. Ltd Vs. Lugazi Town Council.
Appeals - whether fresh evidence may be allowed during the first
appeal.
Held: The local authority could not levy rates beyond its rating area,
however, whether the appellant company was within or without the
retable area was a question that would be proved by fresh evidence
and therefore a retrial would be order in the valuation court.
A Government valuer has statutory formula for rating hereditaments and
once the formula is known, it is incumbent on him to show how he
applied the particular formula to arrive at a given value.
Since this was first appeal fresh evidence would not be allowed and
therefore the production of maps to prove whether the appellant
company was within a ratable would not be allowed.
Sole Electronic (u) Ltd Vs. Town Clerk K.K. & Nakibuka
Enterprises.
Cause of action - whether the plaintiffs company which sues
alleging to have unfairly lost a bid which bid was made by one
of the Directors of the company in his own names, has a cause
of action.
Held: When a Director in the plaintiff company bided for the acquisition
of the suit premises, in his own names, it did not mean that it was the
plaintiff company that bided because of the principle of separate
personality between the company and its members.  Therefore plaintiff
did not have a cause of action to bring the suit.
The question whether there was a subsisting tenancy between the
applicant and the plaintiff company was a triable issue because the
applicant was a successor in titled to the former landlord of the
plaintiff company. On this ground the plaint would not be stuck off.
Nkuyahanga Frank Vs. Esso (u) Ltd
Temporary injunction - application thereof without the injunction
being sought in the main suit - whether a temporary injunction
may be granted.
Held: The relief sought in the main action must be for an injunction in
order for an applicant to seek a temporary one before the case is hard.
In the instant case the suit is for the recovery of a motor vehicle or its
value but not for an injunction restraining the respondents or otherwise
disposing of the said vehicle.  This thereby defeated the application.
The application had failed to show that he would suffer irreparable
damage if the vehicle was sold and in fact he had prayed for the return
the vehicle or its value.  This means that if he proved his case he can
be compensated with damages.
East African General Insurance Co.Ltd Vs. U.E.B
Limitation - whether the plaintiff  company was time barred from
demanding arrears of rent from the defendant company which
is a scheduled corporation on grounds that such a claim should
have been brought within three years of non-payment rent and
breach of tenancy.
Held: The plaintiff's right to recover rent existed before and after the
enactment of Act 20/60.  The plaintiff's proprietary rights as registered
owner were prior to 1969 not challenged nor even now as per s.114 the
Evidence Act.  The plaintiff would prima facie be entitled to claim rents
due beyond the period excluded or barred either by s.18 of the
Limitation act or after commencement of Act 20 of 1969.
Ismail Dabule Vs. Wildon Osuna Otwanyi.
Res Judicata a Magistrate's Court dismissing a suit under O.9 r.19
for non appearance of counsel for the plaintiff which Magistrate's
Court had no jurisdiction to try the suit - whether such dismissal
bars further suits from being filed in respect of the same claim-
whether suit was resjudicata.
Held: The issue of res judicata was irrelevant because the suit was
dismissed under s.8 of the CPA and O.9 r.19 for want of prosecution.
S.8 CPA and O.9 r.20(1) create disability preventing a plaintiff from
filing a fresh suit but must apply to have the dismissal set aside, and
this was irrespective of whether the court dismissing the suit had
jurisdiction or not.  The preliminary objection would therefore be upheld.
Faucett Arthur Ocatum Engole Vs. Attorney General.
Amendment of pleadings - whether amendment of written
statement of defence may be allowed by an oral application.
Held: The proposed amendment would be allowed to be made orally
rather than by chamber summons to save court time.  The proposed
amendment, further, would be allowed because it did not introduce a
new defence there having been previously filed one containing a general
denial.  Moreover, the amendment would not in anyway deprive the
plaintiff of any accrued rights, the action having been filed within the
limitation period, and more so no justice would the plaintiff suffer if the
amendment is allowed.
Zamu Nalumansi & anor Vs. Sulaiman Lule.
Appeals-extension of time to appeal - whether negligence by
counsel for the appellant to file notice of appeal
and record of appeal in time is sufficient ground for court of appeal
out of time.
Held: Since the applicants are laymen, they relied on the assurances
of their negligent counsel.  And their new counsel, who eventually
discovered the former counsel's error of omission was guilty of such
delay as would justify depriving the applicants of the right to have their
intended appeal adjudicated on its merits.  Therefore, this was sufficient
reason according to r. 4 of the rules of the Supreme Court to extend the
time for filing the Notice of Appeal and Record of approval out of time.
Kiwana Margaret Vs. The Chief Registrar of Titles.
Residual powers - whether evocable where there is a specific
procedure in place.
Held: The application was improperly before court because s.197 of the
RTA empowers the ordinary Civil Procedure Rules to be applicable to
proceedings under this Act if there are no rules made by the Chief
Justice for the purpose.  Under the rules, all applications to court shall
be by Notice of Motion under O.48 r.1 of the Civil Procedure Rules.
Chukwuma F.Obidegwu Vs. Daniel B. Ssamakadde.
Pleadings - written statement of defence generally denying the
grounds of the claim - whether this offended against O.6r -7
requiring specific dealing with allegations of fact.
Held: The defendant's pleadings did not deny the existence of the lease
agreement because they just denied generally the grounds of the claim
of the plaintiff, without being specifics as to whether the alleged lease
agreement existed or not.
The defendant's failure at the deliver possession of the said demises
was a clear breach of the lease agreement because where there is an
actual demise of a term the lessor impliedly contracts to give the lease
possession at the commencement of the term.
Since the lessor at the commencement of the term agreed to deliver
possession of a house that was in good and tenantable repair and
condition, there was therefore a covenant express by the landlord to put
the tenant into effective possession, and occupation of a tenantable
house buy the 1st August 1991.
Kayoboke Christopher Vs. Amos Agaba Joseph & others.
Joinder of causes of action - whether suit was bad for misjoinder
where a plaintiff brings an action against the defendants and
directions in a company but one of them is not a shareholder.
Held: Since Dr.Byamugisha was defendant number 2 and was and was
as a result likely to give evidence in this suit, it would not be proper for
Dr. Byamugisha to act in person for the there 2 defendants as their
Counsel.
The plaintiff had two causes of action properly brought before court I.e.
a personal action by which he sought court's protection of his pecuniary
interest is the company and a derivative action by which he sought
court's protection of the good of the company generally against waste
by the directors.  Therefore court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
The question of whether the plaintiff was estopped from complaining
against the manner of running the company because it was a long
established mode to which he himself was party, would be a question to
be determined at the trial.
Badiru Kabalega Vs. Sepiriano Mugangu.
Appeals - whether the first appellate court had done it's duty of
evaluating strictly the record of evidence before it and whether
it had arrived at a correct decision.
Held: The duty of the second appellate court is to consider whether the first
appellate court properly, re-evaluated the evidence on record.  In the instant
case it was on record that the first appellate court found part of the record
before the trial court was missing and yet did not consider the effect this had
had on the appeal before it.  In the absence of this vital evidence the learned
Ag. Chief Magistrate could not be said to have examined the evidence
before it exhaustively.  This would be sufficient to deprive the respondent of
the judgment.
The purpose of visiting the locus in quo is for each party to indicate what he
is claiming.  Each party must testify on Oath and be cross-examined by the
opposite party.  In the instant case the record did not show that either party
had testified on oath and had been cross-examined.  The procedure adopted
by the trial court at the locus in quo was not in conformity with the accepted
procedure.  The whole trial was fatally vitiated by this irregularity.
Shelton Okabo Vs. Standard Chartered Bank Ltd.
Affidavit - failure to file affidavit in reply whether there statements of
facts contained in the supporting affidavit remain uncontradicted.
Held: The duty of the second appellate court is to consider whether the
first appellate court properly, re-evaluated the evidence on record.  In
the instant case it was on record that the first appellate court fount part
of the record before the trial court was missing and yet did not consider
the effect this had on the appeal before it.  In the absence of this vital
evidence the learned Ag. Chief Magistrate could not be said to have
examined the evidence before it exhaustively.  This would be sufficient
to deprive the respondent of the judgment.
The purpose of visiting the locus in quo is for each party to indicate what
he is claiming.  Each party must testify on oath and be cross-examined.
The procedure adopted by the trial court at the locus in quo was not in
conformity accepted procedure.  The whole trial was fatally vitiated by
this irregularity.
Kayondo David Vs. The Co-operative Bank (u) Ltd
Jurisdiction - whether the High Court has no original jurisdiction to
determine a dispute between an employee of the cooperative
Bank and the Bank.
Held: O.13 r5 clearly requires the trial judge to frame the issues to be
determined right at the beginning of the trial.  The prime duty to frame the
relevant issued lies on the court trying the case although the Advocates
in the case also ought to comply with the requirement.
The appellant was an officer of the respondent bank because s.87 of
the co-operative Societies Act defined officer to include Chairman,
Secretary and Treasurer.
Dispute though not defined by the Act, it is not a term of Art and it
must therefore be given its ordinary meaning of a controversy or quarrel.
S.73 (1) of the Co-operative Societies Act did not oust the jurisdiction
of the High Court in disputes concerning the Co-operative Societies or
its members past and present.  This is because the Constitution of
Uganda gives the High Court unlimited original Jurisdiction in all matters
subject to any written law.  The written law to oust such Jurisdiction
it must expressly state so, which was not the case with s.73 of the
Co-operative Societies Act.
Mutaawe Samson Sekabanja Vs. Samuel Mwazike & ors.
Pleadings - cause of action, whether plaint disclosed a cause of
action.
Held: The plaint disclosed a cause of action because it stated
material facts concisely in a summary from as required by the cardinal
rules of pleadings.
The particulars of fraud alleged against the defendants were sufficiently
set out in the amended plaint and enough to enable the defendants
know the accusation brought against them.
Estoppel by judgment did not arise because the previous judgment
material to this case was not from court in its exercise of its probate,
matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction; secondly, the
defendants derived title from a person who was not party to the suit for
which estoppel by record is pleaded.
Notay Engineering Industries Vs. Superior Construction &
Engineering Ltd.
Notice of motion containing no grounds in it's body but the ground
appearing in the affidavit filed in support of the application -
whether notice of motion bad in law as offending the provisions of
O.48 r.3 CPR.
Held: According to the interpretation of the rule in Naume Nandege Vs.
Busoga District Administration HCCS No.142 of 1971 (Unreported) the
grounds of the applications should be stated in the Notice of Motion and
where evidence by affidavit is considered essential a copy thereof
should be attached to the Notice of Motion, to support the grounds set
out in the Notice of Motion, to support the grounds set out in the
Notice of Motion.
However, in Castelino Vs. Radrigues (1972) EA 223 at page 225 letter it
was held that a reference in a document to an annexure incorporates
the contents of the annexure in the document and accordingly the
Notice of Motion in that case was not in breach for the purpose of this
ruling of 048 r.3. Further that even if the notice of motion had not
contained the grounds it would have  been a minor irregularity
curable by amendment since the respondent in that case would not
have been prejudiced by the form of the notice and hence, leave been
give.
In the present Notice of Motion, it is stated that the ground of his
application sufficiently appears in the affidavit filed.  According to
Casteliono case Supra, the contents of the affidavit filed in support of
the application were incorporated in the Notice of motion.
Clouds 101 Ltd Vs. Standard Chartered Bank (u) Ltd.
Appeal - Extension of time for filing notice of appeal whether
sufficient cause shown for the grant of such an application.
Held: The Court is only entitled to grant an extension of time for
sufficient reason, which must be shown to the Court.  The Supreme
Court would not overrule the decision of a single judge exercising his
discretion unless it is exercised upon a wrong principle of the law or
upon a misdirection as to the facts so that the decision was entirely
unreasonable.  The Advocate had failed to show court sufficient reason
for his delay.
There was no rule in the Supreme Court Rules whereby the parties can
consent to the extension of time within which to file a notice or record
of appeal.
It is not correct that in all circumstances that Advocate whose fees had
not been paid is an Advocate whose fees had not been paid is an
Advocate without instructions.
Libyan Arab (u) Bank Vs. Adam Vassiciandis.
Slip rule - whether an application which would in essence make
court reverse it's own decision in the same matter, may be allowed
Whether this was an instance for re-evaluating evidence on record
or taking additional evidence.
Held: The Inherent powers of the Supreme Court as re-affirmed by Rule
(3) of the Rules of the Supreme Court foes not include the taking of new
or additional evidence but is meant to cure a miscarriage of justice due
to fraud and nullity for new or additional evidence is governed by Rule
29(1) and only empowers the Supreme Court to take new evidence only
at the hearing of the appeal.
The Slip Rule provided in rule 35 (1) only gives Court powers to recall
its judgment and prefect it to give effect to its manifest intention as at
the time of its judgment, or if Court is satisfied beyond doubt as to the
order it would have made had the matter been brought to its attention
at the time of the appeal.
Adam Vassailiandis Vs. Libyan Arab (u) Bank.
Slip rule - whether court may order specific performance by way
of slip order where on appeal it has found that suit contract was
not illegal.
Held: Neither parties had adduced evidence to prove whether or not
"Musoke" was an African, the position was thereby left open and not
order of specific performance would necessarily follow since this in
effect would be to enforce an illegal contract if it turned out that Musoke
was not in fact an African.  It would follow that the remission of the suit
to the High Court for the assessment of damages would only be if the
applicant's transfer was registrable.  In the circumstances the best
thing to do is to refer the matter to the Registrar of Titles to ascertain
the status of Musoke.
Kabanda Connie Vs. Kananula Melvin Consulting Engineering.
Inherent provisions under S.101 of the civil procedure Act -
whether invokable concurrently with specific provisions of the law.
Held: The oral application for amendment by substituting a new law
instead of the one on record would not be granted as it would act to the
prejudice of the other party as they will be taken by surprise.
Since S.101 was only applicable where was no other specific provisions
applicable to the circumstances it would not be permissible to amend
the application by just adding the specific provisions because these two
provisions are exclusive and may not be invoked concurrently.
On record there was no evidence of filing a notice of appeal and
therefore an application for stay of execution pending an appeal was
premature and improper.
Notay Engineering Industries (1981) Ltd Vs. Superior
Construction & Engineering Ltd.
Notice of motion containing no grounds in it's body but the grounds
appearing in the affidavit filed in support of the application -whether
notice of motion bad in law as offending provisions of O.48 r.3 CPR.
Held: According to the interpretation of the rule in Naume Ndagire V
Busoga District Administration HCCS No.142 of 1971 (unreported) the
grounds of the application should be attached t o the Notice of Motion,
to support the grounds set out in the Notice of Motion.
However, in Castelino Vs. Rodrigues [1972] EA 223 at pages 225.
It was held that a reference in a document to an annexure incorporates
the contents of the annexure in the document and accordingly the
Notice of motion in the case was in breach for the purpose of this ruling
of 048 r.3.  Further t hat even if the notice of motion had not contained
the grounds it would have been a minor irregularity curable by
amendment since the respondent in that case would not have been
prejudiced by the form of the notice and hence, leave amend could
have been given.
In the present Notice of Motion, it is stated that the ground of this
application sufficiently appears in the affidavit filed according to
Castelino case Supra the contents of the affidavit filed in support of the
application were incorporated in the Notice of Motion.
Superior Construction & Engineering Ltd Vs. Notay
Engineering Industries (1981) Ltd.
Interest:- plaintiff entitled to interest where there has been gross
delay.
Held: A party who freely enters into a contract with another is expected
to pay that other for the work he has done for that party as a result of
the contract.  In the instant case the plaintiff had done the work for which
he contracted with defendant.  He was therefore entitled to the amount
claimed or its equivalent value.
An award if interest is a matter of discretion of the court.  When the
defendant has been guilty of gross delay, as in the instant case where
the defendant withheld money which to his full knowledge would be put
by the plaintiff to some other investment, the plaintiff's entitled to
interest which should neglect the current commercial value of money.
Like interest, costs are also a matter of discretion of the court.  It is
generally awarded to a successful party unless there is a special
reason to despite him of his costs.
Zaituni Kawuma Vs. George Mwalurum.
Slip order - whether having allowed the appeal by finding that the
contract was null and void ab initio, the judgment should be
corrected by an order that refund of the purchase price be made
to the defendant.
Held: Had the matter of refund of the purchase price been brought to the
attention of Court at the time of prosecution of the appeal, an order for
refund would have been made when judgment was given on the appeal.
Therefore this was a proper case for allowing an application for a slip
order that the said refund be made.
The currency Reform Statute was not a devaluation.  It was a statutory
Reform of the currency.  By that Statute sh. 6,000/= was, after 1st
May, 1987 the value of shs. 600,000/= of the old currency.  The
defendant/applicant was, after 1987 entitled to a refund of sh. 6,000/=
new currency.
Stephen Lubega Vs. Barclays Bank (u) Ltd.
Parties to suit - whether misjoinder or non joinder can be rectified
by court.
Held: The receiver, thought appointed by the respondent, was an agent
of the debtor company, which should have been the right party to be
sued and not the respondent.
Where a wrong party has been sued, the misjoinder can be rectified by
court under the Civil Procedure Rules.  This power of court to deal with
joinder issues includes adding or striking out parties.
The sale was clearly fraudulent and in breach of the covenant pertaining
to the sale of the lorry, the consequent transfer of the lorry was
consequently of no effect as the fraud and the breach of covenant had
vitiated the sale.
A floating charge crystallizes the moment there is default and a receiver
is appointed.
An endorsement on the registration card of a car is good notice for
those dealing with the car.
Fraud cannot be imputed from the facts but must be specifically
pleaded and proved.
B.B Mbabali Vs. Bwanika Ddungu.
Temporary injunction - whether the applicant/plaintiff had satisfied
the condition required for the grant of the temporary injunction.
Held: The temporary injunction would be granted since the applicant had
proved that he would suffer irreparable damage if the suit lands were
alienated before the head suit was finally heard and determined;
secondly the applicant's case had a prima-facie probability of success.
J.W.R Kazzora Vs. M.L.S Rukuba.
Lis pendens rule - whether a pending suit about the disputed
property necessarily precludes registration of transfer of the same.
Held: A caveat that merely stated that the caveator had an interest in
the material property did not necessary preclude a sale subsequent
since the caveat itself was not evidence of sale.
The registration of the transfer on various dates was not evidence of
fraud because it was only the transfer registered subsequent to the
expiry of the notice to the caveator that was valid and moreover since
fraud had not been pleaded in the trial court it could not be a ground
of appeal in the Supreme Court.
The respondent was a bona fide purchaser for value notwithstanding
that he was aware of the existence of the plaintiff's/appellant's caveat
because the alleged sale to the appellant which the caveat was
registered to protect was not shown to exist.  There was no evidence
about the sale to support the caveat.
A document dully addressed to the sender is presumed received at the
time which the document would be delivered in the ordinary course of
the post.  In the instant case, the trial judge found that the appellant
was served with the notice under consideration on 12/10/87 and that
therefore the notice expired on 12/12/87, but because the plaintiff
claimed that he took delivery of the said notice on 16/12/87, even then
the said notice should have expired on 16/2/88.  The appellant then had
until 14/1/88 within which to obtain an order from the court extending
the caveat but did not do so.
By the 15th May 1989, the appellant's application to extend his caveat
had already been disposed of and moreover the existence of the
application in court to extend the caveat did not preclude the effecting
of a transfer because there does not exist in Uganda any pendency
legal rule to the effect that transfers or other dealings in land should not
be registered before a suit contesting such a transfer or dealing cannot
lodge the same caveat as already removed.
The second caveat was in exactly the same terms as the first but the
appellant submitted that the second caveat was different from the first
one in that it was lodged on the basis of the suit he had filed, as a
chose in action, to be protected.  However, even the first caveat sought
exactly the same thing to protect a chose in action namely, the
benefit of the verbal agreement for sale of land.  This was tantamount to
renewing the same caveat which is contrary to the provisions of S.149(3)
of the RTA which states that as caveator cannot lodge the same caveat
as already removed.
Had there been evidence of sale, prior to that one between the
respondent and the administrator, then the subsequent transaction
would have been vitiated by mistake.  But no evidence was adduced to
support it.
It is established that a party relying on fraud must specifically plead it
and that particulars of the alleged fraud must be stated on the face of
the pleading.  In the instant case frauds was not specifically pleaded,
nor was fraudulent intent pleaded or the facts set out in the plaint such
as to create fraud.  Therefore the appellant was not entitled to rely on
fraud because it was different from the original case.
The Standard of proof of fraud is that it must be strictly proved although
not beyond reasonable doubt but something more than a mere balance
of probability is required.
Non-compliance with O.18 r7 which requires that a partly extracting an
order should submit it to the other party for approval, was not fatal
because it was not the order extracted that was the removal of the
appellant's caveat but the caveat had merely lapsed.
The Principle of law is that the first person to register land takes better
title than a person to whom the land was first sold but failed to register
it provided that there was no fraud in the registration.  And in the instant
case there was no fraud proved against the respondent.
Kananura Mielvin Consultant Engineers & 7 ors Vs. Connee Labanda
Joinder of parties - whether court's leave is necessary to add defendants.
Held: The respondent was not allowed by the rules to join new
defendants as partners in the appellant firm, without leave of court as
per O.1 r10 (2) and 13.  This empowers the court either to add or strike
out parties on its own motion or may be moved to do so.
It was improper for the respondent, having amended the plaint not to
have served all the partners as defendants as this offended against O.1
r.10(4) that requires services to be effected on added parties when the
plaint is amended.
The trial court improperly admitted the tenancy agreement because it
was of a certified copy and the requisite stamp duty had not been paid
Moreover, court had not been shown why the original of the agreement
was not available.
The respondent/plaintiff was precluded from raising the rent because
when she asked to be paid the rent in advance for the second year if
followed that she did not wish to increase it.  It is settled that once at
the request of his landlord a tenant pays rent which is not due, then that
rent is commuted or fixed and cannot be increased.
The trial judge misdirected herself when she awarded special damages
that had not be strictly proved.
A submission o9f no case to answer in civil cases means that the judge
should not rule on the submission before the hearing the other party.
The judge should first ask the other party whether he intends or not to
give evidence before ruling on the submission so that the submission
is made on all the evidence.  But since the judge directed counsel for
the defendant/appellant to give evidence, the ruling on the submission
was proper.
Attorney General Vs. Milton Obote Foundation Ltd & Uganda
house investments Ltd.
Constitutional cases - whether a formal application is required to
move a constitutional court to hear a reference.
Held: The procedure of the Constitutional Court, the one which deals
with the interpretation of the Constitution is regulated by the
Constitutional cases (Procedure) Act in matters relating to the
interpretation of the Constitution, S.2(1)(9), (b) (2) (9), (b) and (3) of the
Act provide the procedure to be followed which does not involve
requirement of a formal application to move the Constitutional Court.
Therefore formal application was required to move the Constitutional
Court to hear the reference made to it.
Yunusu Ismail t/a Bombo city store Vs. Alex Kamukamu &
ors t/a Okabazaari.
Entry of appearance by partners - whether all the partners had
effectively entered appearance when through their Advocate they
entered one appearance.
Held: The entry of appearance by the defendants was effective because
partners they were represented by the same counsel who stated in
court the names of the individual partners he was appearing for.
Since Kyeyune's affidavit stated that he had authority from the other
partners to swear the affidavit on their behalf and this had not be
contradicted contrary evidence and since the affidavit of Kyeyune also
showed that he was the managing Direction or the active partner of the
firm, Kyeyune's affidavit was proper.
Counsel Jombwe's affidavit was defective because as counsel he could
not in the same cause depone of matters substantive and contentious
pertaining to the allocation of the suit premises and this offended
against regulations 8 of the Advocates (Professional conduct)
Regulation 1977.  But this did not in any way render the notice of
motion defective because it was still supported by affidavit of Kyeyune.
The seventh ground of appeal would fail because it was too general and
unsustainable and offended against r84 of the rules of Court of Appeal
which requires that a memorandum of appeal should state concisely
the grounds of objection to the decision appealed against and specify
the point which are alleged to have been wrongly decided.
Francis Babumba & ors Vs. Erusa Bunjo.
Evidence by affidavit of counsel - whether counsel's evidence by
affidavit touched on a contentious matter and therefore should be
rejected.
Held: The affidavit by counsel for the respondents contained contentious
matters, and should therefore be rejected because counsel could not
also be a witness in the same cause, as this offended against
regulation 8 of the advocates (Professional conduct) regulations 1977.
The grant of a temporary injunction will not decide the whole suit
because the question of the alleged breach of the lease Agreement
would still have to be settled even if the temporary injunction is granted.
Since the affidavit of one of the applicants sworn in support of the
application showed that there was an expired Lease Agreement
between the parties; that the plaintiffs/applicants were out in breach of
any covenant of the said agreement and since there was no evidence to
contradict this affidavit because counsel for the respondent's affidavit
was rejected, this showed that the plaintiffs/Applicants had shown a
prima-faces case as the evidence revealed a triable issue.
Professor Timothy Wangusa Vs. Edward Muloosi.
Thrown away costs - whether costs of the petition may be
included in the meaning of thrown away costs.
Held: The costs of the petition from its commencement could not be
included in thrown away costs because these were not costs
stemming from all costs occasioned by or thrown away in consequence
of the non appearance of the Petitioner.
As long as the taxing officer acted judicially and not capriciously and
followed the proper principles in the taxation of costs, he should not be
divested of his wide discretion in the taxation and allowance of costs.
Rajimpex Vs. National Textiles Board and Nyanza Textile
Industries Ltd.
Execution - notice to non-party to show cause why execution
should not issue against it - whether notice can issue.
Held: Execution cannot issue against a non-party to a suit, and the
notice, therefore, could not issue.
Assignment of a statutory body's liabilities to another statutory body
could only be done by statute. It could happen if there is absolute,
written evidence and notice to the debtor to the effect.
Estoppel by record means-a parson is not permitted to dispute facts
upon which a judgment against him is based.  The submission did not
fall within this meaning.
A ruling inter-parties is a ruling in personam, not in rem.
M/s Nakabago Co-op society Vs. Livingstone Kyanga.
Jurisdiction over a subject matter of shs 460,000 under summary
procedure whether a Magistrate grade II has jurisdiction.
Held: the Civil Procedure rules which provide for summary suits, are
inapplicable in courts presided over by magistrates grades II and III; the
applicable Rules are set out in schedule 3 of MCA.
The entire proceedings were a nullity, and the property was to be
restored to the rightful owner pending the outcome of property filed suit.
Barugare Vs. Attorney General.
Framing issues - whether court is bound and restricted to
counsel's agreed issues.
Held: Court is not bound and restricted to counsel's agreed issues.
The photocopies were secondary evidence and inadmissible under s.63
of the evidence Act be presumed.
A bill of lading made to order of 2 persons does not establish sole
ownership of either.
Esero Bukenya Vs. Administrator General.
Court vacation - Application for temporary injunction - respondent
disposing off subject matter of suit - whether urgent matter.
Held: The disposal of the cattle amounted to defeat of the suit, and was
an urgent matter, and a proper one to be heard during Court vacation.
Disputed property is not part of the estate of a deceased, and did not
vest in the administrator of the estate.
In re Dr.John Chrisestom Kiyimba Katto.
Review under O.42 .7.1
The application to come before the judge who made the order it is
sought to review.
Held: Under O.42 r.1, the application for review should come before the
very judge who made the order it is sought to review.
Lusiano Lippi Vs. Venice (u) Ltd.
Service of summons affidavit to show that a copy of plaint and
affidavit in support were served with summons.
Triable issue - suit for debt - part of it repaid to shareholder in the
plaintiff company - triable issue disclosed.
Held: The affidavit of service must show whether a copy of the plaint and
supporting affidavit were served.  The time of services was immaterial
in the circumstances in that the exparte judgment was entered much
later after expiry of the prescribed period.
That the applicant has effected part payment of the debt disclosed a
triable issue.
Uganda Commercial Bank Vs. Akamba (u) Ltd.
Discovery - Agreement in possession of defendant court
empowered under O.10 r.14 to order production.
Held: To use r.14, there had to be proceedings pending.  Proceedings
included actions and matters.  An application to join another defendant
was a matter.  Also court was empowered to order the production of
the document.
R.14 referred to production in court and was narrower than r.12 and 13
which concern discovery before hearing commences.
Lawrence Musiitwa Kyazze Vs. Eunice Busingye.
Application for stay of execution - whether the supreme court has
jurisdiction to entertain it before the High Court has done so.
Held: The Supreme Court would prefer the High Court to deal with the
application for stay on the its merits first, before the application is made
to the Supreme Court.  However, if the High Court refuses to accept
jurisdiction or refuses jurisdiction for manifestly wrong reasons, or
there is great delay, the Supreme Court may intervene and accept
jurisdiction in the interests of justice.
The Supreme Court may in special and probably rare cases entertain an
application for a stay before the High Court has refused a stay, in the
interests of justice to the parties.  The court can so act only after it has
been apprised of all facts.
Francis Nansio Micar Vs. Nuwa Walakira.
Stay of execution - whether the High Court has power to stay it's
own decree.
Held: Though there is no specific provision in the Civil Procedure Rules
enabling the High Court to grant a stay of execution against its decree
pending an appeal the court has inherent jurisdiction to grant such stay
under Section 101 of the Civil Procedure Act.  The Supreme Court also
has similar jurisdiction under the Court of Appeal Rules.  Since both the
High Court and the Supreme Court have the jurisdiction to grant such
stay, it is always desirable that applications first be made in the High
Court, but direct applications can still be entertained by the Supreme
Court in exceptional cases.
Though the Court of Appeal Rules provide that the address for service
upon the respondent should be stated upon the Notice of Appeal the
requirement is a matter of good administration rather than a fundamental
necessity, and failure to observe it does not render the notice invalid.
Shiv Construction Co. Ltd Vs. Endesha Enterprises.
Appeal - extension of time to lodge a notice of appeal- whether
where there is no in ordinate delay the merits of the appeal are
relevant court's considering to extend or otherwise the time within
which to lodge an appeal.
Held: The delay through Counsel's absence would be a ground upon
which court would allow an extension on time for the applicant to file a
notice of appeal.
If the delay is quite short as in this case, the merits of the appeal do
not arise, if it is the ordinary type of appeal like this one to be argued on
the merits.
Attorney General Vs. Oriental construction Co. Ltd.
Appeal - extension of time within which to appeal - whether the
public importance of the appeal was sufficient ground for which
to allow an extension of time within which to file a notice of appeal.
Held: the failure by the learned State Attorney in informing the Attorney
General that Government had lost the suit which the applicant sought to
appeal against was no ground to have the time within which to file notice
of appeal extended because neither bad faith nor fraud had been alleged
and proved on the part of the State Attorney.
The disputed contract was of public importance because it was entered
into by or on behalf of the former East African Community and the
Uganda Government inherited this contract along with other assets and
liabilities of the defunct Community.  The obligation to pay under this
contract was a part of the public responsibilities of the Government.
The Uganda citizenry would legitimately be concerned with the payment
of such a large sum of money in foreign currency.  The applicant had
proved a ground of public importance for which extension of time in
which to file a notice of appeal out of time be allowed.
Attorney General Vs. N.M.Huda & ors.
Appeal - extension of time within which to appeal - whether
sufficient cause shown.
Held: In order that the Supreme Court may extend the time within
which to file a notice of time sufficient cause relating to the applicant's
inability or failure to take a particular step must be shown.  In the
instance case the applicant's lack of stationary, the length and
complexity of the judgment sought to be appealed from, all these were
irrelevant to the issue of the applicant's inability or failure to file a notice
of appeal in time, because the filing of the notice of appeal did not
require al or any of the above.
The applicant's submission that the appeal was of paramount importance
would not be the basis for the extension of time because sufficient
cause had not been shown for the delay or failure.
The High Court had jurisdiction to entertain an application for extension
of the time to file a Notice of Appeal under s.37 of the Judicature Act
1967, where an appeal was from its judgments.  Therefore the Supreme
Court had concurrent jurisdiction with the High Court on this matter as
provided by Rule 4 of the Court of Appeal for East African Rules.
Matendegyere & ors Vs. Y.Kasikura & ors.
Appeals - third appeals - whether the Supreme Court has
jurisdiction to entertain a third appeal.
Held: S.74 of the Civil Procedure Act provides the grounds upon which
second appeals may be lodged.  Ss. 75 and 76 of the Act state that no
appeal shall lie except on grounds expressed in s.74.  This logically
means that the legislature never intended third appeals because no
provisions therefore were made.  This invariably means that the
Supreme Court has to jurisdiction to entertain a third appeal.
Hannington Wasswa & anor Vs. Maria Ochola & ors.
Appeals - time within which to appeal - failure to file an appeal
after the elapse of 60 days from the receipt of record of
proceedings - whether therefore notice of appeal should be struck
off the record under rules 80 and 81 of the East African Court of
Appeal Rules.
Held: Under R.80(1) of the Rules of this Court, the appeal should have
been filed within 60 days from the date of receipt of the proceedings.
A person on whom a notice of appeal has been served is entitled under
rule 80 of the same rules to apply to this court to strike off the notice
of appeal on the ground that some essential step in the proceedings
has not been taken within the prescribed period.  The failure to file the
appeal within the prescribed 60 days from the date of receipt of the
record of proceedings was sufficient ground to have the notice of appeal
struck off.
Atulkumar Patel Vs. American International Banking Corp.
Further security for costs - whether sufficient grounds adduced
for the order for further security for costs.
Held: Mr. Patel had shown good cause why he should have further
security for costs and security for past costs.  The fact that the
respondent corporation had no known assets in Uganda and was foreign
compounded by the fact that the sums earlier deposited had been made
adequate by the subsequent currency reform grounds for court to order a
further security for costs were established.  Moreover counsel for the
respondent corporation had canceled that a lot more work was still
pending for the appeal which would invariably cause the bill for further
costs to go up.
Barclays Bank (U) Ltd Vs. Eddy Rodgrigues.
Additional evidence from lower court sought to be added on record
appeal - whether it is supplementary record.
Held: A supplementary record is a record of any further documents or
additional parts of documents which may be required for determination
of the appeal.  A supplementary record merely supplements a defective
or insufficient original record of appeal and is not itself a basic
document required for the original record of appeal.  The record sought
to be added was one of the documents put in evidence at the hearing in
the lower court.
The only way to introduce such a document to the appeal proceedings
is by way of supplementary records under rule 89 of the Court of Appeal
Rules.
The notice of appeal was fled out of time by one day.  Since no leave to
extend time within which to appeal was granted, the appeal was
incompetent.
The appellant failed to extract and file both the order appealed against
and the order granting leave to appeal.  It is settled law that no appeal
lies to this court until the decree or order appealed from has been
extracted.
Livingstone Sewanyana Vs. Martin Aliker.
Inherent jurisdiction of Supreme Court - whether Supreme Court
has jurisdiction to set aside it's own judgment on the basis of
new evidence alleging fraud.
Held: The Supreme Court as par rule 1(3) of the RSC is empowered to
prevent a miscarriage of justice and abuse of court process.  This
means that a judgment based on ground would invariably be set aside
and an order for setting aside the judgment in the High Court would
follow with a further order for a new trial.  In the alternative under Rule
1(3) of the said rules the applicant may be ordered to take fresh
proceedings in the High Court to prove the alleged fraud.  Therefore the
Supreme Court has jurisdiction to do so.
The court would not order a retrial, nor the setting aside either or its
judgment on appeal or the High Court judgment because the applicant
had not established that a fraud had in fact been omitted.
The proper procedure open to the applicant since he had failed to
establish before the supreme court that fraud had been omitted, was to
bring a fresh suit in the High Court to challenge its judgment alleging
and providing fraud.  The shorter way of proceeding namely by motion
was not open to the applicant in this case.
Roza Muwangala Vs. Roza Nabirye
Appeals - second appeal - inconsistency of evidence - ground
succeeds.
Held: A ground of inconsistency of evidence on a second appeal
succeeds.
The procedure at the locus in quo is that parties and witnesses should
be present, and the evidence taken there together with any other
observations by Court should be written as part of the court record.
A certificate of title is conclusive proof of title, but may impeached for
for fraud.  When issued in the course of proceedings they should cease
unless to prove fraud in another suit.
Christopher Katuramu Vs. Maliya and others.
Counter claim - heading - counter claim must have a heading like
in the plaint.
Held: O.8 r.8 CPR is mandatory, and the counter claim should be
headed like in the plaint.  A further title should be added to the defence.
Estoppel applies where Counsel admits replying to the disputed
pleading.
No action is filed unless the court fees is paid, but the registry staff's
fault is not appropriately recording payment should not be paid against
parties.  Registry staff may be called as witnesses to prove payment.
Eridadi Otabong Waimo Vs. Attorney General.
Limitation - exemption therefrom on grounds of disability -
mandatory to specifically plead the exemption and disability.
Held: Torts of unlawful detention were severable.  Time for unlawful
detention begun to run upon release, for the tort was a continuous tort.
A party can sue on much of this as happened within the time limit.
Where a plaint is filed out of time, the exemption on ground of disability
must be specifically pleaded.  If it is not, the plaint should be rejected.
Ismail Dabul Vs. Mrs.Georgia Pankelakis.
Retrial - best evidence i.e of vital witness not called - advocate
was supposed to be witness - fresh evidence discovered retrial to
be ordered.
Held: The case should be referred back to the High Court for retrial.
Adonia Nakudi Vs. Christ K.Mukasa.
Appeals - grounds of appeal - rules for framing grounds of appeal-
argumentative ground - improper - grounds to be concise.
Held: The appellant Court can on its own motion consider a point of law
which is not argued by Counsel.
The amendment was improper, and the proceedings were incurably
defective and there would be a retrial.
Grounds of appeal should be framed concisely, and should not be
argumentative.
Attorney General Vs. Silver Springs Hotel Ltd & others.
Injunctions - Injunctions against government - not available under
the law of Uganda, both temporary and permanent.
Held: The Cardinal rules of Statutory Interpretation in this matter were -
a specific legislation is not repealed by a general legislation which does
not specifically so state and where no necessary implication can be
drawn.
Subsequent legislation does not repeal an earlier legislation without
explicitly stating so and where no necessary implications can be drawn.
Where the two statutes are consistent, no intention of repeal should be
drawn.
Government is not bound by statutes which do not clearly say so.
An injunction (temporary or permanent) cannot lie against Government
under the laws of Uganda.  The rationale is that the Government
machinery should not be brought to a halt, and it should not be
subjected to embarrassment.
An amices curiae is invited by Court and he should be a person without
interest in the case.  Mr. Kayondo was not invited, and was an
interested party who therefore did not qualify.
Christopher Sebuliba Vs. Attorney General.
Vicarious liability - ministry of defence personnel - whether
Government liable vicariously.
Held: This was a case of holding over and the appellant was entitled to
be paid rent.  The rent should reflect the market rental.
The Defence Ministry was liable for the acts of the army me.  This made
Government vicariously liable, and the proper defendant was the
Attorney General.
An eviction order against Government or its officers is prohibited by
S.15 of the Government Proceedings Act.
However, the protection afforded Government can be waived (per PLATT,
JSC) (Monitory view).
Mugenyi & Company Advocates Vs. National Insurance
Corporation.
Stay of execution - appeal to Court of Appeal from High Court
order - execution for costs in underlying useful purpose to be
served stay discharged.
Held: The High Court has inherent power to stay its order including
those for execution, irrespective of whether there is an appeal to the
Court of Appeal.  The Court of Appeal can order a stay in exercise of the
jurisdiction exercised by the High Court.
an order for a stay of execution must serve a useful purpose.
Letithian Megembe Vs. Uganda Electricity Board.
Enlargement of time to file to defence - defaulting person
secretary of corporation -distinction drawn between him and other
defendants.
Held: Corporation Secretaries have multifarious duties, and should be
treated differently from other defaulters, but the discretion must be
exercised judicially.
The proposed defence should be shown where a good defence is reason
for seeking the enlargement.
No "sufficient cause" is required under O.47 r.6 which is therefore wider
than O.9 r.24.
John Ntambi Vs. Attorney General & Board of Governors of ST.
Mary College Kisubi.
Pleadings - amendment of pleadings - oral application - proper.
Held: An oral application is proper for O.6 r.30 only provided for
interlocutory applications without being exclusive.
The principle governing amendments before the hearing is that they
should be freely allowed if no injustice is caused to the other party.
No injustice arises if costs is adequate compensation.
An amendment of the plaint which does not disclose a cause of action
against a defendant is unjust and should not be allowed.
Rose Nabirye Vs. Rose Muwangala.
Appeal - delay within which to appeal caused by the applicants
misunderstanding of judgments - whether extension of time
within which to appeal is justifiable.
Held: It would be denial of justice under the given circumstances not to
extend the time in favor of the applicant.
Rhoda Kalema Vs. Departed Asians Property Custodian Board.
Withdrawal of suit application to withdraw pending suit - whether
it is necessary to adopt court procedure.
Held: After the defendants/respondents had surrendered management
of the subject matter of the suit to the plaintiff it was unnecessary for the
plaintiff to adopt the most expensive and even lengthy procedure of
discontinuing the suit.  Instead of involving court in the process it
would have been sufficient for counsel for the applicant to write the
Registrar withdrawing the suit, with a copy to counsel for the
respondent. Alternatively counsel for the applicant could have notified
Counsel for the respondent with a copy of the withdrawal to the
Registrar.
Since it was apparent that Counsel for the applicant adopted a procedure
that put the opposite party to avoidable expenses, the costs for
withdrawing the suit would be payable to the defendant/respondent.
Magem Enterprises Ltd Vs. Uganda Breweries Ltd
Whether section 101 of the civil procedure Act applies where
there are specific provision applicable.
Held: There would be no conflict of roles for a Principal Judge to
entertain the application as he was neither biased nor interested in the
case nor did he personally allocated the hearing of the case to himself.
Section 101 of the Civil Procedure Act has no place in the application
as there were specific provisions applicable to the situation.
It is possible and proper to apply for setting aside and staying of
execution in one application demand.  After entering the interlocutory
judgment, the case should have been set down for formal proof, albeit
in an ex parte manner.
The case raises a triable issue regarding the two conflicting amounts of
money due to the plaintiff/respondent which is a factor justifying the
setting aside of the judgment and the staying of the execution.
David Sejjaka Nalima Vs. Rebecca Musoke.
Appeals issue in trial court not answered - first appellate court
can assess evidence and answer it.
Held: A later Statute on a specific matter modified an earlier general
statute.  The RTA was enacted in 1922, later than the Succession Act
which was enacted in 1906.  The former deals with the specific matter
of the registered land, whereas the latter is on the general matter of
succession to moveable and immovable property.  The RTA therefore
modified the Succession Act.
A bonafide purchaser for value is one without notice of fraud.  The
appellant was not one because he had the imputed fraud from his above
and avoid discovering who the rightful owner was.
Francis Butagira Vs. Deborah Namukasa.
General prayer - whether relief against forfeiture should not be
granted because of not having been specifically prayed for.
Costs - whether refusal to award costs against forfeiture was
proper.
Held: S.22(5) (c) of the Public Lands Act 1969 does not contain an
absolute prohibition against the controlling authority.  This means
therefore that failure to obtain consent of the controlling authority only
renders the lease avoidable at the instance of the controlling authority.
The learned trial Judge therefore erred in holding that absence of
consent made the transfer null and void.
Under the Public Land Act, the lesser is the controlling authority and it
is the only authority that can enforce the covenant against subletting
and not the landlord.  The respondent did not have power to enforce the
obligations of the controlling authority under s.22 (5) of the Public Land
Act.
The Landlord/respondent/lessor was not the controlling authority,
because the term controlling authority was defined in s.54 of the Public
Lands Acts to mean in relating to lands vested in freehold, the
commission, I.e. the Uganda Land Commission.
Though it would have been better had the appellant prayed specifically
for relief against forfeiture, such relief would nevertheless be considered
under the general payee for further or other relief more so that the
issue of relief against forfeiture had been canvassed at the trial.
A lessee according to S.24 of the Judicature Act, may by his own
action pray for relief against forfeiture had been canvassed at the trial.
It is trite Law that the proviso for re-entry on no-payment of rent is
regarded in equity as merely a security for rent and therefore provided
the lessor can be put in the same position as before, the lessee is
entitled to relief against forfeiture.  The fact that the appellant had
acted high handedly is an extraneous matters when considering prayer
for relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent.
The period of seven years during which the appellant failed/refused to
pay rent was a period long enough to show the appellant's callous
disregard of his obligations as a lessee.  Though he assumed there was
no lessor, who the lessor could be nor did he pay the rent upon the
discovery that the respondent was the lessor.  This was however not
enough to be the basis of the refusal to grant relief against forfeiture.
Equity would intervene to grant relief against forfeiture where the lessee
would suffer serious personal consequences if he lost the land.  The
fact that the property to be lost was very valuable was not in itself
evidence of serious personal consequences.
Bona vacancies is where there was no one claiming an interest in the
property.  It is when a person dies intestate without leaving anybody to
claim an interest in the property, in which case such property would
belong to the state.  In the instant case the respondent was executrix
of the will of the original freeholder and according to S.143 of the
Succession Act her acquisition of the title to the property was deemed
to have issued at the demise of the testator.  Therefore, the appellant
could not claim that at the time he sub-let the property it was bona
vacantia.
In the head lease operating between the appellant and the respondent
not to sublet the property without the consent of the lessor.  Therefore
the appellant breached the covenant against subletting and there was
no excuse in doing so.  The appellant could not under S.24 of the
Judicature Act be aided under S.32 of the Public Lands Act which deals
with relief against forfeiture for breach of covenant if the controlling
authority has re-entered the land.
The Learned Trial Judge erred in depriving the respondent who acted
who was the successful party of her costs without good cause.  It was
not only the respondent who acted unreasonably before the institution
of the proceedings but also he appellant.  It could therefore not be said
that it is only the respondent who was guilty of misconduct or whose
conduct might have been averted.  Secondly the respondent was
entitled to re-enter the premises upon the appellant's breach of
covenants in the lease and the appellant cannot complain that it is the
conduct of the respondent that led to this litigation.  This means that
the trial Judge exercised his discretion on wrong principles in refusing to
award the respondent her costs and this Court was therefore entitled to
interfere.
Since the appellant's suit against the respondent was not based on
trespass but on breach of covenant for quiet enjoyment, the point
whether a tenant can sue his Landlord in trespass need not be decided
in the instant case.
Samuel Dheyongera Vs. Charles Mutyabule
Pleadings - material particulars - whether failure to plead that a
car over turned as a material particular renders the pleadings.
Held: Material facts must be pleaded and a plaint failing to do so must
be struck out but failure to plead material particulars may still leave the
Court with the discretion in the matter to adjudicate on it.  The fact of
the overturning of the car was a material particular and the trial judge
decided the case against the appellant on the balance of probabilities
after considering all the evidence.
Katalemwa Traders Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Appeals - whether ground unsustainable for being general.
Held: An advertisement calling for tenders is not an offer but an invitation
to treat or offer.
Where parties agree that they shall subsequent to their negotiations
reduce their agreement into a formal document, their antecedent
negotiation may nevertheless amount to a valid and binding contract
notwithstanding that no such formal document has been drawn up after
all, if, such negotiations in themselves, whether oral or in writing can
clearly indicate the existence of a definite acceptance of all terms of
an offer and the acceptance is unqualified.  Since the appellant did not
produce in evidence a copy of the advertisement, a copy of the letter of
offer, and there was no evidence of what kind of electrical equipment
the purpose, the quantities, and the price, the subsequent offer thereby
vague, indefinite, and incapable of identification, and there was therefore
no binding agreement.
Grounds 3 + 5 were unsustainable for offending against Rule 84 (1) of
the Rules of Supreme Court for being too general.  The Rules require
the memorandum of appeal to particularize matters complained of and
and appellant represented by counsel may not be allowed to argue a
general ground of appeal.
The alternative argument by the appellant for a separate contract outside
the tender agreement amounted to the alteration of the appellant's case
as pleaded in the lower Court and this was unsustainable.  This was not
an instance for court to exercise its discretion to allow a new matter to
be argued before it.
Esso Standard (u) Ltd Vs. Mike N. Nabudere.
Conversion - whether when given facts disclose both an offence
and a civil wrong criminal proceedings should take precedence.
Held: The plaintiff petroleum company did not seek compromise with t
the defendant to the prejudice of public justice because his demand
for damages in the civil court did not in any way prejudice the criminal
proceedings in the criminal court.  There was no justification in the
plaintiff's action being stayed pending determination of the criminal
case because the plaintiff had not compromised with the defendant to
flout the criminal case.
Secondly the plaintiff was only to prove his case on the balance of
probability and the resultant judgment had no evidencible value in the
prosecution of the defendant, since then, proof beyond reasonable
doubt was required.  Therefore it was not necessary to stay the civil
case.
Thirdly, the present circumstances in Uganda were such that the police
were taking several months and years before investigations are compete.
This should therefore not be the basis of action against the completion
of criminal proceedings as it would defeat justice.
Since the abolition of the distinction between a felony and a
misdemearnour by the Criminal law Act 1967 of England, a defendant
could now be sued for an act that was both civil and criminal, for
damages, even before criminal prosecution has taken place.  The old
common law principle was no longer applicable in England.  That
principle should no longer be applicable in Uganda as well.
Attorney General Vs. Oriental Construction Co. Ltd.
Appeals - whether grounds of appeal should be struck out for
raising new issues of fact and law not considered in the lower
court, or they should be argue in view of the public importance of
the matter.
Held: Grounds sought to prove whether there was a subsisting contract
or otherwise would not be allowed because the defendant/appellant not
admitted the contract and liability hereunder the only sought to
contest the extent of the liability, in the lower Court.
Ground three of the appeal was sustainable since it sought to contest
the extent of the liability defence had stated to do at the trial.  Even if
it were to be said that ground three raised new issues it would still be
considered in view of the that that payment out of public funds is
exceptional treatment.
Oriental Construction Co. Vs. Attorney General.
Jurisdiction - execution - stay of execution. Pending abroad in
England - Uganda High Court cannot directly order it's stay.
Held: There was no jurisdiction to order a stay of execution of judgment
registered in England.  The applicant could resort to the reciprocal
enforcement.
The court, however, had jurisdiction to order a stay in Uganda pending
judgment in the appeal before the Supreme Court.
Fida Birabwa Vs. Sulaiman Tigawalana.
Application for leave to appeal based on grounds that the R.C
courts did not properly conduct proceedings - whether it is a
substantial point of law requiring consideration by a higher court.
Held: The question "whether the RC II Court properly exercised its
jurisdiction and whether the RC III Court was properly constituted" is
a substantial point of law requiring consideration by a higher Court.
Ibrahim Juma Vs. Donasiano Nyeko.
Revision - application for revision - respondent absent - application
can be heard.
Held: The application could proceed under O.9 r.17 CPR.
A decision of a chief Magistrate exercising appellate Jurisdiction is
subject to revision under s.83 of the CPA.
T.M.K Vs. Jack Businge & 2 others.
Application for stay of execution made before any party has applied
for execution whether application is premature.
Held: Though there are no provisions in the laws that expressly
authorize institution of applications for stay of execution before an
application for execution is made, there appears to be nothing
inherently irregular in applying for stay of execution where justifiable
circumstance exist.  The application for stay of execution was therefore
not prematurely made.
Selestine Lwanga Vs. Stephen Baitwababo.
Suit not prosecuted due to mistaken impression regarding time of
hearing on the part of counsel - whether sufficient cause to justify
it's reinstatement.
Held: In absence for contrary evidence, counsels non appearance
caused by mistake regarding time of hearing of suit it sufficient cause
to justify its reinstatement where it has been set aside for lack of
prosecution.
A suit is interpreted under section 2 of the Civil Procedure Act (Cap.65)
as meaning all civil proceedings commencing in any manner prescribed.
An application by Notice of motion is for purposes of the Civil procedure
Act a civil suit.
Edward Frederick Sempebwa Vs. Attorney General.
Constitutional court - whether the court that makes the reference
may as well sit as a constitutional court.
Held: it was not settled whether the court that makes the reference of
matters to the Constitutional Court should as well act as the
constitutional court to decide on the substantive matters thereby referred.
There is no laid down procedure as to how the questions framed by the
Court for reference may be brought before the constitutional court.
Neither of the respondents did not contest the method used, i.e., the
notice of motion however.
On or about the 26th day of January 1986 an armed group known as the
National Resistance Army entered Kampala the capital of Uganda and
by force of arms took its control and seized the reigns of power.
Therefore, this amounted in law to a successful revolution through extra-
constitutional means, and that the proclamation (LN 1/86) establishes
a new legal order, in accordance with which the validity of laws in
Uganda has to be determined.
The authorities that made the successful revolution set up conditions for
the basis of the new legal order, and spelt these conditions in Legal
Notice No.1 of 1986 and the saved provisions of the 1967 constitution.
Once this was done, the authorities were precluded from departing from
these conditions and any subsequent legislation by them was to be in
conformity therewith, or otherwise legislative framework.  Therefore the
validity or otherwise of Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 must be viewed within
the perimeters of the legal order already in place.
Since Legal Notice no.6 of 1986 was a proclamation and not a decree
promulgated by the National Resistance Council as required by Legal
Notice No.1 of 1986, and since the proclamation was not signed by the
President of Uganda but by the Chairman of the National Resistance
Council who was also president of Uganda meant that the Legal Notice
was made not in accordance with the rules already laid down.
Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 would be declared invalid because it was not
made in accordance with the Legal Legislation framework put in place
by the revolution.  The court's pronouncement of invalidation would be
necessary to avoid uncertainty in legislation and cause government to
follow the rule of law in exercising legislative powers and others and
moreover the declaration would not prejudice the security of the state
and that the situation would easily be corrected retrospectively by the
state putting in place the right legislation in accordance with the law.
Shah's case set a precedent and defined a judgment debt/decree to be
property protected by the constitution and this precedent would be
followed since the court in the instant caser is of co-ordinate jurisdiction
with the court in Shah's case which was a court of first instance on the
issue of judgment debt being property protected by the first instance
should as a matter of judicial comity follow the decision of another
judge of first instance unless he is convinced that the judgment was
wrong.  The view of the Court is that the decision in Shah's case was
correct and should apply to the instant case.
Since the applicant's judgment debt is property protected by the
constitution, para 12(2) of Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 conflicted with and
infringed upon the constitutional rights of the applicant and consequently
that paragraph cannot be valid unless article 8 (2) (c ) and 13 of the
constitution are repealed or modified by paragraph 13 of Legal Notice
No.6 of 1986.  But paragraph 13 does not expressly repeal the said
articles, let alone its being retrospective.  The cardinal principles of
Statutory Interpretation require that legislation that infringes upon
constitutional rights must expressly state so.
Edward Frederick Sempebwa Vs. Attorney General.
Amicus curria e - whether conditions for inviting an anicus curiae
to court, satisfied.
Held: Amicus curiae is a person who calls the attention of the court to
some point of law or fact which would appear to have been over looked,
or a member of the bar not engaged in a case or bystander who calls
the attention of the court to some decision reported or unreported which
would appear to have been over looked.  Since Mr. Kayondo had not
pointed out what point of law was over looked inspite of his credentials
in support of his suitability to be invited as a friend of the court, at that
stage of the proceeding there was no threat to over look fact or law,
since the parties were very ably represented.
Edward Frederick Sempebwa Vs. Attorney General.
Reference to a constitutional court - whether by appeal against the
ruling of the court of the single judge refusing to make the
reference.
Held: When the application pointed out that S.12(1) of the legal Notice
No.6 of 1986 was unconstitutional and should not be given any force of
law, at that point, the issue before the court was transformed into a
question of interpretation of the Constitution under Art 87 (1) and S.19(1)
and 92) of the Act.  Here a doubt or dispute had arisen as to whether
the matter should go to a constitutional court and the application was
for the determination of this doubt.  The determination by the single
judge aggrieved the applicant because his application to refer the matter
to the constitutional court was refused.  That is why the same matter
was referred to a court of three judges as required by S.19(5) of the Act.
Therefore the applicants' application was properly before the court.
Charles Mpiima Vs. Attorney General.
Pleading limitation - whether must be in WSD.
Plaint - whether severable.
Held: The torts of assault/battery and wrongful imprisonment were
time barred.
The plaintiff was released on bail and a pending criminal charge was not
a disability.
Limitation does not have to be pleaded.  Court can in its discretion take
cognizance of the fact of limitation.
A plaint is severable where the causes of action are different in duration
and nature, as in this case.
Jack Wamanga Wamayi Vs. Interfreight Forwarders (u) Ltd.
Amendment - paragraph substratum of plaint and it's amendment would
cause amendment of others - whether it's amendment permissible.
Held: Court had discretion to allow amendments at any stage of the
proceedings provided no injustice is caused to the other side.
There is no injustice caused if costs is adequate solace, and there are
hardly situation where it is not.
Kabaseke Stores Company Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Pleading - issues of fact not arising out of the pleading - whether
admissible.
Held: The negotiations did not conclude a contract.
The LPO was the offer which was accepted and the contract was
performed the very day be delivery of the beans.
The LPO and delivery note constituted a written contract.
An unpaid seller is entitled under s.49(9) of the Sale of Goods Act to
recover the price.
O.6, r5 CPR renders issued of fact not arising out of the pleadings
inadmissible.
The Omnibus traverse did not include the defence of part payment.
In a contractual breach, a party is entitled to only foreseeable loss.
Expected profit is recoverable as foreseeable loss.
Ben Kiwanuka Vs. Haji Nurdin Matovu.
Extension of time - certified copy of record of appeal provided by
Registrar - discovered record lacked decree at preliminary
objection at hearing - mistake of registrar and counsel who filed
the appeal - intended appellant vigilant and innocent - whether
sufficient reason.
Held: The test is - was there a failure to appreciate the legal necessity
for getting the decree or was it a lack of diligence in seeing that it was
done in time?  Here it was neither but rather a failure to realize that the
record as obtained from the Deputy Registrar contained no decree.
Sufficient cause had been shown.
NOTCO Ltd Vs. Hope Nyakairu.
