Temporary Injunction - propose and conditions ownership of a plot
land was subject of the suit. The defendant was carrying thereon
constructions to meet the condition of development - within - 5
years. The plaintiff sought a temporary injunction to restrain the
defendant's construction.
Held: The purpose of a temporary injunction is to preserve the status quo.
It will issue when there is evidence of likelihood of causing irrespirable
damage to the subject matter that is, a damage/injury substantial or
incapable of remedy or atonement in damages; and a probability of
succeeding in the main suit; and the claim in the suit; and the claim in
the suit is not or vexatious or illegal.
The defendant stood to lose the plot if she failed to meet the
development condition, whereas the applicant could obtain an order to
demolish the structure and remove the debris.
James Fredrick Pool Nsubuga Vs. Attorney General.
Pleading - defence not pleaded in WSD - in admissible.
Amendment - sought after close of examination of witnesses for
plaintiff-whether permissible.
Subject matter petroleum products whose prices increased due to
Gulf War-whether amendment to cater for increase permissible.
Held: A defence not pleaded in the WSD is inadmissible.
Amendment is allowed any time before judgment to resolve the real
issues in controversy provided no injustice is caused to the other party,
and an amendment to reflect the increase in fuel prices due t o the Gulf
war was proper.
Without a relevant warrant, an arrest or search is unlawful within the
provisions of ss.20 and 28 of the CPC unless it is arrest for a cognizable
offence or felony committed in the presence of the arresting person.
The soldiers were acting in the course of their duties, and the defendant
was vicariously liable.
Minor contradictions caused by lapse of time can be ignored in proof of
specific damages but cogent evidence, though not a bank statement is
required to prove the items.
General damages are within court's discretion, and are awarded to put
the plaintiff in the position before the wrong.
Considering the plaintiff's status period spent in custody manner of
treatment and inflation 40,000-is fair.
J.K. Patel Vs. Speak Motor Ltd.
Pleading - defence not pleaded but adduced evidence and not
cross - examined upon - whether implicitly admitted.
Held: There was an enforceable contract.
The onus was on the defendant to prove payment.  It is difficult to prove
a negative.
There was implicit admission of the defence of part-payment.
For equivalents or foreign currency, the operative rate is the Bank of
Uganda exchange rate.
A successful party should be awarded costs if not the reasons must be
stated and the discretion exercised judicially.
The Attorney General Vs. Oriental Construction Co. Ltd.
Extension of time - delay of about 14 months obscure reasons -
whether sufficient cause shown - matter of public importance -
Government to pay a large sum of money - whether if so facts
matter of public importance.
Held: In an application under N.4 of E.A.C.A. Rules the delay and
reason for the delay must be set out.
Short delays caused understandable lapse of human fallibility may be
excusable, but long delays attract careful scrutiny.  Here, no sufficient
reason was shown.
Payment of a large sum of money is not a matter of public importance,
though it may be of importance to the parties themselves.
Fida Birabwa Vs. Sulaiman Tigawalana.
Application for leave to appeal based on grounds that the R.C
Courts did not properly conduct proceedings - whether it is a
substantial point of law requiring consideration by a higher court.
Held:  The question "whether the RC II Court properly exercised its
jurisdiction and whether the RC III Court was properly constituted" is a
substantial point of law requiring consideration by a higher court.
Richard Kaijuka Vs. Teddy Ssezi Cheeye & 2 others.
Verbal application to stay civil proceedings pending determination
of a criminal suit based on the same facts - whether it is a legally
correct form of application.
Held: The verbal application is procedurally wrong for want of form and it
takes the other side by surprise.  There are express provisions in order
48 rule 1 of the civil procedure Rules dealing with such a situation which
require such as application to be made formally and to be supported by
an affidavit.
Ntege Mayambala Vs. Christopher Mwanje.
Stay of execution pending on grounds that if payment on effected
it may be difficult to recover them in the event of a successful
appeal - whether sufficient cause to stay the execution.
Payment of security by judgment debtor for due performance of decree-
whether advocates are exempted.
Held: The ground that if payments are effected by the applicant before
the appeal it may be difficult to recover them in the event of a success-
full appeal is a relevant ground which amounts to sufficient cause to
stay the execution.
All the three conditions laid down in Order 39 rule 4(3) must be fulfilled
before an execution can be stayed, namely that the application was
made without unreasonable delay that substantial loss may result to the
applicant if the application is not granted and that security has been
given by the applicant for due performance.  The applicant is an
Advocate of the High Court, he cannot be exempted from payment of
security.  The reasons for payment of security is to maintain status Quo
among the parties to ascertain that the purpose of the application is
not merely to defeat the course of justice by delaying tactics and to
prove that the judgment debtor is serious with his application for stay
for execution.
John Okello Vs. Mulodokanyi Mudukany & Ereneti Serubugo.
Application to set a side exparte judgment due to non service -
affidavit in support of application not sworn by the person who
effected service - whether such affidavit is of use to court.
Application to set aside exparte judgment due to FACT THAT
THERE is a good defence - whether setting a side is justifiable
where applicant does not reveal the nature of the defence.
Held: The affidavit sworn by the person other than the one who was
engaged in serving/as the service of summons to enter appearance
upon the applicant is concerned.  It is the person who served the
applicant who should have sworn the affidavit indicating what effort he
made to indicate the nature of the defence the fact that the subject
matter of the suit is a piece of land in Kampala which is a big fortune
demanded that the exparte judgment be set aside and each party be
given a change is hear say and of no use to the court in as far to state
his case before depriving any party of it.
Shaftsbury International Freight & Transport Vs. Andrew T.
The issue of fees regarding transportation of goods - whether it is
of commercial importance to warrant determination on merit and
justify an application to set a side an exparte judgment.
Held: The issue of fees regarding transportation of goods is not a point
of cardinal legal or commercial importance to justify setting aside an
aparte judgment.
The fact that the applicant challenged the jurisdiction of court to
entertain the suit presupposes that he was served and thus contradicts
his claim that he was not.  The procedure to be adopted when
challenging court jurisdiction should be to enter an appearance and then
challenge the jurisdiction of court in the written statement of defence.
The challenge of jurisdiction by Notice of motion was therefore improper.
1.Management Committee Mengo Primary School
2. Executive Committee of PTA of Mengo Primary School
3. Teachers of Mengo Primary School. Vs. Ngabo Newspaper
& 2 others.
Capacity to sue and be sued - whether the management
committee of a Primary School can sue or be sued.
Held: The management committee, a body which governs primary
schools was created by an Act of Parliament and can therefore sue and
be sued.  The parents Teachers Association (PTA) is a body not known
under the law and is therefore not a corporate person to sue or be sued
Since the PTA was not refereed to in the plaint as being defamed, it
had no cause of action.
There is want of form in bringing up the action by the 13 teachers which
though saved by Order 6 rule 16 of the civil procedure rules needs to be
rectified following the correct procedure.
Andrew Lutakome Kayira & Paul Kawanga Semogerere Vs.
Edward Rugumayo,Omwony Ojok, Dr.F.E.Sempebwa & 8 ors.
Further and better particulars - whether further and better
particulars may not be furnished on the ground that the point
pleaded was a point of law.
declaratory judgment -whether the plaintiff had no legal right nor a
tangible benefit to weren't a declaratory.
Capacity to be sued -whether members of the National consultative
Council was not a legal entity capable of being sued.
Held: There was no dispute as to the efficacy of legal Notice N.o.1 of 79
because it was a proclamation by which the new government came into
power.  However legal Notice No.2 as a proclamation purporting to
amend Legal Notice No.1 in substance was of no legal consequence in
as it sought to legislate a function reserved only for the National
consultative council, which was in session at the time the president
issued the said proclamation.  Since Legal Notice No.1 of 1979 did not
suspend article 1 of the Constitution of Uganda, the constitution
remained the supreme Law of Uganda.  Therefore neither the Legal
Notice affected the supremacy of the constitution to the extent of the
non suspended provisions of the constitution.
The National consultative Council was both a legislature and a political
organ of the Uganda National Liberation Front.  As a legislature it could
only be a creature of statute, I.e. Legal Notice No.1 of 1979, which legal
Notice never at all provided the powers and or duties to the National
Consultative Council to ratify Ministerial appointment made by the
President.  It is true that the constitution of the Uganda National
Liberation Front by virtue of Article 5.4. (a) (iv) thereof provided for the
ratification and approval of appointment made by the executive of the
Front to the various organs of the Front.  But this constitution never
become part of the law of Uganda by whichever means.  And the said
provisions only affected the UNLF as an organization and not the
government of Uganda as by law (Legal Notice No.1 of 1979) established.
In deciding whether or not the National consultative council acted legally
in removing the President of the Republic it must be noted that the issue
calls into question the legitimacy or otherwise of the incumbent
government.  The consequences of issuing such a declaration are very
serious.  Court should be reluctant to inquire into questions of a
political nature bearing in mind the gravity of the consequences that
could result from such a declaration.
Under Art.31, of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda the
President may be removed from Office for mental or physical incapacity
to discharge the functions of his office in the manner indicated in Article
31.  All these provisions are contained in chapter 4 of the constitution
of the Republic of Uganda which was suspended under section 1 of the
proclamation in Legal Notice No.1 of 1979, provided that the President
shall be head of state.  Legal Notice No.1 of 1971 is silence as to how
YK Lule became President and is silent as to how he can be removed.
Under the non suspended provisions of the Constitution and Legal
Notice No.1 of 1979 there is no power given to the NCC to remove the
President.  Therefore the NCC had no power to remove the President.
The application for further and better particular would be disallowed
because the applicant did not say what further and better particulars he
required and moreover the defence pleading raised a straight forward
point of law that the action was not maintainable in law.
S. 40 (2) of the Judicature Act, 1967, clearly conferred upon court
original Jurisdiction to the exclusion of all other courts in all matters
concerning the enforcement and or interpretation of the Constitution.
And O.2 r7 of the Civil Procedure Rules provided that no suit shall be
open to objection on grounds that merely a declaratory judgment or
order is sought and the court could make binding declaration whether
any consequential relief is sought nor not.  Moreover, the member of the
National consultative Council are entitled to know whether the actions of
the body of which they are members in a given situation are legal.
Unless a proclamation falls within the provisions of S.14 of the inter-
predation Decree, it is not law but an announcement of the executive
will of the sovereign and in so far as that will have to be obeyed it has
the force of law.  Such a proclamation is not the same thing as a
statutory instrument.
It was not acceptable that the members of the National Consultative
Council could not be sued collectively on the ground that the acts
complained of against them were not committed by them collectively.
The members of the National Consultative Council had no parliamentary
privilege to protect them form suits because Legal Notice No.1 of 79
by which the NCC was created was silent on the question of privilege
when the motion of no confidence in the President was carried.
Eddie Rodrigues Vs. The British High Commission
Jurisdiction - sovereign immunity - whether the British High
Commission could be sued in the Uganda Courts.
Held: If a Government or one of its departments goes into the market
places of the world and engages in straight forward commercial
transactions then it is completely within the territorial jurisdiction of the
courts of the foreign sovereign.  The Sovereign cannot claim immunity
in respect of such transactions.
Posiyano Semakula Vs. Susane Magala & ors.
Res Judicata s.7 CPR - whether a suit for the recovery of land
is res judicata where the defendants are transferees subsequent
to an order in the first suit to transfer land to the plaintiff.
Held: The principle parties involved in the first suit are the same in the
second suit.  The send and third respondents had no independent root
of title to the land except as purchasers and transferees from the first
respondent.  The appellant had no other cause of action as against
them.  This meant that the plaintiff in the second suit was trying to
bring before the court, in another way and in the form of a new cause
of action a transaction which he had already put before a court of
competent jurisdiction in other proceedings.  The suit was thereby
resjudicata.
The judgment tendered constituted estopped by judgment because
counsel for the plaintiff did not object to that procedure and he could
therefore not raise the issue on appeal.  Secondly, the judgment in the
first suit exhaustively discussed the issues pertaining to the ownership
of the suit lands and was thereby sufficient in itself to be relied upon
to constitute estoppel by judgment and or resjudicata.
Moses Katuramu Vs. Attorney General & Uganda Posts &
Telecommunications.
Pleadings - reply - whether a reply to a WSD is part of the plaint
and may cure another wise time barred action.
Limitation - reply to WSD-whether a reply to a WSD is part of the plaint
and may cure otherwise time barred action.
Held: The learned trial judge having considered s.8 (2) of the civil
Procedure Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act 1969 that that section does not
limit the categories of exemption to minority and unsoundness of mind
he should have considered the reasons given in the reply that he was in
prison confinement in conformity with order 7 rule 6 and that within a
year after his confinement he filed action against the respondents in
accordance with s.4 of the same Act.
S.B Kyeswa Vs. Gerald M.Sebunya.
Review under s.83 CPA and O.48 rr 1,2,3 CPR - whether High
Court may review a decision of the magistrates court refusing to
review an order.
Appeal - whether the decision of the Magistrates Court refusing to
review an order may be reviewed by the High Court or appealed against.
Revision under s.84 CP\A - whether the High Court may revise an order
which would otherwise be appealed from.
Held: Order 42 r.7 makes untenable applications for review of Orders or
decrees made on review.  The proper procedure is to appeal against an
order made on review but the applicant would be made to suffer because
of the blunder of his Advocate therefore court would involve its inherent
powers under s.101 of the CPA and proceed under s.84 CPA and make
an order for revision of the magistrate decision.
Uganda National Examination Board Vs. Okello - Okello.
Service Summons on Attorney General-whether validly done where the
registry clerk receives and indorses summons.
Application to vacate judgment and restore appeal as per RSC r99(2)
and 93 (3) - whether tenable.
Held: By virtue of its functions the applicant Uganda National
Examinations Board was a government department since it was an
independent body seeking to observe the Government overall objectives
in Education.  However by its very set up as a corporation sole, the
respondent litigant had a choice whether to sue the Board as an
emanation of the Government or as an independent body.  He chose the
Attorney General was not thereby governed by the Government
proceedings Act but by the Civil Procedure Act and Rules.  This meant
that the endorsement of the hearing Notice by the Attorney General's
registry clerk was sufficient evidence of service.  Therefore the Attorney
General was not prevented from attending court by sufficient cause and
therefore his application to restore the appeal would thereby be refused.
Isaac Bishari Vs. Vitafoam.
Notice of appeal - enlargement of time to serve notice of Appeal -
whether application may be granted.
Held: The applicants previous counsel were guilty of dilatory conduct
which could amount to negligence of his counsel.  And moreover no
injustice would be caused to the respondent in extending the time
within which the applicant should serve the relevant documents to the
respondents.
Yahaya Lukyamuzi & anor Vs. Godfrey Oddy Beijuka.
Injunction O.37 rrl,2 and 9 - whether order thereunder may be
combined with orders for furnishing security for anticipated
decentralism and the attachment of property.
Held: The procedure adopted by the court prejudiced the appellants as
they were denied the opportunity to be heard.  The learned Judge
earned in making the omnibus order that gave three alternative courses
of action in one.  The correct course would have been to issue an order
restraining the appellants from breaching the contract.  If this failed
other alternative orders would follow.
Christopher Kiggundu & anor Vs. Uganda Transport Co.
Written submission under r.97 of the Rules of supreme court -
whether oral submission allowed to supplement thereof.
Held: The provision rendering unnecessary counsel after his
presentment or written submissions was unnecessarily prohibitive
and unjust because court often requires points of clarification or even
further argument.  Court would give leave to counsel for oral submissions.
Loss of earning should be claimed as special damages and be proved
strictly.  In this case the claims were vague and were not proved.
The claim with regard to the watch and shoes had not been proved as
required.  Court was not told what type of watch and  they were
and when he bought hem and for how much but the claim for
sh.200,000/= lost from the person of the first appellant was tenable
because it is a practice in this country for people to strip victims of
accidents of their valuables during the period they are unconscious and
sh. 200,000/= was an amount of that could reasonably be found on the
person, and this loss was a foreseeable consequence of the accident for
which the defendant was liable.
Courts of this country have taken the position that normal working life
expectancy is 50-55 years.  In the instant case the first appellant
clearly sustained a severe disabling injury and the award should have
been shs.10 million. Sh. 2 million should be the award for the fractured
leg of the second appellant.
Robert Kavuma Vs. Hotel International Ltd.
Temporary injunction - prima-facie case - whether made out.
Temporary injunction-discharge thereof before another judge-whether
that judge may assume appellate jurisdiction.
Held: An application to set aside, vary or discharge an interlocutory
injunction may be granted on evidence of sufficient cause and sufficient
cause may be that the injunction was granted ex-parte and the
applicant did not have an opportunity to adduce certain matters of law
or fact which have influenced the court to grant the injunction; or that
new facts had come to his knowledge which had been concealed from
the court by the plaintiff and or could not reasonably have been
ascertained at the time of the hearing; or that owing to fresh
circumstances, the injunction had become unduly harsh or unnecessary
or unworkable.  The court of co-ordinate jurisdiction on an application to
set aside, vary or discharge an interlocutory injunction granted by
another, may not consider that the other court misdirected itself or
erred on the law of facts set aside the injunction on the ground that his
learned brother erred in law and fact while granting the injunction was
wrong because then he assumed appellant jurisdiction.
Appeal allowed-costs in cause-order discharging the injunction set aside.
Nicholas Roussos Vs. Gulam Hussein Habib Virani & anor.
Setting a side exparte Judgment - whether application under
O.9 r.9 of CPR was properly before court.
Held: There are specific provisions in our law governing applications to
set aside exparte judgments these provisions contained in rr9 and 24
of O.9 of the CPR. The failure to decide which rule applies to particular
matter does not mean that there is a lacuna in the law.
There is a line of authorities which establish that the principles
applicable to r.9 and 24 of O.9 are different and that the discretion
under r9 is wide whereas under r.24 it is limited to showing sufficient
cause.  The learned judge therefore erred in holding that the principles
are the same.
Since the respondent's application was grounded on non service of
summons, the respondents were presenting evidence of non service of
summons as sufficient cause for their failure to appear and defend the
suit.  Therefore the respondents had in mind r 24 since it is the one
under which sufficient cause must be shown.  And there is authority for
hearing exparte under r.8 or r8A of Order 9 and obtains judgment, the
proper rule under which to bring an application for setting aside the
exparte judgment is r.24.  Therefore the learned trial judge erred in law
to have held that the application to set aside was properly before court
when brought under r 9 of Order 9.
Theresa Okoth - Ofumbi & anor Vs. Haji Hamedali Ahmed K.
Joinder of parties - whether the advocate appellant was liable for
the fraud of his principal and was thereby properly joined as a
defendant.
Held: The second appellant/advocate's party in the case would cover the
same ground as proving the fraud against the company and under O.1
r3 of CPR as per the pleadings the advocate had been properly joined
as defendant as it was him together with other defendants against
whom the right to relief, I.e. fraudulent breach of contract, had been
claimed.  The advocate/appellant had specific instructions from the
plaintiff respondent to effect a transfer of the suit property in his favour.
Instead he neither effected the said transfer nor stopped or declined to
act for the defendant company when making the second sale of the
same property to the fourth defendant.
The director of a company had a fiduciary duty to act in utmost good
faith but the first appellant herein as director of the defendant company
that had fraudulently deprived the plaintiff/respondent company of its
property was not guilty of the breach of such fiduciary duty since this
duty is owed to the company above.  Secondly, the first appellant could
not be liable for the tortuous interference in the contract between the
plaintiff/respondent and the defendant company because this tort had
not been pleaded by the plaintiff/respondent.
Kyotera Coffee Growers Ltd. Vs. Leonsio Kaggwa & others.
Jurisdiction - whether court has jurisdiction to give an order for
injunction against one set of directors of a company from the
management of the company.
Interest jurisdiction - whether court has jurisdiction to give an order for
injunction against one set of directions of a company from the
management of the company.
Expart injunction - whether validly granted.
Held: The Procedure of obtaining the order without serving the other
party was most irregular.  The application did not pray for the
dispensations of any sort.  And the allegation of the urgency of the
matter was not real since the notice of the meeting was given some
days before the court application there was time to serve the
respondents.
S.101 of CPA confers no powers on the parties nor rights on litigants.
The section does not invest the court with jurisdiction where the court
would otherwise have no jurisdiction.  The section only saves the
inherent powers of the court first to make orders as the ends of justice
may require and secondly to prevent abuse of its process.  The court in
granting the injunction in this case was doing neither of the above since
the Companies Act S.131 does not give court power to issue injunctions
to stop the holding of the Annual General meeting.  The best way to
nullify resolutions passed at a meeting by rival directors would be for
the complainants of file a suit against the order seeking a declaration to
nullify such resolution.  Therefore the order of the trial judge was made
without jurisdiction.
New Way Traders Co. Ltd & ors Vs. Alidina Valimahomed & ors.
Temporary injunction O.37 rr1 & 9 - whether may be granted
experte.
Held: As the evidence on record stands the applicants appear to have a
case to put before court for consideration.  Due to the short notice given
to them in contravention of the law, the applicants would suffer
irreparable damage if the injunction were not granted and they were
evicted and damages would not atone for the situation and moreover
ownership of the suit premises was being contested.  This was a proper
case for which an injunction should be granted.
Boniface QUINTO Ojok Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority.
Court vacation rules - application there under whether by chamber
summons or notice of motion.
Affidavit - whether invalid for being merely argumentative.
Held: Court vacation Rules do not fall under Civil Procedure Rules of
Cap 65 O.48 of CPR governs procedure under CPR.  Court vacation
Rules do not stipulate the procedure to be followed in applications
thereunder.  Therefore, the applicant under r.4 of Court vacation Rules
was free to bring his application either by Chamber Summons or notice
of motion.
O. 17 r 3(1) requires affidavits to be confirmed to such facts as the
deponent is able of his knowledge to prove and excludes argumentative
contents.  The affidavit for the applicant did not offend against O.17 r3(1)
as it was not argumentative nor setting forth matters of hearsay.
Okello-Okello Vs. Uganda National Examination Board.
Fraud-pleading thereof - whether the plea in the WSD that an act
done was unlawful amounted to the plea of fraud.
Issues framing of issues-whether wrongly framed issues may be struck
out.
Held: O.6 r 2 mandatorily requires the particularization of fraud in any
pleading thereof.  The allegation that the instruments effecting the re-
entry by the land commission were unlawful does not mean that it is
fraudulent.  It was enough for the appellant/plaintiff to produce the
certificate of Title and then the onus of proof of fraud was upon the
defendant/respondent to show that the certificate was fraudulently
obtained.  Therefore the learned Trial judge erred in refusing to strike
out the pleadings in the WSD which alleged fraud without stating the
particulars thereof.
The Court has a discretion under O.13 r.5 (2) to strike out wrongly
framed issues but in the instant case it was the learned trial judge that
had inadvertently wrongly framed the issues she should have proceeded
under O.13 r 5(1) to amend the wrongly framed issues.
The certificate of Title to the suit property was issued in the names of
the appellant/plaintiff.  It was therefore incumbent upon the respondent
to adduce evidence to show that the issuance of the certificate of Title
was tainted with fraud.  This evidence was not tendered.  Therefore as
s.56 of the Registration of Title Act deems such certificate as a
conclusive proof thereof, the learned trial judge should have found in
favour of the appellant/plaintiff.
Sh.50,000/= general damages awarded by the trial judge immediately
after the currency reform could not be said to be in adequate on grounds
of inflation and moreover the appellant had not shown which principles
the learned trial judge had violated in the assessment of the damages
not had he shown the extent and convenience the ground of the
damages prayed for.
Dr.Rubinga Vs. Yakobo Kato & anor.
Time - within which to appeal from the chief magistrate court to
high court - whether may be extended.
Extension of time within which to appeal from the Chief Magistrate to the
High Court - whether may be done.
Appeals-extension of time within which to appeal-whether once leave
has been granted, it remains in place even though the ensuing appeal
is struck out.
Held:  The leave to appeal which the High Court granted on 20 Feb.1990
ought not to have been given, because the proceedings in which the
application for leave to appeal was rejected by the Chief Magistrate was
ultra vires section 232 (4).  The section provides that an application for
leave to appeal to the High Court against a judgment of a Chief
Magistrate passed in appeal should be made in the first place to the
Chief Magistrate passed in appeal should be made in the first place to
the Chief Magistrate within 30 days beginning with the date of the
judgment sought to be appealed from:  This means, therefore, that the
Appellant's application in the instant case ought to have been made on
or before 18th January 1989, but it was not.  It was made on 25th
August, 1989, over seven months outside the prescribed period.
Consequently, the leave to appeal on the basis of which the appeal
which was struck out had been made was irregular.  The irregularity
was fatal.
The appellant having failed to apply to the Chief Magistrate for leave
within the prescribed period, it was open to him to seek extension for
extension of time within which to make such an application, but as the
provisions of the Civil Procedure Act are extended to proceedings in
Magistrates' Courts by virtue of the provisions of section 1(2) of the
C.P.A. Section 99 of the Act, read together with section 231(1) of the
M.C.A. would form the basis for extension of time for the purpose of an
application for leave before a Chief Magistrate under Section 232(4) of
the M.C.A.
This appeal raises short but difficult points of procedure; whether time
can be extended for leave to appeal from the Chief Magistrate's Court
to the High Court, and whether, once leave has been granted, it remains
in place even though the ensuing appeal is struck out.
Associated Architects Vs. Uganda Tea Authority.
Inherent powers of court - whether invocable where a specific
provision exists.
Held: S.101 CPA was improperly invoked and the application was
thereby not properly before Court because it was not possible to invoke
court's inherent jurisdiction when there was a specific provision in place,
namely applications to remove an arbitrator are governed by r.16 of the
Arbitration Rules which provides that such applications must be by
Chamber Summons.
The allegations of likelihood of bias at this stage would not result in the
removal of the arbitrator since in the proceedings so far he had shown
no proved bias and moreover since the Arbitration Act S.14 provided
that an open to the applicants once they alleged and proved bias.
Tereza Namakula Vs. Kyaterekera Growers Co-op Society Ltd
Appeal-extension of time within which to lodge a record of appeal-
whether may be allowed.
Affidavit -whether invalid for stating the civil registry as the source of the
material information without disclosing the name of staff in the Civil
Registry.
Held: It was not necessary to depend to the name of the member of staff
in the civil Registry who informed the applicant of the absence of the
judge and lack of Stationary.  It was enough in the affidavit to state that
the civil Registry was the source of that information.  The absence of the
judge and lack of stationary were genuine reasons which caused the
delay and court's discretion would be exercised in favour of the
applicant and record of appeal would be granted.
WW.Kaggwa & 16 others Vs. Yowana Kiwanuka & 2 ors.
Revocation of grant - whether application therefore must be by
originating summons.
Held: S.265 of the Succession Act provides that whenever there is a
contention in any case, it shall take the form of an ordinary suit.  This
provision however applies where an application for grant of probate or
letters of administration is contested by the caveat.  But in the instant
case the grant of probate was made already to the respondent.
Therefore s.265 of the Succession Act was not applicable but the
originating summons under O.34 r1, 2 CPR where the instant case
properly fitted.
T.W.R.Kazzora Vs. M.L.S Rukuba.
Stay of execution - whether supreme court may make orders
therefore pending appeal where no judgment has been filed
together with application.
Held: A stay of execution should be granted for good reasons and the
reasons can only be found in the judgment sought to be appealed
against.  Therefore, the application was in competent for lack of the
judgment sought to be appealed against.
M.L.S.Rukuba Vs. J.W.R.Kazzora
Memorandum of appeal - whether this may in itself constitute a
record of appeal.
Held: The filing of the memorandum of appeal without the requisite
papers as per r 85 RSC did not help the appellant since to no appeal
was commenced thereby nor his efforts were defeated because of his
lack of the necessary accompanying papers because it was due to
administrative delays and the period could only begin to run against the
appellant after he had obtained the record from court.
Godfrey Muyonjo Mukasa and ors Vs. Registered Trustees of
Namirembe Diocese.
Interlocutory judgment - whether passed under a wrong rule and
should be set aside.
Held: It was clear that the provisions of r.3.0.9 do not authorize the
registrar to enter an interlocutory judgment.  Therefore the interlocutory
judgment entered was a nullity and the subsequent proceedings for
formal proof were invalid.
J.W.R.Kazzora Vs. M.L.S Rukuba.
Taxation of costs - whether costs excessive and disproportionate
with regard to subject matter.
Taxation of costs-whether appeal complex and involved and there by
leading to high costs.
Taxation of costs-extraneous matters-whether the income of the
Advocate is an extraneous matter in as far as the taxation of costs is
concerned.
Taxation of costs-whether taxation was a matter of opinion.
Taxation of costs -value of subject matter-whether this is as at the time
of taxation of costs.
Costs -quantum-whether manifestly excessive as to require the
intervention of Court.
Cost-whether applicant should pay 2/3 of the costs because of having
succeeded on firm grounds.
Held: The decision of a taxing officer with regard to quantum of costs in
final and court may only interfere with it in exceptional circumstances
such as when the quantum allowed for instructions fees is so manifestly
high as to reflect the application of a wrong principle and to amount to
an injustice to one party.  In the instance case the value of the subject
matter was only seventy million, the hearing lasted only two days, the
appeal raised difficult issues but not of exceptional nature.  Therefore
taking into account all the circumstances of the case, it is judged that
the fee of 15 million as instructions fees was excessive as to reflect
an application of a wrong principle and would thereby be reduced to sh.
The English Rules of Procedure do not apply in the taxation of costs in
Uganda Courts.  However, the English rules are similar to the Uganda
Rules of the Supreme Court and the cases decided on them provide a
persuasive guide to the principles governing taxation of cost in the
Supreme Court of Uganda.
The income of counsel was an extraneous matter which could not be
properly taken into consideration in assessing the instructions fee.
Clearly taxation of costs was at the entire discretion of the taxing officer
which discretion is to be exercised judicially in accordance with the
law and rules of the court but the actual estimation of the costs was
not mathematical but was based entirely on the opinion and experience
of the taxing officer.  Therefore the registrar taxing officer was right in
holding that taxation was a matter of opinion based on experience.
The value of the subject matter was the value at the material time that
the matter comes into question, in this case at the time of taxation.
therefore the Registrar was justified in basing his taxation of instruction
fee on the value as indicated in the valuation Report submitted by the
respondent.
Costs follow the event and the court awarded the respondent full fasts
despite the fact that the applicant succeeded on two grounds.  The
Registrar has no power to alter the order of court.
Mbabali Muyanja Mohamed Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Temporary injunction - whether may be granted without the head
suit first being filed.
Statutory notice-whether suit may be filed against a scheduled
corporation without a statutory notice.
Held: The head suit had been filed without the requisite statutory notice
to the defendant/respondent Bank, which was a schedule corporation.
This defect was fatal and rendered the head suit void ab initio.  Without
the head suit no temporary injunction may be issued.
Haji Badru Wegulo  2 ORS Vs. Attorney General.
Statutory notice - whether the furnishing of a statutory notice a
requirement under s.1 of the civil procedure and limitation (misc.
prov.) Act, applied to cases concerning the protection of
fundamental freedoms under Act 22(1) of the Constitution.
Statutory Notice-issuance thereof informing Attorney General of bills
alleged contravention of applicants fundamental freedoms -whether fresh
notice required where the bill is enacted into law.
Held: The object of the Statutory notice under s.1 of Act 20/60 was to
give an opportunity to government to investigate the claim and if
possible have it settled out of court.  The facts constituting the claim
could have occurred in a single transaction or could be a series of acts
some of which were in the process to occur like in this present
application where the rules to the Bill complained of were only
precursory to the rules in the subsequent statute.  There was no need
for a fresh notice since the Attorney General was already informed of
the complaint against the rules to the Bill which become the rules to
the statute.
Moreover in an action founded on Article 22 of the Constitution there
was no need to serve a notice upon the Attorney General under s.1 of
Act 20/69 because the jurisdiction granted to the High Court under
Article 22 (1) of the Constitution is only subject to Art.22 (5) which
provides for the enactment of Law to provide the practice and procedure
in relation to claims rising under Art 22(1).  If Act 20/69 were to apply to
applications rising under Art 22 (1) like this application it would be
restricting access to the High Court which is not the intention of the
constitution.
Asha Chand Vs. Attorney General.
Whether the applicant can be party to an appeal  when she was
not party to the proceedings before.
Held: The applicant can not joined as a party to the appeal since under
S.14 of the Expropriated Act she was not the person aggrieved by the
minister's decisions and therefore her counsel had no locus Standi for
adjournment.
Alfred Olwora Vs. Uganda Centre Co-operative Union Ltd.
Whether an advocate practicing with out a valid certificate during
the grace period is not entitled to costs and his filed documents
are invalid.
Held: An advocate that practice during the period of grace cannot
recover his costs through the courts but the papers he signs and files
are valid.
Foods & Beverages Ltd Vs. Srael Musisi Oponya.
Pleading - general damages for trespass - whether may be a
waited when not pleaded.
Held: The evidence showed that the respondent's lorry at the time it was
detained by the appellants in Running condition but when it was
released to the police it could not run and was missing some parts.
This was proof of a trespass to the Chattel on the balance of
probabilities.  Trespass is a remedy affording compensation for injury to
Chattel.  This is upon proof that the defendant has interfered with the
plaintiff's possession of the Chattel and trespass remedies any damage
thus caused.  Trespass is actionable per se without proof of damage
therefore it was not necessary to plead general damages.
The award so shs. 20,000,000/= was on the high as damages for tress-
pass shs.10,000,000/= would surface.
Libyan Arab Uganda Bank & anor Vs. ADAM Vassiliads.
Record of proceedings - counsel's notes - whether these may be
admitted to supplement the court's record of the proceedings.
Held: Where counsel intends or wishes to supplement the official record
of proceedings as taken down by the trial judge, with his own notes or
by affidavit counsel must seek the consent of the opposite party before
the appellant court is able to give leave to such counsels application.
The issue of a judge's inability to perform his judicial duties due to
infirmity of body or mind or misbehavior can only be inquired into by a
tribunal appointed under Art.85(5) of the Constitution.  However, if it is
alleged on appeal that the mental infirmity or misconduct of a judge has
denied the aggrieved party a fair trial, the appellate Court has jurisdiction
to determine the matter to ensure that justice is done between the
parties by remedying miscarriage of justice.
Counsel should at the outset have raised the objection that the judge
was biased against the cause of their clients and that he should not
hear their case.  Even if they were overruled on this counsel would be
on record.  But to allege bias midway the proceedings and infact
withdraw there from was not proper.  The allegation of bias was not
proved because the appellants had not shown that the judge has a
pecuniary interest in the matter before him or that he was likely to
favour the respondent against the appellants.  Bias must be objectively
proved by showing that any right thinking reasonable man would have
believed the judge is biased.  In the instant case the appellants have
not shown that the judge had direct pecuniary benefit or at all nor had
they shown that naturally he would favour the respondents.
Excessive intervention in the proceedings by a trial judge may amount
to misconduct justifying the grant of a new trial.  A judge should not
descend into the arena where his vision may be clouded by the dust of
the conflict.  In the present case the judge interrupted counsel during
cross examination and this caused the failure of court from enlisting the
necessary material facts upon which to adjudicate.  The judge struck
too soon and denied the appellants the fair opportunity of presenting
their case.
Daniel Mukwaya Vs. Administration General.
Temporary injunction - whether subject matter of the suit in danger
of alienation.
Held: There was no evidence that the plaintiff's shares, if any, in his late
father's Company now being administered by the Administrator General
were in danger of being sold, wasted or alienated by the defendant.
Therefore the applicant had not proved his case for the grant of an
injunction.
Betty Owaraga Vs. George William Owaraga.
Summons - service thereof - whether validly done on a member
of the family 16 years old whether defendant could not be found.
Held:  O.5 r.14 CPR allows service on an adult member of the family if
the defendant cannot be found.  Before service can be effected it must be
established that the defendant cannot be found.  In the instant case no
proper inquiry as to the appellant's whereabouts and no sufficient steps
were taken to establish that the appellant court not be found.  And
moreover the rule requires that service be done on an adult member of
the family.  In this case the girl served was minor just 11 years old.
Therefore service was bad and the appeal would be allowed.
Sipiya Kyamulesire Vs. Justus Bikanculika.
Special and general damages for trespass to land.
Held: Fraud must be strictly proved ant eh plaintiff must show that the
defendant dishonestly dealt with the plaintiff's land as to have it included
in his lease.  However, the evidence on record proves that the defendant
passed through all the procedure to validly acquire the lease and the
plaintiff was not unaware of what was going on.  The plaintiff's action
would be dismissed.
Had the plaintiff succeeded he would have no award for special damages
since these had not been proved let alone needed.  Shs. 200,000/
would have been awarded as general damages for trespass.
Sarah Nabagala & anor Vs. Joyce Naku & anor.
Pleading - fraud - whether evidence may be led to prove fraud
when not pleaded.
Held: The second was neither named in the will as beneficiary nor was
he related to the deceased.  Therefore as per ss.24,200, and 201 of the
Succession Act, the second defendant had no legitimate interest in the
estate and was thereby precluded from lodging a caveat against the
grant of letters of administration.
By arguing that the will was a forged, the defendants were imputing fraud
on the part of the plaintiffs and yet the particulars of fraud were not
pleaded in the written of defence, fraud requires strict  proof and yet the
defendants did not call a handwriting expart to prove the signature of the
testator.  The argument by counsel that the will was a forgery departed
from the provisions of O.6 rr 1 and 2 of CPR and would thereby fail.
The evidence of the plaintiffs proved that the deceased did not sign the
Will in their presence as required bylaw, I.e. s.50(1) (c ) of the
Succession Act not did the plaintiffs receive personal acknowledgment
of the testator's signature.  Therefore the Will was invalid and hence not
enforceable by court.
The devise was made to the first plaintiff as a guardian of the deceased's
children and widow as long as the children wanted to stay in the devised
home but if they wanted to leave this home the devise would lapse.
Therefore the devise was conditional and not absolute.
Musis Dirisa & 3 ors Vs. SIETCO (U) Ltd.
Departure from pleadings - whether plaintiffs had departed from
their pleadings.
Held: The evidential burden does not shift to the defendant unless there
is cogent and credit evidence produced by the plaintiff on the issue.  In
this case the mere claim that the plaintiffs were fare paying passengers
who sustained injuries due to the defendant's negligence, did not
occasion the shifting of the evidential burden to the defendant so as to
necessitate her to produce the police account reports to disprove the
testimony of the plaintiff.
The trial judge was right in holding that the plaintiffs had abandoned their
pleading in as far as the particulars of injuries were concerned because
their different testimonies at the trial were at variance with their pleading
in the plaint.  This offended against O.6 r6 CPR as it constituted a
departure.
The learned trial judge was correct to have rejected the evidence of the
expert doctor who testified for the plaintiffs because the doctor had only
made a casual examination of the appellants but not a detailed medical
examination.  A doctor or any expart witness must provide a scientific
base for his opinion before his findings can be accepted by court.  This
scientific base was lacking.  There appeal would be dismissed.
Edward Bowazi Vs. Grindlays Bank.
Attachment - whether attachment involves a car that has not been
removed from the judgment debtor.
Taxation of Court Bailiff' costs - whether the serving of judgment debtor
with an attachment warrant and the judgment debtor paying the fees is
attachment.
Held: Attachment is the distress of a man's goods and chattels for debt
and involves the act of taking property out of the possession of the debtor
to compel him to pay the debt.  Since the judgment debtor's car was not
removed from his possession it was therefore not attached.  Therefore
the proper rule regarding the taxation of costs for a bailiff that has not
attached the property in execution is r 1(A) and the fee payable there-
under was sh. 9000/=.  The taxing Officer was therefore wrong in taxing
the bailiff's fees under r.1(B) (1) (b) which led her to taxing the applicant
excessively.
Coffee Marketing Board Ltd Vs. Frank Kizito.
Amendment of pleading to incorporate counter claim-whether
should be disallowed because the omission to file counter claim
with the WSD was not shown to be bonafide.
Held: It is not necessary to show that the omission to file the counter
claim was bonafide but what is necessary on the part of the plaintiff is to
show that if the amendment was allowed would prejudice his case and
may not be compensated in costs.  Counsel for the plaintiff had or
shown this and therefore his objection to the counter claim would be
overruled.
Mable Mabumba Vs. Haruna Semakula.
Written statement of defence - filing thereof out of time -whether
leave may be granted.
Held: Where a defendant who has entered appearance but filed no WSD
in time but has a good defence on the merits, unless the defendant is
simply trying to delay the action court should normally exercise its
discretion in favour of such defendant and let him put forward his defence
but punish him severely in costs.  In the instant case it would not serve
the ends of justice if the defendant was shut out and moreover allowing
the defendant to file this defence would not prejudice the case of the
plaintiff. leave would therefore be granted.
Ephraim Ongom & anor Vs. Francis Benega.
Time within which to file appeal - whether appellants appeal filed
out of time.
Duty of first appellate court-whether first appellate court failed in its duty
out of time.
Held: The appellants appeal for the copy of the proceedings within the
prescribed period and the Deputy Registrar issued a certificate of
completeness of the record.  Under the proviso of r.81(1) of the RSC,
where an application for a copy of the proceedings has been made, the
period within which the appeal must be instituted does not include the
period taken by the registrar in preparing the copy of the proceedings.
Therefore the appellant's appeal was in time.
The duty of the first appellate Court is to consider and evaluate the
evidence and come to its own conclusion.  In so doing it subjects the
judgment clearly re-evaluated the evidence and came to his own
conclusion.  The fact that his consideration of this evidence was done in
merely one paragraph did not point to the in adequacy of the
consideration but merely the form.  The learned trial judge came to the
conclusion that the respondent had proved his case to the required
standard. The appeal must therefore be dismissed.
Emmanuel Bukenya Vs. Ereneo Kasozi Salongo.
Appeals - extension of time within which to appeal - whether
consideration of principles of natural justice may be a ground for
such extension.
Held: The fact that there could be a denial of justice by the refusal of this
application, coupled with other reasons advanced by the applicant, was
sufficient reason for granting the application.
Twaibu Kigongo Vs. Kabogere Coffee Factory & anor.
Order - whether the notification by a single judge that an aggrieved
party wishes to apply for a reference is an order.
Held: A single judge has no power to grant or refuse leave for a reference
but must note that an informal application therefore has been made.
The note of this cannot be called an order.
Hussein Mohamed Vs. Augustine Kyeyune.
Appeals - certificate of delay by registrar - whether impeachable.
Appeal-service of record-whether served out of time.
Held: The applicant was wrong and discourteous to the court by bringing
an indeterminate argument seeking to impute the Registrar's certificate
of delay without stating so expressly in the motion so that the Registrar
could be called upon to explain whether by evidence or by affidavit.  His
action was taking both the respondent and curt by surprise and would
not thereby not be condoned.
R. 87 of the RSC requires that the record of appeal be served upon the
respondent within 7 days of its lodgment but this applies to the
respondent who has observed R.78 of the RSC by furnishing his address
of service to the appellant/court.  Since in his affidavit or opening address
the applicant had not shown that he had complied with R.78 of the RSC
his objection that the respondent had not observed R.87 would not be
upheld.
Lawrence Musitwa Kyazze Vs. Eunice Busingye.
Party to suit - whether Attorney General proper defendant in a
suit for recovery of land where the defendant government officer is
in possession.
Held: Under common law rules of pleading and practice, in suits for
recovery of possession a person found in possession of the suit Land is
the proper defendant.  The appellant was the one in physical possession
and was properly sued.  It was upon him to claim indemnity from those
those that put him in possession by serving upon them third party notice.
S. 15 (1) (b) prohibits orders of recovery of Land against a government
officer such as the appellant, if the effect of the order would be the same
as an order against Government.  The appellant was in possession in his
official capacity as a Government officer.  The order of recovery against
him was therefore misconceived and a declaration of ownership by the
respondent would be substituted instead.
S.15(1) (b) Constituted a restriction on the rights of citizens and would
thereby be construed narrowly.  Accordingly to imply that the order for
the order for the payment of damage and mesne profit is veiled under
what is expressly prohibited under s.15(1)(b) would not be tenable.
Therefore these orders would not be interfered with.
Interfreight Forwarders (u) Ltd Vs. East African
Development Bank.
Pleading - whether the defendant could be found liable as a
summon carrier when this was not pleaded nor framed among the
agreed issues nor evidence led at the trial for proof thereof.
Damages in foreign currency-whether award of damages in foreign
currency was lawful.
Interest-whether court may order payment of interest where this was not
prayed for in the plaint.
Decree and judgment-whether Decree was invalid for being in conflict
with the judgment.
Held: Inevitable accident is a proper defence to a charge in negligence
whereby the defendant must show that what happened could not have
been avoided by the exercise of care and skill.  In the instant case the
defendant/appellant gave a plausible explanation of the causes and
effect of the accident as being the rough, old road, the on coming
speeding bus and the perforce sudden braking which led to the plaintiff's
car on the carrier to be thrown off.  This evidence was not rebutted.
It proved that what happened was beyond the control of the defendant
exercising due care and skill.
A common carrier is under a Common Law strictly liable for loss or injury
to goods, in damages, because of a warranty to ensure safe delivery of
the goods entrusted to him.  However, the defendant could not be held
to be a common carrier because the plaintiff did not plead that the
defendant was a common carrier, nor did the plaintiff at the hearing lead
evidence to show that the defendant was a common carrier nor was the
issues.  Therefore the learned principal judge misdirected himself when
held that the defendant was in the alternative a common carrier and
thereby strictly liable in damages for injury to the plaintiff's Volvo.
Where it is not specified as to the currency for the satisfaction of the
obligations under the contract, like in the instant case, damages would
be awarded in the currency which most truly expressed the plaintiff's
loss, I.e. the currency that nearly as possible compensates the plaintiff
in accordance with the principle of restitution in integrum.  The learned
trial principal judge was justified in awarding damages in currency in
which the item injured was to be replaced.  Secondly, it was foreseeable
on the part of the defendant that since the injured car was purchased
from abroad, it was a foreign currency needed to be awarded in damages.
The award of replacement value was justified because the principle of the
Law is that in cases of destruction of goods the measure of damages is
the Market value of the goods destroyed at the date of judgment, this is
the principle of restitution in integrum.
Although interest had not been pleaded, it had prayed for at the hearing
by the plaintiff.  Therefore court was justified in awarding the interest and
the amount of 36% did not appear to be excessive.
The decree as appearing on record was defective for being not in
agreement with the judgment as required by the mandatory provisions of
0.18 r 7 but since this defect was caused by the Registrar, it should not
have been the subject of appeal in the Supreme Court but in the High
Court as provided for under O.46 r.8.
Matiya Byabalema & 2 ors Vs. Uganda Transport Co. Ltd.
Admitted facts - whether court may depart there form and base it's
decision on it's own finding.
Held: The trial judge erred when he based his assessment of damages
on cases decided 10 years ago because due to the drastic devaluation
the shilling has suffered, the awards made 10 years ago were of little
guidance in assessing damages.  The court ought to assess damages
taking into consideration the current value of money in terms of what
good and services it can purchase at present.  Therefore court ought to
follow the most recent decision as a guide.
It is trial law that when considering leg injuries where amputation has
been effected, it important to bear in mind.  The distinction between an
injury which involves an amputation below the knee and one which
involves amputation above the knee.  As a rule there is greater disability
where amputation takes place in the thigh and larger sums are awarded
in those circumstances.  Therefore, since the appellants disability was
assessed at 60% the award of shs.4m would be raised to shs.9m as
general damages.
The trial judge erred when he dismissed the claim for the 3rd appellant
on grounds that she had not proved her case.  This is because liability
was not in issue since the respondent had admitted 80% liability and the
case was merely for assessment of damages.  Once liability is admitted
it is not proper for the trial judge to reverse that admission unless there
are valid grounds for doing so.
Fida Birabwa Vs. Suleiman Tigawalana.
Appeals - whether decision and occasional a miscarriage of
justice.
Held: Grounds one and two should not have been raised in the High
Court because they were not raised in the Chief Magistrates Court.
However, since the case originated from the RC Courts it was necessary
that the High Court makes pronouncements on those issued so that
they could act as guidelines for those involved in those courts.
S.26 of the RC Judicial Powers Statute empowers RC appellate court
call witnesses and even try the case de novo.  Therefore RC Courts are
not bound by the procedure laid down in the Magistrates Courts Act.
The RC II Court was in line with the law when they required the cross
examination of the witnesses afresh.
Since the sub-county Chief though present in the RC III Court did not take
part in the deliberations of the court, it cannot be said that the presence
of the sub-county Chief in any way affected the decision of the Court.
There this could not be a basis for stating that the RC III Court was not
lawfully constituted.
Substantial miscarriage of justice is said to occur where there has been
a misdirection by the trial court on matters of fact relating to the evidence
given or where there has been unfairness in the conduct of the trial.
This instant case did not at all indicate that there was a misdirection by
the Chief Magistrates Court on the evidence.
Rosette Kizito Vs. Administrator General & ors.
Extension of time to furnish security for costs u/r 4 Rsc -whether
delay of 18 months excusable.
Held: Under r4 of the RSC court has discretionary powers to extend time
for the appellant to furnish security for costs, inter-alia upon sufficient
cause.  In the assistant case there was no sufficient explanation as to
the delay of 18 months.  Therefore no sufficient reason had been shown
upon which court could exercise its discretion in favour of the applicant.
Rashid Kibirige Vs. Dr. Lubega.
Withdrawal of appeal - whether counsel had no instructions to
withdrawal the appeal- whether appeal should be reinstated u.r 67 RSC.
Held: Counsel for applicant was not advancing his client's case when he
withdraw the appeal without instructions.  The application for reinstating
the appeal must be allowed.
Steven Kasozi & 2 ors Vs. People Transport service.
Compromise by counsel - whether court may reject a compromise
by counsel.
Held: In case involving disputes arising out of judiciary relationships, the
court must sanction the compromise arrived at by counsel or parties
involved.  The instant case was dispute arising out of a commercial
relationship between a transporter and passengers and it had not been
shown that counsel for the defendant/respondent had acted without
authority when he entered the compromise.  Therefore it was not open to
the trial court to reject the compromise.
The trial court could not reject the compromise and go ahead and pass
judgment without calling for faster evidence from the defendant/
respondent who had not given any evidence.
The trial court could not hold that the plaintiff/appellants were trespassers
when this had not been an issue raised by the parties and no evidence
had been recorded therefore from the defence.
Departed Asians Property custodian board Vs.Issa Bukenya.
Whether claim for lost business not pleaded should be disallowed.
Held: There was no claim in the body of the plaint that the plaintiff made
a business loss.  Accordingly the prayer for loss of business was not
supported by any allegation of that nature and no particulars of the loss
were given.  Therefore, the learned trial judge erred in making the award
for lost income.
Although the plaintiff had prayed for general damages for trespass to his
goods, the trespass claim consists in the unlawful possession of the
goods by seizure, removal or damages there to which actions were not
alleged in the plaint nor proved in evidence.  Therefore the plaintiff's
prayer for damages for trespass could not be a basis for the award of the
value of the goods claimed detained or converted by the appellant/
defendant.
Natin Jayant Madhvan VS. East African Holdings Ltd & ors.
Adjournment - whether refused judicially.
Held: Application for adjournment may or may not be allowed by a judge
in the exercise of her own discretion and an appellate court would be
reluctant to interfere unless it is proved that the judge did not exercise
the discretion judicially.  In the instant case, if the trial judge was not
inclined to allow the adjourned she would have let the plaintiff to continue
to prosecute the case himself but should not have dismissed it.
Therefore the trial judge's discretion was not exercised judicially and the
plaintiff's case would be re-instated for hearing before another judge.
Peragio Munyagira Vs. Andrew Mutayitwako.
Rules of procedure-whether failure to cite the role under which an
application is brought renders that application defective.
Held: Every application must specify the actual rule under which it is
brought.  S.18 of the CPA as cited was too general.  The application was
thereby defective for failure to cite the specific rule under which it was
brought.  S.18 of the CPA as cited was too general.  The application was
brought.
T.S Muwanga Vs. East African Steel Corporation Ltd.
Temporary injunction - whether may be granted temporary
injunction - irreparable damage - whether established where loss
may be ascertainable monetarily and compesatable.
Held: Since the applicant in the main suit was not claiming any interest
in the house, the status quo to be maintained pending the trial of the
main suit did not involve the house and therefore to order for a temporary
injunction against eviction would be granted.
It was possible to ascertain the loss in money terms the plaintiff/
applicant would suffer if he were evicted.  It was possible to ascertain
that the loss computed in monetary terms would not be such as no
ordinary person would afford to compensate because of the magnitude.
Therefore, the ground of irreparable damage was not sustainable.
Ronald Kayara Vs. Hassan Ali Ahmed.
Third party notice - whether the defendant should apply for a third
party notice.
Held: The plaintiff was not a bare lincensee because the council by
conduct had led the plaintiff to believe that his renewal of his T.O.L was
permanent.  This meant that the plaintiff's license was coupled with a
proprietary interest which was protected by equity and the principle of
estoppel would operate to prevent revocation of a right which one party
has led the other to suppose it was permanent.  Moreover Art.13 of the
Constitution disallowed expropriation of any ones proprietary interest
without compensation.  Therefore the municipal council acted ulter-vires
when they made a grant of a lease to the defendant on the plaintiff's
premises, he occupied under a T.O.L. without due regard to
compensation.
The law requires a higher standard of proof of fraud than in ordinary Civil
cases.  The learned trial judge, had he in the instant case applied the
requisite standard of proof to the facts it cannot be said that the evidence
would be sufficient to prove fraud.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself on the standard of proof of fraud and thereby arrived
at a wrong conclusion of a finding on fraud.
A third party Notice under O.1 r14 issues where the defendant claims to
be entitled to contribution or indemnity from the Third party.  In the
instant case the defendant never claimed anything from the municipal
council but it is only the plaintiff who claimed that the council had acted
ultra vires or arbitrarily.  Therefore it is the plaintiff under O.1 r3 CPR who
should have joined the council as a co-defendant.  Therefore the learned
trial judge misdirected himself to have held that it was the defendant to
apply for court's leave to issue a third party notice.
Ugantico Supermarket Vs. The Registrar of Titles & 2 ors.
Affidavit - whether sworn on behalf of another and therefore
defective.
Temporary injunction O.37 rr 1&2-whether application therefore defective
because made under Notice of Motion instead of Chamber Summons.
Held: The second defendant's affidavit was not defective or incompetent
since he swore it in his personal capacity and not on behalf of his co-
defendant.  He merely swore what he knew about the affairs of his
co-defendant.
Where there is non compliance with any prescribed form as long as it is
not calculated to mislead, such non compliance is not to make an
application or suit void; secondly as long as no injustice is caused non
compliance with the rules of procedure is not to be held to be fatal to an
application or suit; thirdly, O.48 rr8 and 9 of CPR allow the judge to
accept an application which would otherwise by the rules be brought by
notice of motion or chamber summons whatever the case may be.  In the
instant case thought the application should have been brought by
Chamber Summons the want of form would not preclude the supremacy
of substance and the application would be allowed to proceed.
Wycliffe Kiggundu Vs. Attorney General.
Rejecting plaint - whether the trial judge misdirected himself to
reject the plaint on the ground that the action therein contained
was not maintainable in law.
Held: Rejected the plaint under O.7 r11 (a) CPR must be primarily and
only the result of constructing the plaint as it stands and no other
extraneous matter must be considered.  The plaint must be found
defective such that if fails to disclose a cause of action.  In the instant
case the argument that the action was not maintainable at law was a
preliminary point of law and not a result of a defect in the plaint.
Therefore the preliminary point of law should have been set down for
hearing and the plaintiff's suit should have been dismissed if the court
found that his action not maintainable but his plaint should not have
been rejected.  The trial judge misdirected himself when he rejected the
plaintiff's plaint.
Regulation no 36 of the Public Service Regulations provides that a Public
Servant may be interdicted if proceedings for his dismissal are about to
be taken or if criminal proceedings are being instituted against him.
The gap between either of these proceedings and his interdiction must
be reasonably short.  Therefore the plaintiff had a maintainable cause of
action for a declaration and or damages for having been on interdiction
for more than 2 years.  The trial judge misdirected himself in rejecting
the plaintiff's plaint.
Again Regulation no.36 of the Public Service Regulations provides that a
public servant may be interdicted if proceedings for his dismissal are
about to be taken or Criminal Proceedings are being instituted against
him.  The plaintiff was interdicted upon the commencement of police
inquires against his conduct and not upon the determination of the
authorities to institute actual proceedings for dismissal or prosecution.
Therefore, his interdiction was commenced on an illegal basis.  The
plaintiff has a maintainable action for a declaration and or for damages
upon the unlawful interdiction.  The trial judge misdirected himself in
rejecting the plaintiff's plaint.
The trial judge misdirected himself when he held at the plaintiff's cause
of action was not maintainable at law due to the Presidential prerogative
under Art.104 of the Constitution to dismiss the plaintiff in public because
the plaintiff's action did not seek impeach the Presidential prerogative but
the conduct of the Public Service Commission which had acted outside
the law in interdicting him and advising the president to dismiss him in
Public interest.
Departed Asian Property Custodian Board Vs. Issa Bukenya.
Setting aside expart decree - whether good or substantial reasons
enlisted therefore-whether for getting hearing date was a good
reason justifying setting aside expert decree.
Judgment-whether it was proper for court to issue a judgment without
reasons.
Fixing by consent-whether a hearing notice is required where hearing
date has been fixed by consent.
Held: For an application to set aside an expert decree to succeed, the
applicant must show that Summons had not been duly served upon him or
was prevented by an sufficient cause from appearing at the date fixed
therefore.  Forgetting the hearing date is not sufficient cause justifying
setting aside the expart decree.  Therefore the learned judge of the
High Court was correct in refusing to set aside the decree.
The learned judge of the High Court erred in law and fact when she failed
or refused to give reasons for her ruling because a ruling without reasons
is defective.
Where the hearing date is fixed by consent there is no need for hearing
notice.  In the instant case the hearing date had been fixed by consent
and the Court was not to issue a further hearing notice unless the hearing
date taken by consent was not acceptable to the court which was not
the case.
A.K.Detergent Vs. G.M Combined.
Security for costs - whether order thereof may issue because
plaintiff company is highly indebted what is the quantum there for.
Held: The receivers and managers that sold the plaintiff's property acted
according to the powers that were conferred upon them by the
debentures.  These powers were not power to hold and dispose of the
company's property comprised in the debenture.
Therefore the contention of the respondent that their suit contesting the
sale on the ground that it was not valid for having taken place after the
institution of winding up proceedings, was likely to succeed was not
correct.  Therefore, taking into account the fact that the respondent/
plaintiff was heavily indebted most of her assets charged, was under
receivership, winding up proceedings had commenced, it was necessary
that she furnishes security for costs of the suit on which the defendant/
applicant would fall back in event the suit went against the plaintiff/
respondent.
Since the monetary value of the subject matter of the suit, this is, the
property sold to the application/defendant was very big and the litigation
likely to be vast, shs.50 million would be paid as security for costs.
Tabb Trading Company Vs. Fid Hussein.
Court vocation - whether matter was urgent.
Held: The applicant's failure to depose in his affidavit as to whether he had
been served with a notice of eviction rendered his application untenable
because no urgency had been disclosed.  The application would be
allowed.
Patrick Macomb & anor Vs. Sole Electrics (u) Ltd.
Taxation of costs - whether instruction fees manifestly excessive.
Held: An appellate court will only interfere with an assessment of costs
by a taxing officer if the quantum of the assessment is manifestly
extravagant because it is then that an inference that the taxing officer
misdirected himself in principle will be made.  In the respondent which
therefore meant that the appeal was not very involved.  Therefore the
the award of shs.12 million as instruction fee was excessively and
manifested a misdirection in principles.  The award would be reduced to
2 million.
The respondent were not claiming a proprietary interest in the suit
property.  Therefore, it was a misdirection on the part of the taxing officer
to take into account the value of the suit property when assessing
instruction fees.
Since no evidence had been led before the appellate court to prove that
the first respondent was not capable of paying costs, the financial status
of the first applicant was irrelevant in assessing the costs.
CAL can only be awarded to the advocate or his client as a disbursement
upon proof of receipts.  Therefore, it was a misdirection of the part of the
taxing master to award CAL when the advocate had not prove that he
had made such a disbursement.
Everest Mugabi Vs. Attorney General.
Leave to appeal to the supreme court - whether mistake of law is
a ground for leave.
Held: Since Mugabi's suit had been struck out, there was no pending
case before court for which leave to appeal against could be granted to
the Supreme Court.
The decision against which an extension of time to file notice of appeal
to the Supreme Court was being sought had been made 12 months
before this application which statutorily could be brought within 60 days.
Therefore there was inexcusably inordinate delay.
Kabogere Coffee Factory Ltd Vs. Haji Twaibu Kinongo.
Appeals - tendency of incompetent appeal - whether bar to an
application for extension of time to appeal.
Held: The defects in the incompetent appeals were so judgmental that
they were incurable even by extension of time within which to appeal.
The fundamental defects concerned the inability of the Advocate without
a valid appeal.  This defect was incurable even by extension of time.
Therefore in this instance the pendency of an incurably incompetent
appeal was a bar to an application for extension of time.
The pending of an incompetent appeal was a bar to filing a fresh appeal.
Even if the applicants had succeeded on a number of grounds, since
they failed on the ground that disposed of the application in the award
costs to the respondents.
The learned single judge misdirected himself when he dismissed the
applications.  He would instead have had them struck out since they
were not decided to their merits as per r4 of the Rules of the Supreme
Court.
Francis Nansio Micah Vs. Nuwa Walakira.
Preliminary objection - appeals - whether an appeal against a
preliminary objection on an issue of limitation may lie without
leave of court - whether claim for specific performance barred by analogy.
Limitation -pleadings-whether failure to plead limitation in WSD was fatal.
Held: The learned single judge misdirected himself when he rejected the
defence of limitation on grounds that it had not been pleaded.  The trial
judge should have afforded the parties an adjournment so that the
plaintiff could reply to the contention by the defendant that the plaintiff's
action was time barred instead of rejecting the defence that it had taken
court and the other party by surprise.
The appeal against the preliminary objection that the plaintiff was time
barred could not lie as a right without leave of court but an appellant
court in order that it is not fettered from its duty to give effect to the
statute of limitation, would entertain the ground of appeal against the
preliminary objection.  Moreover s.78(1) empowered an appellate court to
entertain an appeal from a decree that is defective, erroneously given, or
is long as it was set forth in the memorandum of appeal.
The plaintiff's action was for breach of contract and s.4(1) of the
Limitation Act required such action to be brought before the expiry of six
years from the date of the cause of action.  In the instant case the
action was commenced almost nine years from the date of accrual of the
cause of action.  However, s.4(6) exempts equitable claims like claim
for specific performance from the application of the six years limitation
period and a party will take advantage of this exemption when he is not
guilty of laches.  In the instant case the plaintiff/respondent was not
guilty of unreasonable delay since he pursued his rights under the
contract as soon as the first opportunity presented itself.
Plaxenda sembatya Vs. Tropical Africa Bank.
Appeals - striking out notice of appeal under r.8 RSC - whether
application tenable - whether appellant failed or refused to take the
essential steps in the proceedings.
Held: Since Counsel for the applicant had been aware of the appellant's
interest in obtaining the record of proceedings from the High Court, the
failure by the appellant to copy to him the letters to the High Court
Registrar applying for the said record did not cause him any prejudice
and was therefore not fatal to the proceedings.
Since the appellant had exercised all due diligence in taking the
necessary steps to prosecute the appeal but was frustrated by the
inordinate delay of the High Court in preparing and delivering the record
of proceedings as required by law, it would be a denial of justice to strike
out the appellant's notice of appeal.
Paulo Lutalemwa Kakooza Vs. Attorney General.
Witness - recalling witness - whether permissible.
Held: The action of the learned trial judge in recalling the defence witness
for further cross-examination was permissible because of the general
power for Court to recall a witness either under O.16 r.12 CPR or S.163
of the Evidence Act.  No injustice was thereby caused.
J.K.Patel Vs. Spear Motors Ltd.
Pleadings - written statements of defence failing specifically to plead part
