payment of the debt - whether evidence may at the trial be led to prove this.
Interest-quantum-whether court may award interest assessed at market
value or official Bank of Uganda exchange.
Costs-failure to award costs to the successful party-whether a mis-
direction.
Held: The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he held that there
was no definite valid and enforceable contract merely by looking at the
documents tendered and the parties oral testimony.  The parties conduct
definitely showed that an offer on definite terms had been made by one
party and accepted by the other.  There was a valid enforceable contract.
The plaintiff had testified that he had been contracted by the defendant
company to build an assembly plant.  There plaintiff showed that he had
been part paid for this work.  The burden of proof thereby shifted to the
defendant to disprove this allegation.  But the defendant in his testimony
claimed that it had part paid more than the plaintiff had shown.  But
since the defendant's part payment had not been pleaded in his written
statement of defence, its evidence of part payment would be inadmissible.
Therefore the defendant had not discharged its burden of proof and would
have judgment against it.
The parties evidence at the trial amply showed that the defendant's
general manager was a key witness in this case.  But since the
defendant refused to call him as a witness, an adverse inference would
be drawn against the defendant.
The defendant's evidence of a set off, when he claimed that the plaintiff's
four years occupation of the defendant's home was upon an
understanding that the rent would act as a set off and the plaintiff's wife's
air ticket given by the defendant, such evidence was admissible even if
the defendant had not pleaded it in its WSD because the plaintiff at the
trial never objected to it nor did the plaintiff cross examine the
defendant's witness on it.
Rent would be assessed at the market rate for the purpose of the set off.
Court had the discretion to award interest and in this case court would
award interest at the official Bank of Uganda rates.
The trial judge misdirected himself when he failed to award costs to the
successful party.  Though the judge has a discretion not to award costs
to the successful party or at all his discretion must be exercised
judiciously and the reasons given in his judgment for his refusal to award
costs to the successful party.
Henry Bukomeko & 2 ors Vs. State-wide insurance Co. Ltd.
Application for extension of time to lodge record of appeal -
whether delay in excusable.
Held: Where the subject of the application is an interlocutory appeal
great care must be exercised in getting the appeal on as quickly as
possible in order that the trial may proceed with a minimum delay; so as
not to have it prejudiced.  In the instant case, the duty to act
expediciously as required was not fulfilled by the applicant.
Libyan Arab Uganda Bank Vs. Adam Vassiliandis.
Taxation of costs - Taxation by consent - whether order may be
set a side because of the excessive quantum of costs under
Consent order-whether a consent order may be set aside without an
application or fresh suit to that effect.
Held: Under r.109(2) RSC an application challenging only the quantum of
costs cannot be entertained.  The application must also involve a
principle of the law alleged to have been breached.  In this case, the
contention that counsel had not mandate to consent to the bill of costs
as taxed, would not be a matter of the law to be referred to a simple
judge under r.10992) RSC because it would involve to an inquiry into the
facts of that consent.  This kind of inquiry can only be entertained by the
full court.
The application seeking to set aside the taxation by challenging the
consent order is not proper because the consent order must first be set
aside.  But a consent order can only be set aside after a fresh suit or
an application to that effect is made and is successful.
Though r 108 RSC gives the discretion to the Registrar to tax costs, the
parties thereto can consent to such costs.  The consent does not
purport to oust the jurisdiction of the registrar in the matter.
The parties to any suit, appeal, application or petition before court can
consent to any contentions matter before them except matters that
should tend to oust the jurisdiction of the court or to confer upon court a
jurisdiction it does not have.
Application dismissed.
Uganda Commercial Bank Vs. General Parts (u) Ltd.
Originating summons O.34 rr 34 and 7 CPR - whether the question
as to the appointment of a receiver is proper for originating
summons.
Held: The application would not succeed because o.34r 3A does not
provide for the determination as to whether a receiver of mortgaged
property has been appointed among the relief's provided by the rule.
Application dismissed.
E.Kishoga & others Vs. Fenekansi Mugasha.
Extension of time to file notice of appeal u/r 4 Rcs - whether good
cause shown.
Held: The appeal had been fixed and heard experte which prevented the
applicant from knowing in time that the appeal had been dismissed.
This coupled with the fact that the applicant had occupied the suit lands
since childhood, was sufficient cause to justify the extension of time
within which to file a Notice of Appeal.
Application allowed.
Esso Standard Ltd Vs. Semu Amanu Opio.
Submissions - whether it is proper not to let counsel make final
submissions.
Held: The learned trial judge was entitled to reach the decision that the
appellant company was in breach of its contract with the respondent for
failure to give the respondent the agreed notice before the termination
of contract.
The learned trial judge erred in law when he awarded exemplary damages
for breach of contract because firstly, this had not been pleaded by the
respondent/plaintiff, secondly, an award for exemplary damages may not
be awarded for breach of a contract unless it involves the commission of
a tort of trespass and since no tort of trespass had been proved as
committed by the appellant, in this case the award for exemplary
damages was improper and would be set aside.
The tort of detinue is a continuing tort and damages therefore are
assessed as at the date of judgment as equivalent to the value of the
chattel in issue as at the date of judgment.  Therefore, the damages to
be awarded to the respondent of his detained chattels would be the value
of the chattels as at the date of judgment.
The glaring mistake in the Currency Reform Statute would be corrected
by court by mere application of logic since the only conversion rate
application of logic since the only conversion rate applicable to s.1 (a) is
that in S.(b)) and the courts have since taken that view.
Since detinue was a continuing tort, damages awardable therefore were
to be assessed as at the date of judgment and therefore the Currency
Reform Statute did not apply to the prayer of damages for detinue.
Since it was the learned judge's mistake to ward exemplary damages,
no party should pay costs of setting the award aside.
The learned trial judge erred when he failed to allow counsel to address
court after each had closed their case.
Appeal allowed in part.
Shabani Matovu Vs. Sikindar Hussein Esmail & 5 others.
Appeals - whether the plaintiff's suit not maintainable because it
should have come as an appeal and not a suit as required by s.14
of the expropriated properties Act.
Special damages-whether proved.
Held:  The compensation of the valuation was to be done by a Board of
Valuers appointed by the Minister as required by S.12 of the
Expropriated Properties Act and S.2(1) of the Properties and Business
(Acquisition) Decree no.11 of 1975.  Since the plaintiff had not had his
claimed compensation valued as such his claim must fail.
S.14 of the Expropriated Properties Act required that the claim for
compensation must be placed before the Custodian Board's validation
Committee for processing and the plaintiff can only come to court as an
appeal against the decision of the validation committee.  Therefore the
plaintiff's case cannot succeed.
Though the plaintiff pleaded the claim for special damages his failure to
invite the valuer that had prepared the bill of quantities for purposes of
computing the compensation to testify in court, meant that the plaintiff had
not specifically proved his claim for the special damages.
Case Dismissed.
Daniel Oboth Vs. The New Vision Newspaper.
Grounds of appeal - whether ground not sustainable because
argumentative.
Held: Since the defendants had published the article only once and had
not refused to apologies since they were not asked to do so, there was
no ground upon which the defendants could have punitive damages
awarded against them.
The humble beginnings of the plaintiff cannot be a basis for calculating
the quantum of general damages awardable in defamation cases but the
actual status of the plaintiff at the date of the publication.  The learned
trial judge therefore erred in taking into account the humble beginnings
of the plaintiff and the award for general damages would be increased
The fourth and fifth grounds of appeal were defective for being
argumentative.
Appeal allowed in part.
Henry Munyanganizi Vs. General Machinery Ltd.
Review - whether court may retry issue not the subject of the
review order.
Pleadings-amendment-whether amendment of pleadings may be allowed
after closure of proceedings.
Held: Where a case is admitted to review by one judge and is afterwards
tried by another the new judge must confine himself to the points
directed by the other for review.  A Judge granting a review on one point
has no power to go into or decide a matter already finally adjudicated
upon.
Parties should not have been allowed to amend pleadings after the order
for review had been made because at the time of the review the
proceedings had been closed and therefore to allow amendment at that
stage would be an abuse of court process since there should be an end
to litigation.
A company is a legal entity irrespective of the motives of its promoters,
once it is formed under the provisions of the law the rules governing it
must be followed.  The company property is clearly distinguishable from
the member's property and therefore the plaintiff could not be said to be
the owner of the tractor bought by the company in which he was a
shareholder.
S.29 of the Sale of Goods Act provides that unless otherwise agreed
delivery of the goods and payment of the price are concurrent conditions.
The plaintiff having paid for a tractor which the defendants had defaulted
in delivery, the plaintiff, buyer is entitled to damages, namely the
estimated loss directly and naturally resulting in the ordinary course of
events from the seller's breach.  In this case the plaintiff should be
awarded damages that may enable him purchase a new tractor.
Arconsult Architects Vs. Bauman (U) Ltd
Time - enlargement of time within which to file a notice of appeal-
whether application tenable - under s.37(1) (a) of the Judicature
Act.
Held: S.37(1) (a) of the Judicature Act gives the High Court power where
any appeal lies from its judgment to extend the time for giving notice of
intention to appeal as long as the applicant gives sufficient reason for the
failure to file his notice in time and the dishonest pocketing of court fees
by the clerk leading to failure to file the notice in time was a sufficient
ground to allow such an extension.
Famous cycle Agency & ors Vs. Mansukhulala Rariji Karia & anor
Registrar - powers thereof in execution under O.46 R 4 CPR -
whether registrar has no power to revoke a warrant of attachment.
Held: The Decree was against several judgment/debtors severally and
not jointly therefore the registrar should have made a formed order
detailing which judgment debtor was to pay what and by what method.
This is because the registrar acts as a court in execution proceedings,
he should have formally judicially considered the application for
execution.  But since he did not consider the application for execution
judicially he could not as well make a formal order rescinding the first
informal order.  However, a registrar has powers of supervision over court
bailiffs and may legitimately intervene in execution proceedings.
Turn Sidpra & anor Vs. Uganda Rehabilitation Development
Foundation.
Cause of action - whether a done of powers of  Attorney may sue
as a plaintiff with regard to an executed tenancy.
Oral application - whether application for leave to proceed with suit in the
name of one plaintiff after the other is dead may be done orally.
Held: Powers of attorney had to be strictly interpreted.  In this case the
particular power did not confer upon the plaintiffs to institute legal
proceedings in their names.  Moreover the powers were defective for the
failure of the witness thereto to give his particulars.  However, the
proceedings were not thereby invalid because the subject matter of the
suit was a contract of conveyance which was partly executed and
therefore it was the duty of the court to adjudicate on the dispute relating
to the contract and so give effect to the wishes of the parties.
The application for leave of court for an action to continue in the name of
the living plaintiff after the death of the other, is supposed to be by
Chamber Summons under O.21 r 12 but because the defendant had not
objected to the application and since both plaintiffs were joint parties to
the tenancy agreement, the subject matter of the suit, the Oral
application would be allowed.
Phoebe Megabit Vs. Print Pak (u) Ltd.
Arbitration - whether civil proceedings must invariably be stayed
pending arbitration.
Held: Jurisdiction - whether court has no jurisdiction in dispute which
requires arbitration prior to court proceedings-whether arbitration
necessarily ousts the jurisdiction of court.
The tenancy agreement the subject matter of the suit contained an
arbitration clause requiring arbitration precedent upon court proceedings.
At the hearing of the suit counsel for the defendant objected to the
proceedings contending that they were premature because arbitration
had not taken place.
Attacker Edgar Vs. Uganda Railways Workers Union & Uganda
Railways Corporation.
Appeal - against ruling that the suit did not disclose a cause of
action under O.6 r.29 - whether appeal as of right or with leave.
Held: the appellant could proceed to appeal as of right against the ruling
and order of the trial judge because O.6 r 29 under which the trial judge
struck out the plaintiff's proceedings provides that such appeals shall be
as of right and not by leave of court.
The learned trial judge correctly interpreted S.19(1) (b) of the Trade
Union Decree which bars any suit against a registered Trade Union in
respondent was a registered Trade Union and the defamatory letter was
written and published by its officer on its behalf.  It follows that the
appellant had no cause of action against the first respondent.
It is true a Trade Union can be liable in cases where it is proved to have
acted outside its scope as a Trade Union but in the instant case the
defamatory letter was written for purposes of security for the officials of
the Union and since protecting the lives of Union officials is a legitimate
function of a trade Union, the Union could not be said to have acted
outside its scope.
The learned trial judge correctly held that the Union as registered was a
separate legal entity from the second respondent which could not be
held to be vicariously liable for the acts of the first respondent.
The learned trial judge was correct in not requiring first to hear evidence
before striking out the appellants pleadings against the first and second
respondents since the pleadings did not disclose a cause of action
against them.
American Express International Banking Corporation Vs.
Atulkumar Patel.
Additional evidence - whether leave may be granted to the
applicant so that he can adduce additional evidence.
Held: Leave to adduce additional evidence may be granted under r.29(1)
(b) of the Rules of Supreme Court for sufficient reason such as the
benefit of a new statute or new judicial decision but the new evidence
was in possession of the applicant at the trial, and therefore no
opportunity in producing that evidence ought to be given by a new trial.
Eriaza Magala Vs. Reverend Kefa Sempangi.
Admission of facts O.11 r.6 - whether proved to warrant entry of
judgment in applicant's favour.
Held: Under O.11 r6 court has wide discretion to give judgment for relief
prayed for by a party if the opposite party admits it.  Admission can be
by pleading or a letter he essential point to note is that for a judgment to
be given the admission to which such judgment can be claimed must
be unequivocal.  In the instant case the defendants in their WSD denied
the plaintiff's claim and the letter referred to did not admit liability clearly
or unequivocally or at all.  The application was misconceived and must
be rejected.
Festo Kassamba & sons Ltd Vs. Margaret Mbabazi.
Witness - failure to call a material witness - whether adverse
inference may be drawn.
Held: Gujwaheru being an active manager in the affairs of the bust
company would in no doubt be in possession of vital information about
the property or finances of the plaintiff has a choice as to who to call a
witness who would have been called.
National Insurance Arilitects Vs. Arconsults Arilitects.
Arbitration - non existence of arbitration agreement - whether
parties may non the less submit themselves to an arbitration.
Arbitration-whether award improperly procured where it is alleged there
was no binding contract between application and respondent.
Arbitration -whether award may be set aside.
Costs-arbitration-whether arbitrator may award costs.
Held: It is true that the parties at the beginning conduced their relation-
ship rather casually without for example having a written agreement in
relation to the suit projects or even providing for a settlement of such an
eventuality by arbitration as provided by SS.2 and 16 of the Arbitration
Act but because the parties did not contest the arbitrator's Jurisdiction
the dispute was properly before the arbitrator.  Parole submission is
sufficient for arbitration.
Though the terms of reference under which the applicants and the
respondents were to deal did not indicate the scale of fees to be charged
by the respondent, the respondent did at the earliest behest indicate his
fees and the applicant did not object.  This was a finding of fact by the
arbitrator based on evidence.  A perusal of the arbitrator's ruling together
with other documents on record show that there was binding contract
between the applicant and respondent to perform the responsibilities of
an architect.  The Arbitrator's award would thereby not be impeachable
since it was not alleged that the arbitrator misconduct himself or the
award was improperly procured other than the fact that the arbitrators
had misdirected themselves in law.  If the parties choose to refer the
determination of their dispute to an arbitrator then they have chosen their
own tribunal and neither would have the right save for very good reasons
to set aside the award.
The costs of the arbitration are governed by r9 of the first schedule to the
Arbitration Act which gives the arbitrator discretion to award costs.  In
the instant case the arbitrator was empowered to award costs as he did.
Acaali Manzi Vs. Nile Bank Ltd.
Adjournment O.15 r.1 CPR - whether sufficient cause shown for
adjournment.
Adjournment by letter-whether proper.
Setting aside-experte Decree-whether defence had merits and whether
there was sufficient cause for absence or any good cause.
Held: It was now accepted that applications for adjournment by letter
would not be acceptable under normal circumstances.
O.15 r.1 gave court discretion to grant adjournment or sufficient cause
under ordinary suits.  Motions for adjournment may be made under O.48
r.5 upon Court's discretion.  The inconsistence between the applicant's
affidavit and the doctor's none as to when the applicant was prevented
by sufficient cause not to be in court at the time judgment was passed
against him and therefore court's action to refuse the adjournment was
exercised properly.
In deciding whether to set aside experte judgment under O.33 rr11 court
has no consider whether the applicant had sufficient reason for absence
or whether there was another good cause I.e. good defence.  Since the
applicant's failure to attend court was not justified, the other cause for
setting aside would be a good defence.  However the applicant having
admitted liability he could not be said to be having a good defence.
moreover his assertion than he had a good defence was not backed by a
draft thereof on record.  It has repeatedly been said that when applicants
apply for leave to defend, the applicant should attach a draft WSD
showing what defence.  All these circumstances taken together do not
show any other good cause to justify setting aside the experte decree
and or granting unconditional leave to defend.
application dismissed.
Haji Twaibu Kigongo Vs. Haji Bruhan Mugerwa.
Affidavit in reply - failure to file - whether respondent therefore has
no contrary evidence - whether respondent has no right of being
heard.
Held: In proceedings that require evidence from both parties like affiliation
proceedings and originating summons failure to file a reply in form of
affidavit or otherwise could disentitle the respondent from giving evidence
at the trial because such proceedings take the form of a suit but
proceedings under O.9 r 26 do not require the respondent to file
affidavit in reply.
The applicant must prove to court that there are circumstances that in
the interest of justice would militate against permitting the respondent
to enjoy the benefits of the Decree and both parties must be heard.
Transami (u) Ltd Vs. Transocean (u) Ltd.
Third party notice - whether third party was liable to indemnify defendant.
Held: It is settled that in Third Party proceedings for indemnity to be
claimed the cause of action as between the defendant/plaintiff must be
the same as between defendant/Third party.  In the instant case the
plaintiff action against the defendant was for eviction, mesne profits,
general damages, etc all founded on trespass and yet the defendant's
claim against the third party was misrepresentation.  These were entirely
different causes of action.  Secondly apart from the causes of action
being the same, the right to indemnify the defendant by the third party
must have been provided by the original contract either impliedly or
expressly.  In the instant case, the mere allocation mistakenly of the
suit premises did not create an obligation upon the third party to
indemnify the defendant.
Mayfair Import & Export Ltd Vs. Inaprodex London Ltd  & anor.
Setting aside exparte Decree U/99 rr17( c) and 24 CPR - whether
sufficient cause shown for non appearance - whether a material
factor appears to have entered into the passing of the exparte
decree.
Held: O.9 r 24 gives a remedy to the defendant against whom an ex-prate
decree has been passed but was prevented from appearing fro sufficient
cause. In this case no material factor entered into the passing of the
exparte judgment, which would not have been, had the judgment not
been exparte.  Therefore, no sufficient cause were shown to have
prevented the applicant from appearing and his application would be
dismissed.
Uganda Oxygen Ltd & 2 ors Vs. Salim Jamal & 2 ors.
Withdrawal suit of by consent under O.22 r2 - whether binds all
the parties in inclusive of those not signatory to withdrawal.
Held: The respondent/defendants could not commit the 1st and 2nd
applicant/plaintiffs who were not signatory to the consent order entered
under O.22 r 2 because the consent is required to be signed by all
parties so as to bind them.
S.80(1) gives Court discretion for good cause to entertain an appeal out
of time without the appellant first having had to seek leave Court to
appeal out of time.  In the instant case the conflict between the parties
had precipitated a disturbing trend of events and this was good cause for
court to admit the appeal.
When the Deputy Registrar entered the consent order withdrawing the
suit, he acted as a civil court under O.46 r2 CPR which, even though it
were not a statute, nevertheless it was a rule of law which clearly
provided that any person aggrieved by any order of a Registrar may
appeal there from to the High Court and the consent order was such an
order appealable from.
Lake Victoria Bottling Co. & 2 ors Vs. Crown Bottlers Ltd.
Third party Notice - whether application therefore tenable whether
subject matter between the third party and defendant same as
that between the plaintiff and defendant.
E.Kangye Vs. E.Bwana.
Decree - whether same as order.
Pleading-whether memorandum of appeal is a pleading.
Held: The terms, decree and order, are mutually exclusive.  However,
whether the memorandum of appeal is a pleading so as to entitle the
appellant to seek amendment thereof under O.6 r 18 was not necessary
to decide since the amendment if allowed so that the term "order" is
substituted for "decree" no miscarriage of justice would arise, the
amendment would be allowed.
The standard of proof required to prove fraud in civil cases was higher
than in ordinary cases.  The learned trial magistrate directed himself
properly as no miscarriage of justice resulted.
The trial magistrate precisely followed the observations he made at the
locus quo and properly directed himself as to the evidential value of
observations as they conformed to the descriptive evidence of the
boundaries of the suit land as given by the parties and their witnesses
both in court and at the locus in quo.  Therefore , court was not
improperly conducted at the locus in quo.
When a witness is sworn in court and he is called upon to give evidence
at the locus in quo it is not necessary to have the witness take another
oath since he continues to be on oath right from court to the locus in quo
Therefore the trial magistrate did not misdirect himself when he did not
require the witness at the locus in quo to take a fresh oath when they
had already taken one in court.
Hajati Ziribagwa & anor Vs. Yakobo Ntate.
Cause of action - recovery of land - whether cause of action close
when defendant became registered proprietor or when plaintiff
discovered the alleged fraud.
Held: The action was brought after the expiry of 12 years since the
defendant acquired the land.  Since this is an action for recovery of land,
the action must have arisen at the date the defendant acquired the land.
The plaint was therefore time barred and must be rejected.
Dr.Willy Kaberuka Vs. Attorney General.
Issues - whether court may frame issues of it's own motion.
Held: Under O.13 r5(1) CPR court may amend of frame issues additional
at any time before passing a decree to enable the parties controversy to
be determined.  Therefore, an additional issue whether the plaintiff was
prosecuted by the defendant would be framed.
The plaintiff received criminal summons and was formally charged before
the traffic court Magistrate and released on bail and continued reporting
to court until the proceedings were determined.  Therefore the plaintiff was
prosecuted and the proceedings entered in his favour.
The record of the lower court showed that no traffic police officers
testified to show how the plaintiff was connected with the motor accident.
Therefore there was no evidence or nay facts in which a reasonable
inference could be made that the plaintiff was in any way party to the
offence.  Nor did the police honestly believe in the guilt of the plaintiff.
Since there was no reasonable or probable cause for prosecuting the
plaintiff, the prosecution was malicious.
Whether the plaintiff suffered damages from the prosecution is an
inference as a natural and foreseeable consequence of the defendant's
conduct.  This, couple with the plaintiff's status in society, shows that
the plaintiff suffered some damage and shs. 3million would be awarded
as damages for malicious prosecution.
G.W.Mulindwa Vs. J.J.Kisubika.
Setting a side dismissal O.9r20 - whether negligence of counsel
for non-appearance is ground therefore.
Held: The professional negligence of counsel leading to the suit being
dismissed under O.9 r.19 CPR, when the applicant plaintiff has engaged
another counsel, should not act as a bar to justice.  Therefore, for
purposes of justice court was empowered under S.101 of CPA to set
aside the dismissal.
Mohamed Yahu Vs. Abdunur Khamis.
Temporary injunction - whether prima-facie case must be
established.
Held: There was no rule that the applicant must establish a prima-facie
case as a condition for the order of a temporary injunction because this
would turn the application into a trial.  In the instant case, though the
applicant had not discharged the onus on him to prove that the balance
of inconvenience if the injunction was not granted was against him, on
this ground the applicant would be granted an order for a temporary
injunction since there were serious matters to be investigated.
Edwin Otile Ojungu Vs. Acan llwete Co-op society Ltd & anor.
Execution - objector proceedings - whether the objector Bank
could successfully object to the attachment  of a lorry over which
the Bank had a lien.
Held: The execution creditor must first pay off the objector bank's out-
Standing loan so that he can validly seize and attach the lorry over which
the Bank had a lien, because goods pledged by the judgment debtor as
security for a loan cannot be lawfully seized.
H.G. Gandesha & anor Vs. G.J.Lutaya.
Evidence - affidavit in reply - whether failure to file affidavit in reply
means that the other party's evidence stands unchallenged.
Held: The facts as deponed to in the affidavit of the applicant were not
intrinsically incredible and therefore since they were not answered, they
stood unchallenged.
Intraship (U) Ltd Vs. G.M.Combaine (u) Ltd & anor.
Objector Proceedings O.19r55 CPR - whether application can
succeed where auctioneers have already sold the attached property
in execution - whether proceeds of the sale can be surrendered
to objectors.
Res judicata-whether issue was res judicata where parties were
different in the former application.
Held: Objector proceedings under O.19 r 55 CPR, require Court to
investigate the objector's interest in the attached property.  Since the
return on the court's record showed that most of the property attached
had been sold, there was nothing to investigate and application cannot
thereby succeed.
Where property has already been sold in execution an application by an
objector under O.19 r 55 cannot properly be brought before court for an
order that the applicant goes after the proceeds of the sale.
Even if the parties in the prior application were different, since one of the
parties, I.e. the judgment debtor under which applicants are claiming is
still the same, the issue as to whether the applicants should have brought
the suit in the names of the company as their principle since the
applicants were agents, was substantially similar as in the present
application. That issue had been adjudicated upon and it was res judicata.
Osuna Otwani Vs. Abdul Ziwa.
Temporary injunction - whether conditions therefore satisfied.
Held: Even though the applicant had shown that he had a prima facie
case with probability of success in the main suit, the fact that the suit
lorry had already been vandalized would render the order for an injunction
an order in vain since the status quo to be preserved would not serve
any reasonable purpose.  Moreover, the injury suffered in atonable by
way of damages which means that the damage is not irreparable.
Application Dismissed.
Mohamed Yahu Vs. Abdur Khamis.
Temporary injunction triable issues - irreparable damage-
whether an order for temporary injunction may be granted.
Held: There is no rule that the applicant for a temporary injunction must
first establish that he has a prima facie case because this would lead
to the trial of the suit without evidence to establish it.  It is enough to
show that there are triable issues to be investigated on either side and
that the suit was not frivolous.  The applicant had shown that there were
triable issues on either side.
The applicant has proved that he would suffer irreparable damage if the
suit lands were alienated before the final disposal of the main suit
because of his anticipatory concern that should the land be
disposed of, there would be nothing of value in view to compensation.
Robert Byaruhanga Vs. Rukungiri District Administration.
Time O.47r.3 - appeals - taxation of costs whether appeal against
the order of the taxing master was not out of time.
Held: O.47 r 3 provides that where the time for doing any act expires on a
Sunday or other day where offices are closed then the following day shall
be deemed to be the time when the doing of the act is to expire.
therefore it is not valid to exclude all the Sunday as the appellant herein
had done.  Therefore, the appeal was incompetent for being our of time.
Appeal dismissed.
Foods & Beverages Ltd Vs. Isreal Musisi Opoya.
Pleadings - damages for trespass - whether failure to plead
general damages fatal.
Held: The learned trial judge was entitled to hold that conversion and not
been proved because the defendant/appellant had held on to the lorry
with an honest claim or right.
At the time the appellant/defendant seized the lorry it was in premises
after it was cannibalized.  The learned trial judge was therefore entitled to
hold that trespass to the plaintiff's lorry had been proved.
The learned trial judge was entitled to award general damages for
trespass is actionable parse without proof of damage.
Shs. 20 million general damages for trespass would be reduced to
shs. 10 million.
Nicholas Roussos Vs. Gulam Hussen Habib Virani & anor.
Setting a side exparte - judgment - application therefore -
whether under O.9r.9 CPR or O.9r24 - whether these rules may
be relied upon inter changeably - whether same in the both rules-
whether no specific legislation governed the matter.
Held: The trial judge erred in law when she held that there was no
specific legislation governing applications to set aside ex prate
judgments.  The correct position is that there are specific provisions of
the law governing application to set aside ex parte judgments and O.9
r 9 and O.9 r 24 each governed a specific matter.
The learned trial judge erred in holding that the principles involved in rr9
and 24 of the Civil Procedure Rules of O.9 were the same.  The principles
involved are different and the discretion under O. 9 r 10 is unrestricted
but the discretion of court under r 24 is restricted to proving sufficient
cause.
When an applicant under r 24 proves that he was not duly served with
summons to enter appearance or that he was prevented by sufficient
cause from physically appearing when the case came for hearing, it is
mandatory for court to set aside the ex parte judgment.
An applicant under r 9 does not need to prove that he was prevented by
sufficient cause from entering appearance but may prove that his in
allowing or refusing the application to set aside the ex parte judgment
already passed under r.4, 5, 6 or 7.
Seraphin Obwolo Vs. Barclays Bank.
Pleadings - special damages - whether salaries and pension
should be claimed as special damages, particularized and
specifically proved.
Held: An employee on permanent terms is entitled to know charges
against him and to be given an opportunity to give any grounds to
exculpate himself.  In the instant case the bank's summary dismissal of
its permanent member of staff without notice was a breach of natural
justice entitling the plaintiff to be heard.
Moreover, clause 7(a) of the agreement between the plaintiff and the
bank provided that the bank was entitled to dismiss the plaintiff
summarily if the plaintiff was guilty of misappropriating funds but the
wrongful crediting of a customer's account was not misappropriating
bank funds.
Terminal benefits pension unpaid salary, and leave allowance must be
particularized and claimed as special damages.  Therefore, since the
plaintiff did not do this his prayer for these items must fail.
Since the defendant was in breach of agreement, the plaintiff was entitled
to general damages, the equivalent of 4 months pay in lieu of notice.
Fam International Ltd & Ahmed Farah Vs. Mohamed El-Faith.
Pleadings - fraud - whether the defendants plea of fraud in his
counter claim was defective - whether defendant failed to
particularize the items of fraud complained of - whether there was
actual fraud imputable on the appellant.
Framing of issues-after evidence is taken - whether proper-whether a
prayer was not a pleading and therefore could not constitute an issue.
Held: Paragraph 4 of the written statement of defence gave the appellants
sufficient particulars of what fraudulent acts the respondent was alleging
against them, namely the backdating of the incorporation of the first
appellant, with intent to defraud the respondent.
The fraudulent acts complained of were imputable on the second plaintiff/
appellant because he stood to gain from them.
In fraud cases the standard of proof is more than a mere balance of
probability though less than proof beyond reasonable doubt.  The learned
trial judge was alive to this provision of the law when he said that he was
satisfied by the evidence which was more than a balance of probabilities.
Therefore the trial judge applied the correct standard of proof of fraud as
required.
The main ground upon which a court can go behind the certificate of
incorporation is fraud and once fraud is alleged the court is entitled to
extend its enquiry to matters precedent and incidental to registration.
The learned trial judge was therefore correct in going behind the
certificate of incorporation, because a certificate of incorporation may
be impeached on the grounds of fraud.
The learned trial judge erred in making a winding up order of the first
appellant because there was no such application properly before the
court as provided by ss 218 and 224 of the Companies Act.
The failure to gazette and entry of the change of name were two
irregularities in procedure which would not vitiate the change of name
property made.  The trial judge was correct in holding so.
It is always better to frame issues at the beginning of the hearing before
evidence is led so that evidence that is led is guided by the framed issues.
A prayer was not an assertion nor a material statement which one party
must allege or the other must deny to constitute an issue.  The trial judge
was right in holding that the issue as to the appellant's holding out as a
shareholder in the respondent's company was a won issue because, it
only appeared as a prayer.
the respondent could not claim his company's property by an action in
his own name as this would offend against the rule of corporate
personality, since the company that owned the property had its own
independent existence.  The trial judge was correct in refusing the prayer
in the counter claim and was also correct in not granting the order for the
recovery of the property in favour or the plaintiffs because they had not
made that prayer.
Pyarali Abdylla & Sons Vs. Fiba (U) Ltd.
Affidavit - Regulation of Advocates (Professional Conduct)
Regulations S.I 79/77-whether affidavit offended against regulation
8 of the regulations and was thereby defective for depending to
contentious matters.
Temporary injunction-irreparable injury-participation in settlement
negotiations-whether evidence that damages may atone for injury-
whether injury not irreparable.
Temporary injunction -irreparable injury-whether developing the suit
premises was an injury to the premises.
Temporary injunction-national interest-whether protection of national
interest may be ground for rejecting a temporary injunction.
Temporary injunction-balance of convenience-whether balance of
convenience favoured respondent.
Held: Where parties to the suit are available it is desirable that they
themselves swear the relevant affidavits.  However, in the instant case
counsel's affidavit was not defective since he swore to matters that were
within his own knowledge and were not contentious.
Developing the suit premises enhanced their value and it was not an
injury to the premises.
Since the applicants prior to the hearing to this application sought a
settlement, it could not be said that the applicants would suffer
irreparable damage since by so participating it meant that their injury,
as result of the temporary injunction, could be atoned in damages.
It was in the national interest that the construction of a unique building on
the suit premises, should continue, though national interest per se would
not be a ground to grant a temporary injunction.
The balance of convenience favoured the respondents since they had
gone too far in developing the suit premises.
W.E Kiwalabye Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank & anor.
Objector proceedings O.19 rr55,56,57 - whether possession
proved - whether objector proceedings were interlocutory.
Interlocutory proceeding-whether objector proceedings were interlocutory.
Affidavit-hearsay - whether affidavit was defective for deponing to hearsay
matters-whether the disclosure of the source of information cured the
defect-whether objector proceedings were interlocutory and therefore
accompanying affidavit's defect of containing hearsay evidence was cured
by the disclosure of the source of information.
Held: Before court can decide that the veil of corporate personality should
be lifted, there must be facts to assist court concluded that the director
of the company was one and the same with his company.  In this instant
case those facts did not exits.
Fancy Stores Ltd & anor Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Government proceedings Act - statutory notice - failure to file
statutory notice whether fatal.
Pleading - whether WSD pleaded non service of statutory notice.
Held: The defendant having denied the contents of paragraph 25 of the
plaint which alleged that service of the statutory notice had been done, the
service of the statutory notice was an issue.
The suit was barred by law because of non service of the statutory notice
as required by S 1(1) of the Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc./Prov.)
Act 1969 and the plaint must be rejected.
Samson Mayanja Vs. Arisa Musoke & anor.
Parties to the suit - death of one of the defendants - whether
personal representative must be joined.
Held: Before the application to set aside the exparte decree dismissing
the suit may be heard, since the action survived after the death of the
first defendant, the deceased first defendant's personal representative
must be added as co-defendant as required by O.2 r.4 Civil Procedure
Rules.
Joseph Mukisa Vs. Kamagu Muwanga.
Temporary injunction O.37 rr.2(1) of civil procedure Rules -exparte
whether grounds existed for the dispensation of service to the
opposite party.
Held: The order of the learned Chief Magistrate was in error because he
had not considered whether service to the respondent should be dispersed
with.  It was imperative for the Chief Magistrate to decide as per O.37 r.3
whether or not grounds existed for the dispensation of service to the
opposite party before making the interim order of injunction.
Dispensation of service to the opposite party can only be justified if the
service would defeat the purpose of the injunction and if the resultant
injury may not be redeemable.  In the instant case no such evidence had
been led.
Alemayehu Degafa Vs. Kim Buwerman.
Serving summons outside jurisdiction - O.5 rr 23, 27 & 33 CPR -
whether application not proper because defendant not ordinarily
resident in court's jurisdiction.
Held: The rule under which the application was brought requires that the
defendant upon whom service of summons is sought, should be ordinarily
resident within the jurisdiction of the court to which the application is
brought.  The plaintiff's application instead said that the defendant was
resident  in U.K. this was not proper and the application would not
succeed.
The application must stat that the applicant has a good cause of action
which the instant application failed to do.  Application dismissed.
Ebuneiri Waisswa Kafuko, Deceased.
Costs - whether costs should follow the event.
Held: Since the respondent's affidavit was intrinsically false for being
contradictory, court would be inclined to believe the applicant's case that
the respondent was not furnishing accounts and order him to do so.
Since the applicants were successful they would have the costs of the
application.
S.A.Zaver Vs. A.Bamanya.
Amendment of defence - whether amendment could be allowed.
Held: The proposed new defence did not introduce a really new and
different element in the defence which would occasion injustice to the
respondent, therefore the amendment will be allowed.
Nyanza Garage Vs. Attorney General.
Pending suit - s.6 civil procedure Act - whether suit was barred
by another pending suit between the same parties and litigating
under the same cause of action.
Res judicata - S.7 (5) Civil Procedure Act - whether the plaintiff's claim not
having been granted in the previous suit, was thereby refused and the
subsequent suit is barred.
Held: Since the court in previous suit left the determination of the amount
of mesne profits open, the present suit was not res judicata and not
barred by S.7 (5) of the Civil Procedure Act but the present suit was
barred by the previous pending suit in which the same parties litigating
under the same issues, the question of the amount of mesne profits was
left to be determined.
Frederico Sebirumbi Vs. Joseph Konde.
Execution-arrest in execution O.19 r34(1) whether notice to show
cause why arrest should not issue necessary.
Execution - arrest in execution - payment of subsistence- whether
payment of subsistence into court by judgment creditor was a condition
precedent to issuing a warrant of arrest in execution.
Held: O.19 r 34 (1) requires that a judgment debtor is served with the
notice to show cause as a condition precedent to his arrest.  In the
instance case the appellant was arrested and asked to explain why he
should not be detained.  This was irregular and the arrest would be
quashed.
It is mandatory that the decree holder as par O.19 r 36 (1), should pay
into court a sufficient sum for the subsistence of the judgment debtor in
civil prison, before the judgment debtor is committed to civil prison.
This procedure was not adhered to.  Therefore the arrest and detention
in civil prison was unlawful and would be quashed.
Shiv Construction Co. Ltd Vs. Endesha Enterprises Ltd.
Appeals - notice of appeal - filing notice of appeal first in the
High Court - whether appeal incompetent.
Temporary injunction - whether order therefore made on mere suspicion-
whether irreparable loss proved when disputed property is land - whether
balance of convenience proved in favour of the respondent.
Held: Rule 74 of the Supreme Court Rules requires that a notice of appeal
must first be lodged in the court of Appeal.  In the instant case even if the
notice of appeal was first lodged in the Supreme Court, it was later lodged
in the High Court within time.  Therefore the appeal was competent.
The learned trial judge was correct in ordering a temporary injunction
against alimentation because the property in dispute was land in disputes
over land damages are usually not sufficient as compensation.  This
meant that the respondent/plaintiff would suffer irreparable injury if the
injunction did not issue. Appeal dismissed.
National Union of Clerical, Commercial & Technical
Employees Vs. National Insurance Corporation.
Inherent powers to the High Court - whether invocable when
specific remedy provided.
Preliminary objection-whether court may defer ruling on a preliminary
objection.
Held: The question whether a court should invoke its inherent powers in a
given case is a matter for the court's discretion to be exercised judicially
and the availability of an alternative remedy or specific provision is only
one of the factors to be taken into account, but does not limit or remove
the court's jurisdiction.  Therefore, the learned trial judge did not error in
exercising his discretion to invoke the High Court's inherent powers under
S.101 CPA even though there was a specific remedy provided.
The learned trial judge erred with he deferred ruling on the preliminary
objection and proceeded to hear the application on its merits and ruled on
the merits and preliminary objection at the same time.  The judge should
have ruled on the preliminary objection but deferred the reasons to be
given with merits of the application.
National Insurance Corporation Vs. National Union of Clerical
Commercial Professional & Technical Employees.
Cross application - whether cross application was not properly
before court because was founded on merely affidavits in reply.
Held: 8(1) of the Trades Disputes (Arbitration and Settlement) Act allows
the applicant to apply to the Industrial Court to interpret its award within
28 days from the date of the award.  Therefore notwithstanding S.11 of the
same Act that requires gazetting, the applicants application to interpret
the Industrial Court's award before it was gazetted was proper since it
was done within 28 days as required by s.8(1) of the Act
The Industrial Court was empowered like any ordinary court to review is
own decisions while exercising its powers to interpretation under S.11 of
the Act.
The failure by the Industrial Court not to allow cross examination of the
witness on a new piece of evidence was not proper and it was a breach
of natural justice.  But, it did not occasion a miscarriage of justice since
the applicant's complaint was merely the procedure by which the
respondent had applied to Industrial court for the interpretation of the award
instead of applying to the High Court for certiorari.
Hannigton Wasswa & anor Vs. Maria Onyango Ochola & 3 ors.
Appeals - jurisdiction - whether court of appeal can grant players
of which the decree court had no jurisdiction.
Limitation S.3 of the Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc Provisions) Act
court broker - whether a court broker was a public officer and therefore
the action against him was time barred by S.3 of the Act.
Limitation - fraud-whether the action against the court broker was not time
barred because of fraud.
Notice of motion-suit-whether commencement of a suit by notice of
motion to prove fraud against a court broker acting in execution of a court
order was proper.
joinder of parties - court broker and auction purchaser - whether these
may be sued jointly.
Held: S.8(2) of the Civil Procedure Act only empowers the court  of appeal
to perform only the duties conferred on the court of first instance, the
court of original jurisdiction.  In the present case the Chief Magistrate's
Court as court of first instance to order for the cancellation of certification
of Title.  The appellate therefore had not jurisdiction to order for the
cancellation of the certificate of Title.
S.3 of the Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Prov) Act 10/69 requires
that any action brought against a public officer challenging any act done
in execution of his public duty, be brought within six months next after
the act being challenged.  Since a court broker was a public officer
executing a public duty, the action against him brought in 1982 was time
barred.
Even if it court be said that since the action brought against the court
broker was based on fraud, then time started running when the fraud
could have been discovered.  According to the facts of the case, the
alleged fraud must have been discovered by May 1981 and yet the motion
on notice was brought in September 1982 which was definitely out of time.
it was not proper to commence proceedings to challenge the alleged acts
of fraud by notice of motion because the standard of proof of fraud must
be high.  This therefore requires an ordinary suit where witnesses may be
cross examined.
A court broker is an agent of the court and not an agent or the parties.
Therefore it is necessary that the court broker should be sued separately.
Wycliffe Kiyingi Vs. Augustine Kajuna.
Pleadings - representative capacity O.7 r 4 CPR whether plaintiff
must plead that he possesses letters of Administration or
probate to show his representative capacity.
Pleadings-fraud O.6 r2-whether plaintiff failed to plead particulars of fraud-
whether therefore the plaintiff's suit had no probability, of success and
therefore no temporary injunction would issue.
Temporary injunction-probability of success of suit-whether suit would not
succeed because of failure to provide particulars of fraud.
Held: Where a litigant sues in representative capacity it is required by
O.7 r4 CPR for him to plead that he possesses letters of administration or
probate, if he is representing the estate of the deceased.
Particulars of fraud and dates thereof must be pleaded failing which, even
if fraud if pleaded, no evidence be lead to prove it.  The applicant/plaintiff
suit therefore could not succeed.
Since fraud at the trial would not be proved because particulars thereof
were not pleaded, the applicant/plaintiff's suit had no probability of
success and therefore the application for temporary injunction could not
succeed.
Ugantico Supermarket Vs. Registrar of Titles & 2 ors.
Temporary injunction - serious triable issues whether the issue as
to whether the suit lands had developments thereon was a triable issue.
Temporary injunction-irreparable damage-whether construction works on
the suit land enhanced its value therefore it was irreparable damage.
Held: It was apparent that there were serious issues of law and fact to
be determined in the main suit, particularly whether or not the applicant had
developments on the suit land or not at the time its certificate of title was
cancelled and the land reallocated.
It is not necessarily correct to say that construction of buildings on the
suit property enhances its value and therefore no (irreparable) damage is
caused.  Each case must be looked at on its own facts.  In the present
case the applicant wanted to construct a supermarket and yet the
respondents want residents want residential houses.  And yet it is not
always easy to find the desired spot for a supermarket.  Therefore, the
applicant would suffer irreparable damage is the injunction were not
granted. Applicant for a temporary injunction allowed.
Oriental Insurance Brokers Vs. Transocean (U) Ltd.
Issue - agreed issues - whether court may on own volition go
beyond agreed issues.
Pleadings-departure-whether in a claim for unpaid premium evidence of
unpaid insurance commission is a departure.
Held: Court is not limited only to issues agreed upon by the parties but
was free to go beyond them where the agreed issues do not go to the
crux of the matter to be resolved.  Court in this case would therefore
formulate its own issues.
The plaintiff was entitled to be paid a commission in percentage terms, on
every item of a paid premium.  However, the plaintiff brought suit in its
pleadings for the recovery of unpaid premiums.  The plaintiff brought suit in
its pleadings for the recovery of unpaid premiums.  The plaintiff instead led
evidence at the trial to prove its unpaid commission.  This was a departure
from its pleadings and would not be allowed where no amendment of the
pleadings was done.
The plaintiff had not proved that there existed a custom or practice
entitling a broker to sue the insured for unpaid premiums where the
insurer had defaulted on the payment thereof.
Even if it could be said that the plaintiff insurance brokerage firm was an
agent of the insurer as principal, it was not legally possible for an agent
to institute a suit in its own name on behalf of the principal without the
principal's authority. Case dismissed.
Specioza Nassuna Vs. Kampala City Council.
Withdrawal of suit - terms of discontinuance - whether since leave
to withdraw was sought during hearing the suit a term that no new
action should brought should be imposed - O.22r(1) & (2).
Held: O.22 r(2) requires that a plaintiff wishing to discontinue her suit
after the hearing has commenced must do so with leave of court and court
is empowered to impose terms such as payment of costs and barring
further suit.  In the instant suit, the plaintiff sought leave to discontinue her
suit when hearing had commenced.  Therefore, court would give the leave
upon the plaintiff's payment of costs of the suit and the barring of further suit.
Makerere University Vs. St. Mark Education Institute Ltd & ors.
Affidavit no opposing affidavit - whether thereby application stands
unchallenged.
Affidavit -no authority to swear affidavit on behalf of another - whether
therefore affidavit is defective -O.3 r2(9).
Affidavit -falsehood-whether an affidavit that contains lies in untenable and
defective.
Held: In a application proceeding by evidence supplied by affidavit, where
there is no opposing affidavit, the application stands unchallenged.  And
this was the case here.
However, the unchallenged application must intrinsically be tenable on its
own.  In this case the application was grounded on an affidavit sworn on
behalf of others where the deponent did not show that he had authority to
swear the said affidavit on their behalf.  The application was therefore
untenable with regard to the other co-applicants.
An affidavit that contains lies and untruths cannot be relied upon.  In the
instant case the applicant/deponent deponed in his affidavit to the effect
that he was a co-administrator to the estate of the original owner of the
suit land and yet the letters of Administration did not refer to him at all.
the was a clear falsehood that would render the affidavit defective and
unreliable.
Since the plaintiff is the dominus limits in a very suit he cannot compelled
to sue a person he does not wish to sue.  Therefore the application to be
added as defendants in this case was wrong and would not be allowed.
Polycarp Sekiboobo Vs. Clare Obonya.
Appeals - dismissal of appeal r 93(4) RSC - whether tenable.
Held: The application was incompetent and untenable because the
original appeal was still pending since a registrar (of the Supreme Court)
had no powers to dismiss an appeal. Application dismissed with costs.
Bob Ludu Vs. Multiline Suppliers.
Preliminary objection O.6 r27 CPR - whether sustainable when not
pleaded in written statement of defence.
Held: This was not the type of matter where a preliminary point of law
would be raised without prior pleading in the Written Statement of
Defense because the question of illegality or otherwise of the contract
was not apparent on the face of the record and was not among the agreed
issues not agreed upon by the parties.
Attorney General Vs. Milton Obote Foundation.
Inherent powers of court s.101 CPA-Application for leave to appeal
to supreme court - whether inherent powers of court may not be
invoked where matter was improperly before court.
Held: S.101 CPS for courts exercise of its inherent powers is not
invocable where a matter is not properly before court, or where the remedy
sought is barred by limitation.  In the instant case the application was
time barred and was thereby improperly before court.
Resty Nantongo Vs. David Kayondo.
Interim injunction - discharge thereof equitable owner of land
against the lessee should be discharged.
Held: The plaintiff respondent had not even attempted to challenge the
existence of the lease of the appellant herein.  The lease therefore
sidestepped the issue as to who of the parties had purchased the land.
The lessee had legal title as lessee and yet the respondent/plaintiff had
no title at all but could only claim in equity.
The plaintiff respondent failed to show such a case as would be the basis
upon which court should interfere with an admitted legal rights to the lease
in favor of merely alleged equitable right of the purchaser without transfer.
Therefore, the learned trial judge erred in granting the order for an interim
injunction when the applicant had not shown substantial grounds for
denoting the existence of the respondent/appellant's legal right to the
lease in the suit property.  Therefore the interim injunction would be
discharged.  Appeal allowed.
Famous Cycle Agency Ltd &ors Vs. Manshulular Ramji &2ors.
Interpleader - O.31rr1+2 - adverse claims for rent by different land-
lords - whether the proper procedure was by inter-pleader u/o.31rr
1&2 CPR.
Held: O.3 r2(a), (b) and ( c) provides that a litigant that claims no interest
in the subject matter of the suit but is merely concerned with court's
directions as to which of the various claimants he should make the
required satisfaction, then the proper procedure is by interpleader.
Therefore, in the instant case since the tenants/plaintiffs were interested
in knowing as to whom to pay rent, they should have bought the suit by
way of interpleader.
S.58 of the Registration of Titles Act provides that a Certificate of Title is
conclusive evidence of ownership.  In the instant case it was the first
defendant who had a Certificate Title in his names and was therefore the
owner of the suit property to whom rent must be paid.
G.M Combined Vs. A.K.Detergents.
Leave to appeal- informed leave R 39(A) 12c - formal o.40 r1 (4)
CPR - whether o.40 r1(4) Controls the procedure when applying for
leave or whether r.39(a) Rsc controls the application.
Citing wrong rule-striking out application - whether the citing of a wrong
rule should lead to the striking of the application.
Held: It was clear that when counsel for the applicant/plaintiff cited 0.40
42 CPR in an application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against
the order for security for costs, he did not mean to cite that particular rule
because that particular rule had nothing to do with the application.  He
must have meant 0.40 r1(2) CPR since it was the specific rule that dealt
with the requirement for leave of court to appeal.  This misunderstanding
by counsel should have been put right since the actual provision of the
law was known, so as not to embarrass or prejudice the parties
concerned. The bench and the bar are bound to give the parties their best
consideration so as to avoid ignorance of law from adversely affecting them.
The party making an application for leave to appeal to the Supreme court
has the choice to apply informally immediately after the order of the lower
court under O.39(a) RSC or formally under O.40 r1(4). The choice is with
the applicant.  The respondent or court can only oppose the merits of the
application.  Therefore, it was misdirection on the part of the learned judge
to have refused applicant counsel's informal application for leave.
Application allowed with costs against the respondent.
Uganda Commercial Bank Vs. Kyagambiddwa Growers Ltd.
Objector proceedings O.19r55-action for ejectment s.184 RTA -
whether a respondent in objector proceedings may rely on fraud
without a specific action for ejectment.
Held: Allegations of fraud were only appropriate in an action for ejectment
under S.184 of the Registration of Titles Act.  The instant proceedings
were merely objector proceedings in which it was not possible to impeach
the registered proprietor/objector's title.
Uganda Oxygen Ltd & 2 Ors. Vs. Salim Jam & ors.
Appeal against order by the registrar - appeal without leave -
whether appeal was not properly before court O.46 rr 7 + 8.
Consent order-appeal against consent order entered by the Registrar
was not an order but merely an extract and therefore not appealable,
since right of appeal was a creature of statute.
Held: When Registrar entered the consent to withdraw he acted as a
civil court U/046 r 6 Car and therefore the consent was an order and not
merely an extract.
While it is true that a right of appeal is a creature of statute, 0.46 r8 under
which the present appeal was filed was a rule of law that made orders
entered by the Registrar appealable.
S.80 (1) CPA, the proviso thereto is a substantive provision to the effect
that no leave is required to accept an appeal as valid without leave having
first been sought for the enlargement of time to appeal, as long as there is
good cause.  In the instant case the contradictory decisions made by the
management of the respondent was good cause for court to base its
decision to allow the appeal as validly before it without leave having first
been sought for the enlargement of time.
George Paul Emenyu & anor Vs. Attorney General.
Party to the suit - plaintiff not registered over a suit vehicle
whether therefore plaintiff could not sue for damage.
Held: The sale agreement established that the plaintiff was the owner of
the suit motor vehicle since it was common knowledge that vehicles are
sold but the transfers thereof take time much later.
If a motor vehicle swerves to the wrong side of the road and causes an
accident, the driver must explain how his position on the wrong side was
consistent with reasonable care on his part.  In the case instant, the
defendant failed to discharge this burden and the logical conclusion is
that he failed in his duty of care to other road users and was thereby
liable negligence.
A person is guilty of contributory negligence if he ought reasonably to
have foreseen that if he did not act as reasonable prudent man he might
hurt himself and he must take into account that others may be careless.
In the instant case the first plaintiff who was the driver swerved further left
from his lane to avoid the defendant's motor vehicle which came wobbling
towards his side of the road.  Therefore the plaintiff's driver acted
prudently to avoid the accident.
Shs. 8, million would be paid by the defendant as replacement value of
the motor vehicle damaged repair.  Further shs.42 million would be paid
as lost income for none use of the plaintiff's mini-bus for four years.
George William Katatumba Vs. Uganda Co-operative
Transport Union Ltd.
Pleading - O.6r 1 CPR - local currency whether pleadings must be
invariably in Uganda currency or must state minister's permission to
convert currency.
Held: Annexure "F" had supported paragraphs 5 and 6 of the plaint when
it stated that fees ware to be paid in Uganda shillings at the reigning forex
rate at time of shillings the claims in paragraphs 5 and 6.  therefore the
learned trial judge erred when he held that annexure 'F' was not part of
the plaint.
Judgment may be allowed in foreign currency.  Therefore the learned trial
judge erred in holding that claims in foreign currency are unenforceable in
law because of illegality.  The Foreign Exchange Control Act did not
prohibit ab-initio the payment in foreign currency but provided that the
minister's permission must be sought.  So, judgment could still be made
awarding the claimed amount in foreign currency but require the Decree
holder to seek ministerial license to that effect.
Yahaya Kariisa Vs. Attorney General & anor.
Adjournment - judicial discretion to refuse or allow adjournment
whether exercised judiciously.
Held: Court has discretion to allow or refuse an adjournment but the
discretion must be exercised judiciously.  Discretion is the faculty of
determining in accordance with the circumstances what seems just fair,
right equitable and reasonable in the given set of circumstances.  In the
instant case the alleged series of adjournments should have been put into
their proper context.  Had this been done court would have concluded that
the previous adjournments were all justified and should not have been the
basis upon which the court should have exercised its discretion to refuse
this particular adjournment.  Therefore the learned trial judge misdirected
herself when she failed to pout the previous adjournment in their context
and thus injudiciously exercised her discretion to disallow the
adjournment.
Bosa & Co. Advocate Vs. Vero Nassanga & ors.
Pleadings - undue influence whether undue influence must be
pleaded with particulars.
Costs-costs in probate action whether may not follow the event.
Held: In deciding upon the capacity of a testator to make a Will it is the
soundness mind and not the particular state of the bodily health that is to
be considered.  In the instant case, the deceased's mental power could
have been reduced below the ordinary standard by his illness, yet he was
seized with the requisition intelligence to understand and appreciate the
testamentary act he had undertaken and accomplished.
Undue influence or duress is when the testator is induced to make
disposition, which he did, not really intend to make even where force is not
used or threatened.  When pressure of whatever nature is exerted on the
testator as to overpower his own volition without convincing his judgment.
The defendant had not proved that the testator's widow had brought such
pressure upon the testator.  It was not enough for them to show that the
widow had power to unduly press the testator.  It must positively be
shown that she exercised power or pressure.
Moreover the burden of proof of the existence of undue influence lay on
the party alleging the same.  The defendant had not discharged it.
Thirdly the defendant were supposed to have pleaded particulars of
respective acts of undue influence complained or, with necessary dates,
which they did not.  This is because undue influence must be positively
proved and not merely assumed.
Where the testator or those interested in the residue have been the cause
of the litigation, for instance where in the testator used words that were
difficult to understand and required construction by the courts for such
litigation will be paid out of the estate.  In the case before us, the
defendants that the testator's Will was made under undue influence, with-
out attempting reasonably to prove their allegations.  Therefore the two
defendants should be ordered to pay the costs of the whole action.
Suit allowed defendant to pay costs of suit.
Gaso Transport service (Bus) Ltd Vs. Martin Abdala Obene.
Amendment of pleadings O.6r 18 amendment after close -
whether too belated and untenable.
Held: The more advanced the proceedings are, the greater the burden
upon the applicant who seeks leave to amend to prove to court that the
leave ought to be granted. However, court should be more inclined to
allow the amendment of the defect in a pleading rather than give
judgment in ignorance of facts which ought to be known before rights
are definitely decided.  In the instant case the amendment ought to have
been allowed to show whether it was the appellant who owned the bus
or some other similarly called company.  After all the amendment would
not prejudice the other party.
Nile Bank Ltd Vs. Akalu Enterprises.
Summary suit O.33rr3 & 4 - triable issue - whether application for
leave to appear and defend the suit may be granted on grounds
that the loan contract had been frustrated because the money
was borrowed for the export of beans but government had subse-
gently imposed a ban on the exportation of beans.
Held: Since the defendant applicant in substance admitted the claim but
contested the amount not subtracted, which he had repaid, there was no
need for the defendant to appear and defend the suit.  The defendant
should pay the loan amount claimed by the plaintiff less the amount
repaid.
Secondly since the defendant had repaid some money and further
negotiated a rescheduling of the loan repayment his action were
inconsistent with a frustrated contract where the loss ought to lie where
it fell.  Application dismission with costs.
Sarah Nakabate Serubugo Vs. Robina Nakidali Kibebere & 3 ors.
Pleadings O.6 R2 - particulars of fraud - whether plaintiff had not
given particulars of fraud and therefore could not prove it.
Held: Although the plaintiff did not explicitly plead non est. factum, it was
clear that her claim was based thereto as she pleaded that she had
signed documents presented to her by her daughter who had informed her
that the purpose of the documents was to help her daughter the daughter
the defendant to collect the plaintiff had successfully pleaded non est
factum.
While locally there is no standard form precedents for pleadings,
particularly the pleading of fraud, and resort is often had to English
precedents, particulars of fraud may nevertheless be found sufficiently
given in any pleading even if a particular format has not been adhered to.
In the instant case the plea that the defendant had informed the plaintiff
that she should sign the documents she had given her to enable the
defendant collect the certificate of title from Mukono Land Officer,
whereas, the plaintiff was in effect signing a transfer and consent
S.184 Registration of Titles Act empowers court to order the cancellation
of a Certificate of Title where fraud has been proved as the cause for a
contested dealing in land.  In the instant case fraud had been sufficiently
proved and cancellation of the Certificate of Title would be ordered.
Case allowed Order of Cancellation of Certificate given.
Intraship (u) Ltd Vs. G.M Combined (u) Ltd.
Inherent powers of court - citation of a wrong rule - whether court
may use it's discretionary power to entertain an application where
a wrong rule was cited.
Held: It is true that the application was wrongly before court because the
law cited, i.e. S.352 (1) Companies Act and O.34A r 6 Civil Procedure
Rules concerned themselves with a situation where receivers had been
appointed and yet the application before court was for stay of execution
and the setting aside of the decree.  However, the citing of a wrong rule
does not in itself bar the court from using its discretion to entertain the
merits of the matter where it is shown that no injustice would result.
But in the instant application the matters were so confusing and were not
clear even to the applicant than tit would be unjust to entertain the
application where the pleadings were unclear and unpredictable.
Application dismissed.
Loi Bagyenda & anor Vs. Loyce Kikunja Bagyenda.
Suit by minor - next friend - whether a 19 year old co-applicant for
grant of letters of administration without a next friend rendered the
application a nullity even if the other joint applicant was an adult.
Misjoinder of parties-striking out improperly joined party O.1 r 10(2) CPR-
whether application untenable because the joinder of a minor without a
next friend was a fatal defect.
Held: The striking off of one of the parties for misjoinder does not render
the suit a nullity as long as the removal of the party leaves the cause of
action intact.  In the instant case the party seeking to be removed was a
son of the co-plaintiff albeit, a minor for purposes of succession but the
co-plaintiff mother was entitled in her own right to the grant to Letters of
Administration.  Therefore the removal of the son from the suit would leave
the case of action intact.
Application allowed but counsel to pay costs personally.
Aloysius Tibamanya Vs. Januario Tibamanya.
Temporary injunction - O.37rr1,2, & 9 CPR whether fatally defective
because brought by notice of motion.
Notice of motion - chamber summons - whether temporary injunction may
be applied for by Notice of Motion.
Affidavit-source of information - whether affidavit defective of failure to state
source of information.
Held: The application was wrongly before court since the application for a
temporary injunction must be by chamber summons.  In the instance
case the application was by notice of motion which rendered it defective.
The applicant's affidavit was defective for failure to disclose his source of
information when his affidavit was about information.
Application dismissed.
Joyce Kasule Kweguya Vs. Apollo Matovu & 3 ors.
Fraud O.6 r2 CPR swearing statutory declaration that duplicate
certificate of title is lost by a person other than the administrator -
whether evidence of fraud.
Held: Though the deceased died intestate, he died testate to the extent
that the Will did not define the property it purported to devise to the
beneficiaries.
No trust was created because the Will never defined the property the
subject of the trust.  Since no trust was created the first defendant was
free to make a statutory declaration of the loss of the duplicate Certificate
of Title pursuant to s.67 RTA.  This section allowed any person to make
a statutory declaration. Case dismissed with costs.
Charles Acire Vs. Mary Anne Engola.
Interlocutory judgment - application to set a side interlocutory
judgment O.9 r9, O.47 r1 civil procedure rules - whether this
invariably includes setting a side exparte final judgment.
Held: Since the applicant had not applied to set aside the final exparte
judgment but merely only the interlocutory judgment the application was
intenable because the interlocutory judgment was merely a step to the
final exparte judgment which was not the subject of this application.
Application struck out with costs.
Silas Majyambere Vs. Cargolux (u) & anor.
Right to begin - O.16 r3, 55, 100 & 101 evidence Act - whether
where the plaintiff sued for breach of contract and the defendant
alleged lack of title, the defendant was enjoined to begin first and
prove lack of title.
Held: According to O.16r3, where there are issues that burden of proving
some of which lies not on the plaintiff but the defendant, the plaintiff is
still required to begin his case but in so doing the plaintiff has an option
to elect not to lead evidence on some of those other issues to be proved
that the defendant so that the plaintiff only replies thereto.  This rule does
not take away the plaintiff's obligation to prove his case under ss.100 and
101 Evidence Act.  Plaintiff ordered to begin his case.
David Kayondo Vs. Resty Nantongo.
Adding a defendant to the proceeding s.O.1 r10 (2) and 13…and13 civil
procedure Rules - whether court can add a defendant to theanother defendant
Held: A plaintiff cannot be forced to sue a party he does not wish to sue.
Therefore the application was misconceived.
Application dismissed with costs.
Gabriel Njaukana Vs. Attorney General.
Ex-parte proceeding - reversal or order thereto - whether thereby
other consequent orders stand reversed.
Held: When the order allowing the plaintiff to proceed exparte was
reversed, it put both parties in their original position, logically meaning
that the order allowing the plaintiff to proceed outside the limitation period
was reversed too.  Therefore the preliminary objection as to limitation was
properly raised.
The plaintiff had not proved that he was prevented by disability to institute
the suit in time because the disability claimed occurred outside the
limitation.  Suit dismissed with costs.
Jocelyn Barugare Vs. Attorney General.
Framing of issues O.13 rr1-5 -whether only parties to the suit must
frame issues and court is bound thereto.
Held: The procedure of framing issues is provided for under O.13 rr 1-5 of
the Civil Procedure Rules.  The parties to the suit may frame agreed
issues before or after evidence is taken and court may opt to adopt
parties' agreed issues but it is the duty to the court to frame issues which
in its opinion from the basis upon which the right decision of the case
depends.
This means that court must consult the parties as to what are the issues
in controversy interprets but inspite of the consultation court ultimately
must decide which issues whether those frame and agreed upon by the
parties or framed by it are the basis upon which the right decision of the
case depends.  If in the opinion of the court the agreed issues by the
parties are not sufficient for a proper finding of the case then court will
