frame its own issues or strike out some or vary some at any stage of the
proceedings before passing judgment.
Sarah Kawino Vs. Rutaisire.
Non suit of plaintiff - contract based on an unproved document -
whether plaintiff non-suited.
Held: Neither party was able to prove the contract they alleged was made
and the contractual intentions of the parties cannot be ascertained.
Therefore the plaintiff was non-suited as she failed to prove her case.
Case dismissed.
W. Nuwemugizi Vs. National Water & Sewerage Corporation.
Pleadings - written statement of defence - whether because the
written statement of Defence never pleaded lawful termination
judgment could not be based on it.
Held: The learned trial Judge misdirected himself on the evidence when he
held that the plaintiff/appellant had accepted voluntary retirement.  The
acceptance of the emoluments as suggested in the letter the defendant
did not mean that the plaintiff had accepted to retire voluntarily.  There
was evidence that the plaintiff wanted the contrary situation but the
Managing Director showed him that he could not change the decision of
the Board of the defendant.
Moreover, the terms of service of the defendant stipulated that where a
given situation was not adequately covered by the Terms of Service
Regulations, recourse should be had to the Government standing Orders.
It happens that the terms of service of the defendant did not provide the
procedure for voluntary retirement and therefore resort must be had to the
Government Standing Orders, 1968 chapter one, regulation one, which
provides that an officer cannot voluntarily retire until he applied for the
purpose and acceptance therefore given.  In the instant case the
appellant never applied for voluntary retirement.  Therefore the trial Judge
misdirected himself on the law when he held that the appellant had
voluntarily retired.
The defendant/respondent never pleaded in its Written Statement of
Defence that the plaintiff/appellant had had his contract of service
terminated.  However, the same was framed as an issue for trial and the
plaintiff never protested.  Evidence thereafter was led and the issue was
resolved on the evidence.  Therefore since the plaintiff never objected to
the issue being framed at all nor evidence being led to prove the issue the
irregularity of lack of pleading had been cured.  The learned trial Judge
was entitled to hold that the plaintiff's contract of employment had been
terminated.
Godfrey Muyonjo & anor Vs. The Registered Trustees of
Namirembe Diocese.
Setting a side exparte judgment - exparte judgment entered
under O.9 r3 - whether this ground for setting a side expart
judgement.
Held: The interlocutory judgment entered under O.9 r3 CPR was illegal
and void as it was entered under a wrong rule.  The judgment would
therefore be set aside.  Appeal allowed.
William Mufumu Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority.
Costs - payment of costs by counsel may pay costs personally
for ill - advising the plaintiff to file an unsustainable suit.
Held: S.12 of the Uganda Revenue Authority Statute provides that the
Uganda  Revenue Authority Board shall be responsible for recruitment of
the Authority's staff.  The District Revenue Officer therefore had no
authority to recruit the plaintiff as an employee of the defendant.
Therefore the plaintiff was not recognized as an employee of the defendant
and his suit for damages for  wrongful dismissal was unsustainable.
The facts of the case were such that there was no reasonable cause why
the plaintiff had been advised to file the suit.  Therefore his counsel would
be personally liable for the payments of the costs.
Fatuma Osman Hussein Vs. Mahendra Umadbai Patel.
Parties to a suit O.1 r3 - whether a person against whom the
plaintiff has no claim and does not desire to prosecute can be
joined as a co-defendant.
Held: O. 1 r.3 has no application to a situation where a person whose
legal rights will be directed affected by the granting of the relief claimed
goes to court asking to be joined as a defendant.
Even if the application in question was brought under O.1 r.10(2), r the rule
rule required that the defendant to be added must be a defendant against
whom the plaintiff has some cause of complaint which ought to be
determined in the suit.  It was never intended to apply where a person to
be determined in the suit. It was never intended to apply where a person
to be added as a defendant is a person against whom the plaintiff has no
claim and does not desire to prosecute.
Application dismissed.
Isaac Bishari T/A Isaac Trading store Vs. Vitafoam (u) Ltd.
Costs - taxation of costs - whether Ush 8 million as institution fees
was manifestly excessive and should be reduced.
Held: An appellate court will not interfere with an assessment of costs by
the taxing master unless he has misdirected himself on a matter of
principle and manifestly excessive and extravagant assessment may
result in the interference of a misdirection of principle.
In the instant case the appeal lasted only one morning, and counsel for
the respondent only did the barrister's work of arguing the appeal but the
appeal was prepared and filed by another advocate and only one point of
law was involved which was easily disposed off by the justices who heard
the appeal.  Therefore, the figure of Ush 8 million was manifestly high and
was of misdirection in principle and should be reduced to Ush 2.5 million
appeal allowed with costs.
Birumi Wilson Vs. Akamba (u) Ltd
Adjournment - O.15 r1-whether injudiciously refused.
Held: The Uganda Contract Act came into force on 1st January 1963 and
S.2 thereof ceases the application of the Indian Contract Act to contracts
in Uganda and S.3 (1) thereof provides the application of the Common Law
of England relating to contracts.  The learned trial judge in the case
instant based his decision on the Common Law doctrine that no suit can
be entertained against a stranger to the contract.  The trial judge
considered the common law doctrines of offer acceptance and
consideration and found that there was no contract between the appellant
and the respondent.  Therefore, even if the Judge cited Parker's case, he
relied on the Common Law Doctrines of Contract.
Under the adversarial system, where parties are represented by counsel,
it would be extremely rare for a trial Judge on his own motion to order the
joining or substitution of a third party to the proceedings.  Therefore, the
learned trial Judge did not err in not considering the joining of Messey
Ferguson (UK) Ltd as co-defendant.
The Court of Appeal will interfere with the exercise of discretion of the trial
Judge in refusing an adjournment if the result of his exercise of discretion
in refusing the adjournment will occasion injustice.  In the instant case
counsel for the plaintiff applied for adjournment without specifically
disclosing the purpose, his application being vague and half hearted and
the trial Judge was justified in refusing the adjournment.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Yozefu Kashongorize Vs. China Sichuan Corporation.
Application for adjournment - whether application by letter is
acceptable by court.
Held: It is practice that any advocate has to seek adjournment of his case,
he must brief a colleague to hold a brief and seek adjournment on his
behalf.  Application for adjournment by letter is not accepted mode of
applying for adjournment.
There is enough evidence on record to prove that 3936 trees belonging to
the plaintiff were uprooted by the defendant. Considering the fact the
young trees and old stumps were uprooted with no chance of young trees
sprouting from the cut stumps, an estimated price of Ush 5, 000/= per
tree would be adequate compensation.
Regarding the soil, which was removed, this item was not proved on the
balance of probabilities.  It was not enough to write down the particulars.
The onus of proof was on the plaintiff to prove by calling quality surveyors
to tell how much soil had been removed and the value thereof.  The claim
for soil, stones, murram therefore fails.
Judgment is accordingly given in favour of the plaintiff and the defendant
is ordered to pay Ush 19, 640,000/= special damages plus costs of costs
of the suit.
Yokoyakimu Mwene Habyene Vs. Attorney General
Survival of causes of action - false imprisonment - whether false
imprisonment may survive as a cause of action.
Held: Since the plaintiff's son was dead the father was entitled to continue
the proceedings on behalf of the son's estate.  Even though the plaintiff's
pleadings were affected by bonafide mistake, since the plaintiff was not
represented, it was unnecessary for court not to be stifled by
technicalities and to let substantive justice take its cause.
The plaintiff could not maintain a cause of action on his own behalf for
damages for travel and subsistence expenses incurred by him while
seeking the release of his son.  This is because Art. 15 of the Constitution
provided only for a cause of action for unlawful imprisonment to be brought
by the person imprisoned or for his estate in case of his death.
Appeal allowed-file re-submitted to the trial court for assessment
damages.
Francis Micah Vs. Nuwa Walalira.
Appeal - service of notice of Appeal on persons directly affected by
the appeal r 76(1) S.C.R whether mandatory.
Execution - court bailiff - whether court complaint against excess
execution should be filed u/s 35(1) and (2) Civil Procedure Act as an
interlocutory proceeding and not by a fresh separate suit-whether
executing court bailiff may be joined with judgment creditor in a
complaint against excess execution.
Execution-court bailiff-whether court bailiff was a representative of the
judgment creditor or court for purposes of execution - whether the
judgment creditor was responsible for the acts of the court bailiff.
Held: R. 76 (1) of the RSC is mandatory.  An intending appellant must
serve copies of the notice of appeal on all persons directly affected by the
appeal.  In the instant case the appellant should have served the copy of
the notice of appeal on the Court bailiff since he had been party to the
proceedings in the court below and would there by be affected by the
results of the appeal.  However, since the appellant refrained from taking
any further step in respect of the court bailiff, the present appeal would
not be decided basing on that objection.
O. 19 rr8 to 11 Civil Procedure Rules illustrate the point that it is the
Judgment Creditor who initiates the process of execution and it is the
Judgment Creditor who points out to the Court bailiff is an officer of court,
he is the representative of the Judgment Creditor to the extent of excess
attachment, since it is he who directs to him the kind of property to be
attached.  In the instant case the respondent was responsible for the
excess attachments done by the court bailiff and was therefore a rightful
party to be shed under S.35 (1) Civil Procedure Act in the suit complaining
of excessive attachment.
S. 35 (1) Civil Procedure Act requires that all matters relating to
execution be determined by the court executing the Decree and not by a
separate suit.  The case of Hanningtone Wasswa & Anor Vs,. Maria
Onyango Ochola & 3 Ors SCCA 22/93 which started that the Court
Bailiff should be sued separately, should distinguished from S.35 (1)
C.P.A. because the case of Wasswa dealt with a prayer for damages for
fraud against the court bailiff.  The application complaining of excess
attachment was rightfully brought under S.35 (1) in this instant case by
motion.
Application allowed and motion remitted to the lower court for hearing.
Hadija Nakibuuka Vs. Attorney General.
Issues - frame of issues O.13 r 1(1),(2),(3),(4) and (5) C.P.R
whether when a matter is not framed as an issue it means that
the defendant has admitted the material proposition by the plaintiff.
Held: An issue as per O.13 r 1 (1) CPR is a material proposition of law or
fact affirmed by the one party and denied by6 the other.  Since the
defendant/respondent in his Written Statement of Defence denied that the
accident happened when the same had been arrested as having happened
by the plaintiff/appellant, it was an issue have framed it as an issue did
not mean it was not an issue to be determined by court whether or not the
accident happened.  The failure to have framed it as an issue did not mean
it was not an issue to be determined by court.  And the learned trial
Judge was correct in dodging that the plaintiff/appellant had not proved
that the accident happened.
The trial Judge was correct to find that the plaintiff had failed to prove that
she had been married to that deceased because according to her evidence
she had got married to the deceased in 1966 when she was 11 years old,
which was not  possible.
The failure by the plaintiff/appellant to produce the alleged dependants of
the deceased in Court meant that there was no sufficient evidence
before Court for a conclusion that the alleged dependants existed and as
to their particulars, which are essential in determining the quantities of
damages.  This should invariably be the case unless there is sufficient
explanation regarding failure to produce the alleged dependants in Court,
which was not given in the instant case.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
NEC & 2 Others vs. Nile Bank Ltd
Execution - objector proceedings O.19 r 5 - whether appellant
instead of filing a suit to contest the defendant's attachment of it's
vehicles under debenture should instead have filed objector
proceedings - whether objector proceedings may only follow
attachment in execution of a decree of court.
Assessment of damages-whether rule of law or practice for a trial court to
asses damages awardable to the plaintiff who has lost the suit.
Held: A contract made before a company is formed cannot bind the
company formed afterwards.  In the instant case the first appellant
executed the debenture before NEC Bakery came into existence.
Therefore the learned trial Judge was correct in holding that the debenture
was a nullity.
Though a subsidiary company is an independent entity from its parent, in
the instant case the trial Judge was correct in lifting the veil of the
subsidiary NEC Bakery and to find that it was owned and controlled by the
first appellant who had majority shareholding in it and that therefore the
first appellant was liable on the debenture.
If a person contracts essentially as an agent for non-existing Principal
that person may be found personally liable on the contract.  In the instant
case learned trial Judge was correct in finding the appellant who ostensibly
contracted on behalf of NEC Bakery which was not in existence at the
time of the debenture, liable on the debenture.
The learned trial Judge erred in holding that the respondent/defendant was
empowered under the debenture to exercise a right of seizure under
clause 6 of the debenture because clause 6 of the debenture did not
provide for seizure but only stated the conditions under which the
appellant shall immediately be liable to repay the loan.  It is only clause 7,
which provided for a right to appoint a receiver by the respondent.
therefore they respondent was not entitled to seize the appellant's motor
vehicle it was only entitled to appoint a receiver.
The learned trial Judge misdirected himself when he observed that the
plaintiff/appellant should instead have filed objector proceedings to contest
the seizure instead of a suit.  Objector proceedings may only follow when
there is an execution of a decree of court.
The Mortgage Decree does not apply to moveable property and therefore
the argument that the seizure of the appellant's vehicles was done under
the powers of the Mortgage Decree Ss.2, 7 was misconceived. And more-
over there was no order of foreclosure as required by S.7 Mortgage Decree.
Even if it is not a rule of Law that the trial Court should invariably assess
the damages it would have awarded the party succeeded, it was an
important rule of practice because the party is given an opportunity to
appeal against the award by the trial court.
Kakinga Co-operative society Ltd & 6 ors Vs. Begumanya & 3 others
Arbitration - jurisdiction - co-operative societies statute s.72 -
whether the provision in s.72 of the co-operative societies statute
is to the effect that disputes arising there under must be submitted
to arbitration, ousted the court's jurisdiction.
Held: A provision for arbitration does not oust the jurisdiction of the High
Court which has unlimited civil jurisdiction throughout Uganda.  Therefore
the plaintiffs suit was not barred.
The dismissal of the plaintiff was wrong since it was counter to the rules
of natural justice that require that a person should be given a right to be
heard.  Therefore, the plaintiffs were justified to instruct their counsel to
file suit in the name of Co-operative Society.
James Ajai Atare & ors Vs. Bellie Okadameri & the Editor in
Chief New Vision Newspaper.
Setting a side ex-parte decree - O.9r24 - where applicants went
aware of hearing date but had other urgent matters to attend to-
whether this was sufficient ground for setting a side the ex-parte
judgment.
Held: The applicants should have known that count appearance in Uganda
should take precedence over other engagements.  Even if their advocate
was indisposed, any of the applicants would have informed court which
would have adjourned the hearing.
The evidence on record clearly shows that the applicants had chances of
applying to defend themselves but that they did not use the chances.
In the result the applicants were solely responsible for the court's decision
to hear the defamation case ex-parte.
The attachment in execution of vehicles belonging to the New Vision
Corporation was in order because suing the Editor - in - chief of the
corporation is another way of suing the corporation.
Application dismissed with costs to respondents.
Professor Syed Sufderal Huq Vs. Attorney General.
General damages - whether plaintiff entitled to general damages in
respect of injuries suffered, illegal arrest, detention and deportation-
exemplary damages - whether plaintiff is entitled to exemplary
damages in respect of the high handed manner in which state
against treated him.
Held: The basis for an action of unlawful arrest and detention is the mere
imprisonment itself.  The plaintiff has to prove that he was arrested and
imprisoned by the defendant and the burden shifts to the defendant to
justify the action taken.  In order for an arrest to be lawful, the person
arrested should be informed of the reasons for so doing unless the
circumstances are such that he either knows or he creates a situation
makes it practically impossible for him to be informed.  The evidence in
this case clearly shows that the plaintiff was not told why he was being
arrested.  In failing to give the plaintiff reasons for their conduct, the police
acted illegally in arresting and detaining him.
The contention by the defense that the plaintiff lost his diplomatic
immunity status upon his dismissal cannot stand because the immunity
accorded to the plaintiff arose from duties owed by the Uganda
Government to the Organization of Islamic Conference and the agreement
they had entered into.  The Uganda Government had the obligation to
accord the plaintiff his immunity until he left the country or give him
reasonable notice to leave the country.  The government did neither of
these.  Accordingly, the arrest, detention and subsequent deportation of
the plaintiff were unlawful and it was done in flagrant violation of his
diplomatic status.
The law imposes a duty on a person driving a vehicle on a road to use
reasonable care to avoid colliding with other road users.  In the absence
of a police accident report coupled with the fact that the vehicle overturned
several times shows that it must have been driven in a negligent manner.
The evidence available shows that the defendant's driver did not take
reasonable care to avoid the accident.  He is accordingly liable for the
accident and subsequent injuries suffered by the plaintiff.
The plaintiff has also succeeded in proving that he was illegally arrested,
detained and deported, he also suffered injuries as a result of an accident
caused by negligent driving of the defendant's agents.  For all this he is
entitled to be compensated; damages both general and exemplary are
accordingly awarded.
Uganda Development Bank Vs. Kasirye Byaruhanga & Co.Adv.
Advocates (professional conduct) regulations r.8 - whether
proceedings by an advocate who depones to contentious matters are void
Held: Regulation 8 of the Advocates (Professional Conduct) Regulations
is not a primitive regulation and therefore it does not provide that an
affidavit deposing to contentious matters by counsel is thereby defective.
It simply provides that counsel must choose either to be witness in the
case or to be counsel but not both.  In the instant case, counsel for the
applicant deposed to matters that would not necessarily require him to
appear as a witness since the matter deposed to where on court record.
There, there was no need or authority to strike out the appellant's motion.
Appeal allowed.
The New Vision & anor Vs. Luka Bamiango.
Appeals s.232 (1) (a) MCA - order, S.2 CPA - whether an appeal
is not sustainable where no order is extracted prior to the
institution of the appeal.
Order S.2 CPA- Preliminary objection-whether the ruling on a preliminary
objection resulted in an order or decree.
Decree S.2 CPA - preliminary objection - whether the ruling on a
preliminary objection resulted in an order or decree.
Held: Where a preliminary issue fails and the suit is allowed to proceed
no preliminary decree arises but only an order as par S.2 CPA.  In the
instant case ruling on the preliminary objection in the lower court have
resulted in an order.
However, S.232 (1) (a) MCA provides that unless a formal order or decree
embodying the decision complained of is extracted the appeal there from
is not competent.  Therefore the preliminary objection by counsel for the
respondent would be upheld since no order embodying the decision
complained of was extracted.
Preliminary objection upheld with costs.
Jimmy Kisule Vs. Steel Rolling Mills.
Summary suit O.33 CPR -existence of triable issues - whether
suit properly filed under summary procedure.
Summary suit O.33-claim for interest - whether claim properly brought
when payment of interest was not earlier on agreed upon by the parties.
Held:  It is trite that summary procedure should only be resorted to
in clear and straight forward cases where the demand is liquidated and
where there are no points for the court to try.  In the instant case, the
issue as to whether the defendant/applicant took delivery of the foods or
not was a triable matter requiring court to take evidence in order to
conclude on it.
A party wishing to proceed under O.33 can only claim interest if that
interest has been agreed upon by both parties in their earlier contract, the
subject of the litigation.  Therefore this suit was irregularly bought under
o.33 CPR.
Application allowed with costs.
Jastine Lutaaya Vs. Stirring Civil Engineering Co. Ltd.
Amendment of pleadings O.6r 18 - substitution of party O.1r 10 -
whether application to amend pleadings by substituting the
plaintiff was not tenable because there was no proof of bonafide
mistake.
Held: An application to substitute a plaintiff under O.1 r 10 (1) CPR must
show that the suit was instituted in the name of the wrong plaintiff through
a bona fide mistake.  In this instant case the applicant should have known
that the original plaintiff had no locus to institute the suit since as lessee
its lease was a nullity for lack of ministerial consent.  Therefore there was
no proof of bona fide mistake and the application would fail.
Application dismissed with costs.
Asha Shaban Vs. Vadgama Ltd & 2 others.
Security for costs - O.23 rr 1 & 3 CPR - dismissal of suit for failure
to pay security for cost - whether a new suit on the same facts
against the same parties is tenable.
Held: O.23 r 2 (2) stipulates that where a suit is dismissed for default by
the plaintiff to pay security for costs the plaintiff may apply to court for
setting aside the dismissal.  This means that the plaintiff cannot file a
new suit on the facts against the parties for the same relief.  Therefore the
plaintiff's subsequent suit was misconceived and an abuse of the court
process.
Suit dismissed.
Scoul Vs. Kanobolic Group of Companies Ltd.
Res judicata - application to set a side award under an arbitration-
whether the application was res judicata - whether judge was
functus officio.
Inherent jurisdiction - application to set aside award under an arbitration -
whether though the application could be resjudicata, court inherent
jurisdiction to entertain the application on its merits.
Preliminary objection - pleadings-whether because the respondent had
not raised the preliminary objections in its reply to the notice of motion, it
was barred from raising them during the hearing.
Stay of execution O.19 r26-pending suit-whether the application for the
stay was incompetent because there was no pending suit.
Held: The present application was about the same parties who sought
the same remedy arising out of same transaction as in the previous
application 17/95 was res judicata and therefore untenable.
The application for say of execution was incompetent, as it was not
based on a pending suit, as the application for setting aside the award
had been adjudicated upon and dismissed and therefore it was not a
pending suit any more.
it is not requirement of the law that preliminary objections must be
pleaded first.
S.101 CPA gives Court inherent jurisdiction but only for the matters that
are properly before it.  An application to set aside an award under
arbitration, which similar application had been adjudicated upon previously
and was thereby resjudicata, could not be entertained by court under its
inherent powers.
Application dismissed.
J.K.Sentongo & anor Vs. Shell (u) Ltd.
Temporary injunction - O.37 rr1&9 CPR -whether the requirement
to preserve the status quo, existence of prima facie case,
irreparable injury and balance of convenience were in favour of
applicant.
Held: The status quo actually as per affidavits of the respondent which
were not challenged is that the respondent was building on the suit
premises.  Therefore the status quo to preserve was for the respondent
to continue building on the premises till determination of the head suit.
It was too early as far as the proceedings of the head suit were concerned,
to tell whether the applicant had a prima facie case with a probability of
success. To delve into the question of the existence or otherwise of the
prima facie case would require going into the merits of the case which
require evidence.
Since the respondent was developing the suit premises, it was enhancing
the value thereof.  Therefore there was no injury to the premises and
therefore there was no irreparable injury to complain about.
Moreover the defendant/respondent was the richest oil company in
Uganda and was fully capable of atoning whatever damage would befall
the applicant in damages should the head suit be decided in favour of the
applicant.
Since the respondent had already invested so much in developing the suit
premises it would suffer a greater inconvenience if its activities were
stopped by injunction more than what the second plaintiff/applicant would
suffer.
Application dismissed with costs.
Abendego Absolom Ongom Vs. Amos Kaheru.
Exparte proceedings - pleadings - whether because the defendant
has not come to court to lead evidence to contradict the plaintiff's
case therefore remedies may be granted as prayed.
Pleadings - particulars of contributory negligence-whether failure to provide
particulars of contributory negligence meant it was not proved.
Held: Where a defendant does not appear, having filed a Written
Statement of Defence and the trial proceeds ex parte, remedies cannot
be granted to the plaintiff just as prayed unless they are sufficiently
supported by the pleadings.
As per S.26 (2) of the Sale of Goods Act, the transfer of title and payment
of purchase price in a contract of sale are not concurrent conditions.
Therefore the defendant having bought the car and having obtained
possession of it with the consent of the vendor, he had become its owner
even though he had not paid all the installments.
Even though the defendant in his WSD attempted to plead contributory
negligence he failed because no particulars there were provided.
Moreover, the burden of proof of contributory negligence lay on the
defendant, who failed to discharge the burden when he failed to come to
court and testify.
The plaintiff had proved as special damages, the cost of private medical
treatment Ush 1,240,000/=; loss of sitting allowances ush 180,000/=.
The plaintiff had failed to prove the claim for the cost of transport to and
from hospital for himself and his wife who visited him regularly.  This is
because no evidence had been led to that effect.
In case of destruction of goods the measure of damages is taken to be
the market value of the goods destroyed at the time and place of
destruction.  Therefore the plaintiff's claim for a replacement value of a new
car would fail since his damaged car was old.
The plaintiff's disability assessed at 60% was quite an exaggeration
because the plaintiff suffered potts fracture, which healed nicely. However,
the plaintiff was in plaster of Paris for four months and had screws in his
body and suffered posttraumatic arthritis.  He would therefore be awarded
Ush 5 million general damages.
Case allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Makerere Properties Ltd Vs. Mansukhlal Ranji Karia.
Pleadings - failure to plead in WSD that suit instituted without
authority - whether therefore defence may not rely on that point of law.
Held: A suit instituted in the names of a company without the authority of
the directors is not maintainable in law.  In the case instant, though
Mohamed Amin claimed that he had a resolution signed by some of the
shareholders as authority for the suit, there was no evidence that there
was a meeting where the resolution was passed.  Therefore, the
resolution did not amount to authority for the suit.
Moreover the resolution had not been tendered in evidence which meant
that after all it did not exist.
Further, before the registrar of  companies could rectify the register, to
reinstate the original shareholders and directors, the purported original
had no powers to authorize the institution of the suit.
Article 36 of the company's Articles of Association provides that the
management of the business of the company shall be vested in the
directors.  In the instant case at the time when PW1 instructed
M/s Mulira & co. Advocates to institute the action he was not a director
and had never been a director of the company.  He could not therefore
instruct counsel to file proceedings in the name of the Company.
Failure to plead by the defendant in his WSD that the plaintiff's suit had
been filed without authority did not preclude the defendant from raising it
during submissions after evidence had been led on both sides because
that fact had been clear in evidence.  Therefore court would rely on that
finding and strike out the action of the plaintiff Company.
Action struck off for want of authority to institute it.
Matico Store Ltd & anor Vs. James Mbabazi and anor
Amendment of pleadings O.6 r18 CPR - amendment of plaint-
whether application tenable where two witnesses have testified
on behalf of the plaintiff.
Held: As long as allowing the amendment shall not prejudice the other
and as long as the other party can be compensated by costs, amendment
of pleadings should be freely allowed.  In the instant case on those
reasons the application to amend will be allowed.
Application allowed.
Tom Mukalazi Vs. Davis Kisule.
Evidence - lack of evidence for defence- whether thereby the
plaintiff's account of what happened has to be accepted.
Held: A driver that drives a motor vehicle is presumed to be driving it with
the authority of the owner or employer.  This is a presumption of fact,
which can be rebutted by evidence.  However since the defence called no
evidence at all, this presumption remained that the driver was authorized
to drive the motor vehicle and therefore the defendant was liable.
Contributory negligence or particulars were not pleaded in the defendant's
written statement of defence and therefore the defendant could not rely on
it at the trial.
Because the plaintiff suffered an amputation of the arm at the wrist, and
his permanent disability was assessed at 70% when he was only 26
years old Ush 9 million would be awarded general damages.
In absence of the evidence of the employer, special damages for lost
income from employment would not be awarded.
Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
David Kabungu Vs. Zikarenga & 4 others.
Transfer of suit s.18(1) (b), CPA - balance of convenience - whether
the allegation that the plaintiff would be put to prohibitive expense
if the suit is not transferred was a ground for the transfer of the suit.
Transfer of suit S.18(1) (b) CPA-lack of jurisdiction whether the allegation
that the Chief Magistrate had no jurisdiction to cancel a certificate of title
was sufficient ground for transferring the suit to the High Court in Kampala.
Held: A suit which is filed in a court that has no jurisdiction cannot be
transferred from that court.  In this case it was not true that the Chief
Magistrate had no jurisdiction to try a suit where the subject matter is
land under the Registration of Titles Act.  Therefore, the Chief Magistrate
had jurisdiction to try the suit.
A plaintiff has the right to choose his court.  The expense which the
plaintiff/applicant was likely to incur in transporting and maintaining the
numerous various senior public officers from Kampala to Kabale to attend
as witnesses was bound to be prohibitive as to deny him justice. Therefore
if this application was not allowed, it would amount to shutting the plaintiff
behind the doors of justice.
Application allowed.
Alcon International Vs. Kasirye, Byaruhanga & Co. Advocates.
Stay of execution of a taxation order pending appeal O.39 r 4 CPR
invocation of inherent powers of court s.101 CPR - whether
procedure wrong.
Appeals - notice of appeal-whether a notice of appeal amounted to an
institution of an appeal.
Stay of execution of a taxation order pending appeal O.39 r.4 CPR-
invocation of inherent powers of court S.101 CPA-whether procedure
wrong.
Stay of execution pending appeal O.39 r 4 CPR-sufficient cause-whether
a pending appeal was sufficient cause for an order for stay of execution-
whether taxation was done outside the proper principles and law for
taxation of costs.
Held: Where there is a specific provision of the law in place governing the
situation, the invocation of the inherent powers of court was untenable, in
the present case the application for stay of the execution of a taxation
order pending appeal was governed by O.39 r 4 CPR.  The application was
instead brought under section 101 of the Civil Procedure Act and was a
wrong law.
However the application though brought under a wrong law, was not
therefore fatally incompetent because no prejudice was therefore
occasioned to the respondents; secondly the application was commenced
by notice of motion, which it would still have been had it been filed under
O.39 r 4 thirdly the procedural defect was curable by the invocation of Art
126 (2) (e) of the constitution; fourthly, the rules of procedure are
handmaids of justice and should not be used to defeat it.  Therefore,
procedural defect of the application would be ignored.
Appeal describes a procedure started by filing a notice of appeal.  Once a
notice is filed then the procedure of appeal is put in place.  Therefore the
applicant's application was competent because there existed already a
pending appeal commended by the notice of appeal.
A pending appeal is not in itself sufficient cause for stay of execution.
For purposes of an application for stay of execution of an order taxation
of costs, pending appeal, sufficient cause would be manifested by
evidence or allegation that the taxing master improperly addressed
himself to the law relating to the taxation of costs.  The instant application
had failed to prove sufficient cause and would be refused.
Application dismissed.
Christopher Kisembo Vs. G.W Byaruhanga & Onor.
Amendment of pleadings - application therefore during
submissions - whether not tenable because in ordinarily late.
Held: It is trite law that in Uganda vehicles must be driven on the left-hand
side of the road.  The fact that the first defendant's vehicle knocked that
of the plaintiff on the left hand side of the Mbarara Fort Portal road, in
absence of an explanation or excuse from the first defendant, this was
sufficient to constitute negligence on the part of the first defendant.
Driving a vehicle in dangerous mechanical condition such as having a bad
tyre cannot per se constitute negligence on the part of the driver unless it
is shown by evidence that it was the mechanical condition that of
necessity caused or contributed to the accident.  In the instant case even
if the driver of the plaintiff was convicted of driving a vehicle in a dangerous
mechanical condition because of a bad tyre, it was not shown that he had
negligently failed to control the vehicle because of a bad tyre.  Therefore
contributory negligence was not proved.
The first defendant was within the scope of his employment when he
caused the accident while returning home after dropping the veterinary
surgeon to the farm of the second defendant.  Returning home did not
alter the essence of the first engagement, that of dropping a surgeon at
the farm.
The oral application to amend the plaint would be refused because it was
inordinately late and would necessitate fresh investigations on the part of
the defendants to make a rebuttal.
Where the value of repairs is higher than the replacement value, court
would only award the replacement value.
A plaintiff is enjoined to mitigate his damages.  Thus court would compute
damages for lost income from the date of collision to the period when with
due diligence the repairs ought to have been completed.  In the present
case it would be the period when the vehicle ought to have been replaced.
Ush 1,000,000/= would therefore be awarded because the plaintiff had
testified that the date of the accident he had already made money to buy
another vehicle.
Raymond Katabakya Vs. Attorney General.
Pleadings - special damages - whether proof of higher sum of
special damages than pleaded without amendment of pleadings is untenable.
Held: The plea of res ipsa loquitor was rightly raised since the lorry which
crushed the plaintiffs leg was under the sole control of the defendant's
driver and the defendant had offered no explanation to show that there was
no negligence.  Therefore negligence on part of the defendant's driver was
presumed.
Ush 5 million would be awarded as general damages for an amputation
above the knee and permanent disability at 40%.
A plaintiff is precluded from leading evidence to prove a higher amount of
special damages than pleaded.  Therefore only the pleaded amount would
be awarded.
Suit allowed with costs.
Sheikh Kateregga & anor Vs. UEB.
Pleadings - particulars of negligence - whether failure to itemize -
particulars of negligence was fatal.
Held: In an action founded in negligence particulars thereof must be given
of the alleged negligence, showing in what respects the defendant was
negligent.  Though in the instant case the pleadings did not follow the
conventional itemization of the particulars, nevertheless, the pleadings
set out clearly what the plaintiffs were alleging against the defendant.
He who affirms must prove the truth of his affirmations.  Since the
plaintiffs alleged that Lugoloobi was acting  in the course of his
employment, it was incumbent upon them to prove the allegation.  Yet the
plaintiffs did not even produce Lugoloobi as a witness to testify as to
whether he was acting on his own frolic or not.
To make an employer liable for the act of a person alleged to be his
servant the act must be one of the class of acts which the person was
authorized or employed to do, even if the act is done wrongly or negligently
or wantonly. In the instant case it was not sufficient to show court that
Lugoloobi was an employee of UEB but it was incumbent upon the
plaintiff's to show that the class of duties of the servant of the defendant
were the duties the doing of which resulted from the tortuous damage to
the plaintiffs.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Toro & Mityana Tea Co. Ltd Vs. Ibingira Charles.
Leave to appear and defend summary suit O.33 rr3 + 4 - triable
issue - leave to appear and defend wrongly refused because there
were triable issues.
Leave to appear and defend summary suit O.33 rr3 & 4 defence-whether
merits of the defence should not be entertained for purposes of an
application for leave to appear and defend.
Held: An applicant for leave to appear and defend the suit need not show
that he has a good defence on the merits.  He only needs to show that
there is an issue or question in dispute, which ought to be tried.  In the
instant case the defendant alleged that the plaintiff treated some
employees of the defendant without the defendant's authority.
Appeal allowed.
Elizabeth Nakanwagi Vs. Sterling Civil Engineering (u) Ltd.
Stay of execution - permanent injunction - whether court has no
jurisdiction to stay execution of a permanent injunction.
Stay of execution - likelihood of success of appeal whether failure to
show likelihood of success of appeal was a ground to refuse application
for execution.
Held: Court has inherent powers to stay its own orders including a
permanent injunction.
Though the applicant had successfully shown court that the stay was
necessary so that the intended appeal is not rendered nugatory, and that
the failure to grant the stay would visit irreparable damage upon the
applicant, the application would nonetheless be refused because of failure
to show that the pending appeal had probability of success.
Catherine Nakkazi Vs. Kirunda & anor.
Execution - attachment of immovable property O.19 r15 CPR
whether immovable property may be attached against a warrant of
attachment of movable property O.9 r40.
Taxation -Bailiff's bill of costs - travel expenses-whether court would not
allow unjustified expenses.
Execution-eviction of tenants -whether lawful where warrant was for
attachment of movable property.
Held: A warrant of attachment and sale of movable property is issued
under O.19 rr40 + 61 CPR and it must be for attachment and sale of
movable property had in its schedule a residential house in one heap
with household property.  This was illegal and improper because
attachment and sale of immovable property can only be dealt in a
separate warrant under O.19 r 51.  Therefore the attachment of the
residential property was null and void and no costs should be allowed for
the auctioneers for having done illegal work.
The warrant for attachment and sale of movable property does not confer
upon a bailiff to evict tenants without a further order of court.  Therefore the
item for eviction expenses would not be allowed.
R.15 Court Bailiffs Rules as amended required a Court bailiff to justify his
travel expenses incurred outside the limits of the place where he has his
ordinary business office.  In the instant case the taxing master should not
have allowed the expanse of travel beyond the jurisdiction of the
executing court because there were other bailiffs within the local
geographical extents of the executing court.
Appeal allowed with costs to the respondent.
George Kanyamukama Vs. Karora Mixed Farmers Co-op Soc. Ltd
Temporary - injunction O.37 r2(3) - committed to civil prison for
disobedience of temporary injunction - whether not proper because
injunction was exparte and never served on respondent.
Temporary Injunction - ex-parte-whether improper because offending
practice direction 217/94.
Held: Temporary injuntion-ex-parte-whether improper because offending
practice direction 217/94.
Since the temporary injunction was ex-parte; it must have been served on
the applicants.  Since this was not done, the applicants could not be held
to have disobeyed the temporary injection.  Therefore the committal to
prison of the applicants was improper.
Order of detention set aside and applicants set free.
Noble Builders (u) Ltd Vs. SIETCO.
Notice of appeal, r78(1) (a) & (2) notice of full and sufficient address
for service - whether respondent who has not served his notice and
sufficient address for service is not entitled to be served with the
memorandum and record of appeal.
Held: Where a person fails to file a notice of a full and sufficient address
of service, that person is not entitled to be served with the Memorandum
and Record of appeal.
This is a requirement of r78 (1) (a) (2) RSC and is mandatory and could
not be circumvented by filing a notice of legal representation under rr 22 &
23 RSC.
Application dismissed with costs.
Y.Kamuhuka Vs. E.Kagongo.
Appeals evidence by affidavit on appeal - whether tenable.
Held: Adjournment by endorsement on the notice of hearing indicating
inability to attend court is not tenable.  Counsel should have asked
another lawyer to hold a brief on his behalf or at least the appellant
should have attended court.
Proceeding by affidavit on appeal was not tenable because it would deny
the respondent the opportunity to cross-examine the deponent.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
HMB Kayondo Vs. Somani Amirali.
Pleadings - written statement of defence - whether failure to
transverse pleadings in paint - whether therefore facts admitted.
Held: It is a rule of pleading that an averment not expressly or implicitly
traversed is deemed to have been admitted.  It is a rule of evidence that a
fact admitted need not be proved.  The plaintiff in para 5 of the plaint had
pleaded that he gave notice of dishonour to the defendant.  The defendant
in his WSD did not traverse either explicitly or implicitly that plea.
Therefore the defendant had admitted that the plaintiff gave him notice to
dishonour the cheque as required by S.48, the Bills of Exchange Act.
A company duly registered is a legal entity distinct from the subscribers
or those who formed it.  This is the rule of incorporation.  Therefore the
dishonoured cheques on the account of Uganda Consumer Supplies Ltd
belonged to the Company.  However the defendant being managing
director thereof would not be allowed to use incorporation as a cloak for
fraud.  Therefore, the veil incorporation would be lifted by court so that
the defendant is found personally liable for the dishonoured bills.
S.30(1) Bills of Exchange Act provides that every party whose signature
appears on a bill is a prima facie deemed to have become a party thereto
for value.  Sine the defendant admitted having drawn the cheques, the
burden of proof lay on him to prove that the plaintiff had passed no
consideration to the defendant for the cheques.  The defendant failed in this.
Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Mangalita Namirembe Vs. Kalamatu Tebukola.
R.C Courts - jurisdiction - whether RC Courts had jurisdiction to
collect a debt of shs.200.000/=.
Held: The matter in controversy was a debt of Ush 200,000/= old currency
which had been reduced to Ush 200/= by the Currency Reform Statute
of 1987.  therefore the debt being Ush, 2,000/=, the RC Courts had
pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain the suit as per S.4 RC Judicial Powers
Statute.
However the Chief Magistrate and the RC Courts erred to have found that
the money required to be paid to her by the clan elders' meeting.
Therefore there was no contract constituted by the clan elders' meeting.
Since there was no contract, if the appellant mistakenly was paid part of
the money required to be paid to her by the clan elders' meeting, it was
money received for no consideration, received under a mistake of fact and
was recoverable.
In absence of evidence to the contrary a payer of rates in whose names
receipts appear, is the owner of the property and the Chief Magistrate
erred in ignoring the appellant's receipts to prove the ownership of the
property in absence of evidence to the contrary.
Appeal allowed with costs.
G.M Combined (u) Ltd Vs. A.K.Detergents (u) Ltd.
Dismissal  of suit for failure to pay security for costs - application
therefore - whether must be formal.
Setting aside dismissal of suit dismissed for failure to pay security for
costs-whether by review under O.42 r 1 CPR.
Review O.42 r.1-application to set aside order of dismissal of a suit for
failure to pay security for costs.
Lis pendeus - stay of suit-whether lodgment of notice of appeal acted as
a stay of proceedings.
Held: The application to review the order of dismissal of the suit for failure
to finish security for costs brought under O.42 r.r 1 & 8 was misconceived
since O.23 r 2 (2) required the applicant to show court that he was
prevented by sufficient cause from furnishing security for costs as the
only ground for setting aside the dismissal.
The lodgment of a notice of appeal is an intention to appeal and cannot
amount to appeal, that must be lodged by filing a memo of appeal, record
of appeal, payment of fees, and security of costs as per r.81 RSC.
There the applicant was precluded from stating that there was a pending
appeal which should have acted as a stay of the order of payment of
However, even if the notice of appeal was to amount to an appeal, a mere
appeal against an interlocutory order cannot amount to a stay of
substantive proceedings.
Application dismissed with costs.
Famous Cycle Agencies Ltd  & 4ors Vs.Mansukhalal Ramji.
Adjournment of suit O.15(1) CPR -sufficient cause - whether
sufficient cause shown where counsel for the appellants in court in
absence of the appellants applies for an adjournment to be able to
receive fresh instructions from his clients.
Withdrawal of defence O.22 rr 1(3) + 7-application by letter whether
tenable.
Held: O.15 r (1) CPR provides that court, has discretion for sufficient
cause shown to grant adjournment.  The discretion is judicially
reasonably exercised upon proper material, thus considering the party's
conduct in the case and the opportunity he had in getting ready and the
truth and sufficiency of the reason alleged by him for not being ready.  In
the instant case the trial judge was correct in refusing the adjournment
because the reason given for the adjournment, that the second
respondent had withdrawn from the case, was not a surprise to the
plaintiffs/appellants.  This fact had been known by counsel for a long time.
O.22 rr 1 (3) +7 provide to the effect that a defendant's withdrawal can
only be by leave of court upon application by chamber summons.
Therefore the trial Judge in accepting the withdrawal of the 2nd
respondent's defence without a formal application.  However, this did not
occasion a miscarriage of justice.
A certificate of title is conclusive evidence that the registered person is
the owner therefore, except upon proof of fraud, as per the provisions of
SS.56 and 184 RTA.  Therefore, the learned trial Judge was correct in
finding that the first respondent was the true landlord of the appellants.
The learned trial Judge erred when he found that rent payable to the first
respondent was from 1st July 1991 instead of from 15th December 1992.
Appeal Dismissed except for amount of rent payable.
Trans Road Ltd Vs. Bank of Uganda.
Further security for costs r104(3) SCR - inordinate delay - whether
the application for further security for costs was presented after
inordinate delay - whether thereby may prejudice respondent's
appeal.
Held: Rule 104(3) RSC permit court to make an order for further security
for costs at any time if it thinks fit.  However, that order should not
prejudice the respondent's case.  Inordinate delay such as in the present
case would cause such prejudice.
Application dismissed with cost to the respondent.
Fr.Francis Payer Vs. Josephat Kawalya Mwebe & ors.
Setting a side ex-parte judgment and Decree O.9rr 9 and 24
whether an application to set a side judgment and decree may be
made simultaneously under O.9 r9 and r2 CPR-whether ex-parte
judgment may be set aside although there was service.
Stay of execution - letter by registrar staying execution-whether letter did
not amount to in order.
Held: A mere letter from the Deputy Registrar is an administrative request
to stay execution but cannot amount to an order of court to stay
execution.  The plaintiff/respondent could have ignored it and gone ahead
to execute.
O.9 r9 and O.9 r 24 CPR are in respect of two different situations.  Under
O.9 r 9 an application to set aside exparte judgment and Decree in
default appearance is brought when judgment has been entered by the
registrar, and there under, the court to which the application is brought
has wider discretion to allow or refuse the application than under O.9 r 24
where court is limited only to being shown sufficient cause for non
appearance.  Therefore it was wrong in Law to bring the application under
both rules simultaneously.  However, it was not fatal to the case.
Rule 8 of the Advocate (Professional Conduct) Regulations preclude
counsel from deponing to contentions matters in which he acts or
appears.  However, in the instant application, counsel's affidavit in reply
deponed to matters already agreed by the opposite party and therefore
the matters were not contentious.
O.9 r 9 under which the application was filed (inter alia), gives court wide
discretion in allowing or refusing applications to set aside exparte
judgment and decree entered in default, upon such terms as to costs as
the justice of the case demands.  In this application, it was apparent that
the defendants were in fact served with summons to enter appearance.
However justice required that the defendants who had shown an interest
in being heard should be given the opportunity as long as they can be
penalized in costs.
Application allowed with costs to the respondent.
Edward Seninde Vs. Fred Luwaga.
Amendment - oral application O.6 r.18 - whether application to
amend orally not tenable - whether should have been by chamber
summons.
Amendment - application therefore O.6 r 18-whether too late because
brought during submissions.
Held: The equitable defence of bonafide purchaser for value does not
apply to chattels but only to real property.  Therefore the defendant could
not lawfully claim to have passed good title to the plaintiff as a defence.
The equitable doctrine of tracing proves that a plaintiff can recover from
the defendant money (or property) that the plaintiff paid to the defendant
when the defendant had no right to receive it.  In the present case the
plaintiff was entitled to recover the money he paid to the defendant for the
purchaser of the suit car when in fact the suit car was subsequently
impounded.  However the doctrine of tracing would not allow the plaintiff
to recover what he did not lose.
An oral application for amendment is tenable under O.6 r 18.
Nanguga Livestock Coop-Society Ltd Vs. Energo Project.
Stay of execution pending appeal to supreme court - whether by
chamber summons u/o 19r26 or by notice of motion s.101 CPA.
Held: Proceedings by an advocate, who has no practicing certificate outside
the grace period, are illegal and must be set aside.  A retrial is ordered.
Appeal allowed, a retrial ordered.
In re Sir John Bagaire
Reciprocal Enforcement Act s.3(1) - limitation whether the
application for the registration of judgment passed by the Queen's
Bench Division was after 12 months and therefore barred by the
limitation.
Reciprocal Enforcement Act s.3 (2) - residence and business place of the
respondent -voluntary submission to jurisdiction whatever respondent not
shown to be ordinarily resident or carrying on business within jurisdiction of
the original court whatever the respondent did not voluntarily submit to
jurisdiction-whatever therefore application not maintainable.
Held: S.3 (1) Reciprocal Enforcement Act requires that a judgment to be
registered in the High Court of Uganda having been obtained in a superior
Court in the United Kingdom must be registered within 12 months after date
of judgment unless a further period has been granted by Court.  In this
instant case the judgment was passed on 27th October 1991 and this
application for registration was filed in 1994.  Therefore the application was
not maintainable.
S.3 (2) (b) Reciprocal Enforcement Act requires a judgment passed by the
superior Court in the United Kingdom that is sought to be registered in the
High Court of Uganda to have been passed against the defendant/
respondent who or has voluntarily submitted to the jurisdiction of the original
Court where such defendant/respondent is neither resident nor carries on
business in the United Kingdom.  In the instant case, the suit was exparte
and therefore, the respondent/defendant had not voluntarily submitted to the
jurisdiction of the original court.
Application dismissed.  No order as to costs.
Alia Babwa Vs. Abdul Halimu
Affidavit - defective affidavit - whether failure to indicate place -
where affidavit was sworn rendered affidavit defective and the
application supported thereby unsupported and untenable.
Held: It is true that the affidavit was defective but the application was not
thereby fatally defective since the applicant could still file a supplementary
affidavit to correct the defect by indicating where the affidavit was sworn.
Moreover, no prejudice was occasioned to the respondent.
Leave to amend application by filing supplementary affidavit granted.
Rohini Sidipra Vs. Freny Sidipra & ors.
Security for costs against litigant resident outside jurisdiction -
suit property in the hand of the respondent/defendant - whether
order for security for costs against plaintiff should be lifted.
Held: The plaintiff who seeks to avoid an order for security for costs must
show to the satisfaction of the court that he or she has fixed assets within
the jurisdiction to satisfy a possible order for costs in event of losing the
case.  In the instant case the assets allegedly in the hands of the defendant
were neither fixed nor determined as to their value.  Therefore, the order for
security for costs would not be vacated against the plaintiff who did not
ordinarily reside within jurisdiction.
An affidavit that is prolix in extreme or argumentative is not tenable.
Therefore, court would strike it as par O.17 r3 (1) CPR.
Application for review refused. Plaintiff to pay security for costs.
John William Kihuku & 2 ors Vs. Personal Representative of
Rt.Rev.Eric Sabiti.
Res judicata S.7 CPR - competent court - whether because trial
magistrates court had no powers to cancel certificate of title
based on fraud, suit was not res judicata.
Limitations Act - disability-whether a harassment by government
functionaries proved as disability.
Held: Where a person procures registration to defeat an unregistered
interest on the part of another person of which he is proved to have had
knowledge then such person is guilty of fraud.  Therefore the defendant was
guilty of fraud in the instant case when she procured registration of the piece
of land over which the plaintiffs were known customary tenants, in
possession of an offer to lease the same land.
However, since the issue of fraud had arisen in an earlier suit between the
same parties and the same issue was litigated upon on its merits and
concluded in favour of the defendants where fraud was found not to have
been proved, then the present suit was res judicata and not maintainable.
Even if it could be said that the trial magistrate court before which the
parties first litigated was not a competent court for purposes of res judicata
because the Magistrate court had no powers to cancel a certificate of title,
it should be known that the matter went to the High Court on appeal, the
court possessed of the competent jurisdiction.  The High Court on appeal
held that fraud had not been proved.  Therefore, it would still be held that
case was res judicata and maintainable.
There was no evidence on balance of probabilities that the plaintiffs were
disable to file the suit within 12 years because of harassment by
government functionaries.  Therefore the plea of disability would not hold.
Cases dismissed with costs.
Gold Trust Bank Ltd Vs. Banx Ltd.
Costs - taxation of costs - appeal against quantum - whether not tenable.
Costs-taxation of costs-whether amount so excessive that a principle of law
is infringed-whether taxed amount may not exceed value of decree.
Reference - time - whether a reference is governed by the provisions of law
regarding appeals and that therefore the reference was incompetent for
being out of time and for failing to follow the form of an appeal.
Held: Reference is governed by R.109 SCR and is supposed to be less
elaborate than an appeal and does not require any other documents other
than the proceedings before the taxing master which include the bill of costs
or documents upon which the taxing officer based his taxation addition to
the application for the reference.
The rules of the Supreme Court do not provide for the time within which a
reference must be instituted.  This was a matter of the Rules committee.
However, S.34 (2) interpretation Decree provides that where no time is
prescribed or allowed within which something may be done, then it must
be done with a reasonable time.  Therefore the two references were
competent and the preliminary objection would be overruled.
It does not necessarily follow that because the appeal lasts a whole 3 days
therefore the appeal was important and difficult and attracting the amount
awardable. The time was consumed by the manner in which the respondent
counsel presented the appeal.  Therefore, there was an extent an error of
law which led the taxing master to award an excessive sum of ush 5 million
as instructions fees whereas the appeal did not present my novel issue to
be decided.  The amount would be reduced to Ush. 2 million.
That taxing master instead of considering the provisions of the rules
governing taxation of costs in application, the considered appeals, thereby
misdirecting himself as to the amount he should have awarded for the
application that was withdrawn. Amount would therefore be reduced to
The reference on quantum only would be dismissed because it was not
tenable in law.
Reference allowed and costs reduced to shs. 2 million and 750,000/=
respectively for each reference.
Kiwanuka Nsereko Vs. Returning Officer & Nsubuga Nsambu.
Time - computation of time for s.34(1) (a) Interpretation Decree-
whether election petition action not limited  because time therefore
reckoned exclusive of the first day.
Court fees-payment by installments-whether action is deemed filed at the
payment of the last installment.
Held: S.34 of the Interpretation Decry and O. 47 r 8 CPR both provide that
for purposes of limitation of actions, the reckoning shall be made exclusive
of the first day.  Therefore, the learned trial Chief Magistrate was correct
when he held that the petition filed on 27th April when the polling was on
28th March was within time.
However, a suit or petition or nay action is deemed to have been filed when
the court fees is paid in full.  Therefore since the court fees was paid fully on
4th May 1994 the action purported to have been filed when the court fees
was paid in full on 4th May.  This time was beyond the limitation period,
and therefore the action was time barred.
Revision allowed and petition struck out with costs.
Allen Nsibirwa Vs. National Waters & Sewerage Corporation.
Limitation - disability - whether negotiations between the parties
regarding settlement of the matter outside court constituted disability O.7 r6.
disability O.7 r.6.
Pleadings - limitation - whether limitation must be pleaded by defendant -
s.4 Civil Procedure & Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act.
Held: Though limitation was not raised in the defence the defendant was
entitled to raise it at the trial since it was an issue of law.
Disability must be pleaded as required by O.7 r 6 CPR.
The negotiations between the parties with a view to reaching an out of court
settlement did not constitute disability since this fact would not disable a
party from filing the suit.
Preliminary objection upheld.  Plaint rejected.
Yahaya Lukyamuzi & anor Vs. Godfrey Beijuka.
Temporary injunction O.37 rr,1,2&9 CPR-furnishment of security
pending judgment attachment, pending judgment, arrest
pending judgment - whether orders available under O.37 r37
O.36 CPR.
Temporary injunction O.37 r 3-exparte-whether notice to respondent
mandatory.
Held: The application which sought orders of attachment and funishment of
security pending judgment should have been brought under O.36 and not
order 37.
Notice to the opposite party in an application for an injunction is mandatory
unless the application or court invoke the provisions of O.37 r3 for
dispensing notice.  Therefore the learned trial judge misdirected herself
when she admitted the application.
The omnibus order where furnshment of security' attachment and arrest
pending judgment was not proper.
The three different courses of action should have been ordered as
alternatives.  Appeal allowed.
Samwiri Iyamulenge Vs. Jovanis Nyirakamarande.
Suit by minor O.29 r1-plaintiff aged 20 years whether a married
woman aged 20 years was a minor and required to sue through a
next friend for purpose of divorce.
Jurisdiction of LC Courts -whether ousts the jurisdiction of courts of higher
grades.
Held: S.3 (5) of the Contract Act provides that a minor is a person below 18
years.  Since the plaintiff/respondent was 20 years, she was entitled to file
the suit for purposes of enforcing a contractual obligation without the next
friend.
Consent by parents or guardians where at least one of the parties is a minor
is not a requirement for the validity of a customary marriage unless at least
one of the parties does not belong to any indigenous tribe of Uganda.
Therefore, the appellant was from contending that his marriage was void due
to luck of consent since both parties to the marriage were Bafumbira from
Uganda.
Local council courts have jurisdiction to try cases invoking a customary
marriage.  However this does not oust the jurisdiction of a magistrate court
Grade 1 which has similar jurisdictions.  Therefore, the learned trial
magistrate was not precluded from trying the case as he was possessed
the requisite jurisdiction.
Where bride price is not paid in full, customary marriage is void.  Since in
the instant case the appellant/respondent had paid only1/2 a cow, leaving a
balance of a full cow, the marriage was void and the divorce proceedings
were uncalled for.
Appeal allowed.  Each party to meet its own costs.
Charles Kabunga Vs. Christopher Baryaruha & 3 ors.
Affidavit O.17 r3 - facts within knowledge of deponent - whether
counsel deported to matters outside his knowledge and whether
thereby the affidavit was defective.
Recovery of land against a registered proprietor-whether it is an action in
rem or persona.
Held: An Advocate is not allowed to depone to matters that are not purely
formal but contentious as per 8 of the Advocates (Professional Conduct)
Regulations 1997.  When counsel deponed to the value of the land he was
deponing to a contentious matter since this was not a formal fact in his
knowledge.  Therefore his affidavit was materially defective and would not be
relied upon in court.
The procedure of originating summons applies to questions that arise
between the executors, administrators or trustees on one hand and creditor,
devisee or next of kin who sets up a claim on the other.  In the instant case
the applicant's claim does not fall in that category of question because
the applicant is a person who has obtained judgment for the recovery of
interest in land against a registered proprietor under S.185 RTA.  The
application by notice of motion was properly brought by notice of motion.
A decree for the recovery of land is a decree in rem.  When the trial court
ordered the 1st respondent to redistribute the land to include the applicant
in the distribution, the second respondent, though not a party in the court
court that issued the original decree, his interest had to be affected because
he derived title from the first unlawful distribution.
Application allowed. Registrar to council the relevant certificates of title and
transfer the same to the applicant.
Bat (U) 1984 Ltd Vs. Selestino Mushongore
Pleading - contributory negligence - whether contributory
negligence must be pleaded.
Held: Contributory negligence should be pleaded and particulars thereof
given.  In the instant case the defendant neither pleaded contributory
negligence in defence nor did court frame it as an issue.  However,
contributory negligence arose but of the evidence and the learned trial Judge
was entitle to have been held 55 years as the working life expectancy but
the trial Judge should not have used 20 as the multiplier but 15 due to
imponderables in life.
The United Nations Development Program (UNDP)'s alleged indicators with
regard to life expectancy due to AIDS pandemic, had not been proved in
court as no evidence had been led. Therefore the trial Judge was entitle to
have been held 55 years as the working life expectancy but the trial Judge
should not have used 20 as the multiplier but 15 due to imponderable in life.
The photographs were not admissible in evidence because the photographer
was not called as a witness.  Therefore, the trial Court was entitled to
reject him.
The learned trial Judge erred when he held that the deceased's income
being Ush 20,000/= per day, therefore he spent all the 20,000/= per day on
his family.  The trial court should have found that the deceased spent
shs 5000/= per day on his family.  This should have been multiplied by 365
days.  This would give about shs 27 million.  This should have been taxed to
Ush 20 million. This Ush 20 million should have been apportioned to the
three dependants.
Appeal allowed only in part. File ordered back to trial court to apportion the
award between to the three dependants.
Registered Trustees of Kampala Institute Vs. Departed Asian
Property Custodian Board.
Costs - taxation of costs -whether because judgment was a
declaration of a legal principle that did not confer a proprietary
interest, the award of instruction fees should not take account the
value of the suit property.
Held: Where the judgment of taxation in merely declaratory of a legal
principle and that declaration does not confer proprietary interest, then a
taxing master may not base his taxation of instruction fees on the value of
the property about which the declaration may have been made.  In the
instant case reference, the appellate court only declared that the
repossession of the suit property was governed by the Expropriated
property.  Therefore, the judgment was only declaratory and did not confer a
proprietary interest to the applicant and the learned Judge of the Supreme
Court's reduction of the instruction fees from Ush 70 million to 7 million was
based on correct principles of the law and there was not basis upon which
the full court would interfere.
Reference dismissed with costs.
Elizabeth Imagara & 2 ors Vs. Attorney General.
Pleadings-failure to file defense - whether thereby liability admitted
Held: Since no defense was fixed by they defendant, no issues were joined
with regard to liability.  Liability is deemed to have been admitted. Therefore
court had only to resolve on the issue of damages.
Damages for wrongful dismissal should normally be based on the wages,
which the employer would have received if a valid notice had been given to
him on the date of dismissal.  Since the contracts of the plaintiffs would be
paid their one month's salary in lieu of notice.  Further their salary arrears
would be paid.
Suit allowed. Payment for unexpired contract period refused.
John Nagenda Vs. The Editor of the Monitor Newspaper & onor.
Pleadings O.6 rr 2,5,7 & (CPR-specific pleading-whether defendant
had not specifically thus precluded form leading evidence on it.
Issues O.13 r 5 (1) CPR-issues for the determination of court -whether an
issue not pleaded nor framed may not be a matter for the determination of
court.
Held: A defendant that offers an apology is precluded from raising the
defence of justification.  However in the instant case the alleged apology
by the defendant was the correction published later that the words
complained were not uttered to the surveyors wife but to DW1.  this in
substance did not amount to an apology.
Even if any issue is not specifically raised in the pleadings or framed for the
decision of the trial court, if evidence is lead during the trial of the case on
the unpleaded issue and parties canvas the issue or one of the parties does
canvas the issue in the trial Court, unless the party complaining about the
irregular procedure was prejudiced by the irregularity, an appeal court will
not interfere.  In the instant case though justification was neither pleaded nor
made an issue for the determination of court, nevertheless the parties did
canvas the issues which was left to court to determine.
Therefore the learned trial Judge did not err in law or fact when he allowed
the defence of justification.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Prince J.D.C Mpuga Rukidi Vs. Prince Solomon Iguru & ors.
Declaratory judgment - whether appeal had been overtaken by
events and was incompetent because the respondent had already
been crowned.
Frame of issues - failure to issues at the commencement of the trial-whether
proper.
Costs-whether order of costs against the unsuccessful party was erroneous
because the hotly contested dispute was between members of the same
family.
Held: the learned trial Judge's admission in evidence of the photocopied Will
could not be impeached because there was evidence before court that the
original will was lost.  Secondly, the will was photocopied which is the kind
of mechanical method that insures accuracy of the copy; there was
evidence that tended to prove that the signature on the will was that of the
testator and the contents of the Will had not been seriously challenged by
the adverse party.
S.13(2) (b) Interpretation Decree provides that when any enactment repeals
another, unless a contrary intention appears, the repeal does not affect
anything previously duly done in pursuance of the repealed enactment.
Therefore when the late King named the Will unattested, such a mode of
making Wills was permissible under S.50(2) Succession Act which
provision allowed Africans to make unattested Wills.  Though the exemption
was repealed by Decree 22/72 Succession Act (Amendment) Decree the
repeal did not affect the act already performed by the late King, the act of
nominating the respondent by a Will unattested.
Moreover, even if the document nominating the respondent as heir was to
be found wanting as a Will, the document could be relied upon as evidence
of nomination of the respondent as heir because paragraph 2 schedule 3 of
the 1962 Constitution under which the nomination was done did not provide
any specific mode by which nominations of successors to the throne of
Bunyoro Kitara could be made.
O.13 r 3 gives discretion to court to frame issues from among or all the
allegations made on oath, allegations made in the pleadings and contents
of documents from the parties.  This rule does not mean that when court is
framing the issues it should look at all the allegations.  It is own discretion
to choose from among the allegations or all of them.  This further means
that court may frame the issues at any stage of the proceedings before
judgment.  Therefore, the learned trial Judge in framing only one issued did
not err since he had the discretion to do and in his opinion, it was enough
to decide whether or not the respondent was qualified to be heir to the
throne of Bunyoro Kitara.  And once this was answered in the affirmative
there was no further need to decided on the other allegations.
S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act provides that the court has the discretion in
determining who may be awarded costs though the costs should follow the
the event.  The instant case involved members of the same family, a family
whose importance went beyond its borders.  Therefore, for the sake of
peace and harmony in the family and community of the Kingdom, to assist
in the process of reconciliation, no costs should have been awarded!
The order awarding costs would be set aside.
The granting of a declaration is a discretionary remedy and the court should
not easily grant a declaration that would serve no useful purpose or seriously
prejudice the security of the state or affect the confidence between the
parties. Had the appellant succeeded, the court would have had to consider
whether to grant the declaration or not in view of the possible repercussions.
Appeal, save as to costs, dismissed.
Ococi Jungula & 5 ors Vs. Dhugira Esther Opoti & 3 ors.
S.6 Civil Procedure Act, stay of suit where suit with similar matters
in issue is also in issue in a previously instituted suit-whether the
provision applied where earlier suit was allegedly withdrawn.
Parties to a suit - whether a newspaper (New Vision has capacity to sue or
be sued.
S.1(1) (c), S.8 Civil Procedure & Limitation (misc. prov.) Act 20/69-Statutory
Notice to sue corporations-whether the notice was sufficiently served.
Held: There is sufficient evidence on record to show that Civil Suit No.651/94
was duly withdrawn by the plaintiffs and that the non payment of the costs
occasioned by it by the plaintiff did not affect the validity of the withdrawal
of the suit.
A newspaper name does not fall within the Provisions of O.27 r.1 for the
purpose of suing or being sued under the business name.  The inclusion of
the 2nd defendant who has no legal personality enabling him to sue or to be
sued is accordingly unnecessary.
There is sufficient evidence on record to show that the Statutory Notice was
duly served or being sued under the business name.  The inclusion of 2nd
defendant, a scheduled corporation.  1st and 3rd preliminary objections
dismissed.
In re messrs Katende Sempebwa, Exparte.
Originating inter pleader summons - s.60 civil procedure Act O.31
r1(a), whether conditions for the issue of the summons satisfied.
Held: The application complied with the section 60 Civil Procedure Act and
O.31 r2 CPR and would be granted since the applicant had no interest in the
money claimed.  There was collision between the applicant and the claimant
and the applicant was willing to pay the money into court or as to court's
direction.
G.M Combined (U) Ltd Vs. A.K.Detergents (u) Ltd.
Security for costs - O.23 r1 CPR and s.404 companies Act
whether trial court erred in ordering the plaintiff/appellant to pay
security for costs where the plaintiff was a limited liability company
under liquidation.
Security for costs-quantum where the subject matter of the suit is above
ush 2 billion-whether Ush 50 million as security for costs was excessive.
Held: A plaintiff's impecunity and being under liquidation interalia justify an
order for security for costs unless the defendant has admitted liability, offers
to settle the claim or that the defendant has no reasonable chance to
success.
Appeal dismissed in part and security for costs reduced to Ush 30 million.
Mparo Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Admissions-O.11 r6 whether defendant may pray for dismissal
of suit after admitting liability except as to quantum.
