Witness-cross-examination thereof - failure to cross examine witness on
evidence adduced by him whether therefore his evidence is unchallenged.
Special damages-recovery thereof-whether special damages arising out of
money not provide spent may be awarded.
Interest -whether interest may not be awarded because the parties did not
agree it upon.
Held: The defendant's prayer to dismiss the plaintiff's suit was not tenable
because liability had already been admitted as per O.11 r 6.
Since counsel for the defendant did not cross examine the expert witness
as to the valuation report made by him the witness evidence stood
unchallenged and counsel for the defendant was precluded from impeaching
the evidence from the bar.  The witness's evidence had been accepted by
court as the truth.
Any estimate expertly arrived at cannot be said to be an act of guesswork
as long as the witness expertise is not denied.  Therefore, the evidence as
to the estimates of the value of repairs was a valid estimate and would be
awarded as special damages.
Special damages may be expenditure to be incurred or expenditure already
incurred.  Therefore, even if the plaintiff had not expended the sum claimed
as special damages it was proved as the sum expendable in effecting the
repairs which liability the defendant had admitted.
Interest is awarded by court at its discretion.  In commercial transactions
the rationale is to compensate the litigant for what he would probably earn
if his money were not withheld, like in this case.  Therefore interest would
be awarded on rent arrears and costs of repairs at 22% p.a.
Suit allowed.
Obadi Enterprises Ltd Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority & anor.
Revision u/s 84 civil procedure Act - taxation of costs - whether
taxation officers orders may be revised because it was unjust.
Costs-revision u/s 84 Civil Procedure Act - whether the taxation of costs
was excessive requiring a revisional order.
Held: S.84 (c ) Civil Procedure Act empowers court to make an order of
Revision where it is shown that the lower court acted in exercise of its
jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity or injustice. In this case the
taxation of costs was based o the amount claimed but not subsequently
awarded.  This lead to the excessive taxation of costs where the award was
Ush 1, 500.000/= and the cost over 17million. This did not represent fairness.
Therefore this was a clear case for Revision and the taxed bill of costs would
no set aside.
Application allowed and bill of costs set aside and respondent asked to
present a fresh bill of costs for taxation.
Transroad Ltd Vs. Bank of Uganda.
Reciprocal enforcement of judgments Act s.3(b) - Jurisdiction -
whether the respondent Bank of Uganda had submitted to the
jurisdiction of the court in England - whether therefore the
judgment of the England court may be registered and enforced in
Uganda u/s 3(b) reciprocal enforcement of judgments Act.
Held: Since the respondent bank was party to a consent order dismissing
its challenge of the jurisdiction of the English Trial Court, it meant that it had
submitted to the jurisdiction of the English Court as provided by the
Reciprocal Enforcement of judgment Act S.3(b).  The conduct of the
respondent and consequent upon the order obtained by consent dismissing
its challenge of jurisdiction showed that the respondent was cognizant of
the judgment it set out to settle in the subsequent negotiations.  The
respondent was therefore estopped from denying jurisdiction at such a late
stage.
The respondent bank would not be permitted to hide behind the veil of
technicalities to escape liability contrary to Art. 125(2) (e) of the Constitution
Substantive justice demanded that obligations voluntarily entered into should
be honoured.  Therefore the application would be allowed so that the
judgment obtained in the English court is enforced in Uganda.
Isaac Kasiba Lule Vs. Administrator General & anor.
Limitation Act s.20 - whether suit for an order to redistribute estate
was barred by s.20 of the limitation Act because filed after 6 years
from date of distribution.
Held: present application was not subject to S.20 Limitation Act because
the beneficiary applicant does not seek to recover from the trustee
Administrator General trust property but the application merely impugned
the scheme of distribution of the deceased's personal estate by the
administrator general.  Therefore the applicant's application was not time
barred.
To hold that the proceedings as commenced by counsel for the applicant
were a nullity because he lacked a practicing certificate would be to deny
the administration of substantive justice as required by the Constitution Art.
Preliminary objections overruled.
All Ports Freight Service (u) Ltd Vs. Julius Kamanyi & anor.
Defence - application to strike out defense - whether no defense
was disclosed - whether defense was frivolous and vexatious
because it made admissions of liability.
Defense-application to strike out defense U/O 6 r 29-whether application
may be made by co-defendant.
Held: O.6 r29 does not say who may make an application to strike out a
defence.  In ordinary rules of Statutory Interpretation, what is not expressly
excluded is permitted and therefore a defendant may apply to have defence
of his co-defendant struck out under O.6 r 29 on grounds that no defence is
disclosed of the defence is merely vexatious and frivolous.
O.13 r 1 (1) (2) provides that issues arise when material propositions of law
or fact are affirmed by one party and denied by another and  material
propositions of law or facts are those that a party must allege in order to
show a right to sue or defend and the purpose of a trial is to decide these
are no issues necessitating a trial and such a defence is no defence as it is
frivolous, vexatious and disclose no defence in law.  Therefore, the first
defendant's defence would be struck out as provided by O.6 r 29.
Application to strike out defence u/O 6 r 29, O.13 r 1 (1) (2).
James Kabateraine Vs. Charles Oundo & anor.
Execution - court bailiff selling attached property after a stay had
been agreed between the parties and selling on credit and below
the value of the property - whether bailiff liable in trespass - whether
sale may be set a side and restoration ordered.
Held: The sale was in flagrant violation of Rule9(2) of the Court Bailiff's Rules
1987 which requires that any sale at a price below the value of the attached
property must have the approval of court.  The bailiff having sold the tractor
valued at Ush 8 million at only Ush 3 million without the approval of court
violated the law and the sale was wrongful.
R 13 (1) of the Court Bailiff's Rules, 1987 enjoins the bailiff not to sell the
property in execution on credit.  The bailiff violated this rule when he sold the
property of the judgment debtor/plaintiff on credit, by post-dated cheque.
The execution was wrongful when it was levied after the stay had been
agreed between the parties.
The whole execution was irregular and would be set aside for having violated
the rules of court.  This would still be so even if only one rule had been
violated.
A wrongful execution is trespass and the plaintiff is entitled to an order of
restoration.  Therefore the defendant would be ordered to return to the
plaintiff his tractor or its value as at the date of judgment.
Ush 10 million would be awarded as general damages in trespass, detinue
and conversion.
Ush 2 million would be awarded as punitive damages.
Suit allowed with costs.
Maria Kevina Sentamu Vs. Kikondo Kyaterekera.
Jurisdiction - L.C Court - registered land - whether an L.C.Court has
has jurisdiction to try a case involving land registered under the
RTA.
Res judicata-jurisdiction of L.C Court - whether the suit concerning
registered land was res judicata when initially tried by L.C. court.
Held: Since the subject matter of the suit concerned land registered under
the Registration of Titles Act, the L.C. court did not have jurisdiction to try it
and therefore the L.C. was not a court of competent jurisdiction for purposes
res judicata.
Preliminary objectives dismissed.
Kameal Ltd Vs. Management Training & Advisory Center &anor.
Government proceedings s.1(2) Act 20/69 - pleadings - whether
failure to plead that statutory notice was served and failure to
attach the copy of the notice to the plaint was a material irregular-
rity.
Held: While it was true that the requirement to plead that the Statutory
Notice was served was mandatory the requirement was nonetheless only
ancillary to the requirement to serve the Statutory Notice, which in this case
was served.  Therefore the omission in the pleadings that the Statutory
Notice was curable by was of amendment and the application for leave to
amend would be granted.
Further the amendment would be allowed since no injustice would be
caused to the other party; the application was made bonafide; the
amendment was not expressly or impliedly prohibited by law; and the
amendment would help in avoiding a multiplicity of proceedings.
Application to amend under O.6 r 18 granted.
Abbey Semakula Vs. Eldad Rubarenzya.
Jurisdiction - chief magistrate pecuniary jurisdiction s.219 MCA -
whether the aggregate decretal amount of Ush4,645,000/= plus
Ush. 800.000/= cost together exceeding Ush. 5.000.000/= meant
therefore jurisdiction to make such an award as per s.219 of the
magistrate's court.
Service of summons-affidavits of service-whether discrepancies therein was
no effective service.
Held: The allegation that the respective Commissioner for Oaths did not
have valid practicing certificates at the time they commissioned the
affidavits, was not substantiated or proved either by an affidavit of counsel
alleging the same or by any other evidence.  Therefore, the Learned Chief
Magistrate was correct in law in not considering the same.
Costs are never taken into account in computing the sum in a decree.
Therefore since the decretal award did not exceed Ush 5,000,000/= the
Learned Chief Magistrate did not exceed his jurisdiction.
The discrepancies in the affidavits of service as to their dates in which it
appeared that the dates of deponing preceded the dates of service were
clearly typographical errors, which could be ignored.  Therefore this did not
render the affidavits incurably defective.
However, the ambiguities and discrepancies in the process servers' affidavits
of service and reply tended to show that there was no effective service and
that is why the defendant did not appear to defend the suit.
Appeal allowed.
Stephen Mabosi Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority.
Appeals - notice of appeal - application to strike out notice of
appeal on grounds that no appeal has been instituted sixty days
from the date of filing notice of appeal - whether application tenable
where respondent did not specifically apply for records of the
proceedings but merely stated that he intended to appeal as soon
as he was availed the trial court record by the registrar.
Appeals-record of proceedings application therefore -whether statement in
the notice of appeal to the effect that the respondent intends to formulate
grounds of appeal on receipt of the record of proceedings amounted to an
application for the proceedings-whether the respondent's appeal was not out
of time.
Held: R 81 did not provide the form by which an application or request for
the record of proceedings may be made as long as it is in writing addressed
to the Registrar, made within 30 days from the date of judgment.  Therefore
the respondents' notice of appeal in its form also amounted to a request of
proceedings.  Therefore the respondent was entitled to rely on the proviso
to r 81(1) (2) RSC and its appeal was not out of time and the notice of
appeal would therefore not be struck out.
Application dismissed.
Nicholas Roussos Vs. Gulam Hussein Habib Virani & anor.
Taxation of costs - instruction fees - whether manifestly excessive
and unjust.
Held: The instruction fees ought to take into account the amount of work
done by the advocate, subject matter of the suit and the prevailing economic
conditions.  In the case instant counsel for appellant stated the matter from
scratch the original counsel and plaintiff having died and the suit property
was quite valuable.  Therefore even though the taxing officer's assessment
was manifestly excessive and the learned trial judge was right to intervene
his reassessment was manifestly on the low side.  Ush 6,000,000/= should
have been allowed.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Joseph Mulenga Vs. Fiba (u) Ltd
Objector proceeding O.19 r55 - civil procedure Rules - possession-
whether proved.
Held: Applications brought under r 55 of O.19 Civil Procedure Rules restrict
court to investigate only the issue of possession as at the date of
attachment.  If the objector was in possession on account of the objector
then the property will be released as required by r 57 of O.19.  since the
objector herein had not shown by affidavit that it was in possession of the
rice as at the date of the warrant of attachment, its application would be
disallowed.
Application dismissed with costs.
Herbal international & ors Vs. Ibraham Alarakhia.
Execution - application to set aside - whether improperly brought
under review O.42 r 1CPR.
Execution-sale of immovable property-whether sale unlawful because not
done at the exact time of sale-whether selling some hours after advertised
time was a material irregularity.
Execution-court bailiff-whether failure to deposit money into court after sale
was a material irregularity as per S.49(1) Civil Procedure Act.
Execution - sale of immovable property-whether failure to deposit certificate
of titles was irregular as per O.29 r(2) S.49(1) CPA.
Held: S.35(1) Civil Procedure Act requires that any question arising between
the parties concerning execution be decided by the court executing the
decree and not by a separate suit.  Therefore the application was properly
before court.
Since an affidavit in support of an application is no evidence but merely
supports prima facie allegations raised in the application, oral evidence may
be allowed in addition to the affidavits to explain the contents of the affidavit.
The sale would be annulled for being contrary to law because it was done
not at the exact time advertised.  This meant that the purchaser might not
been the highest bidder, since there was no re-advertisement and therefore
the sale was by private treaty.  This offended against r 9(2) Court Bailiffs'
Rules 1987.  Secondly the failure to deposit the land title into court, and the
proceeds of the sale within 7 days of the alleged sale were material
irregularities necessitating the annulments of the sale.
Sale annulled.
Multi Contractors Ltd Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Party to the suit - agency whether the respondent/defendant
debenture holders & mortgagee bank was a wrong party to the
suit for the recovery of possession of property sold by the
defendant should have been the receiver.
Held: Since the appellant company still owed money to the respondent its
debenture could not be said to have been discharged.  Therefore that sale of
the suit property over which the respondent had a debenture was validly
done.
The receiver/managers once they were appointed became the agents of the
appellant and therefore when the receiver sold the property he did so as the
agent of the appellant.  The debenture terms and the law provided this.
S.9(c) (ii) of the Banking Act allows a bank to buy its security in hold.  In
the instant case when the respondent bank bought the suit property it did
so in hold.  But the hold could not be forever, the property eventually could
be and was taken over by the bank lawfully.
Appeal dismissed.
Amina Musoni Vs. Akamba (u) Ltd & Gaso Transport Service.
Parties to the suit - registered proprietor was properly joined as
co-defendant where there was evidence that the suit bus has been
sold to the second defendant by the time of the accident.
Held: The transaction by which the first defendant sold the bust to the
second defendant was a normal business transaction.  Therefore the first
defendant could not be held liable for an accident caused by the bust a
already sold to the second defendant.  Therefore the first defendant even
though a registered proprietor did not own the bus at the time of the
accident and was therefore wrongly sued.
The defence of novus actus grounded on the alleged sudden seeing and
knocking by the second defendant at the stationary lorry in the middle of the
road at a dark spot was not available to the defendant because the second
defendant's driver was negligent in driving the bus at night with poor head-
lights and at excessive speed.  This means, had the second defendant's
driver not been negligent he cold have avoided colliding with the lorry.
However, the owner of the lorry having parked the same in the middle of the
road without any sign for on coming traffic to be warned of its presence in
the middle of the road was negligent contributory by 40% and the bust
driver contribution negligent by 60%.
Since the plaintiff was 54 years old, a businessman in private employ, court
would assess his life expectancy at 60 years and his working life
expectancy at 6 years.
Since the plaintiff widow could not tell court consistently and credibly about
the number of children their ages and schools had not produced them in
court she had failed to prove who the dependant relatives were except the
widow.
The inconsistencies by which the plaintiff showed court that her husband
spent more on her family than he earned meant that the plaintiff had failed
to prove to court what her deceased husband's income was.
Had the plaintiff succeeded she would have been awarded Ush 100,000/=
(as she pleaded in the plaint being her late husband's income) multiplied by
12 months (since the income was monthly) multiplied by 6 (the years of her
deceased husband's working life expectancy).  This would have been
reduced by 30% (being imponderables like death or fall in income and the
fact that the award was lump sum).  This would have been further reduced
by 40% (being the contribution of the third party lorry owner who was not
joined as co-defendant by the plaintiff or defendant).  The figure would have
come to Ush 3,024,000/=.
Suit dismissed.
Joweria Namaganda Vs. Attorney General.
Government proceedings - survivor of causes of action - whether
application to substitute deceased plaintiff was not tenable
because the deceased plaintiff's action against government was
time barred because failed after 12 months from the date of
discharge from hospital - whether plea of disability by deceased
plaintiff was a triable issue requiring allowing the applicant to be
substituted for the deceased plaintiff.
Limitation - S.2 (1) Civil Procedure and Limitation(Misc. Prov.) Act- whether
action against government was statute barred,.
Held: Since the deceased plaintiff had pleaded disability, disability was a
teriable issue requiring both parties to the suit so that the issue of disability
be tried.
Application allowed.
Administrator General VS. Akello Joyce Otti & anor.
Memorandum of appeal - failure to state nature of order sought in
memorandum of appeal - whether thereby defective.
Held: S.6 of the  Administrator General Act is provides that a widow or a
widower may apply for and obtain letters of Administration of her or his
deceased's spouse's estate without having sought a certificate of no
objection from the Administrator General (AG).  In the instant case, the trial
court was entitled to grant the letters of administration in preference to the
AG's application because the first respondent was the widow of the intestate.
R. 84 (1) of the rules of the Supreme Court require that a Memorandum of
Appeal should set out interalia the nature of the order sought from the
appellate court.  The appellant's Memorandum of Appeal was defective for
failure to point out the nature of the order required from court.  Therefore the
appeal would be dismissed.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Israel Kabwa Vs. Martin Banoba Musiga.
Pleading - fraud - whether trial court may entertain an issue of
fraud wherein the same though pleaded is not particularized.
Held: A beneficiary of the estate of the intestate has locus to sue in his own
name to protect the estate of the intestate for the own benefit without first
having letters of Administration.  Therefore the respondent being heir to the
estate of his father had locus to bring this suit without having first sought
Letters of Administration.
Moreover the belated grant of the Letters of Administration validated all the
intermediate actions related to the estate including the filing of the suit.
The trial Judge was entitled to frame fraud as an issue and to decide the
same as proved against the appellant even though the respondent's
pleadings had given no particulars thereof because the respondents led
evidence at the trial to prove fraud without any objection from the appellant
and the appellant submitted on the same.  Therefore the appellant was never
prejudiced by the Judge's approach.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Joseph Mpamya Vs. Attorney General.
Vicarious liability of government s.4 law reform (miscellaneous
provisions) Act - torts committed by a local government official-
whether central government (Attorney General) liable because
officer is appointed by the minister of local government.
Cause of action-plaint in the name of wrong defendant-whether therefore
plaint discloses no cause of action-whether plaint must be rejected -whether
plaint not amendable.
Held: S.3 of the Local Government (Resistance Councils) Statute 1993
provides that the District Executive Secretary shall be the Chief Executive
Officer of the Local Government Council.  Therefore the DES is a servant in
the government and was performing a function related to housing which
function is reserved to district authorities.  Therefore the AG was wrongly
sued.
A plaint in the names of a wrong defendant cannot be amended but can only
be rejected.
Preliminary objection upheld.  Plaint rejected with costs.
Kibona Enterprises Vs. Departed Asian Property Custodian
Board & anor.
Vicarious liability of government - contracts entered by departed
Asian property custodian Board - whether because DAPCB is a
department of ministry of Finance therefore it is government which is liable.
Held: Even though the agreement of sale showed that it was the Ministry of
Finance that was the vendor, SS.1and 16(1) (b) Expropriated Properties Act
and S.5 (3) assets of Departed Asian Decree provide that the management
of departed Asian properties lay with the 1st defendant, a corporation sale.
Therefore the first defendant was rightly sued.
Where one party makes a firm offer and accepted by the other in all its term
a valid contract is established.  In this case, the plaintiff an advert pursuant
to which he bided successfully for the purchase of the property and paid
accordingly.  Therefore was a valid contract.
Since the plaintiff could be atoned by damages specific performance being
an equitable remedy would not be granted.  Ush 4 million would be paid as
general damages for breach of contract.
Suit allowed with costs to defendant.
Kaggwa Mpanga Vs. Zzimula Mugwanya & 2 others.
Rules 5(6) Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules,
1996-Registry for filing election petitions- whether filing petition in
High Court Registry other than the provided district registry renders
petition incompetent fatally.
Transfer of suit-transfer of a petition filed in a wrong registry-
whether thereby court has no jurisdiction to transfer the same but
may only strike it out.
Held: R5(6) Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules, 1996
mandatorily provides that the election petition shall be filed in the district
registry respective of the constituency in which the petitioned election is
held, were such a registry exists.  In the instant case the registry for filing
was Mpigi and not the High Court at Kampala.  Therefore the petition was
wrongly filed in a wrong registry.
a suit filed in a wrong registry is incompetent and the court to which it is filed
had no jurisdiction to transfer the same and can only strike it off the register.
Petition struck off register with costs.
Tumushabe Abaho Vs. Stanley Beineababao.
Appeals-decree-failure to file decree together with memo of appeal-
whether an irregularity - S.232(1)(9) Magistrates Courts Act -
decree- extraction thereof - whether invariably by the appellant-
0.18r 7CPR.
Held: S.232(1)(a) Magistrate Courts Act requires that an appeal must be
from a decree, that at the time the appeal is lodged, a decree appealed from
must be in existence.  In the instant case, the decree appealed from was on
court record and this was sufficient compliance with s.232(1)(a)MCA.
O.18 r7 puts the duty of extracting a decree on the successful party.  It was
therefore erroneous for the respondent to argue that the intending appellant
has the duty to extract the decree.
Preliminary objection overruled with costs.
Crown Bottlers Vs. Lake Victoria Bottling Co & 2 others.
Application strike out notice of appeal r80 RSC-whether may be
amended to include application to strike out appeal.
Held: The application to strike out the notice of appeal could not be
amended under r 80 RSC but could be withdrawn and a fresh application
for striking out the appeal instituted.
Application dismissed with costs.
Yoakim Mwene Habyene Vs. Attorney General.
Extension of time r4 RSC-likelihood of success of main application
whether a ground to refuse or grant an application for extension of
time.
Costs-taxation-whether court may interfere with discretion of taxing officer
where the complaint is the inadequacy of amount taxed.
Affidavit O.17 r3(1)-opinion-whether affidavit was defective for merely stating
opinions of the deponent.
Held: Under r4 RSC for an application for extension of time, likelihood of
success is not a ground.  However, likelihood of success may strengthen
the applicant's case when proved.  However, in the instant case, there was
likelihood of success because the applicant had already approbated the
court's award of the so called inadequate costs and taken benefit of it.  He
was now estopped from reprobating the same award which he had already
taken benefit of by afterwards claiming that the award was wrong.
Moreover, a judge hearing a reference may not interfere with the discretion of
the taxing master on the ground of alleged inadequacy of the amount taxed.
Only the complaint that the taxing master deviated from the principles
governing taxation of costs would enjoin the reference judge to interfere with
the discretion of the taxing applicant is to quantum of costs taxed and this
was not a ground for a reference judge to interfere.
And the affidavit accompanying the application offended against O.17 r3(1)
for deponing to matters of personal opinions only, therefore there was no
accompanying affidavit.
Application dismissed.
Gulyetonda Jesse Vs. Henry Muganwa Kajura & 2 others.
Registry - filing in wrong registry - whether petition thus filed is
incompetent-45(6) Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions)
Rules 1996.
Held: An advocate who neglects to renew his certificate does not get
de-registered but his name continues on the roll of advocates.  It would be
an injury to hold that the absence of a certificate had the effect of invalidating
all proceedings taken in the suit, whereas the litigants would find it almost
impossible to investigate the existence of the certificate before handing
down their instructions.  Therefore, lack of an advocate's practicing
certificate does not invalidate proceedings and the petition was validly before
court.
S.2(4) of the Commissioner for Oaths (Advocates Act) provides that where
an Advocate Commissioner for Oaths ceases to practice as an Advocate
then such commissioner shall cease to be commissioner for Oaths.  Since
the Advocate who commissioned the affidavit had never been de-registered
as an Advocate, inspite of his lack of a practicing certificate he validly
continued to act as Commissioner for Oaths and the affidavit he
commissioned could not be impeached merely because of lack of a
practicing certificate.
R5(6) of the Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules 1996
provides mandatorily that where a constituency to which a petition relates is
within a district registry of the High Court then the petition must be
presented in that District Registry.  In the instant case the presentation of
the petition at Kampala instead of Masindi where the relevant constituency
had its district registry, was fatal and on that account the petition was
incompetent.
Petition struck off the court record with costs for having been in wrong
registry.
Mutekanga Asumani Haji Vs. Equator Growers (U) Ltd.
Interlocutory judgment-formal proof-whether formal proof include
proof of liability or quantum of damages.
Entry of appearance-failure to enter appearance-whether thereby
party precluded from taking part in proceedings.
Formal proof-standard of proof - whether the plaintiff had less
burden to prove special damages because there was no defence
to his claim.
Held: A defendant who neither enters an appearance nor files a written
statement of defence is precluded from taking part in proceedings during
formal proof hearing, when there is subsisting an interlocutory judgment.
The learned trial judge therefore erred when he allowed counsel for the
respondent to participate in the proceedings and cross examine witnesses.
Where an interlocutory judgment has been entered in favor of the plaintiff,
the question of liability of the defendant is no longer in issue.  What is in
issue is the assessment of the quantum of damages.  Therefore the learned
trial judge misdirected himself when he required the appellant to prove
breach of the agreement, when there was a subsisting interlocutory
judgment in favor of the plaintiff.
Special damages must be specifically pleaded and strictly proved
irrespective of whether there is a defence to the claim or not.  Proof of
special damages consists evidence of particular losses.  In the instant case
the appellant's witnesses had taken part in running the factory and testified
with first hand knowledge.  The appellant had proved his claim for special
damages on a balance of probabilities.
Since no attempt was made to prove loss of profit non would be awarded.
Sh. 1 million would be awarded as general damages for breach of contract.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Allibhai Mohamed Vs. Bukenya Mukasa & Departed Asian
Property Custodian Board.
Review O.41 r1(1)(b), 8 Civil procedure Rules, ss.83 & 101 Civil
procedure Act - aggrieved party-where a person not party to the
proceedings may claim to be aggrieved by the judgment.
Held: Under S.83 Civil Procedure Act and O.42 rr 1(1)(b) & 8, an aggrieved
person is a person who had suffered legal grievance as a result of a
judgment and this includes a person not a party to the proceedings.
However, the grievance must be a legal grievance.  In the instant case at
the time of the consent judgment whose review is sought, i.e. February
1994 the appellant had no Letters of Administration to the estate of the
lessee.  Therefore, the appellant had no locus standi in the management of
the property of the lessee and therefore could not validly claim to have
suffered legal grievance as a result of the consent judgment.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Mulenga Joseph Vs. Photo focus Ltd & Anor.
Objector proceedings - possession - whether objector was in
possession of the attached property on account of the judgment
debtor-whether property therefore properly attached.
Held: a debenture hold has a superior interest or security over the executing
judgment creditor where the property sought to be attached is a subject of
a debenture.
However, the interest granted by the debenture to the objector is limited to
only the amount advanced to the judgment debtor as loan/overdraft by the
objector.  In this case the sum advanced was shs.135 million and yet the
total value of rice over which the objector had the debenture was above
shs.500 million.
But in order for excess value of a debenture to be a subject of attachment in
execution of a judgment debt, the charge created must be a floating charge
and the judgment debtor must be in possession of the asset(s)).
In the Instant case the charge created was a floating charge because it
covered assets both present and future, which assets could be changing
as in ordinary course of business, for instance the rice could be sold and
more bought and this would continue to he the case until the debenture
holder, i.e. the Bank/objector took a step to intervene and thus have the
charge crystallized.
Secondly, though the rice was in the possession of the objector bank since
it was in its bonded warehouse as required by the terms of the debenture,
nevertheless the rice was in possession of the objector on account of the
judgment debtor.  Therefore according to the requirement in O.19 r58 CPR
regarding the situation, the rice in excess of the objector's interest was
attachable in execution of the judgment debt.
Application dismissed with costs.
Gulyetonda Jesse Vs. Henry Muganwa Kajura.
Costs-election petitions-whether costs in elections do not follow the
event-S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act and r27 Parliamentary Elections
(Election Petitions) Rules, 1996.
Held: It is not true that in election petitions a petitioner has no personal
interest in the matter.  In the instant case the petitioner personally wanted
the respondent's sit.  Therefore, costs may follow the event even in election
petitions as it was in the present petition.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Luwero Green Acres Ltd Vs. Marubeni Corporation
Appeals O.39 r 14(2) - Exparte appeal- application to rehear
appeal heard exparte O.39 r18 where the application is dismissed-
whether applicant may instead appeal against exparte judgment
or must appeal against the refusal to rehear appeal on merit.
Held: S.74(2) Civil Procedure Act permits the appellant to appeal against
exparte decree.  This permission does not exclude the appellant from
appealing against the refusal to rehear appeal on its merits. The appellant
in entitled to follow either of the two choices.  Therefore the preliminary
objection was misconceived.
Preliminary objection dismissed with costs.
Photo focus Ltd Vs. Mulenga Joseph
Registrar's powers, O.46 r2 CPR-entry of final judgment under
O.9 r4 CPR-whether registrar had no powers to enter final judge-
ment because the case was not a liquidated demand.
Liquidated demand O.9 r4 CPR -entry of final judgment-whether
registrar had no power to enter final judgment - whether registrar
had no power to enter final judgment-whether claim was not liquidated.
Setting aside exporter judgment O.9 r9 CPR-whether it would be
just and reasonable.
Authority to borrow money-whether a director is not authorized to borrow
money without a company resolution.
Inherent powers of court S.101 Civil Procedure Act-whether it was
just and equitable that the exparte judgment be set aside and the
applicant be heard in defence of his case.
Held: A liquidated demand is in the nature of a debt, a specific sum of
money due and payable under or by virtue of a contract ascertained or
capable of being ascertained as a mere matter of arithmetic.  In the present
case the respondent was only claiming a specific amount of money loaned.
Therefore the claim was a liquidated demand and the registrar was entitled
to enter judgment and Decree under O.46 r2 CPR in favour of the plaintiff
due to the defendant's failure to enter appearance and file defence when
served.
Under O.9 r9 CPR Court has unlimited discretion as to the reasons for
setting aside exparte judgment but the discretion must be exercised
judicially and for that matter court sets two tests while considering whether
or not to exercise its discretion in favour of setting aside, namely, whether
there was a material factor that could have influenced the judgment,
which factor might not have existed had the judgment not been exparte,
and secondly, whether it would be just and reasonable to set aside.  In the
instant case the applicant does not, deny service of summons but contends
that the judgment should be set aside because the registrar had power to
enter final judgment whereas it was not a liquidated demand.  This
contention is not true.  Therefore taking all the circumstances of the case
into consideration it would not be just and reasonable to set aside the
judgment.
A director has powers to borrow money in the name of the company where
the Articles of Association do not prohibit the transaction.  Therefore, the
loan acquired by the director in the name of the company was finding on the
company and the company was liable to repay it.
Application dismissed with costs.
Uganda Revenue Authority Vs. Stephen Mabosi.
Interest S.26 Civil Procedure Act-whether 40% excessive because
above bank rate.
Held: When as provided by S.90 of the Evidence Act, the terms of a contract
or other disposition of property, have been reduced to the form of a
document, no other evidence is admissible to exclude or add onto what is
contained in the document.  The document speaks alone and by itself.
Therefore, the appellant was estopped from claiming that in fact the goods
seized were less than what was recorded in the seizure notice.  The only
admissible evidence was the seizure notice.  The learned trial judge was
correct in rejecting the appellant's evidence that derogated from the seizure
notice.
Moreover, an omission or neglect to challenge the evidence in chief of a
material proposition by cross-examination would lead to the inference that
the evidence as given is accepted.  In the instant case the appellant never
cross-examined the respondent on the number of trips involved in ferrying
the impounded goods.  Therefore, the respondent's testimony was
unchallenged.
However, the award of 40% interest, being far above the bank interest was
excessive and would call for the intervention of the appellate court.  Instead
30% would be ordered.
Appeal dismissed accept as to rate of interest. Respondent awarded 80% of
the taxed costs of the appeal.
Yekoyakim Mwene Habyene Vs. Attorney General & anor.
Part heard case O.16 r10(1)-retrial of suit-application to retry part
heard suit de novo-whether tenable-whether may be allowed under
S.3(2)( c) Judicature Act and S.101 CPA.
Appeals-leave to appeal-against order refusing to retry suit de novo,
without leave of court-whether tenable -whether may be allowed
under inherent powers of the supreme court r1(3) RSC.
Disqualification of presiding judge-application therefore -whether
grounds exist to disqualify a presiding judge.
Held: The appeal against the ruling where the trial judge refused to try the
case de novo was irregularly before the Supreme Court because no leave
had been granted therefore.  However, owing to the special circumstances of
the case, the said irregularity was not fatal to the appeal as the defect was
curable by court exercising its inherent powers under r1(3) RSC.
O.16 r 10(1) confers discretionary powers to a judge succeeding to a pert
heard case to try the case from point where his/her sister judge left from.
this means the succeeding judge may exercise his inherent powers
considering the circumstances of the case, to try the case de novo, as
provided by S.101 Civil Procedure Act and S.3(2)(c) of the Judicature Act.
In the instant case the circumstantial of the case justified a retrial.
No satisfactory reason had been shown to justify the disqualification of the
judge from hearing the case.
Appeal allowed in part.  Case ordered to be tried de novo.  Costs in cause.
All Ports Freight Service (U) Ltd Vs. Julius Kamanyi & anor
Striking out pleadings O.6r 29 CPR-application therefore by co-
defendant-whether untenable-whether must be only by adverse party.
Written statement of defence-striking out thereof under O.6r 29
CPR for failure to disclose a defence and for being frivolous and
vexatious-whether WSD failed to disclose a defence under O.13 r1
Issues O.13r1 (1, (2)CPR-whether WSD failed to make any answer
to the claim, and therefore no issue was constituted requiring the
answer of court.
Held: According to the rules of statutory interpretation, what is not expressly
excluded, is permitted.  Therefore since O.6 r 29 CPR does not exclude a
defendant from applying to court for striking out the WSD of his
co-defendant on grounds that it does not disclose a defence, is vexatious or
frivolous, such an application is permitted.
A defence is an adverse answer to the claim of the plaintiff it is the adverse
propositions of law and fact as between the litigants that constitute issues
under O.13 rr 1(1) and (2) CPR that must be decided by court.  When a
defence does not constitute an adverse answer to the plaintiff's claim then it
is no defence and may be struck out under O.6 r 29.  a defendant may
make an application to strike out a co-defendant's defence under this rule.
Since the 1st defendant's WSD was in fact an admission of the claim, it
was in fact an admission of the claim, it was no defence and his
co-defendant rightly applied to strike it off.
Application allowed with costs.
Uganda Mineral waters Ltd Vs. Kampala Mineral Water Ltd.
Objector proceedings O.19 rr55, 56 & 57 Civil Procedure Rules-
possession-whether objector was in possession through its tenants.
Held: Questions of legal title are not relevant as to the investigation that
must be made by court under O.19 rr55, 56, and 57 CPR.  Therefore court
would not veer into the relevance of adverse claims of title by the parties.
Under O.19 rr 55, 56, & 57, court must answer the sole question as to
whether at the date of the attachment the debtor was in possession either
on his won account or on the account of the objector or the objector was in
possession on account of the debtor.  In the instant case it was not
conceivable that a party would get an order of vacant possession in its favor
when in fact it is already in possession.  Therefore, the claim that the
judgment creditor was in possession through its tenants and yet was
granted an order of vacant possession in its favor, showed that the claim
was not true.  But, the objector presented a tenancy agreement which
showed that it was in possession through its tenants.
Application allowed.
Mark Extraction Enterprises Ltd Vs. M/S Nalongo Orphanage
Interest S.26 CPA-whether rate of 25% was just and reasonable.
Held: The plaintiff had proved that he supplied foodstuffs to the defendant to
the tune of shs.8,240,000/= and the money was still owing.  Therefore the
defendant was liable to pay the debt.
S.26 of the Civil Procedure Act provides that where interest is not agreed
between the parties, court could award interest at a rate that is just and
reasonable.  In the present case the defendant was an orphanage which
took the supplied foodstuffs for purposes of needy children and not to make
profit.  Therefore, the rate of interest of 25% as prayed for by he plaintiff was
neither just nor reasonable.  The defendant would pay interest at a rate of
Suit allowed with costs and interest at 18% p.a.
In re Mustapha Ramathan.
Certiorari-time-whether application out of time-whether application
not tenable because other statutory remedies exist.
Held: S.34(b) Judicature Act requires an application for leave to file for a
writ of certiorari to be filed within 6 months from the date of the happening of
the act sought to be quashed.  In the instant case the repossession order is
dated 16th October 1995 and yet the application is filed on 25th April, 1996,
well beyond the statutory 6 months.  Therefore the application was out of
time since the provisions of the law are mandatory.
Where a statutory remedy by way of appeal is available then the prerogative
jurisdiction of the court cannot be invoked.  S.14 of the Expropriated
Properties Act 1982 provides that any person aggrieved by the order of the
minister in granting repossession may appeal to the High Court.  Therefore
the instant application could not be entertained when another statutory
remedy was available.
The writ of prohibition is a preventive writ, by which court's prerogative
jurisdiction is invoked to prevent happening of an act complained of.  The
writ is not corrective.  In the instant case the application to prohibit the
Registrar of Titles from registering the third respondent as owner of the suit
property was misconceived since the registration already took place;
likewise, the application to prohibit the third respondent from taking
possession of the suit premises was misconceived, since upon registration
the third respondent took constructive possession.
Application dismissed.
Tekiike Yafeesi Vs. Jamada Wakafutuli.
Review, S.83 Civil Procedure Act, 0.42 r1 Civil Procedure Rules-
discovery of new and important evidence-whether ground established.
Judgment-citing wrong date of judgment-whether fatal.
Substitution due to death of plaintiff-whether proceeding in the
name of deceased irregular.
Affidavits-source of information-failure to disclose source of inform-
action-whether thereby affidavit incurably defective for being based
on hearsay.
Held: Citing of a wrong date of a judgment sought to be reviewed is a
serious irregularity.  Also, bringing the application in the names of a
substituted deceased party was a serious irregularity.  These two
irregularities would have rendered the application fatally defective had the
respondent complained.
The failure by affidavit of counsel for the applicant to disclose the source of
information where he had based his affidavit on information was a material
irregularity rendering the affidavit totally defective for being based on hearsay.
The alleged discovery of new and important evidence, the basis of the
application for review, was false because what is alleged to be new had
been exhaustively considered and decided upon in the judgment sought
to be reviewed.
Application for review refused and dismissed.
All Ports Freight Service Vs. Julius Kamanyi & anor
Joinder of parties-partners-whether all partner must be joined in suit.
Held: If two or several persons jointly purchase goods for resale with a view
to dividing the profits arising from the transaction, a partnership is created
and each of them will be liable to third parties.  In the instant case it was
clear that both defendants obtained cement from the plaintiff, for resale at a
profit to be shared.  Therefore, a partnership relationship was established as
under s.3 (1) of the Partnership Act.
A partnership need not be established formally and in writing.  It is sufficient
to establish that a community of interest exists between the parties.  This
was amply proved in this case.
The doctrine of holding out also provided for under S.18 of the Partnership
Act, states that where a person holds himself out as a partner, thus
including third parties, acting on such representations, to deal with him as
such, then he is liable to the third parties.  In the instant case it was not
necessary to apply the doctrine because the partnership had already been
established.
Although S.30 of the Bills of Exchange Act provides that when a person's
signature appears on a bill of exchange then that person is prima facie a
party, it was not applicable to the instant case because the plaintiff was not
suing on the cheque, the cheque was only of evidential value of the
transaction.  Therefore, the non appearance of the second defendant's
signature on the cheque, did not absolve him from liability for the debt
incurred for the unpaid cement.
O. 1 r 6 empowers a plaintiff to elect whom to sue.  Therefore the plaintiff
was free not to join the said cook to the proceedings as another defendant.
Sh. 15 million would be awarded as general damages for breach of contract.
Suit allowed with costs.
Asiimwe Sarah Vs. Festo Byenkya.
Appeals-time-whether memorandum of appeal was out of time.
Seal of court-seal of Magistrate's Court on a High Court document
whether irregularity fatal.
Held: In absence of evidence showing that the record of the proceedings
was availed to the appellant within 30 days of the date of judgment, it
would not be proper to hold that the appeal was lodged out to time.
A memorandum of appeal must be stamped with the stamp or seal of the
High Court.  However since it was explained that because of the absence of
the High Court District Registry stamp or seal, the Chief Magistrate Courts
stamp was used, the irregularity would be excused under Art.126(2) of the
Constitution that enjoins court to administer substantive justice without
undue regard to technicalities.
Preliminary points overruled.  Court to proceed with the appeal.
Uganda Development Bank Vs. National Insurance Corp. &
G.M Combined.
Adjournment-discretion of judge-whether appellate court may
interfere therewith.
Security for costs-application thereof-whether only available to
defendant-whether plaintiff counter claimed against becomes defendant.
Leave to appeal interlocutory order-whether must stay proceedings.
Refusal of advocate to proceed after adjournment refused-whether
suit may be dismissed under O.14 r19 Civil Procedure Rules.
Held: An appellate court should not interfere with the exercise of the
discretion of a judge unless it is satisfied that the judge in exercising his
discretion has misdirected himself in some matter and as a result had
arrived at a wrong conclusion.  In the instant case the trial judge refused the
adjournment to counsel for the appellant who sought to file a formal
application for an order of security for costs against the second respondent.
The trial judge based his refusal on the reasoning that the counterclaim, the
subject of the application for security for costs, would be tried later in time
after the disposal of the main suit and that the plaintiff would only at that
time present his application.  This was a misdirection on the part of the trial
judge because a counterclaim is not a separate suit to be tried separately.
Therefore, the trial judge's discretion to refuse the adjournment was
exercised on a misdirection of law and fact and for that matter he arrived at
wrong conclusion.
A plaintiff is served with a counterclaimed becomes a defendant to the extent
of the counterclaim.  Therefore the plaintiff/appellant was proceedings.
Therefore the plaintiff/appellant was correct in filing the application for
security for costs as it had become a defendant to the counterclaim.
Leave to appeal an interlocutory order does not of itself operate as a stay of
the proceedings.  Therefore the learned trial judge was entitled to order that
the suit proceeds while the plaintiff/appellant pursues his appeal against the
judge's refusal to adjourn the case.
O.14 r 19 empowers court with various alternative while dealing with party
that is refusing to proceed with the trial of the case, and dismissal of the
suit is just one of the alternatives but the severest of all the alternatives.
In the present case it would have been proper to ask the party represented
by counsel to proceed by themselves without their counsel instead of
dismissing the suit.
Appeal allowed.  No order as to costs.
Gubaza William Vs. Uganda Electricity Board.
Reinstatement of dismissed suit O.9 r20 whether application
tenable-whether negligence of counsel was sufficient cause.
Held: Under O.9 r 20 court has a discretion to consider whether mistake of
counsel may be treated as sufficient for non appearance of the plaintiff when
his case was called for hearing.  In the circumstances of this case it would
not be proper to penalize the plaintiff for the negligence of his counsel.
Therefore the dismissal would be set aside.
Application allowed.
Mulenga Joseph Vs. Photo Focus (U) Ltd.
Objector proceedings-possession O.19 rr55, 57 and 89 Civil
Procedure Rules-whether failure to plead that application was in
possession of the suit property on the date of attachment was
final.
Affidavit-falsehood-whether entire affidavit suspect.
Held: It is trite law that in an objector application under O.19 r55 the
investigation the court does is restricted to the issue of who was in
possession on the date of attachment.  In the instant application the
objector never pleaded that it was in possession of the attached property on
the date of attachment though at the prosecution of the application the
objector claimed that it was in possession.  This was an afterthought which
would not convince court to rule in favour of the objector.
Secondly, the objector's affidavit in support contained obvious falsehoods.
Such falsehoods rendered the entire affidavit suspect and an application
based on such an affidavit must fail.
Application dismissed with costs.
Transroad Ltd Vs. Bank of Uganda.
Reciprocal Enforcement of judgments Act S.3(1)-application to
extend time within which to register a foreign judgment-whether
it should be considered as a preliminary issue if the respondent
submitted to the jurisdiction of the foreign court before the
application for extension of time within which to register the
judgment is considered.
Reciprocal enforcement of judgments-extension of time within which to
apply to register a foreign judgment-whether the period of 4 years was an
ordinate delay.
Held: The learned judge in the lower court misdirected himself when raised
the submission to the jurisdiction of the foreign court by the respondent.
This issue was not pertinent to the interlocutory application for leave to
extend time.  The issue of jurisdiction was only relevant in the main
application to have the judgment registered and executed in Uganda.
The learned trial judge in the High Court was wrong to hold that the delay to
register the judgment for execution was inordinate because looking at the
history of the case it was the respondent who had given the appellant the
impression necessary to register the judgment for execution.
Appeal allowed.  Time extended within which to register the foreign
for execution in Uganda.
Poojara Dinesh Vs. Vacu-Lug (U) Ltd.
Striking out unnecessary or scandalous matter O.6 r17 CPR-
whether the defendant's pleading a set off for developments on the
suit property, in a claim for rent arrears, was a matter scandalous
or unnecessary and should be struck off under O.6 r17 CPR.
Held: S.14 of the Expropriated Properties Act relate to a situation where the
Minister has made a decision concerning the expropriated property which
decision has aggrieved the party.  Such a party can appeal the decision of
the minister to the High Court.  In the instant case the minister had made no
decision to appeal from.  The defendant was entitled to claim a set off in its
WSD.
Moreover, there was nothing unnecessary or scandalous abut the pleading.
Preliminary objection overruled.  Case to proceed.
Nakadde Imelda Ndiwalungi Vs. Roy Busuulwa Nsereko & anor
Temporary injunction O.37 r1(a) CPR-whether sentimental
attachment to the property is evidence of a possibility of irreparable injury.
Held: The applicant had proved she has a prima facie case with good
chances of success and she had further proved that the suit property was in
danger of being alienated and further that she had sentimental attachment to
the property which sentiments were not compensatable by way of damages
and this would therefore amount to irreparable injury.
Application for a temporary injunction allowed to subsist for 6 months.
Muluya Mustapha Haji Vs. Alupakusadi W. Wamulongo & ors
Jurisdiction of the High Court Act 86 Constitution of Uganda-
election petitions-whether an election petition filed in a district
registry other than the one in which the election was held was a
fatal irregularity contrary to rule 5(6) Election Petition Rules.
Held: Although on the face of it rule 5(6) is mandatory in its provision that
the election petition shall be presented  in a district registry where the
election was held, the rule does not provide the consequences of non
compliance.  Therefore regard must be had as to the intentio9n of the
legislature.  When the results of an election are petitioned Art. 86 of the
Constitution gives Jurisdiction to the High court to hear and determine the
merits of the petition and rules of procedure providing as to which registry the
petition may be filed are only enabling and to interpret them in such as to
make the court prohibited from exercising its jurisdiction as conferred to it
under Art. 86 of the Constitution would be to defeat the intention of the
legislature.  Therefore, in the instant case the petition was rightly before the
court of competent jurisdiction to hear and determine the same.
Objection overruled with costs.
Mapro Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Special damages-whether relate to only money already spent.
Admissions, O.11 r 6 CPR-whether proved.
Interest-whether payable when not agreed.
Held: Where only quantum is framed as an issue for the determination of
the court, then liability is admitted under O.11 r6.  Therefore counsel for
defendant was estopped from contesting the prayers for special damages.
Special damages may be expenditure already incurred or expenditure to be
incurred.  The repair costs required as certified by the government valuer
was expenditure to be incurred and was competently prayed for as a special
damage.
In commercial transactions the rationable is to compensate the plaintiff for
what he would probably earn if his money was not held. Court is empowered
to award interest even where it is not prayed for or agreed between the
parties, to meet the ends of justice.
Suit allowed. Repairs & rent to be paid as special damages and interest at
Uganda Journalists Safety Committee & 2 others Vs. A.G.
Affidavit-non-disclosure of source of information-whether affidavit
incurably defective.
Cause of action-failure to disclose by affidavit the nature of the
grievance and unconstitutional-whether no cause of action
disclosed.
Held: Art. 137(3) of the Constitution gives jurisdiction to the constitutional
court to entertain a petition that seeks to challenge the constitutionality of a
given law.  The procedure provided for this kind of petition is legal notice
No.4/96 "The Rules of the Constitutional Court (Petitions for Declarations
1996.  Under Art 137(3) the Constitutional Court has original jurisdiction to
make declarations of the constitutionally of laws and acts of the executive.
However, under Art 50 it is the High Court that has original jurisdiction to
entertain petitions that require the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights
and Freedoms.  Therefore the two articles deal with different jurisdictions
and may not be invoked simultaneously in the same petition.  The petition
was therefore irregularly before court.
Rules of Procedure must be adhered to even in constitutional cases, and
only minor irregularities may be ignored where a petition prima facie disclose
a cause of action and the individual's liberty is at stake.  But proceeding
under the wrong provisions of the law was not such a minor irregularity as in
the instant case.
Rule 12(1) of the Rules of the Constitutional Court (Petitions for Declarations
under Art 137 of the Constitution) Directions 1996, provides that all evidence
at the trial in favour of or against the petition shall be by affidavit.  Therefore,
the cause of action must be discernible from the affidavits.  In the instant
case, one of the two affidavits only claimed that the provisions were
restrictive, prohibitive and unconstitutional without showing this by affidavit.
And in the second affidavit it was deponed that journalists were being
harassed, without the affidavit disclosing which journalists were actually
harassed. Therefore the petition failed to disclose a cause of action.
When averments are based on information the source of information should
clearly be disclosed, and if it is on belief, the grounds of belief should be
stated, so that court is enabled to judge whether it would be safe to act on
the deponent's affidavit.  In the instant case both supporting affidavits failed
to satisfy the non disclosure rule and were thus defective and could not be
relied upon.  The petition cannot stand as the supporting affidavits had fallen
by the way side.
Petition struck out with costs.
Gulu Municipal Council Vs. Nyeko Gabriel & others.
Statutory notice-suit against a local authority S.1 Civil Procedure
& Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act-whether suit filed before the expiry
of 60 days notice is barred.
Revision, S.84 Civil Procedure Act-whether a party aggrieved by a
Magistrate's Court's decision may apply to have it revised.
Held: There is no prescribed procedure to initiate revision proceedings under
S.84 CPA, however an applicant aggrieved by the decision of a Magistrate's
Court may apply to the High Court to have the decision of the Magistrate's
Court revised.  In the instant case, though counsel for the applicant was
wholly to blame when he refused to enter appearance on behalf of applicant,
court would not sanction an illegality by stand.  This is because the
provisions of S.1 of the Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act
requiring that the suit against a local authority may only be filed after the
expiry of 60 days, were mandatory.
Application allowed.  No order as to costs.
Genda John & 53 ors Vs. Coffee Marketing Board.
Review O.42 r1, CPR, SS.83 and 101 Civil Procedure act-consent
judgment-whether reviewable.
Inherent powers of court S.101 CPA-consent judgment-whether
court may vary consent judgment to prevent unjust enrichment.
Held: O.42 r 1(1) CPR & S.83 Civil Procedure act Provide that a person
considering himself aggrieved by a judgment or order, which is not
appealed from, may apply to have such upon proof of discovery of new and
material evidence not available after due diligence of the party before the
judgment or order is made.  However, a person aggrieved, must legally be
aggrieved.  In the instant case the applicant cannot be said to be legally
aggrieved when the judgment was recorded by the consent of both parties.
However, under S.101 Civil Procedure Act, court has inherent powers to
make such order as may be necessary for the ends of justice.  In the instant
case, the respondents in their plaint never prayed for the payment of gratuity.
If later the payment of gratuity found its way in the consent judgment, it
must amount to unjust enrichment, which court has inherent powers to
prevent.
Application allowed under S.101 CPA and not under O.42 r1(1), with costs.
Chebet Augustine Vs. Torokoch Erieza.
Dismissal of suit for want of prosecution O.9 r19-appeals-whether
party may appeal against dismissal of suit for want of prosecution
or must apply for reinstatement of the suit under O.9 r20 CPR.
Held: The appeal was incompetent because under O.9 r 20 CPR when a suit
is dismissed because of non attendance of the plaintiff, the plaintiff can only
apply for reinstatement of the same by the court dismissing it but such
plaintiff (or applicant as in the present case) cannot appeal against the
dismissal as of right.
Appeal struck out with costs.
Tororo District Administration Vs. Andalalapo Industries.
Application for an order to postpone payment of decretal amount-
O.18 r11(2)-whether invariably by consent of decree holder.
Inherent powers of court S.101 Civil Procedure Act-application for
an order to defer payment of decretal amount-whether because
procedure provided under O.18 r11(2) inherent powers of court not invokable.
Held: O.18 r 11 (2) require that for an applicant who seeks a court's order to
the effect that he being a judgment debtor, the satisfaction of the decree be
deferred or be satisfied in installments, must bring that application with the
consent of the judgment creditor.  In the instant case since the applicant
did not have the consent of the judgment creditor.  In the instant case
since the applicant did not have the consent of the judgment creditor the
application was misconceived and must fail.
Court's inherent powers under s.101 CPA are not inviolable where there is a
particular legislation dealing with the matter.  In the instant case the
legislation applicable was O.18 r 11(2) CPR.
Art. 126(2)(e) of the Constitution require that substantive justice must be
administered without undue regard to technicalities.  However, the Article
does not do away with rules of procedure which must be adhered to.
Application struck out with costs.
Ibingira Monica Ntarumbana & 3 ors Vs. Muriel Baingana
& 3 others.
Costs S.27 Civil Procedure Act - whether because of filial
reconciliation, costs may not follow the event.
Held: The general rule is that costs follow the event.  However, court is
empowered with discretion under S.27 CPA when deciding whether a loosing
party may not pay costs, looking at the peculiar circumstances of the
case.  In the instant case the parties are very close relatives and ordering
the defendants to pay costs would be failing to help the process of
reconciliation amongst the parties.  Therefore, this was the proper case for
refusing to order the loosing party to pay the costs of the suit.
It is ordered that each party meets its own costs.
Namwandu Catherine Vs. Sulaiman Musisi
Interlocutory judgment under O.9 r 6 CPR-claim for order of eviction
and general damages for trespass-whether interlocutory judgment
wrongly entered and may be set aside.
Service of summons O.5 r14 CPR-service on brother of defendant-
whether service impeachable.
Held: O.9 r 6 CPR provides that a registrar may enter an interlocutory
judgment in default of entry of appearance by the defendant where the
plaintiff's claim is for pecuniary damages.  In the instant case the claim was
for an order of eviction and general damages.  Therefore, the registrar had no
jurisdiction to enter the interlocutory judgment under O.9 r 6 CPR and the
judgment so entered was a nullity and must be set aside.
The affidavit of service did not sufficiently prove that there was effective
service of the summons because it deponed that service was done on the
brother of the defendant without showing that the defendant himself could
not be found, nor showing that the brother was an adult.
Interlocutory judgment set aside.  Service of summons to be done afresh.
Janmohamed Jaffer Ltd Vs. Kemisa Senya.
Time-appeals-whether appeal filed out of time-whether time begins
running when decision read to the parties or when reason for the
decision are given later.
Held: Computation of time for purposes of appeal starts from the day a
decision is pronounced but not when the reasons for the decision are
delivered.  In the instant case time started running on 28th February 1995
when the decision was delivered and expired on 31st March, 30 days hence,
and therefore the appeal filed on 12th September 1995 was clearly out of
time, and therefore incompetent.
Application allowed with costs.  Appeal struck out.
Musoke Lwanga Sanyu Vs. Yakobo Ntate Mayanja
Fraud-pleading O.6 r2-notice of motion-whether a case where fraud
is pleaded cannot be determined by notice of motion-whether
fraud can only be determined by proceeding under a plaint and
written statement of defence.
Held: O.6 r2 CPR requires that where an action is based on fraud, the
particulars must be set out in the pleadings and proved in court strictly.
therefore, in an action involving fraud, proceedings by affidavit is not possible.
Therefore, the learned trial Judge misdirected himself when he proceeded to
entertain a matter where fraud was pleaded basing on affidavits.
Where a notice to remove a caveat is set by the registrar, under S.149(1)
RTA, it is required by S.205 of the RTA that a memorandum, being a copy
of the notice and when it was sent, be made.  In the instant case no such
memorandum existed and therefore there was no proof that the notice was
sent as alleged.
Moreover, even if there was no affidavit from M/s Mulira and Co. Advocates
deponing that they never received the notice, the affidavit was not necessary
because the burden of proof as required by SS.100, 101, 102 and 105 of the
Evidence Act, was on the person alleging that the notice was sent to prove
that actually the notice was sent.
Moreover, a caveat instituted for the beneficiary under a will does lapse after
the expiration of 60 days under S.149(1) of the RTA, the operation of the
caveat must be determined before this removal.  Therefore, the learned Judge
misdirected himself when he found that failure by the said Magala Efulaimu
to apply to court for the delay of the registration of the respondent as
proprietor was a ground to remove the caveat.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Mugenyi & Co. Advocates Vs. Attorney General
Pleadings-estoppel-whether must be pleaded.
Held: S.4(1) Companies Act requires at least 2 shareholders to form a
private limited liability company.  The 2 government ministers signed as
shareholders and thus fulfilled the requirements of the Act and it was not
competent to inquire as to whether or not the two ministers were
Shareholders.  Therefore the company was duly incorporated and the
learned trial judge erred when he held otherwise.
In order to lift the veil of incorporation personality so as to find that in fact
there was no company but a government extension, one must allege fraud
on the part of government.  In the instant case there was no fraud or illegality
alleged in the pleadings against government.  Therefore, the veil of
incorporation would remain uplifted and UTC 1975 would be dealt with as an
independent company separate from its owner the government and the
appellant must proceed to recover his fees in liquidation and not against
government.
Unless estoppels is a fact in issue at the trial, it cannot be raised when not
pleaded.  The defendant must plead estoppel and the plaintiff must reply in
order for it to be considered at the trial.  The learned trial judge erred to
have based his judgment on estoppel when the same had not been
pleaded and was not a fact in issue at the trial.
Appeal dismissed in part.  Appellant ordered to recover against the company
in liquidation.
Salim Jamal & 2 others Vs. Uganda Oxyen Ltd & 2 others.
Appeal-whether appeal commenced by notice of appeal or
memorandum of appeal.
Joinder of parties O.1 rr10(2), (4) CPR-whether party may be joined
without amending pleadings.
Held: Corporate personality cannot be used as a cloak or mask for fraud.
Where this is shown to be the case the veil of incorporation may be lifted to
ensure that justice is done and the court does not look helplessly in the
face of such fraud.  In the instant case it was necessary to disregard the
veil of incorporation and when that was done it would immediately be
apparent that respondent No.3 was a shareholder in OHL was not a director
and could therefore not remedy and loss occasioned by the directors
therein though ordinary mechanisms of internal management of the
company and the wronging directors were the ones in control, and could not
therefore bring an action to impeach themselves.  Therefore the learned
trial judged correctly found that respondent No.3 had a derivative right to
bring the derivative action against the wronging directors.
Where directors are being used by a derivative action, it is necessary to add
the company as a co-defendant.  O.I rr10(2) + (4) give court the discretion to
add a party where the circumstances of the case so demand.  In this case
the learned trial judge was right to add UOL as fourth defendant.  However,
when this is done the other party must be afforded an opportunity to amend
its pleadings.  In this the trial judge misdirected himself with he did not give
the plaintiff the opportunity to amend.
An appeal is commenced by a notice of appeal and not by a memorandum
of appeal.
Appeal dismissed except to the issue of whether the parties should have
been allowed to amend their pleadings after court had joined a fourth
defendant.
Katwiremu Yorokamu Engineer Vs. Mushemeza Elija & others
Time-notice of motion and affidavit in support bearing different
dates-whether a material irregularity.
Affidavit grounded on matters of knowledge of the law-whether
affidavit false because deponent not a lawyer.
Review O.42 rr1(1)(a) & (b) CPR - interlocutory orders from election
petitions-Parliamentary Elections Statutes, 1996-whether such
orders not reviewable because not appealable.
Review O.42 CPR-sufficient reason to necessitate a review -
whether presence of a decision of the court of appeal contrary to
that of the High Court was "sufficient reason" for review.
Held: There was no evidence that the deponent had no knowledge of the
matters of law.  A statement that the deponent engineer was not a lawyer
was no such evidence.  Therefore this did not impeach the validity of the
affidavit.
Where the (notice of motion) application and its accompanying affidavit
bear different dates, it does not vitiate the application when the application
and affidavit are filed in court on the same day.
The applicant's application for review does not fit under O.42 r 1 (1) (a).  This
sub-rule provides that in order for a matter to be reviewable there under, the
order must be one from which appeal is allowed but from which no appeal
has been preferred.  In the instant case, as the Court of Appeal had already
held, no appeal against interlocutory orders of the High Court was allowed
by the Court of Appeal.  Therefore, this application for review under O.42 rr1
(1)(a) under which this application was filed, was not allowed.
Under paragraph (b) of the same sub-rule it is provided that an application
for review may be made where the order of Civil Procedure Rules, O.39.
However, the instant case was an election petition not provided for under
O.39 CPR.  It is the Parliamentary Elections Statute 1996 that prohibited
the appeal of interlocutory orders from the High Court to the Court of Appeal,
and not the Civil Procedure Rules.  Therefore, even under O.42 rr1(1)(b) the
applicant's application for review was not feasible.
On top of the requirement to fit the application in O.42 rr1(1)(a) or (b),
application for review further requires the applicant to show that thee has
been a discovery of new and important matter not available before even with
due diligence or that there was an error on the face of the record, application
the applicant sought to plead that there was sufficient reason for review.
The term "sufficient reason" must be interpreted ejusdem generis with the
first 2 requirements.  To this end the mere presence of a decision of the
Court of Appeal in a different case altogether perse cannot amount to
sufficient reason" within the meaning of O.42 r1.
Application dismissed.  Costs in cause.
Wamboya Abu Vs. Gidima Sulaiman
Stay of execution O.39 r4(3) CPR-whether grounds exist.
Held: An applicant for an order of stay of execution must demonstrate to
court that his pending appeal has a likelihood of success.  This is because
the remedy of stay of execution exists to avoid rendering nugatory the result
of a successful appeal.  In the present case however the applicant had not
by affidavit or otherwise demonstrated that his appeal had a likelihood of
success.
An applicant for an order or a stay of execution must further show that
substantial loss may result against him if the order is not given; that the
application has been made without unreasonable delay and that security
has been given by the applicant for due performance of the decree should
the appeal not succeed.  In the present case the applicant failed in all the
three respects.
Application dismissed with costs.
Mirieri Sanyu Vs. Moses Bukenya.
Contempt of court-disobedience of an order of a temporary
injunction-O.37 r2(1), (3) CPR -whether person disobeying an order
of temporary injunction may invariably always be committed to Civil Prison.
Temporary Injunction-disobedience of order thereof-whether
respondent may be committed to Civil Prison for contempt.
Held: Under our law, courts are quite cautious in invoking the process of
committal to civil custody in civil matters.  An applicant for an order of
committal to Civil Prison must not only show that the respondent has
disobeyed the court's order, but that the act of disobedience has prejudiced
the interest of the opposite party, and that obstruction of justice complained
of is such that committal for contempt would be a proper remedy.  In the
instant case, though the respondent had disobeyed the orders of court, the
disobedience was not prejudicial to the interest of the applicant since he had
the interest of the applicant since he had prayed for general damages that f
could atone for his injured interest.
Appeal dismissed.  No order as to costs.
British India General Insurance Co. Ltd Vs. Dolatrai Solanki.
Stay  of execution -good cause-whether shown-whether special
circumstances exist.
Held: The court can grant a stay of execution when satisfied that there is
good cause and that special circumstances exist to justify such a cause.
And the likelihood of success of the applicant's appeal and the consequent
fear of rendering an appeal likely to succeed, nugatory, consist of special
stay.  In the instant case the appeal was not likely to succeed because it
was instituted by an applicant who had no capacity to institute it.
A company can only authorize the commencement of legal proceedings in
its name by way of a resolution.  In the instant case there was no such
resolution and therefore, the counsel who purported to act on behalf of the
applicant who had not made any resolution to that effect, must be personally
liable for the costs arising from such proceedings where the Advocates is
apparently acting without instructions.
Application dismissed.
Hotel International Ltd Vs. The Administrator of the Estate of
the Late Robert Kavuma.
Interest S.26 CPA-whether court may not award interest on own volition.
Held: The learned trial judge erred in fact when he held that there was the
respondent's caveat on the suit land as a notice of the respondent's
unregistered interest.  This is because the evidence was to the effect that
the Registrar of Titles though she had received the application to register a
caveat she had not done so.  S.51 RTA provides that no unregistered
instruments is effectual.  Therefore, the respondent's caveat did not exist
and therefore his unregistered interest was not protected and was thus
available legally for appropriation to the appellant who had no notice thereof.
No fraud could be imputed on the appellant since he had no knowledge of
the existence of the respondent's unregistered interest.
The learned trial Principal Judge erred when he shifted the burden of proof by
requiring the appellant/defendant to deny whether or not he had inflicted
damage on the suit premises for purposes of assessing mesne profits.  This
was contrary to the requirements of SS.100, 102 & 102 Evidence Act that
required the person alleging to prove the truth of his allegations.
The learned trial Judge erred when he awarded interest when the same had
not been prayed for.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Mukasa Vincent & ors Vs. Mary Musoke.
Time-reply to WSD filed expiry of 15 days-whether filed in time
because WSD received "under protest".
Held: The phrase "under protest" is meaningless when not viewed in context.
In the instant case counsel for the plaintiffs received the WSD though under
protest, were bound to reply thereto as provided under the law.  Therefore
his reply to the WSD outside the statutory period of 15 days as provided
by O.8 r11 was not valid.
Reply struck out with costs.
Oriental Insurance Brokers Ltd Vs. Transocean (U) Ltd
Issues O.13 r 5(1)-amendment by court-whether invariably by
notifying the parties-whether judgment passed on amended
issues without parties being notified, is prejudicial.
