Held: (By a majority of 2 to 1) The learned trial judge erred in introducing
new issues at the time of making judgment without affording the parties the
opportunity to be heard and this error prejudiced the appellant's case.
S.43(3), (4) Insurance Decree impose a duty on the Insurance Broker to
remit the collected premiums to the insurer not later than 21 days.  since
the broker was under a duty to remit premiums to the insurer, it means that
the broker an implied duty to collect the premiums from the insured to the
insurer and even to sue the insured to compel him to pay the premiums.
The learned trial learned trial judge erred when he held that the broker could
not sue the insured to compel him to pay the unpaid, agreed premiums.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Ntungamo District Local Council Vs. John K. Karazarwe.
Amendment of proceedings O.6 r18-whether because amendment
may cause injustice and introduce a new cause of action may not
be allowed.
Affidavit O.17-affidavit in reply-whether failure to file affidavit in reply
meant that averments of facts are uncontroversial.
Held: The requirement to file an affidavit in reply is not a rule of law but a
rule of practice.  This is because the non complying party has a right to
disprove the contents of the other party through cross examination by leave
of court under O.17 r2.
O.6 r 18 confers a very wide discretion to courts to grant leave to parties to
amend their pleadings.  However an amendment that would introduce a new
distinctive cause of action or would prejudice the right to the other party
would not be allowed. In the instant case the amendment of the proceedings
drop the declaration of the legality or otherwise of the removal from office of
the applicant and the introduction of the prayer for an order stopping the
applicant from using the applicant's vehicle would not be allowed because a
new distinctive cause of action would emerge and the respondent would be
prejudiced in the defence on the validity or otherwise of his removal.
Application dismissed with costs.
Acak Smith Opon Brigadier Vs. Attorney General
Amendment of plaint O.6 r 18-cause of action-whether plaint may
not be amended because it does not disclose a cause of action.
Cause of action-vicarious liability-whether where a plaint does not
plead that a servant was acting in the course of employment no
cause of action is disclosed against his master.
Held: Where the plaint omits to aver that the acts complained of were
committed by the servants of the defendant in the course of their
employment, it does not mean that the plaint does not disclose a cause of
action, where the servants have been described as servants of the defendant.
This is because whether a servant did or did not do the acts complained of
in the course of his employment was a fact peculiarly within the knowledge
of the defendant to be pleaded by him in his defence.  Therefore in the
instant case the plaint disclose a cause of action because the defendant's
servants were described in the plaint as servants of the defendant for whose
tortuous actions the defendant was vicariously complained of.
Since the amendment would not prejudice the respondent the application to
amend was filed in time, it would be allowed.
Application for leave to amend allowed with costs against the applicant.
The Non-performing Assets Recovery Trust Vs. General
Industries (U) Ltd.
Security for costs rr 42, 43(1) and 104(1), (3) Court of Appeal Rules-
whether allegation of failure to pay past costs was a ground for an
order for security for costs.
Held: It was not sufficient to allege that the respondent had not paid past
costs.  The applicant for an order for security for costs must show that the
respondent cannot pay the costs past and future.  In the present case the
applicant had merely stated that the respondent had not paid past costs.
This was not sufficient.
Application dismissed with costs.
Ngirabakunzi Kwera Stella Vs. Ntabgoba.
Election petition appeals, r19 Parliamentary Elections (Elections
Petition) Rules 1996-application to enlarge time within which to file
memo of appeal-whether death of wife of counsel was a special
circumstance enjoining court to extend time.
Held: Rule 19, Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules 1996 gives
court wide powers to extend the period to file a memo of appeal provided
special circumstances are shown.  And the death of a wife of a counsel was
such a circumstance.
Application allowed and costs awarded against applicant.
Ddegeya Trading Stores (U) Ltd Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority.
Revision S.84 CPA-Order of Registrar as taxing master-whether
revisable by High Court Judge-whether Registrar neither subordinate
nor magistrates court.
Costs-consent as to costs-whether consent order for costs may be
set aside-whether the policy of the High Court was against
exaggerated bill of costs-whether thereby consent order may be
set aside.
Approbating and reprobating court's decision-an appeal against the
order of court for a fresh bill of costs and presentation of the fresh
bill of costs for taxation-whether this amounted to approbating and
reprobating court's decision.
Held: The Registrar of the High Court under O.46 r 4 is an officer of the High
Court and therefore cannot be called a subordinate or a magistrate's court
and therefore his decision cannot be revised by the High Court judge under
S.84 CPA.  Therefore the judge erred to have proceeded under S.84 CPA.
However, a consent judgment or order may be set aside if it is against the
policy of the Court.  And the policy of the court was against exaggerated
bills of costs.  In the instant case a bill of costs of Ugshs. 17 million for the
recovery of shs. 1.5 million was exaggerated and the judge in the High Court
was entitled to invalidate it.
Moreover, and most important, a person cannot approbate and reprobate a
decision of court's decision it amounts to a waiver of that person's right of
appeal at common law.  When the appellant presented a fresh bill of costs
and had it taxed, pursuant to the order of the judge in the High Court, he
was precluded from appealing against the order of the judge as this would
amount to approbating and reprobating a court's decision.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Shell (U) Vs. Agip (U) Ltd
Arbitration-a step in the proceedings -S.17 Arbitration Act-whether
notice under O.10 rr 15 & 16 to produce documents was a step in
the proceedings-that therefore court was correct to dismiss
application for stay of proceedings.
Stay of proceedings pending arbitration - whether application validly
refused because defendant had taken a step in the proceedings.
Notice of grounds for affirming the decision of the trial court-opting
out of arbitration agreement -whether proved.
Held: A notice to produce documents under O.10 rr15 & 16, even if filed in
court does not amount to taking a step in the proceedings as provided under
S.17 of the Arbitration Act.  A step in the proceeding must be an act
involving a court summons as under O.10 r18.  in the present case the
notices to produce documents and to inspect the same was mere discourse
between counsel of both parties and did not amount to taking a step in the
proceedings as envisaged by S.17 Arbitration Act.  Therefore the learned
trial judge erred in holding that the defendant/appellant had taken a step in
the proceedings when he filed the notice to produce documents and thus
misdirected himself on that basis to refuse to grant a stay of the
proceedings.
A notice to confirm the decision of the trial court arises when a party wishes
the appellate court to hold the same conclusion as the trial court on reasons
other than what the trial court gave, but arising from the evidence of facts
and law during the proceedings in the trial or lower court as the case may
be.  In the instant case counsel for the respondents wanted the appellant
court to hold that the trial judge could still have dismissed the appellant's
application on another ground directly arising from the evidence in that court,
that is, that the parties had opted out of the arbitration clause when they
chose to submit the dispute to the auditors.  However, there was no
evidence that the appointment of the auditors amounted to opting out of the
arbitration clause.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Prof. Syed Huq Vs. Islamic University in Uganda.
Preliminary objection as to competence of the appeal, r101(b)
RSC-whether must be raised with leave of court r80 RSC.
Held: An Advocate that practices without a valid practicing certificate after
the grace period, practices illegally and is liable to prosecution as provided
by S.14(1) Advocates Act.  And all proceedings taken by such counsel and
documents signed by him are invalid, because to say otherwise would
amount to a perpetuation of an illegality.
However, in this case, the issue of the competence of the appeal could not
be raised as a preliminary objection without the leave of the court according
to the provisions of r10(b) RSC.  Therefore the lack of a practicing certificate
by counsel who extracted the decree, would not interfere with the
competence of the appeal.
Where two parties to a contract have agreed to contract, then there is a
contract which non of the parties may deny.  In the instant case the
respondent's WSD admitted that the appellant was appointed Rector by
the Governing Council of the respondent.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself when he held that the appointment was null and void
due to lack of quorum by the appointing council.
However, S.13  of the Employment Decree provides that a foreign contract
of employment shall not be enforced unless it had been approved or attested
in accordance with the Employment Decree.  In the instant case since the
appellant was not a Ugandan and the respondent was a corporation that
that belonged to a foreign contract and the contract was unenforceable due
to lack of it having been approved or attested in accordance with the
Employment Decree.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Tororo District Administration Vs. Andalalapo Industries Ltd.
Revision, S.84 CPA - orders of High Court Registrar-whether
revisable.
District Registrar, O.46 r8-whether may finally determine rights
between parties.
District Registrar-appeal against orders thereof-whether under O.46
r8 or O.44 r7.
Notice of motion-grounds therefore O.48 r3-whether failure to state
grounds in notice of motion renders the same detective.
Unconditional leave to appear and defend-triable issue-whether
shown with sufficient particularity.
Held: Though it is mandatory that a notice of motion under O.48 r3 must
state the grounds of the application the irregularity caused by non
compliance is curable if the grounds of the application or appeal are set out
in the accompanying affidavit as was the case in the instant.
Even if it were true that the appellant did not comply with the O.44 r 7 by
bringing this appeal under O.46 r7, this by itself would not lead appeal being
struck out because rules of procedure are formulated for purposes of giving
effect to the rights of the parties and where no injustice has been caused
to any of the parties a mere irregularity in relation to rules of procedure
should not be allowed to vitiate the proceedings.
Ordinarily failure to file an affidavit in reply would mean the contents of the
affidavit of the applicant are taken as unchallenged and truthful.  However,
this general rule is subject to whether the contents pass the test of evidence
that is cogent and of probative value.
A District Registrar proceeding under O.44 r 6 may take formal steps
preliminary to the trial and handle applications interlocutory, and fix the case
for hearing.  In the instant case by the learned Registrar entertaining an
application for leave to appear and defend and dismissing the same,
exceeded his jurisdiction and his orders must be set aside.
However, looking at the merits of the application to appear and defend the
suit under summary procedure, the applicant/respondent failed to show by
affidavit that it had triable issues of fact or law.  An applicant in such a
matter must show that there is a question which ought to be tried.  Such
defence when raised should be stated with sufficient particularity as to
appear genuine.  General or vague statements denying liability will not
suffice.  In the instant case it as not enough to state that there were
irregularities in the contract the subject of the suit.  It was incumbent upon
the applicant for leave to appear and defend to state with sufficient
particularity the nature of the irregularities in the contract.
Application for unconditional leave dismissed.  Each party to bear own
costs.
Nalukwago Joeri Vs. Administrator General
Res judicata S.222(1) MCA-case pending before appellate LC III
Court-whether case res judicata.
Pending suit S.221 MCA-whether appeal pending before the
appellate LCIII court was a pending case.
Pecuniary jurisdiction of L.C.Court S.4(2) RC Court's Statute-
unregistered land-whether LC Court pecuniary jurisdiction in
unregistered land matters was limited.
Held: S.221 Magistrate's Court Act provides that no court shall try another
case when the same case between these parties is still pending before
another court.  In this instant case the section precludes the case filed by
the Administrator General before the Chief Magistrate's Court at Mengo,
when another case was still pending before the Rubaga LCIII Court.
The LC Court has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction to try cases involving
unregistered land.
Appeal allowed.  Case at Mengo stayed pending appeal from Rubaga LIII
Court.
Uganda Posts & Telecommunications Vs. Abraham Kitumba.
Stay of stay of suit S.6 Civil Procedure Act - pleadings-whether
issue of pending suit may be raised after evidence has be led.
Held: The issue of stay of suit should be pleaded in the written statement of
defence or be raised as a preliminary point of law before calling evidence.
The appellant having allowed the respondent's witnesses to testify and
conclude their case, could not any more raise the issue of the pending suit
under S.6 Civil Procedure Act.
However, if a person purchases an estate which he knows to be in the
occupation of another other than the vendor, such person is bound by all the
equities which the parties in such occupation may have in the land.  In the
instant case the respondent acquired the suit land when the appellant was
in occupation.  Therefore, this was notice of the claim the appellant might
have over the suit property.  Therefore, the respondent was not a bonafide
purchaser without notice.
There is no law that government cannot own land by Kibanja tenure system.
Therefore, even if the appellant's interest was unregistered, it could lawfully
own and hold land by way of Kibanja.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Arua Motor Dealers Vs. Attorney General
Limitation-Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Prov.)Act S.2(2) -
whether claim in contract was time barred-whether war was a
disability, O.7 r6.
Pleadings O.7 r1(e) CPR-failure to plead date of execution of
contract-whether thereby claim fails.
Pleadings-documents O.7 r14(1) - failure to annex document relied
upon - whether fatal irregularity.
Held: S.2(2) Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act bars actions
founded on contract against Government after the expiry of 3 years from the
date the cause of action arose.  However, before it is concluded that a
cause of action is time barred, it must be shown when the said cause of
action arose.  In the present case the plaint did not concisely plead the
terms of the contract nor the date of its execution as required by O.7 r1(e).
Therefore, it is difficult to conclude that the plaintiff's cause of action had
been accrued.
However, S.23 Limitation Act provides that where there is acknowledgement
of the debt the cause of action is revived from the date of acknowledgement.
However, O.7 r 14(1) requires that where a party wishes to sue on a
document must annex the same to the plaint at the date of filing.  In the
instant case the plaintiff while submitting from the bar that it was in
possession of documents showing that government had acknowledge the
date, the documents were never annexed to the plaint.  Therefore, the
alleged acknowledgement and consequent revival of the cause of action was
not proved.
The submission by the plaintiff that there was a war going on in Arua and
this was a disability preventing the plaintiff to file its action in time, would
not succeed because there was no evidence that the whole of Uganda was
engulfed in war.  Courts in many parts of the country were open.
The action in tort was barred by Legal Notice No.1/86.
Objection upheld.  Plaint rejected.
Kiyingi Francis Vs. & ors Vs. Bank of Uganda.
Pleadings O.6 r2 CPR - representation-whether not pleaded.
Held: O.6 r 2 CPR requires that where a party wishes to rely on any
representation made by the other, such party must plead the particulars of
the same.  Herein, the plaintiffs pleaded that the defendant induced the
plaintiffs to opt for the voluntary retirement scheme by representing to the
plaintiffs that their housing loans would not be deducted.  Therefore, the
plaintiffs pleaded the requisite particulars of the representation.
The bank could not plead that it was not intended that the plaintiffs should
act on the representation.  This is because it was not an occasion of social
or domestic relations but business and the plaintiffs acted on the
representation made by the defendant and the defendant was thus bound by
its own representation.
Suit allowed with costs.
SIETCO Vs. Noble Builders (U) Ltd.
Amendment O.6 r 19 CPR-amendment without leave-whether
amending the name of the party was mere description not requiring
leave of court-whether amending prayer for interest did not require
leave, S.26(2) CPA.
Adjournment O.15 r (1) CPR-sufficient cause -whether shown.
Pleadings-fraud O.6 r1, & 2 CPR-lack of particulars-whether
thereby claim fails.
Pleadings-departure -whether evidence was departure and was
rightly rejected.
Amendment of pleadings O.6 r18-failure to state exact nature of
claim-whether amendment may be rejected.
Interest on liquidated claim-whether must be from date of filing suit
or date of judgment.
Held: The respondent's amendments of its pleadings beyond what was
allowed by court, was contrary to the law but the appellant did not challenge
this when it filed its amended WSD nor at the trial.  This means that the
appellant was not prejudiced by the respondent's act.
O.15 r1(1) CPR gives court discretion to adjourn cases for sufficient cause.
In the instance complained about court refused the adjournment which was
premised on the allegation that counsel for the defendant was out of the
country.  The trial court was entitled to refuse the adjournment because it
was not disclosed before it as to why counsel for the appellant had to be
outside the country when the case was coming for trial.  The learned trial
judge exercised his discretion judicially when he refused the adjournment.
O.6 r2 requires that for every instance where fraud is pleaded particulars
thereof must be given.  In the instant case the appellant having pleaded fraud
it was incumbent upon it to supply particulars to the respondent because
this was not pleaded in its WSD. The trial court rightly rejected the evidence.
Every application for leave to amend must contain the exact nature of the
claim or defence sought. In the instant case the application was only for
leave to amend the WSD without stating the exact nature of the defence
sought to be amended or introduced.  The learned trial judge was entitled to
reject the same.
Where there is a lump sum contract (like the building contract in this case)
and there is substantial performance thereof and the complaining party
has taken benefit of the work, liability cannot be repudiation on the ground
that the work though substantially performed is in some respects not in
accordance with the contract.  In the instant case the UNDP had already
entered the buildings, thus taking benefit thereof.  Therefore the learned trial
judge was entitled to award the full contract price even though there was
evidence that the performance by the respondent of the contract work was
not absolutely as per contract.
Where a person is entitled to a liquidated claim, he should be awarded
interest from the date of filing the suit.  Therefore the learned trial judge erred
in awarding interest from the date of judgment.
Appeal dismissed with costs.  Cross appeal allowed.
Lwanga Sanyu Musoke Vs. Sam Galiwango
Appeals-failure to appeal against grant of lower court-whether there-
fore High Court may not interfere.
Held: S.233(1),(2)(b)( c) Succession Act provides that a grant may be revoked
where it was obtained fraudulently by making a false statement.  In the
instant case there was ample evidence on record to show that the deceased
left a Will which fact the respondent was privy to.  By making a false
allegation to the effect that the deceased left no Will, which allegation was
the basis of the grant of Letters of Administration to the respondent, it
means that the grant was obtained by fraud and should be revoked.
S.187 Succession Act precludes a claimant to take benefit of the provisions
of an unproved Will but the section does render inadmissible in evidence a
Will that has not yet been proved by grant of probate.  Therefore the trial
court misdirected itself when it refused to admit in evidence the alleged Will
for purposes of proving its existence.
It is not necessary to appeal against an interlocutory ruling separate from
the final decision.  Therefore, it was not necessary for the appellant to have
pleaded against the trial judge's upholding of the objection to tender in
evidence the Will.  It was enough that this was incorporated in the
memorandum of appeal against the whole final decision of the trial court.
Therefore, the appeal against the introductory order could not be caught by
time before the final decision on the matter is made.
Under S.32 Judicature Act, the High Court has unlimited jurisdiction to inter
alia take any step to rectify any wrong findings on the face of the record
which comes to its attention.  In the instant case even if there was no
appeal against the grant of the lower court, the High Court could have
interfered against the grant on grounds that the grant was based on a
fraudulent misrepresentation of an essential fact and that the Chief
Magistrate had no jurisdiction to make a grant where the estate was above
Moreover, court countenance an illegality and leave it standing.
Appeal allowed.  Grounds to affirm decision dismissed.
Hassim Hassani Vs. Nobaf Construction Co. Ltd & Another
Held: For court of exercise its discretion in favour of the plaintiff/applicant
who wishes court to order for the attachment of the defendant/respondent's
property pending judgment pursuant to the provisions of O.36 r5(11) CPR
the applicant must satisfy court that the respondent is about to leave the
country or remove its property from jurisdiction of the court.  In the instant
case, the alleged removal of the defendant's property from Kumi to Mbarara
was not the removal of the property from the local limits of jurisdiction
because the High Court has unlimited geographical jurisdiction throughout
Uganda.
Application dismissed.
Aisha Babita Vs. Akamba Public Transport Ltd
Special damages - pleading - failure to attach receipts - whether damages
nonetheless awardable.
Held: The fact that the skid marks covered 60 meters was evidence that the
defendant's but was running at very high speed and this was manifest
evidence of negligence.  Moreover the scene of the accident was near a
market where the defendant's driver should have known that it was a busy
place and thereby taken the necessary caution.
The deceased was knocked a few meters before he was able to cross the
road, at a point which was not a zebra crossing.  This means that the
deceased failed to make sure that he would successfully cross the road
before he ventured to do so.  Therefore, the deceased was guilty of
contributory negligence, which in the circumstances would be assessed at
Funeral expenses as pleaded would be awarded although as special
damages proof thereof is strict.  The failure to attach receipts of expenditure
in proof of funeral expenses was excusable because at the time of
bereavement, it is not possible to attend to details such as asking for receipts.
Moreover, the items pleaded are such as the ones that must be available
when someone dies.
Although the plaintiff claimed that her husband earned Ugshs. 1.5m/=, no
proof was presented and although the plaintiff claimed that the deceased
looked after his family adequately, no evidence was presented as to the lost
benefit likely to be suffered by his family.  However, it is understandable that
a wife may not know quite well the income of her husband.  Therefore court
would follow the precedent in Agnes Nakawooya Sebalamu Vs. Attorney
General HCCS 505/96 where court found itself in a similar situation and
awarded Ugsh. 150,000/= as the money spent by the deceased on his
family per month.
Suit allowed with costs.
Maliam Adekur and Anor Vs. Attorney General & Anor.
Parties to the suit-agent of Local Government-whether thereby Attorney
General liable, S.4(2)(a) Local Government Act.
Proceedings Against Government -liability of Attorney General for malicious
prosecution and false arrest where prosecution was private-whether therefore
Attorney General not liable.
Held: Art 128(4) Constitution of Uganda provides that a person Exercising
judicial power cannot be liable for any act or omission arising therefrom.
Therefore it was preposterous for the petitioners to argue that the trial
magistrate who  presided over the prosecution acted unconstitutionally.
Secondly, the prosecution was a private one.
Moreover the arrest and detention were effected by local administration
personnel.  S.4(2)(9) establishes a local government as a body corporate
capable of suing and being sued.  Therefore, the Attorney General was not
liable.
Preliminary objection upheld.  No cause of action established. Counsel to
bear costs personally.
In Re Edith Nassazi
Application for adoption by notice of motion-whether defective -
whether irregularity curable by Art 126(2) Constitution of Uganda.
Held: At the time of hearing this application, no procedure regulations had
been made as provided by S.50 of the Children's Statute. Therefore, the law
applicable was the Adoption of Children Rules, S.I. 216-1, which required
that the application be by petition and not by notice of motion as was the
case therein.  However, the irregularity was not fatal to the application as it
was curable under Art 126(2) Constitution of Uganda, that enjoined court to
do substantive justice and not to pay undue regard to technicalities.
S.49(1)(b) Children's Statute provides that before court makes an order for
adoption of a child it must be satisfied that it will be for the welfare of the
child.  In this case the applicant had already shown his noble intentions
when he took custody of the child and care for her.
Application allowed.  Costs to be paid by the applicant.
Rwanyarare James & anor Vs. Attorney General
Representative action-lack or leave of court to file representative
action-whether thereby petition wrongly in court.
Held: Rules of Procedure are landmarks of justice, including justice sought
from the constitutional court.  Therefore, though rule 4(1) of the Modifications
to the Rights & Freedoms (Enforcement Procedure) Rules, were rules of
procedure, they applied to constitutional petitions with the effect in the
present case the petition was time barred in as far it sought the declaration
of the unconstitutionality of certain provisions of the constitution because
the petition should have been filed 30 days from the promulgation of the
constitution; and the elections of the president and parliament should have
been challenged within 30 days.
Secondly, the constitutional court has no original jurisdiction to entertain
petitions that challenge the elections of the president and parliament, as
such jurisdiction is vested in the Supreme Court and the High Court
respectively.
The Constitutional Court has no original jurisdiction to entertain petitions
under Art.50 of the constitution for the enforcement of rights and freedoms
under the constitution, except by way of reference to it from another court.
Under O.1 r8 (1) Civil Procedure Rules a litigant may file a representative
action with leave of court.  Therefore, the petition in so far as if sought to be
representative of persons other than the litigants, was wrongly before court.
Petition dismissed with costs.
Teddy Sseezi Cheeye & anor Vs. Tumusiime Enos.
Stay of execution, jrr5(2) (b), 41(2) & 43(1) CAR (Court of Appeal
Rules) -impecuniously of applicant is instance of sufficient cause to
stay of execution.
Held: For an applicant for an order of stay of execution to succeed he must
prove that there exists sufficient cause for the application.  Impecuniosity is
not an instant of sufficient cause to allow an application to stay execution.
Application dismissed with costs.
Bitwire Emmanuel Vs. The Representative of the Zaire
Represented by its Embassy.
Attachment in execution O.19 CPR-Diplomatic property-whether
attached property was diplomatic property was diplomatic property
and therefore immune from attachment.
Held: For the premises to be said to be immune from attachment in
execution as per the premises house the mission or are the private
residence of a Diplomatic agent but not the kind of staff like the accountant
and his relatives as it were in this case.
Application dismissed.  Each party to bear its own costs due to importance
of the point of law raised by the applicant.
Chamute Agencies Co. Ltd Vs. Mbale District Administration
Parties to the suit O.1, r10 CPR-Substitution of parties-whether
Court may substitute parties.
Held: Since the enactment of the Local Government (Resistance Councils)
Statute 1993, Districts ceased being referred to, as District Administrations
instead are to be referred to as District Councils.  Therefore the suit was in
wrong name but Court was empowered by O.1 r 10 CPR to substitute the
name of the party with the correct one.
A trade usage is established where there is a practice among people who
normally deal in a particular line of business and the practice is generally
known to all persons who enter into that relationship.  In the present case
the plaintiff had failed to prove that there was a trade usage of issuing
suppliers with LPO's after the delivery of tendered goods merely because
that had happened on some occasions.
However because the defendant represented to the plaintiff that it could
supply and receive the LPO on delivery and that there was a clear intention
on the defendant that the plaintiff should act upon the representation
believing in its truth and actually the plaintiff did indeed act upon the
representation, by the doctrine of equitable estoppel, the defendant was
estopped from denying the contract.
The measure of damages for breach of contract where the buyer refuses to
accept some of the goods, is the difference between the contract price and
the market price.  In the instant case there is no market price since the
goods, i.e. the assessment forms are peculiarly designed for the defendant.
Therefore, the measure of damages for breach of contract is the contract
price, i.e. Ush. 22 million, which was the value of the assessment forms.
Suit allowed with costs.
Maximov Oleg Petrovich Vs. Premchandra Shenoi & anor.
Cause of action, O.7 r11 (a) CPR - corporate personality-whether
the plaint does not disclose a cause of action against a director
personally when the transaction concerns the company - whether
this is a triable issue calling for evidence and not preliminary.
Frivolous and vexatious action, O.7 r.11 (e) CPR-whether action
was frivolous and vexatious and plaint must be rejected.
Representative action O.1 r.8(1) -whether because transaction
concerned 3  persons, the plaintiff can only bring a representative
action and with leave of Court.
Preliminary objection O.6 r.29 CPR-whether plaint may be rejected
for disclosing no cause of action.
Held: As per O.7 r 11 (a) CPR a plaint that does not disclose a cause of
action must be rejected. In considering that the plaint discloses a cause of
action only the plaint, must be looked at so that it is apparent on its face
that the plaintiff appears as a person aggrieved by the violation of his rights
and that it is the defendant who is liable.  In the instant case the pleadings
disclose that the plaintiff paid some money to the defendant so that they
could jointly trade in precious stones.  The pleadings further show that the
defendants acknowledged receipt though of a lesser sum.  Therefore it was
apparent on the face of the plaint that the plaintiff was aggrieved by the
defendants.  As to whether it was the 1st or 2nd or both defendants was a
triable issue after evidence had been led.  Therefore there was a cause of
action disclosed.
O.7 r 11 (e) CPR provides that a suit that is shown by the plaint to be
frivolous and vexatious must be rejected.  The plaint must show that to a
reasonable person, the plaintiff has no the kind of grievance that is entitled
to be adjudicated upon but that the plaintiff is actuated by malafide to harass
the defendant.  In the instant case the plaint discloses a reasonable
grievance against the plaintiff by the defendant.  Therefore the suit is not
frivolous and vexatious.
Since the plaintiff never sued in representative capacity, but brought the
action for his own benefit, it was not incumbent upon Court to order him to
sue in representative capacity.
Further O.1 r 8 (1) is properly invoked only where the person suing claims in
the plaint the same rights as those he wishes to represent.  In the instant
case the plaintiff claimed that it is only him who provided the money for the
transaction.
Moreover, rejecting the plaint and deciding an action before trial should be
sparingly done and only in such instances where the action is a clear abuse
of the process of Court per Fletcher Maulton, LJ in Dyson V. Attorney
General [1911] 1 KB 418.
Preliminary objection overruled with costs.
Kwesigabo, Bamwine & Walubiri Advocates Vs. Nytil Picfare
Review O.42 r.1-error apparent on record-whether proved.
Attachment where subject matter is several times more valuable
than the debt -whether unjust and unconscionable.
Held: A lien is a kind of attachment and the value of the property to be
attached must be commensurate to the amount of the debt.  In the instant
case the land title were the applicants sought to exercise alien was valued
at ush.400 million and yet the debt of Ush. 2.3 million was disproportionately
too small such that the attachment would be unjust and unconscionable.
The ground for review to the effect that there was an error apparent on the
record was not proved because no error was proved when the applicant
merely dated the items for which fees was claimed whereas in the earlier
bill of costs no date was supplied.  This meant that the dictates of O.42 r 1
were not satisfied.
Where an advocates receives instructions to represent his client in a matter
that advocate is not certificated his subsequent certificate ness does not
render the instructions lawful.
Application dismissed with costs.
Banco Drabe Espanol Vs. Bank of Uganda.
Appeals-fees-whether appeal incompetent because filed without fees.
Appeals-order appealed from-extraction thereof-whether
incompetent because not submitted to the other party for approval.
Appeal - order appealed from bearing different date from that of the
decision-whether order defective and accompanying appeal incompetent.
Held: No document is properly filed until fees thereof has been paid, as per
Unta Export Ltd Vs. Customs [1970] E.A. 648. In the case instant Rule 75
(2) of the CAR (Court of Appeal Rules) provided that an appeal shall be
lodged within 14 days the decision sought to be appealed from and since the
fees was paid within 14 days though later than the date that appeal was
lodged, the appeal was filled in time since it was deemed to have been filed
at the time fees was paid.
It is true the order accompanying the Memorandum of Appeal was defective
and a nullity because it bore a different date from that when the decision
was made, and was extracted without the other party approving the
contents thereof.  However, that complaint could only be taken to the Court
that heard the application and made the order and not the appellant Court.
That not withstanding, the defect of the order did not affect the competence
of the appeal because ultimately the appeal lies from the ruling, i.e. the
reasoned order or judgment made by Court as per the provisions of R 86(1)
(9) CAR, and not from the order extracted by a party or parties.
Application to strike off appeal dismissed with costs.
J.P.Balindawa Vs. J.W. Ziritwawula & anor.
Fixing hearing date for Election Petition, S.143(2) Local Govern-
ment Act-whether duty on petitioner or Registrar-whether
proceedings fixed for hearing after 90 days untenable.
Pleadings-fraud O.6 r2-failure to supply particulars thereof-whether
pleading defective.
Held: It was incumbent upon the petitioner or his counsel to apply for an early
hearing date.  He neglected to do so and applied for the hearing 11 days
from the expiry of the hearing period of 90 days as provided for in S.143 (2)
Local Government Act.  The proceedings fixed after the expiry of 90 days
were clearly stale and untenable.
O.6 r 2 CPR requires that where a litigant plead fraud, inter alia, such
pleading should state particulars of the fraud.  In the instant case the
petitioner just stated that the 1st respondent forged the names of the
persons whom he alleged nominated him.  No particulars of the forgery were
stated.  The pleadings were therefore defective.
Objection upheld.  Petition dismissed with costs.
Nsambu Sulaiman Vs. Fred Balinda.
Setting aside ex-parte Decree, O.33, r.11 - whether defence on
merits established.
Held: Once an applicant for an order to set aside an ex-parte decree under
O.33, r.11 establishes that he has a defence on the merits of the case, then
in light of all the facts and circumstances both prior and subsequent, it is
just and reasonable to set aside the decree.  In the case instant the
applicant had shown that he had counter claim to the suit and therefore the
applicant had established that he had a triable issue, sufficient for the
purposes of granting leave to appear and defend the suit.
Application allowed.
Print and Stationary Supply Vs. Kitgum District Administrator
Setting aside ex-parte judgment, O.9 r9 CPR-non service of
hearing notice -whether sufficient cause.
Held: Since the application was grounded on non-service of the hearing
notice, it should have been brought under O.9 r 24 CPR which provides that
the applicant for an order to set a side ex-parte judgment may show that for
sufficient cause he was prevented from attending Court.  However, since the
publication was brought under O.9 r 9, which is wider than O.9 r 24, the
alleged ground of failure to attend Court to due to non-service and the hearing
notice, was covered there under.
And since the application was grounded on non-service of hearing notice
that was only relevant issue to consider.  In the instant case the applicants
promptly brought this application immediately they became aware of the
existence of judgment against them.  This meant they were not guilty of
obstructing or delaying justice.  Since the hearing notice allegedly signed
by the applicant was not on Court record there was no proof of service.
Therefore the application to set aside would be allowed.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Zaabwe Fredrick Vs. Mars Trading Co. & anor.
Temporary injunction, O.37, rr.1 & 2 CPR-irreparable damage-
whether proved.
Held: Irreparable damage is damage not atonable in damage. However, in the
present application the applicant had not shown any special circumstances
that exist as proof that the alienation of the property was injury not atonable
in damages, because the fact is that the loss of the property by the
applicant was compensatable in damages.
Application dismissed with costs.
Attorney General Vs. Sanyu Television.
Capacity to sue or be sued-suits in the name other than a natural
or legal person-whether suits tenable under O.27, r.10 CPR.
Parties to the suit-substitution of parties O.27, r.10(2) CPR-whether
Court may substitute or add a party.
Held: O.27 r.10 CPR provides that a person carrying on business in a name
or style other than his own may be sued in such name or style.  In the
instant case, the respondent, Sanyu Television has so clothed its outside
personal with all the indicia and trappings of a legal entity as to be
indistinguishable from one by conducting all its business in the name of
Sanyu Television.  Therefore it was a right party to be sued and the suit
against it was properly before court.
Secondly even if Court did not apply O.27, r.10(2) hands to do justice
against Sanyu Television could not be tied since O.1, r.10(2) empowers
Court to substitute or add parties.  Since according to the facts of the
instant case the parent organization to which Sanyu Television belongs is
International Television Network Ltd, that name would be joined as the
second defendant.
Application for the injunction allowed. Second defendant added, with costs.
Okello Eric & anor Vs. Wade Adams Ltd.
Documents relied on by plaintiff, O.7, r14(2)-failure to annex the
same to the plaint-whether may not be relied upon at the trial.
Held: O.7 r 14(2) provides that no reliance in Court shall be allowed on a
document not mentioned in the plaint or annexed there to.  In the present
case since the expert was giving oral evidence it was sufficient without
relying on the document.
It is true that African children, who are educated, often at considerable
sacrifice by their parents, are expected to make contribution to the welfare
of their parents in return.  However such a custom is not static and the
changes may result in the parents not necessarily expecting contribution to
their welfare from their educated children.  Therefore ush. 5 million would be
awarded for the lost of life.
Ush. 1,500,000/= would be awarded as general damages for the swollen
tibia where permanent disability was calculated at 10%.
Kawere Sulaiman Haji Vs. Emmanuel Pinto.
Summary suit-application to appear and defend, O.33 r4 whether
triable issue disclosed.
Held: S. 91 (d) Evidence Act makes admissible the existence of a
subsequent oral agreement to rescind or modify a contract, disposition or
grant which is originally in writing.  Therefore the allegation that by an oral
agreement the defendant discharged the contract by giving the plaintiff motor
spares in evidence at the trial and this was a triable issue necessitating the
granting to leave to the applicant to appear and defend the suit.
Application allowed with costs.
Katabalwa Philip Vs. Ntege Ssebagala & anor
Security for costs, O.23, r.1 CPR-election petition-whether
application for security for costs may not be granted because
petition not frivolous-Insolvency-whether ground for order for
security for costs.
Held: Since the grounds of the application in the chamber summons were at
variance with grounds mentioned in the affidavit, the chamber summons was
not accompanied by an affidavit as required by O.48, r.3 CPR.  Therefore
the application was not supported by evidence.
Insolvency of the litigant is not a ground for an order for security for costs.
An order for security for costs would be granted if the petition is merely
vexatious and frivolous.  In the present petition the issues to be resolved by
Court are of great public importance and are neither frivolous nor vexatious.
Application dismissed.
Trade Investments (U) Ltd Vs. M/S Magezi Ibale & Co. Adv.
Costs taxation-whether instruction fees of Ush.20M/= excessive
where subject matter is about Ush. 800M/= - whether proviso to
6th schedule of Advocates (Remuneration and Taxation of Costs)
Rule allowed a higher figure.
Held: The proviso to the 6th schedule of the Advocates (Remuneration and
Taxation of Costs) Rules allows an Advocates to claim a higher figure than
provided in the schedule but only on condition that the presiding Judge/
arbitrator/Magistrate as the case may be has given a certificate of complexity
to the concerned counsel allowing him to therefore claim a higher figure.
Therefore, the award of ush.20m/- as instruction fees was excessive and
arbitrary and would be set aside and substituted therefore the award of
ush. 8.9m/- as provided by the rules in the 6th schedule since the subject
matter was valued at about Ush. 800m/- but no certificate of complexity had
been obtained.
The award of Ush. 500,000/- as telephone costs would not be considered to
be arbitrary because the case spanned over two years and the respondent
Advocate had to keep in touch with his clients who were spread as far as
Dar-Es-Salaam.
Appeal allowed in part.
Nile Safaris Ltd Vs. Hot Ice Ltd & Grahamed Denis
Costs-whether losing party was entitled to costs.
Held: The trial Judge was correct in finding that failure to use the fire
extinguisher if any existed, was not the cause of fire, nor the class of the
driving permit of the driver.  Therefore the appellant had failed to prove
negligence on the part of the respondent.
The burden of proof of inevitable accident is on the defendant pleading the
same. However, the defendant only needs to plead inevitable accident where
the plaintiff has established a prima facie case of negligence.  In the present
case the appellant failed to establish a prima facie case of negligence and
therefore the respondents were not bound to plead nor prove inevitable
accident.
Costs followed the event unless a successful party proves to court to its
satisfaction that special reasons do exist to warrant him getting the costs
from the successful party.  In the present case the appellant had not
discharged the burden of proof that special circumstances exist to warrant
that appellant be awarded the costs from the successful.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Rwenzori Investment Ltd Vs. N.P.A.R.T.
53(1) 76 & 87 of the Court of Appeal Rules-whether court may
enlarge time of file appeal-whether sufficient cause shown-whether
likelihood of success of appeal is a ground.
Held: Rule 4, Court of Appeal Rules empowers court to extend time to do
an act required under the rules including time to file an appeal out of time
where sufficient reasons have been shown.  The errors of omission by
counsel should not necessarily of omission by counsel should not
necessarily defeat the rights of the litigant, and where it is shown that
counsel who let down his otherwise vigilant client sufficient reason exists to
allow an application for extension of time to file the appeal.  However in the
present case the applicant was guilty of dilatory conduct when he instructed
his Advocates long after the time for taking the essential steps in the appeal
had lapsed.  Therefore, no sufficient reason had been proved to move court
to extend the time for the appeal.
Once sufficient reason for extending the time for appeal has not been shown,
then other considerations like the likelihood of success of the appeal are
irrelevant.
Application dismissed with costs.
Sebugwawo Julius Vs. Electoral Commission & anor
Inherent jurisdiction of court S.101 CPA whether court may ignore
defects and do Substantial Justice.
Held: Articles 139(3)(b) & 140 (c ) (d) do not exist in the Constitution of
Uganda though the petitioner had purported to have filed this petition under
their provisions.  This means that the petition was brought under a non-
existing Law and since no amendment was applied for to correct what
counsel for the petitioner called a typing error, the petition was untenable
and would be struck off because it was not properly  before court.
In the instant case what was infringed was not only procedural but also
substantive law therefore Art 126 (2) (e) constitution would not properly be
called in aid to save the petition.
Defaulters of procedure and substantive law should not be allowed to run to
s.101 CPA asking court to invoke its inherent power where the matter or
proceeding has been improperly brought to court.
Preliminary objection upheld petition struck out with costs.
Uganda Bankers (Employers Association) Vs. National Union
of Clerical, Commercial, Professionals &Technical Employers.
Costs-taxation-Advocates (Remunerations and taxation of costs)
Rules 1982-whether Rules applicable as at the date the order was
made or as at the date of Taxation when amended Rules were
in force.
Costs-principles involved in taxation of costs-whether because
they are a matter of law they need not be stated as grounds of
appeal from the order of the taxing master.
Held: The Remuneration Rules and the mode of assessing instruction fees
were matters of law, which the learned Judge was presumed to know and
had been argued before him when he sat in his appellant capacity.
Therefore, the learned Judge erred in holding that the appellants had not
stated the principles of taxation, which the taxing master is alleged to have
breached.
S.13(2) Interpretation Decree provides that where a law is repealed, the
repeal does not affect a right, privilege, obligation or liability which had
accrued before the repeal came into effect.  In the present case the
appellant's liability to pay costs accrued on 17th August 1995 when the
order to pay costs was made against the appellant & not when the bill was
taxed on 31.3.96.  Therefore the law applicable was the Advocates
(Remuneration and Taxation of Costs) Rules, 1982 which provided for a
minimum scale of Ush. 1500/- for arguing or defending a chamber summons
and not the Advocates (Remuneration and Taxation of Costs) (Amendment)
Rules, which came in force on 22/2/96, which provided for Ush.75,000/- as
the minimum scale for arguing or defending a chamber summons.  Therefore
the learned Judge erred to have applied the later rules and therefore applied
wrong principles of taxation of costs.
Moreover, because no value had been given of the subject matter, it was
wrong for the learned Judge to speak of value of billions.  Of shillings.
Therefore he was influenced by wrong assessment of the instruction fees.
Proviso number one to the sixth schedule provides that where an advocate
claims that a given matter was specifically complicated and for that matter
wishes to claim as instruction fees, a fee higher than provided in the scale,
must first obtain a certificate of complexity from the presiding Judge or
Magistrate (trial or appellate as the case of may be).  In the instant case for
the taxing master to have allowed instruction fees to defend a chamber
summons at Ush. 40m/- from the minimum scale provided or Ush. 1500/-
required a certificate of complexity from the presiding Judge the taxing
master, without which, as it was in the case instant no higher fee should
have been allowed.
Appeal allowed with costs to the appellants.  Taxation to be done devovo
before another taxing master.
Mitwalo Magyengo Vs. Medadi Mutyaba
Appeals-second-appeals S.74(1) Civil Procedure Act-whether not
tenable on evidence.
Held: S.74 (1) Civil Procedure Act precludes second appeals against
findings of fact made by the High Court acting as an appellate court.
Therefore the grounds of appeal against findings of fact by the High Court
would not be entertained.
According to the evidence on record it was not clear whether the cultivation
by the appellant covered new grounds or only grounds previously cultivated
by the appellant before the respondent purchases the land.  Since the
evidence did not delineate the land previously occupied and cultivated by the
appellant, he could not be called a trespasser and the order for damages
awarded against him for trespass is set aside.
However though the appellant could not be called a trespasser he had failed
to prove that he was a customary tenant to Kibanja holder.  The evidence
clearly showed that the appellant was either a squatter or licensee.
Therefore the order granting the respondent a permanent injunction against
the appellant would be up held.
Appeal allowed just in part and respondent and appellant to share costs in
halves.
COMMERCIAL LAW
Stephen Lubega Vs. Barclays Bank (u) Ltd.
Debentures - whether a receiver appointed under a debenture is an
agent of debtor.
Held: The receiver, though appointed by the respondent, was an agent
of the debtor company, which should have been the right party to be
sued and not the respondent.
Where a wrong party has been sued, the misjoinder or non joinder can
be rectified by court under the Civil procedure Rules.  This power of
court to deal with joinder issues includes adding or striking out parties.
The Sale was clearly fraudulent and in breach of the  covenant
pertaining to the sale of the lorry; the consequent transfer of the lorry
was consequently of no effect as the fraud and the breach of covenant
had vitiated the sale.
A floating charge crystallizes the moment three is default and a Receiver
is appointed.
An Endorsement on the registration card of a car is good notice for
those dealing with the car.
Fraud cannot be imputed from the facts but must be specifically
pleaded and proved.
HMM Kayondo Vs. Somani Amirali.
Bills of exchange - notice of dishonor s.48 bill of exchange Act -
whether drawee did not give notice of dishonor of the cheque.
Bills of Exchange - consideration s.30 (1) Bills of Exchange Act - whether
plaintiff must prove consideration for the cheques.
Held: It is a rule of pleading that an averment not expressly or implicitly
traversed is deemed to have been admitted.  It is a rule of evidence that a
fact admitted need not be proved.  The plaintiff in para 5 of the plaint had
pleaded that he gave notice of dishonour to the defendant.  The defendant
in his WSD did not traverse either explicitly or implicitly that plea.
Therefore the defendant had admitted that the plaintiff gave him  notice of
dishonour of the cheque as required by s.48, the Bills of Exchange Act.
A company duly registered is a legal entity distinct from the subscribers
or those who formed it.  This is the rule of incorporation.  Therefore the
dishonoured cheques on the account of Uganda Consumer Supplies Ltd
belonged to the Company.  However the defendant being managing
Director thereof would not be allowed to use incorporation as a cloak for
fraud.  Therefore, the veil of incorporation would be lifted by court so that
the defendant is found personally liable for the dishonoured bills.
S.30 (1) Bills of Exchange Act provides that every party whose signature
appears on a bill is a prima facie deemed to have become a party for
value.  Since the defendant admitted having drawn the cheques, the
burden of proof lay on him to prove that the plaintiff had passed no
consideration to the defendant for the cheques.  The defendant failed in
this.  Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Banax Ltd Vs. Daniel Mulika.
Company law - memorandum and articles of association - whether
form a contract between members of the company interse.
Held: The plaintiff company had a separate existence from its
members and the former sought to enforce its rights in its capacity
as such.  The memorandum and Articles of Association formed a
contract between the members interse and the members and the
company but it was possible for a shareholder to deal with the
company in his private capacity and not as a member and this was
the case in the instant.  Therefore the requirements of plaintiff
company's Articles were inapplicable.
Esso Standard (U) Ltd Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Banking - whether a cheque is banked when it is received and
deposited at the collecting bank or when it is presented for
payment at the drawing Bank.
Held: A drawer cannot recall cheques that he has drawn but can only
countermand payment by his bankers of the cheques.
The respondent Bank was vicariously responsible for whatever loss that
would be occasioned by their employee's fraudulent refusal to present
cheques deposited for payment in time.
A cheque is banked when it is received and deposited at the collecting
bank and not when it is presented for payment at the drawing Bank.
A cheque presented 25 days from the time it was banked for payment
was not presented within a reasonable time having regard to the fact
that the respondent and drawing bank were to be fund in the same
location.
The respondent bank's presentment of the cheques for payment 25 days
after they were banked, failed to act diligently and was in breach of its
contractual duty to its customer.
The drawer was not discharged on the liability of the cheques merely
because the respondent delayed in presenting the cheques for payment
because even if had the cheques been presented in time there were no
sufficient funds to have the cheques paid.
Reamaton Ltd Vs. Uganda Corporation Creameries & anor
Partnership -share of profit-whether therefore this was evidence that
a partnership existed-s.4(3).
Held: The receipt by a person of share of the profits of a business is strong
evidence that he is a partner but not conclusive ipso facto.  Court must take
into account the agreement and intention of the parties. In the instant case
other co-existing factors show that there was no partnership.  There co-
existing factors include the fact that the first defendant had borrowed money
for the coffee business which loan was only the liability of the first defendant
and yet if the business were a partnership the two said parties would be
jointly liable.
To constitute a contract of guarantee there must be a promise to answer
for the debt of another under s.4(1) of the Contract Act.  In the instant case,
documents which would otherwise have constituted the requisite promise
by the second defendant to answer for the debt of the first defendant, were
signed by the second defendant in his capacity as executive director of the
first defendant. Therefore no such guarantee had been proved against the
second defendant personally.
A contract to pay a commission to Government Civil Servants was illegal
and unenforceable as it infringed S.1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Therefore the claimed set off constituting commissions supposed to be
paid to the second defendant for onward transmission to the civil servants
was illegal and unenforceable.
Further, there was no proof of unpaid commission as a set off from the claim
of the plaintiff to the defendants.
Suit allowed with costs.  Both defendants found jointly and severally liable
to the plaintiff.
Allibhai Ismail Jaffer & 2 ors Vs. Nandlal Harjivan Karia & anor
Agency-undisclosed principle-whether agent may take benefit of
the contract.
Held: In a sale of immovable property, upon payment of a deposit, property
passes to the purchaser who acquires an equitable interest in the property
and the vendor becomes a trustee who holds the property in trust for the
purchaser.  The legal title remains with vendor until the final payment when
the legal title passes to the purchaser.  Therefore, the 1st respondent was a
lawful purchaser of the suit property who acquired an equitable interest in
the same when he paid the deposit to the appellants.
Where an agent does not disclose the principal for whom he acts, such an
agent acts for himself.  Such an agent is liable for all the liabilities that may
occur in the transaction but also may take full benefit of the contract.  In
the instant case, though the 1st respondent, when he paid the deposit to the
appellants, claimed to be acting as broker for another buyer, because the
first respondent failed or refused to disclose the actual purchaser for whom
he claimed to be working, the law would recognize him as the purchaser of
the suit premises.
In order that a person may be found guilty of fraud, the alleged fraud must be
visited on the person alleged to have committed the same.  In the instant
case the alleged forgeries were not proved to have been committed by the
1st respondent.  Therefore the trial Principal Judge was entitled to hold that
the 1st respondent was a bonafide purchaser who had in turn passed clean
titled to the 2nd respondent.
S.1(2)(a) of the Expropriated Properties Act nullified dealings in property
expropriated by Government after the Expropriation Decrees 29/72 and
27/73, which dealing could include the transfer of the property to the
purchaser by the Custodian Board as was the fact in the instant case.
However, since the purchaser had acquired his equitable interest for before
the Expropriation Decrees, and was therefore not subject of the
Expropriation Decrees, and was therefore not subject of the Expropriation
Decrees, and was therefore not subject of S.1(2) (a) of Expropriated
Properties Act.  The Custodian Board was entitled to effect a transfer in
favor of the 1st respondent because the 1st respondent was the owner of
the property in law since property passed to him before the law prohibiting
transfer and sales of such  property was promulgated.
Mulenga Joseph Vs. Photo focus Ltd Ltd & anor
Charges-whether charge was floating or fixed.
Held: A debenture holder has a superiors interest or security over the
executing judgment creditor where the property sought to be attached is a
subject of a debenture.
However, the interest granted by the debenture to the objector is limited to
only the amount advanced to the judgment debtor as loan/overdraft by the
objector.  In this case the sum advanced was shs. 135 million, and yet the
total of rice over which the objector had the debenture was above shs. 500
million.
But in order for the excess value of a debenture to be a subject of
attachment in execution of a judgment debt, the charge created must be a
floating charge and the judgment debtor must be in possession of the
asset(s)).
In the instant case the charge created was a floating charge because it
covered assets both present and future, which assets could be changing as
in ordinary course of business, for instance the rice could be sold and more
bought and this would continue to be the case until the debenture holder,\
i.e. the Bank/objector took a step to intervene and thus have the charge
crystallized.
Secondly, though the rice was in the possession for the objector bank since
it was in its bonded warehouse as required by the terms of the debenture,
nevertheless the rice was in possession of the objector on account of the
judgment debtor.  Therefore according to the requirement in O.19 r58 CPR
regarding the situation, the rice in excess of the objector's interest was
attachable in execution of the judgment debt.
Application dismissed with costs.
All Ports Freight Service Vs. Julius Kamanyi & anor.
Partnership-S.3(1) Partnership Act-whether proved-whether partner-
ship must always be in writing .
Partnership-holding out S.18 Partnership Act-whether second
defendant was bound by the acts of the first defendant because he
held out as his partner.
Bills of Exchange Act S.30-parties to the bill- whether because the
second defendant did not sign the cheque therefore is not bound.
Bills of Exchange Act S.30-cheque-whether evidence that it was
issued for value.
Held: If two or several persons jointly purchase goods for resale with a view
to dividing the profits arising from the transaction, a partnership is created
and each of them will be liable to third parties.  In the instant case it was
clear that both defendants obtained cement from the plaintiff, for resale at a
profit to be shared.  Therefore, a partnership relationship was established as
under s.3 (1) of the Partnership Act.
A partnership need not be established formally and in writing.  It is sufficient
to establish that a community of interest exists between the parties.  This
was amply proved in this case.
The doctrine of holding out also provided for under S.18 of the Partnership
Act, states that where a person holds himself out as a partner, thus
including third parties, acting on such representations, to deal with him as
such, then he is liable to the third parties.  In the instant case it was not
necessary to apply the doctrine because the partnership had already been
established.
Although S.30 of the Bills of Exchange Act provides that when a person's
signature appears on a bill of exchange then that person is prima facie a
party, it was not applicable to the instant case because the plaintiff was not
suing on the cheque, the cheque was only of evidential value of the
transaction.  Therefore, the non appearance of the second defendant's
signature on the cheque, did not absolve him from liability for the debt
incurred for the unpaid cement.
O. 1 r 6 empowers a plaintiff to elect whom to sue.  Therefore the plaintiff
was free not to join the said cook to the proceedings as another defendant.
Sh. 15 million would be awarded as general damages for breach of contract.
Suit allowed with costs.
Grindlays Bank (U) Ltd & Kampala Bottlers Ltd Vs. Uganda
Bottlers Ltd.
Revivers-appointment-whether receivers not validly appointed.
Mortgages -Mortgage Decree-appointment of receivers-whether
receiver not appointed as required by the Mortgage Decree.
Debentures-mortgages-whether debenture was not a mortgage
because not registered with registrar of titles.
Receivers-whether agents of the bank or debtor.
Held: The receivers were validly appointed by the bank pursuant to the
powers conferred upon the Bank by the debenture.  The document of
appointment having been written by on of the receivers with authority of the
bank, the receivers were thus appointed in writing.  The relevant document
concerning the appointment need not include "appointment" in its body.
The Mortgage Decree was not applicable to the debenture as it was not
registered with the register of titles but only with the company registry.
S.113 Evidence Act provides that a person is estopped from complaining
against the act of another, which act has been done with the acquiescence
of that person.  In the instant case, the Managing Director of the respondent
was present in the meeting where the bank appointed the receivers and in
fact handed over to the receivers the keys and cash and books of account
of the respondent.  He never protested against the appointment of the
Directors then.  The respondents were therefore estopped from challenging
the validity of the appointment.
Since the appointment of the receivers was valid, so was their transfer of the
suit property to the appellants in appeal No.16/95.
S.184 gives fraud as the only basis upon which title may be impeached.
Since by the time the respondents filed the suit the appellants in appeal
No.16/95 were already registered sufficient to impeach the appellant's title.
Appeals allowed with costs.
Alfa Insurance Consultants Ltd Vs. Empire Insurance Group.
Insurance-broker and agent S.57 Insurance Decree-whether
plaintiff was an insurance broker and not agent.
Insurance broker-remuneration-rate of commission-whether fixed by
insurance Decree S.57-whether quantum meruit.
Insurance broker-whether must solicit and negotiate the policy in
order to merit the full brokerage commission-whether broker was
the efficient cause of the transaction.
Held: S.57 Insurance Decree (19/78) defines insurance broker as an
independent contractor soliciting or negotiating insurance policies on behalf
of the insured for a commission.  This means that the appellant when it
negotiated the insurance policies, it was not acting for the insurance
company but for the insured American Embassy. That is, the appellant was
not the agent of the insurance company and therefore the respondent was
wrong to argue that it chose to pay 7.7% to the appellant because it was
not their contracted producer who should have first undergone training to
deserve to be the respondent's contracted producer.  The appellant was on
the facts and the law an insurance broker and not an agent, and was
therefore entitled to full commission.
Where a broker is claiming a commission upon a certain transaction the
broker must show that he was the efficient cause of the transaction coming
about.  To be an efficient cause the broker need not necessarily complete or
take part in all the negotiations.  It is sufficient to prove that he introduced
the insurer to the insured.  In the instant case the appellant company
actually negotiated the transaction with the insured and sold it to the
respondent, the insurer.  The insured split it two phase for ease of payment
but it was one and the same transaction.  Therefore the appellant was
entitled to the full brokerage commission for both covers.
According to the evidence there was no known fixed rate of commission for
brokers by law at the time the policy was negotiated.  Therefore, the
appellant was entitled to what was reasonable in the circumstances.  And
12% would be reasonable in the circumstances since the transaction was
not shown to have been very difficult to negotiate.
Appeal allowed.  Commission to be paid on the full policy at 12%.
Oriental Insurance Brokers Ltd Vs. Transocean (U) Ltd
Insurance-broker S.34 Insurance Decree-whether insurance broker
has a cause of action against the insured for unpaid premiums.
Held: (By a majority of 2 to 1) The learned judge erred in introducing new
issues at the time of making judgment without affording the parties the
opportunity to be heard and this error prejudiced the appellant's case.
S.43(3) (4) Insurance Decree impose a duty on the Insurance Broker to
remit the collected premiums to the insurer not later than 21 days.  Since
the broker was under a duty to remit premiums to the insurer, it means that
the broker has an implied duty to collect the premiums from the insured to
the insurer and even to sue the insured to compel him to pay the premiums.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Wamala Growers Co-operative Union Vs. Attorney General
Sale of goods-sale of future goods S.7(3) Sale of Goods Act-
whether the sale was for future goods.
Held: S.7(3) Sale of Goods Act, provides that where the seller purports to
effect a present sale of future goods, the contract operates as only an
agreement to sale goods.  However in the instant case, the relevant facts
were that the agent of the defendant accepted payment for the animals and
allowed the plaintiff to select from a herd of over 500 heifers.  Therefore there
was created an express contract which was breached.
Where the party in breach of a contract knows the special circumstances
under which the contract was concluded, after having been so informed by
the injured party at the conclusion of the contract, the measure of the
damages the injured party is entitled to as a result of that breach is what
was reasonably contemplated as would naturally arise from the breach.
In the instant case the very nature of in-calf heifers is for diary farming where
milk is expected to be produced for sale.  The value of the expected mild
from 20 in-calf heifers for 9 years would be Ushs.194.4 million.  This amount
would be paid by the defendant to the plaintiff.
Case allowed.  Defendant to pay Ugshs 194.4 million and costs to plaintiff.
Kavuma F.W Vs. Sembule Investments Bank
Business Names Registration Act S.5-particulars of owners of business
name.
Partnership-whether a co-owner can commit conversion in respect of
joint property.
Agency - principal - ratification-whether proved.
Held: A person is guilty of conversion who without lawful excuse, deprives
another of his goods by giving some other person a lawful title to them.
In the present case, the third party had only defective title to the cheques
as the true owner was the plaintiff.  The defendant dealt with the cheques in
a manner inconsistent with the rights of the plaintiff who was the true owner,
and are therefore prima facie, liable to him for the conversion of the cheques.
S.82(1)(2) Bills of Exchange Act protects a bank from liability in conversion
where the bank has acted in good faith and without negligence and the
cheque in question is a crossed cheque.  In the instant case though the
bank sought to rely on Section 82 Bills of Exchange Act for protection and
pleaded to have acted in good faith and without negligence, the bank did not
lead evidence to show that the cheques in question were crossed.
Secondly, the bank's failure to investigate the particulars of the customer
who purported to be the owner of the cheques was evidence in question
were crossed.
The plea that the plaintiff had ratified the act of the third party cannot stand.
A principal can only ratify the act of a person who is his agent.  In the
instant case the third party never acted for the plaintiff and never said so.
The plead that the plaintiff was a partner of the third party cannot stand
because even if it were true that the third party and the plaintiff were partners
a co-owner can commit conversion in respect of joint property.  However,
neither the third party nor the plaintiff claimed that they were partners.
The alleged indemnification of the defendant by the plaintiff when he agreed
to drop his complaint against the defendant cannot be said to have been
done voluntarily because, the plaintiff had had no legal counsel; the plaintiff
was desperate for accessing even the little balance to offset his debts, so
it was a corrupt bargain and it was unenforceable and moreover the
defendant never performed his part of the bargain.
The measure of damages for conversion of (a chattel) cheques is their face
value.  Therefore, the defendant would pay Ugshs.31 million to the plaintiff
the face value of the cheques.
Case allowed with costs against the defendant.
COMPANY LAW
Muwumba Kabire &anor Vs. H.H.Abidi &sons Transporters Ltd.
Corporate personality - whether objector's property wrongly
attached where objector is shareholder in a company which is the
judgment debtor.
Held: Where an application is made for the attachment of any
moveable property belonging to a judgment - debtor, but not in his
possession, the decree-holder shall annex to the application an
inventory of the property to be attached, containing a reasonably
accurate description of the same.  In the instant case it was improper
not to specify the properties to be attached.
As regards the motor-vehicle attached it is well established that the
property of the company is distinct from that of its members.
Therefore the attachment of the objector's property was wrong.
A power of attorney is defined as an authority given by one to
another to act for him in his absence e.g. to convey land, sue etc.
The attorney like in the instant case does not necessarily have
to have any interest in the thing to be done or transaction to be
executed.
Johnson Samson Senseko Kulubya Vs. Uganda Transport
Shareholders right to compensation for share in company divested
by Government - whether existed.
Held: Since by Decree 11/75 Government became trustee to the
assets and liabilities it vested in the defendant company, the
plaintiff was entitled to compensation for his shares by the
defendant company.
All evidence pointed to the fact that the plaintiff was General Manager
and was regarded as such and was entitled to his terminal benefits
in that capacity.
That since the defendant company had allowed the plaintiff to stay in
the house until payment, terminal benefits, the defendant was now
stopped from evicting him before the payment, terminal benefits.
Christopher Kayoboke Vs. Amos Agaba, Joseph Byamugisha
and Baryaruha.
Company's internal management - whether court had no
jurisdiction to entertain an action brought by a member -personally
against the directors of a company, concerning the internal
management of the company.
Held: Since Dr. Byamugisha was defendant number 2 and was as a
result likely to give evidence in this suit, it would not be proper for
Dr. Byamugisha to act in person for the there 2 defendants as their
Counsel.
The Plaintiff had two causes of action properly brought before court I.e.
a personal action by which he sought court's protection of his pecuniary
interest is the company and a derivative action by which he sought
court's protection of the good of the company generally against waste by
the directors.  Therefore fourth had jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
The question of whether the plaintiff was estopped from complaining
against the manner of running the company because it was a long
established mode to which he himself was party, would be a question
to be determined at the trial.
Nile Bank Ltd Vs. Gomba Machinery and General Equipment
Lifting the veil - whether the veil can be lifted for the purpose of
enabling the judgment creditor applicant to recover it's docretal
sum from the managing director, instead of recovering it from
the judgment debtor company.
Held: Whether or not Mr. Gombya, the Managing Director was the
proper judgment debtor, the correct mode of executing a decree by
arresting the judgment debtor would be made under s.39 (d) of the
Civil Procedure Act and Order 19 r.8 (2) (j) (m) but not under Order 19
Rule 34 (1) of Order 19 is applicable as an alternative mode of execution
where there has been an application properly made for the arrest of a
judgment debtor under section 39(d) and O.19 r.8 (2) (I) (iii) when the
court may, instead of issuing a warrant of arrest for the judgment
debtor, issue a notice calling upon him to appear before court and show
cause why he should not be committed to civil prison.  Further, Rule
34 (7) of Order 19 cannot be invoked by the judgment debtor.  The rule
is explicitly within the discretion of the court and this is explicitly I
indicated in form 11 of Appendix D to Civil Procedure Rules at page 13/2.
The notice is issued and signed by the Judge.
As far as Lifting of veil for the purpose of enabling the judgment creditor
Applicant to recover its decretal sum from the managing Director instead
of recovering it from the J/d company, this would probably be done if the
applicant, J/c in his affidavit proved that the defendant company was as
it was described in Jones V. Lipman (1962) 1 W.L.R. 832 at page 838,
the creature of the Managing Director, a device and a sham, a mask
which he held before his face in an attempt to avoid recognition by eye
of equity.
Henry Kawalya Vs. Dan Semakadde.
Winding up-petition for winding up by court.
Held: A contributory may petition for winding up within the provisions of
ss.214 and 224 of the companies Act, which are not fulfilled here.
A deadlock in management to justify winding up must not be caused by
a bona fide act intra vires the Articles and Memorandum.
The just and equitable rule dos not apply where the deadlock, at the time
of hearing the petition, has been resolved by resignation of one director
and his replacement by another.
It is proper for a director to initiate a change in a deal, if it is in the
interest of the company.
A shareholder cases to be such upon payment to him of a consideration
for his interests of the company.
S.100 of Table A empowers a director to appoint others to meet the
minimum number of directors where some directors resigns.
In re Lukerere Coffee factory Ltd.
Restoration of a company's name on the registrar of companies.
The Company defaulted on debentures it issued to Grindlays Bank
whereupon the bank appointed M/S Chandubhai Rambhai Patel as
Receiver and Managers.  These later withdrew following the expulsion of
Asians in 1972 and no person was appointed to fill the vacancy.
No annual returns were filed with the result that the Registrar struck the
company's name off the Register.  This was a petition to restore the
