company's name , on the ground that it were the receivers to file the
returns, not the directors who therefore took no blame for the omission.
Sole Electric (u) Ltd Vs. Town Clerk K &Nakibuka Enterprises.
Separate personality - whether bidding for the purchase of a
premises by a director of a company in his own names is
bidding by the company.
Held: When a Director in the plaintiff company bided for the acquisition
of the suit premises, in own names, it did not mean that it was the
plaintiff company that bided because of the principle of separate
personality between the company and its members.  Therefore the
plaintiff company did not have a cause of action to bring the suit.
The question whether there was a subsisting tenancy between the
applicant was a successor in title to the former landlord of the plaintiff
company.  On this ground the plaint would not be stuck on.
Eriya Milling Protect Ltd Vs. Wade Adams Construction Ltd.
Ostensible authority - whether the official of the company who
signed on beheld of the company had ostensible authority to bind
the company.
Held: The signature on the invoice that constituted the alleged contract
had not been proved and the alleged signatory had not been called to
testify.  Therefore, this is not the contract that falls under S.90 of the
Evidence Act which precludes oral contracts from contradicting
documentary contracts.
The alleged agent of the defendant company could not have either
actual or ostensible authority of the company to bind it because the
defendant company had never introduced the alleged agent to the
plaintiff as holding the said position.  Therefore, the question of estoppel
did not arise.
Uganda Blanket Manufacturers(1973) Ltd Vs. A.G
Enforcing company's rights - whether action should be commenced
by company or minority shareholders where the minister
purporting to replaces forcefully it's management.
Held: Decree 22 of 1974 provided that the Minister of Industry shall control
the management of the appellant company through the Board of Directors,
therefore for the Minister to purport to have wound up the Board which was
a statutory body so that he could control the management of the company
directly was illegal.  A statutory body can only be wound up by statutory
provision.
An action to enforce the company's rights was properly commenced in the
company's name because a new group had assumed the control of the
company which was allowing it to be run on an ultra-vires basis.  And more-
over neither the Ministry, nor the Board of Directors nor the general meeting
could have commenced these proceedings in the circumstances.
The conduct of the Minister did not occasion the award of exemplary
damages because the Minister merely misconceived his task.  He thought
he was operating a Government owner Company by virtue of Decree 2 of
1974 and thought he was preserving Government property and looking to the
wider interests of the textile industry.
Sheikh Ali Senyonga & 7 others Vs. Sheikh Hussein Rajab
Kakooza and 6 others.
Private company -membership subject to religious criteria -
body is private not public company.
Held: The council was registered as a company and was subject to
company law.  It was a private company because membership was
restricted according to religious criteria.
The constitution of the Council should be interpreted to give reasonable
business efficacy.
The elected chairman met the requirement of the Degree as he had an
equivalent of a B.A. in Dawa obtained from Libya.  The Deputy Mufti
did not need any specific academic qualifications but had to be of good
character, fluent in Arabic, a practicing Muslim and Ahlisunnah Wal-
Jama'h.  He needed some experience in Sharia matters.
The burden of proving qualifications lay on the person who alleges he
had he same.
Theresa Okoth - Ofumbi & anor Vs. Haji Hamedali Ahamed
Karim
Liability of director for the fraud committed by the company -
whether director was liable.
Held: The second appellant/advocate's party in the case would cover the
same ground as proving the fraud against the company and under O.1
r3 of CPR as per the pleadings the advocate had been properly joined
as defendant as it was him together with other defendants against
whom the right to relief, I.e. fraudulent breach of contract, had been
claimed.  The advocate/appellant had specific instructions from the
plaintiff respondent to effect a transfer of the suit property in his favour.
Instead he neither effected the said transfer nor stopped or declined to
act for the defendant company when making the second sale of the
same property to the fourth defendant.
The director of a company had a fiduciary duty to act in utmost good
faith but the first appellant herein as director of the defendant company
that had fraudulently deprived the plaintiff/respondent company of its
property was not guilty of the breach of such fiduciary duty since this
duty is owed to the company above.  Secondly, the first appellant could
not be liable for the tortuous interference in the contract between the
plaintiff/respondent and the defendant company because this tort had
not been pleaded by the plaintiff/respondent.
Kyotera Coffee Growers Ltd Vs. Leonsio Kaggwa & ors.
Directors - dispute between two sets of directors - whether one set
may abstain an injunction against the other for the management of
company.
Held: The Procedure of obtaining the order without serving the other
party was most irregular.  The application did not pray for the
dispensations of any sort.  And the allegation of the urgency of the
matter was not real since the notice of the meeting was given some
days before the court application there was time to serve the
respondents.
S.101 of CPA confers no powers on the parties nor rights on litigants.
The section does not invest the court with jurisdiction where the court
would otherwise have no jurisdiction.  The section only saves the
inherent powers of the court first to make orders as the ends of justice
may require and secondly to prevent abuse of its process.  The court in
granting the injunction in this case was doing neither of the above since
the Companies Act S.131 does not give court power to issue injunctions
to stop the holding of the Annual General meeting.  The best way to
nullify resolutions passed at a meeting by rival directors would be for
the complainants of file a suit against the order seeking a declaration to
nullify such resolution.  Therefore the order of the trial judge was made
A.K Detergents Vs. G.M Combined.
Winding up proceedings - whether no valid sale of company's
assets in possible when winding up proceedings are commenced
whether sale under debenture valid.
Held: The receivers and managers that sold the plaintiff's property acted
according to the powers that were conferred upon them by the
debentures.  These powers were not revocable.  The Law is that winding
up proceedings do not affect the receiver's power to hold and dispose of
the company's property comprised in the debenture.  Therefore the
contention of the respondent that their suit contesting the sale on the
ground truth it was not valid for having taken place after the institution
of winding up proceedings, was likely to succeed was not correct.
Therefore, taking into account the fact that the respondent/plaintiff was
heavily indebted most of her assists charged, was under receivership,
winding up proceedings had commenced, it was necessary that she
furnishes security for costs of the suit on which the defendant/applicant
would fall back in event the suit went against the plaintiff/respondent.
Since the monetary value of the subject matter of the suit, this is, the
property sold to the application/defendant was very big and the litigation
likely to be vast, shs.50 million would be paid as security for costs.
Henry Munyangizi Vs. General Machinery Ltd.
Corporate personality - whether plaintiff may claim ownership of a
tractor purchased by a company of which he is a shareholder.
Held: Where a case is admitted to review by one judge and is afterwards
tried by another the new judge must confine himself to the points
directed by the other for review.  A Judge granting a review on one point
has no power to go into or decide a matter already finally adjudicated
upon.
Parties should not have been allowed to amend pleadings after the order
for review had been made because at the time of the review the
proceedings had been closed and therefore to allow amendment at that
stage would be an abuse of court process since there should be an end
to litigation.
A company is a legal entity irrespective of the motives of its promoters,
once it is formed under the provisions of the law the rules governing it
must be followed.  The company property is clearly distinguishable from
the member's property and therefore the plaintiff could not be said to be
the owner of the tractor bought by the company in which he was a
shareholder.
S.29 of the Sale of Goods Act provides that unless otherwise agreed
delivery of the goods and payment of the price are concurrent conditions.
The plaintiff having paid for a tractor which the defendants had defaulted
in delivery, the plaintiff, buyer is entitled to damages, namely the
estimated loss directly and naturally resulting in the ordinary course of
events from the seller's breach.  In this case the plaintiff should be
awarded damages that may enable him purchase a new tractor.
Namuco Ltd VS. Tri-Star International Ltd.
Director - whether a person who is not registered as a director with
the registrar of companies may nevertheless act as a director and
swear an affidavit on behalf of the company, validly.
Held: The affidavit in reply to Kagoro was valid because he had a general
power of attorney to transact business on behalf of the company and
he was thereby no stranger to the affairs to the company and he could
validly depene to matters regarding the company whether as director or
agent therefore.
It was the applicant who had the obligation to obtain the requisite
consent and therefore their failure to obtain the consent could render the
agreement for a sublease was a valid contract interpreters and it conferred
a right to the respondent's caveat was valid to prevent any dealing in the
land before the respondent was able either to claim for specific
performance or damages.
Contraction Engineers & Builders Ltd Vs. The New Vision
and 3 others.
Institution of suit - company resolution -whether invariably required
to constitute a suit.
Held: A board resolution is merely evidence that the company has
authority to institute a suit but lack of a board resolution does not
necessarily mean that the directors of a company have no authority to
institute the suit.  Therefore, the plaintiff's case before court was not
improper merely because there was no resolution to that effect.
A among the words complained of was that "shs 257 million had been lost
in A.T.M. deal".  The ordinary and the natural meaning discerned by an
ordinary man reading the article is that the said money had been cheated
by whoever was written about in the article.  Therefore, the words
complained of were defamatory.
A publication even if defamatory, must refer to the plaintiff in order that it
is defamatory of him.  In the present case the article complained of
referred to the plaintiff company and was therefore defamatory of the
plaintiff.
For a defence of justification to succeed, the words complained of must
be shown to be substantially true at the time of the publication and the
burden to prove so is on the defendant.  In the instance case the
payment alleged to be a shady deal came from a decree of court
consequent upon a consent judgment.  This means the deal was not
shady but a genuine one.  Therefore the defence of justification must fail.
For the defence of fair comment to succeed it must be shown that the
words complained of were merely a comment and not a statement of fact
and the fact commented upon must have been truly and accurately stated.
In the instant case, the editorial was an expression of an opinion from the
facts stated and it was an objective and fair comment made in public
interest without malice but the rest of the article and the cartoon were
statements of fact and could not be held to be fair comment.
An occasion is privileged where the parson making the communication
has a duty or interest to make the communication to the person who has
a corresponding interest or duty to receive the communication.  This gives
rise to the defence of qualified privilege.  In the instant case the defendant
made the publication in the course of its journalistic engagements.
Though the matter was of public interest, it was not of a public nature.
Therefore the occasion was not privileged and the defence of qualified
must fail.
It was not a correct statement of the law that a company as plaintiff in an
action in defamation, must first prove that they suffered special damages
or financial loss in order that the plaintiff company can qualify to be
awarded general damages.  In the instant case the defamation regarded
the plaintiff's business where it was alleged that the plaintiff was corrupt
and incompetent.  The plaintiff was entitled to damages without proof of
special damages.  An award shs. 3,500,000/= would be made to the
plaintiff company.
Banax Ltd Vs. Gold Trust Bank Ltd.
Company resolution - whether Bank could refuse to accept a
resolution of it's customer duly registered with the registrar of
companies.
Held: The reorganization of the company was an internal matter and the
respondent bank should only have looked at the resolution which had
been duly registered with the registrar of companies.  Therefore, the
bank would not be said to have had notice of something irregular and
was thereby in breach of contract to freeze the appellant's account.
The plaintiff appellant must prove that it had suffered actual damage due
to its non-use of its account as a basis for the award of general damages.
This had not been the case and Shs.100,000/= would be awarded for
inconvenience suffered.
Fam International Ltd & Ahmed Farm Vs. Mohamed El-faith
Certificate of incorporation-s.17 of the companies Act whether
trial judge erred in going behind the certificate of incorporation -
whether certificate of incorporation is not conclusive evidence as
to the incorporation - whether fraud is a ground for going behind the
certificate of incorporation.
Held: Paragraph 4 of the written statement of defence gave the appellants
sufficient particulars of what fraudulent acts the respondent was alleging
against them, namely the backdating of the incorporation of the first
appellant, with intent to defraud the respondent.
The fraudulent acts complained of were imputable on the second plaintiff/
appellant because he stood to gain from them.
In fraud cases the standard of proof is more than a mere balance of
probability though less than proof beyond reasonable doubt.  The learned
trial judge was alive to this provision of the law when he said that he was
satisfied by the evidence which was more than a balance of probabilities.
Therefore the trial judge applied the correct standard of proof of fraud as
required.
The main ground upon which a court can go behind the certificate of
incorporation is fraud and once fraud is alleged the court is entitled to
extend its enquiry to matters precedent and incidental to registration.
The learned trial judge was therefore correct in going behind the
certificate of incorporation, because a certificate of incorporation may
be impeached on the grounds of fraud.
The learned trial judge erred in making a winding up order of the first
appellant because there was no such application properly before the
court as provided by ss 218 and 224 of the Companies Act.
The failure to gazette and entry of the change of name were two
irregularities in procedure which would not vitiate the change of name
property made.  The trial judge was correct in holding so.
It is always better to frame issues at the beginning of the hearing before
evidence is led so that evidence that is led is guided by the framed issues.
A prayer was not an assertion nor a material statement which one party
must allege or the other must deny to constitute an issue.  The trial judge
was right in holding that the issue as to the appellant's holding out as a
shareholder in the respondent's company was a won issue because, it
only appeared as a prayer.
the respondent could not claim his company's property by an action in
his own name as this would offend against the rule of corporate
personality, since the company that owned the property had its own
independent existence.  The trial judge was correct in refusing the prayer
in the counter claim and was also correct in not granting the order for the
recovery of the property in favour or the plaintiffs because they had not
made that prayer.
W.E.Kiwalabye Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank & anor.
Corporation personality-lifting the veil-whether grounds existed for
lifting the veil.
Held: Before court can decide that the veil of corporate personality should
be lifted, there must be facts to assist court conclude that the director of
the company was one and the same with his company.  In this instant
case those facts did not exist.
Ishasha Mines Ltd Vs. National Enterprises Corporation.
Subsidiary company - liability - whether a parent company may
be found liable for the acts of it's subsidiary.
Held: A subsidiary company has in law its independent corporate
existence and may be sued for acts its liable for.  However where as a
question of fact it is established that the subsidiary was merely a means
through which the parent company conducts its business, then an action
may be properly instituted against the parent company for acts done by
subsidiary.  In the instant case it was clear that officers of the subsidiary
were all appointed by the defendant.  Therefore, the suit was properly
brought against the defendant.
The purported final settlement agreement smacked of duress because the
plaintiff negotiated from a very weak position.  Secondly the agreement
was ambiguous because it merely stated that the subsidiary had agreed
to pay so much for the plaintiff's claim without stating what the claim was.
Therefore the plaintiff's action was not estopped by the purported final
settlement agreement.
Suit allowed and the plaintiff to be compensated for 450 tones of lime
mines the 80 tones already compensated for.
Wahabe Tamari & sons LTD Vs. Green House Ltd.
Lifting the veil of incorporation s.33 companies Act - fraud -
whether veil of incorporation may be lifted for fraud.
Held: The respondent company was incorporated well before the suit
agreement was executed.  Therefore it cannot be said that it was
incorporated for the purpose of defrauding others.  Therefore no valid
reason had been proved for purposes of lifting the veil of incorporation of
the respondent company.
Application dismissed with costs.
N.K.Radia Vs. Kakkybhai & co.Ltd.
Institution of suit - authority therefore whether board resolution
must invariably be filed as evidence that the company has
authority to institute a suit.
Held: In order to bring an action in the name of a company there must be
authority to do so other wise the suit is a nullity.  But where lack of
authority to sue does not plainly appear at the commencement of the trial
and determine the issue of lack of authority or otherwise, after evidence
has been heard.  In the instant case the learned trial Judge was correct in
overruling the preliminary objection since the alleged lack of authority to
bring the proceedings did not to him plainly appear at that stages the suit.
NEC & 2 others Vs. Nile Bank Ltd
Corporate personality-lifting the veil - whether a subsidiary
company was an independent entity from it's holding and therefore
the holding company was not liable for it's acts - whether the veil
of corporate personality should be lifted to find that the holding
company was responsible for the acts of it's subsidiary.
Pre-incorporation contract-whether could bind the company subsequently
incorporated.
Debenture-Mortgage Decree SS.2 and 1-whether debenture holder could
attach movable property in exercise of its right under debenture - whether
such debenture holder could rely on the mortgage to attach the plaintiff's
vehicles.
Held: A contract made before a company is formed cannot bind the
company formed afterwards.  In the instant case the first appellant
executed the debenture before NEC Bakery came into existence.
Therefore the learned trial Judge was correct in holding that the debenture
was a nullity.
Though a subsidiary company is an independent entity from its parent, in
the instant case the trial Judge was correct in lifting the veil of the
subsidiary NEC Bakery and to find that it was owned and controlled by
the first appellant who had majority shareholding in it and that therefore
the first appellant was liable on the debenture.
If a person contracts essentially as an agent for non-existing Principal
that person may be found personally liable on the contract.  In the instant
case learned trial Judge was correct in finding the appellant who
contracted on behalf of NEC Bakery which was not in existence at the
ostensibly time of the debenture, liable on the debenture.
The learned trial Judge erred in holding that the respondent/defendant was
empowered under the debenture to exercise a right of seizure under
clause 6 of the debenture because clause 6 of the debenture did not
provide for seizure but only stated the conditions under which the
appellant shall immediately be liable to repay the loan.  It is only clause
7, which provided for a right to appoint a receiver by the respondent.
therefore they respondent was not entitled to seize the appellant's motor
vehicle it was only entitled to appoint a receiver.
The learned trial Judge misdirected himself when he observed that the
plaintiff/appellant should instead have filed objector proceedings to contest
the seizure instead of a suit.  Objector proceedings may only follow when
there is an execution of a decree of court.
The Mortgage Decree does not apply to moveable property and therefore
the argument that the seizure of the appellant's vehicles was done under
the powers of the Mortgage Decree Ss.2, 7 was misconceived. And more-
over there was no order of foreclosure as required by S.7 Mortgage Decree.
Even if it is not a rule of Law that the trial Court should invariably assess
the damages it would have awarded the party succeeded, it was an
important rule of practice because the party is given an opportunity to
appeal against the award by the trial court.
Teddy Ssezi Cheeye & 2 others Vs. Emmanuel Tumusiime
Mutebile & 2 others.
Defamation - whether a company could not maintain a cause of
action in libel.
Held: The Judge in libel disputes acts as the jury by finding by himself
whether or not the words complained of were in their ordinary and natural
meaning defamatory of the plaintiff and he makes this finding without
calling for the aid of private witnesses whether for or against the plaintiff
or defendant. It is only when the words complained of are a legal innuendo
where certain facts are known to specific persons, that the Judge may
call in the aid of witnesses who are among the specific persons who know
the specific facts.  In the instant case, since the plaintiffs complained that
the inference from the ordinary and natural meaning of the words
complained of were defamatory of them, the trial Judge was entitled to
formulate his own conclusion without the aid a witnesses.
A trading corporation or company may maintain an action in respect of
imputation of corruption or any other wrongful conduct if such imputation
is calculated to injure it in its trading character.  In the instant case since
it was alleged that the third plaintiff company was dealing in underhand
and corrupt practices, its trading character was concerned and therefore
rightly brought an action on its behalf for damages.
A libel in a newspaper is prima facie evidence of publication.  Since the
defendants did not rebutt this presumption, the learned trial Judge was
entitled to find that the defendants had indeed published the libel
complained of.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Makerere Properties Ltd Vs. Mansukhlal Ranji Karia.
Institute of suit instruction to advocate by a person not a director
nor shareholder-whether such suit is maintainable.
Held: A suit instituted in the names of a company without the authority of
the directors is not maintainable in law.  In the case instant, though
Mohamed Amin claimed that he had a resolution signed by some of the
shareholders as authority for the suit, there was no evidence that there
was a meeting where the resolution was passed.  Therefore, the
resolution did not amount to authority for the suit.
Moreover the resolution had not been tendered in evidence which meant
that after all it did not exist.
Further, before the registrar of companies could rectify the register, to
reinstate the original shareholders and directors, the purported original
directors had no powers to authorize the institution of the suit.
Article 36 of the company's Articles of Association provides that the
management of the business of the company shall be vested in the
directors.  In the instant case at the time when PW1 instructed
M/s Mulira & Co. Advocates to institute the action he was not a director
and had never been a director of the company.  He could not therefore
instruct counsel to file proceedings in the name of the Company.
Failure to plead by the defendant in his WSD that the plaintiff's suit had
been filed without authority did not preclude the defendant from raising it
during submissions after evidence had been led on both sides because
that fact had been clear in evidence.  Therefore court would rely on that
finding and strike out the action of the plaintiff Company.
Action struck off for want of authority to institute it.
H.M.B Kayondo Vs. Somani Amirali.
Corporate personality - lifting the veil - whether the veil of incorporate-
action of the defendant's company would be lifted to find on the
dishonoured bills.
Held: It is a rule of pleading that an averment not expressly or implicitly
traversed is deemed to have been admitted.  It is a rule of evidence that a
fact admitted need not be proved.  The plaintiff in para 5 of the plaint had
pleaded that he gave notice of dishonour to the defendant.  The defendant
in his WSD did not traverse either explicitly or implicitly that plea.
Therefore the defendant had admitted that the plaintiff gave him  notice of
dishonour of the cheque as required by s.48, the Bills of Exchange Act.
A company duly registered is a legal entity distinct from the subscribers
or those who formed it.  This is the rule of incorporation.  Therefore the
dishonoured cheques on the account of Uganda Consumer Supplies Ltd
belonged to the Company.  However the defendant being managing
Director thereof would not be allowed to use incorporation as a cloak for
fraud.  Therefore, the veil of incorporation would be lifted by court so that
the defendant is found personally liable for the dishonoured bills.
S.30 (1) Bills of Exchange Act provides that every party whose signature
appears on a bill is a prima facie deemed to have become a party for
value.  Since the defendant admitted having drawn the cheques, the
burden of proof lay on him to prove that the plaintiff had passed no
consideration to the defendant for the cheques.  The defendant failed in
this.  Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Mukasa Lubansa & ors Vs. Combined Building Company.
Corporate personality -departure of shareholders-whereby
company ceased to exist.
Held: A Company is a legal entity separate from its shareholders.
Therefore, the departure of the shareholders of the defendant company
did not affect its capacity to own the property in its names under Decree
The law is that relief against forfeiture cannot be granted where the parties
parties have altered their positions.  In the instant case the land had been
leased to a third party.  Therefore the prayer for relief against forfeiture
would not succeed.
Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff and relief against forfeiture refused.
Mattec Ltd Vs. Joseph Duyck & anor.
Institution of suit - management - whether institution of suit by a
company was an act of management and not a decision of the
company 's general meeting.
Institution of suit-instruction of counsel-whether must be by resolution of
the shareholders in a general meeting.
Held: It is trite law that to bring an action in the name of a company there
must be authority to that effect.  However, that authority need not be by a
resolution of the Board of Director unless the Articles of Association of the
the Company expressly require so.  The resolution can be made by
management since institution of a suit is a decision of management and
not shareholders.  Therefore the applicant was lawfully entitled to bring
this action.
Objection overruled.
Coffee Marketing Board Vs. Kizezi Growers Coop Union.
Ostensible authority - liability of co-op union - whether union not
liable to repay a loan contracted on it's behalf by it's officers.
Held: The principle of ostensible authority applicable to companies equally
applied to cooperative Unions.  The principle of ostensible authority is to the
effect that where an agent acts without actual authority or outside his actual
authority a third party can enforce the contract against the company where
there is a representation on by persons who possess the actual authority
that the agent has the authority to enter into that kind of contract on behalf
of the company and the third party is thereby induced to act of the
representation.
In the instant case there was evidence that the officers who acted as the
agents the company has previously ever borrowed on behalf of the company
money for company use.  Therefore, the plaintiff as third party had no
obligation to inquire into the limits of the authority of the agents since that
concerned the internal management of the cooperative Union.  Therefore the
defendant was liable on the loan agreement and must pay it. The loan
agreement was lawful and enforceable.
Where an instrument is on the face of it regular persons dealing with the
company have a right to presume that the seal so affixed has been duly
fixed.  Therefore the plaintiff as a third party was entitled to treat the loan
agreement dully executed by the agents of the defendant cooperative Union.
Even if it were to be held that the loan agreement was illegal, where the
parties to an agreement are not in parid elicto, as in the instant case, the
defendant would still be required to repay the money as had and received.
Suit allowed.  Loan ordered to be repaid by the defendant.
United Assurance Co. Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Instructional of counsel - single director s.177 companies Act-
whether single director had powers to legally instruct counsel file
a suit in the name of the company.
Corporate personality-ownership of company property-whether company
property- whether company property is owned by the company and not
shareholders-whether therefore suit property remained vested in the
company and not appropriated.
Held: Company property belongs to the company and not the shareholders.
Since the suit property belonged to the company, it was not expropriated.
What was expropriated were the shares of the Asians in the company.
Therefore the suit property registered in the names of the company was not
managed under the provisions of the Expropriated Properties Act.  Therefore
the learned trial judge erred when he ruled that the suit was not maintainable.
The suit was properly brought to contest the constitutional propriety of the
compulsory acquisition.
The management of a private company is in the board of directors who under
S.177 of the company's Act can manage the affairs of the company under
regulation 80 of Table A of the Act.  The management includes instructing
counsel to file proceedings in the name of the company.  In the present
case board of directors of the appellant company consisted of a single
director and it is in this director who instructed counsel and no resolution
was required to evidence the instructions to counsel to file the suit.
The learned trial judge misdirected himself in law and fact when he rule that
the case had no substantial constitutional issues requiring the interpretation
of the Constitutional Court.
Appeal allowed.
Imulti Constructors Ltd Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Receiver - agency - whether a receiver/manager of company's
assets is an agent of the Debtor company.
Held: Since the appellant company still owed money to the respondent its
debenture could not be said to have been discharged.  Therefore the sale of
the suit property over which the respondent had a debenture was validly
done.
The receivers/managers once they were appointed became the agents of the
appellant and therefore when the receiver sold the suit property he did so as
the agent of the appellant.  The debenture terms and the law provided this.
S.9(c ) (ii) of the Banking Act allows a bank to buy its security in hold. In
the instant case when the respondent bank bought the suit property it did so
in hold.  But the hold could not be forever, the property eventually could be
and was taken over by the bank lawfully.
Appeal dismissed.
British India General Insurance Co. Ltd Vs. Dolatrai Solanki.
Instructions to institute proceedings by non existing company-
whether counsel personally liable for costs.
Held: The court can grant a stay of execution when satisfied that there is
good cause and that special circumstances exist to justify such a cause.
And the likelihood of success of the applicant's appeal and the consequent
fear of rendering an appeal likely to succeed, nugatory, consist of special
stay.  In the instant case the appeal was not likely to succeed because it
was instituted by an applicant who had no capacity to institute it.
A company can only authorize the commencement of legal proceedings in
its name by way of a resolution.  In the instant case there was no such
resolution and therefore, the counsel who purported to act on behalf of the
applicant who had not made any resolution to that effect, must be personally
liable for the costs arising from such proceedings where the Advocates is
apparently acting without instructions.
Application dismissed.
Mugenyi & Co. Advocates Vs. Attorney General
Number of members of private company S.4(1) Company's Act-
Government private company-whether Government Ministers were
not shareholders-whether therefore there was no statutory
minimum of 2 shareholders-whether-therefore company not
incorporated.
Lifting the veil of incorporation-Salomon Vs. Salomon-whether
because fraud was not pleaded veil may not be lifted.
Held: S.4(1) Companies Act requires at least 2 shareholders to form a
private limited liability company.  The 2 government ministers signed as
shareholders and thus fulfilled the requirements of the Act and it was not
competent to inquire as to whether or not the two ministers were
Shareholders.  Therefore the company was duly incorporated and the
learned trial judge erred when he held otherwise.
In order to lift the veil of incorporation personality so as to find that in fact
there was no company but a government extension, one must allege fraud
on the part of government.  In the instant case there was no fraud or illegality
alleged in the pleadings against government.  Therefore, the veil of
incorporation would remain uplifted and UTC 1975 would be dealt with as an
independent company separate from its owner the government and the
appellant must proceed to recover his fees in liquidation and not against
government.
Unless estoppels is a fact in issue at the trial, it cannot be raised when not
pleaded.  The defendant must plead estoppel and the plaintiff must reply in
order for it to be considered at the trial.  The learned trial judge erred to
have based his judgment on estoppel when the same had not been
pleaded and was not a fact in issue at the trial.
Appeal dismissed in part.  Appellant ordered to recover against the company
in liquidation.
Salim Jamal & 2 others Vs. Uganda Oxygen Ltd & 2 others.
Corporate personality-lifting the veil of incorporation-fraud-whether
fraud for lifting the veil of incorporation.
Internal management of the company-locus to institute suit by
person not a director-whether such a person has locus to institute
a derivative action to protect his interest in the company.
Held: Corporate personality cannot be used as a cloak or mask for fraud.
Where this is shown to be the case the veil of incorporation may be lifted to
ensure that justice is done and the court does not look helplessly in the
face of such fraud.  In the instant case it was necessary to disregard the
veil of incorporation and when that was done it would immediately be
apparent that respondent No.3 was a shareholder in OHL was not a director
and could therefore not remedy and loss occasioned by the directors
therein though ordinary mechanisms of internal management of the
company and the wronging directors were the ones in control, and could not
therefore bring an action to impeach themselves.  Therefore the learned
trial judged correctly found that respondent No.3 had a derivative right to
bring the derivative action against the wronging directors.
Where directors are being used by a derivative action, it is necessary to add
the company as a co-defendant.  O.I rr10(2) + (4) give court the discretion to
add a party where the circumstances of the case so demand.  In this case
the learned trial judge was right to add UOL as fourth defendant.  However,
when this is done the other party must be afforded an opportunity to amend
its pleadings.  In this the trial judge misdirected himself with he did not give
the plaintiff the opportunity to amend.
An appeal is commenced by a notice of appeal and not by a memorandum
of appeal.
Appeal dismissed except to the issue of whether the parties should have
been allowed to amend their pleadings after court had joined a fourth
defendant.
Kkaaya Jjingo Haji & 2 others Vs. Mufti of Uganda-Sheikh
Saad Luwemba.
Proceedings against the company-applications for an order that
company holds Annual General Meeting-S.135(1) Companies Act,
O.34A r6(h)-whether individuals have locus-whether suit maintain-
able against managing director personally.
Annual General Meeting S.135(1) Companies Act-application for
an order to convene it by individuals against managing director
personally-whether maintainable.
Held: Where a wrong has been done to the company an individual member
has locus to bring an action to restrain or rectify the wrong.  However since
the wrong id done to the company and not the individual, the action must
be brought in the name of the company.  In the instant case the failure to
hold the mandatory Annual General Meeting was a wrong done to the
company and the applicants should have brought the application in the
name of the company and not themselves.  The court has power under O.1
r10 (2) CPR to add the UMSC as a party but in the instant case counsel for
the applicants refused to see the necessity thereof.
Application struck out with costs.
Lusse Joseph Vs. Uganda
Held: Art. 23(b) (c ) of the Constitution provides that where a person has
been on remand for more that 360 days before he is committed, after the
committal, brought this application for release on bail.  This means that even
where a person is committed after he has been on remand for more than
360 days such person shall be released on bail.
Application allowed.
Dharamsy Morarji & Sons Ltd Vs. Suman Naresh Kara
Transmission of shares, S.84 Companies act-whether to transfer
shares refusal was malafide.
Resolution of company-quorum-whether resolution impeachable by
one direction in presence of non members.
Held: S. 187 of the Succession Act provides that no right of executor or
legatee is established unless a court of competent jurisdiction has granted
probate of the will or letters of Administration.  Therefore since High Court
refused to grant probate of the Will that established he respondent's right
to claim shares in the respondent company, the respondent's claim for the
shares could not succeed.
The appellant company being a private company that restricted the
transmission of shares, the single director who formed the quorum for the
meeting and subsequent resolution not to transmit the respondent because
the Articles of Association gave the director a discretion to do so and no
bad motive was proved against the director.
The participation of two more persons in the meeting of the director where
the resolution not to transmit shares was reached, did not invalidate the
decision of the director since he alone formed the requisite quorum.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Maximov Oleg Petrovich Vs. Premchandra Shenoi & anor.
Corporate personality-personal liability of director-whether conversed as a
preliminary point of law or after evidence, O.7 r 11 CPR.
Held: As per O.7 r 11 (a) CPR a plaint that does not disclose a cause of
action must be rejected. In considering that the plaint discloses a cause of
action only the plaint, must be looked at so that it is apparent on its face
that the plaintiff appears as a person aggrieved by the violation of his rights
and that it is the defendant who is liable.  In the instant case the pleadings
disclose that the plaintiff paid some money to the defendant so that they
could jointly trade in precious stones.  The pleadings further show that the
defendants acknowledged receipt though of a lesser sum.  Therefore it was
apparent on the face of the plaint that the plaintiff was aggrieved by the
defendants.  As to whether it was the 1st or 2nd or both defendants was a
triable issue after evidence had been led.  Therefore there was a cause of
action disclosed.
O.7 r 11 (e) CPR provides that a suit that is shown by the plaint to be
frivolous and vexatious must be rejected.  The plaint must show that to a
reasonable person, the plaintiff has no the kind of grievance that is entitled
to be adjudicated upon but that the plaintiff is actuated by malafide to harass
the defendant.  In the instant case the plaint discloses a reasonable
grievance against the plaintiff by the defendant.  Therefore the suit is not
frivolous and vexatious.
Since the plaintiff never sued in representative capacity, but brought the
action for his own benefit, it was not incumbent upon Court to order him to
sue in representative capacity.
Further O.1 r 8 (1) is properly invoked only where the person suing claims in
the plaint the same rights as those he wishes to represent.  In the instant
case the plaintiff claimed that it is only him who provided the money for the
transaction.
Moreover, rejecting the plaint and deciding an action before trial should be
sparingly done and only in such instances where the action is a clear abuse
of the process of Court per Fletcher Maulton, LJ in Dyson V. Attorney
General [1911] 1 KB 418.
Preliminary objection overruled with costs.
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW
Wycliffe Kiggundu Vs. Attorney General.
President's prerogative - whether the President's prerogative to
retire a public servant in public interest was unfitted.
Held: Rejected the plaint under O.7 r11 (a) CPR must be primarily and
only the result of constructing the plaint as it stands and no other
extraneous matter must be considered.  The plaint must be found
defective such that if fails to disclose a cause of action.  In the instant
case the argument that the action was not maintainable at law was a
preliminary point of law and not a result of a defect in the plaint.
Therefore the preliminary point of law should have been set down for
hearing and the plaintiff's suit should have been dismissed if the court
found that his action not maintainable but his plaint should not have
been rejected.  The trial judge misdirected himself when he rejected the
plaintiff's plaint.
Regulation no 36 of the Public Service Regulations provides that a Public
Servant may be interdicted if proceedings for his dismissal are about to
be taken or if criminal proceedings are being instituted against him.
The gap between either of these proceedings and his interdiction must
be reasonably short.  Therefore the plaintiff had a maintainable cause of
action for a declaration and or damages for having been on interdiction
for more than 2 years.  The trial judge misdirected himself in rejecting
the plaintiff's plaint.
Again Regulation no.36 of the Public Service Regulations provides that a
public servant may be interdicted if proceedings for his dismissal are
about to be taken or Criminal Proceedings are being instituted against
him.  The plaintiff was interdicted upon the commencement of police
inquires against his conduct and not upon the determination of the
authorities to institute actual proceedings for dismissal or prosecution.
Therefore, his interdiction was commenced on an illegal basis.  The
plaintiff has a maintainable action for a declaration and or for damages
upon the unlawful interdiction.  The trial judge misdirected himself in
rejecting the plaintiff's plaint.
The trial judge misdirected himself when he held at the plaintiff's cause
of action was not maintainable at law due to the Presidential prerogative
under Art.104 of the Constitution to dismiss the plaintiff in public because
the plaintiff's action did not seek impeach the Presidential prerogative but
the conduct of the Public Service Commission which had acted outside
the law in interdicting him and advising the president to dismiss him in
Public interest.
Professor Isaac Newton Ojok Vs. Uganda.
Presidential pardon-whether plea in arrest of judgment proved.
Held: While Art.73 of the constitution empowered the president to grant
pardon or amnesty, it is clear from the evidence that the appellant was
one of a select few who was to appear in court charged in the treason.
Therefore, the trial judge directed herself correctly on the evidence and
law when she rejected the appellant's plea in arrest of judgment, that
he had been pardoned while on remand.
When the trial judge was invited to disqualify herself on the basis of the
likelihood of partiality in favour of the state on the grounds that she was a
blood sister of the first Deputy Prime Minister, a pillar of the government,
the appellant was alleged to be fighting, she should have made a record
of the application and her decision to refuse the application should have
been reached judicially and recorded.  It was a misdirection on the part
of the trial judge not to have put on record an application of so serious a
nature.
In order to find whether a judicial officer was biased it is necessary to
consider whether there was a real likelihood of bias by considering
whether the judicial officer laboured under a pecuniary or kindred interest.
After the judicial officer has passed that test, then it may be necessary
to verify whether the particular judicial officer's act or conduct satisfied
reasonable persons that the court was impartial and unbiased.  In the
instant case the allegation of kinship interest because it was not he
own brother in court nor was the National Resistance Movement itself in
court directly.  However, a reasonable man taking into account the
learned trial judge's premature findings of fact before the accused gave
his defence would have conclude led the judge was probably biased in
favour of the state consciously or unconsciously.
Georgia Wavamuno Vs. Parali Bhimji, & anor.
Jurisdiction - whether a constitutional court may entertain matters
that are otherwise provided for under other laws.
Held: Art.22(2) of the constitution of Uganda provides that as long as
there are adequate means of redress for the contravention of ones
constitutional rights, under any other law, then a constitutional court has
no jurisdiction in the matter.  In the instant case the applicant sued the
respondents against reposing hire property without compensation and
yet the Expropriated Properties act provided that such an aggrieved party
may appeal to the High Court against the order to repossession and the
same statute provided for the means of compensation.  Therefore the
constitutional court had no jurisdiction in the matter.
United Assurance Co. Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Right to property Art.13 Constitutional 1967 - reference to constitute-
tional court - whether the alleged compulsory acquisition of
appellant's property was a substantive constitutional issue
requiring reference to interpretation.
Held: Company property belongs to the company and not the shareholders.
Since the suit property belonged to the company, it was not expropriated.
What was expropriated were the shares of the Asians in the company.
Therefore the suit property registered in the names of the company was not
managed under the provisions of the Expropriated Properties Act.  Therefore
the learned trial judge erred when he ruled that the suit was not maintainable.
The suit was properly brought to contest the constitutional propriety of the
compulsory acquisition.
The management of a private company is in the board of directors who under
S.177 of the company's Act can manage the affairs of the company under
regulation 80 of Table A of the Act.  The management includes instructing
counsel to file proceedings in the name of the company.  In the present case
case board of directors of the appellant company consisted of a single
director and it is in this director who instructed counsel and no resolution
was required to evidence the instructions to counsel to file the suit.
The learned trial judge misdirected himself in law and fact when he rule that
the case had no substantial constitutional issues requiring the interpretation
of the Constitutional Court.
Appeal allowed.
H.M.B Kayondo S.C Vs. Attorney General.
Whether crown's prerogative to dismiss at will absolute or qualified.
Held: In an application to strike out pleadings which do not disclose
a cause of action or defence, the court would only look at the
pleadings as filed by the parties to the action and no formal
application is required.
That a preliminary objection could be raised even after the pleadings
were closed, since,  if argued as a preliminary, could dispose of
he suit.
That the Government Standing Orders do not constitute a contract
between the President as appointing authority and public officers and
therefore such public officers  may not sue for breach of contract.
That the plaint failed to disclose a cause of action and that this
incurable and would be struck out.
In re: An Application for a writ of habeas corpus
Ad Subjuciendum by Mpiso Fred.
Detention - applicant alleged to be produced to a court martial
which was under dissolution - refusal by the respondent to produce
applicant before court.
Held: Since the charge sheet showed that the applicant was charged
with dissertation on dates when he was in Military custody smacked of
bad faith and showed that the motive of the charge was bad.
Since the Court Martial before which the applicant was supposed to
appear was under dissolution it would be unconstitutional for the
applicant to continue under detention indefinitely.
Ontario Ltd Vs. Crispus Kiyonga & ors.
Hans Kelsen's pure theory of law - revolutionary movements legal
entities before they assume power.
Held: Revolutionary movements are not legal entities until they assume
power;
The Government was a wrong party to the suit because the movement
was non-existent in law prior to its assumption of power.  A non-existing
entity cannot be a party to a contract and cannot thereby bind
government.
For a contract to be binding, it must be between persons existing at the
time the contract is made.  "The NRM interim Government" did not exist
in law at the time of the alleged contract.  Therefore there was no valid
concluded contract.
The NRM interim Government could not have acted as agent of the
Government because the Government was not capable of entering into
such a contract.  An act which cannot be done by the principal cannot
be done by him through an agent.
The contract was unenforceable for being illegal because it was made
to commit a crime against the established government of the day.
The alleged contract could not be said to have been ratified by
Government because the subsequent government was established by
a proclamation in legal notice No.1 of 1986, which did not act
retrospectively to legalize acts done by the Interim Government of NRM.
The contract was frustrated by impossibility of performance since by
subsequently assuming power the then "Interim Government of NRM"
had now to act legally within the confines of the law; this thereby meant
that the contract could not be performed as envisaged by the parties.
Attorney General Vs. Milton Obote Foundation Ltd.
Interpretation of the Constitution - whether a formal application is
required to move a Constitutional court to hear a reference.
Held: The procedure of the Constitutional Court, the one which deals
with the interpretation of the Constitution is regulated by the
Constitutional case (Procedure) Act in matters relating to the
interpretation of the Constitution, s.2(1)(9), (b)(2)(9), (b) and (3) of the
Act provide the procedure t o be followed which does not involve the
requirement of a formal application to move the Constitutional Court.
Therefore no formal application was required to move the Constitutional
Court to hear the reference made to it.
Edward Fredrick Sempebwa Vs. Attorney General.
Hans Kelsen's pure theory of law-whether legal notice no.1 of 1986
established a new legal order.
Proclamation - whether same as proclamation.
Decree-whether same as proclamation or legal Notice,
Proclamation -whether valid when signed by a chairman of a political
organ and not by a head of state.
Declaratory judgment whether proclamation should be invalidated.
Right to property -whether a judgment decree is properly protected by
the Constitution of Uganda.
Held: it was not settled whether the court that makes the reference of
matters to the Constitutional Court should as well act as the
constitutional court to decide on the substantive matters thereby referred.
There is no laid down procedure as to how the questions framed by the
Court for reference may be brought before the constitutional court.
Neither of the respondents did not contest the method used, i.e., the
notice of motion however.
On or about the 26th day of January 1986 an armed group known as the
National Resistance Army entered Kampala the capital of Uganda and
by force of arms took its control and seized the reigns of power.
Therefore, this amounted in law to a successful revolution through extra-
constitutional means, and that the proclamation (LN 1/86) establishes
a new legal order, in accordance with which the validity of laws in
Uganda has to be determined.
The authorities that made the successful revolution set up conditions for
the basis of the new legal order, and spelt these conditions in Legal
Notice No.1 of 1986 and the saved provisions of the 1967 constitution.
Once this was done, the authorities were precluded from departing from
these conditions and any subsequent legislation by them was to be in
conformity therewith, or otherwise legislative framework.  Therefore the
validity or otherwise of Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 must be viewed within
the perimeters of the legal order already in place.
Since Legal Notice no.6 of 1986 was a proclamation and not a decree
promulgated by the National Resistance Council as required by Legal
Notice No.1 of 1986, and since the proclamation was not signed by the
President of Uganda but by the Chairman of the National Resistance
Council who was also president of Uganda meant that the Legal Notice
was made not in accordance with the rules already laid down.
Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 would be declared invalid because it was not
made in accordance with the Legal Legislation framework put in place
by the revolution.  The court's pronouncement of invalidation would be
necessary to avoid uncertainty in legislation and cause government to
follow the rule of law in exercising legislative powers and others and
moreover the declaration would not prejudice the security of the state
and that the situation would easily be corrected retrospectively by the
state putting in place the right legislation in accordance with the law.
Shah's case set a precedent and defined a judgment debt/decree to be
property protected by the constitution and this precedent would be
followed since the court in the instant caser is of co-ordinate jurisdiction
with the court in Shah's case which was a court of first instance on the
issue of judgment debt being property protected by the first instance
should as a matter of judicial comity follow the decision of another
judge of first instance unless he is convinced that the judgment was
wrong.  The view of the Court is that the decision in Shah's case was
correct and should apply to the instant case.
Since the applicant's judgment debt is property protected by the
constitution, para 12(2) of Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 conflicted with and
infringed upon the constitutional rights of the applicant and consequently
that paragraph cannot be valid unless article 8 (2) (c ) and 13 of the
constitution are repealed or modified by paragraph 13 of Legal Notice
No.6 of 1986.  But paragraph 13 does not expressly repeal the said
articles, let alone its being retrospective.  The cardinal principles of
Statutory Interpretation require that legislation that infringes upon
constitutional rights must expressly state so.
Andrew Lutankome & Paul Kawanga Semogerere Vs. Edward
Rugumayo, Omwony Ojok, Dr.F.E.Sempebwa & 8 ors.
Supremacy of constitution - whether the non-suspension of Art.1
of the Constitution of the republic of Uganda by legal notice No.1 of
1979 meant that the Constitution remained the supreme law of
Uganda.
Ratification -whether the National Consultative council had power to
ratify ministerial appointments made by the President.
Legality of government -whether a declaration therefore should not be
made because it may call for political rather than legal considerations.
Remove of the President-whether the National Consultative council had
power to remove a President.
Proclamation-whether it is a statutory instrument.
Parliamentary privileges-whether members of the National Consultative
Council could not be sued as a constitutional privilege.
Held: There was no dispute as to the efficacy of legal Notice N.o.1 of 79
because it was a proclamation by which the new government came into
power.  However legal Notice No.2 as a proclamation purporting to
amend Legal Notice No.1 in substance was of no legal consequence in
as it sought to legislate a function reserved only for the National
consultative council, which was in session at the time the president
issued the said proclamation.  Since Legal Notice No.1 of 1979 did not
suspend article 1 of the Constitution of Uganda, the constitution
remained the supreme Law of Uganda.  Therefore neither the Legal
Notice affected the supremacy of the constitution to the extent of the
non suspended provisions of the constitution.
The National consultative Council was both a legislature and a political
organ of the Uganda National Liberation Front.  As a legislature it could
only be a creature of statute, I.e. Legal Notice No.1 of 1979, which legal
Notice never at all provided the powers and or duties to the National
Consultative Council to ratify Ministerial appointment made by the
President.  It is true that the constitution of the Uganda National
Liberation Front by virtue of Article 5.4. (a) (iv) thereof provided for the
ratification and approval of appointment made by the executive of the
Front to the various organs of the Front.  But this constitution never
become part of the law of Uganda by whichever means.  And the said
provisions only affected the UNLF as an organization and not the
government of Uganda as by law (Legal Notice No.1 of 1979) established.
In deciding whether or not the National consultative council acted legally
in removing the President of the Republic it must be noted that the issue
calls into question the legitimacy or otherwise of the incumbent
government.  The consequences of issuing such a declaration are very
serious.  Court should be reluctant to inquire into questions of a
political nature bearing in mind the gravity of the consequences that
could result from such a declaration.
Under Art.31, of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda the
President may be removed from Office for mental or physical incapacity
to discharge the functions of his office in the manner indicated in Article
31.  All these provisions are contained in chapter 4 of the constitution
of the Republic of Uganda which was suspended under section 1 of the
proclamation in Legal Notice No.1 of 1979, provided that the President
shall be head of state.  Legal Notice No.1 of 1971 is silence as to how
YK Lule became President and is silent as to how he can be removed.
Under the non suspended provisions of the Constitution and Legal
Notice No.1 of 1979 there is no power given to the NCC to remove the
President.  Therefore the NCC had no power to remove the President.
The application for further and better particular would be disallowed
because the applicant did not say what further and better particulars he
required and moreover the defence pleading raised a straight forward
point of law that the action was not maintainable in law.
S. 40 (2) of the Judicature Act, 1967, clearly conferred upon court
original Jurisdiction to the exclusion of all other courts in all matters
concerning the enforcement and or interpretation of the Constitution.
And O.2 r7 of the Civil Procedure Rules provided that no suit shall be
open to objection on grounds that merely a declaratory judgment or
order is sought and the court could make binding declaration whether
any consequential relief is sought nor not.  Moreover, the member of the
National consultative Council are entitled to know whether the actions of
the body of which they are members in a given situation are legal.
Unless a proclamation falls within the provisions of S.14 of the inter-
predation Decree, it is not law but an announcement of the executive
will of the sovereign and in so far as that will have to be obeyed it has
the force of law.  Such a proclamation is not the same thing as a
statutory instrument.
It was not acceptable that the members of the National Consultative
Council could not be sued collectively on the ground that the acts
complained of against them were not committed by them collectively.
The members of the National Consultative Council had no parliamentary
privilege to protect them form suits because Legal Notice No.1 of 79
by which the NCC was created was silent on the question of privilege
when the motion of no confidence in the President was carried.
Smith Opon Achak & Ahmed Ogeny Vs. Uganda.
Instrument of pardon - whether invariably in writing.
Held: The Resident may grant pardon according to Article 73 (9) of the
Constitution which does not state that the pardon must be in written but
the fact that the exercise of the Presidential prerogative has to be acted
upon by officers of government prison authorities, it means that the
pardon must be a signed instrument.  It was incumbent upon the
appellants to prove on the balance of probabilities whether they had
been pardoned by the General Presidential pardon.  They appellants had
failed to prove this.
Haji Badru Wegulo & 2 ors Vs. Attorney General.
Fundamental freedoms - Art.22 (1) of the Constitution - whether
the provisions of s.1 of the civil procedure & limitation (misc.
provisions) Act, 1969 apply to application made under Art 22(1) of
the Constitution.
Held: The object of the Statutory notice under s.1 of Act 20/60 was to
give an opportunity to government to investigate the claim and if
possible have it settled out of court.  The facts constituting the claim
could have occurred in a single transaction or could be a series of acts
some of which were in the process to occur like in this present
application where the rules to the Bill complained of were only
precursory to the rules in the subsequent statute.  There was no need
for a fresh notice since the Attorney General was already informed of
the complaint against the rules to the Bill which become the rules to
the statute.
Moreover in an action founded on Article 22 of the Constitution there
was no need to serve a notice upon the Attorney General under s.1 of
Act 20/69 because the jurisdiction granted to the High Court under
Article 22 (1) of the Constitution is only subject to Art.22 (5) which
provides for the enactment of Law to provide the practice and procedure
in relation to claims rising under Art 22(1).  If Act 20/69 were to apply to
applications rising under Art 22 (1) like this application it would be
restricting access to the High Court which is not the intention of the
constitution.
Libyan Arab Uganda Bank & anor Vs. Adam Vassiliads.
Right to affair trial under Art 15(9) of the Constitution - whether the
trial judge was biased, misconduct himself and or was
mentally ill such as to deny the appellants affair trial - whether
appellate court had jurisdiction to inquire into the mental
incapacity of the trial judge.
Held: Where counsel intends or wishes to supplement the official record
of proceedings as taken down by the trial judge, with his own notes or
by affidavit counsel must seek the consent of the opposite party before
the appellant court is able to give leave to such counsels application.
The issue of a judge's inability to perform his judicial duties due to
infirmity of body or mind or misbehavior can only be inquired into by a
tribunal appointed under Art.85(5) of the Constitution.  However, if it is
alleged on appeal that the mental infirmity or misconduct of a judge has
denied the aggrieved party a fair trial, the appellate Court has jurisdiction
to determine the matter to ensure that justice is done between the
parties by remedying miscarriage of justice.
Counsel should at the outset have raised the objection that the judge
was biased against the cause of their clients and that he should not
hear their case.  Even if they were overruled on this counsel would be
on record.  But to allege bias midway the proceedings and infact
withdraw there from was not proper.  The allegation of bias was not
proved because the appellants had not shown that the judge has a
pecuniary interest in the matter before him or that he was likely to
favour the respondent against the appellants.  Bias must be objectively
proved by showing that any right thinking reasonable man would have
believed the judge is biased.  In the instant case the appellants have
not shown that the judge had direct pecuniary benefit or at all nor had
they shown that naturally he would favour the respondents.
Excessive intervention in the proceedings by a trial judge may amount
to misconduct justifying the grant of a new trial.  A judge should not
descend into the arena where his vision may be clouded by the dust of
the conflict.  In the present case the judge interrupted counsel during
cross examination and this caused the failure of court from enlisting the
necessary material facts upon which to adjudicate.  The judge struck
too soon and denied the appellants the fair opportunity of presenting
their case.
Vincent Rwamwaro Vs. Uganda.
Right to representation - whether appellant denied his constitutional
right to representation.
Held: The existence or otherwise of a grudge between the appellant and
the prosecution witnesses due to the differences based on political
parties was a matter of fact and not law.  Therefore it was not an issue
such as would be determined by the second appellate court.
An accused person should take all reasonable steps to ensure that his
counsel appears for him and if he is unable to appear to offer a
satisfactory explanation to court for his absence.  In the instant case
though the appellant's counsel was absent, the appellant did not furnish
any explanation as to why his counsel was not in court.  Therefore the
trial Magistrate exercised his discretion judicially when he refused an
adjournment because there was no explanation before him as to why
the appellant's counsel was not in court.
The issue that the learned justice of the first appellate court misdirected
himself when he set aside the order of compensation, was an issue that
affected the legality of the sentence and would therefore be considered
even if no cross appeal was preferred.
S.331(2) (b) and ( c) of the Criminal Procedure Code empower an
appellate court to vary the sentence imposed by the lower court, even
to specify the amount payable as compensation mandatory after a
convocation for robbery where no death sentence is made.  Therefore the
learned justice of the first appeal misdirected himself when he set aside
the order for compensation on the basis that the order was prejudicial
since it dis not specify the amount of compensation.  Therefore, the
appellant would be ordered to pay shs. 30,000/= to the victim of the
robbery.
Further both the learned justice of the first appeal and the learned trial
Magistrate misdirected themselves when they did not impose the
mandatory order as provided in S.26 of the MCA which provides for an
order of police supervision on the person convicted or robbery. The court
would therefore order that the appellant undergoes police supervision for
a period of 2 years from the date of expiration of his sentence.
Esau Namanda Vs. Uganda.
Suspect's right to defend himself Art15(2) (b) and ( c) of the
Constitution whether breached.
Human Rights-the right to be tried by an independent tribunal - whether
breached.
Held: The conviction of the appellant was illegal as it was contrary to his
constitutional right art.15 (2) (b) ( c) to be informed of his offence and to
permit him to prepare his defence.  The conviction would therefore be set
aside.  Secondly, the charge of perjury formed a distinct charge from the
material trial and therefore the convict was entitled to be tried by an
independent tribunal.  This had not been the case.
For the accused to be convicted of perjury the discrepancy in the
appellant's evidence must be material to the case or that it affected the
credibility of the appellant.  In the instant case the trial judge did not
show that the discrepancy in the accused's evidence was material to
the case.
Ronald Kayara Vs. Hassan Ali Ahmed.
Right to property - whether the plaintiff's license could be terminated
without compensation.
Held: The plaintiff was not a beer licensee because the council by
conduct had let the plaintiff to believe that his renewal of his T.O.L was
permanent.  This meant that the plaintiff's license was coupled with a
proprietary interest which was protected by equity and the principle of
estoppel would operate to prevent revocation of a right which one party
has led the other to suppose it was permanent.  Moreover Art. 13 of the
Constitution disallowed expropriation of any ones proprietary interest
without compensation.  Therefore the municipal council acted ultra-vires
when they made a grant of a lease to the defendant on the plaintiff's
premises, he occupied under a T.O.L without due regard to
compensation.
The law requires a higher standard of proof of fraud than in ordinary Civil
cases.  The learned trial judge, had he in the instant case applied the
requisite standard of proof to the facts it cannot be said that the evidence
would be sufficient to prove fraud.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself on the standard of proof of fraud and thereby arrived
at a wrong conclusion of a finding on fraud.
A third party Notice under O.1 r14 issues where the defendant claims to
be entitled to contribution or indemnity from the Third party.  In the
instant case the defendant never claimed anything from the municipal
council but it is only the plaintiff who claimed that the council had acted
ultra vires or arbitrarily.  Therefore it is the plaintiff under O.1 r3 CPR who
should have joined the council as a co-defendant.  Therefore the learned
trial judge misdirected himself to have held that it was the defendant to
apply for court's leave to issue a third party notice.
Prince J.D.C Mpuga Rukidi Vs. Prince Solomon Iguru & ors.
Traditional rulers - nomination of successor - whether validly done
by respondent was an eligible member for nomination, him not
being the son of the lawfully wedded wife.
Held: the learned trial Judge's admission in evidence of the photocopied Will
could not be impeached because there was evidence before court that the
original will was lost.  Secondly, the will was photocopied which is the kind
of mechanical method that insures accuracy of the copy; there was
evidence that tended to prove that the signature on the will was that of the
testator and the contents of the Will had not been seriously challenged by
the adverse party.
S.13(2) (b) Interpretation Decree provides that when any enactment repeals
another, unless a contrary intention appears, the repeal does not affect
anything previously duly done in pursuance of the repealed enactment.
Therefore when the late King named the Will unattested, such a mode of
making Wills was permissible under S.50(2) Succession Act which
provision allowed Africans to make unattested Wills.  Though the exemption
was repealed by Decree 22/72 Succession Act (Amendment) Decree the
repeal did not affect the act already performed by the late King, the act of
nominating the respondent by a Will unattested.
Moreover, even if the document nominating the respondent as heir was to
be found wanting as a Will, the document could be relied upon as evidence
of nomination of the respondent as heir because paragraph 2 schedule 3 of
the 1962 Constitution under which the nomination was done did not provide
any specific mode by which nominations of successors to the throne of
Bunyoro Kitara could be made.
O.13 r 3 gives discretion to court to frame issues from among or all the
allegations made on oath, allegations made in the pleadings and contents
of documents from the parties.  This rule does not mean that when court is
framing the issues it should look at all the allegations.  It is own discretion
to choose from among the allegations or all of them.  This further means
that court may frame the issues at any stage of the proceedings before
judgment.  Therefore, the learned trial Judge in framing only one issued did
not err since he had the discretion to do and in his opinion, it was enough
to decide whether or not the respondent was qualified to be heir to the
throne of Bunyoro Kitara.  And once this was answered in the affirmative
there was no further need to decided on the other allegations.
S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act provides that the court has the discretion in
determining who may be awarded costs though the costs should follow the
the event.  The instant case involved members of the same family, a family
whose importance went beyond its borders.  Therefore, for the sake of
peace and harmony in the family and community of the Kingdom, to assist
in the process of reconciliation, no costs should have been awarded!
The order awarding costs would be set aside.
The granting of a declaration is a discretionary remedy and the court should
not easily grant a declaration that would serve no useful purpose or seriously
prejudice the security of the state or affect the confidence between the
parties. Had the appellant succeeded, the court would have had to consider
whether to grant the declaration or not in view of the possible repercussions.
Appeal, save as to costs, dismissed.
Uganda Journalists Safety Committee & ors Vs. Attorney General
Interpretation of the Constitution, Act 137 of the Constitution-
whether petition for interpretation may not be joined with petition
for enforcement because constitutional court has no jurisdiction,
except by way of appeal, to entertain a petition for redress.
Enforcement Art 50 of the Constitution-whether a petition for
interpretation of the constitution under Art 137(3) may not be
joined with a petition for enforcement under Art 50 of the
constitution.
Held: Art. 137(3) of the Constitution gives jurisdiction to the constitutional
court to entertain a petition that seeks to challenge the constitutionality of a
given law.  The procedure provided for this kind of petition is legal notice
No.4/96 "The Rules of the Constitutional Court (Petitions for Declarations
1996.  Under Art 137(3) the Constitutional Court has original jurisdiction to
make declarations of the constitutionally of laws and acts of the executive.
However, under Art 50 it is the High Court that has original jurisdiction to
entertain petitions that require the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights
and Freedoms.  Therefore the two articles deal with different jurisdictions
and may not be invoked simultaneously in the same petition.  The petition
was therefore irregularly before court.
Rules of Procedure must be adhered to even in constitutional cases, and
only minor irregularities may be ignored where a petition prima facie disclose
a cause of action and the individual's liberty is at stake.  But proceeding
under the wrong provisions of the law was not such a minor irregularity as in
the instant case.
Rule 12(1) of the Rules of the Constitutional Court (Petitions for Declarations
under Art 137 of the Constitution) Directions 1996, provides that all evidence
at the trial in favour of or against the petition shall be by affidavit.  Therefore,
the cause of action must be discernible from the affidavits.  In the instant
case, one of the two affidavits only claimed that the provisions were
restrictive, prohibitive and unconstitutional without showing this by affidavit.
And in the second affidavit it was deponed that journalists were being
harassed, without the affidavit disclosing which journalists were actually
harassed. Therefore the petition failed to disclose a cause of action.
When averments are based on information the source of information should
clearly be disclosed, and if it is on belief, the grounds of belief should be
stated, so that court is enabled to judge whether it would be safe to act on
the deponent's affidavit.  In the instant case both supporting affidavits failed
to satisfy the non disclosure rule and were thus defective and could not be
relied upon.  The petition cannot stand as the supporting affidavits had fallen
by the way side.
Petition struck out with costs.
Tororo District administration Vs. Andalalapo Industries.
Art 126(2)(e)-procedural technicalities-whether unconstitutional.
Held: O.18 r 11 (2) require that for an applicant who seeks a court's order to
the effect that he being a judgment debtor, the satisfaction of the decree be
deferred or be satisfied in installments, must bring that application with the
consent of the judgment creditor.  In the instant case since the applicant
did not have the consent of the judgment creditor.  In the instant case
since the applicant did not have the consent of the judgment creditor the
application was misconceived and must fail.
Court's inherent powers under s.101 CPA are not inviolable where there is a
particular legislation dealing with the matter.  In the instant case the
legislation applicable was O.18 r 11(2) CPR.
Art. 126(2)(e) of the Constitution require that substantive justice must be
administered without undue regard to technicalities.  However, the Article
does not do away with rules of procedure which must be adhered to.
Application struck out with costs.
