Kataryeba Zachary & 3 ors Vs. Uganda.
Representation by counsel-refusal of court to adjourn to enable
accused instruct another charge-whether material irregularity.
Held: S.12 Penal Code Act deals with insanity and not intermeddling.
Therefore, the accused were charged with non existent section.  This was a
material irregularity.
Moreover, after the court had allowed the charge sheet to be amended to
read S.12 (1), (2) of the Administrator General's Act, the accused were
never invited to plead afresh to the new amended charge.  This was irregular.
The refusal by court to adjourn the case to enable the accused engage
another counsel was a denial of the accused constitutional right to be
represented.
A collective defence was unconstitutional as per Art 28 of the Constitution.
The evidence showed that the accused retained the property of the
deceased and dealt with it for the purpose of preserving the same, since the
since the accused worked with the deceased before his demise.  Therefore,
the offence of intermeddling was not proved by the prosecution as required
by law.
A retrial would not be ordered since the prosecution had failed to prove their
case beyond reasonable doubt and a retrial would only aid the prosecution to
fill in the gaps to the prejudice of the appellants.
Appeal allowed.
Uganda Journalists Safety Committee & anor Vs. A. G
Interpretation of the Constitution Art.137 Constitution of Uganda-
enforcement of fundamental human rights Art 50 Constitution
of Uganda-whether constitutional court may entertain both
proceedings simultaneously.
Sedition Ss.37,41,42 & 50 Penal Code-whether inconsistent with
Art 29(1) (a) & (b) of the Constitution.
Petition-time-whether petition brought out of time-Rule 4 Legal
Notice No.4.
Held: The Constitutional Court was created by Art.137 of the Constitution
for the sole purpose of interpreting the constitution but not for redress under
Art 50 of the Constitution.  Therefore the petition was wrongly before court
as it had been brought under Art.50 of the Constitution.
The petition even if it could be said to be properly before court, which it was
not, it was brought our of time as rule 4 of the Fundamental Rights &
Freedoms (Enforcement Procedure) Rules requires the petition to be filed
within 30 days from the date of the act sought to be redressed.  In this case
the petition was filed 5 months later.
The 1st petitioner's failure to accompany its petition with an affidavit was
contrary to rule 3(b) of the Fundamental Rights & Freedoms (Enforcement
Procedure) Rules which requires every such petition to be accompanied by
an affidavit.
Petition struck of with costs.
Rukundo Sarapio Vs. Attorney General
Limitation rA(1) Modifications to the Fundamental Rights and
Freedoms (Enforcement Procedure) Rules - whether there is no law
of limitation to constitutional matters.
Locus standi in a petition to challenge the constitutionality of a
judgment-whether locus standi open to a person not a party to the
case.
Held: R.4(1) of the Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Enforcement
Procedures) Rules, 1996, provides that a petition shall be lodged within 30
days after the breach of the constitution complained of.  This petition
offended against the said rule because it was presented more than 30 days
from the date of judgment complained of.
Art 119 of the Constitution sets out the functions of the Attorney General
and particularly Clause 4(c) provides that the Attorney General represents
Government in Courts or any other legal proceedings where government is
a party.  The Attorney General could not be a party to a petition against a
judgment to which Government was not a party.
Moreover; the petition sought to challenge the exercise of the judicial
functions of courts.  S.4(5) Government Proceedings Act bars any action
against Government in respect of an act or omission done by a person in
discharge of a judicial function. The petition was untenable.
However, Art 137(3) of the Constitution, notwithstanding the rule of locus
standi, allows any person who alleges that any law or act is inconsistent
with the constitution to file a petition for a declaration to that effect.
Therefore the petitioner had a cause of action in that sense but no more.
Petition struck out with costs.
Andekur Maliam & anor Vs. Attorney General & anor
Judicial power-liability for omission or commission in exercise of
judicial power - whether Attorney General liable, Arts 128(4) and
250 Constitution of Uganda.
Held: Art 128(4) Constitution of Uganda provides that a person Exercising
judicial power cannot be liable for any act or omission arising there from.
Therefore it was preposterous for the petitioners to argue that the trial
magistrate who presided over the prosecution acted unconstitutionally.
Secondly, the prosecution was a private one.
Moreover the arrest and detention were effected by local administration
personnel.  S.4(2)(9) establishes a local government as a body corporate
capable of suing and being sued.  Therefore, the Attorney General was not
liable.
Preliminary objection upheld.  No cause of action established. Counsel to
bear costs personally.
Rwanyarare James & anor Vs. Attorney General
Enforcement of rights and freedoms by courts Art 50 Constitution-
procedure-whether invariably by reference - whether constitutional
court has no jurisdiction therein except by way of reference.
Rules of Procedure-whether do not apply to constitutional matters.
Limitation, r4(1) Modification to the Rights & Freedoms (Enforce-
ment Procedure) Rules-whether petitions to the Constitutional
Court for interpretation of the constitution must be lodged within 30
days from the date of the occurrence of the act complained of.
Election Petitions-Constitutional Court-whether has no jurisdiction
to entertain election petitions.
Held: Rules of Procedure are landmarks of justice, including justice sought
from the constitutional court.  Therefore, though rule 4(1) of the Modifications
to the Rights & Freedoms (Enforcement Procedure) Rules, were rules of
procedure, they applied to constitutional petitions with the effect in the
present case the petition was time barred in as far it sought the declaration
of the unconstitutionality of certain provisions of the constitution because
the petition should have been filed 30 days from the promulgation of the
constitution; and the elections of the president and parliament should have
been challenged within 30 days.
Secondly, the constitutional court has no original jurisdiction to entertain
petitions that challenge the elections of the president and parliament, as
such jurisdiction is vested in the Supreme Court and the High Court
respectively.
The Constitutional Court has no original jurisdiction to entertain petitions
under Art.50 of the constitution for the enforcement of rights and freedoms
under the constitution, except by way of reference to it from another court.
Under O.1 r8 (1) Civil Procedure Rules a litigant may file a representative
action with leave of court.  Therefore, the petition in so far as if sought to be
representative of persons other than the litigants, was wrongly before court.
Petition dismissed with costs.
Uganda Co-Operative Transport Union Ltd Vs. Roko
Construction Ltd.
Art 28(1) fair and public hearing-whether failure to allow a party an
opportunity to cross-examine breached the constitution.
Held: Art 28(1) Constitution of Uganda provides that a person has a right to
a fair and public hearing before an impartial tribunal and the failure by the
trial judge to afford an opportunity to the appellant to cross-examine and
challenge the evidence of accounts presented by the respondent meant that
the trial was neither fair nor public.
Secondly, s.136(1) Evidence Act mandatorily provides for the opportunity to
a party to challenge evidence adversely given by the other party at the trial.
Appeal allowed.  Judgment set aside. Retrial ordered.
Lawrence Kasaka Kasekese & Ors Vs. Uganda.
Substantive justice - Art. 126(e) Constitution - trial de novo S.142
MCA-whether application of S.142 MCA was not a technicality.
Held: As per Eustace Vs. Republic [1970] E.A. 393 the interpretation of
S.142 (1) of the Magistrate Courts Act is such that an accused can only be
tried by the first and second Magistrates in succession but not the third.
The third Magistrate has no jurisdiction to try the accused except by way of
a de novo trial.  Therefore in the case instant the accused could not be tried
let alone be convicted by the Chief Magistrate who was the forth in
succession to try the accused basing on the evidence already recorded by
other previous successive Magistrates.
Appeal allowed.  A fresh trial de novo ordered.
Sebugwawo Julius Vs. Electoral Commission & anor.
Art. 126 (2) (e) - Legal technicalities-whether though the application
was brought under a wrong Law, may be entertained.
Held: Articles 139(3) (b) & 140 ( c) (d) do not exist in the Constitution of
Uganda though the petitioner had purported to have filed this petition under
their previsions.  This means that the petition was brought under a non-
existing Law and since no amendment was applied for to correct what
counsel for the petitioner called a typing error, the petition was untenable
and would be struck off because it was not properly before court.
In the instant case what was infringed was not only procedural but also
substantive Law therefore Art 126(2) (e) constitution would not properly be
called in aid to save the petition.
Defaulters of procedure and substantive Law should not be allowed to run to
S.101 CPA asking court to invoke its inherent power where the matter or
proceeding has been improperly brought to court.
Preliminary objection upheld petition struck out with costs.
CONTRACT
H.M.B Kayondo S.C Vs. Attorney General.
Whether state breached contract.
Held: In an application to strike out pleadings which do not disclose
a cause of action or defence, the court would only look at the
pleadings as filed by the parties to the action and no formal
application is required.
That a preliminary objection could be raised even after the pleadings
were closed, since,  if argued as a preliminary, could dispose of
he suit.
That the Government Standing Orders do not constitute a contract
between the President as appointing authority and public officers and
therefore such public officers  may not sue for breach of contract.
That the plaint failed to disclose a cause of action and that this
incurable and would be struck out.
Bamweyana Lulent Vs. Segujja Hamisi.
Breach of contract - whether contract based on memorandum of
agreement duly signed by both parties - whether contract voluntary
whether defendant liable therein.
Held: The defendant was party to the agreement since he
acknowledge that the signature thereon was his.
The defendant has failed to persuade court to the view that he was
coerced into signing the agreement because the agreement was
signed in December 1987 and did not report to the authorities that
he was coerced into signing an agreement nor did he mention this
fact in his affidavit while applying for leave to appear and defend.
The signing of a contractual document implied consent, therefore
the defendant was bound by it since he had failed to prove that his
signing was under a misapprehension as to the essential nature of
the document.
Obonyo Vs. Chilington Tool Co. Ltd.
Plaintiff suspected to be in breach of stealing stores and dismissed-
whether breach of contract of employment - whether wrongful
dismissed.
Held: Where an employee is guilty of sufficient misconduct in his
capacity as employee he may be dismissed summarily without
notice and before the expiry of the fixed period employment.
A dismissed servant is entitled recover any arrears which had been
accrued due by the time of dismissal even though they were in
respect of a period after he had been guilty of misconduct.
Tushabagha Enterprises Vs. Nyanza Textile Ltd.
Breach of sale of goods contract budget proposal subsequent to a
concluded contract increasing costs of production - whether
contract frustrated -proforma invoice with wards "price were
subject of the contract was not specified.
Held: When the defendant made out the Proforma Invoice they thereby
made an offer to sell the goods to the plaintiff at the prices stated in
the invoice at the time and in so doing there was an effective intention
to contract to sell on the terms indicated at the time.  The evidence
indicated that the price on the receipt was the price prepared for the
cloth and it was not a mere deposit.  This therefore was a complete
and binding agreement not dependent on any future alteration on any
future alteration in prices.
A mere difficulty of performance or an increase in prices of expense or
unprofitable ness is not enough to relieve one party from carrying out
the contract.  Therefore the Budgetary Proposals even if they operated
to make the venture unprofitable for the defendants the plea of
frustration would not be upheld.
Specific performance is an equitable remedy in the discretion of the
court granted where damages are not likely to compensate the
plaintiff adequately for the contract.  Where court can determine like
in this case the amount of profit lost by the plaintiff, such damages
would be awarded since they would adequately cater for the situation.
Washaki Serapio Vs. Kasolo Louis.
Breach - whether defendant's refused to refund the plaintiff's part
payment for a house which plaintiff subsequently failed to buy
but the defendant sold it to someone.
Held: Where there is no forfeiture, as it was in the instant case, if
money is paid in part of the purchase price and then the buyer makes
default as to the balance, then so long as the seller keeps the contract
open and available for performance, the buyer cannot recover the
the money, but once the seller rescinds the contract or treats it as at
an end owing to the buyer's default, then the buyer is entitled to recover
his money by action at Law, subject to a counter - claim by the
seller for damages, who in the instant had not counter-claimed.
The plaintiff was clearly in breach but since the defendant sold the
house, the plaintiff can recover his initial payment.  The defendant
could not be enriched twice.
Sam Engola Vs. Christine Nabitalo.
Oral contract of hire - breach of contract - whether war of force
majeure frustrated the contract.
Held: There was evidence that the defendant hired the plaintiff's car
at the rate agreed and that in pursuance of the said agreement the
defendant took possession of the car and paid the installments as
pleaded by the plaintiffs.
The suit car was seized from the defendant by armed robbers and such
seizure amounted to the destruction of the foundation of the contract
and thus its performance was frustrated and could not be effected any
more.
The seizure was not as a result of the negligence of the defendant and
she could therefore be absolved from liability as a bailee.
Suit against the defendant dismissed each party meet his/her costs.
Edmund Khakale Vs. Owor Opio Peter.
Assessment of damages - breach of contract and conversion.
Held: Value of 32 drums at shs.16,000/= @ (now currency)
Hiring charges for the lorry 7,000/= (new currency)
Deposited paid shs.17,300/= (new currency)
Loss of profit shs.40,000/=
Nakintu Annet Vs. Haji Bagye.
Assessment of damages - breach of contract.
Held: Since the plaintiff has to be put back to the position she was in
at time of the breach of contract there will be judgment for the
plaintiff for the delivery of 19 bags of sugar or their value at the time of
the contract.
General Damages for loss of profit at shs. 300,000/= Matovu for the
plaintiff.
Karim Hirji Vs. m/s Pan African.
Offer to purchase property and an acceptance contingent upon a
board subsisted a binding contract before such resolution had not
yet been obtained.
Held: After backing the offer with the letter of guarantee, the condition
annexed by the defendant it was necessary that the offer be
communicated to the defendant within the time fixed by the plaintiff, to
accept it.  Therefore, since this time had elapsed there was no
complete contract between the parties, but only a bargain of a highly
conditional nature.
A banker's (letter of) guarantee is where the Banker gives financial
backing of a payment on first demand.  The plaintiff's banker testified
truthfully that he had to block up funds on the plaintiff's account for
this purpose. Therefore, the plaintiff did indeed open letters of
guarantee.
Evidence by an affidavit to prove an important point in a case, where the
other party has not been given a chance to reply should not admitted
in court.
Sam Engola Vs. Christine Nabitalo.
Subject matter looted - whether contract frustrated.
Held: The looting caused frustration of the contract and discharged the
parties of obligations thereunder since the event.
the coup was unexpected by the defendant, and the dangerous
circumstances of the loss of the car absolved her of responsibility for
the loss.  This was a complete defence to an action for detinue and
conversion.
A bailee is to act as agent of necessity to prevent loss of the subject
matter if he cannot cause the owner to intervene.
Failure to report to police in the circumstances, given that she had
been threatened, was not negligence on her part and did not cause her
liability therefore.
John Nagenda Vs. Sabena Belgian World Airline.
Breach of contract - plaintiff not issued with a rebate ticket he paid
for payment subsequently refunded- whether this was breach of
contract.
Held: There was clearly a breach of contract on the part of the defendant.
Damages is compensation in money for the loss of that which he would
have received had the contract been performed.  There is no
compensation for disappointment of mind or vexation caused by the
hurtful and humiliating manner in which the defendant broke the contract
and no exemplary damages are awardable.
Special damages must be strictly proved.  Lack of receipts and
inconsistency between the testimony and pleadings left the claims
unproved.
Cecelia T.S.Sule Vs. Administrator General & ors
Breach of contract -whether breach of contract proved where
evidence shows no conducted contract.
Held: Since there was no contract, there was no breach and therefore
no cause of action accrued to the plaintiffs late husband or his
successors or anybody claiming to derive title from him.
Even if the court found that there was a sale of the suit property on the
fact of the pleadings, no breach had yet occurred as the terms of the
contract were not pleaded and no cause of action had yet accrued to
the plaintiff.
Eriya Miling Project Ltd Vs. Wade Adams Construction Ltd.
Breach of contract - plaintiff entering into contract - with an official
of a company who did not have authority to bind the company -
whether there was a valid contract.
Held: The signature on the invoice that constituted the alleged contract
had not been proved and the alleged signatory had not been called to
testify.  Therefore, this is not the contract that falls under S.90 the
Evidence act which precludes oral contracts from contradicting
documentary contracts.
The alleged agent of the defendant company could not have either
actual or ostensible authority of the company to bind if because the
defendant had never introduced the alleged agent to the plaintiff as
holding the said position.  Therefore, the question of estoppel did not arise.
Ontario Ltd Vs. Crispus Kiyonga & others
Validity - whether a rebel movement can enter into a valid contract
that may subsequently bind government.
Held: Revolutionary movements are not legal entities until they assume
power;
The Government was a wrong party to the suit because the movement
was non-existent in law prior to its assumption of power.  A non-existing
entity cannot be a party to a contract and cannot thereby bind
government.
For a contract to be binding, it must be between persons existing at the
time the contract is made.  "The NRM interim Government" did not exist
in law at the time of the alleged contract.  Therefore there was no valid
concluded contract.
The NRM interim Government could not have acted as agent of the
Government because the Government was not capable of entering into
such a contract.  An act which cannot be done by the principal cannot
be done by him through an agent.
The contract was unenforceable for being illegal because it was made
to commit a crime against the established government of the day.
The alleged contract could not be said to have been ratified by
Government because the subsequent government was established by
a proclamation in legal notice No.1 of 1986, which did not act
retrospectively to legalize acts done by the Interim Government of NRM.
The contract was frustrated by impossibility of performance since by
subsequently assuming power the then "Interim Government of NRM"
had now to act legally within the confines of the law; this thereby meant
that the contract could not be performed as envisaged by the parties.
HIMACO Ltd Vs. Crispus Kiyonga & others.
Conditional contract - plaintiff paying money against a proforma
invoice for the purchase of a motor vehicle-whether conditional
contract.
Held: For a condition precedent to exist both parties to the contract
must understand it and agree to it at the time of concluding the contract
Since the plaintiff stated in court that he would not have parted with his
money if he had been informed of the requirement of foreign exchange for
the importation of the motor vehicle, it cannot be said that there was a
condition precedent to the contract.
The profoma invoice and receipt were the only documents incorporating
the contract since the invoice stated that the plaintiff was paying for a
fully registered motor vehicle.  Therefore the parole evidence to state that
the contract was precedent upon availability of foreign exchange was
inadmissible.
For the defendant to sit back without initiating the process of obtaining
foreign exchange early enough, the plea of frustration for inability to
acquire foreign exchange would not avail him.
Base Electronic centre Vs. Energo Project.
Quantum maruite - contract for services where the price is not
agreed upon before formation thereof.
Held: Where a contract exists without the price for it being agreed upon
prior to the performance thereof, the price to be charged should be
calculated on the quantum maruit basis.  In the instant case, since the
plaintiff had not proved that the charge for installing a satellite was 30%
of the CIF price of the Satellite itself and had not proved that he knew
the CIF price of the Satellite Disc, it was reasonable to say that what
the defendant had paid him was enough.
S.B.Kibirige Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Wrongful dismissal - plaintiff manager of defendant company
dismissed before being given opportunity to defend himself before
the commendation and disciplinary committee-whether dismissal wrongful.
Held: An employer under common law has an inalienable right to d
dispense with the services of an employee.  He cannot be forced to
employ anybody.
It is a fundamental requirement of the rules of natural justice that a
person properly employed would be entitled to a hearing before
dismissal on charges, like in this case, involving misconduct. An
employee on permanent terms was also entitled to know the charges
against him and to be given opportunity to give any grounds on which
he relied to exculpate himself.
In the instant case, the plaintiff's negligence of this duty resulted in a
big loss of over shs.7 million.  Dismissal without notice in the
circumstances was justifies.  Moreover in his own testimony, the
plaintiff admitted that fraud and negligence justified summary dismissal.
The defendant dismissed the plaintiff for good cause.
Superior Construction and Engineering Ltd Vs. Notay
Engineering Industries (1981) Ltd.
Sub-contract - where a party enters into a contract with another
to do some work that party is expected to be paid for the work he
has done for that party.
Held: A party who freely enters into a contract with another is expected
to pay as a result of the contract.  In the instant case the plaintiff had
done the work for which he contracted with defendant.  He was therefore
entitled to the amount claimed or its equivalent value.
An award if interest is a matter of discretion of the court.  When the
defendant has been guilty of gross delay; as in the instant case where
the defendant withheld money to his full knowledge would be put by
the plaintiff to some other investment, the plaintiff's entitled to interest
which should neglect the current commercial value of money.
Like interest, costs are also a matter of discretion of the court.  It is
generally awarded to a successful party unless there is a special
reason to despite him of his costs.
Produce Marketing Board Vs. Uganda Railways Corporation.
Bailment - whether the defendant's failure to deliver the plaintiff's
goods to the agreed destination was in breach of contract of
bailment.
Held: There was evidence from both sides that the suit goods were
never delivered to their destination and this was in breach of the
common law duties, which begin with the carrier accepting the goods
for carriage and end when there has been delivery whether actual or
constructive.
The Conduct of the 1st defendant's employee in labeling the wagon
containing the plaintiff's goods to 7th Street railway siding instead of
the contracted 5th Street, and delivering the same to a third party,
constituted willful misconduct and therefore made the 1st defendant
liable for the loss thereby occasioned.
The first defendant would not hide under the exemption clause contained
in the Tariff Book No.5 which upon proof of their willful misconduct,
because it was guilty of fundamental breach of contract.
General damages awardable would be those arising from loss actually
resulting as was at the time of the contract reasonably foreseeable as
liable to result from that breach.  In instant case sh. 2 million would be
awarded for breach of contract.
J.W.R.Kazzora & M.L.S Rukuba.
Mistake - whether sale of property by an Administrator who said
he did not know of another prior sale of the same property was a
mistake that vitiated the second sale.
Held: A caveat that merely stated that the caveator had an interest in
the material property did not necessary preclude a sale subsequent
since the caveat itself was not evidence of sale.
The registration of the transfer on various dates was not evidence of fraud
because it was only the transfer registered subsequent to the expiry
of the notice to the caveator that was valid and moreover since fraud
had not been pleaded in the trial court it could not be ground of appeal
in the Supreme Court.
The respondent was a bona fide purchaser for value notwithstanding
that he was aware of the existence of the plaintiff's/appellant's caveat
because the alleged sale to the appellant which the caveat was
registered to protect was not shown to exist.  There was no evidence
about the sale to support the caveat.
A document dully addressed to the sender is presumed received at the
time which the document would be delivered in the ordinary course of
the post.  In the instant case, the trial judge found that the appellant
was served with the notice under consideration on 12/10/87 and that
therefore the notice expired on 12/12/87, but because the plaintiff
claimed that he took delivery of the said notice on 16/12/87, even then
the said notice should have expired on 16/2/88.  The appellant then had
until 14/1/88 within which to obtain an order from the court extending
the caveat but did not do so.
By the 15th May 1989, the appellant's application to extend his caveat
had already been disposed of and moreover the existence of the
application in court to extend the caveat did not preclude the effecting
of a transfer because there does not exist in Uganda any pendency
legal rule to the effect that transfers or other dealings in land should not
be registered before a suit contesting such a transfer or dealing cannot
lodge the same caveat as already removed.
The second caveat was in exactly the same terms as the first but the
appellant submitted that the second caveat was different from the first
one in that it was lodged on the basis of the suit he had filed, as a
chose in action, to be protected.  However, even the first caveat sought
exactly the same thing to protect a chose in action namely, the
benefit of the verbal agreement for sale of land.  This was tantamount to
renewing the same caveat which is contrary to the provisions of S.149(3)
of the RTA which states that as caveator cannot lodge the same caveat
as already removed.
Had there been evidence of sale, prior to that one between the
respondent and the administrator, then the subsequent transaction
would have been vitiated by mistake.  But no evidence was adduced to
support it.
It is established that a party relying on fraud must specifically plead it
and that particulars of the alleged fraud must be stated on the face of
the pleading.  In the instant case frauds was not specifically pleaded,
nor was fraudulent intent pleaded or the facts set out in the plaint such
as to create fraud.  Therefore the appellant was not entitled to rely on
fraud because it was different from the original case.
The Standard of proof of fraud is that it must be strictly proved although
not beyond reasonable doubt but something more than a mere balance
of probability is required.
Non-compliance with O.18 r7 which requires that a partly extracting an
order should submit it to the other party for approval, was not fatal
because it was not the order extracted that was the removal of the
appellant's caveat but the caveat had merely lapsed.
The Principle of law is that the first person to register land takes better
title than a person to whom the land was first sold but failed to register
it provided that there was no fraud in the registration.  And in the instant
case there was no fraud proved against the respondent.
Frank Rwakijanju Vs. Prince Patrick Kaboyo.
Specific performance - sale of land by oral contract - specific
performance available only if there has been an possession of the land.
Held: The remedy of specific performance is available only when there
has been an act of performance by taking possession of the land.
Inspection of the land and introduction did not amount to taking
possession.
Hardship to thirty parties not prior to the contract, in this case squatters,
was not a bar to the remedy of specific performance.
Acknowledgement of payment in writing did not constitute a written
contract, but was merely an acknowledgement.
Special damages must be specifically pleaded and proved.
General damages is available for breach of an oral contract thought
there has been no act of performance by taking possession.
Sheikh Mohammed Lubowa Vs. Kitara Enterprises Ltd.
Sale of land - want of consideration sale agreement ineffective.
Held: Trespass to land is constituted where entry onto the land by the
defendant was without the consent of the owner.  Where there is a valid
sale agreement, there is no trespass.
\Where the initial entry is unlawful in that there was no consent, a
subsequent sale agreement legalizes it.
There was no valid sale agreement for want of consideration.
Katalemwa Traders Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Offer - whether the news paper advertisement amounted to an offer.
Acceptance - whether there was a definite offer to accept for the
formation of a valid contract.
Held: An advertisement calling for tenders is not an offer but an
invitation to treated or offer.
Where parties agree that they shall subsequent to their negotiations
reduce their agreement into a formal document, their antecedent
negotiation may nevertheless amount to a valid and binding contract
notwithstanding that no such formal document has been drawn up after
all, if, such negotiations in themselves, whether oral or in writing can
clearly indicate the existence of a definite acceptance of all terms of an
offer and the acceptance is unqualified.  Since the appellant did not
produce in evidence a copy of the advertisement, a copy of the letter of
offer, and there was no evidence of what kind of electrical equipment,
the purpose, quantities, and the price, the subsequent offer thereby
vague, indefinite, and incapable of identification, and there was therefore
no binding agreement.
Ground 3+5 were unsustainable for offending against Rule 84 (1) of the
Rules of Supreme Court for being too general.  The rules require the
memorandum of appeal to particularize matters complained of and an
appellant argue a general ground of appeal.
The alternative argument by the appellant for a separate contract outside
the tender agreement amounted to the alteration of the appellant's
unsustainable.  This was not an instance for court to be argued before it.
Somali Democratic Republic Vs. Snoop Sunderial Treon.
Duress - whether proved where it is by a third party not privy to the contract.
Held: The part played by the Attorney General on behalf of the
appellant in the negotiations which would otherwise have been private
between the purchaser and vendor and the fact that the appellant and
the President of Uganda had reached an agreement that the appellant
would have full use of the property in question, without first seeking the
view of the duress by a third party.
Kabaseke Stores Company Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Invitation on the treat-negotiation prior to tender of local purchase
order (LPO) -whether offer.
Held: The negotiations did not conclude a contract.
The LPO was the offer which was accepted and the contract was
performed the very day by delivery of the beans.
The LPO and delivery note constituted a written contract.
An unpaid seller is entitled under s.40(9) of the sale of Goods Act to
recover the price.
O.6, r5 CPR renders issues of fact not arising out of the pleadings
inadmissible.
The Omnibus traverse did not include the defence of part payment.
In a contractual breach, a party is entitled to only foreseeable loss.
Expected profit is recoverable as foreseeable loss.
J.K.Patel Vs. Spear Motors Ltd.
Construction work in phase - amount and time of payment not
agreed upon-whether there was a contract.
Held:  There was an enforceable contract.
The onus was on the defendant to prove payment.  It is difficult to prove
a negative.
There was implicit admission of the defence of part-payment.
For equivalents of foreign currency, the operative rate is the Bank of
Uganda exchange rate.
A successful party should be awarded costs, if not the reasons must
be stated and the discretion exercised judicially.
Wilson Nuwemugizi Vs. National Water & Sewerage
Corporation.
Employment contract - whether breached when 3 months salary
in view of notice has been paid to the plaintiff among other retire-
ment emoluments.
Held: The plaintiff had permanently left the service of the defendant
because the defendants' Board of Directors advised him to retire and he
verbally accepted without any verbal or written protest.  Therefore the
plaintiff had voluntary retired and the defendant was thereby not in
breach of the service contract.
Okumu & sons Vs. Attorney General.
Hire contract - whether established when not reduced in writing.
Held: Where there is an offer by one party and acceptance of the offer by
the other then there is a contract.  In the instant case though informal,
there was an offer by the plaintiff to let the vehicle for here at an agreed
rate, and an acceptance by the Army to hire it at that rate.  There was
a valid contract of hire.
The plaintiff had the onus to prove that the frustration of the contract was
self induced.  The plaintiff had to prove that the suit lorry had broken
down due to non-servicing by the defendant and that it was the defendant
who had cannibalized the lorry to render it a Scrap.  But the plaintiff when
he failed or refused to call the witness who had authorized the letters to
the effect that the defendant had admitted liability in this respect,
rendered his evidence hearsay and valueless in as far as proving that the
defendant was liable for the disrepair of the lorry.  Therefore, the plaintiff
had not proved that the frustration of the contract of hire was self induced.
Esso Standard Ltd Vs. Semu Amanu Opio.
Employment contract - whether breached.
Damages-exemplary damages for breach of contract-whether awardable.
Held: The learned trial judge was entitled to reach the decision the
appellant company was in breach of its contract with the respondent for
failure to give the respondent the agreed notice before the termination
of contract.
The learned trial judge erred in law when he awarded exemplary damages
for breach of contract because firstly, this had not been pleaded by the
respondent/plaintiff, secondly, an award for exemplary damages may not
be awarded for breach of a contract unless it involves the commission of
a tort of trespass and since no tort of trespass had been proved as
committed by the appellant, in this case the award for exemplary
damages was improper and would be set aside.
The tort of detinue is a continuing tort and damages therefore are
assessed as at the date of judgment as equivalent to the value of the
chattel in issue as at the date of judgment.  Therefore, the damages to
be awarded to the respondent of his detained chattels would be the value
of the chattels as at the date of judgment.
The glaring mistake in the Currency Reform Statute would be corrected
by court by mere application of logic since the only conversion rate
application of logic since the only conversion rate applicable to s.1 (a) is
that in S.(b)) and the courts have since taken that view.
Since detinue was a continuing tort, damages awardable therefore were
to be assessed as at the date of judgment and therefore the Currency
Reform Statute did not apply to the prayer of damages for detinue.
Since it was the learned judge's mistake to ward exemplary damages,
no party should pay costs of setting the award aside.
The learned trial judge erred when he failed to allow counsel to address
court after each had closed their case.
Appeal allowed in part.
J.K.Patel Vs. Spear Motors Ltd.
Offer and acceptance - whether there was a valid enforceable
contract.
Held: The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he held that there
was no definite valid and enforceable contract merely by looking at the
documents tendered and the parties oral testimony.  The parties conduct
definitely showed that an offer on definite terms had been made by one
party and accepted by the other.  There was a valid enforceable contract.
The plaintiff had testified that he had been contracted by the defendant
company to build an assembly plant.  There plaintiff showed that he had
been part paid for this work.  The burden of proof thereby shifted to the
defendant to disprove this allegation.  But the defendant in his testimony
claimed that it had part paid more than the plaintiff had shown.  But
since the defendant's part payment had not been pleaded in his written
statement of defence, its evidence of part payment would be inadmissible.
Therefore the defendant had not discharged its burden of proof and would
have judgment against it.
The parties evidence at the trial amply showed that the defendant's
general manager was a key witness in this case.  But since the
defendant refused to call him as a witness, an adverse inference would
be drawn against the defendant.
The defendant's evidence of a set off, when he claimed that the plaintiff's
four years occupation of the defendant's home was upon an
understanding that the rent would act as a set off and the plaintiff's wife's
air ticket given by the defendant, such evidence was admissible even if
the defendant had not pleaded it in its WSD because the plaintiff at the
trial never objected to it nor did the plaintiff cross examine the
defendant's witness on it.
Rent would be assessed at the market rate for the purpose of the set off.
Court had the discretion to award interest and in this case court would
award interest at the official Bank of Uganda rates.
The trial judge misdirected himself when he failed to award costs to the
successful party.  Though the judge has a discretion not to award costs
to the successful party or at all his discretion must be exercised
judiciously and the reasons given in his judgment for his refusal to award
costs to the successful party.
Charles Lwanga Vs. Xaverio Ddaulira.
Time - whether time was essence.
Held: The respondent could not be said to be a bona fide purchaser when
he knew that the appellant was in possession of the suit house and did
not inquire from him as to the position.  Possession was notice to the
respondent upon which he should have made the necessary inquiries.
Therefore the appellant took priority.
when time is not of the essence to the contract it is necessary to
stipulate clearly when time will become of essence to the contract.  In
the Landlord's stipulation as to the period of the last installment was
necessary to bring the period of payment to an end, when time became
of essence.
Henry Munyanganizi Vs. General Machinery Ltd.
Special damages for breach of contract - whether calculated as at
the value of the money at the date of breach.
Held: Where a case is admitted to review by one judge and is afterwards
tried by another the new judge must confine himself to the points
directed by the other for review.  A Judge granting a review on one point
has no power to go into or decide a matter already finally adjudicated
upon.
Parties should not have been allowed to amend pleadings after the order
for review had been made because at the time of the review the
proceedings had been closed and therefore to allow amendment at that
stage would be an abuse of court process since there should be an end
to litigation.
A company is a legal entity irrespective of the motives of its promoters,
once it is formed under the provisions of the law the rules governing it
must be followed.  The company property is clearly distinguishable from
the member's property and therefore the plaintiff could not be said to be
the owner of the tractor bought by the company in which he was a
shareholder.
S.29 of the Sale of Goods Act provides that unless otherwise agreed
delivery of the goods and payment of the price are concurrent conditions.
The plaintiff having paid for a tractor which the defendants had defaulted
in delivery, the plaintiff, buyer is entitled to damages, namely the
estimated loss directly and naturally resulting in the ordinary course of
events from the seller's breach.  In this case the plaintiff should be
awarded damages that may enable him purchase a new tractor.
Turn Sidra & anor Vs. Uganda Rehabilitation Development
Foundation.
Conveyancing -whether a done of powers of Attorney may sue as
a plaintiff with regard to an executed tenancy.
Held: Powers of attorney had to be strictly interpreted.  In this case the
particular power did not confer upon the plaintiffs to institute legal
proceedings in their names.  Moreover the powers were defective for the
failure of the witness thereto to give his particulars.  However, the
proceedings were not thereby invalid because the subject matter of the
suit was a contract of conveyance which was partly executed and
therefore it was the duty of the court to adjudicate on the dispute relating
to the contract and so give effect to the wishes of the parties.
Nakawa Trading Co. Ltd Vs. Coffee Marketing Board.
Breach - whether established - whether contract - repudiated.
Held: A breach of contract occurs when one or both parties fail to fulfill
the obligations imposed by the terms. The terms of the contract in the
instant case were reduced in writing and provided inter-alia that lorries
belonging to the plaintiff only were eligible for the transporting of the
defendant's cargo and the defendant would be presented with particulars
of the plaintiff's lorries for inspection and verification which the plaintiff
failed to do.  The defendant was thereby entitled to repudiate the contract.
Shillings 5 million would be awarded as damages to the defendant
against the plaintiff's breach of contract because such amount reasonably
would have been had in contemplation of both parties at the execution of
the contract as the probable result of the breach of I, since the contract
involved the public importance of the opening of an alternative route for
Uganda a landlocked country the fact that the plaintiff ought to have known.
Banax Ltd Vs. Gold Trust Bank Ltd.
Breach of contract - whether bank breached it's contract with it's
customer by freezing it's account.
Held: The reorganization of the company was an internal matter and the
respondent bank should only have looked at the resolution which had
been duly registered with the registrar of companies.  Therefore, the
bank would not be said to have had notice of something irregular and
was thereby in breach of contract to freeze the appellant's account.
The plaintiff appellant must prove that it had suffered actual damage due
to its non-use of its account as a basis for the award of general damages.
This had not been the case and Shs.100,000/= would be awarded for
inconvenience suffered.
Spear Motors Ltd Vs. Banyakore Kweterana.
Sale of goods -frustration - currency devaluation - failure to obtain
foreign exchange - anarchy - whether these events frustrated the contract.
Held: S.55 of the Sale of Goods Act allows parties to a contract to vary
their contract by interalia, express agreement.  In the instant case, the
meeting in June 1987 between the parties led to a new agreement by
which the appellant could not therefore claim that the contract had been
frustrated.
The learned trial judge's decree for specific performance can only be
impeached if it is proved that it was not just and reasonable or one which
justice demanded.  It is not enough to claim that it would be costlier to
perform the contract.  The learned trial judge used his discretion correctly
and there was no misdirection.
Seraphin Obwolo Vs. Barclays Bank.
Employment - whether breached due to lack of reasonable notice
of termination - whether principles of natural justice breached.
Held: An employee on permanent terms is entitled to know charges
against him and to be given an opportunity to give any grounds to
exculpate himself.  In the instant case the bank's summary dismissal of
its permanent member of staff without notice was a breach of natural
justice entitling the plaintiff to be heard.
Moreover, clause 7(a) of the agreement between the plaintiff and the bank
provided that the bank was entitled to dismiss the plaintiff summarily if
the plaintiff was guilty of misappropriating funds but the wrongful crediting
of a customer's account was not misappropriating bank funds.
Terminal benefits, pension, unpaid salary, and leave allowance must be
particularized and claimed as special damages.  Therefore, since the
plaintiff did not do this his prayer for these items must fail.
Since the defendant was in breach of agreement, the plaintiff was entitled
to general damages, the equivalent of 4 months pay in lieu of notice.
Banax Ltd Vs. Gold Trust Bank Ltd
Breach of contract - whether Bank breached its contract with its customer
by freezing its account.
Damages for breach of contract -quantum.
Held: The reorganization of the company was an internal matter and the
respondent bank should only have looked at the resolution which had
been duly registered with the registrar of companies.  Therefore, the
bank would not be said to have had notice of something irregular and
was thereby in breach of contract to freeze the appellant's account.
The plaintiff appellant must prove that it had suffered actual damage due
to its non-use of its account as a basis for the award of general damages.
This had not been the case and Shs.100,000/= would be awarded for
inconvenience suffered.
Mbabazi & Co. Vs. Uganda Railways Corporation.
Bailment - whether contract established where defendant took
custody of the plaintiff's goods for a consideration.
Held: To establish a contract of bailment, the subject matter must be a
chattel whose custody must have been transferred to the bailee
temporarily for the consideration.  In the instant case the subject matter
was hoes in the custody of the defendant who expected to be paid a
storage charge.  Therefore the contract of bailment was established and
the defendants breached this contract when they failed to return the hoes
to the plaintiff.
The special damages awardable would be the replacement market value of
the hoes as at the time of judgment.
The general damages for the plaintiff's loss occasioned by the defendant
would be shs. 5, 000, 000/= (five million).
George William Katatumba Vs. Uganda Cooperative
Transport Union Ltd.
Enforceability - illegality -whether contract was on enforceable
because it violated the provision of exchange control Act.
Held: Annexure 'F' had supported paragraphs 5 and 6 of the plaint when it
stated that fees were to be paid in Uganda Shillings at the reigning forex at
time of settling the claims in paragraphs 5 and 6.  therefore the learned
trial judge erred when he held that annexure 'F' was not part of the plaint.
Judgment may be allowed in foreign currency.  Therefore the learned trial
judge erred in holding that claims in foreign currency are unenforceable in
law because of illegality.  The Foreign Exchange Control Act did not
prohibit ab-initio the payment in foreign currency but provided that the
minister's permission must be sought.  So, judgment could still be made
awarding the claim amount in foreign currency but require the Decree
holder to seek ministerial license to that effect.
Appeal allowed case sent back for hearing to High Court with paragraph
5 & 6 of the plaint reinstated.
Arconsult Architects Vs. Bauman (u) Ltd.
Building contracts -scale of fees payable to architect - whether
contract breached whether fees payable may be based on value of
abandoned works.
Held: Where an architect has complied with instructions and produced
the work for which he was commissioned he is entitled to payment even
if the plans are not utilized.  In the instant case even if thee respondent/
defendant had abandoned the works on the premises, the architect should
still have been paid that agreed percentage based on the total value cost
of the works i.e. Ush 241 million.  Therefore the trial judge erred in not
awarding the US$14,156 as the percentage value of the works, as fees
for the architect.
Nile Bank Ltd Vs. Akalu Enterprises.
Frustration - bank loan - whether defendant was entitled not to
repay a bank loan because the money was borrowed for the
exportation of beans but government subsequently imposed a ban
on the exportation of beans - whether loan contract had been
frustrated.
Held: Since the defendant applicant in substance admitted the claim but
contested the amount not subtracted, which he had repaid, there was no
need for the defendant to appear and defend the suit.  The defendant
should pay the loan amount claimed by the plaintiff less the amount repaid.
Secondly since the defendant had repaid some money and further
negotiated a rescheduling of the loan repayment his action were
inconsistent with a frustrated contract where the loss ought to lie where
it fell.
Application dismissed with costs.
Ishasha Mines Ltd Vs. National Enterprises Corporation.
Estoppel - agreement that the plaintiff's claim against the
defendant has been finally settled - whether therefore the plaintiff is
estopped in filing an action for a further claim.
Held: A subsidiary company has in law is independent corporate
existence and may be sued for acts its liable for.  However where as a
question of fact it is established that the subsidiary was merely a means
through which the parent company conducts its business, then an action
many be properly instituted against the parent company for acts done by
its subsidiary.  In the instant case it was clear that officers of the
subsidiary were all appointed by the defendant.  Therefore, the suit was
properly brought against the defendant.
The purported final settlement agreement smacked of duress because the
plaintiff negotiated from a very weak position.  Secondly the agreement
was ambiguous because it merely stated that the subsidiary had agreed
to pay so much for the plaintiff's claim without stating what the claim was.
Therefore the plaintiff's action was not estopped by the purported final
settlement agreement.
Suit allowed and the plaintiff to be compensated for 450 tones of lime
minus the 80 tones already compensated for.
Isaac Bishari Vs. Vitaform Ltd.
Sale of goods -specific goods s.2 sale of goods Act - whether the
contract mattresses sold against a proforma invoice describing
their, sizes and other descriptions were, specific and a ascertained
goods.
Specific performance - S.52 Sale of Goods Act-whether the contract
mattresses sold against a proforma invoice stating the price and
describing the sizes of the mattresses, were specific and ascertained
goods - whether the remedy of specific performance was applicable.
Price-rise in price after the contract - whether the buyer was enjoined to
pay the extra rise in price.
Held: The contract goods (Mattresses) were so particularized as to
quantity, size and price and the part delivery corresponded to these
particulars.  Therefore the goods were ascertained.  Therefore had the
learned trial judge made a finding as to whether there was a breach of
contract he would have found that the remedy of specific performance
was available.
Where a contract of sale stipulates the price payable for goods to be the
ruling price, it cannot be price other than the price agreed upon at the
time of the contract.  The price therefore cannot depend on the vagaries
of the future.  The respondent/defendant was pre-cluded form basing the
suit contract on the fact of fluctuation of price.
Appeal allowed.  File to be remitted to the trial Court for finding whether
there was breach of contract.
William Mufumu Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority.
Employment contract -breach thereof whether employment
contract was breached where plaintiff was employed on temporary any
terms.
Held: S.12 of the Uganda Revenue Authority statute provides that
the Uganda Revenue Authority Officer therefore had no authority to
recruitment of the Authority's staff.  The District Revenue Officer therefore
had no authority to recruit the plaintiff as an employee of the defendant.
Therefore the plaintiff was not recognized an employee of the defendant
and his suit for damages for wrongful dismissal was unsustainable.
The facts of the case were such that there was no reasonable cause why
the plaintiff had been advised to file the suit.  Therefore his counsel would
be personally liable for the payments of the costs.
Willy Ogwanga Vs. Ringa Enterprises Ltd
Special damages for breach of employment contract - payment in
foreign currency s.5 foreign exchange control Act -whether lack of
consent for payment in foreign currency by the minister meant that
the plaintiff could not be paid.
Held: There was a valid service contract between the appellant and the
respondent and the respondent was obliged to pay the appellant.  It was
the responsibility of the respondents to seek the necessary permission
from the Minister and moreover the appellant sought to be paid only the
equivalent of 7200 pounds in Uganda currency.
Birumi Wilson Vs. Akamba (u) Ltd
Private of contract - whether defendant was a privy to the contract.
Law applicable -Indian Contract Act - whether applicable to the law of
contract in Uganda.
Held: The Uganda Contract Act came into force on 1st January 1963 and
S.2 thereof ceases the application of the Indian Contract Act to contracts
In Uganda and S.3 (1) thereof provides the application of the Common Law
of England relating to contracts.  The learned trial Judge in the case
instant based his decision on the Common Law doctrine that no suit can
be entertained against a stranger to the contract.  The trial Judge
considered the common law doctrines of offer acceptance and
consideration and found that found that there was no contract between the
appellant and the respondent.  Therefore, even if the Judge cited Parker's
case, he relied on the Common Law Doctrines of Contract.
Under the adversarial system, where parties are represented by counsel,
it would be extremely rare for a trial Judge on his own motion to order the
joining or substitution of a third party to the proceedings.  Therefore, the
learned trial Judge did not err in not considering the joining of Massey
Ferguson (UK) Ltd.  As co-defendant.
The Court of Appeal will interfere with the exercise of discretion of the trial
Judge in refusing an adjournment if the result of his exercise of discretion
in refusing the adjournment will occasion injustice.  In the instant case
counsel for the plaintiff applied for adjournment without specifically
disclosing the purpose, his application being vague and half hearted and
the trial Judge was justified in refusing the adjournment.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
NEC & others Vs. Nile Bank Ltd.
Agency - non existent principle- whether agent was liable
personally for ostensibly acting for a non - existent principle -
whether the holding company was liable for ostensibly acting for a
non-corporate subsidiary.
Held: A contract made before a company is formed cannot bind the
company formed afterwards.  In the instant case the first appellant
executed the debenture before NEC Bakery came into existence.
Therefore the learned trial Judge was correct in holding that the debenture
was a nullity.
Though a subsidiary company is an independent entity from its parent, in
the instant case the trial Judge was correct in lifting the veil of the
subsidiary NEC Bakery and to find that it was owned and controlled by the
first appellant who had majority shareholding in it and that therefore the
first appellant was liable on the debenture.
If a person contracts essentially as an agent for non-existing Principal
that person may be found personally liable on the contract.  In the instant
case learned trial Judge was correct in finding the appellant who ostensibly
contracted on behalf of NEC Bakery which was not in existence at the
time of the debenture, liable on the debenture.
The learned trial Judge erred in holding that the respondent/defendant was
empowered under the debenture to exercise a right of seizure under
clause 6 of the debenture because clause 6 of the debenture did not
provide for seizure but only stated the conditions under which the
appellant shall immediately be liable to repay the loan.  It is only clause 7,
which provided for a right to appoint a receiver by the respondent.
therefore they respondent was not entitled to seize the appellant's motor
vehicle it was only entitled to appoint a receiver.
The learned trial Judge misdirected himself when he observed that the
plaintiff/appellant should instead have filed objector proceedings to contest
the seizure instead of a suit.  Objector proceedings may only follow when
there is an execution of a decree of court.
The Mortgage Decree does not apply to moveable property and therefore
the argument that the seizure of the appellant's vehicles was done under
the powers of the Mortgage Decree Ss.2, 7 was misconceived. And more-
over there was no order of foreclosure as required by S.7 Mortgage Decree.
Even if it is not a rule of Law that the trial Court should invariably assess
the damages it would have awarded the party succeeded, it was an
important rule of practice because the party is given an opportunity to
appeal against the award by the trial court.
Jean Francis Piva Vs. Habitat
Privity of contract - whether stranger can claim under a contract to
which he did not provide any consideration.
Offer and acceptance - whether a binding contract existed where the
parties did not specifically agree to the terms made in the counter offer.
Held: According to our law, where a firm offer is given by one party and is
accepted in all its terms by another the existence of a valid contract
between such parties would be a difficult fact to deny.
It is clear from the evidence on record that Cataco made rejection of the
defendant's offer and made a counter offer.  Accordingly, there was no
binding contract between the defendant and Cetaco.
From the evidence on record, the reason why the plaintiff demanded for a
commission was because he was convinced that he had arranged a valid
contract between the defendant and Cetaco, but since Court has found
otherwise, the plaintiff is according to any commission from the defendant.
Had there been a valid contract, the plaintiff's claim would still not have
been honored since according to the evidence on record he did not
provide any consideration to the contract and as such could not claim
under it.
Godom Builders & Constructors Ltd Vs. Departed Asian
Property Custodian Board.
Work stipulated under building contract not completed because the
building was repossessed by former Asian owner - whether
contract was frustrated.
Frustration of contract-whether plaintiff is entitled to interim payment for
works already executed.
Held: The plaintiff did not complete the  contract as agreed because
the property was repossessed by its former owner, and therefore the
contract was frustrated.  The evidence adduced however did not indicate
when the property was returned, as this would have help to determine
when the contract did not provide for such eventually, the plaintiff is
is entitled to payment on certificates No.6 and 7.
The allegations by the defendant that the work done was sub-standard
and that certificates No.6 and 7 were not authentic were not proved.
Neither was it indicated how the certificates were to be authenticated nor
was it a term of the contract.  If the defendant was dissatisfied with the
work done, it should have sought a reduction in contract price.
in the absence of that, the plaintiff is entitled to the amount of money
contained in both certificates since it is apparent that the work
substantially carried out.
Judgment in favour of plaintiff for Ush 21,598,353 with 45% interest from
date of judgment till payment in full.
Coffee Marketing Board Vs. Kigezi District Growers.
Acts by an agent - whether, the acts of the chairman of a co-opera
Co-operative union bond the union where he obtained a loan purportedly on
behalf of the union but put the loan to his personal use.
Privity of contract-whether there is no cause of action against the
defendant-whether the Union is not privy to the alleged contract.
Held: It is without doubt that an agent or servant or employee who sets
out to act within the scope of his authority and in so acting deviates and
does things not for the benefit of his principal, or master would still render
such principal or master liable under the doctrine of vicarious liability.
Where the agent has actual authority, express or implied, the ostensible
authority coincides with the actual authority.  Where he has no actual
authority but a representation of the kind that has been just described,
the agent has ostensible authority although actual authority may be
lacking.
In the instant case, mahirane was the chairman of the defendant Union
he had previously borrowed money from the plaintiff on behalf of the
Union and the Union had duly repaid the loan.  The plaintiff need not delve
into the Union's bye-laws to find out whether Mahirane had the power to
contract on behalf of the Union.  See rule in Royal British Bank Vs.
Turquand [1856] ER 327.  There is evidence to show that the cheque for
the loan was credited to the favour of the defendant, that later on it was
removed from the defendant's account by Mahirane and Turyatemba who
were officers of the Union, authorized by its bye-laws to sign, inter alia
cheques on behalf of the Union.  In that regard their conduct bound the
Union.
The defendant Union's bye-laws 51 and 52 create no compulsion for the
affixing of its common seal by the Union on its contracts so as to render
them a nullity in case no such affixation is made.  Therefore the fact that
no genuine seal was affixed to the loan agreement with the plaintiff does
not render the agreement a nullity.
Accordingly the loan agreement concluded between Mahirane on behalf of
the defendant and the plaintiff was legal. The defendant shall repay to the
plaintiff the loan sum of Ush 20/= m plus interest at the rate of 40% p.a
and the service charge of 1% p.a.  The defendant will recover the Ush
4,120,743 rental from the plaintiff.
Patrick Kirunda Vs. Bernard Mawanda.
Damage for breach of contract - quantum for lost earrings -quantum
for general damages.
Held: The plaintiff was rightly entitled to the amount it cost him to put the
house.  However the plaintiff had not proved specifically the claim of loss
of earning from his butchery and would thereby fail in that claim.
Ush 200,000/= as general damages for breach of contract.
suit allowed.
Abendego Absolom Ongom Vs. Amos Kaheru.
Sale of goods Act s.26(2) - whether therefore new buyer is not
owner of the Vehicle because he has not completed payment of
contract price.
Held: Where a defendant does not appear, having filed a Written
Statement of Defence and the trial proceeds ex parte, remedies cannot
be granted to the plaintiff just as prayed unless they are sufficiently
supported by the pleadings.
As per S.26 (2) of the Sale of Goods Act, the transfer of title and payment
of purchase price in a contract of sale are not concurrent conditions.
Therefore the defendant having bought the car and having obtained
possession of it with the consent of the vendor, he had become its owner
even though he had not paid all the installments.
Even though the defendant in his WSD attempted to plead contributory
negligence he failed because no particulars there were provided.
Moreover, the burden of proof of contributory negligence lay on the
defendant, who failed to discharge the burden when he failed to come to
court and testify.
The plaintiff had proved as special damages, the cost of private medical
treatment Ush 1,240,000/=; loss of sitting allowances ush 180,000/=.
The plaintiff had failed to prove the claim for the cost of transport to and
from hospital for himself and his wife who visited him regularly.  This is
because no evidence had been led to that effect.
In case of destruction of goods the measure of damages is taken to be
the market value of the goods destroyed at the time and place of
destruction.  Therefore the plaintiff's claim for a replacement value of a new
car would fail since his damaged car was old.
The plaintiff's disability assessed at 60% was quite an exaggeration
because the plaintiff suffered potts fracture, which healed nicely. However,
the plaintiff was in plaster of Paris for four months and had screws in his
body and suffered posttraumatic arthritis.  He would therefore be awarded
Ush 5 million general damages.
Case allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Lydia Lwanga Vs. Mawolis Dimitrikos
Tenancy agreement - notice of termination without notice of
termination amounted to breach of tenancy agreement.
Damages for breach of tenancy agreement-quantum.
Held: Where notice is provided for in the covenants of the tenancy
agreement, failure to give such notice of termination of the tenancy is a
breach of the covenant.  In the instant case the plea that the defendant
left the house for security reasons did not amount to a plea of frustration
of contract because the defendant was liable for breach of the covenant
to give notice of termination.
The defendant was also liable for failure to deliver up the premises in
tenable repair as required by the tenancy agreement.
a letter written "without prejudice" is inadmissible in evidence as an
admission.  Therefore the plaintiff should not have relied on it.
Where a tenant abandons the demised premises he is liable to pay rent
for the period the premises are unoccupied.
Where a tenant abandons the demised premises he is liable to pay rent
for the subsequent repairs necessitated by the concomitant vandalisation
of the premises.
Ush 500,000/= would be awarded as general damages for breach of
tenancy agreement.
Stephen Byaruhanga Vs. Mbarara Municipal Council.
Offer - consider offer - whether there was a contract where the
original after were not accepted.
Held: In law, a counter offer operates as a rejection of the original offer.
a rejection of the original offer means that no contract is concluded since
there was no acceptance.  Since the respondent inter alia offered that the
applicants must pay the balance within one year and yet the applicants
counter offered to pay it within two years, it means that no contract was
concluded between the applicants and the respondent.
Certiorari is a prerogative with which will issue to quash a decision of a
tribunal exercising judicial or quasi judicial functions, which tribunal is
found to have acted ultra-vires its powers or its decision is vitiated by
error on the face of the record.  Prohibition issues to forbid some act
some act or decisions which would be ultra vires.  In the case instant the
decision by the respondent Municipal Council to rescind its decision to
sell the houses was a legislative act, exercising its powers to make
subordinate legislation.  Therefore, the writs of certiorari and prohibition
could not apply to a decision which was purely to a decision which was
purely legislative and not judicial or quasi judicial.
Mangalita Namirembe Vs. Kalamatu Tebukola.
Consideration -money had and received whether it was money had
and received with no consideration.
HELD: The matter in controversy was debt of Ush 200,000/= old currency
which had been reduced to Ush 2000/= by the Currency Reform Statute
of 1987.  therefore the debt being Ush 2,000/=, the RC Courts had
pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain the suit as per s.4 RC Judicial Posers
Statute.
However the Chief Magistrate and the RC Courts erred to have found that
the appellant was bound by the Clan Elders' decision.  This is because
the appellant did not sign the minutes of the clan elders' meeting.
Therefore there was no contract constituted by the clan elders' meeting.
Since there was no contract, if the appellant mistakenly was paid part of
the money required to be paid to her by the clan elders' meeting, it was
money received for no consideration, received under a mistake of fact and
was recoverable.
In absence of evidence to the contrary a payer of rates in whose names
receipts appear, is the owner of the property and the Chief Magistrate
erred in ignoring the appellant's receipts to prove her ownership of the
property in absence of evidence to the contrary.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Alex Olwor Vs. Registered Trustees of Arua Catholic Diocese
Agency - liability - whether agent was liable as well as the principal
to the same contract - whether principal notified contract.
Held: S.5 Sale of Goods Act requires a contract of sale of goods of the
amount of or above shs 200 to be in writing.  The suit contract was a
validity enforceable contract as it fulfilled the requirements of the sale of
Goods Act.
Where the agent does not indicate in a contract that he is contracting
personally but as an agent, then he is personally liable to the contract.
In the instant case the principal ratified the contract by making part
payment in pursuance thereof.  Therefore both the agent and the principal
were liable.
It is a rule of law and practice that special damages must not only be
pleaded but proved strictly.  Though a receipt of Ush. 540,000/= was
tendered in evidence, the amount pleaded was Ush 810,300/=.  The
plaintiff was precluded from recovering the lesser amount of Ush
540,000/= evidence for which had been adduced because that proved
amount was not pleaded.
A plaintiff will recover damages for loss of profit as damages foreseeable
by the parties at the time they made their contract, as the probable
result of the breach.  In the instant case there was no evidence that the
defendant had knowledge of the plaintiff's nature of business.  It was not
mentioned in evidence that the plaintiff was a regular or casual Timber
Trader.  Therefore the defendant could not foresee loss of profit as the
natural consequence of the breach of the contract.
Suit allowed for the payment of the balance on the contract price and
Ush 100,000/= as compensation for delayed payment and costs.
Yona Kanyomozi Vs. Motor Mart Ltd & ors.
Privity of contract - subcontract - whether a plaintiff has a causes of
action against a sub contract - whether a subcontractor is privy to
the contract between a contractor and the plaintiff.
Time breach - whether the defendant was not in breach of the contract
because there was no stipulation as to time for performance.
Held: The invoice that showed the repair cost estimates was from the first
defendant.  Therefore there was a subsisting contract between the
plaintiff and the first defendant.
The second defendant acted as an officer of the first defendant Company
and was therefore not liable personally.
The third defendant was subcontracted by the first defendant to work on
the plaintiff's vehicle.  Therefore there was no contract between the
plaintiff and the third defendant.
Since 1992 September the plaintiff urged the defendants to go on repairing
repairing the vehicle without stipulating a time limit of the performance of
of the contract, the plaintiff by conduct had led the defendants to believe
that he would not insist on the stipulation as to time and was therefore
estopped from complaining.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Cases dismissed with costs.
Kadu Enterprises (U) Ltd Vs. U Prebil.
Sale of goods - unconditional talking of delivery - whether thereby
the purchase must pay for the goods.
time unconditional taking of delivery - whether thereby purchaser cannot
claim breach of condition of stipulation as to time.
Held: The defendant being fully aware of all the facts and circumstances
attending the sale did accept and took exclusive delivery of the suit goods
unconditionally.  Therefore the defendant was bound by the contract and
must pay for the goods.  Stipulation as to the time was irrelevant since the
defendant unconditionally took delivery of the goods.
Yona Kanyomozi Vs. Motor Mart (U) Ltd & ors.
Privity of contract - subcontract - whether a plaintiff has a cause
of action against a subcontractor - whether a subcontractor is
privy to the contract between a contractor and the plaintiff.
Time to breach - whether the defendant was not in breach of the contract
because there was no stipulation as to time for performance.
Held: The invoice that showed the repair cost estimates was from the first
defendant.  Therefore there was a subsisting contract between the plaintiff
and the first defendant.
The second defendant acted as an officer of the first Defendant Company
and was therefore not liable personally.
The third defendant was subcontracted by the first defendant to work on the
plaintiff's vehicle.  Therefore there was no contract between the plaintiff and
the third defendant.
Since in 1992 September the plaintiff urged the defendants to go on
repairing the vehicle without stipulating a time limit of the performance on the
contract, the plaintiff by conduct had led the defendants to believe that he
would not insist on the stipulation as to time and was therefore estopped
from complaining.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Cases dismissed with costs.
Nuru Sabiti Vs. Uganda.
Breach of contract - whether mounted to obtaining credit by
fraud c/s 291 (1) PCA.
Held: the tenor of evidence showed that the accused had no intent to
defraud but honestly failed to deliver the cocoa within ordinary course of
commercial transactions.  This was a civil transaction conjured into a
criminal contravention. The subsequent conviction and sentence were illegal.
Revision allowed.  Conviction quashed.  Sentence set aside.
Samwiri Iyamuleng Vs. Jovanis Nyarakamarande.
Marriage - age of consent s.3 (5) contract Act - whether a woman
aged 20 had attained the age of consent for purposes of a marriage
contract.
Held: S.3 (5) of the Contract Act provides that a minor is a person below 18
years. Since the plaintiff/respondent was 20 years, she was entitled to file
the suit for purposes of enforcing a contractual obligation without the next
friend.
Consent by parents or guardians where at least one of the parties is a minor
is not a requirement for the validity of a customary marriage unless one of
the parties does not belong to any indigenous tribe of Uganda.  Therefore,
the appellant was precluded from contending that his marriage was void due
to lack of consent since both parties to the marriage were Bafumbira from
Uganda.
Local council courts have jurisdiction to try cases invoking a customary
marriage.  However this does not oust the jurisdiction of a magistrate court
Grade 1 which has similar jurisdictions.  Therefore, the learned trial
magistrate was not precluded from trying the case as he was possessed
the requisite jurisdiction.
Where bride price is not paid in full, the customary marriage is void.  Since
in the instant case the appellant/respondent had paid only one and half a
cow, leaving a balance of a full cow, the marriage was void and the divorce
proceedings were uncalled for.
Justine Olijo Vs. Attorney General.
Sale of goods, s.49(1) sale of Good Act - damages for non
payment of price - whether loss of profit and interest on borrowed
money may be awarded as general damages for breach of
contract to pay price for goods supplied.
Held: General damages for non payment of the contract price are only
recoverable where the alleged loss must have been within the reasonable
contemplation of the parties at the time of making the agreement, and the
alleged loss must be the direct result of the breach of contract by non
payment of the price.  In the present case loss of profit and interest on
borrowed money was not recoverable.  However, only the unpaid price
would be ordered paid.
Suit allowed. Ush 4.7 million as unpaid ordered to be paid costs.
Elizabeth Imagara & 2 ors Vs. Attorney General
Employment - breach of contract - whether salary for un expired
contract period may be claimed as special damages.
breach of contract of employment -special damages - whether salary for
un expired contractual employment period may be claimed as special
damages.
Held: Since no defense was fixed by the defendant, no issues were joined
with regard to liability.  Liability is deemed to have been admitted. Therefore
court had only to resolve on the issue of damages.
Damages for wrongful dismissal should normally be based on the wages,
which the employer would have received if a valid notice had been given to
him on the date of dismissal.  Since the contracts of the plaintiffs' stipulated
one-month's notice or salary in the lieu thereof, the respective plaintiffs
would be paid their one month's salary in lieu of notice.  Further their salary
arrears would be paid.
Suit allowed.  Payment for unexpired contract period refused.
Kibona Enterprises Vs. Departed Asians Property Custodian
Board & anor.
Offer by advertisement - acceptance by being highest bidder -
whether valid contract established.
Held: Even though the agreement of sale showed that it was the Ministry of
Finance that was the vendor, SS.1 and 16 (1) (b) Expropriated Properties
Act and S.5 (3) assets of Departed Asian Decree provide that the
management of departed Asian properties lay with the 1st defendant, a
corporation sale.  Therefore the first defendant was rightly sued.
When one party makes a firm offer and accepted by the other in all its
