terms, a valid contract is established. In this case, the plaintiff saw an advert
pursuant to which the bided successfully for the purchase of the property
and paid accordingly.  Therefore there was a valid contract.
Since the plaintiff could be atoned by damages specific performance being
an equitable remedy would not be granted. Ush 4 million would be paid as
general damages for breach of contract.
Suit allowed with costs to defendant.
Shariff Osman Vs. Haji Haruna Mulanga.
Sale of land - unpaid balance - whether there for purchaser not
entitled to vacant possession - whether vendor had lien over contract
land whether specific performance may be ordered.
Held: A vendor of real property retains a lien in the property for the unpaid
balance of the purchase money. However, in the instant case the agreement
of the parties provided a specific time when the purchaser would take
possession.  Since the agreement was prepared by counsel for the
appellant the clause providing for taking possession would strictly be
construed against the vendor/appellant so that it is taken that delivery of
possession was not contingent upon completion of purchase price; since
upon payment of the deposit property passed to the purchaser.
The principle at Common Law is that in absence of a contrary intention
time is of essence of a contract even though the parties have not expressly
provided it.  In the case instant however, it took two years for the appellant/
vendor to claim to rescind the contract.  This was evidence that time of
payment of the purchase price was not of essence to the contract and
therefore the respondent/purchaser was not in breach of the contract for
failure to pay the balance by the agreed date.
If the appellant/vendor had successfully rescinded the contract he would not
be entitled to keep the deposit.
The respondent/purchaser was not entitled to mesne profits and general
damages because he had in ordinarily delayed in enforcing specific
performance.
Appeal dismissed except as to general damages.
Reamanton Ltd Vs. Uganda Corporation Creameries & anor
Partnership Act-guarantee- whether there existed a promise to
answer for the debt of another -whether the promise must
invariably be in writing.
Illegality - whether agreement to pay a commission to public servants was
illegal and unenforceable - S.I. Prevention of Corruption Act.
Held: The receipt by a person of share of the profits of a business is strong
evidence that he is a partner but not conclusive ipso facto.  Court must take
into account the agreement and intention of the parties. In the instant case
other co-existing factors show that there was no partnership.  There co-
existing factors include the fact that the first defendant had borrowed money
for the coffee business which loan was only the liability of the first defendant
and yet if the business were a partnership the two said parties would be
jointly liable.
To constitute a contract of guarantee there must be a promise to answer
for the debt of another under s.4(1) of the Contract Act.  In the instant case,
documents which would otherwise have constituted the requisite promise
by the second defendant to answer for the debt of the first defendant, were
signed by the second defendant in his capacity as executive director of the
first defendant. Therefore no such guarantee had been proved against the
second defendant personally.
A contract to pay a commission to Government Civil Servants was illegal
and unenforceable as it infringed S.1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Therefore the claimed set off constituting commissions supposed to be
paid to the second defendant for onward transmission to the civil servants
was illegal and unenforceable.
Further, there was no proof of unpaid commission as a set off from the claim
of the plaintiff to the defendants.
Suit allowed with costs.  Both defendants found jointly and severally liable
to the plaintiff.
Mutekanga Asumani Haji Vs. Equator Growers (U) Ltd.
Breach - damages - quantum.
Held: A defendant who neither enters an appearance nor files a written
statement of defence is precluded from taking part in proceedings during
formal proof hearing, when there is subsisting an interlocutory judgment.
The learned trial judge therefore erred when he allowed counsel for the
respondent to participate in the proceedings and cross examine witnesses.
Where an interlocutory judgment has been entered in favor of the plaintiff,
the question of liability of the defendant is no longer in issue.  What is in
issue is the assessment of the quantum of damages.  Therefore the learned
trial judge misdirected himself when he required the appellant to prove
breach of the agreement, when there was a subsisting interlocutory
judgment in favor of the plaintiff.
Special damages must be specifically pleaded and strictly proved
irrespective of whether there is a defence to the claim or not.  Proof of
special damages consists evidence of particular losses.  In the instant case
the appellant's witnesses had taken part in running the factory and testified
with first hand knowledge.  The appellant had proved his claim for special
damages on a balance of probabilities.
Since no attempt was made to prove loss of profit non would be awarded.
Sh. 1 million would be awarded as general damages for breach of contract.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Gwebatuma Badru Haji Vs. Bwayo Joseph
Duress-obtaining money from plaintiff so that his son may not be
prosecuted-whether money obtained by duress.
Undue influence or extortion-civil action-whether a plaintiff has no
cause of action in a civil court for the recovery of money obtained
through extortion because extortion is a criminal felony.
Money had and received-extortion-whether money obtained through
extortion may be recovered as money had and received by a civil
action.
Illegality-recovery of money obtained through extortion-whether
plaintiff was estopped from claiming recovery of money paid to rescue
his son from prosecution because it was money paid for an illegal purpose.
Held: Where money is obtained by duress or extortion the plaintiff who
seeks the recovery of the money has a cause of action on the principle of
money had and received.  Therefore, the learned trial Chief Magistrate was
correct in finding that the plaintiff had a cause of action.
Where a person threatens to prosecute an individual, his wife or close
relation for an offence not committed, it may amount to duress of the
promise from the defendant in that he will discontinue the threatened
prosecution if some gratification is paid.  In the instant case the appellant
withdrew the threatened prosecution when he was paid the shs.2 million
without any evidence that indeed the respondent's son was guilty of the
alleged defilement.  Therefore the appellant was liable for obtaining money
by duress.
The payment by the respondent to the appellant was under duress but not
illegal since the respondent's son was not guilty of the alleged offence.
Appeal dismissed.
All Ports Freight Service Vs. Julius Kamanyi & anor.
Consideration-cheque-whether presumption that issued for value.
Damages-breach -quantum.
Held: If two or several persons jointly purchase goods for resale with a view
to dividing the profits arising from the transaction, a partnership is created
and each of them will be liable to third parties.  In the instant case it was
clear that both defendants obtained cement from the plaintiff, for resale at a
profit to be shared.  Therefore, a partnership relationship was established as
under s.3 (1) of the Partnership Act.
A partnership need not be established formally and in writing.  It is sufficient
to establish that a community of interest exists between the parties.  This
was amply proved in this case.
The doctrine of holding out also provided for under S.18 of the Partnership
Act, states that where a person holds himself out as a partner, thus
including third parties, acting on such representations, to deal with him as
such, then he is liable to the third parties.  In the instant case it was not
necessary to apply the doctrine because the partnership had already been
established.
Although S.30 of the Bills of Exchange Act provides that when a person's
signature appears on a bill of exchange then that person is prima facie a
party, it was not applicable to the instant case because the plaintiff was not
suing on the cheque, the cheque was only of evidential value of the
transaction.  Therefore, the non appearance of the second defendant's
signature on the cheque, did not absolve him from liability for the debt
incurred for the unpaid cement.
O. 1 r 6 empowers a plaintiff to elect whom to sue.  Therefore the plaintiff
was free not to join the said cook to the proceedings as another defendant.
Sh. 15 million would be awarded as general damages for breach of contract.
Suit allowed with costs.
Omari Mohamed Captain Vs. Attorney General.
Misrepresentation-government issuing certificate of purchase to a
leasehold property where the landlord has re-entered due to non
payment of rent-whether misrepresentation proved.
Breach of contract-damages-quantum.
Held: Because of the re-entry substratum of the contract was non-existent.
And yet the defendant had represented to the plaintiff that he had the suit
property available for sale and because of this representation, the plaintiff
had paid money to the defendant, and yet the representation was false.
Therefore, the defendant is liable for misrepresentative and the breach of
contract.
the defendant would pay to the plaintiff the market value of the property as at
the date of judgment as special damages plus shs. 650,000/= per month
from date of breach as mesne profits.
Shs. 2 million would be paid as general damages.
Kasasa Mohammed Vs. Uganda.
Breach of contract-obtaining goods by false pretence under S.289
Penal Code Act-whether criminal proceedings wrongly brought a
instead of civil proceedings.
Held: It is up to the person taking legal action to choose whether to institute
it as civil or criminal proceeding.  Either choice does not exclude the other
as long as there is evidence that disclose both civil and criminal triable
issues.
A contention that the matter before the criminal court should only have been
commenced in civil court is not a proper submission of no case to answer.
A submission of no case to answer is to the effect that the evidence
disclosed on the record is not sufficient to put the accused to his defence.
There is no rule of law requiring the trial Magistrate to give an exhaustive
evaluation of the evidence and law while ruling on a submission of no case
to answer except when the ruling is in the affirmative, that there is no case
to answer.   Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate was entitled to make
her ruling in the two sentences.
Application dismissed.
Wakida Edward Vs. Adeodata Kekitiinwa & 3 others.
Time-whether time was of essence in the lease contract.
Illegality-unenforceability-whether subsequent lease unenforceable
because illegally granted.
Held:  When time has not been made of essence of the contract, one party
cannot avoid the contract on grounds of unreasonable delay by the other
until notice has been served, making time of essence.  When the offer for
the lease was made to the plaintiff on 26 November 1987, it stipulated that
the plaintiff must accept the same within one month by paying all fees
including premium.  The plaintiff accepted the offer 6 months later when he
paid the fees which was accepted by the 3rd defendant Uganda Land
Commission.  Even then the lease agreement was only ready in January
1989 and the certificate of title in November 1989.  This meant that the
parties had not regarded time as being the essence to the contract.  And
third defendant (ULC) could only make time of essence by giving notice to
the plaintiff, which was never done.  Therefore the ULC was in breach of the
lease agreement.
S.51 of the Registration of Titles Act provides that only when an instrument
is registered that it is effectively able to pass estate of interest in land.  In
the present case the plaintiff became the registered lessee of the suit
property not in 1987 when the offer was made but in November 1989 when
the plaintiff was registered as lessee and granted a certificate of title.
Therefore, the 5 year period began to run from November 1989 and not 1987.
Therefore, when the plaintiff's lease was re-allocated in 1993 it had not
expired because it was due to expire in November 1994.
Rule 2 of the Public Lands Miscellaneous Regulations define reasonable
development as being at least one third of the projected development.  In the
instant case, though the covenant in lease required the plaintiff to erect as
shs. 12m building on the suit land within 5 years, the fact that the plaintiff
had ferried building materials on the site as he awaited the approval of his
building plans from KCC, would amount to reasonable development
disentitling the controlling authority from claiming breach of the
development covenant in the lease by the plaintiff.
S.184(e) Registration of Titles Act provides that a person can bring an action
to recover land where that person has a certificate of title prior in time as
against the other person from whom recovery is claimed.
Moreover, it was against public policy to deprive a lessee of his property
without notice and without any blame on his part with regard to the lease
covenants.
The subsequent lease granted to the 1st defendant was unenforceable
because it was granted illegally in breach of public policy, and the 1st
defendant was privy to the illegality because she knew the property had
been previously leased to the plaintiff which fact should have given notice to
her to act prudently.
Suit allowed with costs.
Mutanda Julius Vs. Kampala City Council.
Enforceability-illegality-S.31 Urban Authorities Act-whether tender
to collect debts on behalf of KCC required advertising first and
whether therefore contract unenforceable because of lack of
advertising.
Held: The contract existed between the parties, the plaintiff had performed
his part, therefore it was enforceable.
Suit allowed.
Mbalire Simon Vs. Moses Mukiibi.
Damages for breach of contract-restitution in intergrum - quantum.
Held: The fundamental principle by which the courts are guided in awarding
damages is restitution in integrum.  By this principle the law endeavours, so
far as it can be done, to place the injured person in the same situation he
occupied before the occurrence of the breach (or tort).  In the present case
the plaintiff parted with so much money but did not get the motor vehicle and
the income he expect therefrom.  Shs. 5 million would be awarded as
general damages for breach of contract on top of the order of the refund of
Suit allowed with costs.
Wamala Growers Co-operative Union Vs. Attorney General.
Agreement to sell goods S.7(3) Sale of Goods Act-whether because
it was an agreement to sell future goods there was no contract.
Breach-damages-quantum.
Held: S.7(3) Sale of Goods Act, provides that where the seller purports to
effect a present sale of future goods, the contract operates as only an
agreement to sale goods.  However in the instant case, the relevant facts
were that the agent of the defendant accepted payment for the animals and
allowed the plaintiff to select from a herd of over 500 heifers.  Therefore there
was created an express contract which was breached.
Where the party in breach of a contract knows the special circumstances
under which the contract was concluded, after having been so informed by
the injured party at the conclusion of the contract, the measure of the
damages the injured party is entitled to as a result of that breach is what
was reasonably contemplated as would naturally arise from the breach.
In the instant case the very nature of in-calf heifers is for diary farming where
milk is expected to be produced for sale.  The value of the expected mild
from 20 in-calf heifers for 9 years would be Ushs.194.4 million.  This amount
would be paid by the defendant to the plaintiff.
Case allowed.  Defendant to pay Ugshs 194.4 million and costs to plaintiff.
Prof. Syed Huq Vs. Islamic University In Uganda.
Consensus ad Idem-whether because both parities agreed to
contract there was a contract.
Employment S.13 Employment Decree-foreign employment
contract-enforceability-whether contract was foreign and whether
it was unenforceable.
Held: An Advocate that practices without a valid practicing certificate after
the grace period, practices illegally and is liable to prosecution as provided
by S.14(1) Advocates Act.  And all proceedings taken by such counsel and
documents signed by him are invalid, because to say otherwise would
amount to a perpetuation of an illegality.
However, in this case, the issue of the competence of the appeal could not
be raised as a preliminary objection without the leave of the court according
to the provisions of r101(b) RSC. Therefore the lack of a practicing certificate
by counsel who extracted the decree, would not interfere with the
competence of the appeal.
Where two parties to a contract have agreed to contract, then there is a
contract which non of the parties may deny.  In the instant case the
respondent's WSD admitted that the appellant was appointed Rector by the
Governing Council of the respondent.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself when he held that the appointment was null and void
due to lack of quorum by the appointing council.
However, S.13 of the Employment Decree provides that a foreign contract of
employment shall not be enforced unless it has been approved or attested
in accordance with the Employment Decree.  In the instant case since the
appellant was not a Ugandan and the respondent was a foreign contract and
the contract was unenforceable due to lack of it having been approved or
attested in accordance with the Employment Decree.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Mutenyo Paul Vs. Mary Grace Akot
Misrepresentation-whether acted upon.
Warranty that goods are fit for purpose-whether warranty existed.
Rescission-whether suit property kept for too long and could not be
rescinded.
Held: The learned trial Chief Magistrate correctly held that there was no
authoritative inspection of the suit vehicle by the respondent and that
therefore the respondent entirely depended on the representations made by
appellant.  The appellant represented to the respondent that the suit vehicle
was fit for the purpose the respondent wanted it for.
Where goods sold are described in the invoice as a car, a warranty is to be
inferred that the goods answered the known mercantile description of a car.
In the instant case the appellant sold do the respondent a mere scrap.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Kavuma F.W. Vs. Sembule Investments Bank
Held: A person is guilty of conversion who without lawful excuse, deprives
another of his goods by giving some other person a lawful title to them.
In the present case, the third party had only defective title to the cheques
as the true owner was the plaintiff.  The defendant dealt with the cheques in
a manner inconsistent with the rights of the plaintiff who was the true owner,
and are therefore prima facie, liable to him for the conversion of the cheques.
S.82(1)(2) Bills of Exchange Act protects a bank from liability in conversion
where the bank has acted in good faith and without negligence and the
cheque in question is a crossed cheque.  In the instant case though the
bank sought to rely on Section 82 Bills of Exchange Act for protection and
pleaded to have acted in good faith and without negligence, the bank did not
lead evidence to show that the cheques in question were crossed.
Secondly, the bank's failure to investigate the particulars of the customer
who purported to be the owner of the cheques was evidence in question
were crossed.
The plea that the plaintiff had ratified the act of the third party cannot stand.
A principal can only ratify the act of a person who is his agent.  In the
instant case the third party never acted for the plaintiff and never said so.
The plead that the plaintiff was a partner of the third party cannot stand
because even if it were true that the third party and the plaintiff were partners
a co-owner can commit conversion in respect of joint property.  However,
neither the third party nor the plaintiff claimed that they were partners.
The alleged indemnification of the defendant by the plaintiff when he agreed
to drop his complaint against the defendant cannot be said to have been
done voluntarily because, the plaintiff had had no legal counsel; the plaintiff
was desperate for accessing even the little balance to offset his debts, so
it was a corrupt bargain and it was unenforceable and moreover the
defendant never performed his part of the bargain.
The measure of damages for conversion of (a chattel) cheques is their face
value.  Therefore, the defendant would pay Ugshs.31 million to the plaintiff
the face value of the cheques.
Case allowed with costs against the defendant.
Arua Motor Dealers Vs. Attorney General
Government Proceedings - limitation-whether claim in contract was
time barred-whether war a disability -S.2(2) Civil Procedure and
Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act.
Limitation-acknowledgement of debt-whether this revives cause of
action.
Held: S.2(2) Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act bars actions
founded on contract against Government after the expiry of 3 years from the
date the cause of action arose.  However, before it is concluded that a
cause of  action is time barred, it must be shown when the said cause of
action arose. In the present case the plaint did not concisely plead the
terms of the contract nor the date of its execution as required by O.7 r 1(e).
Therefore, it is difficult to conclude that the plaintiff's cause of action had
been accrued.
However, S.23 Limitation act provides that where there is acknowledgement
of the debt the cause of action is revived from the date of acknowledgement.
However, O.7 r 14(1) requires that where a party whishes to sue on a
document must annex the same to the plaint at the date of filing.  In the
instant case the plaintiff while submitting from the bar that it was in
possession of documents showing that government had acknowledge the
date, the documents were never annexed to the plaint.  Therefore, the
alleged acknowledgement and consequent revival of the cause of action was
not proved.
The submission by the plaintiff that there was a war going on in Arua and
this was a disability preventing the plaintiff to file its action in time, would
not succeed because there was no evidence that the whole of Uganda was
engulfed in war.  Courts in many parts of the country were open.
The action in tort was barred by Legal Notice No.1/86.
Objection upheld.  Plaint rejected.
Kiyaga Francis & ors Vs. Bank of Uganda.
Representation-whether proved that defendant made representation-
ton-whether not pleaded.
Held: O.6 r2 CPR requires that where a party wishes to rely on any
representation made by the other, such party must plead the particulars of
the same.  Herein, the plaintiffs pleaded that the defendant induced the
plaintiffs to opt for the voluntary retirement scheme by representing to the
plaintiffs that their housing loans would not be deducted.  Therefore, the
plaintiffs pleaded the requisite particulars of the representation.
The bank could not plead that it was not intended that the plaintiffs should
act on the representation.  This is because it was not an occasion of social
or domestic relations but business and the plaintiffs acted on the
representation made by the defendant and the defendant was thus bound by
its own representation.
Suit allowed with costs.
Winchester Procurement Ltd Vs. Mega Holdings Ltd.
Privity-whether third party was privy to the contract.
Breach-damages-whether plaintiff may claim interest above a refund
of money had and received.
Held: It is a fundamental principle of the law of contract that no one can sue
or be sued on a contract unless he is privy to the contract.  In this case the
contract was between the defendant and the plaintiff and the defendant
could not rely for his defence against the breach, on third parties who were
not privy thereto.  How the defendant was supposed to procure the cement
was not concern of the plaintiff.
A defendant in an action for recovery of damages in breach of contract is
liable to such damage that was reasonably contemplated at the time of the
execution of the contract, to be the natural consequence of the breach.  In
this case, it was reasonably inferable from the circumstances that the
plaintiff intended to re-sale the cement at a profit.  That means the plaintiff's
loss was more than the money had and revived.  However, since the loss
of the plaintiff was a special damage it had to be proved strictly, which the
plaintiff failed.  However, in the circumstances the plaintiff would be awarded
Ugshs. 2m/= general damages.
Suit allowed with costs.
Chamute Agencies Co. Ltd Vs. Mbale District Administration
Trade usage-whether the doctrine of trade usage established where
defendant some times took delivery to goods not formally ordered for.
Estoppel by conduct-whether established where Defendant took
delivery of some goods not formally ordered for and rejected others
on the ground that there were not ordered for.
Breach of contract-damages quantum for refusal to take delivery
of goods duly supplied.
Held: Since the enactment of the Local Government (Resistance Councils)
Statute 1993, Districts ceased being referred to, as District Administrations
instead are to be referred to as District Councils.  Therefore the suit was in
the wrong name but Court was to as District Councils.  Therefore the suit
was in the wrong name but Court was empowered by O.1r10 CPR to
substitute the name of the party with the correct one.
A trade usage is established where there is a practice among people who
normally deal in a particular line of business and the practice is generally
known to all persons who normally enter into that relationship. In the present
case the plaintiff had failed to prove that there was a trade usage of issuing
suppliers with LPO's after the delivery of tendered goods merely that had
happened on some occasions.
However because the defendant represented to the plaintiff that it could
supply and receive the LPO on delivery and that was a clear intention on the
part of the defendant that the plaintiff should act upon the representation
believing in its truth and actually the plaintiff did indeed act upon the
representation, by the doctrine of equitable estoppel, the defendant was
established from denying the contract.
The measure of damages for breach of contract where the buyer refuses to
accept some of the goods, is the difference between the contract price and
the market price.  In the instant case there is no market price since the
goods, i.e. the assessment forms are peculiarly designed for the defendant.
Therefore, the measure of damages for breach of contract is the contract
price, i.e. Ush. 22 million, which was the value of the assessment forms.
Suit allowed with costs.
Ruth Omara Atubo Vs. Uganda Land Commission.
Enforceability-mistake-whether contract was unenforceable because
of the mistake on the part of the defendant.
Breach - Damages-quantum
Held: A Contract can only be made on account of mistake if the mistake
was due to ambiguity or if special circumstances exist to render the mistake
of the defendant excusable or where the plaintiff must heave known of the
defendants' mistake at the execution of the contract.  And where the
defendant cannot rely on any excuses and the mistake is merely the result
of his own carelessness, he cannot avoid performance of the contract by
merely pleading mistake.  In the present case the defendant pleaded
mistake but did not give evidence to show that the plaintiff contributed
thereto.  Therefore the mistake was solely by the defendant and therefore
the lease was not void.
S.56 of the Registration of Titles Act provides that a Certificate of Title is
conclusive evidence that the person named therein is the proprietor and
S.184 Registration of Titles Act provides that impeachment of a Certificate
of Title as in this present case must be based on proof of fraud against the
registered proprietor in a Court action.  Therefore the Registrar of Titles had
no power to cancel the plaintiffs Certificate of Title without an Order of Court.
Therefore the plaintiff was entitled to compensation from the defendant to the
tune of the open market value of the suit Land plus her expenditure on the
suit of the Land as special damages.
Since the plaintiff suffered inconvenience and mental anguish as a result of
the cancellation of her Certificate of Title she was entitled to Ush. 6 million
as General Damages.
Suit allowed with costs.
Abdalla Faraj Vs. Ali Omar & Odimbe Advocates.
Legality-Ss.3 & 4 Illiterates Protection Act-failure by Advocate to
certify that he was the author of the document, which relates to the
illiterate-whether-therefore contract illegal and unenforceable.
Held: S.4 Illiterates Protection Act requires that the author of an agreement
where an illiterate is a party must certify on that document that he is author
thereof and appendage his full name and address after explaining the
contents of the document claiming that he was not party to the contents
thereof.  The Court can only resolve the contents in favour of the literate if the
literate fulfilled the requirements of S.4 of the Illiteratates Protection Act.
It was not enough for the 2nd defendant as Advocate to subscribe his
signature as witness and his firms stamp.  He should have gone further to
certify explicitly that he was the author of the agreement, in which the 2nd
defendant failed.
The Advocate would pay 60% of the costs and damages.
Ush. 50m/- would be awarded as damages for deprivation of business.
Case allowed with costs.
Dhushime Henry Vs. S.M. Tours & Travel Ltd
Breach of hire contract-damages-quantum
Held: In applying "Aguis V. G.w. Colliery Co. [1899] 1 QB 413, the measure
of damages is what would have been contemplated of a reasonable man,
when the contract was made, as the probable result of the breach thereof.
In the instant case the plaintiff was clearly entitled to the repair costs, the
balance on the hire per day for the days the vehicle was under repair, this
discounted by a factor of 30% to allow for the imponderables.  This not with-
standing, the plaintiff was further entitled to general damages of Ush.1.5M/-
for breach of contract for the inconveniences suffered by the plaintiff.
Case allowed with costs.
Pyrari Shunji Ganyi & 3 ors Vs. Coffee Development Authority
Sale of land and execution of transfer-deferment of payment of
purchase price-whether contract not binding.
Held: Once a transfer is executed there is a binding contract inter-parties
and the time to register the transfer is not of essence.  In the instant case
the sale of the property and execution of transfer were concluded before the
expulsion Decrees came into force.  Therefore the appellants did not have
the property to be expropriated as the property had passed to the purchasers
and in the same vein the appellants could not repossess the property, as
they had no interest therein.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
M/S Afro Print Ltd Vs. The New Vision Printing & Publishing
Corporation.
Breach - implied term-whether term may be implied so that
machinery is provided for carrying out the intention of the parties-
whether term may be implied to give business efficacy to the
contract-whether defendant breached implied term.
Breach-fundamental breach, "Tiger Night Guard Services Vs.
Opoka & Co. Ltd" whether fundamental breach same as breach of
implied term.
Concurrent or alternative liability in tort whether tenable-whether
excluded by time limit on tort.
Held: In "Tiger Night Guard Services Vs. Opoka & Co. Ltd", [1978] HCB 156,
it was held that a party who alleges and proves a fundamental breach of the
terms of a contract is at liberty to terminate that contract.  However the
instant case was not about termination of a contract but about breach of an
implied term and not even an express term of the contract. Case
distinguished.
Courts will imply terms in contracts providing the machinery to carry out the
intention of the machinery to carry out the intention of the parties.  While the
court is grafting an implied term of a contract it must not do so arbitrarily,
capriciously or forcefully, but must rely upon the requirements or dictates of
some applicable law.  In the present case the plaintiff did not adduce such
a law yet on the other hand the defendant has stated that if a term were to
be implied that the defendant should not publish the news as it were in this
case it would be country to the right and freedom of the defendant of
expression enshrined in the constitution.  Public policy dictates that no term
of a contract whether express or implied should require the parties to do an
unlawful act.  Therefore the doctrine of the "implied term to provide a
machinery for carrying out the intentions of the parties" was not applicable.
The efficiency doctrine states that court may imply a term that is necessary
in the business sense to give efficacy to the contract.  This kind of implied
term is something so serious and obvious that it goes without saying, a term
the court will hold that the parties must have intended it to form part of their
contract through not expressed.  However, the test for the application of the
doctrine is the test "officious bystander" i.e., if at the time the parties were
making the contract an officious by stander had asked the parties whether
such a term (in the present case whether the defendant should not publish
case it is obvious that because of their conflicting interests the parties
would not have agreed as to the obviousness of the term.  Therefore the
"efficacy" doctrine was not applicable because of the obvious conflicting
interests of the parties in the present case.
Our Law recognizes the notion of concurrent or alternative liability in tort and
contract and the plaintiff has the liberty to choose the cause of action that
appears to be the most advantageous to him in respect of any particular
legal consequence.  However, this must not permit the plaintiff to circumvent
or escape a contractual exclusion or limitation of liability for the act or
omission that would constitute the tort.  In the instant case the plaintiff had
the option to sue in tort for misfeasance since the defendant had clearly
bungled his business but as per S.21(1) of the Civil Procedure and Limitation
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, his cause of action in tort was time barred
since the defendant was a scheduled corporation.
Suit dismissed.  Each party to bear own costs.
COPYRIGHT
Attorney General Vs. Sanyu Television
Infringement thereof - whether proved.
Held: O.27, r. 10 CPR provides that a person carrying on business in a
name or style other than his own may be sued in such name or style.  In
the instant case, the respondent, Sanyu Television has so clothed its
outside person with all the indicia and trappings of the legal entity as to be
indistinguishable from one by conducting all its business in the name of
Sanyu Television belongs is International Television Network Ltd, that name
would be joined as the second defendant.
Secondly even if Court did not apply O.27, r.10 its hands to do justice
against Sanyu Television could not be tied since O.1, r 10 (2) empowers
Court to substitute or add parties.  Since according to the facts of the instant
case the parent organization to which Sanyu Television belongs is
International Television Network Ltd, that name would be joined as the
second defendant.
Application for the injunction allowed. Second defendant added, with costs.
CRIMINAL LAW
Ocoke Francis Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code whether malice aforethought
established.
Held: The failure of the trial judge to compile a memorandum of agreed
facts did not occasion a miscarriage of justice since there was other
evidence adduced at the trial.
There was no sufficient evidence to establish malice aforethought.
The evidence for the defence on the issue of accident was quite
contradictory and unworthy of belief and therefore be rejected.
Looking at the evidence as a whole the degree of negligence was so
high as to establish the offence of manslaughter.
Wamala William Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the penal Code Act - whether conviction based
on fanciful theories or attractive reasoning and adduced - intention
to kill - whether nature of the blow inflicted is evidence of intention
to kill.
Held: The trial judge was of the view that the Panga, which loomed
large in the testimony of the key eye witness could have been used.
So, his theory as to the use of the Panga was not far fetched as to
appear fanciful theories or attractive reasoning but on evidence
adduced before him.
A person who inflicts a heavy blow on another person causing grievous
harm has intention to kill and therefore since the appellant inflicted
upon the deceased at a deep cut he intended to kill him.
The fact that all witnesses were relatives did not call for the
corroboration of their evidence.
Andrew Isingoma Vs. Uganda.
Murder - whether established beyond reasonable doubt - whether
malice aforethought established.
Held: The admission of the evidence of the child of tender years
irregular since the trial judge held neither a voui dire nor warned
himself but in the light of other corroborative evidence on record, this
irregularity was not fatal.
The admission of the post mortem report from a Doctor other than the
one who performed it was not fatal since the appellant was
represented and his counsel cross-examined the Doctor.
Common intent in the murder of the deceased was established by the
confession of the appellant implicating the co-accused in the murder
and their being found together at a home eating from which home the
stolen bicycle and blood stained clothes were found.
The vouir dire had proved that the confession was voluntary and
correctly admitted and corroborating it was not lawful necessary,
thought there was ample evidence to corroborate.
Where the appellant was found possession of recently stolen property
belonging to the deceased it was corroborative of the fact that the
appellant was guilty of the murder of the deceased.
Rushoma Thomas Vs. Uganda.
Theft of cattle c/s 245 and 255 of the penal code Act -ingredients
of theft appeal - duty of appellate court - severity of sentence -
whether appeal able in supreme court - Alibi - duty of prosecution
to disprove it- identification - whether properly done.
Held: The prosecution had proved that it was the appellant who had
taken the cattle and that it was with intent to deprive them permanently
of their owner.
The appellant court made extensive evaluation of the evidence and
arrived at the same conclusion as the trial court.
The second appellate court would not interfere with the concurrent
finding of fact by the trial and first appellate courts.
Kanalusasi George Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The admission by the appellant of killing the deceased did not
weaken his plea of guilty and therefore the prosecution still had to
discharge its burden to prove that the killing was with malice
aforethought.
Since the prosecution did not adduce evidence to contradict the
appellant's defence of self-defance the appellant's account should have
been accepted.
Donozio Kiiza Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether prove.
Held: The inconsistency in the date of the incident was not of serious
consequence since it did not prejudice the appellant in his defence.
That taking into account that the identification circumstances were
poor the trial judge erred in relying on such a single, identification
witness.
The learned trial judge erred is not addressing himself to the need to
establish a common intention between the appellant and the gang in
which he was seen.
Mugisha Joseph Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act -circumstantial evidence -
whether sufficient for a conviction -assessors - whether trial
continuing with one assessor is a nullity.
Held: Counsel for the appellant misconstrued the provisions of the law
regarding assessors.  The interpretation Decree required that reference
to the plural must be construed as referring to the particular. Therefore
"assessor" could also mean "assessor".
The deceased persons evidence has been amply identified by the
witnesses who were relatives of the deceased.
The circumstantial evidence left no doubt whatsoever that the
deceased persons had died at the hands of the appellant who killed
them because they were implicating them with the death of one
Mariya, thereby with malice aforethought.
Kataka James Vs. Uganda.
Attempted smuggling c/s 301 D(1) of the Penal Code Act -
evidence - burden and standard of proof - proximity material in
customs officers.
Held: The evidential burden as imposed upon the appellant was
discharged when the appellant gave a probable explanation that the
goods were destined to Iganga and Jinja in Uganda.
The law requires that all the evidence and facts should point to the
guilt of the accused.  In the instant case it could not be maintained there
was an attempt to smuggle goods to Kenya.  Proof of smuggling goods
entails proof of an overt act and proximity to the border of the country
where the alleged smuggling of the goods is to take place is very
material.
A mere act of preparation for commission of an offence is not enough.
In the instant case the offence of smuggling is not proved by the acts
of loading the goods on the trailer and the driving of the trailer to Lubiri
in Kampala because these acts were not sufficiently proximate to the
commission of smuggling the goods to Kenya.  The proximate
principle is material in customs offences.
Kalyowa Moses & 3 ors Vs. Uganda.
Aggravated robbery c/s 272 and 273 of the Penal Code Act and
murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act -whether it is the appellants
who committed the offences.
Held: The circumstantial evidence that would otherwise implicate the
first appellant as outline by the learned trial judge fell short of
irresistibly pointing to the guilt of the first appellant and to no other
reasonable hypothesis.
A confession by a co-accused can only be used to lend credence and
strength to other evidence already on record against the co-accused
which only falls short by a very narrow margin of the standard of proof
necessary for a conviction.
The admission of the theft of the property by the appellants and the
blaming of the first appellant for the murder amounted to accomplice
evidence which evidence was of the weakest kind and could only be
used to lend assurance to the evidence against the appellant.
Uganda Vs. Kizza Ephraim & another.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - submission of no case to
answer-establishment of a prima facie case.
Held: A submission of no case to answer may be properly upheld
where the evidence as presented to court, any reasonable court cannot
call upon the accused to stand defense.
A Prima facie case cannot be made out where at the close of the
prosecution case evidence hangs on a mere possibility, contradictions.
Muzoora Rafairi Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s of the Penal Code Act -whether the intent to kill by the
appellant proved.
Held: The prosecution failed to show that the appellant formed the
specific intent to kill because it is strange that the appellant would just
walk into his father's house and hack him to death in the manner
described by the prosecution without reason.  Therefore the conviction
of murder was unsafe.
Uganda Vs. Waswa Moses.
Burglary and theft c/s 281(2) and 252 of the Penal Code -plea of
guilty - confirmation of sentence.
Held: The words used by the accused only amounted to a plea of guilty
to the court of theft only and not burglary which involved "breaking" and
"entering".  But this anomaly had been corrected when the prosecution
explained to the accused the charge in detail and the accused replied
"facts correctly".
For purposes of deterring from further communication of the offences
the sentencing of the magistrate would be confirmed.
Wandera David Vs. Uganda.
Stealing by a servant c/ss 257 and 258 of the Penal Code Act -
sentencing - young offender sentenced to 19 months imprisonment
whether sentence unlawful.
Held: A magistrate's court shall not pass a sentence of imprisonment
of any person who is in the opinion of the court under the apparent age
of 18 years.  The court shall when in its opinion that have regard all the
circumstances including the character and gravity of the offence, if no
other method is appropriate order him to be detained for safe custody
pending an order by the Minister under the provisions of s. 190 (2) of
the Magistrates Courts Act, in such a place as it thinks fit…
The birth certificate produced was a photocopy which was not certified
therefore the court should have proceeded to make its own independent
inquiries.
Since the state did not contest the appeal and the appellant had been
custody for about 3 months, and the subject matter of the charge was
recovered, the sentence 19 months should be substituted for a caution.
Lukwago Joseph Vs. Uganda.
Burglary c/s 281 (2) of the Penal Code Act 3 years sentence of
imprisonment - whether excessive where accused pleads guilty
and is a first offender inter-alia.
Held: Whether the complaint was already committing a breach of the
Foreign Exchange Control regulations should not excuse the
appellant or anyone else to steal the foreign currency.  And moreover
he had stolen credit cards inclusive.
Since the accused had pleaded guilty to the charge thus saving court's
time, and prayed for mercy, these factors were mitigating as far as the
severity of sentence was considered.
Bagamuhunda Reuben Vs. Uganda.
Murder -whether proved -provocation - whether defense available.
Held: The learned trial judge erred in presuming the deceased dead
since the evidence of this left some doubt.
The discrepancies in the evidence about the arson were minor and
therefore the appellant was rightly convicted.
The defence of provocation was not available because the appellant's
brother had long died before the crime.
Obong Richard s/o Ocen Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The learned trial Judge's omission to examine PW3 properly on
whether she understood the nature of an oath was not fatal since her
evidence was corroborated.
The deceased's assault of the appellant was sufficient to constitute
provocation.
The defence of self-defence would not avail the appellant as he was
clearly not in any danger when he struck the deceased fatally as he
had already disarmed him.
Uganda Vs. Kasujja Emmanuel.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act identification of accused
defense of alibi - discrepancy in evidence of prosecution -whether
deceased dead.
Held: Accused was identified properly by the prosecution witness
because there was candle light, the daughter of the deceased shouted
his name and the accused never escaped from the scene of the crime.
The discrepancies within the evidence of the prosecution were minor
and explainable.
The doctor who performed the antopsy and the Police who made the
the sketch map of the scene of the crime and other witnesses proved
that the deceased was dead.
The fact that the accused used a fatal implement and the manner he
used it by cutting several times, it left no doubt that he intended to kill
the deceased and this established malice aforethought.
Uganda Vs. (1) Byansi Sempson & anor.
Robbery c/s 272 and 273 (2) of the penal Code Act - whether
proved.
The admitted evidence contained absolutely nothing to connect the
accused with the offence in the remotest way since no mention is
of any of them in the summary of evidence.
The exhibits tendered were not marked as required by law and there-
fore it was difficult to say whether the exhibits were partly the stolen
goods.
A submission of no case to answer is properly made and upheld where
there is no evidence to prove an essential element of the offence and
or when the evidence adduced has been discredited. In this case the
prosecution evidence was utterly insufficient to place the accused
on their defence.
Okitoi Epilu Vs. Uganda.
Traffic and Road Safety Act, Ss.115 (1) and 5 (b) and 128 (9) and
138(2)(9) - one equivocal pleas of guilty - sentence - whether
excessive.
Held: The Magistrates Courts (Amendment) Act 4/85 amended S.192
(d) and provided that for any fine not exceeding shs.2000/= to be met
with a maximum period of imprisonment not exceeding seven days in
default. Therefore the default sentence of one month would be set
aside and substituted with 7 days.
Any fine exceeding shs.2000/= but not exceeding shs.10,000/= carries
a maximum of one month's imprisonment in default.  The sentence of
six months is illegal and should be substituted with one month.
Boona Majidu Vs. Uganda
Aggravated robbery c/s 272 and 273 (2) of the Penal Code Act -
conviction basing on identification entirely whether there is enough
evidence to safely convict.
Held: Inspite of the inconsistencies in the evidence of the Prosecution
the witnesses were credible and given the fact that the witnesses were
testifying to facts that had happened more than two years back the
inconsistencies were explainable.  Therefore the prosecution evidence
would be believed.
The trial court must satisfy itself before making a conviction based on
identity that the identification was not erroneous.  The two prosecution
witnesses had known the appellant before and the candle light and
moon light in the kraal helped the prosecution witnesses to identify the
appellant properly.
Specioza Nabasumba Vs. Uganda.
Receiving stolen property c/s 298 (1) of the Penal Code Act
whether proved.
Held: The evidence being wholly circumstantial it did not prove the
charge beyond reasonable doubt since there were other probable
explanations.
Uganda Vs. Sulaiman Ndamagye.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code - whether proved murder c/s 183
of the Penal Code Act - whether proved on circumstantial evidence.
Held: The facts and the circumstances looked at together are in-
compatible with the innocence of the accused and irresistibly point to
causing the deceased's death with malice aforethought.
Wagama Amisi & 2 ors Vs. Uganda
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - aggravated robbery c/s
272 and 273 of the Penal Code Act -accused inflicting multiple
bruises on different parts of the body -whether assault occasioning
actual bodily harm or grievous harm.
Held: Though a conviction can be founded on the dying declaration
courts have almost invariably always insisted on need to corroborate
the dying declaration.  This is more so in the instant case where the
identification circumstances were poor and therefore the deceased
could have been mistaken in his identification.
Business, however multiple could not amount to main or dangerous
harm and therefore such injury could not be classified as grievous
bodily harm.
It is a settled Law that mere presence at the time of the commission
of the crime does not make a person a party to the crime without
participation in some way.
Theft was a minor and cognate offence to robber and therefore an
accused could be convicted thereof when not charged therewith.
Uganda Vs. Paddy Kalenzi.
Kidnap with intent to murder - whether victims being arrested by
soldiers and taken to barracks and later murdered, at the spur of
the accused - whether kidnap with intent to murder by accused.
Common intention - the accused's instigation of soldiers to arrest
and later murder the decease - whether there was sufficient
evidence of common intention between the an accused.
Held: Since the victims were arrested at the instigation of the accused
and the allegations made by the accused to the soldiers that the
deceased were guerillas, the accused was fully aware of the
consequences of such allegations.
It was not necessary that the accused should make a prior arrangement
with the soldiers. It was enough that the accused had a common
intention with the assailants and the accused's action especially in
point out the deceased to the assailants would help the inference that
the accused had a common intention with the assailants in murdering
or exposing the deceased to the danger of being murdered.
Uganda Vs. Kulabako Night Jennifer.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act -whether proved burden of
proof - presumption that a homicide is unlawful, unless circumstances-
make it excusable.
Held: The presumption is that every homicide is unlawful, unless
excusable.  In the instant case  apart from the prosecution
proving that the deceased died as a result of the rapture of the uterus
there is no irresistible evidence that it was the accused's beating of the
deceased that caused the death of the deceased.
In absence of any medical report indicating the nature of injuries
sustained by the deceased as a result of the assault, the only possible
offence that the accused committed is common assault.
Magezi Joseph Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved. Murder -
provocation whether defence of provocation negative by
prosecution.
Held: Looking at all the evidence in this case, it was as likely to be a
case of provocation as was not and the benefit of doubt would be in
favour of the appellant.
Kalisit Sebugwawo Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act -whether proved.
Held: The repetition of a dying declaration by different witnesses is not
corroboration but since the learned Trial Judge based his conclusion of
the truthfulness of the dying declaration on the fact that the identification
circumstances of the appellant by the deceased were good and looking
at other evidence on the record, the dying declaration had been
corroborated.
In spite of the fact that no weapon was produced in court there was
ample evidence from the witnesses to show that a spear was used.
Rujumba Joseph Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: There was no evidence that the stick alleged to have caused the
death was described to the doctor or observed actually by him,
performing the post mortem examination, that the stick was consistent
with the nature and time of the assault and its estimation of the mens
rea of the accused.
The death was an unusual result from such a blow as described.  That
being the case, there was not the requisite mens rea murder within the
working of s.186 of the Penal Code.  It was at most a case of
manslaughter.
Kanyolo Patrick & ors Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The evidence on record as a whole was enough to fovaourably
identify the accused.
The learned trial Judge properly cautioned himself before accepting the
evidence of co-accused and accomplice by having this evidence
corroborated in material particulars.
SGT. Shaban Birumba & anor Vs. Uganda.
Aggravated robbery c/ss.272 and 273 (2) of the Penal Code Act-
whether proved beyond doubt where the pistol alleged to have been
used in the robbery was neither produced in court nor testified.
Held: Since the investigation of the case did not include proof that the
pistol was much a weapon capable of causing death, aggravated robbery
had not bee proved beyond reasonable doubt that the pistol was deadly
weapon.  Therefore the case fell within the ambit of s.273(1) (b) of the
Penal Code, i.e. robbery.
An limitation fire arm, or one unloaded, or otherwise incapable of
discharging any shot cannot be deadly weapon within the meaning of
s.273 (2) of the Penal Code.  It is at best a dangerous weapon
according to s.31(5) of the Fire Arms Act.
That Penal code provisions must be interpreted strictly and where there
is any doubt as to the meaning of a given provision the doubt must be
resolved in the favour of the accused.
W. Rushegyera Vs. Uganda.
Reckless driving of motor vehicle c/s 118(1) (a) and s.65(1)(a), 66
of the traffic and Road safety Act - and s.143 of the MCA. whether
sentence of 6 months imprisonment was illegal, high handed and
ill motivated.
Held: That in the absence of any reason advanced as to why he
administered both, the sentence was harsh in the circumstances.
Since the appellant has had his permit cancelled, he paid the fine in full
and served more than half of the imprisonment sentence, the sentence
of he Court below is set aside and substituted with a sentence equivalent
to what he has so far served.
Uganda Vs. Juma Rukuma Masudi Isabirye.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - accused entering house
and shot the deceased.
Held: Where the accused sets up a defence of alibi he does not
assume responsibility of proving it.  It is incumbent on the prosecution
to destroy or disprove it by adducing evidence placing him at the sconce
of the crime at the material time.
Where the accused are jointly charged the prosecution must either
prove common intention as provided under section 22 of the Penal Code
Act or each accused is a principal offender under section 21 of the
Penal Code.
In law for an act to amount to an attempt some actus reus must have
been done by the accused.  The text to apply is the common law
principle of proximity as it was reiterated in the case of Everest Mugabi
V. Uganda (1976) HCB 124.  The prosecution must prove both an overt
act sufficiently proximate to the intended offence.
As regards attempted murder, an overt act and positive intention to
cause the death must be established Republic Vs. Luseru Wandera s/o
Wandera (1948) 5 EACA 101.
In deciding whether common intention exists the court is guided by
both evidence and conduct of the accused.  Common intention may be
inferred from presence, conduct and omission by anyone of the accused
to disassociate himself from attack.  Actual participation is not essential.
It is for the prosecution to establish the guilt of the accused beyond
reasonable doubt.  The grave discrepancies and inconsistencies in the
evidence of the prosecution witness especially than of P.W.3, Nuru
Mutesi and P.W. 4 which were unresolved and the minor numerous
deliberate lies on the part of the prosecution witnesses coupled with
the failure to produce the first report to the names of the accused and
the first report of the names of the accused and the inordinate deal to
record statements from the chief witnesses.  It would be usage to
base a conviction on the prosecution evidence.
Uganda Vs. Harry Musumba.
Murder contrary to the provisions of section 183 of the Penal Code
Act - factors to be beyond reasonable doubt in a murder case.
Held: The burden of proof in criminal cases, with the exception of a few,
lies on the prosecution and that burden never shifts to the defence.
R V. Mazabia Bin Mukomi Republic (1941) 8 EACA 85, Woolimington
In a murder case like one under consideration the prosecution must
prove beyond reasonable doubt inter-alia, the following:
(a) that a human being was killed.
(b) that the killing was unlawful
(c ) that the killing was with malice aforethought
that the accused participated in the killing of that human being.
Sarapio Tinkamanyire Vs. Uganda.
Kidnap with intent to murder s.235 (1)(9) of the Penal Code Act
whether ingredients proved.
Held: Unless there is some particular issue or conduct raised by the
defence that requires a preliminary decision, it preferable that while
writing the judgment for the judge to proceed with the setting out the
prosecution case first as it is stated, by the witness, then to set out the
defence case as set out by the appellant and his witnesses, it any and
subsequently to indicate the court's findings on the whole of the evidence
In the instance case the learned the judge's approach however
undesirable did not cause him to come to the wrong conclusions, as
his conclusions were supported by the evidence.
The learned trial judge's direction to the assessors as to the ingredients
of the offence of kidnapping with intent to murder was misleading
because he seemed to understand that the ingredients have an intention
to murder the victims or to put him in danger of being murdered.
The ingredients of the offence of kidnap with intention to murder c/s235
(1)(a) of the Penal Code are not that the appellant has formed the
intention to murder - victims or to put them in danger of murdered.
The section provides a broader intent than the intent to murder or to put
in danger of being murdered because it states; "may be murdered or be
disposed of as to be murdered".  However, on all the evidence the facts
proved that the appellant disposed of the victims so as to put them in
danger murdered.  Therefore, the learned judge's misconduct on did not
occasion a miscarriage of justice.
The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he held hat the
appellant was guilty of aggravated robbery merely because he had been
seen by the complainants stab and kidnap two victims with intent to
have them murdered at about 9.00 am, and when he returned at about
12.00noon and threatened the complainants to part with their money
and they did part with it, the learned trial judge considered the lapse of
3 hours to be "soon after" and then deemed "soon" to be equivalent to
"immediately" as used in s.273 (2) of the Penal Code.  The learned
trial judge mis-conducted himself when he deemed that an act of
violence committed in the course of a kidnapping constituted one
transaction with a threat to kill in a robbery some hours later.
The use of evidence to support the findings that the appellant committed
the offence of aggravated robbery.  The use of a deadly weapon was not
sufficiently proximate in time to support a finding of simple robbery.
The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he convicted the
appellant on four counts but instead passed only one sentence, even if
pm courts 3 and four as per his findings, he imposed the mandatory
death sentence, he should have passed sentence on each count.
Uganda Vs. Isingoma Ziresire & ors.
Receiving or retaining stolen property c/ss.298(f) of the Penal Code
Act - whether proved.
Held: To sustain a charge of receiving or retaining the prosecution must
prove theft, possession and guilty knowledge.
Where an accused offers an explanation which might possibly be true
tying to show that he was not possessed of guilty knowledge regarding
the circumstances by which the property said to be stolen came into
his possession then the charge is not proved.
A man who merely handled property which he knew had been stolen
was not necessarily a receiver.  The physical possession had to be
such as to give him control as against the person he was assisting or
if not against him joint control with him.
It is the law that proof of possession of recently stolen articles will
necessarily in every case justify an inference of guilt.  What constitutes
recent possession depends on the nature of the property and
circumstances of the particular case.
The doctrine of recent possession would not be applied where property
alleged to be recently stolen was found on the accused four months
after the alleged theft.  Secondly the goods allegedly stolen were
common households items found in anybody's home.  There was
special about them to justify applying the doctrine.
The accused had offered probable explanations to rebut the imputation
of guilty knowledge.
Richard Ogola Vs. Uganda.
Embezzlement -whether theft minor and cognate to embezzlement.
Held: The offence of theft was minor and cognate to that of
embezzlement as both belonged to the same family.  Theft is minor in
a sense that the gravity of punishment therefore prescribed is minor to
that of embezzlement and the two offences are cognate because both
offences involve a fraudulent taking away of someone's property.
It is not mandatory that the items stated in the charge sheet in an
offence of theft must all be proved in order to convict the accused.
The prosecution need to prove that some of more of the items in the
charge sheet were stolen by the appellant.
The trial magistrate failed to exclude hearsay evidence from his
judgment before finding the appellant guilty of theft since the said
hearsay evidence was incriminating to the appellant, it did occasion of
justice, and was fatal to the conviction.
The conduct of the accused in running away from the scene of the
crime was circumstantial evidence pointing to the guilt of the accused
but it required corroboration.  The only would be corroborative evidence
connecting the appellant with the theft was that one by a person who
was not called to testify.  Therefore there was a break in the chain of
the circumstantial evidence and would not properly be relied upon to
irresistibly point to the guilt of the accused.
It was not proper for the trial Magistrate to require the accused to
challenge the evidence of the prosecution that some thefts occurred.
This tended to put the burden of proof on the accused and a conviction
based on the weakness of the defence instead of the strength of the
prosecution case would not stand.
Uganda Vs. Acca Poline.
Manslaughter - considerations.
Held: The exercise of the power to impose a lesser sentence is guided
by the circumstances in which the offence was committed, and the
antecedents of he accused.
Appeal of guilty, and the time spent by the accused on remand in
custody are matters to be considered in favour of the accused.
Here, the offence was committed with extreme brutality, and concealed
up to the following day.  These circumstances outweigh the mitigating
factors.
Sam Salongo Sepuya Vs. Uganda.
Forcible entry c/s 72 of the Penal Code Act - whether offence
proved where appellant dug and laid pipes on land alleged to
belong to the complainant without his consent.
Held: Mens rea was an essential element to prove forcible entry and the
appellant honestly believed that he had the authority of RCs and water
Board to dig and lay pipes on a land he considered was a public right
of way, which therefore constituted an easement and an encumbrance
on the title of who ever claimed ownership.
David Turyahirayo Vs. Uganda.
Embezzlement - intention to permanently deprive ownership - selling
employer's goods on credit - whether such intention is constituted.
Held: The elements of embezzlement are-being an employee of the
complainant, receiving property by reason of the employment, and
intention to permanently deprive employer of the said property.
The selling of goods on credit was not in itself conclusive evidence an
intention to permanently deprive his employer of them.
In the appellant's signing for cash, the cashier was an accomplice and
the practice requiring collaboration and warning was not followed.
A possibility of access by 2 other people raised doubt on the guilt of
the appellant.
The prosecution did not discharge the burden of proof beyond
reasonable doubt.
No issue of witness summons was improper.
Mohammed Yasin Sekajolo Vs. Uganda.
Attempted murder - complainant arm badly cut with a pang -
maimed and could have bled to death - dangerous weapon used-
offence of attempted.
Held: The appellant was properly convicted but the sentence was
excessive and it would be reduced to 6 years.
Appeal against conviction dismissed.
Esso Standard (u) Ltd Vs. Mike N.Nabudere.
Conversion - whether when given facts disclose both an offence and
a Civil wrong, criminal proceedings take precedence.
Stare decisions-whether it was necessary for court in Uganda to
over-rule the common law principles of the precedence of criminal
proceedings over civil proceedings.
Held: The plaintiff petroleum company did not seek compromise with
the defendant to the prejudice of public justice because his demand for
damages in the civil court did not in any way prejudice the criminal
proceedings in the criminal court.  There was no justification in the
plaintiff's action being stayed pending determination of the criminal case
because the plaintiff had not compromised with the defendant to flout the
criminal case.
Secondly the plaintiff was only to prove his case on the balance of
probability and the resultant judgment had no evidencible value in the
prosecution of the defendant, since then, proof beyond reasonable
doubt was required.  Therefore it was not necessary to stay the civil
case.
Thirdly, the present circumstances in Uganda were such that the police
were taking several months and years before investigations are
complete.  This should therefore not be the basis of pegging the
plaintiff's right of action against the completion of criminal proceedings
as it would defeat justice.
Since the abolition of the distinction between a felony and a
misdemearnour by the Criminal law Act 1967 of England, a defendant
could now be sued for an act that was both civil and criminal, for
damages even before criminal prosecution has taken place.  That
principle should no longer be applicable in Uganda as well.
Charles Dickens Eweku Vs. Uganda.
Forfeiture - accused acquitted of charge of stealing by public serv-
ant -no-satisfactory evidence of ownership of vehicles subject
matter of alleged stealing - whether order of forfeiture of vehicles to
state proper.
Held:  The order of forfeiture, in the circumstances was proper.
Discretions to be exercised honestly and in the spirit of the statute.
"According to his discretion" means according to the rules, reasons and
justice, not private opinion.
Uganda Vs. Yowasi Kiiza.
Robbery c/ss.272 and 273 (2) of the Penal Code Act - Demanding
money with menaces is a minor and cognate offence to robbery.
Held: The circumstances embodies in the major charge of robbery
necessarily imputed the offence of demanding Money with menace as
a minor offence since both offences have as their necessary ingredients,
violence and theft.  The accused demanded money with threats
calculated to force his late uncle to part with his money against his will.
Uganda Vs. Muhammad Kasoma.
Soliciting a bribe or gratification c/ss.1 (a), 5(1) of the prevention of
the corruption Act - whether proved.
Held:  The Chief Magistrate misdirected himself to have concluded that
since a committee of ten officials were to decide on the tender bids the
accused could not make a sole decision.  He failed to appreciate that
at the time the letter of 8th March 1989 was written the Committee or
perhaps the EEC representatives on behalf of the committee, had
decided in favour of the firm from whom the accused was soliciting a
bribe and that the accused could have been claiming the credit for the
award of the tender.  The appeal therefore succeeds since the evidence
shows that the accused had a case to answer.
Salvatano Ayoo Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code - whether proved.
Common intention to commit murder-whether proved.
Provocation -whether allegations of witchcraft were sufficient defence
to a charge of murder.
Held:  At the point somebody intervened to stop the beating of the
deceased and the appellant complained against the intervention and in
fact pushed aside the intervener, at that stage the first appellant could
be said to have associated himself with the cuts of those people who
assaulted the deceased.  He quite clearly had a common intention with
them to kill or to do grievous harm to the deceased.  His appeal against
the conviction must thereby fail.
The trial judge quite correctly considered and rejected a belief in
witchcraft on the part of the first appellant as constituting provocation.
As regards the conviction of the second appellant the trial judge
misdirected himself on the evidence when he held that it was the
second accused who beat the deceased first after declaring that the
deceased would not live on that day.  This is because there was a
contradiction in the evidence of Omin, the only eye witness to the
incident who first asserted in his evidence that it was the second
appellant who first but the deceased then in cross examination he said
it was the first appellant.  The appeal for the second appellant would be
allowed.
Uganda Vs. Ibrahim Seguya.
Finding not guilty under s.71(1) of the Trail on Indictment Decree-
whether tenable when no witness has been called for the
prosecution.
Trial on indictments Decree S.71(1) finding of not guilty thereunder -
whether tenable when no witness has been called for the prosecution.
Adjournment under S.51 (1) of TID-whether properly refused.
Held: S.51(1) of the TID empowers court to postpone or adjourn a trial
to some future date due to reasonable cause like absence of witness
and s.51(2) provides that if the court's discretion is against further
adjournment, then the trial may proceed on available evidence and s.71
(1) of the TID provides that after the prosecution has called its evidence,
the court may if it considers that there is no sufficient evidence that the
accused committed the offence, record a finding of not guilty.  The trial
judge was in order to acquit the accused under S.71(1) of the Decree
basing himself on the insufficiency of evidence on record against the
accused caused by the prosecution's failure to call witness at the date
of trial.  The appeal must thereby fail.
Harry Isiko Vs. Uganda.
Theft c/s 252 penal code Act and obtaining money by false
pretence c/s of the Penal Code Act - whether they may be altar-
native charges.
Held: S.151 of the Magistrate Courts Act, 1970 empowers a court
hearing a charge of obtaining by false pretences to convict on the
alternative charge of theft even though the accused was not so formally
charged.  But this can only be so where the facts of the case support
the theft.  In the instant case the particulars of the false pretence did
not reflect the possible offence of conversion.  The situation could have
only been saved by having theft as alternative charge to appear formally
as such a charge or for the Court to bring it to the attention of the
defence be prepared to this effect.  This was not the case.  Therefore
Court no proper trial on the issues pertaining to the no alleged theft.
Therefore Court misdirected itself to convict the accused on an issue
where there was no proper trial.
Kanyike Abasi Vs. Uganda
Assault with intent to rob c/s 274(1)(2)(b) - whether proved.
Held: The voluntariness or otherwise of a confession may only be
analyzed at the trial within a trial and this is during the prosecutions
case.  If court has however already admitted the confessions because
they were not objected to during the prosecutions case, it is too late to
challenge them in the defence.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself when he allowed the defence to dispute the
admissibility of the confession, which had already been approved.  This
caused or was evidence of confusion.
Uganda Vs. Mukasa Deogratius
Defilement c/s 123 (1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Age of complainant-birth certificate-whether age proved conclusively
when birth certificate was prepared after commencement of criminal
proceedings.
Intoxication-whether defence available.
Held: A birth certificate as per S.72(a) (ii) and (iii) of the Evidence Act is
a public document and therefore it was not necessary to call the
Assistant Registrar General of Births and Deaths to prove its authenticity
and the authenticity of the document would not be vitiated by the fact
that the document was prepared after the commission of the offence
since the particulars appearing on the document were obtained from the
complainant's hospital of birth.
Intoxication may provide a defence by enabling the accused to prove
temporary insanity or by indicating that the accused was incapable of
forming the intention necessary to constitute the offence.  In the instant
case the accused in his won evidence stated that he was not so drank
as to be incapable of forming the intention necessary to constitute the
offence.
The accused by his conduct admitted the offence when he told PW3
that he was not had been told by PW2 that the accused had defiled the
complainant and yet PW3 being a paternal uncle to the complainant
was rightly concerned.  This coupled with the other evidence on record
proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was guilty as
charged.
Uganda Vs. Christopher Kiziito.
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act -whether proved.
Held: There was evidence that the complainant was distressed which
evidence was not challenged.  The distress condition corroborated the
evidence of PW1, the complainant, this is because in sexual offences
the distressed condition of the complainant is capable of amounting to
corroboration of the complainant's evidence.  This, couple with the other
evidence on record, and the fact that the defendant's alibi was rejected,
shows that the prosecution had proved the case against the accused
beyond reasonable doubt.
Moses Bagada Vs. Uganda.
Attempted rape c/s 119 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The appellants conviction was justified because both the
complainant and PW2 knew the accused very well, they had been
drinking together and there was moonlight to identify the accused at the
scene of the crime.
The sentence of 6 years imprisonment with 12 strokes of the cane was
not proper since the appellant was a young offender who was not
supposed to be imprisoned at the time he committed the offence.  The
sentence would therefore be reduced to 4 years imprisonment 6 strokes
of the cane.
Vincent Rwamwaro Vs. Uganda.
Robbery c/s 272 and 273(1) (9) of the Penal Code Act - whether
proved.
Theft c/s 252 of the Penal Code-whether proved.
Held: The existence or otherwise of a grudge between the appellant and
the prosecution witnesses due to the differences based on political
parties was a matter of fact and not law.  Therefore it was not an issue
such as would be determined by the second appellate court.
An accused person should take all reasonable steps to ensure that his
counsel appears for him and if he is unable to appear to offer a
satisfactory explanation to court for his absence.  In the instant case
though the appellant's counsel was absent, the appellant did not furnish
any explanation as to why his counsel was not in court.  Therefore the
trial Magistrate exercised his discretion judicially when he refused an
adjournment because there was no explanation before him as to why
the appellant's counsel was not in court.
The issue that the learned justice of the first appellate court misdirected
himself when he set aside the order of compensation, was an issue that
affected the legality of the sentence and would therefore be considered
even if no cross appeal was preferred.
S.331(2) (b) and (c) of the Criminal Procedure Code empower an
appellate court to vary the sentence imposed by the lower court, even
to specify the amount payable as compensation mandatory after a
convocation for robbery where no death sentence is made.  Therefore the
learned justice of the first appeal misdirected himself when he set aside
the order for compensation on the basis that the order was prejudicial
since it dis not specify the amount of compensation.  Therefore, the
appellant would be ordered to pay shs. 30,000/= to the victim of the
robbery.
Further both the learned justice of the first appeal and the learned trial
Magistrate misdirected themselves when they did not impose the
mandatory order as provided in S.26 of the MCA which provides for an
order of police supervision on the person convicted or robbery. The court
would therefore order that the appellant undergoes police supervision for
a period of 2 years from the date of expiration of his sentence.
Esau Namanda Vs. Uganda.
Perjury c/ss.81 (1) and 91 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
