Held: The conviction of the appellant was illegal as it was contrary to his
constitutional right Art.15(2) (b) (c) to be informed of his offence and to
permit him to prepare his defence.  The conviction would therefore be set
aside. Secondly, the charge of perjury formed a distinct charge from the
material trial and therefore the convict was entitled to be tried by an
independent tribunal.  This had not been the case.
For the accused to be convicted of perjury the discrepancy in the
appellant's evidence must be material to the case or that it affected the
credibility of the appellant.  In the instant case the trial judge did not
show that the discrepancy in the accused's evidence was materials to
the case.
Godfrey Tinkamalirwe & another Vs. Uganda.
Kidnapping with intent to murder c/s 235,(I) (a) of the Penal Code
Act - whether proved - whether intent to murder to be presumed
u/s 235(2) of the Penal Code Act.
Motive-whether relevant and established.
Kidnapping with intent to confine secretly and wrongfully c/s 236 -
whether proved.
Held: Although S.235(2) provides that the necessary intent that the
victim be murdered in the offence of kidnap under s.235(1)(a) and (b), it
may be presumed if the victim is not seen for a period of more than 6
months.  In the instant case the trial judge held that the intent must be
proved and not presumed.  He was entitled to hold so because the victim
had ended up in police custody meaning that the intent had not been
proved and could therefore not be presumed.
Generally speaking, motive is irrelevant in criminal law except in some
exceptional circumstances, such as prosecution for libel where a
defence of fair comment or qualified privilege is raised.  However, motive
is always useful in showing the probable reason for the commission of
the offence.  The existence of a motive makes it more likely that an
accused person did in fact commit the offence.  Therefore, the learned
trial judge directed himself correctly in taking into account the fact that
the victim and the appellant belonged to rival churches.
The summing up to the assessors must not leave room for a reasonable
man to think that the judge did favour one side unfairly.  In the instant
case the assessors were left with the clear impression that they should
find the appellants guilty not on the strength of the prosecution's case
but on the falsity of the appellant's defence.  The trial judge here
misdirected himself misdirected himself.  However, the irregularity did
not accession a miscarriage of justice.
Since the Kidnap did not fall under S.235(1)9a) of the Penal Code, the
appeal must succeed in part.  However, the evidence clearly proved that
the victim was secretly and wrongfully confined after abduction before
being taken to the police station.  Therefore the appellants were guilty of
kidnapping with intent to confine secretly and wrongfully 236 of the Penal
Code.
Professor Isaac Newton Ojok Vs. Uganda
Treason -whether conviction sustainable.
Bias-whether there was a real likelihood of bias or whether there was a
reasonable suspicion of bias.
Held: While Art.73 of the constitution empowered the president to grant
pardon or amnesty, it is clear from the evidence that the appellant was
one of a select few who was to appear in court charged in the treason.
Therefore, the trial judge directed herself correctly on the evidence and
law when she rejected the appellant's plea in arrest of judgment, that
he had been pardoned while on remand.
When the trial judge was invited to disqualify herself on the basis of the
likelihood of partiality in favour of the state on the grounds that she was a
blood sister of the first Deputy Prime Minister, a pillar of the government,
the appellant was alleged to be fighting, she should have made a record
of the application and her decision to refuse the application should have
been reached judicially and recorded.  It was a misdirection on the part
of the trial judge not to have put on record an application of so serious a
nature.
In order to find whether a judicial officer was biased it is necessary to
consider whether there was a real likelihood of bias by considering
whether the judicial officer laboured under a pecuniary or kindred interest.
After the judicial officer has passed that test, then it may be necessary
to verify whether the particular judicial officer's act or conduct satisfied
reasonable persons that the court was impartial and unbiased.  In the
instant case the allegation of kinship interest because it was not he
own brother in court nor was the National Resistance Movement itself in
court directly.  However, a reasonable man taking into account the
learned trial judge's premature findings of fact before the accused gave
his defence would have conclude led the judge was probably biased in
favour of the state consciously or unconsciously.
Uganda Vs. Alfred Akuku.
Rape c/ss.117 and 118 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Intoxication - whether defence available to an accused who admits
having had sex because he was too drunk.
Mistake of fact - whether defence available to an accused who
admits having had sex with the complainant thinking it was his wife.
Consent - whether defence available to an accused whom the
complainant allowed to share a bed with.
Held: The complainant's allowing his brother in law to share a mat with
her was no evidence of consent to the subsequent unlawful sex but
merely a social obligation to him since the complainant had no where
else to prepare a bed for the accused whom she socially obliged to
house.
S.13(4) of the Penal Code Act allows a defence of intoxication where it
can be shown that the accused was so drunk that he could not form the
requisite intention to commit the offence.  The intention required in this
case was an intention to play sex.  As it was shown, the accused
though drunk was able to find the house of his Sister-in-law, the accused
though among several huts, addressed her by name, gained an erection
and jumped over the two children who lay between them to get to the
victim.  The defence of intoxication was therefore not available.
S.10 (1) of the Penal Code Act provides the basis for the defence of
mistake of fact.  The accused must have done the act or omission in
an honest and reasonable but mistaken belief as to the State of things.
In this case the accused contended that he thought he was at home
with his wife.  Of course there is no dispute that the accused was drunk
but he went to the complainant's house whom he called by name and
asked for accommodation.  Under those circumstances, it cannot be
said that the accused acted under a mistaken though an honest and
reasonable belief.  The defence is thereby not available to the accused.
Uganda Vs. Enoch Babumpabuha.
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Consent -whether defence to a charge defilement.
Age-defilement-whether age of the victim may be inferred common sense.
Identification of accused-whether satisfactorily done.
Held: It was no defence to a charge of defilement that the victim was
marriageable age or that she consented.
The evidence of 2 prosecution witnesses to the effect that they had
known the accused for a long time had not been challenged by the
defence, and the accused himself had admitted having had sex with the
complainant. This showed that the accused had been properly identified.
It was enough for court and the assessors to determine that the
complainant before them was obviously under age and this was possible
by common sense.  It was not necessary for the prosecution to labour
to prove that the complainant was below 18 years.
Uganda Vs. Silver Nabugemu.
Theft c/s 245 of the Penal Code Act - whether sentence of 15
months imprisonment for theft of millet valued at shs.600 was
excessive.
Conviction U/S 13(1) MCA - sentencing accused without conviction-
whether sentence lawful.
Held: Though S.13(1) MCA did not expressly mandatorily provide for a
conviction prior to sentencing, it is a mandatory rule of practice that
before court may sentence the accused, it must first record a finding of
guilt, conviction and then sentence.  The trial Magistrate's imposed
sentence was illegal since the accused had not been found guilty and
convicted.
The sentence of 15 months imprisonment would not be supported in view
of the value of the millet alleged to have been stolen.  Even if it were
assumed that the procedure adopted by the trial Magistrate was proper
the sentence of 15 months imprisonment was out of proportion and
excessive.
The trial Magistrate erred in law to have on his own motion declared the
accused a habitual criminal and yet the accused was never invited to
challenge such an allegation.  The proper procedure before sentence
would have been to invite the prosecution to tell court as to the
antecedents and character of the accused and also to invite the accused
to say something in mitigation of sentence.
Uganda Vs. Peter Akuku.
Defilement c/s 123 (1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Indecent assault C/S 122 (1) of the Penal Code-whether proved.
Held: The injuries in the victims vagina and her immediate private parts
as per medical evidence meant that the victim had fallen, or been
abused, or infected or hand had sexual intercourse and it necessary to
rule out all those other factors as cause of the injuries found on the
victim leaving only sexual intercourse and by the accused in order to
convict the accused as charged.
However the medical examination did not show that the victim had any
infection or that she had fallen as the cause of the injuries.  This meant
that it should either be child abuse or sexual intercourse.  The evidence
also ruled sexual intercourse by the accused out.  This left only child
abuse.  The evidence showed that the victim was left with the accused in
good condition was found injured in the immediate presence of the
accused in dubious circumstances.  Therefore the accused was guilty of
indecent assault of the victim c/s 122 (1) of the Penal Code.
Uganda Vs. Alfred Jurunga.
Bail under s.51 (4) TID - application on remand for more that 730
days - whether bailable.
Held: in view of the failure by the prosecution not only to proceed with
the commencement of the commencement of the hearing of the case but
without offering sufficient excuse court was bound to find that the delay
of the trial was unreasonable and warranted the release of the accused
on bail pending trial.  Article 10 (3) (b) of the Constitution demanded a
trial within a reasonable time.
Uganda Vs. Byekwaso.
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the penal code Act - whether proved.
Held: The prosecution for an indictment of defilement must prove unlaw
ful carnal knowledge age of the victim as being below 18 and the identity
of the accused.  In this case, the victim being 6 years only cold not give
a sworn testimony and her evidence required corroboration strongly which
needed not be direct.  The doctor's evidence showed that the victim was
sexually assaulted and the nature of the injuries rules out assault by a
finger.  And the fact that the victim and her brother picked on the
accused as the person guilty of the defilement, who had together
strongly corroborated the victim's testimony that it was the accused who
had sexually defiled her.
Uganda Vs. Christopher Mugisha.
Rape c/ss 177 & 118 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Rape c/s117 & 118 of the Penal Code-medical evidence whether lack
thereof is fatal.
Rape c/s 117 & 118 of the Penal Code - corroboration - whether lack
thereof is fatal.
Identification - single witness-whether sufficient identification.
Held: The accused was correctly identifies without difficulty since it was
during day time, the accused and complainant were neighbours and the
incident complained of endured long enough for the complainant to
identify the accused sufficiently.
Although there was no corroboration, the complainant told court the truth
to its satisfaction and lack of medical evidence was not fatal to the case
of the prosecution in light of the evidence of the prosecution as a whole.
Uganda Vs. Akut Joseph
Embezzlement c/s 257(c ) of the Penal Code Act - whether
sentence of fine of shs.5000/= was lawful and adequate.
Held: The trial Magistrate Grade II had no discretion to impose less than
3 years imprisonment or a fine since the minimum imprisonment
sentence was 3 years and no option of a fine was provided for.  The
sentence was thereby illegal and would be set aside.
Major John Kazoora Vs. Uganda
Embezzlement c/s 257 (a) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Theft c/s 245(5) of the Penal Code - whether exportation proved against
a customer whose account is credited from another account within the
same Bank.
Held: S.86 (d) of the Magistrates' Courts Act requires that the charge
sheet specifically names or describes the co-charged.  However by long
time practice it has become acceptable to mention in a charge that
somebody unnamed and or undescribed is not joined because he is not
available to be joined.  Therefore, the non disclosure did not occasion
injustice to the appellant in as much as  the charge sheet is nor really
evidence.
Considering that ISO is an intelligence organization whose operations
have of necessity to be covert on the evidence of the prosecution, it
could not rule out the possibility that the sh. 12 million was intended for
ISO purposes such as payment to Jane as an ISO agent.  The
prosecution had failed in their evidence to rule out beyond reasonable
doubt that the said money was not meant for an agent.  The trial Chief
Magistrate clearly erred in law and fact when he failed to scrutinize the
evidence of the prosecution.
Rules 10 of the Evidence (Statement to Police Officers) Rules does not
preclude an oral admission to a police officer of relevant rank provided
the suspect is properly cautioned.  However when the accused denied
having made the admission, the trial Chief Magistrate should have held a
trial within a trial to determine whether the admission was really made by
the appellant.  The trial Chief Magistrate misdirected himself when he
accepted as made a confession the appellant had denied, without first
holding a trial within a trial.
The trial Chief Magistrate erred in law to have held that the debiting of
ISO account and crediting of appellant's account on 25th January 1991
constituted theft because the money which is in the bank belongs to the
bank and therefore mere debiting and crediting does not constitute taking
or asportation which is an element in the offence of theft.
Uganda Vs. Mugenyi Godfrey & another.
Murder -whether proved.
Aggravated Robbery c/s 272 and 273(2) of the Penal Code - whether
proved.
Common intention-whether established.
Aiding and abetting-whether proved.
Theft-whether proved-whether necessary to prove all items appearing
in the indictment.
Held: There was no evidence that the deceased had had any injury
leading to bleeding or vomiting blood.  The sample of blood from the
accused revealed that it was similar in group with the blood stain on the
pillow at the scene of the murder.  Since the blood did not come from the
deceased, it came from the accused.  Even though the accused had
repudiated his confession in which he had confessed to have robbed and
murdered the deceased, who in her struggle bit the accused's finger, the
similarity in the blood group corroborated the confession.
Strangulation and suffocation are not mutually exclusive terms because
strangulation invariably suffocation since it involves the blocking of the
flow of blood as well as blocking the trachea or respiration, by pressing
the neck.  Therefore the accused could not take benefit of the alleged
doubt as to the cause of death since the postmortem Report as proved
showed that the deceased died of acute pulmonary edema.  This
necessarily included strangulation or suffocation.
If some assistance or encouragement is voluntarily done with the
knowledge of the circumstances constituting the offence, that is sufficient
to sustain the conviction and it is irrelevant that the assistance was not
given with the motive of encouraging the crime.  In the present case
though there seemed to be no satisfactory evidence that A2 was at the
scene of the crime, the sharing in the loot fully knowing the
circumstances under which the money had been obtained amounted to
assisting or encouraging the crime.  Therefore A2 took part in the
commission of the offence.
Since the accused caused the death of the deceased by suffocation this
was evidence of malice aforethought because the act of suffocating
another means that the person so acting is fully aware of the
consequence of suffocation, death.
It was not necessary to prove all the items listed in the indictment so as
to prove a charge of theft but some of the items proved stolen as listed
suffices.
Uganda Vs. Kayanja Kizito & another.
Robbery c/s 272 and 273 (2) of the Penal Code Act - whether
proved.
Held: The accused had been amply identified by the witness who were
complainants.  This coupled with the fact that property recently stolen
was found on the accused, plus the glaring untruthfulness in their
defenses all strengthened the inference of the guilt of the accused as
the indictment stood.
Sam Lutaya Vs. Uganda.
Attempted murder c/s 197 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Mens rea - attempted murder c/s 197 of the Penal Code - whether proved.
Held: The circumstances favouring a correct identification had been
properly found by the learned trial judge when he considered as proved by
the witnesses that there was bright moon light the witnesses were very
close, the witnesses knew the accused very well before and all of the
witnesses described the accused's clothing in very similar terms.
The trial judge erred in concluding that the appellant had been
unmistakenly identified without first or at all having considered the
accused's defence of alibi.  This offended against the principle of the law
that before a decision of fact is made the evidence must be looked at as
a whole.  However this was not fatal since the second assessor
considered the defence of alibi in his findings and found that it had not
been provide.
The appellant could not be said not to have had the requisite mens rea
when he took part in a gang that invaded the complaint's house and one
of the attackers with common intent discharged a gun at close range at
the complainant.
Ali Fadul Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 of the penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: When the defence made a submission of no case to answer the
trial judge was not entitled to rule that the prosecution had provide its
case beyond reasonable doubt while rejecting the submission.  This
prejudiced the defence case since the trial judge had formed the opinion
that the accused was guilty before hearing his defence and thereby the
accused was not afforded a fair hearing. Appeal allowed - a retrial ordered.
Bernard Akol Vs. Uganda.
Kidnapping with intent to procure a resume c.s 235(b) of the Penal
Code Act - 14years imprisonment -whether sentence excessive.
Held: The accused/appellant was a first offender, therefore, the trial judge
did not impose a maximum sentence, but since the offence was grave
and was being committed frequently at the time, the sentence of 14 years
was proper.  Appeal Dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Lochiling Lokoro
Theft c/s 255 of the Penal Code Act sentence - whether two years
imprisonment excessive.
Held: Imprisonment for 2 years was excessive.  It will be reduced to 6
months.
Uganda Vs. Wabwire Tools & anor
Theft c/s 252 of the Penal Code sentence - whether imprisonment
for 2 1/2 years was excessive.
Held: In absence of proof of previous convictions, the accused could only
be called a first offender and the sentence imposed was excessive. The
sentence would be reduced to 6 months.
Uganda Vs. Emmanuel Byakatonda
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act whether proved.
Held: The prosecution had proved that the accused had been sexually
intercourse by the accused, and that the victim was below eighteen
years.  Therefore the offence of defilement had been proved.
The accused will be sentenced to 14 years imprisonment.
Patrick Akol Vs. Uganda.
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: While ordinarily a child of apparent age of 14 years was a child of
tender years it still remains a matter of the good sense of the court to
decide whether a particular witness was a child of tender years.  In the
instant case the learned trial judge found that Bonny who 14 years was a
reasonably mature person and therefore the learned trial judge was
entitled to admit Bonny's evidence could rely on Bonny's evidence.
Judith who was 13 years old was a child of tender years and it was
invariably necessary to administer a voire dire to her.  Since the trial court
failed to administer a voire dire to her, her evidence was the kind of
evidence not on oath.
The unsworn evidence of a child of tender years is risky to act upon with
out corroboration but the corroboration is not a requirement of the law.
It is for the court to weight the reliability of the evidence of the particular
unsworn witness.
The medical evidence other than providing the rapture of the hymen did
not connect the appellant to the defilement.
The evidence of Judith and Bonny was intrinsically honest and reliable
and of such quality that the court was entitled to act upon it.  Therefore,
the trial judge was correct to convict the accused. Appeal dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Sebunya Ssekaala
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Defilement-age of the complainant - whether proof of the age of
complainant must be documentary.
Held: There is no law requiring proof of age by birth certificate and it was
enough that the parents of the complainant stated what the age of the
complainant was.
Although it was unsafe to convict on uncorroborated evidence of a child
of tender years, in the instant case the child's evidence was been amply
corroborated and moreover the child's evidence was so truthful and did not
require corroboration.
Blasio Sengendo & anor Vs. Uganda.
Embezzlement c/ss252 and 257(c ) of the Penal Code Act -
whether prove - whether because the appellants were employed by
a limited liability company the change should have been under
s.257(b) and not ( c).
Theft - whether small theft was proved-whether fraudulent intentions shown
accomplice - whether witness was an accomplice.
Bias-cancellation of bail-whether court is at liberty to council bail at any
stage.
Bias-whether trial Magistrate was biased.
Held: Although the charge sheet showed that the appellants had been
charged under S.257 (c ) the correct subsection should have been (b)
since the embezzlement with which they were charged concerned a
limited liability company.
Embezzlement is committed by an employee when he steals
property of the employer before the employer acquires either actual or
constructive possession of that property.  In the present case, the
property alleged to have been stolen was already in the custody of the
employer and therefore the offence of embezzlement was not committed.
The offence of theft was committed when the spares were taken out of the
shop even if they were intercepted at the gate but he issue is whether it
were the appellants who stole the spares.  The fraudulent intent was
indicated by the stranger who ran away when he was intercepted with the
spares.  His running away was evidence that he fraudulently intended to
deprive the owner of the property permanently.
An admission is a statement made by the accused, though not amounting
to a confession but contains gravely incriminating facts against the maker.
In the instant case the alleged apologies were not unequivocal as they
were open to different interpretations, one such interpretation being that
they were sorry for a theft to be committed against the company without
their preventing it.
When the trial Magistrate ruled out the possibility that PW3 was not a
credible witness in light of the contradictions in his evidence and should
have admitted his evidence with caution.
It is trial law that invariably circumstantial evidence must be narrowly
examined to avoid a possibility of a fabrication by ruling out co-existing
circumstances reasonably capable of explaining the situation, before
inferring the guilt of the accused.  In the instant case there were several
contradictions in the prosecution case which were not explained away
and his cast doubt on the guilt of the accused.  The circumstantial
evidence was not water tight.
Counsel holding a watching brief has no right to address court in
opposition to a prosecutor although as an officer of court he may inform
court on matters that can assist court while the interest of justice demand.
A trial magistrate has a discretion under S.98 of the Magistrates Court
Act to decide whether or not to recall a witness.  The trial magistrate was
entitled to refuse the recall of the witness and this did not indicate bias on
plot of the magistrate.
The inference of bias must be as to what a reasonable man would think
given the set of circumstances.  It the reasonable man would thing that
the Magistrate did favour one side unfairly at the expense of another than
bias is proved.  In the instant case there was no evidence of a real
likelihood of bias on the part of the Magistrate.
It is not a correct statement of the law that court is at liberty to cancel
bail at any stage.  Evidence in favour of cancellation of bail must be
evidence on oath and the court must decide judiciously that it is justified
in the present case the trial Magistrate erred when she cancelled the
accused's bail on mere speculative information from prosecution.
Appeal allowed.
Police Constable Olera Vs. Uganda.
Defence - whether court found the accused guilty before consider-
considering his defence whether thereby the trial was fatally flawed.
Held: In evaluating the evidence the court is legally bound to evaluate the
whole evidence both for the state and the defence together.  It was not
correct to look at the case for the prosecution separately and then the
defence.  In the instant case the trial magistrate considered the
prosecution's case and by the time she considered the defence case she
had already believed the prosecution.  This occasioned a miscarriage of
justice.  Appeal allowed.
Livingstone Kakooza Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing - whether lack of remorse after conviction was a proper
principle to take into account while sentencing.
Sentencing-manslaughter c/s 182 Penal Code -whether sentence of 20
years imprisonment was a life sentence-whether a life sentence was
excessive for a first offender convicted of manslaughter.
Sentencing-life imprisonment S.49(7) imprisonment Act-whether a
sentence of 20 years was life imprisonment.
Held: S.49 (7) Prisons Act Provides that imprisonment for life shall be
deemed to be twenty years.  Since the accused had been on remand for
2 years, the sentence of 18 years amounts to life imprisonment.  This was
manifestly excessive for a first offender and would be reduced to 10 years
imprisonment.
The appellant maintained his innocence even after conviction and that is
why he appealed.  Therefore, it is not proper for a trial court to take into
account lack of remorse after conviction when sentencing a convict
because remorseless or otherwise should not have a bearing on the
potential appeal of the appellant.  Therefore, the trial court erred in
applying a wrong principle of the law while sentencing the accused, when
the court took into account lack of remorse on the part of the accused.
Mukwaya Mannasse Vs. Uganda.
Murder c/s 183 penal code Act and aggravated robbery c/ss 272
and 273.
Murder c/s 183 Penal Code and aggravated robbery c/ss 272, and 273.
Alibi-burden, proof-whether accused has burden of proof to disprove alibi.
Recent possession-conviction-whether doctrine of recent possession
correctly applied where accused is alleged to have robbed a motor vehicle
and subsequently arrested with it.
Held: It is trite law that when an accused person sets up an alibi he does
not thereby assume any burden of proving its truth.  It is the prosecution
to disprove or destroy the alibi. The learned trial Judge thereby misdirected
herself to have argued that the accused needed to raise a doubt in
court's mind by producing duplicate receipts so as to establish the truth
of the alibi.
Sula Kasiira Vs. Uganda.
Theft - as potation - whether theft proved where the accused too
robbed a motor vehicle and stole the valuable property if contained
and abandoned the motor vehicle.
Compensation robbery u/s.273(3) Penal Code -whether orders for
compensation properly imposed, where trial court ordered conviction to
pay money value of stolen items.
Held: There was evidence to suggest that both identifying witnesses had
ample time and opportunity to observe their assailants at the scene so as
to enable them to recognize them on the identification parade.  The
accident took place in the early hours of the morning about 7.30 am and
it was not dark.  Therefore, conditions for proper identification existed.
Fore theft to be proved there must be what amounts in law to an
aspiration, i.e. the carrying away of the complainants goods without the
complainant's consent.  In the case before us the learned trial judge
correctly made a judgment of the theft, because, the complainant's cash
of Ush 4 million, some rolls of textile, video cassettes, and the pick up
where the items were loaded had been assorted or carried away from the
complainants by the accused.
The sentence of 10 years imprisonment was not excessive because the
offence with which the appellant was convicted carried a maximum
sentence of life imprisonment, and moreover, the appellant was a police
officer who was supposed to enforce the law and protect people and their
property against criminals.  Here he was doing the very opposite.  The
sentence of 10 years was not excessive.
S.274(A) of the Penal Code Act provides for corporal punishment for the
offence of simple robbery. It is at the discretion of the trial court as to how
many canes may be given to the convict.  Therefore this ground of appeal
had no merit, the trial court having in its discretion sentenced the
appellant to 6 stokes of the cane.
S.123 Trial on Indictment Decree provides for an order of police supervision
for a maximum period of 5 years whenever a person is convicted of simple
robbery under S.272 of the Penal Code and sentenced to a term of
imprisonment lesser than life.  Into the instant case the order was for 4
years.  The appellate court would not interfere with such a powerful order.
Appeal dismissed.
Fred Sabahshi Vs. Uganda.
Manslaughter c/s 182 Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Prima-face case-manslaughter whether trial court correctly put accused
to his defense-whether there was a prima facie case of manslaughter
against the accused.
Common intention c/s.22 Penal Code Act-torture and death of deceased-
whether common intention established.
Held: S.71(1) Trial on Indictment Decree requires that where court is of
the opinion that the available evidence after the close of the prosecution's
case, is not sufficient to support the indictment, court must invite counsel
for both parties to address court before making finding of not guilty to the
original indictment.  In the present case the learned trial Judge erred when
he found that the accused were not guilty of murder as charged without
having first invited both parties to address court on respect.
However, S.7(2) of the Trial on Indictment Decree does not require court
to invariably invite counsel for the defense to make a submission of no
case to answer.  Counsel must make his indication to court that he
wishes to make the submission.  In the instant case counsel for the
defense never indicted to court that he wishes to make that submission
and court was thereby justified in not giving counsel the opportunity in its
own motion.
Nevertheless when court must proceed with a lesser charge than the one
in the original indictment, the accused person must be required to plead
to the altered indictment.  The trial court therefore erred in not letting the
accused plead to the altered indictment.  However this did not occasion a
miscarriage of justice since the accused were offered an opportunity to
defend themselves against the altered indictment of manslaughter.
A submission that there is no case to answer means that no prima facie
case has been made out on the available evidence after the close of the
prosecution's case, against the accused.  That no reasonable court would
convict the accused on that available evidence.  In the instant case the
two accused, including the appellant tortured the accused to death.  The
learned trial Judge correctly inferred that both the accused shared a
common intention to prosecute an unlawful purpose, which resulted in the
death of the deceased and thus put both accused to their defense.
Common intention may be inferred from the failure of the accused from
dis-associating himself from the actions of his co-accused.  In the instant
case it was reasonable to inter that the two accused persons had formed
a common intention to prosecute an unlawful purpose which was to
torture the deceased to death.  The learned trial judge was therefore in his
conclusion.
S.81(3) of the Trial on Indictment Decree provides that the trial court gives
reason for his disagreement with the assessors.  In the instant case even
if the reasons were not explicitly put, they were reasonably inferred from
the judgment. Appeal dismissed.
Sebastino Hakizimana Vs. Uganda.
Insanity s.12 Penal Code Act - whether the appellant had proved
the defence insanity on the balance of probability.
Held: The prosecution was uncertain as to whether the accused acted
under diminished responsibility when he committed the offence or had
malice aforethought. Therefore the prosecution should have called for
medical evidence either during the trial or during the two-year period
pending this appeal.  The evidence of the first impression formed by the
arresting officer, and the impression of mental confusion on the part of the
office that recorded the accused's statement a day later, coupled with the
appellant was laboring under diminished responsibility and was insane
when he committed the offence.
Appeal allowed. Death sentence quashed.  Case file to be remitted to the
responsible minister for action.
Samali Bamutiire & 2 others Vs. Uganda.
Kidnapping with intent to murder c/s 235(1) (a) Penal Code Act -
whether not proved where there is a break in the chain of places
the deceased was taken.
Kidnapping with intent to confine C/s 236 Penal Code-whether proved.
Held: The phrase, "liable to suffer death" only provides the court with a
discretion to impose a death sentence.  The learned trial Judge by
sentencing, "you shall be liable to suffer death" failed to exercise her
discretion.
There was a break in the chain of places to which the deceased was
taken as far as the responsibility of the appellants for the kidnap and
murder of the deceased was concerned.  Therefore, the appellants should
have been found guilty of a lesser offence, C/s 236 Penal Code, kidnap
with intent to confine.
The Trial Court should take into consideration the period of detention of
the appellant in police and military custody and a formal remand in
assessing the term of the imprisonment sentence.  Since the appellants
spent in police, military and remand custody a period of 7 years, this was
near the maximum penalty of 10-year imprisonment.  Therefore the
appellants would be released forthwith.
Appeal allowed, appellants released.
Leo Byaruhanga Vs. Uganda.
Defilement c/s 123 (1) Penal Code Act.
Held: For an appeal against sentence to succeed, the appellant has to
satisfy court that the sentence is manifestly excessive.
In the instant case the trial Judge took into account.  The advanced age
of the appellant as well as the 11-month period during which he had been
on remand.
She rightly observed that defilement, a serious crime carrying a maximum
sentence of death was rampant in the country and courts therefore have to
impose deterrent sentences.
The appellant, who chased the complainant, grabbed her, took her to his
house where he defiled her and denied the incident outright did not deserve
any leniency and was accordingly rightly sentenced.  That is why the
Supreme Court dismissed this appeal.
Uganda Vs. Londoma Feremino.
Plea of guilty - where the accused did not unequivocally admit on
lawfully wounding the victim-whether the plea of guilty was properly
entered.
Held: The trial Magistrate should have encouraged the accused to give
her reasons for inflicting injuries on the victim because they could include
justification in the form of self defence.
It is good practice to record facts constituting the offence, put them to the
accused and only after he has admitted the corrections of those facts,
and when the facts constitute the commission of the offence charged can
a conviction be properly entered.
The facts narrated in this case were admitted by the accused.  He
admitted them without any complaint and said nothing thereafter in his
mitigation.  The admission of those facts by the accused therefore cured
the defect in the plea.  The sentence is therefore confirmed as imposed
by the trial magistrate.
Kwerimba Vs. Uganda.
Robbery c/s 272 & 273 (b) Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Defenses-alibi-whether correctly taken into consideration by trial Judge.
Held: There was overwhelming evidence against the appellant.  PW1
knew the appellant well, although the attack occurred at 3:00 am there
was ample light first from the tadoba and later from the lighted grass
torch to enable PW1 identify the appellant.
The appellant accepts he was traced at his home only.  His claim that the
injury on his shoulder was inflicted by his arresters is clearly invented
story intended to cover up the incriminating injury inflicted by PW1 which
injury fully corroborated PW1 evidence about the identity of the attacker.
There is no evidence to support appellant's claim that PW1's properties
found by PW2 and PW3 hardly 3 hours after robbery were planted on the
appellant at Butenga Police Post.
Accordingly the trial Judge was justified convicting the appellant.
Appeal dismissed.
Capt. Wilberforce Serunkuma Vs. Uganda.
Robbery c/s 272 and 273 (2) Penal Code Act.
Held: Where satisfactory evidence of AIDS is adduced, a court may
consider the circumstance of the case and in the absence of a certificate
from the Medical Board hold that AIDS is grave illness.
To justify grant of bail, the applicant has to prove to the satisfaction of the
court that he was incapable of getting adequate treatment whilst in
custody.
To justify grant of bail, the applicant has to prove to the satisfaction of the
court that he was incapable of getting adequate treatment whilst in
custody.
In the instant case, all the court has is an affidavit of the applicant
supported by some documents from the TASO indicating that the
applicant is an "AIDS" victim.
No affidavit was sworn on report made by any doctor who treat him Luzira
or Mbuya Military Hospital to show that he could get adequate treatment
whilst in custody.
As the record stands therefore the statutory requirement of proof of
exceptional circumstance, in this case grave illness has not been fulfilled.
The bail application is therefore dismissed.
Bimbi Peter Vs. Uganda.
Defilement c/s 123(1) of Penal Code Act -whether proved.
Alibi-whether defence available where appellant was caught red handed
in the sexual act by neighbor.
Held: There is no merit in the appeal against to conviction as the evidence
against the appellant was overwhelming.  The complainant and the
appellant were well known to each other and the incident took place in
broad daylight.  Also a neighbor, Rosemary Nantale, found the two red-
handed in the sexual act and upon seeing her the appellant got up and
ran away.  The appellant had also informed the secretary for defense that
he had talked to the complaint's father about the incident and that it was
going to be settled amicably.
Further, the medical evidence corroborated the complaint's testimony
that the appellant had previously defiled her and that she had sexual
intercourse on or about the day of the incident.
The sentence of 15 years imprisonment was certainly harsh but it is
justifiable given the fact the appellant who was 30 years old had defiled
the title girl (11 years) twice and would most probably have continued to
do so for a long time.
However the order for corporal punishment was illegal since it is neither
provided for by S.123 (1) of the Penal Code and since S.108 of the Trial
on Indictment Decree was in-applicable in this case.  Accordingly the
appeal against sentence succeeds in part.
Appeal against conviction set aside.
Appeal against sentence succeeds only to the extent that the order for
corporal punishment is set aside.
Kasoma Mohammad Vs. Uganda
Criminal Law - Defilement c/s 123 (1) Penal Code - whether proved.
Defenses - alibi-whether taken into consideration by trial Judge.
Held: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and gave the following
reasons for its orders.  There is no substance to the applicant's complaint
that the learned Judge did not take his defense of alibi into consideration.
Despite certain alleged drawbacks to the complainant's evidence, the
learned Judge found that the testimony of the complainant was reliable
and rejected the defense.  Having examined the evidence again we found
that they could be no doubt at all on that point.  There defence is
accordingly rejected.
The learned Judge having warned himself properly of the need for
corroboration, went on to state that if he were satisfied that the
complainant was truthful he could still convict on her uncorroborated
evidence.  It is apparent that the complainant was an exceptionally
persuasive witness her whole narrative was consistent.  The medical
evidence supported her story we could well understand that with or without
corroboration the complainant's evidence must be accepted in favour of
the appellant's alibi.  Consequently this ground of appeal fails.
The appellant a man of 49 years of age cannot be excused for playing
this dangerous and disgraceful trick on a girl of 14 years who knew the
appellant's wife and so trusted the appellant.
Accordingly, thee is no reason to interfere with the sentence imposed.
In any case it was not manifestly excessive.
Appeal dismissed.
Sam Buteera Vs. Uganda.
Defilement c/s 123(1) of Penal Code Act -whether proved.
Held: The victim knew the appellant well, she had seen him at her home
before the incident.  Even if she was in a coffee plantation she saw him
coming to attack her with the help to lantern.  He even talked to her after
sexually assaulting her.  The learned trial Judge therefore rightly directed
herself and the assessors on the law relating to uncorroborated evidence
of a complainant in sexual offence.  The circumstances under which the
offence was committed were such as to render aspects of the case in
relation to the fact of defilement such as the medical evidence and
distressed condition in which the victim was found by her grandmother.
Appellant was therefore properly convicted.
S.123 Penal Code does not provide for corporal punishment for defilement
S.108 Trial on Indictment Decree is inapplicable as it gives the High Court
power to impose corporal punishment to persons under the age of 16
years.  The order of corporal punishment against the appellant was
therefore illegal and is accordingly set aside.
Appeal against conviction fails.
Appeal against sentence succeeds only to the extent that the order for
corporal punishment is set aside.
Uganda Vs. Tandema Philippo.
Murder c/s 183 Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The burden of proving the accused's guilt is on the prosecution and
that burden does not shift to the accused except in a few statutory case-
Woolmington Vs. DPP (1935) AC 462.
There was satisfactory evidence to prove that the first element of murder,
that is a human being by the names of Cecilia Otoda alias Cecilia
Achandere is dead.  The prosecution also proved beyond reasonable
doubt that the cause of the deceased's death was unlawful.
As to whether the accused caused death of the deceased, the evidence
available is circumstantial.  The law dealing with circumstantial evidence
was stated in Simon Musoke Vs. R (1958) EA 715.  the principle is that
where prosecution case is founded on circumstantial evidence, that
evidence must show that the accused is guilty and there are no existing
factors that tend to weaken or destroy the inference of his guilt.  In this
statement to the police, which was admitted by, consent of both sides
the accused admitted having killed his wife with his bare hands.  The
accused himself confirmed in court that he had had a quarrel with his wife.
The circumstantial evidence available therefore leads to the inference that
the accused killed his wife.
The evidence available however does not prove beyond reasonable doubt
that the accused killed his wife with malice aforethought.  The conflicting
prosecution evidence as to how the deceased met her death makes the
situation more uncertain.  Further more there was evidence from both
sides that before the incident the accused was so drunk and might not
have been capable of informing the necessary intention to kill his wife.
Accordingly the accused is acquitted of murder but convicted of
manslaughter c/s 182 Penal code Act and S.86 T.I.D.
Alfred Bumbo Vs. Uganda
Murder - c/s 183 and 184 Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The evidence of eye-witness did not clearly put the first appellant on
the scene of the crime.  His alibi therefore should be truthful and raised a
doubt in the prosecution case.  He was entitled to the benefit of doubt.
His appeal must therefore succeed.
Once an accused person has been positively identified during the
commission of a crime then his claim that he was elsewhere must fail.
In the instant case 2nd and 4th appellants were clearly identified as
being part of the gang that killed the deceased.  The trial Judge correctly
rejected their alibis.
The absence of any evidence of arrest or any evidence from the police
investigating officer did not weaken the prosecution's case because other
evidence was available to provide prosecution's case because other
evidence was available prosecution's case beyond reasonable doubt.
Appeal allowed for appellant number one and dismissed for appellants(2)
and (4).
Uganda Vs. Ikikye Zakaria.
Defilement c/s 123(1) Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The evidence of PW2 and the medical report coupled with common
sense were indeed in agreement that PW1 was far below the age of 18
years.  Though the best way to prove age is a certified birth certificate, the
foregoing have been held to be a conclusive method of proof of age - R Vs.
Recorder of Grimshy Ex-parte Bursar [1951] ALL ER 889.
From the victim testimony and the medial examination report, the
prosecution proved sexual intercourse with the victim beyond reasonable
doubt.  Since it had earlier been proved that PW1, the victim is below 18
years, the sexual intercourse was therefore unlawful by virtue of the
provisions of S.123 Penal Code Act.
From the evidence on record, the testimony of PW1 is corroborated in
every aspect.  Although the corroborating evidence is circulated it is trite
law that circumstantial evidence is good as direct evidence provided that
it irresistibly points to the guilt of the accused and is incompatible with
his innocence; Charles Benon Bitwire Vs. Uganda, Court of Appeal
Criminal Appeal No. 23/85.
Having believed the evidence of the prosecution witness, the alibi put up
by the accused is rejected and the accused is found to have been at the
scene of the crime and defiled PW1 on 5th April 1993.  the accused is
therefore found guilty of the offence of defilement c/s 123 (1) Penal Code
and is accordingly convicted.
Kibuka John Baptist Vs. Uganda
Defilement c/s 123(1) Penal Code Act - Whether proved.
Held: The procedure to be followed by a trial Court which is faced with a
child of tender years as a witness is set out in S.38 (3) Trial on
Indictments Decree.  The most recent decided case to which the trial
judge referred to is Mukasa Deogratius Vs. Uganda, Criminal Appeal
No.21/93 (unreported) where "a child of tender years" has been defined as
any age, or apparent age, of under 14 years, in the absence of any
special circumstances.  In the instant case, PW4 was not a child of
tender years because he was 14 years old when he gave evidence.
There were no special circumstances, which justified him to be regarded
as a child of tender years. It was therefore not necessary for the learned
trial Judge to decide whether PW4 should give sworn or unsworn evidence.
It was self evident from his judgment that the learned trial Judge made a
careful and comprehensive evaluation of all the evidence in the case
before coming to the conclusion he did.  He considered the prosecution
evidence, the most important aspects of which came from P.W.4, an
eyewitness, and the medical evidence.  He also considered the appellant's
alibi, which he found, rightly so in our view, did not create a whole, the
trial Judge, in our view, correctly found that all ingredients of the offence
with which the appellant was charged had been proved to the required
standard.
There was no useful purpose of calling the victim since as the prosecution
State Attorney put it she could not comprehend the proceedings and also
in view of the fact that the evidence of the other witness was sufficient to
prove the case against the appellant to the required standard.
S. 123 (1) of the Penal Code provides for death as the maximum sentence
for the offence of defilement.  Although we are unable to say that the
sentence of 25 years in the instant case is illegal, we are satisfied that it
was manifestly harsh and excessive.  Considering the circumstances of
the case a sentence of 16 years imprisonment would be appropriate.
Regarding Corporal punishment following the decision in the case of
Bambi Vs. Uganda Criminal Appeal No. 33/94, corporal punishment is
neither provided for under S.123(1) Penal Code nor S.108 Trial on
Indictment Decree.  It follows therefore that the order for corporal
punishment was illegal.  The order for police supervision was also illegal,
as the offence of defilement is not one to which S.123 Trial Indictments
Decree, which provides for police supervision applies.
Appeal against conviction dismissed.
Appeal against sentence partly succeeds.
The sentence of 25 years imprisonment, the orders for corporal
punishment and police supervision are set aside.
Abeit Alex & another Vs. Uganda.
Robbery c/s 272 and 273(2) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: Although the blood stained panga was neither examined for blood
grouping nor compared with that of the deceased, it was the first
appellant who, when asked where the murder weapon was, showed the
search party where he had hidden the panga.  There was ample evidence
to show that the cut wounds on the deceased were inflicted by the panga.
Even without the appellant's confessions, the circumstantial evidence
sufficiently connected the panga with the offence.
The learned trial Judge correctly directed himself to the law relating to
circumstantial evidence as laid out in Simon Musoke Vs. R (1958) E.A
715. His holding that the discovery of the panga, gun and ammunition was
sufficient to prove that the gun was robbed from the deceased is therefore
unassailable, and thus was very strong circumstantial evidence against
the first appellant to support the conviction for robbery and even for murder
had it been charged as a separate count.
Regarding the confessions, the statements gave details of the plan to kill
the deceased and the motive for killing.  Both objectives were achieved
by killing the deceased and stilling his gun.  The police officer who
recorded the confessions could not have known all these details because
he was not the investigating officer.  Moreover the alleged assaults and
torture took place at the time of the appellant's arrest and the appellants
did not claimed that the torture had induced them to make or sign the
confessions.  The confessions were therefore made voluntarily and were
rightly admitted in evidence.
The learned trial Judge correctly directed himself and the assessors along
the principles relating to repudiated or retracted confessions as was
summarized in the case of Tuwamoi Vs. Uganda [1967] EA 84.  The
confessions of both the first and second appellants were sufficient to
sustain the conviction of robbery against them and the appellants were
accordingly properly convicted of the offence of robbery.  Their appeal
against the conviction is therefore dismissed.
The conviction on the alternative account of murder was irregular as the
appellants had been found guilty on the main count of robbery, although
the error did not occasion any miscarriage of justice since the appellants
were rightly convicted and sentenced on the main count to robbery.
Steven Mugume & Fred Mutumba Vs. Uganda.
Robbery c/s 272 and 273 (1)(b) of the Penal Code Act -whether proved.
Held: It cannot be said that no miscarriage of justice could have occurred
when the appellants were convicted of simple robbery.  It was most
important that witnesses give their evidence regularly in open court,
wherever it is constituted, for all to hear and see, that witnesses are
cross-examined and tested and that no suspicion is encouraged that the
judge favoured one side or the other by listening to stories off record.
To take into account information off record is to invite evil insinuation
against the Bench, the effect of which is often of which is often very
difficult to refute.
Under the circumstances, the appeals are allowed to the extent that the
convictions are quashed, sentences set aside.  A retrial before another
Judge and deferent assessors on the charge of simple robbery c/s 272
and 273 (1) (b) is ordered.
Uganda Vs. Mukombe Moses Alias Bulo
Kidnapping with the intent to murder c/s 235(1) and (2) of the
Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The child Sandra who was kidnapped was aged about 1-½ years.
At that age she was incapable of forming her won will.  In the
circumstances her will is imputed to be the will of the mother the
complainant PW3.  from the evidence of PW3, which is corroborated by
that of PW4, the accused took away the sick child from PW3, assaulted
PW3 and chased her away by force.  DW3 in cross-examination testified
that the accused's home.  From the evidence on record, the prosecution
has proved beyond reasonable doubt that the seizure and forceful taking
away of the child was against PW3's will.
The accused's claim that PW3 too away the child from his home is
contradicted by the evidence of PW6 and PW5.  owing to the numerous
grave contradictions the evidence of the accused is rejected as being a
pack of lies.  Since the child was kidnapped on 16th May 1992 it has not
been seen or heard of.  The accused is presumed to have had the
intention that the child was to be murdered or to be disposed of as to be
put in danger of being murdered and knowledge that the child will
probably be murdered.  The prosecution has proved beyond reasonable
doubt the guilt of the accused.  Accordingly he is convicted of kidnapping
within intent to murder c/s 235(1) (2) of the Penal Code Act.
Mukasa Deogratuis Vs. Uganda.
Defilement c/s 123 (1) of the Penal Code - whether proved.
Held: The complainant's evidence was properly admitted under S.38 (3)
Trial on Indictments Decree because though the witness was a child of
tender years, the section allows admission of the witness's testimony as
long as the witness through the conduct of a vior dire shows court that
she is of sufficient intelligence to justify the reception of her evidence.
The court record showed that the learned trial Judge conducted a vior dire
and came to the conclusion that though the complainant did not
understand the nature of an oath she had sufficient intelligence to justify
the reception of her testimony.
The age of the complainant though some witnesses said that she was
thirteen and others eleven at the date of the alleged defilement, there was
no material contradiction since they were all agreed that the complainant
was below 18years at the time she was defiled.  (The Supreme Court did
not impeach the finding of the trial Judge that a birth certificate was a
public document and therefore did not require its author to attend court
to prove it).
The accused's beating the prosecution witness who confronted him
wishing to find out the truth about the allegation that the accused had
defiled the complainant was evidence of guilt.  It is trite law that the
conduct of an accused person.  Subsequent to the offence may be taken
against him in considering his guilt or otherwise of that offence.  The
offence committed carried a maximum death sentence, therefore the
sentence of 14 years imprisonment was not manifestly excessive, nor
was it improper or based on wrong principles.
Appeal dismissed.
Leonard Muyingo Vs. Uganda.
Issuing a bouncing cheque c/s 364(1) (b) of the Penal Code Act.
Held: Since the application in the High Court was pending the normal
course to have been taken by counsel was monitor the hearing of the
case in the Chief Magistrate's Court since there is no provision that once
a party has indicated that he is applying for bail, that stays proceedings
in the trial court.
It is clear from the record that the counsel for the accused did not take
trouble to find out the progress of the case, and yet he was aware that
his client's application for bail was not on.  Counsel for the defendant had
ample time to contact his client in between the adjournments.  There is
nothing to show than counsel tried to visit his client while on remand, and
there is no evidence that he was refused access to his client.  The
appellant also had enough time to contact his counsel but chose not to.
Accordingly, the fault lay squarely on counsel and his client.  In the
circumstances, the ground of appeal that there were procedural
irregularities and that the appellant was denied legal representation is
dismissed.
As to whether the bounced cheque was issued to PW! At all or by
presentment of the same for payment, there is no legal requirement that
a cheque paid to an advocate as a trust for his client must be crossed and
not cash.  It is also not anywhere provided in law or precedent that there
is a limit as to the amount of money an advocate is supposed to receive
on behalf of his client.  There is also nothing on record to show the
appellant, and not PW1, is the one who presented the cheque in question
to the bank.  These grounds of appeal also fail.
There is no substance in the allegation that the provisions of S.126 MCA
were not complied with.  From the evidence on record, it is clear that
when the learned chief Magistrate quoted S.125 MCA, he must have
meant S.126 MCA as S.125 MCA deals with discharge of the accused
when there is no case to answer and is obviously irrelevant in the
circumstances.
In view of the fact that the maximum sentence for issuing a bouncing
cheque is 10 years, and more importantly that the accused was also
liable to a civil suit to make good the amount on the bounced cheque the
learned Chief Magistrate should have imposed a lesser sentence, was
accordingly harsh and excessive.  The appeal is dismissed, sentence set
aside substituted for a sentence of one year.
Uganda Vs. Oloya David.
Rape c/s 117 and 118 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The injuries found on the victim were inconsistent with a consented
sexual intercourse as alleged by the accused.  Furthermore, according to
PW3, she met the victim coming from the direction of the alarm and she
was crying.  That evidence of disposition by victim was evidence of her
consistency as to her lack of consent to the sexual intercourse given by
the victim, her evidence from the record is truthful on her lack of consent
to that sexual intercourse.  Accordingly, the accused is found to have had
unlawful sexual intercourse with the victim without her consent.  He is
therefore found guilty as charged and convicted accordingly.
Uganda Vs. Francis Ssentongo.
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: There was no dispute that the complainant was under 18 years. She
told court that she was 14 years.  Therefore she was 12 years at the time
when she was defiled.  The medical evidence corroborated her statement.
The prosecution has therefore proved beyond reasonable doubt that the
complainant was under 18 years.
According to the complainant PW3 the accused chased her, caught her,
pushed her down and squeezed her neck to prevent her from making an
alarm.  He inserted his penis into her vagina and had intercourse with her
for about 10 minutes.  This piece of evidence was not challenged in cross-
examination.  It is conclusive evidence that there was penetration which
for the purpose of the offence of defilement is required to be proved.
The medical report corroborated PW3's evidence on the fact of her
defilement.  The prosecution has thus proved the act of defilement beyond
reasonable doubt.
As to whether PW3 correctly identified the accused as the person who
defiled her, there was sufficient day light to enable correct identification.
Secondly, PW3 told court that she knew the accused by appearance.
Pw3's apparently accurate description of the accused to Sserunkuuma,
secretary for finance RC. 1 Namulanda confirms that she correctly
identified the accused because it was after her description that PW4 and
one katende went to the home of PW6 and had the accused arrested.
The prosecution has therefore proved beyond reasonable doubt that the
accused defiled PW3.  Accordingly the accused is found guilty of the
offence of defilement and is convicted as charged.
Uganda Vs. Happy Godfrey Willy Asiimwe.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: From the medical evidence and the evidence of PW2, PW3 and
PW5 who saw the body of the deceased and buried him the prosecution
has proved beyond reasonable doubt that the deceased is dead.
As to whether the deceased died as a result of malice aforethought; it
should be noted that malice aforethought could be inferred from the nature
of the weapon used and how it was used and the part of the body aimed
at.  From the medical evidence on record, it was stated that a sharp
instrument caused the cut on the right neck of the deceased.  Since the
neck is a vulnerable part of the body, the assailant must have intended to
cause death.
On whether or not the death was unlawful, it is settled law in our criminal
law that every homicide case is unlawful unless it was accidental or
excusable.  In this case it was not shown anywhere that death was
caused by accident or was excusable.
It is generally very unsafe to base a conviction solely on the dying
declaration of a deceased person made in the absence of the accused of
the accused and not subject to cross-examination unless there is
satisfactory corroboration.  Considering the fact that the prosecution is
solely relying on the dying declaration made by the deceased around
4.00am, there is no doubt that there was a possibility of mistaken identity
of his assailant.  This fortified by the inconsistencies and discrepancies
in the prosecution evidence, which go to support the alibi.  Considering
the whole evidence on record, the prosecution failed to negative the alibi
raised by the accused.  The defense of self-defense was also not
negative by the prosecution.  Accordingly, the accused is therefore not
found guilty of murder C/s 183 and 184 Penal Code Act and is therefore
acquitted.
Herbert Turyakira Vs. Uganda.
Indecent assault c/s 122(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: The learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in holding that the alleged
victim's evidence had been corroborated by PW2's evidence yet PW2
was a child and therefore her evidence required to be corroborated.
Evidence that requires corroboration cannot be corroborated by evidence,
which also requires corroboration.
It is true that a court can convict on uncorroborated evidence in sexual
offences and on the uncorroborated evidence of a child of tender years,
after court has warned itself of the danger of relying upon such
uncorroborated evidence, if court is satisfied that though the evidence is
uncorroborated, it is truthful.  However in the case instant, the prosecution
witness having contradicted herself in cross-examination as to the identity
of the accused and in absence of an identification parade, it was clearly
unsafe to rely on such evidence to convict the accused.
The prosecution throughout the trial had the burden to prove beyond
reasonable doubt the guilt of the accused and court would not rely on the
weakness of the defence case.
Appeal allowed.
Raphael Kiiza & another Vs. Uganda.
Forging Land Transfer c/s 327 and uttering a false document c/s
320 of the Penal Code Act.
Fair trial Act 15 Constitution - S.131 MCA failure to hear evidence of some
witnesses - whether thereby the appellants did not receive a fair trial.
Judgment - omission to date judgment-whether proper.
Held: S.13 Magistrate's Courts Act requires the  trial court to hear all
the evidence of the appellant's last two witnesses not withstanding that
the defence had just stated that they had closed their case.  This is
because subsequently court sat again to hear the defence case.  This
means that the appellants did not receive a fair trial.
Every judgment must be dated.  Therefore the trial magistrate
misdirected himself when he omitted to date his judgment.
Appeal allowed.  Retrial ordered.
Deo Bakyenga Vs. Uganda
Causing financial loss c/s 258 of the Penal Code Act - mens rea-
whether mens rea to cause financial loss may be presumed.
Neglect of duty c/s 108(1) Penal Code Act-whether proved.
No case to answer - failure to prove ingredients of the offence whether
therefore accused may not be put to his defence.
Held: Mens rea is an essential ingredient in the offence of causing
financial loss, and cannot be presumed put proved by prosecution.  The
prosecution had the burden to prove that the appellant's omission to carry
out his guard duties were fraught with the knowledge that would cause
financial loss.  Therefore, the trial Magistrate erred in shifting the burden
of proof from the prosecution to the appellant.
There was no sufficient evidence to prove the ingredients of an offence the
accused should not be put to his defence.
Where the prosecution fails to prove the ingredients of an offence accused
should not be put to his defence.  In the instant case the learned trial
Magistrate erred when he put the accused to his defence whereas the
prosecution had failed to prove the ingredients of the offences charged.
A conviction of the offence of causing financial loss attracts a statutory
minimum sentence of 3 years imprisonment.  Therefore the sentence
imposed of 20 months was illegal.
Appeal allowed, conviction quashed sentences set aside.
PC Tito Mukisa Vs. Uganda.
Motive - relevancy - whether failure by trial judge to take into
account the motive of the accused was proper.
Murder c/s 183 Penal Code Act - accident - whether defence available.
Held: Since it was at night when the incident occurred, the circumstances
for a proper identification of the accused while he pointed a gun at the
deceased as alleged by the prosecution, did not exist.  Therefore the
learned trial judges should have warned himself of the danger of relying
on only one identification witness in such difficult circumstances
Though, in an indictment for murder, motive for the murder is irrelevant in
law, it is relevant and available if a particular motive to kill made it likely
that an accused in fact did commit the offence.  In the instant case the
prosecution did not show the motive why the appellant would want to kill
the deceased.  Therefore, the appellant's defence of accident was sound.
Appeal allowed, conviction quashed.  Sentence set aside.
Shaban Mugabi Vs. Uganda
Theft c/s 252 and 245(2) and (3) of the Penal Code Act -whether
complainant gave ush.1,500,000/= by cheque and the accused
converted it to his use.
Held: The trial Court, after the accused had pleaded guilty narrated to the
accused the facts constituting the charge against him and he continued
to admit his guilt.  This shows that the accused was aware of what he
was saying and the trial court was entitled to convict him on his won plea
of guilty.
Under S.213 MCA Court was empowered to make an order of restitution
against the appellant for him to pay the complainant the money he lost
due to the accused's theft.
The sentence of 12 months imprisonment was excessive and harsh in
view of the fact that the appellant pleaded guilty.
Appeal allowed in part.  Sentence reduced to 7 month imprisonment.
Nkwine Jackson Vs. Uganda.
Malicious damage to property c/s 315(1) of the Penal Code Act-
claim of right s.8 of the PCA -whether the offence of malicious
damages to property not proved because of the accused's honest
claim right.
Held: s.8 Penal Code Act provides that a person is not criminally liable in
respect of an offence relating to property if his act or omission is done in
exercise of an honest claim of right.  In the instance case what was at
stake was a dispute over land which dispute could only be settled by a
Civil Court.  Therefore, without the settlement of the issue of ownership
of the land in question, the accused could not be found liable of
malicious damages to property since he claimed that the land was his.
The contradictions between the prosecution witnesses as to what nature
of crops were destroyed by the appellants' cows were not minor and had
to be explained before finding the accused guilty because the
contradictions went to the root as to what garden was destroyed.
Appeal allowed.
Henry Kayondo Vs. Uganda
Prejudicially and unlawfully retaining on official document c/s3(4)
of the official secrets Act -official document - whether communication-
between officials of the movement secretariat was not
"official" as provided by the official secrets Act.
Held: The definition section 15 of the Official Secrets Acts regarding what
an official document is, was inclusive and therefore extensive.  This
means the documents relating to the case could or could not be official
documents as per S.15 of the Official Secrets Act.  It was a question of
evidence could only be deduced at the trial.  Therefore the learned trial
Chief Magistrate was entitled to overrule the preliminary objection.
An alternate charge need not be minor and cognate.
The communication between Advocate and client is absolutely privileged
as per S.124 Evidence Act.  However where an offence is suspected of
having been committed the communication is no longer privileged.
There was no provision in law providing for preliminary objection as to
whether a charge disclosed an offence or not.  Therefore, the preliminary
objection raised by the appellant was misconceived.
Appeal dismissed.
Moses Kalala Vs. Uganda.
Alibi - burden of proof - whether accused to prove his alibi.
Embezzlement c/s 257 (b) Penal Code Act-whether proved.
Held: An accused person who raises the defence of alibi to a criminal
charge does not thereby have the burden to prove the alibi but the burden
lies with the prosecution to disapprove or destroy the alibi by placing the
accused at the scene of crime.  In the instant case the prosecution failed
to produce the head of department who would clearly have shown that the
accused was in fact not on leave.
Under S.257 PCA embezzlement is when a servant receives the chattel,
money or any valuable security on account or in the name of his employer
or master, by virtue of his office, and converts the said valuable security,
money or chattel to his won use.  In the instant case it was shown by the
prosecution that the diesel alleged to have been embezzled was in
possession of the appellant.  The diesel was already in possession of the
appellant.  The diesel was already in possession of the employer.
Therefore no embezzlement was proved.
Appeal allowed conviction quashed.  Sentence set aside.
Uganda Vs. David Livingstone Turyakira alias Rukumba.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - malice aforethought -whether proved.
Defences-intoxication and provocation-whether proved.
Evidence-dying declaration -whether admissible-whether must be
corroborated.
Held: Malice aforethought can be inferred from the nature of the weapon
used in killing the victim and the part of the body where the fatal blow is
inflicted. In the instant case the spear used was very sharp and was
thrown at the victim through his armpit.
It is a rule of prudence to always look for corroboration when a dying
declaration is sought to be relied on.  In the case, the confession, though
retracted but found admissible by court, contained exculpatory elements
to the effect that the killing was due to provocation.  Therefore the dying
declaration had been corroborated.
What provokes a normal person may not be the same as that which
provoke a drunken man.  Therefore, the prosecution had failed to disprove
that the accused's killing of the deceased was die to provocation assisted
by the accused's drunkenness.  Therefore, the accused was guilty of
manslaughter and sentenced to 6 years imprisonment.
Kassim Mpanga Vs. Uganda.
Causing financial loss c/s 258 (1) PCA - unsecured bank credits -
whether failure to recover monies lent as such is an instance of
causing financial loss c/s 258 (1) PCA.
Abuse of office c/s 83(1) PCA-unsecured bank credits - whether a manager
who advances unsecured credits to customers contrary to bank policy of
securing credits is guilty of abuse of office.
Held: The gist of the offence of causing financial loss is the term "loss". A
thing may be said to be lost after a reasonable time has elapsed to allow
diligent search and recovery and such diligent search has been made and
has been fruitless. In the instant case, in respect of 29 accounts inspite of
diligent recovery efforts of several months, recovery was impossible.
Therefore the learned trial magistrate was correct to have found the accused
guilty of causing financial loss c/s 258(1) PCA because the loss was a
natural consequence of the unauthorized and unsecured credit.
Abuse of office is the doing of an act by an accused person's employers,
prejudicial to the interest, in abuse of authority of his office in the instant
case the accused acted arbitrarily by giving out the overdrafts unsecured
and without authority contrary to bank policy.  This act amounted to abuse
of office by the appellant.
S.259 PCA mandatory requires court to consequently impose an order of
compensation against an accused convicted of causing financial loss and
embezzlement.  The order of compensation must be imposed specifically
count by count.  In the instant case the trial magistrate imposed a blanket
order and this was illegal.  However, a court of Appeal is empowered under
S.337(2) CPC to vary a judgment of the High Court on appeal.  Therefore
the order of compensation would be substituted for the order to apply to only
count one.
Appeal dismissed.  Order of compensation to apply to count one only.
Avutia Vs. Uganda.
Attempt theft c/s 370 and 252 of the Penal Code Act - whether
proved where accused was found seated in a car without any
instrument to indicate that he was capable of driving it away.
Minor and corporate offence s.143 MCA-Criminal; Trespass c/s 286(a)
PCA-whether minor and cognate to theft-whether accused could be
convicted of criminal trespass when only charged with attempted theft.
Held; S.143 MCA authorized court to convict an accused of minor and
cognate offence when the facts disclosed reduce the original charge
accordingly.  A minor and cognate offence is of the same genus as the
offence with which the accused is charged, because the ingredients of
the minor and cognate offence are a subset of the major offence.
The accused need not plead independently to the minor and cognate
offence nor defend himself to the major offence because the ingredients
of the minor offence have been tackled in the defence against the major
offence.  In the instant case the trial Chief Magistrate erred with he found
the accused guilty of criminal trespass because it was not a minor
cognate offence to theft.  He should have required the prosecution to alter
the charge and the accused to plead independently to the altered charge.
This misdirection caused a miscarriage of justice.
Revision allowed.  Sentence set aside. Accused set free.
Alex Olwor Vs. Registered Trustees of Arua Catholic Diocese
Sale of goods -contract of sale, s.5 sale of Goods Act -whether
there was an enforceable contract of sale.
S.5 Sale of Goods Act requires a contract of sale of goods of the amount
of or above shs 200 to be in writing.  The suit contract was a validity
enforceable contract as it fulfilled the requirements of the sale of Goods
Act.
Held: Where the agent does not indicate in a contract that he is
contracting personally but as an agent, then he is personally liable to the
contract. In the instant case the principal ratified the contract by making
part payment in pursuance thereof.  Therefore both the agent and the
principal were liable.
It is a rule of law and practice that special damages must not only be
pleaded but proved strictly.  Though a receipt of Ush 540.000/= was
tendered in evidence, the amount pleaded was Ush 810,300/=.  The
plaintiff was precluded from recovering the lesser amount of Ush 540,000/=
evidence for which had been adduced because that proved amount was
not pleaded.
A plaintiff will recover damages for loss of profit as damages foreseeable
by the parties at the time they made their contract, as the probable result
of the breach.  In the instant case there was no evidence that the
defendant had knowledge of the plaintiff's nature of business.  It was not
mentioned in evidence that the plaintiff was a regular or casual Timber
Trader.  Therefore the defendant could not foresee loss of profit as the
natural consequence of the breach of the contract.
Suit allowed for the payment of the balance on the contract price and
Ush 100,000/= as compensation for delayed payment and costs.
Tom Bwete Vs. Uganda.
Attempting to obtain goods by false pretences c/ss 289 and 370
of the Penal Code Act -immovable property - a person can be
found guilty of attempting to obtain goods by false pretences
where the goods are immovable property.
Uttering a false document c/s 330 Penal Code Act-Advocates whether an
accused may utter a false document through his counsel.
Sentencing - uttering a false document c/s 330-whether the sentence of a
fine was illegal because not provided for under the section.
Held: S.330 of the Penal Code Act providing for the offence of uttering a false
document provided for a maximum sentence of 7 years imprisonment but
did not provide the option of a fine.  Therefore the sentence for the fine was
illegal and false document through ones advocates.
S. 289 Penal Code Act providing for the offence attempting to obtain goods
by false pretence provides that such goods must be capable of being stolen.
How ever a house cannot be stolen since it is immovable property.
Therefore, the learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in convicting the appellant
of an offence, which the appellant was not capable of committing.
Appeal succeeds only in part.  Fine set aside. Imprisonment to stay.
Uganda Vs. Kennedy Ovuru.
