Defilement - sentencing -accused 24years, unmarried alleging to
have been encouraged by alcohol.
Held: The established practice of court is not to impose a maximum
sentence on a first offender.  In the instant case the accused pleaded guilty
and was a first offender.
Six years imprisonment imposed.
Mafujja Leus Vs. Uganda.
Embezzlement c/s 257(a) Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: Where a person declines to avail himself of an opportunity to cross-
examine a witness testifying against him on the essential particulars of the
evidence adduced, it must follow that that person against whom testimony
has been given believes the testimony.  Therefore, in the instant case, even
if the extra judicial statement was excluded, sufficient evidence abound on
which the trial Magistrate correctly found a conviction.
A sentence of 5 years for a conviction of embezzlement was not excessive
and harsh.
Appeal dismissed.
Ezra Sebuwufu Vs. Uganda.
Embezzlement c/s 257(d) of the Penal Code Act - circumstantial
evidence - whether offence circumstantially proved.
Sentencing-embezzlement c/s 257(d) Penal Code Act-whether sentence of
12 months illegal.
Embezzlement c/s 257(d) Penal Code Act-Compensation-whether an order
for compensation against the accused is mandatory.
Held: To support a conviction that solely relies on circumstantial evidence,
the incriminating facts adduced must not be capable of any other reasonable
reasonable explanation other than the guilt of the accused.  The evidence in
this case proved that it is the accused as cashier that received the money
alleged to have been stolen, on behalf of the company but did not pass it
over to management. That was sufficient evidence to support the conviction.
As per S.257 (d) Penal Code a conviction for embezzlement carries a
minimum sentence of imprisonment of 3 years.  Therefore the sentence of
12 months imprisonment would be set aside for mandatory illegal.
S.259 Penal Code Act provides for a mandatory order for compensation
against a person convicted of embezzlement.  Therefore, the learned trial
Magistrate erred when he failed to impose the mandatory order.
Appeal dismissed.  File remitted back to trial court to impose the correct
sentences.
Edrisa Sekitoleko Vs. Uganda.
Embezzlement c/s 257 of the Penal Code Act - possession -
whether appellant not in possession of alleged stolen diesel and
therefore not guilty of embezzlement but theft.
Held: The evidence clearly indicated that the appellant remained in
possession of the vehicle and its contents including the diesel at all
material times.  Therefore the appellant was rightly convicted of
embezzlement as charged.
Appeal dismissed.
Kamori Johnson Vs. Uganda.
Threatening violence c/s 76(d) of the Penal Code -whether proved.
Malicious damage to property s.315-whether proved.
Claim of right s.8 Penal Code Act - property of some other person-whether
an accused can successfully make a claim of right over property which he
claims belongs to his mother.
Fresh evidence on appeal-whether admissible.
Held: The contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was
such that the offence of threaten violence was not proved.
The defence of claim of right was not available where the appellant claimed
that the property belonged to his mother and not to him.  Moreover the
mother testified that she never owned the garden.
Fresh evidence may not be adduced on appeal where the opposite party has
had no opportunity to cross - examine on it.  The affidavit on appeal was not
helpful because it raised matters that were never considered at the trial.
Appeal succeeds only in part.  Conviction on count 2 upheld.
Abdi Ali Ahmed Vs. Uganda.
Reckless driving c/s 118(1)(a) and s.138 (2) and (9) and s.65(1)
(a) Traffic & Road Safety Act - whether proved where appellant
pleaded but contradicted the statement later.
Plea of guilty-equivocal plea-whether accused's plea of guilty equivocal.
Held: Where an accused who originally pleads guilty but after court has
recited the facts of the case, denies his original statement, then the
accused cannot be said to have pleaded guilty.  Therefore, the learned trial
magistrate erred in recording a plea of guilty against the accused.
Appeal allowed. Sentences set aside.
Kagube Mohamed Vs. Uganda.
Theft of Cattle c/s 255 Penal Code Act -whether proved where
appellant's plea of guilt is equivocal.
Held: There was no evidence to prove that the alleged plea of guilty was
obtained by duress since there was no body who duressed the appellant as
he stood in the dock to plead to the charge.
Where a person is charged on the main count and an alternative count, and
he pleads guilty to the main count, then he cannot be called upon to plead
to the alternative count.  In the instant case the trial court misdirected
itself to ask the appellant to plead to the alternative count when the
appellant had pleaded guilty to the main count already.  However, this
misdirection would only leave their main count standing.
The facts as put to the accused did not in any way show that he was the
guilty of the theft of the bull.  Therefore his conviction was not proper.
Court misdirected itself when it imposed sentenced on both the main and
alternative counts.  This was irregular.  However, the sentence of 2 years
imprisonment was not excessive.
Appeal allowed.  Sentence set aside.
Nuru Sabiti Vs. Uganda
Obtaining credit by fraud c/s291(1) of the Penal Code Act -
whether offence proved where there was a contract for supply of
goods between accused and complainant
Held: The tenor of evidence showed that the accused had no intent to
defraud but honestly failed to deliver the cocoa within ordinary course of
commercial transactions.  This was a civil transaction conjured into a
criminal contravention. The subsequent conviction and sentence were illegal.
Revision allowed.  Conviction quashed.  Sentence set aside.
Salim Kamyere Vs. Uganda.
Theft c/s 252 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: Hearsay evidence is inadmissible.  The complainant's evidence as to
who took the money was hearsay since the complainant was unconscious
and never saw the appellant take the money but was told by one prosecution
witness.  The prosecution witness's evidence that the appellant took the
complaint's money was also hearsay since he was only told by the
complaint that the black polythene bag contained money.  Therefore the
conviction was based on hearsay evidence and was inadmissible.
Appeal allowed.  Conviction set aside. Acquittal ordered.
Christopher Lubaale Vs. Uganda.
Shop breaking and theft c/ss 252 and 283(a)  of the Penal Code
Act -recent possession -whether offence proved where accused
is found with property recently stolen.
Held: Where an arrest had been made or authorized according to S.68
MCA, police is at liberty to search the place of dwelling or business of the
arrested person or person authorized to be arrested, it police has reason to
believe that material evidence may be obtained threat.  In the instant case,
the appellant's dwelling house was searched after the arrest.  Therefore, the
search did not require a warrant.
The requirement for corroboration for accomplice evidence is requirement
of prudence not one of law.  However in the instant case corroboration was
found in the fact that property recently stolen was found at the home of the
appellant.
Where a person is found in possession of property recently stolen, that
person may be either a thief or may be guilty of receiving stolen property.
In the instant case, property stolen on 24th March 1993 was found at the
appellant's home on 27th March 1993.  the accused's explanation was not
satisfactory to the trial court and the court was entitled to convict the
accused of the theft.
The sentence of 18 months was not excessive.
Stephen Batumbia Vs. Uganda.
Attempting theft c/s 370 and 252 of the Penal Code Act - whether
offence proved where accused presents cheque to the bank for
payment when he has received part payment of the cheque value.
Giving false information to a person employed by the public service c/s 109
(c) Penal Code Act-whether offence proved where accused states to police
that the complainant paid him a cheque that was dishonored when
accused ahs received part payment of cheque value.
Held: Though the trial Court misdirected itself on the amount the accused
is alleged to have attempted to fraudulently recover from the complainant,
nevertheless the court reached the right conclusion by holding that the
appellant attempted to unjustifiably get money that he was not entitled to
when he presented the cheque against which he had been partly paid.
The trial was correct in convicting the appellant of attempted theft.
Conviction on this count is confirmed.
The trial Court misdirected itself when it convicted the appellant of giving
false information to a person employed in the public service because the
appellant's information to the effect that the cheque had been dishonored
was a correct fact.  Conviction on this count is quashed and sentence set
aside.
The appellant court would not interfere in the severity of the sentence
imposed by the trial court on count one as no principal law was offered for a
sentence of 12 months imprisonment for the offence of attempted theft.
Appeal allowed in part.  Conviction and sentence on count one upheld
count 2, conviction quashed.  Sentence set aside.
Waiswa Richard & 3 ors Vs. Uganda.
Assault occasioning actual bodily harm c/s 228 of the Penal Code
Act -whether proved where complainant is examined by a medical
officer.
Common intention-assault occasioning actual bodily harm - whether offence
against appellant who merely commanded the others to beat the
complainant.
Held: Although appellant number one did not physically assault the
complainant, he had a common intention with the other 3 to unlawfully
assault the complainant and his intention was readily inferable from his
conduct.  There was no need to prove express agreement between him and
his co-accused.
Although the phrase medical officer is not well known in the medical
profession, considering the training of the witness and his experience of 5
years practice, he was a witness equivalent to a medical assistant and thus
qualified to examine the victims in this single case of assault. The trial court
was correct in basing her finding the evidence of the medical officer.
The sentencing 2 months imprisonment was not excessive.
Appellant number four did not participate in the assault as there was no
such evidence.
Appeal dismissed for appellants number one, two or three.
Eriya Ngabeki Vs. Uganda.
Causing grievous harm c/s212 of the Penal Code Act -obstructing
police officers in due executing of their duties c/s 106 of the Penal
Code Act -whether offences proved where appellant set up
defenses of alibi.
Common intention S.22 Penal Code Act - grievous harm and obstructing
Police Officers - whether offence proved against appellant-whether
appellant had common intention with the crowd.
Held: The appellant's evidence as to the time he set out for the wedding
party was not consistent.  The prosecution had clearly placed the
appellant at the lead of the mob that assaulted the complainant in
obstruction of police officers in the execution of their duties.  The appellant
had a common intention with the group that perpetrated the criminal acts.
Since the accused was not represented the trial court should have assisted
the appellant to find the possible mitigation circumstances before passing
sentence.
Appeal against sentence allowed.  Sentence reduced to 6 months
imprisonment.  Appeal against conviction dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Richard Mutumba
Uttering a false document c/s 330 of the Penal Code Act -whether
proved where appellant is acquitted of forging the document.
Obtaining money by false pretense c/s 289 Penal Code Act-whether proved
where appellant's acquitted of forging the document.
Held: The admission of evidence of a witness not before court is wrong in law
because it deprives the opposite party the opportunity to cross examine the
witness on the evidence and to test her credibility.  In the instant case the
trial court misdirected itself when it admitted evidence of a witness from a
previous trial.
However, the wrong admission of evidence dos not necessarily render the
trial a nullity unless the admitted evidence was the foundation of the
conviction.  In the instant case the evidence wrongly admitted was
inconsequential in the finding by court of the appellant's guilt.
Where a person is found not guilty of forgery, it does not ipso facto mean
that therefore he is not guilty of uttering a false document.  In the present
case the trial court found that though the chepues were forged there was no
evidence that the cheques were forged by the appellant.  Court was still
entitled to find whether it was the appellant guilty of uttering the forged
cheques.
A person utters a false document when he tenders the same for payment
knowing it to be forged or false and with intent to defraud.  In the present
case the issue was whether the appellant knew that the cheques were
forged and whether he uttered them with intent to defraud. The trial court held
that the appellant must have known that the cheques were forged since he
was an accounts clerk in the Ministry of Internal Affairs and must know
about the process of clearing cheques.  This finding was based on
conjecture and hypothesis.  Therefore, the trial court misdirected itself on
finding was based on conjecture and hypothesis.  Therefore, the trial court
misdirected itself on finding that the appellant knew that the cheques were
forgery as this circumstantial evidence co-existed with other evidence on
record that showed that the cheques were given to the appellant by third
party.
Certain exceptions apart, the burden of proof in criminal proceedings is
thought out on the prosecution.  Therefore, the learned trial Chief Magistrate
misdirected himself when he held that the accused had the burden to prove
that the money was withdrawn to pay the said third party's creditors.
Appeal allowed. Conviction set aside.
Uganda Vs. Tereza Onziru.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Malice aforethought - one death blow-whether because deceased died from
one death blow malice aforethought was not proved.
Murder c/s 183 PCA-common intention-whether established where two
accused jointly caused the death of the deceased.
murder c/s 183 PCA-defence of person whether the defence of defence of
person available.
Held: It is unsafe to convict on uncorroborated dying declaration.  In the
instant case by fleeing from the home where the deceased met his death,
the two accused by that act, corroborated the dying declaration that
pointed out the onus two accused as the assailants of the deceased.
Where two or more persons jointly assail a person, causing his death and
there is no evidence as to who dealt the death blow, prosecution must first
establish existence of a common intention before the accused are jointly
convicted of the murder.  In the instant case there was no evidence of the
existence of common intention between the two accused to murder the
deceased.  Therefore, each individual would be liable individually for her
respective contribution in the assault of the deceased.
The defence of defending is not available where the accused uses force
unproportional to the attack on the person being defended.  In the instant
case A2 used a knife and stabbed the accused in the back allegedly in
defence of her sister who had only been struck with a piece of wood by
the deceased.  Certainly the stabbing was exceedingly unproportional to
the act of the deceased and therefore the defence of defending a person
was not available to A2, who had been accurately identified by the deceased
in his dying declaration.
Use of a deadly weapon per se does not automatically attract inference of
malice aforethought.  In the instant case only one death blow was struck,
though with a deadly-weapon-a knife.  Since there was evidence of a fight
prior to the death blow, malice aforethought had not been proved and
therefore the accused was guilty of manslaughter c/s 182 Penal Code Act.
Accused A2 convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 5 years
imprisonment. A1 acquitted.
Uganda Vs. Kankiruho James & another
Principal offenders s.21 of the Penal Code Act - whether accused
number two was a principal offender where the facts disclosed that
she looked for market for cows which had already been stolen.
Held: S.21 of the Penal Code prescribe circumstances that establish when
an accused is a principal offender in any alleged offence before court.  In the
instant case the prosecution failed to show that A2 fell in any description
envisaged by S.21 to be established as a principal offender.  It was not
proved that she took part in stealing the cows nor did she know that the
cows were stolen.  Her conviction would therefore be quashed.
Interalia for purposes of the Appellant Court it is required that the Trial Court
gives reasons for its sentence.  The Learned Trial Magistrate erred in failing
to give reasons for his sentence of 18 months imprisonment.  However in
the circumstances of the case the sentence cases cited did not occasion a
miscarriage of justice for A1 who was properly convicted.
The Learned Trial Magistrate erred in law when he imposed a compensatory
sentence on the accused because a Criminal Magistrate has no jurisdiction
to impose a compensatory sentence.  This sentence would be set aside.
Uganda Vs. Police Constable Alfred Ogwang.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Defenses - intoxication - S.13 Penal Code-whether defense available where
the accused while at a party got annoyed went back to the barracks and
returned to the party, shot indiscriminately at the revelers and then returned
to the barracks.
Defenses - provocation -whether defense available where accused was
refused entry into a canteen got annoyed went to the barracks returned with
a gun and shot indiscriminately at the revelers killing 13.
Held: Infringement of S.78 TID amounts to adducing evidence to the
evidence already stated in the summary of facts.  In the instant case the
summary of evidence warned the accused that a gun would be tendered in
evidence and the gun was actually tendered in evidence albeit the number
thereof was different.  Therefore this did not amount to new evidence as
such as to mean that S.78 TID had been infringed upon.
The weird story of the accused in defense was indicating of a person who
only wanted to derail the course of justice.  It was clear that it is the
accused who had shot and killed all the deceased.
The prosecution had discretion in choosing what witnesses to bring to prove
its case.  Since the accused wished to rely on the defense of insanity by
intoxication it was a incumbent upon him to prove so.
the accused would not rely on the non-production of particular witnesses by
the prosecution since this by itself was no evidence of a motive deliberate to
hide the truth from the court.
According to the evidence from the witnesses the accused was not so drunk
as not to know what he was doing.  Since the accused was annoyed and
yet was able to go back to the barracks, to collect his gun and go and shoot
the deceased persons and then return to the barracks, it was not reasonable
suppose that the accused was so drunk that he did not know what he was
to doing.  Therefore had failed to rebut the presumption that he intended the
consequences of his acts.
The defense of provocation would be rejected because the accused had
more than sufficient time to cool down and moreover what happened, his
denial of entry into some canteen could not mount to provocation.
Accused convicted as charged.
Uganda Vs. Ronald Mwaka
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Defenses-self-defense-whether defense available where deceased refused to
sell more waragi to the accused and the accused got enraged, chased her
and killed her.
Malice aforethought-whether this may be inferred from the kind of weapon
used-whether there was malice aforethought.
Held: Since the evidence showed that it was the accused who was the
attacker, it could not be said that the accused reasonably feared that his
life was in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm so as to be
entitled use of force to disentangle himself thus by spearing the accused.
Therefore malice aforethought could not be readily inferred.
The law is that malice aforethought may be inferred from the use of a lethal
weapon.  But in the instant case the manner of use of the weapon indicated
one blow and on a less vulnerable part of the body.  The death was due to
internal bleeding due to lack of urgent medical attention.  Therefore malice
forethought could not be readily inferred.
Accused guilty of manslaughter and sentenced to 6 years imprisonment.
Uganda Vs. Apollo George Anyiwar
Defilement - whether proved where the complainant did not
expressly state that the assailant's penis had enter her vagina.
Held: Medical evidence rapture of the hymen and the edematous vaginal
walls of the victim coupled with the victim's statement in court that she felt
pain in her vagina was evidence that sexual intercourse by penetration of a
male penis in the complainant's vagina took place.
Court must be cautious in basing a conviction on the testimony of a single
identifying witness especially where conditions favouring correct
identification are lacking.  In the instant case corroboration must be sought
since there was a single identifying witness and conditions did not favour
correct identification as it was late in the evening and the complainant did
not favour correct identification as it was late in the evening and the
complainant did not know the accused before.  However, there was no
evidence adduced capable of corroborating the evidence of identification of
of the accused by the complainant.
Accused not guilty as charged.
Uganda Vs. Stephen Mulangira
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: It is a requirement to establish sexual intercourse that the hymen
must be proved ruptured.  Any slight penetration is sufficient to establish
intercourse.  In the instant case the edematous vagina was proof of forcible
penile entry therein inspite of the minimal rapture of the hymen.
The complainant at the trial old court that she did not report the defilement
to her aunt PW2 and yet PW2 told court that the defendant had told her that
it was the accused who had defiled her.  These contradictions show that the
person who defiled the complainant was not properly identified.  Since the
complainant, being a child of tender years her evidence was not on oath
and which evidence was not corroborated as required by S.38(3) TID and
S.12 Oaths Act
Not guilty as charged.
Uganda Vs. Aramanzani Mubiru
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code-malice aforethought-whether proved.
Self-defense-S.17 Penal Code - whether defense available-whether
reasonable or excessive force used.
Provocation-S.187 Penal Code - whether defense of provocation available
where no malice aforethought is proved.
Held: Medical evidence showed that there was only one killer bullet that
entered at the left upper arm and exited through the right supras capsular
area.  This meant that the accused never aimed at the deceased since a
more direct wound would have been found on the deceased's body.
Therefore, no malice aforethought, constructive or otherwise was proved
against the accused.  His aim was to shoot in the air and not at any
vulnerable part of the deceased.
A person is entitled to use reasonable force against an attacker, if he is in
reasonable apprehension of serious injury to himself provided he has done
everything reasonably possible in the circumstances to retreat or avoid the
fight.  In the instant case, the accused policeman could not be said to have
used reasonable force in killing the deceased because the deceased even
though he boxed the accused he was not around and yet the accused was
in company of two armed LDU's on the scene.  The accused had an
opportunity to retract and avoid firing the killer bullet.
Even though the accused did not expressly set up the defense of
provocation, it could be gathered from the allegation that the accused shot
the deceased after the deceased had boxed him.  However since it had
already been proved that there was no malice aforethought on the part of
the accused in shooting at the deceased the defense of provocation was
not applicable.
Accused guilty of manslaughter c/s 182 and 185 Penal Code.
Uganda Vs. Gayira Francis and another
Murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Murder-malice aforethought S.186-whether established where accused
boxed the deceased in the chest.
Common intention S.22 Penal Code - whether proved where A1 boxed the
deceased in the presence of the AII.
Assault c/s 227 Penal Code - whether proved.
Held: Invariably, malice aforethought can only be proved circumstantially.
The nature of the weapon used in effecting the death may circumstantially
show whether or not the accused's disposition was such that he intended
the death of the deceased by his act.  In the instant case, even though the
part of the body hit was the face, which is a vulnerable part, but the nature
of the wounds was that the face was bruised meaning a blunt object in fact
a fist was used.  This was no evidence of malice aforethought therefore the
accused were not guilty of murder.
Common intention in inferred from conduct presence and actions of the
accused or from the failure of the accused to disassociate himself from the
commission of the offence.  In the instant case the prosecution witnesses
had showed that when they found both accused and the deceased in a
scuffle they separated them.  It is AI that returned and hit the deceased with
his fist.  Therefore it cannot be said that AII formed a common intention with
AI to murder the deceased.  All was therefore not guilty of murder nor assault
of the deceased AI was guilty of common assault C/s 227 Penal Code.
Uganda Vs. Mukalazi Michael
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Held: By way of common sense by her appearance it was obvious that
complainant was a tiny little girl vary far bellow the age of 18.  the fact was
not challenged by the defence.  Therefore, this coupled by medical
evidence as to the victim's age was proof that the victim was below the of 18.
Major contradictions in prosecution evidence should be resolved in favor of
the accused.  In the instant case the contradictions in the prosecution
evidence were minor and would be disregarded.
Accused convicted as charged.
Uganda Vs. Ocero George
Defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved.
Defences-insanity-whether defense available where the accused claimed to
have had a mental blackout during the time it is alleged he committed the
offence.
Defences-intoxication S.13(2) (b) Penal Code- whether accused was so
intoxicated as to amount to being insane.
Defences-intoxication 13(4) Penal Code-mens rea-whether the accused
was so intoxicated that he could not form the necessary intent to commit
the offence.
Held: While court must cautiously deal with confession that is repudiated in
this case the confession was detailed in material particulars and
corroborated the victim's unsworn evidence that it is the accused who
defiled her.
S.11 Penal Code presumes everybody sane and the accused who sets up
the defence of insanity must rebut the presumption.  In the instant case, the
accused could not be believed when he alleged that he had had a mental
blackout.
The accused had not shown court that the alleged insanity was due to
intoxication as per S.13(2) (6) Penal Code.  Therefore the defense of
intoxication was not available.  Therefore the defense of intoxication was
not available.  S.13(4) of the Penal Code provides that an accused may set
up a defense of intoxication contending that due to intoxication he could not
form the necessary intent to commit the offence.  In the instant defilement
as an offence did not require mens rea for its commission.
Accused convicted as charged.
Uganda Vs. Mucoori Francis.
Failure to pay graduated tax c/s 69(3) Local Administrations Act,
1967-whether proved.
Held: The plea to all the two counts was omnibus and irregular.  A plea
must be for each count separately.
The plea was equivocal because the accused pleaded that he had not paid
the graduated tax, as charged, but in the same breath pleaded he was
unable to pay.  The section creating the offence requires that a person to
be guilty under the section must have failed to pay the tax without lawful
excuse.  Therefore, although the accused pleaded guilty he at the same
time south to say that his failure was due to lawful excuse.  Therefore the
plea was equivocal and should not have been the basis of the conviction.
The trial Magistrate must convict the accused person instead of merely
recommending conviction as it was in this case.  Therefore, the accused
person was not convicted and the sentence was a nullity.
proceedings set aside.  No retrial ordered because the accused has served
the illegal sentence.
Kamuroro Joseph Vs. Uganda.
Causing death by crash or negligent C/S 219A Penal Code-whether
proved where deceased attempted to disarm the arresting policeman
and was hit and killed by a bullet in the scuffle.
Criminal liability-accident S.9(1)+(3) Penal Code Act-whether
accused was arraigned for an act that happened by accident.
Held: S.9(1), (3) of the Penal Code Act provides that a person is not
criminally liable for an act that happens independent of the accused's
exercise of his will.  In the instant case the killer bullet flew from the
accused's gun during a scuffle where the deceased sought to disarm the
accused.  Therefore, the accused was not criminally liable for the discharge
of the killer bullet.
Moreover, for an accused to be guilty of causing death by a rush or
negligent act under s.219A of the Penal Code, it must be shown that his
conduct was such that he cared not whether his act caused death or not.
This was not the case in the instant case.  The facts were that the killer
bullet flew from accused's gun accidentally and not through recklessness or
negligence.
The trial Magistrate misdirected himself when he recorded a plea of guilty
whereas the facts were at variance from the charge.  The charge was that
the accused killed the deceased due to acting recklessly and yet the facts
were that the killer bullet flew the gun by accident.
The trial Magistrate misdirected himself when he held that the fine payable
on conviction under s.219A was shs. 4,000/= whereas it is shs. 70,000/=.
Appeal allowed.  Conviction quashed. Appellant set free.
Zita Jackson Vs. Uganda.
Defilement-C/S 123(1) PCA-whether proved.
Sentencing - 7 years imprisonment for defilement - whether
excessive.
Sentencing-corporal punishment-whether lawful s.123(1) Penal
Code Act.
Held: Failure by a trial judge to record his note of summing up to the
assessors is contrary to s.81(1) TID and this can lead to the quashing of a
conviction if injustice results there from.  In the present case the failure to
make the record did not in itself cause injustice since the assessors in their
opinions gave the salient features of the evidence which meant that they
were properly directed.
S.64(2) requires the trial judge to draw up a memorandum of agreed facts
and in the instant case the trial judge failed to comply with this provision of
the law.  However, since the contested medical report was after being
admitted, signed by both counsel for the prosecution and accused and the
trial judge, the report became part of the record of the court.
It is rule of practice for the trial judge to record submissions of counsel and
when counsel's submissions raise issues of law and fact and the trial judge
does not consider the issues in his judgment, then such an omission is
relevant to the merits of an appeal.  However, in the instant case since the
submissions of counsel were made and closed in the morning and
judgment delivered 3 hours later, it means that the submissions were fresh
in the mind of the judge when he was writing the judgment.  Therefore the
omission to record the submissions did not occasion a miscarriage of
justice.
It is a rule of practice for courts to require corroboration of the evidence
against the accused in sexual offences.  In the instant case the distressed
condition of the complainant was corroborative of the sexual assault upon
her.
Seven years imprisonment were neither illegal nor excessive.
Corporal punishment was not provided for the offence of defilement and the
sentence for corporal punishment was illegal and would be set aside.
Appeal dismissed except as to orders for corporal punishment.
Sekalo John Leonard Vs. Uganda.
Embezzlement C/S 257(b) Penal Code Act-whether proved.
Theft - aspiration-whether embezzlement was proved when asportation was
not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Held: To prove embezzlement, the ingredients of theft i.e. asportation and
the intention to permanently deprive the employer of his product, must be
proved beyond reasonable doubt.  In the instant case the prosecution failed
to prove to the required standard in criminal cases that the diesel alleged to
have been embezzled was actually taken out of the depot.
In terms of s.257 Penal Code Act, to prove embezzlement, the employee
must have received or taken into possession the property in question for or
on account of his employer, and upon receipt or taking into possession the
property, the employee must intercept the property before it reaches the
employer.  In the instant case the diesel alleged to have been embezzled
cannot be said to have been intercepted and stolen before it reached into
the employer's possession.
Appeal allowed.  Appellant set free.
Uganda Vs. Mubiru Aramanzani.
Murder C/S 183 Penal Code-whether proved-whether no malice
aforethought prove.
Manslaughter-whether proved.
Accident-whether defence available.
Constructive malice to murder-whether proved.
Self defence S.17 Penal Code Act - whether defence available -
whether excessive force used-whether reasonable force.
Provocation -whether defence available-S.187 Penal Code Act.
Held: In order for the prosecution to establish malice aforethought, it must
show that the accused intended to kill the deceased.  In the instant case
the prosecution failed to prove this.  And the fact that the killer bullet entered
the deceased at his left upper arm, shows that the accused never aimed to
shoot the deceased but only shot in the air.
Constructive malice was not proved.
Where the accused's assailant does not attempt a violent felony, the
accused is entitled to use reasonable force against his attacker to award off
the attack.  In the instant case the deceased only attacked the accused
only with has bear hands.  Therefore his release of the fatal bullets was use
of excessive force in the circumstances.
The shooting was not accidental, as the accused himself testified that he
shot in the air to scare his assailant.
The defence of provocation was not applicable.
Accused found guilty of manslaughter, sentenced to 4 years imprisonment.
Kasasa Muhammad Vs. Uganda.
Contract-breach thereof-whether cannot be a subject of criminal
proceedings under S.289 Penal Code Act obtaining goods by
false pretence.
Held: It is up to the person taking legal action to choose whether to institute
it as civil or criminal proceeding.  Either choice does not exclude the other
as long as there is evidence that disclose both civil and criminal triable
issues.
A contention that the matter before the criminal court should only have been
commenced in civil court is not a proper submission of no case to answer.
A submission of no case to answer is to the effect that the evidence
disclosed on the record is not sufficient to put the accused to his defence.
There is no rule of law requiring the trial Magistrate to give an exhaustive
evaluation of the evidence and law while ruling on a submission of no case
to answer except when the ruling is in the affirmative, that there is no case
to answer.   Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate was entitled to make
her ruling in the two sentences.
Application dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Pattni Manish
Embezzlement c/s 257(b)-whether proved.
Held: Where a charge does not set out the particulars of the offence, such
charge is defective.  However, since in this case the accused appeared to
understand the substance of the charge, the defect would not be fatal.
S.30(b) Evidence Act does not permit the admissibility of a statement of a
deceased police officer because such is not one of the instances police
officer because such is not one other instances provided for under the
subsection.  This is because the accused has a right to cross-examine his
accuser.
Embezzlement is committed by an employee of the complainant company
when such employee interrupts in transits the movement of money or
reliable article from a third party to the complainant, and the employee
converts the same to his use before the money or valuable reaches his
embezzled had already been paid to the agent of the complainant. Therefore
it was not possible to embezzle what was already in the custody of the
complainant.  The possible offence could have been theft but not
embezzlement.
Appeal dismissed.
Tusingwire Teopista & anor Vs. Uganda
Doing an act intended to cause grievous harm c/s 209(a) Penal
Code Act-whether proved-whether offence minor and cognate to
attempted murder c/s 197(a) Penal Code Act.
Minor and cognate offence-whether doing an act intended to cause
grievous harm c/s 209(a) Penal Code Act was Minor and cognate
to attempted murder c/s 197(a) Penal Code Act.
Assault occasioning actual bodily harm-whether proved.
Charges-amendment thereof S.130(1)(a) Magistrates Courts Act -
whether because trial magistrate found that the evidence disclosed
an offence offer than the one originally charged, should have caused
the charge to be amended and should not have convicted the
accused of the offence for which they were not charged without
amendment.
Conviction of offence not charged and not minor and cognate-
whether conviction a nullity-whether conviction may stand because
no injustice caused under S.331 Criminal Procedure Code.
Attempted murder c/s 197(a) Penal Code Act-whether proved-
attempt defined.
Criminal liability-accident-whether accused not liable for the burning
of the child because child burnt by stove accidentally while running
away from lawful punishment by accused parent.
Held: It is the right of the defence to move court on a motion of no case to
answer.  Where the defence choose not to make the submission of no case
to answer, it does not preclude the trial court in pursuance of S.126(1) of
Magistrates Courts Act to rule that there is a case to answer or not.
Therefore the learned trial magistrate was entitled in the instant case to rule
on own motion that there was a case to answer.
And whereas according to the evidence on record after the prosecution
evidence, there might have been no case to answer, where nevertheless the
trial court rules that there is a case to answer, where there upon the defence
presents its evidence which only affords to strengthen the prosecution case,
the trial court is entitled to act on the evidence as a whole including that of
the defence to convict the accused.  In the instant case the prosecution
evidence had not made out a prima facie case on the original charge of the
offence of attempted murder.  However when the trial court ruled that there
was a case to answer, and indeed the appellants presented the evidence
which showed that they had indeed burned the complainant, the court was
entitled to treat the evidence as a whole and find that in fact an indictable
offence had been committed.
The defence of accident was not available to the appellants because the
prosecution had proved that the complainant was burn deliberately by the
appellants, who intended to extract information from the complainant about
the whereabouts of the lost money.
Even if the defence of accident was to be considered, and say that the
complainant was burnt by the stove as she ran away from being chastised
by her parent, the evidence still would indicate that the running away was
induced by the appellants' deliberate act of endangering their victim in such
a way that she had to run away and in so doing fell in the danger of being
burnt. Still the appellants would be liable for inflicting the consequent injuries.
An attempt to commit is an act done with intent to commit the crime, and
forming part of a series of acts which would constitute its actual commission
If it were not interrupted.  Therefore to support a charge of attempted murder
the prosecution must prove the full intent to murder, i.e. with malice
aforethought, which intent to murder, while being prosecuted, is interrupted
before the death results.  In the present case the complainant's hands and
legs were burnt by the appellants who left her to go with the injuries.
It cannot be said that the appellants had formed the intention to kill the
complainant but were interrupted in their efforts to do so.  Therefore the trial
magistrate was entitled to find that attempted murder had not been proved.
However, S.130(1)(a) Magistrate Courts Act provides that where, during trial,
it appears to court that the evidence discloses an offence than the offence
originally charged, if no injustice may be caused to the accused, the court
may make an order for the alteration of the charge by way of its amendment.
Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in convicting the appellants
of an offence with which they were not charged without having first called
for the amendment of the charge and inviting the appellants to plead thereto.
This was so because the offence of doing an act likely to cause grievous
harm c/s 209(a) Penal Code act was not minor and cognate to the offence
of attempted murder originally charged.
However, the trial was not a nullity because the appellants were not
prejudiced in preparing their defence.  A trial court is empowered to convict
a person of a minor and cognate offence because the major offence
originally charged ipso facto gives notice of the minor offence.  In the instant
case the trial court should have convicted the appellants with the offence of
assault occasioning actual bodily harm c/s 228 Penal Code Act because
the evidence on record disclosed such an offence.
S.331(2)(1) Criminal Procedure Code permits an appellate court to quash a
conviction and substitute it with the one the lower court should have passed.
In the present case the nature of the injuries disclosed the offence of assault
occasioning actual bodily harm therefore the appellants' conviction of doing
an act likely to cause grievous harm would be substituted with committing
an assault occasioning actual bodily harm c/s 228 Penal Code Act.
There was no evidence on record put before sentences.  Since 5 years was
the maximum sentence for the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily
harm, a sentence of 18 months will be substituted from the date of remand.
Appeal against sentence, and conviction for doing an act likely to cause
grievous harm, allowed and substituted with conviction of assault
occasioning actual bodily harm and sentence of 18 months.
Turyamureeba Paskali & anor Vs. Uganda.
Attempted murder c/s 197(a) Penal Code-whether proved -identification-
evidence-whether circumstantially sufficient to found a
conviction-identification by neighbour-whether may be mistaken-
whether judicial notice should be taken of the existence of moon-
right during the month of November
Held: There is no scientific basis for stating that in the month of November
there is always moonlight at 8.00om.
Even if the victim and the appellants were neighbours it is possible to make
mistaken identification of close relatives and friends.  In the instant case
there were irreconcilable and contradictory statements made by the
complainant while describing his assailants.  Therefore there was a real
possibility that he cold be mistaken in his identification of the appellants.
Appeal allowed.
Oketch Mitoto Samya Vs. Uganda.
Attempted theft c/s 370(1) Penal Code Act-whether proved where
accused transferred log book of motor vehicle to other names from
the owner's but did not take the car from the company premises.
Attempted theft c/s 370(1) Penal Code Act-asportation-whether
where there is no asportation an accused may be convicted of
attempted theft.
Attempts-overt act-whether fraudulent transfer of title of a motor
vehicle was an overt act of theft.
Held: The licensing officer was not a handwriting expert nor did he present
to be one.  However, his conclusion was a common sense view from his
routine matching and observation of signatures in the exercise of his duties
as a licensing officer.  Moreover, the trial court based its conviction of the
appellant on his failure or refusal to challenge the testimony through cross-
examination.
Because there was no asportation, an essential ingredient in the offence of
theft was not proved. However, the learned trial Magistrate was correct in
finding the appellant guilty of attempted theft because the act of fraudulently
transferring the ownership of the vehicle amounted to an overt act of theft in
terms of S.369(1) Penal Code Act.
Though 2 years imprisonment sentence was the maximum allowable for the
offence of attempted theft, the trial Magistrate was entitled to impose it
because the appellant never struck court as being repentant and the
appellant had grossly abused his position of trust in the company by
committing the offence.
Appeal dismissed.
Kalange Steven Vs. Uganda.
Store breaking & theft c/s 283(a) and 252 Penal Code Act-circumstantial-
evidence-whether offence proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Held: It is our law that a mere presence at the place where the offence is
committed is not enough to hold somebody liable for the commission of
that offence.  In the instant case it is true the appellant, among others, was
supposed to be on guard at the stores but that does not mean that the
appellant is criminally liable for whatever took place at the store.  The
prosecution had failed to move that the appellant was responsible for the
theft.
Imprisonment for 3 years was not excessive taking into account that the
value of the goods alleged stolen was shs.4 million and that the maximum
sentence for the offence was 7 years.
Appeal allowed.  Appellant to set free.
Banyenzaki John Vs. Uganda.
Defilement S.123(1) Penal Code Act-whether proved where vulva
was bruised but no penetration.
Indecent assault c/s 122(1) Penal Code Act -whether proved.
Held:The trial judge misdirected herself when she received the complainant's
testimony without conducting a voire dire on the complainant knew the
nature of an oath or the value of telling the truth, when, as her evidence on
record it was clear that the complainant was of the apparent age below 14.
And this misdirection on the part of the trial judge vitiated the conviction of
the appellant because it was the complainant's testimony that was the basis
of the conviction.
It was a misdirection on the part of the trial judge to reject the expert's
testimony which showed that there was no penetration without the judge
giving reasons for the departure from the expert opinion.
Appeal allowed.  Conviction for defilement set aside and substituted for
indecent assault c/s  122 of Penal Code Act and sentence of 20 years
substituted for 5.
Kataryeba Zackary & 3 others Vs. Uganda.
Intermeddling with property of deceased c/s 12(1),(2) Administrator
General's Act-whether proved.
Retrial-whether allowable.
Held: S.12 Penal Code act deals with insanity and not intermeddling.
Therefore, the accused were charged with non existent section.  This was a
material irregularity.
Moreover, after the court had allowed the charge sheet to be amended to
read S.12(1), (2) of the Administrator General's Act, the accused were never
invited to plead afresh to the new amended charge.  This was irregular.
The refusal by court to adjourn the case to enable the accused engage
another counsel was a denial of the accused constitutional right to be
represented.
A collective defence was unconstitutional as per Art 28 of the Constitution.
The evidence showed that the accused retained the property of the
deceased and dealt with it for the purpose of preserving the same, since the
accused worked with the deceased before his demise.  Therefore, the
offence of intermeddling was not proved by the prosecution to fill in the gaps
to the prejudice of the appellants.
Appeal allowed.
Nyanga Wilson Kizito Vs. Uganda.
mens rea for causing financial loss-whether not proved that accused
knew financial loss would result.
Causing financial loss c/s 258(a) Penal Code Act-irretrievable loss-
whether irretrievable loss must be moved as a necessary ingredient
for causing financial loss.
Held: According to the provisions of S.258(1) Penal Code Act, knowledge
by an accused employee that financial loss to his employer may result from
his actions or omissions, may be express or implied.  The appellant's
ignoring the long established procedures of verification to avoid fraud was
exculpatory and inconsistent with his innocence.
It is not a rule of law or fact that to prove the offence of causing financial
loss, the loss must be irretrievable.
Appeal dismissed.
Lusse Joseph Vs. Uganda.
Bail Art 23(b) ( c) Constitution of Uganda-committed after remand
lasting more 360 days-whether accused may be released on bail.
Held: Art 23(b)( c) of the Constitution provides that where a person has been
on remand for more than 360 days before he is committed, such person
shall be released on bail.  This means that even where a person is
committed after he has been on remand for more than 360 days such a
person shall be released on bail.
Application allowed.
Olowe Anthony Olotunde Vs. Uganda.
Illegal entry into Uganda c/s 17(2) Immigration Act-whether proved
where particulars of offence of the offence.
Plea-guilty-particulars of the offence-whether an accused person
can be found guilty on his own plea to a charge that does not
disclose the particulars of the offence.
Charges-failure to furnish particulars of the offence in the charge
sheet-whether defective.
Held: Under S.17 (2) Immigration Act the basic ingredients of the offence is
that an accused person must have illegally returned to Uganda when already
ordered to leave and having left Uganda when already ordered to leave and
having left Uganda under a deportation order signed by the Minister of
Internal Affairs under the Act or other written law and must have returned
without the permission of the minister.  In the instant case the charge sheet
only alleged that the appellant had illegally returned to Uganda when he had
previously been deported.  The charge sheet thus did not sufficiently provide
the appellant with reasonable information as to the nature of the offence with
which he had been charged. The appellant was entitled to know under which
law he had been deported and the particulars of the offence to enable him
sufficiently answer the charge.
Where an accused pleads guilty to a non-existing offence, such accused is
entitled to appeal where he is convicted by the trial court.
Where an accused pleads guilty, court is enjoined to explain to such
accused every ingredient of the offence with which he is charged, and the
accused should be required to admit or deny the same and his answer must
be recorded in his own words, in a form to prove to the appellate court that
the accused fully understood the charge and pleaded guilty to every element
of the same unequivocally.  In the present case the facts as narrated by
the prosecution did not disclose the elements of the offence.  Therefore the
appellant's plea was not unequivocal.
Appeal allowed.  Conviction quashed.  Sentences set aside. Appellant freed.
Iyouk Peter Dhour Vs. Uganda.
Knowingly using a counterfeit document c/s 14(h) EA Customs &
Management must testify.
Forfeiture of smuggled goods S.160(2) (b)-whether order lawfully
made.
Held: The lower court based its decision, in concluding that the documents
were counterfeit, on comparing the originals and the alleged counterfeits.
The discrepancies were glaring enough to entitle court to conclude without
calling the author thereof to certify that the documents presented by the
accused to claim the impounded goods, were counterfeit.  However, the
prosecution did not prove that the accused knew or should have known that
the documents were counterfeit.  Therefore the learned trial Magistrate erred
in convicting the accused.
However, since the accused/appellant could not lawfully claim to have
imported the impounded cigarettes, as the documents of claim were counter-
feit, court was entitled to order the goods condemned under S.160(2) (b)
East African Customs & Management Act.
Appeal allowed.  Conviction set aside.  Goods condemned.
Obbo Charles Onyango & Andrew Mwenda Vs. Uganda.
Bail S.74(3) (9) Magistrates Courts Act-Publication of false news
c/s 24 Penal Code Act-whether bail of Ugsh.2m/= for a person
accused of publishing false news c/s 24 PCA is excessive-whether
the Magistrate failed to exercise his discretion judiciously.
Held: While court should take into account the accused's ability to pay,
while exercising its discretion to grant bail on certain conditions, the court
should not impose such tough conditions that bail looks like a punishment
to the accused.  In the case instant, the High Court was empowered to
interfere with the discretion of the lower court while granting bail under S.74
(3)(A) Magistrates Courts Act where it is shown that that discretion was not
exercised judiciously.  The imposition of a condition that each accused
should pay Ugsh. 2m/= was a failure by that lower court to judiciously
exercise its discretion.
Application allowed.  Cash bail reduced to Ugsh. 200,000/=.
Tusiime Twebaze Drake Vs. Uganda.
Uttering a false document c/s 330 Penal Code Act-whether proved
where no handwriting expert's opinion was sort.
Obtaining money by false document and obtaining money by false
pretence - whether sentence of 3 years excessive.
Held: The object of an identification parade is to make sure that the ability of
the witness to recognize the suspect is tested.  However, the identification
parade is not the only such test.  The correctness or otherwise of
indent faction by witness, of the accused will depend on the circumstances,
such as the length of time, the distance, the light, the familiarity of the
witness with the accused.  If the quality of these is good, the danger of
distance identity is reduced. In the instance case the evidence adduced
by the prosecution and not contradicted by the appellant clearly showed that
the complainant and other prosecution witnesses who were involved in the
alleged motor vehicle purchase transaction office hours.  The circumstances
of identification could not come not have been better.  The learned trial
magistrate was correct to come to the conclusion she came to.
It is not necessary for the convicting court to always state that the
prosecuting has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The elements of the offence of uttering a false document and those of forging
a document are different.  Therefore it is possible as it was in the case
instant to convict a person of uttering a false document while acquitting him
of forging the same.  Moreover, there was no requirement that to prove of a
handwriting expert.  The appellant had been seen by witnesses that
testified seeing him uttering the false documents.
The sentence of 3 years was not excessive.  The trial court took into
account the fact that the appellant was a graduate who should have used
his education to do better things.
Appeal dismissed.
Matsanga Deo Vs. Uganda
Attempted murder c/s 197(a) and malicious damage to property
c/s 315 Penal Code Act-whether offences proved.
Sentencing Art 23(8) Constitution of Uganda - whether period of
remand must be taken into account in sentencing accused.
Attempting murder c/s 197(a) and malicious damage to property
c/s 315 Penal Code Act-whether sentences of 4 years and 6
months respectively excessive.
Held: The essential ingredients of the offence of attempted murder are that
the assailant intended to maim or disfigure the complaint and that the
intention was to be carried out with the weapon and that the assailant started
to execute the said intentions.  In the present case there was cogent
evidence that the appellant had been properly identified by the complainant
is the one that shot at his car while he drove it.  Therefore the Chief
Magistrate had been correct to put the accused to his defence and
eventually to convict him of the same.
The essential ingredients of the offence of malicious damage to property are
the damage is inflicted willfully and unlawfully by the accused.  Since the
complainant's car was damaged by the shots aimed at it by the appellant
who had been properly identified, the learned Chief Magistrate was correct
to find that the offence was proved.
The conditions for a proper unmistaken identification existed because the
appellant was known to his assailant; the distance between the two was a
mere 30 meters when the appellant fired the shots at the complainant; and it
was a clear day at 2:19 pm in broad day light.
It is not a requirement of the law that the trial Magistrate must record his
reasons for rejecting or allowing a submission of no case to answer.
Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate did not commit an error of law
in failing to record his reasons for rejecting the appellant's submission of no
case to answer.  Moreover, this failure to record his reasons did not
occasion a failure of justice.
S. 155 of the Evidence Act provides that statements made y the witness
immediately after the occurrence of an event are relevant to corroborate the
truth or otherwise of his latest statements in Court. In the present case the
fact that the complainant did not mention his assailants name in his
immediate statement at Police was not necessarily corroborative of the fact
that the complainant did not know his assailant, because the complainant
explained in his latest statement that he feared for his life since his
assailant was still at large.
The prosecution must produce all witnesses necessary to establish the truth
of a case.  If it fails to do so where the evidence is barely inadequate, the
Court is entitled to draw the inference that the evidence of the uncalled
witness would have tended to be adverse to the prosecution case.  In the
prosecution case.  In the case instant the prosecution proved all the
essential ingredients of the offences charged.  Therefore, the prosecution
evidence was adequate.
The learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in law in not recording the
proceedings in locus in quo.  However, a visit at a locus in quo is only
necessary to corroborate the evidence already on record.  In the instant case
since the evidence already recorded in open court was sufficient to establish
the guilt of the appellant, no miscarriage of justice was occasioned by the
procedural failure to record the proceedings of the locus in quo since the
visit thereto was superfluous.
The learned trial judge erred in not taking into account the period of remand
spent by the appellant prior to his conviction and sentence as this is now
constitutionally mandatory as per Article 23 (8) of the Constitution of the
Republic of Uganda 1995.
The sentences therefore would be reduced by 6 months.
Appeal against conviction dismissed.Appeal against sentence allowed in part.
Okello Florence Joyce Vs. Uganda
Corruptly receiving gratification as an inducement c/s 1(a) & 5(1)
Prevention of Corruption Act-whether proved.
Held: S.142(1) (b) MCA empowers the High Court on appeal or revision, with
discretion to set aside a judgment and conviction by a trial Magistrate
relied on evidence not wholly recorded by him where it appears that the
accused was thereby prejudiced, and may order a retrial.  However, this
power is discretionary and the learned appellate Judge was correct in not
disturbing the holding of the trial sentence on the record before her, which
was sufficient.
The appellant was not correct to argue that the learned appellate Judge erred
in upholding the shifting of the burden of proof to accused by the trial court
because this was not the case according to the facts on record.
The learned appellant Judge exercise the powers of the first appellate court
duly and correctly by subjecting the evidence on record from the trial court
to exhaustive scrutiny and came to the conclusion that the trial court was
correct in convicting the appellant.
Appeal dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Quarish Ggolooba
Bail - Treason and misprision of treason-whether accused on bail
may not travel outside jurisdiction without leave of court.
Held: Even where court has not imposed it as a condition for bail, an
accused should not travel outside jurisdiction without leave of court.
Application to cancel bail allowed.
Esunget Samuel Vs. Uganda
Destroying evidence, c/s 96 Penal Code Act and abuse of office
c/s 83(1) Penal Code Act -  whether proved.
Double jeopardy-whether proved where accused was charged with
two counts arising from the same facts, S.20 Penal Code Act.
Held: S.130(1) MCA empowers court with the discretion to allow amendment
of the charge at any stage of the proceedings.  However where the charge is
amended the court is supposed to call the accused to plead to the altered
charge and the court has the obligation to inform the accused court of his
right to demand the recall of witnesses to be cross examined.  Since the
trial court allowed the altering of the charge without calling upon the accused
to plead afresh thereto and informing him of his right to recall witnesses for
the prosecution for cross-examination the accused was prejudiced.
The record showed that the particular document allegedly destroyed by the
appellant was Police form No.3 from police file of Old Kampala CRB/SD/3/2/
95. the particularity was enough to sufficiently identify the document to the
appellant who was a seasoned police detective.  This ground of appeal would
thereby fail.
S.20 Penal Code Act provides for the defence of double jeopardy to the
effect that a person cannot be punished twice for the same offence.  In the
present case the accused was charged with commission of two-distinct
offences i.e. destroying Evidence c/s 96 Penal Code Act and abuse of office
c/s 83 (1) Penal Code Act.  All the two offences arose from the same facts
and the same incident namely, when the appellant destroyed (or was
alleged to) the police form 3, he thus committed the offences of destroying
employ of the State.  This is perfectly lawful and is an investigating officer
in the punished twice for the same offence c/s 20 Penal Code Act.
Therefore double jeopardy not established.
Though the appellant on appeal pleaded that the trial court convicted him on
suspicion and not on cogent evidence, the record of the trial court provided
ample and sufficient basis for appellant's conviction.  Moreover, an appellate
court must be circumspect about dislodging the lower courts findings on
matters of evidence and fact because it is the trial court that had the
opportunity to examine the witnesses, to hear their evidence & to scrutinize
their demeanor.  In this particular instance no reason is available to disturb
the findings of the trial court.
Since the accused was prejudiced in his not being given the opportunity to
recall prosecution witnesses when the charge was amended, fact his
sentence of 18 months would be reduced to 13 months, the period the
appellant had already served and therefore would be released immediately.
Appeal dismissed.
CRIMINAL PROCEDURE
Ocoke Francis Vs. Uganda.
Summary of evidence -whether this is not incorporated in the facts
at the preliminary hearing - whether such evidence may be relied
upon at the trial.
Held: The failure of the trial judge to compile a memorandum of agreed
facts did not occasion a miscarriage of justice since there was other
evidence adduced at the trial.
There was no sufficient evidence to establish malice aforethought.
The evidence for the defence on the issue of accident was quite
contradictory and unworthy of belief and therefore be rejected.
Looking at the evidence as a whole the degree of negligence was at
the evidence as a whole the degree of negligence was so high as to
establish the offence of manslaughter.
Kanalusasi George Vs. Uganda.
Plea of not guilty where the appellant admits the killing in his plea
of not guilty -whether the prosecution must be deemed to have
proved that fact beyond reasonable doubt.
Held: The admission by the appellant of killing the deceased did not
weaken his plea of not guilty and therefore the prosecution still had to
discharge its burden to prove that the killing was with malice
aforethought.
Since the prosecution did not adduce evidence to contradict the
account should have been accepted.
Bagamuhunda Reuben Vs. Uganda
Sentence for murder -whether a finding of murder may have a
sentence less that death.
Held: The learned trial Judge erred in presuming the deceased dead
since the evidence of this left some doubt.
The discrepancies in the evidence about the arson were minor and
therefore the appellant was rightly convicted.
The defence of provocation was not available because the appellant's
brother had long died before the crime.
Uganda Vs. Byansi Sempason & another.
Submission of no case to answer - when may be upheld.
Held: The admitted evidence contained absolutely nothing to connect
the accused with the offence in the remotest way since no mention is
made of any of them in the summary of evidence.
The exhibits tendered were not marked as required by law and
therefore it was difficult to say whether the exhibits were partly the
stolen goods.
A submission of no case to answer is properly made and upheld where
there is no evidence to prove an essential element of the offence and
or when the evidence adduced has been discredited.  In this case the
prosecution evidence was utterly insufficient to place the accused on
on their defence.
Uganda Vs. Juma Buruma Masudi Isabirye.
Common intention - the accused jointly charged - the prosecution
to prove common intention.
Held: Where the accused sets up a defence of alibi he does not assume
responsibility of proving it.  It is incumbent on the prosecution to destroy
or disprove it by adducing evidence placing him at the scene of the
material time.
Where the accused are jointly charged the prosecution must either
prove common intention as provided under section 22 of the Penal Code
Act or each accused is a principal offender under section 21 of the PC.
In law for an act to amount to an attempt some actus reus must have
been done by the accused.  The text to apply is the common law
principle of proximity as it was reiterated in the case of Everest
Mugabi Vs. Uganda (1976) HCB 124.  The prosecution must prove both
an overt act sufficiently proximate to the intended offence.
As regards attempted murder, an over act and positive intention to
cause the death must be established.  Republic V. Luseru Wandera s/o
Wandera (1948) 5 EACA 101.
In deciding whether common intention exists the court is funded by both
evidence and conduct of the accused.  Common intention may be
inferred from presence, conduct and omission by anyone of the
accused to disassociate himself from attack. Actual participation is
not essential.
Charles Eweku Vs. Uganda.
Forfeiture - whether an order for forfeiture could be validly made
where the appellant has been acquitted of theft.
Held: The learned Chief Magistrate found that the appellant's claim to
ownership of the motor was questionable and was thereby justified in
making the order for forfeiture, this being in inspite of failure by the
prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
Mutyaba Semu Vs. Uganda.
Bail - Advanced age - whether 60 years of age was advanced age
for purposes of granting bail to the applicant.
Held: 60 years per se was not advanced age but this coupled with the
fact that the accused suffered from diabetes, a disease that required a
good diet which could not be provided by prison authorities and the fact
that the accused had been reporting faithfully to court, he could be
granted bail.
Sarapio Tinkamaliirwe Vs. Uganda.
Judgment - whether the trial judge's first stating the case for the
accused and then the case for the prosecution was a valid of
approach in writing the judgment.
Held: Unless there is some particular issue or conduct raised by the
defense that requires a preliminary decision, it is preferable that while
writing the judgment for the judge to proceed with setting out the
prosecution case first as it is stated; by the witness, then to set out the
defense case as set out by the appellant and his witness, if any and
subsequently to indicate the Court's findings on the whole of the
evidence.  In the instant case the learned that judge's approach however
undesirable did not cause him to come to the wrong conclusion as his
conclusion wee supported by evidence.
The learned trial judge's direction to the assessors as to the
ingredients of the offence of kidnapping with intent to murder was
misleading because he seemed to understand that the ingredients have
an intention to murder the victims or to put him in danger of being
murdered.  The ingredients of the offence of kidnap with intention to
murder c/s 235(1)(a) of the Penal Code are not that the appellant has
formed the intention to murder - victims or to put them in danger of
being murdered.  The section provides a broader intent than the intent to
murder or to put in danger of being murdered because it states;
"may be murdered or be disposed of as to be murdered".  However, on
all the evidence the facts proved that the appellant disposed of the
victims so as to put them in danger being murdered.  Therefore, the
learned judge's misconduct did not occasion a miscarriage of justice.
The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he held that the
appellant was guilty of aggravated robbery merely because he had been
seen by the complainants stab and kidnap two victims with intent to
have them murdered at about 9.00 am and when he returned at about
12.00non and threatened the complainants to part with their money and
they did part with it, the learned trial judge considered the lapse of 3
hours to be :soon after" and then deemed "soon" to be equivalent to
"immediately: as used in s.273 (2) of the Penal Code.  The learned trial
Judge mis-conducted himself when he deemed that an act of violence
committed in the course of a kidnapping constitute done transaction
with a threat to kill in a robbery some hours later.  There was no
evidence to support the findings that the appellant committed the offence
of aggravated robbery.  The use of a deadly weapon was not sufficient
proximate in time to the taking of the money from the victims by the
victims by the appellant.  However, there was ample evidence to support
a finding of simple robbery.
The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he convicted the
appellant on four counts but instead passed only one sentence, even if
no courts 3 and four as per hid findings, he imposed the mandatory
death sentence, he should have passed sentence on each count.
Ogola Richard Vs. Uganda
Charge sheet - whether discrepancy between the items listed
stolen in the charge sheet and those sought to be proved by the
prosecution witness was fatal to the trial.
Held: The offence of theft was minor and cognate to that of
embezzlement as both belonged to the same family.  Theft is minor in
a sense that the gravity of punishment therefore prescribed is minor to
that of embezzlement and the two offences are cognate because both
offences involve a fraudulent taking away of someone's property.
It is not mandatory that the items stated in the charge sheet in an
offence of theft must all be proved in order to convict the accused.
The prosecution need to prove that some of more of the items in the
charge sheet were stolen by the appellant.
The trial magistrate failed to exclude hearsay evidence from his
judgment before finding the appellant guilty of theft since the said
hearsay evidence was incriminating to the appellant, it did occasion of
justice, and was fatal to the conviction.
The conduct of the accused in running away from the scene of the
crime was circumstantial evidence pointing to the guilt of the accused
but it required corroboration.  The only would be corroborative evidence
connecting the appellant with the theft was that one by a person who
was not called to testify.  Therefore there was a break in the chain of
the circumstantial evidence and would not properly be relied upon to
irresistibly point to the guilt of the accused.
It was not proper for the trial Magistrate to require the accused to
challenge the evidence of the prosecution that some thefts occurred.
This tended to put the burden of proof on the accused and a conviction
based on the weakness of the defence instead of the strength of the
prosecution case would not stand.
Wini Geyonga Rusheyegera Vs. Uganda.
Minor and cognate offense -whether the accused cab be convicted
of a minor and cognate offence where the prosecution fails to prove
all the ingredients of the offence charged.
Held: The trial Magistrate was fully entitled under section 143 of the
Magistrates' Court Act, 1970 to decide the facts as he did not hold the
appellant guilty of a lesser offence.
Courts have no powers to reduce a sentence below the statutory
minimum sentence.
where there are more than one count in a charge, each charge should
carry its own verdict either of conviction or acquittal and each conviction
should be covered by a sentence to be served either concurrently or
consecutively.
Mohammed Yasin Sekajolo Vs. Uganda.
Sentence - attempted murder - long period on remand -8 years is
imprisonment excessive - reduced to 6 years.
Held: The appellant was properly convicted but the sentence was
excessive and it would be reduced to 6 years.
Appeal against conviction dismissed.
Smith Opon Achak & Ahmed Oceny V Uganda.
Plea in bar -whether the appellants had been granted presidential
pardon.
Held:  The resident may grant pardon according to Article 73 (9) of the
Constitution which does not state that the pardon must be in writing but
the fact that the exercise of the Presidential prerogative has to be acted
upon by officers of government prison authorities, it means that the
pardon must be a signed instrument.  It was incumbent upon the
appellants to prove on the balance of probabilities whether they had been
pardoned by the General Presidential pardon.  They appellants had failed
to prove this.
Harry Isiko Vs. Uganda.
Alternate charge u/s 151 of the magistrates courts Act -whether
accused charged with obtaining money by false pretences may
be convicted by theft even though not so charged.
Held: S.151 of the Magistrate Courts Act, 1970 empowers a court
hearing a charge of obtaining by false pretences to convict on the
alternative charge of theft even though the accused was not so formally
charged.  But this can only be so where the facts of the case support
the theft.  In the instant case the particulars of the false pretence did
not reflect the possible offence of conversion.  The situation could have
only been saved by having theft as alternative charge to appear formally
as such a charge or for the Court to bring it to the attention of the
defence be prepared to this effect.  This was not the case.  Therefore
Court no proper trial on the issues pertaining to the no alleged theft.
Therefore Court misdirected itself to convict the accused on an issue
where there was no proper trial.
Abasi Kanyike Vs. Uganda.
Confessions - whether defence may retract during defence, a
confession it has already admitted as to it's voluntariness during
the prosecutions case.
Held: The voluntariness or otherwise of a confession may only be
analyzed at the trial within a trial and this is during the prosecutions
case.  If court has however already admitted the confessions because
they were not objected to during the prosecutions case, it is too late to
challenge them in the defence.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself when he allowed the defence to dispute the
admissibility of the confession, which had already been approved.  This
caused or was evidence of confusion.
Adonia Zoreka & another Vs. Uganda.
Assessors - whether an assessor who has been absent from part
of the trial may nevertheless give his opinion - whether such a trial
is a nullity.
Held: Once an assessor, has been given leave of absence and the trial
continues, the absent assessor case to be an assessor for that particular
case.  The court is not properly constituted if the absent assessor
returns and resumes his seat, when he has not heard all the evidence.
Therefore, in the instant case having allowed the absent assessor to
resume his seat and give his opinion rendered the trial a nullity.
The appeal would be allowed and a fresh trial ordered.
Moses Bagada Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing -attempted rape - whether a sentence of 6 years
imprisonment of a first young offender was proper.
Held: The appellants conviction was justified because both the
complainant and PW2 knew the accused very well, they had been
drinking together and there was moonlight to identify the accused at the
scene of the crime.
The sentence of 6 years imprisonment with 12 strokes of the cane was
not proper since the appellant was a young offender who was not
supposed to be imprisoned at the time he committed the offence.  The
sentence would therefore be reduced to 4 years imprisonment 6 strokes
of the cane.
Vincent Rwamwaro Vs. Uganda.
Appeals -second appeal-whether the existence of otherwise of a
grudge was a matter of fact not to be entertained by the second
appellant court.
Held: The existence or otherwise of a grudge between the appellant and
the prosecution witnesses due to the differences based on political
parties was a matter of fact and not law.  Therefore it was not an issue
such as would be determined by the second appellate court.
An accused person should take all reasonable steps to ensure that his
counsel appears for him and if he is unable to appear to offer a
satisfactory explanation to court for his absence.  In the instant case
though the appellant's counsel was absent, the appellant did not furnish
any explanation as to why his counsel was not in court.  Therefore the
trial Magistrate exercised his discretion judicially when he refused an
adjournment because there was no explanation before him as to why
the appellant's counsel was not in court.
The issue that the learned justice of the first appellate court misdirected
himself when he set aside the order of compensation, was an issue that
affected the legality of the sentence and would therefore be considered
even if no cross appeal was preferred.
S.331(2) (b) and (c) of the Criminal Procedure Code empower an
appellate court to vary the sentence imposed by the lower court, even
to specify the amount payable as compensation mandatory after a
convocation for robbery where no death sentence is made.  Therefore the
learned justice of the first appeal misdirected himself when he set aside
the order for compensation on the basis that the order was prejudicial
since it does not specify the amount of compensation.  Therefore, the
