appellant would be ordered to pay shs. 30,000/= to the victim of the
robbery.
Further both the learned justice of the first appeal and the learned trial
Magistrate misdirected themselves when they did not impose the
mandatory order as provided in S.26 of the MCA which provides for an
order of police supervision on the person convicted or robbery. The court
would therefore order that the appellant undergoes police supervision for
a period of 2 years from the date of expiration of his sentence.
Andrew Gitau Kimani Vs. Uganda.
Appeals - extending time therefore - whether ignorance of law due
to being a foreigner were sufficient reason for extension of time
within which to appeal.
Held: While it is true that ignorance of the law governing appeals cannot
perse be sufficient ground for extending time in which to appeal, it is a
mitigating factor in favour of the applicant where it is coupled with other
circumstances which make it clear that the delay was not caused by the
appellant's dilatory conduct.  Therefore, this amounted to sufficient
reason for extension of time.
The learned justice's order in the High Court that the appellant pays
costs of the application to the State was strange and improper.
Professor Isaac Newton Ojok Vs. Uganda.
Disqualification of a judge - application thereof -whether must
invariably be decided upon judicially and recorded.
Held: While Art.73 of the constitution empowered the president to grant
pardon or amnesty, it is clear from the evidence that the appellant was
one of a select few who was to appear in court charged in the treason.
Therefore, the trial judge directed herself correctly on the evidence and
law when she rejected the appellant's plea in arrest of judgment, that
he had been pardoned while on remand.
When the trial judge was invited to disqualify herself on the basis of the
likelihood of partiality in favour of the state on the grounds that she was a
blood sister of the first Deputy Prime Minister, a pillar of the government,
the appellant was alleged to be fighting, she should have made a record
of the application and her decision to refuse the application should have
been reached judicially and recorded.  It was a misdirection on the part
of the trial judge not to have put on record an application of so serious a
nature.
In order to find whether a judicial officer was biased it is necessary to
consider whether there was a real likelihood of bias by considering
whether the judicial officer laboured under a pecuniary or kindred interest.
After the judicial officer has passed that test, then it may be necessary
to verify whether the particular judicial officer's act or conduct satisfied
reasonable persons that the court was impartial and unbiased.  In the
instant case the allegation of kinship interest because it was not he
own brother in court nor was the National Resistance Movement itself in
court directly.  However, a reasonable man taking into account the
learned trial judge's premature findings of fact before the accused gave
his defence would have conclude led the judge was probably biased in
favour of the state consciously or unconsciously.
Godfrey Tinkamalirwe & another Vs. Uganda.
Assessors - summing up - whether one sided and biased.
Held: Although S.235(2) provides that the necessary intent that the
victim be murdered in the offence of kidnap under s.235(1)(a) and (b), it
may be presumed if the victim is not seen for a period of more than 6
months.  In the instant case the trial judge held that the intent must be
proved and not presumed.  He was entitled to hold so because the victim
had ended up in police custody meaning that the intent had not been
proved and could therefore not be presumed.
Generally speaking, motive is irrelevant in criminal law except in some
exceptional circumstances, such as prosecution for libel where a
defence of fair comment or qualified privilege is raised.  However, motive
is always useful in showing the probable reason for the commission of
the offence.  The existence of a motive makes it more likely that an
accused person did in fact commit the offence.  Therefore, the learned
trial judge directed himself correctly in taking into account the fact that
the victim and the appellant belonged to rival churches.
The summing up to the assessors must not leave room for a reasonable
man to think that the judge did favour one side unfairly.  In the instant
case the assessors were left with the clear impression that they should
find the appellants guilty not on the strength of the prosecution's case
but on the falsity of the appellant's defence.  The trial judge here
misdirected himself misdirected himself.  However, the irregularity did
not accession a miscarriage of justice.
Since the Kidnap did not fall under S.235(1)9a) of the Penal Code, the
appeal must succeed in part.  However, the evidence clearly proved that
the victim was secretly and wrongfully confined after abduction before
being taken to the police station.  Therefore the appellants were guilty of
kidnapping with intent to confine secretly and wrongfully 236 of the Penal
Code.
Uganda Vs. Silver Nabugemu.
Sentencing -theft of millet valued at shs.600/= whether sentence
of 15months imprisonment was excessive.
Held: Though S.13(1) MCA did not expressly mandatorily provide for a
conviction prior to sentencing, it is a mandatory rule of practice that
before court may sentence the accused, it must first record a finding of
guilt, conviction and then sentence.  The trial Magistrate's imposed
sentence was illegal since the accused had not been found guilty and
convicted.
The sentence of 15 months imprisonment would not be supported in view
of the value of the millet alleged to have been stolen.  Even if it were
assumed that the procedure adopted by the trial Magistrate was proper
the sentence of 15 months imprisonment was out of proportion and
excessive.
The trial Magistrate erred in law to have on his own motion declared the
accused a habitual criminal and yet the accused was never invited to
challenge such an allegation.  The proper procedure before sentence
would have been to invite the prosecution to tell court as to the
antecedents and character of the accused and also to invite the accused
to say something in mitigation of sentence.
Major John Kazoora Vs. Uganda.
Charge sheet - whether defective for failure to mention the name of
co-suspect.
Held: S.86 (d) of the Magistrates' Courts Act requires that the charge
sheet specifically names or describes the co-charged.  However by long
time practice it has become acceptable to mention in a charge that
somebody unnamed and or undescribed is not joined because he is not
available to be joined.  Therefore, the non disclosure did not occasion
injustice to the appellant in as much as  the charge sheet is nor really
evidence.
Considering that ISO is an intelligence organization whose operations
have of necessity to be covert on the evidence of the prosecution, it
could not rule out the possibility that the sh. 12 million was intended for
ISO purposes such as payment to Jane as an ISO agent.  The
prosecution had failed in their evidence to rule out beyond reasonable
doubt that the said money was not meant for an agent.  The trial Chief
Magistrate clearly erred in law and fact when he failed to scrutinize the
evidence of the prosecution.
Rules 10 of the Evidence (Statement to Police Officers) Rules does not
preclude an oral admission to a police officer of relevant rank provided
the suspect is properly cautioned.  However when the accused denied
having made the admission, the trial Chief Magistrate should have held a
trial within a trial to determine whether the admission was really made by
the appellant.  The trial Chief Magistrate misdirected himself when he
accepted as made a confession the appellant had denied, without first
holding a trial within a trial.
The trial Chief Magistrate erred in law to have held that the debiting of
ISO account and crediting of appellant's account on 25th January 1991
constituted theft because the money which is in the bank belongs to the
bank and therefore mere debiting and crediting does not constitute taking
or asportation which is an element in the offence of theft.
Sam Lutaya Vs. Uganda.
Judgment - failure to appraise accused's defense of alibi in the
judgment - whether proper.
Held: The circumstances favouring a correct identification had been
properly found by the learned trial judge when he considered as proved by
the witnesses that there was bright moon light the witnesses were very
close, the witnesses knew the accused very well before and all of the
witnesses described the accused's clothing in very similar terms.
The trial judge erred in concluding that the appellant had been
unmistakenly identified without first or at all having considered the
accused's defence of alibi.  This offended against the principle of the law
that before a decision of fact is made the evidence must be looked at as
a whole.  However this was not fatal since the second assessor
considered the defence of alibi in his findings and found that it had not
been provide.
The appellant could not be said not to have had the requisite mens rea
when he took part in a gang that invaded the complaint's house and one
of the attackers with common intent discharged a gun at close range at
the complainant.
Ali Fadul Vs. Uganda.
No case to answer - whether ruling prejudged the case - whether
accused did not have a fair trial.
Held: When the defence made a submission of no case to answer the
trial judge was not entitled to rule that the prosecution had provide its
case beyond reasonable doubt while rejecting the submission.  This
prejudiced the defence case since the trial judge had formed the opinion
that the accused was guilty before hearing his defence and thereby the
accused was not afforded a fair hearing. Appeal allowed - a retrial ordered.
W.W Mpora & 8 others Vs. Uganda.
Receiving stolen property c/s 298(1) of the Penal Code Act -
sentence - whether seven years imprisonment excessive.
Held: Since the appellants had been on remand for 3 years, seven years
sentence was excessive.  They should be immediately released.
Appeal Allowed.
Bulasio Sengendo & another Vs. Uganda.
Witnesses - recalling a witness - whether trial magistrate erred in
refusing to recall a witness - whether this was evidence of bias
against the appellants.
Held: Although the charge sheet showed that the appellants had been
charged under S.257 (c ) the correct subsection should have been (b)
since the embezzlement with which they were charged concerned a
limited liability company.
Embezzlement is committed by an employee when he steals
property of the employer before the employer acquires either actual or
constructive possession of that property.  In the present case, the
property alleged to have been stolen was already in the custody of the
employer and therefore the offence of embezzlement was not committed.
The offence of theft was committed when the spares were taken out of the
shop even if they were intercepted at the gate but he issue is whether it
were the appellants who stole the spares.  The fraudulent intent was
indicated by the stranger who ran away when he was intercepted with the
spares.  His running away was evidence that he fraudulently intended to
deprive the owner of the property permanently.
An admission is a statement made by the accused, though not amounting
to a confession but contains gravely incriminating facts against the maker.
In the instant case the alleged apologies were not unequivocal as they
were open to different interpretations, one such interpretation being that
they were sorry for a theft to be committed against the company without
their preventing it.
When the trial Magistrate ruled out the possibility that PW3 was not a
credible witness in light of the contradictions in his evidence and should
have admitted his evidence with caution.
It is trial law that invariably circumstantial evidence must be narrowly
examined to avoid a possibility of a fabrication by ruling out co-existing
circumstances reasonably capable of explaining the situation, before
inferring the guilt of the accused.  In the instant case there were several
contradictions in the prosecution case which were not explained away
and his cast doubt on the guilt of the accused.  The circumstantial
evidence was not water tight.
Counsel holding a watching brief has no right to address court in
opposition to a prosecutor although as an officer of court he may inform
court on matters that can assist court while the interest of justice demand.
A trial magistrate has a discretion under S.98 of the Magistrates Court
Act to decide whether or not to recall a witness.  The trial magistrate was
entitled to refuse the recall of the witness and this did not indicate bias on
plot of the magistrate.
The inference of bias must be as to what a reasonable man would think
given the set of circumstances.  It the reasonable man would thing that
the Magistrate did favour one side unfairly at the expense of another than
bias is proved.  In the instant case there was no evidence of a real
likelihood of bias on the part of the Magistrate.
It is not a correct statement of the law that court is at liberty to cancel
bail at any stage.  Evidence in favour of cancellation of bail must be
evidence on oath and the court must decide judiciously that it is justified
in the present case the trial Magistrate erred when she cancelled the
accused's bail on mere speculative information from prosecution.
Appeal allowed.
Karim Bagenda & Ors Vs. Uganda
Appeals-jurisdiction-whether court has jurisdiction to entertain appeal
when there has been no conviction.
Appeals-conviction-whether appellant court has jurisdiction to entertain
appeal when there is no conviction.
Judgment-reservation of reasons-whether a judge may reserve reasons for
judgement-SS.81, 84 & 85 TID.
Held: SS.81, 84, & 85 of the Trial on Indictment Decree do not permit a
trial judge to reserve reasons for her judgment to be given later.
The learned trial judge's judgment was defective in as far as she did not
specifically record the conviction and sentence.
An appellate court has no jurisdiction to entertain an appeal where there
is no conviction.
Record to be remitted back to trial court for a proper recording conviction
and sentence.
Sula Kasiira Vs. Uganda
Identification parade-whether properly conducted.
Sentencing-simple robbery c/ss.272 & 273(1) (b) Penal Code-10 years
imprisonment whether excessive.
Sentencing - Corporal Punishment - 6 strokes of the cane for simple
robbery c/ss.272 & 273(1) (b) Penal Code Act -whether proper.
Held: There was evidence to suggest that both identifying witnesses had
ample time and opportunity to observe their assailants at the scene so as
to enable them to recognize them on the identification parade.  The
accident took place in the early hours of the morning about 7.30am and it
was not dark.  Therefore, conditions for proper identification existed.
For theft to be proved there must be what amounts in law to an
aspiration, i.e. the carrying away of the complainant's goods without the
complainant's consent.  In the case before us the learned trial judge
correctly made a judgment of the theft, because, the complainant's cash
of Ush.4million, some rolls of textile, video cassettes, and the pick-up
where loaded had been assorted or carried away from the complainant's
by the accused.
The sentence of 10 years imprisonment was not excessive because the
offence with which the appellant was convicted carried a maximum
sentence of life imprisonment, and  moreover, the appellant was a
police officer who was supposed to enforce the law and protect people
and their property against criminals. Here he was doing the very opposite.
He sentence of 10 years was not excessive.
S. 274(a) of the Penal Code Act provides for corporal punishment for the
offence of simple robbery.  It is at the discretion of the trial court as to
how many canes may be given to the convict.  Therefore this ground of
appeal had no merit, the trial court having in its discretion sentenced the
appellant to 6 strokes of the cane.
S. 273(3) of the Penal Code provides for compensation in favour of the
victim of the offence of simple robbery.  In the instant case the appellant
was liable to compensate the complainants for his stolen money in cash,
roles of textiles, and videocassettes un recovered.
S.123 Trial on Indictment Decree provides for an order of police supervision
for a maximum period of 5 years whenever a person is convicted of simple
robbery under S.272 of the Penal Code and sentenced to a term of
imprisonment lesser than life.  In the instant case the order was for 4
years.  The appellate court would not interfere with such a powerful order.
Appeal dismissed.
Fred Sabahashi Vs. Uganda
Manslaughter c/s.182 Penal Code - whether proved.
Prima-facie case-manslaughter whether trial court correctly put accused
to his defence-whether there was a prima facie case of manslaughter
against the accused.
Common intention c/s.22 Penal Code -torture and death of deceased-
whether common intention established.
Held: S.7(1) Trial on Indictments Decree requires that where court is of
the opinion that the available evidence after the close of the prosecution's
case, is sufficient to support the indictment, court must invite counsel for
both parties to address court before making a finding of not guilty to the
original indictment.  In the present case the learned trial judge erred when
he found that the accused were not guilty of murder as charged without
having first invited both parties to address court on that respect.
However, S.71(2) of  the Trial on Indictment Decree does not require court
to invariably invite counsel for the defense to make a submission of no
case to answer, counsel must make his indication to court that he wishes
to make the submission.  In the instant case counsel for the defense
never indicated to court that he wished to make that submission and
court was thereby justified in not giving counsel the opportunity in its own
motion.
Nevertheless when court must proceed with a lessser charge than one in
the original indictment, the accused person must be required to plead to
the altered indictment.  However this did not occasion a miscarriage of
justice since the accused were forced on opportunity to defend themselves
against the altered indictment of manslaughter.
A submission that there is no case to answer means that no prima facie
case has been made out on the available evidence after the close of the
prosecution's case, against the accused.  That no reasonable court would
convict the accused on that available evidence.  In the instant case the
two accused, including the appellant tortured the accused to death.
The learned trial judge correctly inferred that both the accused shared a
common intention to prosecute an unlawful purpose, which resulted in the
death of the deceased and thus put both accused to their defense.
Common intention may be inferred from the failure of the accused from
disassociation himself from the actions of his co accused. In the
instant case it was reasonable to infer that the two accused persons had
formed a common intention to prosecute an unlawful purpose which was
to torture the deceased to death.  The learned trial judge was therefore
justified in his conclusion.
S.81 (3) of the Trial on Indictment Decree provides that the trial court gives
reason for his disagreement with the assessors.  In the instant case even
if the reasons were not explicitly put, they were reasonably inferred from
the judgment. Appeal dismissed.
Byaruhanga Leo Vs. Uganda
Sentencing -defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act - whether
sentence of 10 years imprisonment excessive.
Held: For an appeal against sentence to succeed, the appellant has to
satisfy court that the sentence is manifestly excessive.
In the instant case the trial Judge took into account.  The advanced age
of the appellant as the 11-month period during which he had been on
remand.
She rightly observed that defilement, a serious crime carrying a maximum
sentence of death was rampant in the country and courts therefore have to
impose deterrent sentences.
The appellant, who chased the complainant, grabbed her, took her to his
house where he defiled her and denied the incident out right did not
deserve any leniency and was accordingly rightly sentenced.  That is why
the Supreme Court dismissed this appeal.
Uganda Vs. Londoma Feremino
Confirmation of sentence s.167(1)(2) of the magistrates' courts
Held: The trial Magistrate should have encouraged the accused to give
her reasons for inflicting injuries on the victim because they could include
justification in the form of self defence.
It is good practice to record facts constituting the offence, put them to the
accused and only after he has admitted the corrections of those facts,
and when the facts constitute the commission of the offence charged can
a conviction be properly entered.
The facts narrated in this case were admitted by the accused.  He
admitted them without any complaint and said nothing thereafter in his
mitigation.  The admission of those facts by the accused therefore cured
the defect in the plea.  The sentence is therefore confirmed as imposed
by the trial magistrate.
Capt.Wilberforce Serunkuma Vs. Uganda.
Bail - whether AIDS falls under exceptional circumstance of grave
illness under s.14(A) (2)(a) trial on indictments (Amendment) Act
1985 justifying grant of bail.
Held: Where satisfactory evidence of AIDS is adduced, a court may
consider the circumstance of the case and in the absence of a certificate
from the Medical Board hold that AIDS is grave illness.
To justify grant of bail, the applicant has to prove to the satisfaction of the
court that he was incapable of getting adequate treatment whilst in
custody.
To justify grant of bail, the applicant has to prove to the satisfaction of the
court that he was incapable of getting adequate treatment whilst in
custody.
In the instant case, all the court has is an affidavit of the applicant
supported by some documents from the TASO indicating that the
applicant is an "AIDS" victim.
No affidavit was sworn on report made by any doctor who treat him Luzira
or Mbuya Military Hospital to show that he could get adequate treatment
whilst in custody.
As the record stands therefore the statutory requirement of proof of
exceptional circumstance, in this case grave illness has not been fulfilled.
The bail application is therefore dismissed.
Bimbi Peter Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing - defilement c/s 123(1) -whether sentence of 15 years
imprisonment plus 10 strokes of the case was excessive.
Held: There is no merit in the appeal against to conviction as the evidence
against the appellant was overwhelming.  The complainant and the
appellant were well known to each other and the incident took place in
broad daylight.  Also a neighbor, Rosemary Nantale, found the two red-
handed in the sexual act and upon seeing her the appellant got up and
ran away.  The appellant had also informed the secretary for defense that
he had talked to the complaint's father about the incident and that it was
going to be settled amicably.
Further, the medical evidence corroborated the complaint's testimony
that the appellant had previously defiled her and that she had sexual
intercourse on or about the day of the incident.
The sentence of 15 years imprisonment was certainly harsh but it is
justifiable given the fact the appellant who was 30 years old had defiled
the title girl (11 years) twice and would most probably have continued to
do so for a long time.
However the order for corporal punishment was illegal since it is neither
provided for by S.123 (1) of the Penal Code and since S.108 of the Trial
on Indictment Decree was in-applicable in this case.  Accordingly the
appeal against sentence succeeds in part.
Appeal against conviction set aside.
Appeal against sentence succeeds only to the extent that the order for
corporal punishment is set aside.
Mohammed Kasoma Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing -defilement c/s 123(1) of the Penal Code Act-whether
sentence of 91/2 imprisonment excessive.
Held: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and gave the following
reasons for its orders.  There is no substance to the applicant's complaint
that the learned Judge did not take his defense of alibi into consideration.
Despite certain alleged drawbacks to the complainant's evidence, the
learned Judge found that the testimony of the complainant was reliable
and rejected the defense.  Having examined the evidence again we found
that they could be no doubt at all on that point.  There defence is
accordingly rejected.
The learned Judge having warned himself properly of the need for
corroboration, went on to state that if he were satisfied that the
complainant was truthful he could still convict on her uncorroborated
evidence.  It is apparent that the complainant was an exceptionally
persuasive witness her whole narrative was consistent.  The medical
evidence supported her story we could well understand that with or without
corroboration the complainant's evidence must be accepted in favour of
the appellant's alibi.  Consequently this ground of appeal fails.
The appellant a man of 49 years of age cannot be excused for playing
this dangerous and disgraceful trick on a girl of 14 years who knew the
appellant's wife and so trusted the appellant.
Accordingly, thee is no reason to interfere with the sentence imposed.
In any case it was not manifestly excessive.
Appeal dismissed.
Sam Buteera Vs. Uganda
Sentencing -defilement c/s 123(1)of the Penal Code Act -whether
sentence of 12 years imprisonment plus strokes excessive was
rightly passed.
Held: The victim knew the appellant well, she had seen him at her home
before the incident.  Even if she was in a coffee plantation she saw him
coming to attack her with the help to lantern.  He even talked to her after
sexually assaulting her.  The learned trial Judge therefore rightly directed
herself and the assessors on the law relating to uncorroborated evidence
of a complainant in sexual offence.  The circumstances under which the
offence was committed were such as to render aspects of the case in
relation to the fact of defilement such as the medical evidence and
distressed condition in which the victim was found by her grandmother.
Appellant was therefore properly convicted.
S.123 Penal Code does not provide for corporal punishment for defilement
S.108 Trial on Indictment Decree is inapplicable as it gives the High Court
power to impose corporal punishment to persons under the age of 16
years.  The order of corporal punishment against the appellant was
therefore illegal and is accordingly set aside.
Appeal against conviction fails.
Appeal against sentence succeeds only to the extent that the order for
corporal punishment is set aside.
John Baptist Kibuka Vs. Uganda.
Sentence - defilement c/s 123(1) -whether sentence of 25 years
imprisonment with six strokes of the cane plus police supervision
for 5years upon completion of sentence was excessive.
Held: The procedure to be followed by a trial Court which is faced with a
child of tender years as a witness is set out in S.38 (3) Trial on
Indictments Decree.  The most recent decided case to which the trial
judge referred to is Mukasa Deogratius Vs. Uganda, Criminal Appeal
No.21/93 (unreported) where "a child of tender years" has been defined as
any age, or apparent age, of under 14 years, in the absence of any
special circumstances.  In the instant case, PW4 was not a child of
tender years because he was 14 years old when he gave evidence.
There were no special circumstances, which justified him to be regarded
as a child of tender years. It was therefore not necessary for the learned
trial Judge to decide whether PW4 should give sworn or unsworn evidence.
it was self evident from his judgment that the learned trial Judge made a
careful and comprehensive evaluation of all the evidence in the case
before coming to the conclusion he did.  He considered the prosecution
evidence, the most important aspects of which came from P.W.4, an
eyewitness, and the medical evidence.  He also considered the appellant's
alibi, which he found, rightly so in our view, did not create a whole, the
trial Judge, in our view, correctly found that all ingredients of the offence
with which the appellant was charged had been proved to the required
standard.
There was no useful purpose of calling the victim since as the prosecution
State Attorney put it she could not comprehend the proceedings and also
in view of the fact that the evidence of the other witness was sufficient to
prove the case against the appellant to the required standard.
S. 123 (1) of the Penal Code provides for death as the maximum sentence
for the offence of defilement.  Although we are unable to say that the
sentence of 25 years in the instant case is illegal, we are satisfied that it
was manifestly harsh and excessive.  Considering the circumstances of
the case a sentence of 16 years imprisonment would be appropriate.
Regarding Corporal punishment following the decision in the case of
Bambi Vs. Uganda Criminal Appeal No. 33/94, corporal punishment is
neither provided for under S.123(1) Penal Code nor S.108 Trial on
Indictment Decree.  It follows therefore that the order for corporal
punishment was illegal.  The order for police supervision was also illegal,
as the offence of defilement is not one to which S.123 Trial Indictments
Decree, which provides for police supervision applies.
Appeal against conviction dismissed.
Appeal against sentence partly succeeds.
The sentence of 25 years imprisonment, the orders for corporal
punishment and police supervision are set aside.
Steven Mug me & Fred Outnumber Vs. Uganda.
Decree appeal by republic on acquittal and appeal by the
appellants on conviction -procedure to be followed - whether both
appeals may be consolidated or whether each appeal should stand
separately.
Held: It cannot be said that no miscarriage of justice could have occurred
when the appellants were convicted of simple robbery.  It was most
important that witnesses give their evidence regularly in open court,
wherever it is constituted, for all to hear and see, that witnesses are
cross-examined and tested and that no suspicion is encouraged that the
judge favored one side or the other by listening to stories off record.
To take into account information off record is to invite evil insinuations
against the Bench, the effect of which is often very difficult to refute.
Under the circumstances, the appeals are allowed to the extent that the
convictions are quashed, sentences set aside.  A retrial before another
Judge and different assessors on the charge of simple robbery c/s 272 and
273 (1) (b) is ordered.
Leonard Muyingo Vs. Uganda.
Bail -whether application for bail in a higher court stays the
proceedings in a trial court.
Legal representation - whether lack of legal representation for the
appellant amounted to an infringement of the appellant's constitutional
right and a procedural irregularity.
Held: Since the application in the High Court was pending the normal
course to have been taken by counsel was monitor the hearing of the
case in the Chief Magistrate's Court since there is no provision that once
a party has indicated that he is applying for bail, that stays proceedings
in the trial court.
It is clear from the record that the counsel for the accused did not take
trouble to find out the progress of the case, and yet he was aware that his
client's application for bail was not on.  Counsel for the defendant had
ample time to contact his client in between the adjournments.  There is
nothing to show that counsel tried to visit his client while on remand, and
there is no evidence that he was refused access to his client.  The
appellant also had enough time to contact his counsel his counsel but
chose not to.  Accordingly, the fault lay squarely on counsel and his
client.  In the circumstances, the ground of appeal that there were
procedural irregularities and that the appellant was denied legal
representation is dismissed.
As to whether the bounced cheque was issued to Pw1 at all or by
presentment of the same for payment, there is no legal requirement that
a cheque paid to an advocate as a trust for his client must be crossed
and not cash.  It is also not anywhere provided in law or precedent that
there is a limit as to the amount of money an advocate is supposed to
receive on behalf of his client.  There is also nothing on record to show
the appellant, and not PW1, is the one who presented the cheque in
question to the bank.  These grounds of appeal also fail.
There is no substance in the allegation that the provisions of S.126 MCA
were not complied within.  From the evidence on record, it is clear that
when the learned chief Magistrate quoted S.125 MCA, he must have
meant S.126 MCA as S.125 MCA deals with discharge of the accused
when there is no case to answer and is obviously irrelevant in the
circumstances.
In view of the fact that the maximum sentence for issuing a bouncing
cheque is 10 years, and more importantly that the accused was also
liable to a civil suit to have imposed a lesser sentence, the sentence
was accordingly harsh and excessive.  The appeal is dismissed,
sentence set aside and substituted for a sentence of one year.
Yakubu Wabala Vs. Uganda
Plea of guilty - appeal against conviction s.216(3) MCA -whether
appeal tenable - whether plea of guilty properly taken.
Sentencing to imprisonment and a fine in default-whether sentence proper.
Sentencing - accessory after the fact c/s 378 PCA-whether 6 months
excessive.
Held: An accused convicted on own plea of guilty cannot appeal against
conviction but only sentence as per the provision of S.216 (3) MCA.
However the recording of a plea of guilty in this case was not correct as
the accused's words "I have understood the charge.  It is true", did not
amount to a plea of guilty.
For an offence of being an accessory after the fact c/s 378 PCA, an
ordinary misdemeanor, where the accused has purportedly pleaded guilty,
is a first offender, the sentence of 6 months was excessive.
An accused person is supposed to be sentenced to a fine, in default of
which a sentence of imprisonment.  The trial magistrate erred in law when
he sentenced the accused to a sentence of imprisonment of 6 months in
default of which a fine of Ush 100,000/=.
Uganda Vs. Omach Richard
Plea - plea of guilty - whether properly recorded.
Sentencing -being carried in a dangerous position c/s 133(1) and 138
Traffic and Road Safety Act-whether the default sentence of 30 days was
lawful.
Held: The facts constituting the offence were not properly put to the
accused as required by law, and therefore the accused was not given an
opportunity to admit unequivocally all the essential ingredients of the
offence.  Therefore, the plea of guilty was wrongly recorded.
The default sentence was illegal because S.192(a) MCA provided that
where the fine imposed is not above two thousand shillings, then the
default sentence is a maximum of 7 days.  The trial magistrate erred
when he imposed sentence of 30 days imprisonment.  Revision allowed.
Deo Bakyenga Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing -causing financial loss c/s 258 PCA - whether
sentence of 20 months was illegal.
Held: Mens rea is an essential ingredient in the offence of causing
financial loss, and cannot be presumed but proved by prosecution.  The
prosecution had the burden to prove that the appellant's omission to
carry out his guard duties were fraught with the knowledge that that
would cause financial loss.  Therefore, the trial magistrate erred in shifting
the burden of proof from the prosecution to the appellant.
there was no sufficient evidence to prove that the app0ellant neglected his
guard duties.
Where the prosecution fails to prove the ingredients of an offence the
accused should not be put to his defense.  In the instant case the learned
trial Magistrate erred when he put the accused to his defence whereas
the prosecution had failed to prove the ingredients of the offences charged.
A convicting of the offence of causing financial loss attracts a statutory
minimum sentence of 3 years imprisonment.  Therefore the sentence
imposed of 20 months was illegal.
Uganda Vs. Kilama Kennedy
Conviction - failure to record offence subject of conviction c/s 133
(3) MCA - whether this mistake was a subject of a revision order.
Sentencing -stealing from a person c/s 252 and 256 (a) PCA-whether 19
months imprisonment was harsh.
Held: Since the accused was convicted on his own plea, it would have
been redundant and superfluous to record within the conviction the offence
he had been convicted of as required by S.133 (3) MCA.  And the word
robbery was used by the trial Court wrongly put this would not occasion
a revision order.
The sentence of 19 months imprisonment was harsh in view of the
triviality of the item stolen i.e. posho.  However, the sentence was not so
harsh as to call for the intervention of court.
Revision order refused conviction and sentence confirmed.
Shabani Mugabi Vs. Uganda.
Plea of guilty s.216 MCA-appeal - whether where a person pleads
guilty he is precluded from appealing against conviction.
Sentencing-theft c/s 252 PCA-whether a sentence of 12months
imprisonment for a person who has pleaded guilty is excessive.
Held: The trial Court, after the accused had pleaded guilty narrated to the
accused the facts constituting the charged against him and he continued
to admit his guilt.  This shows that the accused was aware of what he
was saying and the trial court was entitled to convict him on his own
plea of guilty.
Under S.213 MCA Court was empowered to make an order of restitution
against the appellant for him to pay the complainant the money he lost
due to the accused's theft.
The sentence of 12 months imprisonment was excessive and harsh in
view of the fact that the appellant pleaded guilty.
Appeal allowed in part.
Sentence reduced to 7 months imprisonment.
Alcon International Vs. Kasirye Byaruhanga & Co. Advocates
Inherent powers of court s.101 civil procedure Act-invocation there
of when there is specific rule in place - whether fatal to the
application.
Held: Where there is a specific provision of the law in place governing the
situation, the invocation of the inherent powers of court was untenable, in
the present case the application for stay of the execution of a taxation
order pending appeal was governed by O.39 r.4 CPR. The application
was instead brought under section 101 of the Civil Procedure Act and
was a wrong law.
However the application though brought under a wrong law, was not
therefore fatally incompetent because no prejudice was therefore
occasioned to the respondents; secondly the application was
commenced by notice of motion, which it would still have been had it has
been filed under O.39 r 4 thirdly the procedural defect was curable by the
invocation of Art 126 (2) (e) of the constitution; fourthly, the rules of
procedural defect of the application would be ignored.
Appeal describes a procedure started by filing a notice of appeal.  Once a
notice is filed then the procedure of appeal is put in place.  Therefore the
applicant's application was competent because there existed already a
pending appeal commenced by the notice of appeal.
A pending appeal is not in itself sufficient cause for stay of execution.
For purposes of an application for stay of execution of an order of
taxation of costs, pending appeal, sufficient cause would be manifested
by evidence or allegation that the taxing master improperly addressed
himself to the relating to the taxation of costs.  The instant application
made no such allegation nor gave evidence.  Therefore the application
had failed to prove sufficient cause and would be refused.
Application dismissed.
Kayondo Henry vs. Uganda
Charges -alternative charges s.86(b) (1) whether an alternative
charge must be minor and cognate.
Charges-preliminary objection as to validity of charges-whether no
preliminary objection may be raised as to whether a charge disclosed an
offence or not.
Held: The definition section 15 of the Official Secrets acts regarding what
an official document is, was inclusive and therefore extensive.  This
means the documents relating to the case could or could not be official
documents as per S.15 of the official secrets Act.  It was a question of
evidence and this evidence could only be deduced at the trial.  Therefore
the learned trial Chief Magistrate was entitled to overrule the preliminary
objection.
An alternate charge need not be minor and cognate.
The communication between Advocate and client is absolutely privileged
as per S.124 Evidence Act.  However where an offence is suspected of
having been committed the communication is no longer privileged.
There was no provision in law providing for preliminary objection as to
whether a charge disclosed an offence or not.  Therefore, the preliminary
objection raised by the appellant was misconceived.
Appeal dismissed.
Kassim Mpanga Vs. Uganda.
Compensation s.259 - blanket order of compensation - whether
order of compensation illegal because not specified in respect of
which count order made.
Appeal - grounds of appeal-whether second appellate court may entertain
ground of appeal that was not raised in the first appellate court.
Held: The gist of the offence of causing financial loss is the term "loss".
A thing may be said to be lost after a reasonable time has elapsed to
allow diligent search and recovery and such diligent search has been
made and has been fruitless.  In the instant case, in respect of 29
accounts inspite of diligent recovery efforts of several months, recovery
was impossible.  Therefore the learned trial magistrate was correct to
have found the accused guilty of causing financial loss c/s 258(1) PCA
because the loss was a natural consequence of the unauthorized and
unsecured credit.
Abuse of office is the doing of an act by an accused person's employers,
prejudicial to the interest, in abuse of authority of his office in the instant
case the accused acted arbitrarily by giving out the overdrafts unsecured
and without authority contrary to bank policy.  This act amounted to the
unauthorized and unsecured credit.
S.259 PCA mandatory requires court to consequently impose an order
of compensation against an accused convicted of causing financial loss
and embezzlement.  The order of compensation must be imposed
specifically count by count.  In the instant case the trial magistrate
imposed a blanket order and this was illegal.  However, a court of appeal
is empowered under s.33 (2) CPC to vary a judgment of the High Court on
appeal.  Therefore the order of compensation would be substituted for the
order to apply to only count one.
Appeal dismissed.  Order or compensation to apply to count one only.
Christopher Lubale Vs. Uganda.
Bail pending appeal c/s 217 )1) MCA -chronic sickness with AIDS-
whether ground sufficient for application for bias pending appeal.
Held: Sickness of whatever nature cannot be a ground for releasing a
person on bail pending appeal.
The burden of proof that an appeal has a good chance of success lies on
the applicant for bail pending appeal.  In the instant case, the applicant
did not establish the grounds upon which he based his motion that his
appeal has a good chance of success.
Application for bail pending appeal dismissed.
Moses Ganya Vs. Uganda.
Sentence - procuring a document by false pretense c/s332 PCA-
whether a sentence of 12 months imprisonment excessively harsh
for an accused of advanced age.
Held: The appellant was correctly found by the trial court as being the
originator of the false recommendations which prompted the Administrator
General to issue the certificate of succession.  Therefore the trial Court
was correct in convicting him as changed.
The accused being of advanced age the sentence of 12 months was
rather harsh.  It would be reduced to only that part the appellant had
served and therefore the appellant is released forthwith.
Walakira Lawrence Vs. Uganda.
Unsworn statement -veracity - whether unsworn statement is no
evidence.
Held: There was no evidence that the accused ever handed the money
meant to purchase the beer for sale.  The complainant withdrew it himself
from his bank and paid it to purchase the beer.  Therefore the conviction
was not supported by evidence.
It is the constitutional right of an accused person to make an unswron
statement and this should not lead the accused person to be penalized.
Appeal allowed.
Conviction quashed, and appellant released.
Avutia Vs. Uganda.
Alteration of charges s.130 MCA - miscarriage of justice -whether
the failure by court to require the prosecution to atter or amend the
charge so that the accused could plead to a new charge relevant to
evidence disclosed caused a miscarriage of justice.
Minor and corporate offence s.143 MCA-Criminal Trespass c/s 286(a)
PCA-whether minor and cognate to theft-whether accused could be
convicted of Criminal Trespass when only charged with attempted theft.
Held: S.143 MCA authorize court to convict an accused of minor and
cognate offence when the facts disclosed reduce the original charge
accordingly.  A minor and cognate offence is of the same genus as the
offence with which the accused is charged, because the ingredients of the
the minor offence.  The accused need not plead independently to the
minor and cognate offence, nor defend himself to the major offence
because the ingredients of the minor offence have been tackled in the
defence against the major offence.  In the instant case the trial Chief
Magistrate erred when he found the accused guilty of criminal trespass
because it was not a minor cognate offence to theft.  He should have
required the prosecution to alter the charge and the accused to plead
independently to the altered charge.  This misdirection caused a
miscarriage of justice.
Revision allowed.  Sentence set aside.  Accused set free.
John Mayengo Vs. Uganda
Grievous harm c/s 209 (g) of the Penal Code Act - whether proved
where appellant poured acid on complainant.
Sentencing -sentence of 7 years imprisonment for an offence of grievous
harm-whether sentence excessive.
Sentencing-compensation s.209(1) MCA whether sentence to pay
compensation unreasonable because appellant indigent.
Held: The trial Magistrate correctly convicted the accused/appellant upon
circumstantial evidence which evidence was incompatible with the
innocence of the accused.  The running away of the accused from the
village after the commission of the offence was incompatible with the
innocence of the accused.
The sentence of seven years for the offence that visited so much injury on
the victim, moreover an offence that attracted a maximum sentence of life
imprisonment, was fair.
The sentence of payment of compensation to the victim of the offence of
Ush 107,000/= was unreasonable.
Appeal for the state/respondent.
Adome John Robert Vs. Uganda.
Confession -uncorroborated and taken without cautioning accused
whether safely relied on to convict the accused.
Held: It is unsafe to convict an accused solely on an uncorroborated
confession.  Moreover the confession statement had been recorded without
caution.  Therefore the conviction is quashed.
Appeal allowed, conviction quashed.
John Mayengo Vs. Uganda.
Grievous harm c/s 209(g) of the Penal Code Act -whether proved
whether appellant poured acid on complaint.
Sentencing-sentence of 7 years imprisonment for an offence of grievous
harm-whether sentence excessive.
Sentencing - compensation S.209 (1) MCA whether sentence to pay
compensation unreasonable because appellant indigent.
Held: The trial Magistrate correctly convicted the accused/appellant upon
circumstantial evidence which evidence was incompatible with the innocent
of the accused.  The running away of the accused from the village after the
commission of the offence was incompatible with the innocence of the
accused.
The sentence of seven years for the offence that visited so much injury on
the victim, moreover an offence that attracted a maximum sentence of life
imprisonment, was fair.
The sentence of payment of compensation to the victim of the offence of
Ush 107,000/= was unreasonable.
Appeal for the state/respondent.
Kagube Mohamed Vs. Uganda.
Pleading -main and alternative counts - whether accused who
pleads guilty to the main count may not plead to the alternative
count.
Pleading -plea of guilty-whether sustainable where the facts put to the
appellant do not disclose the accused as having committed the offence.
Pleading -theft of cattle c/s 255 Penal Code Act - whether sentence of 2
years harsh and excessive.
Pleading -plea of guilty-whether obtained by duress.
Sentencing -main and alternative counts-whether the omnibus sentence of
both the main and alternative counts was illegal.
Held: There was no evidence to prove that the alleged plea of guilty was
obtained by duress since there was no body who duressed the appellant as
he stood in the dock to plead to the charge.
Where a person is charged on the main count and an alternative count, and
he pleads guilty to the main count, then he cannot be called upon to plead
to the alternative count.  In the instant case the trial court misdirected
itself to ask the appellant to plead to the alternative count when the
appellant had pleaded guilty to the main count already.  However, this
misdirection would only leave their main count standing.
The facts as put to the accused did not in any way show that he was the
guilty of the theft of the bull.  Therefore his conviction was not proper.
Court misdirected itself when it imposed sentenced on both the main and
alternative counts.  This was irregular.  However, the sentence of 2 years
imprisonment was not excessive.
Appeal allowed.  Sentence set aside.
Uganda Vs. Obita Christopher
Sentencing C.189 s.189(2) magistrate courts Act fine -whether a
trial magistrate may sentence the accused to a fine beyond the
one prescribed.
Sentencing -alternative sentences-whether a convict may be sentenced to
either pay a fine or to imprisonment.
Held: Court has discretion where the relevant section provides for either
imprisonment of a fine, to sentence the accused to pay the fine in default,
imprisonment.  This discretion cannot be extended to the accused so that
it is him to choose either to pay a fine or serve a term of imprisonment.
Therefore, the trial magistrate erred when he sentenced the accused to
serve six months in prison or pay a fine of Ush 40,000/=.
S.113 (1) of the Traffic & Road Safety Act provides that a person convicted
there under may be sentenced to a fine not exceeding Ush 5000/= or a term
of imprisonment not exceeding two years to both.  Therefore the alternative
sentence of the payment of Ush 40, 000/= fine was an error in law as it was
beyond Ush 5000/= imposed by the section.  Even S.189 (2) MCA did not
help the court because that was a general section under which the accused
is charged.
Revisional order allowed.  Sentence set aside.
Christopher Lubaale Vs. Uganda
Search warrant s.68 magistrate Courts Act - search without -
whether search illegal.
Held: Where an arrest had been made or authorized according to S.68
MCA, police is at liberty to search the place of dwelling or business of the
arrested person or person authorized to be arrested, it police has reason to
believe that material evidence may be obtained threat.  In the instant case,
the appellant's dwelling house was searched after the arrest.  Therefore, the
search did not require a warrant.
The requirement for corroboration for accomplice evidence is requirement
of prudence not one of law.  However in the instant case corroboration was
found in the fact that property recently stolen was found at the home of the
appellant.
Where a person is found in possession of property recently stolen, that
person may be either a thief or may be guilty of receiving stolen property.
In the instant case, property stolen on 24th March 1993 was found at the
appellant's home on 27th March 1993.  the accused's explanation was not
satisfactory to the trial court and the court was entitled to convict the
accused of the theft.
The sentence of 18 months was not excessive.
Stephen Batumbia Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing - attempted theft c/s370 & 25 PCA -whether sentence
of 12 months imprisonment harsh.
Held: Though the trial Court misdirected itself on the amount the accused
is alleged to have attempted to fraudulently recover from the complainant,
nevertheless the court reached the right conclusion by holding that the
appellant attempted to unjustifiably get money that he was not entitled to
when he presented the cheque against which he had been partly paid.
The trial was correct in convicting the appellant of attempted theft.
Conviction on this count is confirmed.
The trial Court misdirected itself when it convicted the appellant of giving
false information to a person employed in the public service because the
appellant's information to the effect that the cheque had been dishonored
was a correct fact.  Conviction on this count is quashed and sentence set
aside.
The appellant court would not interfere in the severity of the sentence
imposed by the trial court on count one as no principal law was offered for a
sentence of 12 months imprisonment for the offence of attempted theft.
Appeal allowed in part.  Conviction and sentence on count one upheld
count 2, conviction quashed.  Sentence set aside.
Waiswa Richard & 3 ors Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing -sentence of 2 years imprisonment whether excessive.
Held: Although appellant number one did not physically assault the
complainant, he had a common intention with the other 3 to unlawfully
assault the complainant and his intention was readily inferable from his
conduct.  There was no need to prove express agreement between him and
his co-accused.
Although the phrase medical officer is not well known in the medical
profession, considering the training of the witness and his experience of 5
years practice, he was a witness equivalent to a medical assistant and thus
qualified to examine the victims in this single case of assault. The trial court
was correct in basing her finding the evidence of the medical officer.
The sentencing 2 months imprisonment was not excessive.
Appellant number four did not participate in the assault as there was no
such evidence.
Appeal dismissed for appellants number one, two or three.
Eriya Ngambeki Vs. Uganda.
Procedure -sentencing -appellant 65 years old -whether 2 years
sentence excessive and harsh.
Held: The appellant's evidence as to the time he set out for the wedding
party was not consistent.  The prosecution had clearly placed the
appellant at the lead of the mob that assaulted the complainant in
obstruction of police officers in the execution of their duties.  The appellant
had a common intention with the group that perpetrated the criminal acts.
Since the accused was not represented the trial court should have assisted
the appellant to find the possible mitigation circumstances before passing
sentence.
Appeal against sentence allowed.  Sentence reduced to 6 months
imprisonment.  Appeal against conviction dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Kankiruho James & another
Sentencing theft of cattle c/s255 of the Penal Code Act -whether
sentence of 18 months proper when no reasons are given for the
sentence.
Sentencing-theft of cattle c/s 255 Penal Code - whether sentence of 18
months proper when no reasons are given for the sentence.
Compensation -whether sentence for compensation was properly passed by
the Criminal Court.
Held: S.21 of the Penal Code prescribe circumstances that establish when
an accused is a principal offender in any alleged offence before court.  In
the instant case the prosecution failed to show that A2 fell in any description
envisaged by S.21 to be established as a principal offender.  It was not
proved that she took part in stealing the cows nor did she know that the
cows were stolen.  Her conviction would therefore be quashed.
Interalia for purposes of the Appellant Court it is required that the Trial Court
gives reasons for its sentence.  The Learned Trial Magistrate erred in failing
to give reasons for his sentence of 18 months imprisonment.  However in
the circumstances of the case the sentence cases cited did not occasion a
miscarriage of justice for A1 who was properly convicted.
The Learned Trial Magistrate erred in law when he imposed a compensatory
sentence on the accused because a Criminal Magistrate has no jurisdiction
to impose a compensatory sentence.  This sentence would be set aside.
Uganda Vs. Police Constable Alfred Ogwang.
Evidence -additional material facts-s.78 Trial on Indictments
Decree-whether the prosecution infringed s.78 TID when they
sought to tender a gun in evidence whose particulars summary of
evidence.
Held: Infringement of S.78TID amounts to adducing evidence to the evidence
already stated in the summary of facts.  In the instant case the summary of
evidence warned the accused that a gun would be tendered in evidence and
the gun was actually tendered in evidence albeit the number thereof was
different.  Therefore this did not amount to new evidence as such as to
mean that S.78 TID had been infringed upon.
The weird story of the accused in defense was indicating of a person who
only wanted to derail the course of justice.  It was clear that it is the
accused who had shot and killed all the deceased.
The prosecution had discretion in choosing what witnesses to bring to prove
its case.  Since the accused wished to rely on the defense of insanity by
intoxication it was a incumbent upon him to prove so.
the accused would not rely on the non-production of particular witnesses by
the prosecution since this by itself was no evidence of a motive deliberate to
hide the truth from the court.
According to the evidence from the witnesses the accused was not so drunk
as not to know what he was doing.  Since the accused was annoyed and
yet was able to go back to the barracks, to collect his gun and go and shoot
the deceased persons and then return to the barracks, it was not reasonable
suppose that the accused was so drunk that he did not know what he was
to doing.  Therefore had failed to rebut the presumption that he intended the
consequences of his acts.
The defense of provocation would be rejected because the accused had
more than sufficient time to cool down and moreover what happened, his
denial of entry into some canteen could not mount to provocation.
Accused convicted as charged.
Uganda Vs. Mucoori Francis
Pleas-equivocal plea-whether plea was equivocal.
Pleas-omnibus plea-whether plea was omnibus.
Conviction-whether a recommendation in a judgment that "let
accused be 'convicted" was not a conviction.
Held: The plea to all the two counts was omnibus and irregular.  A plea
must be for each count separately.
The plea was equivocal because the accused pleaded that he had not paid
the graduated tax, as charged, but in the same breath pleaded he was
unable to pay.  The section creating the offence requires that a person to
be guilty under the section must have failed to pay the tax without lawful
excuse. Therefore, although the accused pleaded guilty he at the same time
south to say that his failure was due to lawful excuse.  Therefore the plea
was equivocal and should not have been the basis of the conviction.
The trial Magistrate must convict the accused person instead of merely
recommending conviction as it was in this case.  Therefore, the accused
person was not convicted and the sentence was a nullity.
proceedings set aside.  No retrial ordered because the accused has served
the illegal sentence.
Kamuroro Joseph Vs. Uganda.
Pea of guilty-whether properly taken where facts were at variance
with the offence.
Held: S.9(1), (3) of the Penal Code Act provides that a person is not
criminally liable for an act that happens independent of the accused's
exercise of his will.  In the instant case the killer bullet flew from the
accusd's gun during a scuffle where the deceased sought to disarm the
accused.  Therefore, the accused was not criminally liable for the discharge
of the killer bullet.
Moreover, for an accused to be guilty of causing death by a rush or
negligent act under s.219A of the Penal Code Act, it must be shown that
his conduct was such that he cared not whether his act caused death or
not.  This was not the case in the instant case.  The facts were that the
killer bullet flew from the accused's gun accidentally and not through
recklessness of the killer bullet.
The trial Magistrate misdirected himself when he recorded a plea of guilty
whereas the facts were at variance from the charge.  The charge was that
the accused killed the deceased due to acting recklessly and yet the facts
were that the killer bullet flew from the gun by accident.
The trial Magistrate misdirected himself when he held that the fine payable
on conviction under s.219A was Shs.4,000/= whereas it is shs.70,000/=.
Appeal allowed.  Conviction quashed. Appellant set free.
Zita Jackson Vs. Uganda.
Assessors-summing up s.81(1) TID-whether failure by trial judge
to record the notes of summing to the assessors was a material
irregularity.
Memorandum of agreed facts-whether court admitted the medical
evidence as though it were part of the memorandum of agreed
fact under s.64(2) TID-whether this caused a failure of justice.
Submission of counsel-failure by trial court to record the same-
whether a material irregularity.
Held: Failure by a trial judge to record his note of summing up to the
assessors is contrary to s.81(1) TID and this can lead to the quashing of a
conviction if injustice results therefrom.  In the present case the failure to
make the record did not in itself cause injustice since the assessors in their
opinions gave the salient features of the evidence which meant that they
were properly directed.
S.64(2) requires the trial judge to draw up a memorandum of agreed facts
and in the instant case the trial judge failed to comply with this provision of
the law.  However, since the contested medical report was after being
admitted, signed by both counsel for the prosecution and accused and the
trial judge, the report became part of the record of the court.
It is rule of practice for the trial judge to record submissions of counsel and
when counsel's submissions raise issues of law and fact and the trial judge
does not consider the issues in his judgment, then such an omission is
relevant to the merits of an appeal.  However, in the instant case since the
submissions of counsel were made and closed in the morning and
judgment delivered 3 hours later, it means that the submissions were fresh
in the mind of the judge when he was writing the judgment.  Therefore the
omission to record the submissions did not occasion a miscarriage of
justice.
It is a rule of practice for courts to require corroboration of the evidence
against the accused in sexual offences.  In the instant case the distressed
condition of the complainant was corroborative of the sexual assault upon
her.
Seven years imprisonment were neither illegal nor excessive.
Corporal punishment was not provided for the offence of defilement and the
sentence for corporal punishment was illegal and would be set aside.
Appeal dismissed except as to orders for corporal punishment.
Rukarwana Fred Vs. Uganda.
Witness-child of tender years-whether it is fatal to admit evidence
of a child of tender years without conducting a voir dire-s.38(3)
Trial on Indictments Decree.
Sentencing-defilement C/S 123 Penal Code Act-whether sentence
of 15 years excessive.
Sentencing-corporal punishment-whether sentence of corporal
punishment was illegal.
Held: The failure by the trial judge to administer a vior dire to the witness
who was a child of tender years contravened the provisions of s.38(3) Trial
on Indictments Decree. However, inspite of this short coming, judging from
the evidence on record, the witness possessed sufficient intelligence to
understand the duty of telling the truth.  Therefore lack of a vior dire was not
fatal.
Moreover there was sufficient corroboration of the complainant's for
reduction by the other witnesses.
The sentence of 15 years was not so manifestly excessive as to call for
reduction by the appellate court.
Corporal punishment for the offence of defilement is illegal and the sentence
should be set aside.
Appeal dismissed except as to sentence for corporal punishment.
Uganda Vs. Nawaswa & anor
Time-notice of appeal-application to lodge notice of appeal out time-
whether sufficient cause therefore shown under s.328A (1) Criminal
Procedure Code Act.
Held: Since the case in the lower court did not proceed exparte and the
DPP was represented no good cause had been shown as to why it took the
DPP 6 months to remember to appeal against the order or acquittal of the
respondents.
Application rejected.
Tusingwire Teopista & anor Vs. Uganda.
No case to answer-whether court on own motion may rule that
there is a case to answer where defence or prosecution have not
submitted on the same.
Submission of no case to answer-whether where the accused and
or prosecution does not submit on whether there is no case to
answer court may not rule on the same.
Sentencing-AIDS-whether trial magistrate must take into account
the health condition of the accused while sentencing.
Sentencing-whether 5 years imprisonment excessive for assault
occasioning actual bodily harm.
Held: It is the right of the defence to move court on a motion of no case to
answer.  Where the defence choose not to make the submission of no case
to answer, it does not preclude the trial court in pursuance of S.126(1) of
Magistrates Courts Act to rule that there is a case to answer or not.
Therefore the learned trial magistrate was entitled in the instant case to rule
on own motion that there was a case to answer.
And whereas according to the evidence on record after the prosecution
evidence, there might have been no case to answer, where nevertheless the
trial court rules that there is a case to answer, where there upon the defence
presents its evidence which only affords to strengthen the prosecution case,
the trial court is entitled to act on the evidence as a whole including that of
the defence to convict the accused.  In the instant case the prosecution
evidence had not made out a prima facie case on the original charge of the
offence of attempted murder.  However when the trial court ruled that there
was a case to answer, and indeed the appellants presented the evidence
which showed that they had indeed burned the complainant, the court was
entitled to treat the evidence as a whole and find that in fact an indictable
offence had been committed.
The defence of accident was not available to the appellants because the
prosecution had proved that the complainant was burn deliberately by the
appellants, who intended to extract information from the complainant about
the whereabouts of the lost money.
Even if the defence of accident was to be considered, and say that the
complainant was burnt by the stove as she ran away from being chastised
by her parent, the evidence still would indicate that the running away was
induced by the appellants' deliberate act of endangering their victim in such
a way that she had to run away and in so doing fell in the danger of being
burnt. Still the appellants would be liable for inflicting the consequent injuries.
An attempt to commit is an act done with intent to commit the crime, and
forming part of a series of acts which would constitute its actual commission
If it were not interrupted.  Therefore to support a charge of attempted murder
the prosecution must prove the full intent to murder, i.e. with malice
aforethought, which intent to murder, while being prosecuted, is interrupted
before the death results.  In the present case the complainant's hands and
legs were burnt by the appellants who left her to go with the injuries.
It cannot be said that the appellants had formed the intention to kill the
complainant but were interrupted in their efforts to do so.  Therefore the trial
magistrate was entitled to find that attempted murder had not been proved.
However, S.130(1)(a) Magistrate Courts Act provides that where, during trial,
it appears to court that the evidence discloses an offence than the offence
originally charged, if no injustice may be caused to the accused, the court
may make an order for the alteration of the charge by way of its amendment.
Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in convicting the appellants
of an offence with which they were not charged without having first called
for the amendment of the charge and inviting the appellants to plead thereto.
This was so because the offence of doing an act likely to cause grievous
harm c/s 209(a) Penal Code act was not minor and cognate to the offence
of attempted murder originally charged.
However, the trial was not a nullity because the appellants were not
prejudiced in preparing their defence.  A trial court is empowered to convict
a person of a minor and cognate offence because the major offence
originally charged ipso facto gives notice of the minor offence.  In the instant
case the trial court should have convicted the appellants with the offence of
assault occasioning actual bodily harm c/s 228 Penal Code Act because the
evidence on record disclosed such an offence.
S.331(2)(1) Criminal Procedure Code permits an appellate court to quash a
conviction and substitute it with the one the lower court should have passed.
In the present case the nature of the injuries disclosed the offence of assault
occasioning actual bodily harm therefore the appellants' conviction of doing
an act likely to cause grievous harm would be substituted with committing
an assault occasioning actual bodily harm c/s 228 Penal Code Act.
There was no evidence on record put before sentences.  Since 5 years was
the maximum sentence for the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily
harm, a sentence of 18 months will be substituted from the date of remand.
Appeal against sentence, and conviction for doing an act likely to cause
grievous harm, allowed and substituted with conviction of assault
occasioning actual bodily harm and sentence of 18 months.
Uganda Vs. I.P.Ogwang.
Revision S.341 Criminal Procedure Code-dismissal of charges
S.121(1)MCA on grounds of non appearance of complainant -
complainant was the state and presence of prosecutor was
presence of complaint.
Dismissal of charges u/s 121(1) MCA-whether this amounted to an
acquittal-whether therefore state may only appeal against acquittal
Revision u/s 341(5) CPC-whether application therefore not tenable
because state has right to appeal.
Held: S.12(1) MCA provides that where the complainant is not in court, on
the day fixed for hearing of the case then the trial court may dismiss the
charges.  In the instant case the prosecutor was in court and since in all
criminal cases the state is the complainant, the existence of the prosecutor
(even though the awaited State Attorney was not in court) in court meant
that the complainant was in court.
S.341(5) Criminal Procedure Code provides that where there is a right of
appeal, it is not competent for the High Court to entertain an application for
a revisional order.  And S.216(5) Magistrates Courts Act gives the DPP the
right to appeal against an erroneous acquittal.  However, dismissal of charges
under S.121(1) MCA does not amount to an acquittal for which the right of
appeal is provided to the DPP.  Therefore, this application was competently
before court.
Application for revisional order allowed.  Charges reinstate.
Kalange Steven Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing-store breaking and theft c/s 283(a) Penal Code-
whether sentence of 3 years excessive.
Held: It is our law that a mere presence at the place where the offence is
committed is not enough to hold somebody liable for the commission of that
offence.  In the instant case it is true the appellant, among others, was
supposed to be on guard at the stores but that does not mean that the
appellant is criminally liable for whatever took place at the store.  The
prosecution had failed to move that the appellant was responsible for the
theft.
Imprisonment for 3 years was not excessive taking into account that the
value of the goods alleged stolen was shs.4 million and that the maximum
sentence for the offence was 7 years.
Appeal allowed.  Appellant to set free.
Shimanya Martin Vs. Uganda.
Functus officio rule-ruling of a case to answer-whether thereby trial
Magistrate functus officio and may not reverse the ruling.
Judicial consultation of a higher court - whether an irregularity
fettering judicial independence.
Bias-application to trial Magistrate to disqualify herself on grounds
that she is biased-whether refusal appealable.
Kataryeba Zachary & 3 others Vs. Uganda.
Charges, S.86(a)(ii)MCA-charge under S.12 Penal Code Act for
the offence of intermeddling with the deceased's property-whether
a charge under an inexistent section a material irregularity.
Pleading to amended charge-failure by court to invite accused to
plead to amended charge-whether material irregularity.
Representation by counsel-refusal of court to adjourn to enable
accused instruct another Advocate-whether infringed accused's
right to be represented by counsel.
Collective defence by accused-whether a material irregularity.
Held: S.12 Penal Code act deals with insanity and not intermeddling.
Therefore, the accused were charged with non existent section.  This was a
material irregularity.
Moreover, after the court had allowed the charge sheet to be amended to
read S.12(1), (2) of the Administrator General's Act, the accused were never
invited to plead afresh to the new amended charge.  This was irregular.
The refusal by court to adjourn the case to enable the accused engage
another counsel was a denial of the accused constitutional right to be
represented.
A collective defence was unconstitutional as per Art 28 of the Constitution.
The evidence showed that the accused retained the property of the
deceased and dealt with it for the purpose of preserving the same, since the
accused worked with the deceased before his demise.  Therefore, the
offence of intermeddling was not proved by the prosecution to fill in the gaps
to the prejudice of the appellants.
Appeal allowed.
Shimanya Martin Vs. Uganda
Appealing out of time-Rule 4 CPR- application to extend time to
file notice of appeal-whether lack of court proceedings on grounds.
Held: Rule 4 of the Court of Appeal Rules (CAR) provides that the court may
extend time within which a given step may be taken or act done, for
sufficient reason.  The applicant's contention that the High Court failed to
supply to his counsel the record of proceedings to enable him file a notice
of appeal was not sufficient reason to extend time within which to file a
notice of appeal because a record proceedings was not required to file a
notice of appeal.
His contention that the appeal involved very substantial questions of law of
public importance would not help him.  This is because his very contention
about the importance of the appeal should have propelled him to do all the
acts precedent to the appeal in time.
Application dismissed.
Sunday Atanasio Vs. Uganda.
Bail-special circumstances-infancy-whether infancy proved, Art 23
Constitution, S.14A Trial on Indictments Decree.
Held: S.14A(1)(b) Trial on Indictments Decree defines exceptional
circumstances to include infancy or advanced aged.  An infant as par S.3
Children Statute is a child below 18 years.  However, the affidavit in support
of the application for bail, thought, it was deponed that the applicant was 16
years, the deponent failed to disclose the source of information for her
assertion.  Therefore the affidavit failed to contract the indictment that the
applicant was above 18.  therefore, bail would be refused as the applicant
had failed to prove the exceptional circumstances of infancy.
Application dismissed.
Tusiime Twebaze Drake Vs. Uganda.
Sentencing-uttering false document and obtaining money by false
pretence -whether sentence of years excessive.
Held: The object of an identification parade is to make sure that the ability of
the witness to recognize the suspect is tested.  However, the identification
parade is not the only such test.  The correctness or otherwise of
indent faction by witness, of the accused will depend on the circumstances,
such as the length of time, the distance, the light, the familiarity of the
witness with the accused.  If the quality of these is good, the danger of
distance identity is reduced. In the instance case the evidence adduced
by the prosecution and not contradicted by the appellant clearly showed that
the complainant and other prosecution witnesses who were involved in the
alleged motor vehicle purchase transaction office hours.  The circumstances
of identification could not come not have been better.  The learned trial
magistrate was correct to come to the conclusion she came to.
It is not necessary for the convicting court to always state that the
prosecuting has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The elements of the offence of uttering a false document and those of forging
a document are different.  Therefore it is possible as it was in the case
instant to convict a person of uttering a false document while acquitting him
of forging the same.  Moreover, there was no requirement that to prove of a
handwriting expert.  The appellant had been seen by witnesses that
testified seeing him uttering the false documents.
The sentence of 3 years was not excessive.  The trial court took into
account the fact that the appellant was a graduate who should have used
his education to do better things.
Appeal dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Mawanda Stephen
Dismissed for want of Prosecution, S 117 MCA - Presence of
Prosecutor in Court-whether because the Prosecutor is present
in Court though not ready to proceed, the case may not be
dismissed for want of prosecution.
Held: Though S.117 of the MCA provides that dismissal of a case there
under must be such that the Prosecutor having had notice of the date of the
case, the appearance in Court envisaged is not merely physical presence
but appearance with readiness and capacity to proceed to prosecute the
case.  Appearing in Court without a police file is no appearance.  Therefore
the learned trial Grade one Magistrate was correct in dismissing the charges
against the accused for want of prosecution.
Revision refused.
Kasekese Lawrence Kasaka & ors Vs. Uganda.
Trial and conviction by 3rd Magistrate - S.142 Magistrates Court
Act - whether a third trial Magistrate has no jurisdiction to try an
accused already tried by two Magistrates.
Held: As per Eustace Vs Republic [1970] E.A 393 the interpretation of
S.142(1) of the Magistrate Courts Act is such that an accused can only be
tried by the first and second Magistrate in succession but not the third.
The third Magistrate has no jurisdiction to try the accused except by way of
a de novo trial.  Therefore in the case instant the accused could not be tried
let alone be convicted by the Chief Magistrate who was the fourth in
succession to try the accused basing on the evidence already recorded by
other previous successive Magistrates.
Appeal allowed. A fresh trial de novo ordered.
Matsanga Deo Vs. Uganda
Submission of no case to answer S.125 MCA-whether improperly
rejected-whether trial Court must give reasons.
Locus in quo-failure to record proceedings at locus in quo-whether
therefore proceedings improper.
Held: The essential ingredients of the offence of attempted murder are that
