the assailant intended to maim or disfigure the complaint and that the
intention was to be carried out with the weapon and that the assailant started
to execute the said intentions.  In the present case there was cogent
evidence that the appellant had been properly identified by the complainant
is the one that shot at his car while he drove it.  Therefore the Chief
Magistrate had been correct to put the accused to his defence and
eventually to convict him of the same.
The essential ingredients of the offence of malicious damage to property are
the damage is inflicted willfully and unlawfully by the accused.  Since the
complainant's car was damaged by the shots aimed at it by the appellant
who had been properly identified, the learned Chief Magistrate was correct
to find that the offence was proved.
The conditions for a proper unmistaken identification existed because the
appellant was known to his assailant; the distance between the two was a
mere 30 meters when the appellant fired the shots at the complainant; and it
was a clear day at 2:19 pm in broad day light.
It is not a requirement of the law that the trial Magistrate must record his
reasons for rejecting or allowing a submission of no case to answer.
Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate did not commit an error of law
in failing to record his reasons for rejecting the appellant's submission of no
case to answer.  Moreover, this failure to record his reasons did not
occasion a failure of justice.
S. 155 of the Evidence Act provides that statements made y the witness
immediately after the occurrence of an event are relevant to corroborate the
truth or otherwise of his latest statements in Court. In the present case the
fact that the complainant did not mention his assailants name in his
immediate statement at Police was not necessarily corroborative of the fact
that the complainant did not know his assailant, because the complainant
explained in his latest statement that he feared for his life since his
assailant was still at large.
The prosecution must produce all witnesses necessary to establish the truth
of a case.  If it fails to do so where the evidence is barely inadequate, the
Court is entitled to draw the inference that the evidence of the uncalled
witness would have tended to be adverse to the prosecution case.  In the
prosecution case.  In the case instant the prosecution proved all the
essential ingredients of the offences charged.  Therefore, the prosecution
evidence was adequate.
The learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in law in not recording the
proceedings in locus in quo.  However, a visit at a locus in quo is only
necessary to corroborate the evidence already on record.  In the instant case
since the evidence already recorded in open court was sufficient to establish
the guilt of the appellant, no miscarriage of justice was occasioned by the
procedural failure to record the proceedings of the locus in quo since the
visit thereto was superfluous.
The learned trial judge erred in not taking into account the period of remand
spent by the appellant prior to his conviction and sentence as this is now
constitutionally mandatory as per Article 23 (8) of the Constitution of the
Republic of Uganda 1995.
The sentences therefore would be reduced by 6 months.
Appeal against conviction dismissed. Appeal against sentence allowed in part.
Okello Florence Joyce Vs. Uganda.
Part heard case S.142(1) (a) (b) Magistrates Court Act-whether
failure by second trial Magistrate to recall witnesses was fatal.
Held: S.142(1) (b) MCA empowers the High Court on appeal or revision, with
discretion to set aside a judgment and conviction by a trial Magistrate
relied on evidence not wholly recorded by him where it appears that the
accused was thereby prejudiced, and may order a retrial.  However, this
power is discretionary and the learned appellate Judge was correct in not
disturbing the holding of the trial sentence on the record before her, which
was sufficient.
The appellant was not correct to argue that the learned appellate Judge erred
in upholding the shifting of the burden of proof to accused by the trial court
because this was not the case according to the facts on record.
The learned appellant Judge exercise the powers of the first appellate court
duly and correctly by subjecting the evidence on record from the trial court
to exhaustive scrutiny and came to the conclusion that the trial court was
correct in convicting the appellant.
Appeal dismissed.
Esunget Samuel Vs. Uganda
Amendment of charge sheet, S.130(1) Magistrates Courts Act-
amendment after closure of prosecution and defence case-whether
tenable-whether prejudicial to defence.
Charges-particulars of offence not supplied.
Destroying evidence c/s 96 Penal Code and abuse of office c/s 83
(1) Penal Code Act-sentence-whether sentence of 18 months
imprisonment excessive.
Held: S.130(1) MCA empowers court with the discretion to allow amendment
of the charge at any stage of the proceedings.  However where the charge is
amended the court is supposed to call the accused to plead to the altered
charge and the court has the obligation to inform the accused court of his
right to demand the recall of witnesses to be cross examined.  Since the
trial court allowed the altering of the charge without calling upon the accused
to plead afresh thereto and informing him of his right to recall witnesses for
the prosecution for cross-examination the accused was prejudiced.
The record showed that the particular document allegedly destroyed by the
appellant was Police form No.3 from police file of Old Kampala CRB/SD/3/2/
95. the particularity was enough to sufficiently identify the document to the
appellant who was a seasoned police detective.  This ground of appeal would
thereby fail.
S.20 Penal Code Act provides for the defence of double jeopardy to the
effect that a person cannot be punished twice for the same offence.  In the
present case the accused was charged with commission of two-distinct
offences i.e. destroying Evidence c/s 96 Penal Code Act and abuse of office
c/s 83 (1) Penal Code Act.  All the two offences arose from the same facts
and the same incident namely, when the appellant destroyed (or was
alleged to) the police form 3, he thus committed the offences of destroying
employ of the State.  This is perfectly lawful and is an investigating officer
in the punished twice for the same offence c/s 20 Penal Code Act.
Therefore double jeopardy not established.
Though the appellant on appeal pleaded that the trial court convicted him on
suspicion and not on cogent evidence, the record of the trial court provided
ample and sufficient basis for appellant's conviction.  Moreover, an appellate
court must be circumspect about dislodging the lower courts findings on
matters of evidence and fact because it is the trial court that had the
opportunity to examine the witnesses, to hear their evidence & to scrutinize
their demeanor.  In this particular instance no reason is available to disturb
the findings of the trial court.
Since the accused was prejudiced in his not being given the opportunity to
recall prosecution witnesses when the charge was amended, fact his
sentence of 18 months would be reduced to 13 months, the period the
appellant had already served and therefore would be released immediately.
Appeal dismissed.
DAMAGES
Agadi Didi Vs. James Namakaso
Assessment of general damages - plaintiffs failure to guide court
in assessment of general damages.
Held: The defendant cannot be heard because he had filled no defence.
That failure to file a defence raises a presumption or constructive
admission, of the claim made in the plaint.
The story told by the plaintiff in absence of a defence to contradict it,
must be accepted as the truth.
Joseph Lukwago Vs. Attorney General
Whether they should be awarded.
Held: Notwithstanding evidence that the chassis number was tempered
with since there was nobody claiming the vehicle, the defence had not
proved that the vehicle did not belong to the plaintiff.
That since the NRA intelligence officers is illegally taking the plaintiff's
vehicle they over act within the scope of their employment.
The defendant was liable in his representative capacity as A.G.
Since the servants of the defendants had acted high handedly, the
case for punitive damages had been proved.
Since the plaintiff had failed to present documentary evidence or other
evidence persuasive as to his having incurred special damage, this
was not proved.
Boniface Oryema Vs. Uganda Muslim Supreme Council
Computation of special damages what factor to be used  in deter-
determining the value of used goods.
Held: Since judgment was entered in in favour of the plaintiff under O.9
r.6 of the Civil Procedure Rules and since such judgment was not
contested and set aside, the interlocutory judgment upheld the plaintiff's
claim to the compensation for his house hold property detained and for
a wrongful eviction.
Special damages shall be computed by a factor of 3/5 of the value of
the detained goods at the current prices of the new such pieces.
An advocate without instructions cannot consent to filing a WSD out of
time and this also meant that there was no WSD filed.
Since there was no WSD the defendant would not be heard.
John Nagenda Vs. Sabena Belgian World Airlines.
Special damages -proof of expense incurred - whether
inconsistency and absence of bills fatal.
Exemplary damages for breach of contract - whether awardable.
Held:There was clearly a breach of contract on the part of the defendant
Damages is compensation in money for the loss of that which he
would have received had the contract been performed.  There is no
compensation for disappointment of mind or vexation caused by the
hurtful and humiliating manner in which the defendant broke the
contract, and no exemplary damages are awardable.
Special damages must be strictly proved.  Lack of receipts and
inconsistency between the testimony and pleadings left the claims
unproved.
Dr. Denis Lwamafa Vs. Attorney General.
Restitution in interim -vehicle damaged in accident - whether
valuation as at the time of commission of the tort or judgment.
Mitigation - suit filed in 1983 and finalized in 1990 - court unable to
sit -plaintiff civil servant and poor - whether liable for not mitigating
damages.
Scaling down damages - receipt of lumpsum and contingencies -
award to be scaled down.
Loss of use and expected income - car used for hire-whether
recoverable.
Held: The plaintiff must be put in the position he would have been had
he not suffered the wrong.  The valuation would be as at the time of
judgment.
It was no fault of the plaintiff who was too poor to repair his vehicle, that
the suit, though filed in 1983 soon after the accident, was only finished
Expected income is recoverable.
Since the plaintiff was to be paid a lumpsum and there were
contingencies that the vehicle could have broken down, the award for
loss of use would be scaled down by 30%.
In fairness, restititio in integrum required that the intricacies of the
currency reform be ignored.
Dr. Fredrick Mutyaba Vs. Jambo Ltd & anor.
Special damages assessment of special damages for the repair of
a motor vehicle negligently damaged by defendant.
Held: Special damages for repairs, spares, valuation report, transport
Hamico Ltd Vs. Republic Motors.
Damage for breach - damages for non-delivery -whether these two
litles were different.
Held: For a condition precedent to exist both parties to the contract
must understand it and agree to it at the time of concluding the contract
Since the plaintiff stated in court that he would not have parted with his
money if he had been informed of the requirement of foreign exchange
for the importation of the motor vehicle, it cannot be said that there was
a condition precedent to the contract.
The proforma invoice and receipt were the only documents incorporating
the contract since the invoice stated that the plaintiff was paying for a
fully registered motor vehicle.  Therefore the parol evidence to state that
the contract was precedent upon availability of foreign exchange was
inadmissible.
For the defendant to sit back without initiating the process of obtaining
foreign exchange early enough, there plea of frustration for inability to
acquire foreign exchange would not avail him.
Charles Acire Vs. Myaann Engola
General damages - regard is had to all circumstances of the case.
Held: In matters of defamation, the statement is first given the ordinary
meaning.  The statement was libelous and had similar implications.
To determine an award for general damages, regard is had to the
standing of the plaintiff, his loss and injury; the conduct of the defendant,
and all circumstances of the case sh.500,000/= would be awarded.
Exemplary damages are awarded against Government where the agents
acted oppressively, arbitrarily or in an unconstitutional manner.
Lutaaya Vs. Attorney General.
Tort -wrongful arrest, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution-
award depends on circumstances of each case.
Held: The evidence in respect of the car was hearsay and therefore in
admissible.
There was no complaint which led to the arrest which was therefore
wrongful.
Awards for general damages for wrongful arrest, malicious prosecution
and false imprisonment are inconsistent are inconsistent because each
case is taken on its own facts.
Kibimba Rice Ltd Vs. Umar Salim.
General damages inconvenience - can be inferred as general
damages.
Held: Since both parties were to blame, the liability would be
apportioned equally.
Inconvenience though not specifically.  For loss of business, accounts
or receipts against outgoings have to be shown.  Where accounts are
not maintained an award for general or purchase of another vehicle.
Special damages for loss of business due to damage on vehicle are
available for the period till completion of repairs or purchase of another
vehicle.
George Zzizinga &Nankumba Zzizinga Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Tort -gravity of injury not shown in evidence - minimal amount awarded.
Held:  Dependency and amount of income must be proved as facts by
evidence. The deceased was not the owner, but a manager and there
was therefore no loss of income by the deceased of the amount of income.
There was no evidence of the gravity of injury suffered by the first
plaintiff.  A minimal award would therefore be made.
Funeral expenses were not incurred by the plaintiff, and they are there-
fore not recoverable.
Esso Standard Ltd Vs. Semu Amanu Opio.
Breach of contract -whether exemplary damages for breach of contract
are awardable.
Held: The learned trial judge was entitled to reach the decision the
appellant company was in breach of its contract with the respondent for
failure to give the respondent the agreed notice before the termination
of contract.
The learned trial judge erred in law when he awarded exemplary damages
for breach of contract because firstly, this had not been pleaded by the
respondent/plaintiff, secondly, an award for exemplary damages may not
be awarded for breach of a contract unless it involves the commission of
a tort of trespass and since no tort of trespass had been proved as
committed by the appellant, in this case the award for exemplary
damages was improper and would be set aside.
The tort of detinue is a continuing tort and damages therefore are
assessed as at the date of judgment as equivalent to the value of the
chattel in issue as at the date of judgment.  Therefore, the damages to
be awarded to the respondent of his detained chattels would be the value
of the chattels as at the date of judgment.
The glaring mistake in the Currency Reform Statute would be corrected
by court by mere application of logic since the only conversion rate
application of logic since the only conversion rate applicable to s.1 (a) is
that in S.(b)) and the courts have since taken that view.
Since detinue was a continuing tort, damages awardable therefore were
to be assessed as at the date of judgment and therefore the Currency
Reform Statute did not apply to the prayer of damages for detinue.
Since it was the learned judge's mistake to ward exemplary damages,
no party should pay costs of setting the award aside.
The learned trial judge erred when he failed to allow counsel to address
court after each had closed their case.
Appeal allowed in part.
J.k Patel Vs. Spear Motors Ltd.
Assessment of rent as set off - whether at market rate.
Held: The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he held that there
was no definite valid and enforceable contract merely by looking at the
documents tendered and the parties oral testimony.  The parties conduct
definitely showed that an offer on definite terms had been made by one
party and accepted by the other.  There was a valid enforceable contract.
The plaintiff had testified that he had been contracted by the defendant
company to build an assembly plant.  There plaintiff showed that he had
been part paid for this work.  The burden of proof thereby shifted to the
defendant to disprove this allegation.  But the defendant in his testimony
claimed that it had part paid more than the plaintiff had shown.  But
since the defendant's part payment had not been pleaded in his written
statement of defence, its evidence of part payment would be inadmissible.
Therefore the defendant had not discharged its burden of proof and would
have judgment against it.
The parties evidence at the trial amply showed that the defendant's
general manager was a key witness in this case.  But since the
defendant refused to call him as a witness, an adverse inference would
be drawn against the defendant.
The defendant's evidence of a set off, when he claimed that the plaintiff's
four years occupation of the defendant's home was upon an
understanding that the rent would act as a set off and the plaintiff's wife's
air ticket given by the defendant, such evidence was admissible even if
the defendant had not pleaded it in its WSD because the plaintiff at the
trial never objected to it nor did the plaintiff cross examine the
defendant's witness on it.
Rent would be assessed at the market rate for the purpose of the set off.
Court had the discretion to award interest and in this case court would
award interest at the official Bank of Uganda rates.
The trial judge misdirected himself when he failed to award costs to the
successful party.  Though the judge has a discretion not to award costs
to the successful party or at all his discretion must be exercised
judiciously and the reasons given in his judgment for his refusal to award
costs to the successful party.
Daniel Oboth Vs. The New Vision News Paper.
Defamation -whether the humble beginning of the plaintiff is a
factor to be considered in awarding general damages.
Held: Since the defendants had published the article only once and had
not refused to apologies since they were not asked to do so, there was
no ground upon which the defendants could have punitive damages
awarded against them.
The humble beginnings of the plaintiff cannot be a basis for calculating
the quantum of general damages awardable in defamation cases but the
actual status of the plaintiff at the date of the publication.  The learned
trial judge therefore erred in taking into account the humble beginnings
of the plaintiff and the award for general damages would be increased
The fourth and fifth grounds of appeal were defective for being
argumentative.
Appeal allowed in part.
Ibrahim Bachu & 3 others Vs. Foods & Beverages Ltd.
General damages for inconvenience -quantum.
Held: The defendant carried out extensive improvement on the suit
premises which were found incomplete at the time they were occupied
by the defendant.  Since these improvements would benefit whoever was
the rightful owner since they enhanced the value of the property, the
defendant would be entitled to vacant possession and mesne profits.
Since the defendants were informed of the plaintiffs claim of the premises
immediately they came back from exile in 1986 and the defendants
never cared to investigate their claim; the plaintiffs were entitled to
general damages of shs.1,000,000 for the inconvenience they had
suffered for non possession of their premises.
Foods & Beverages Ltd Vs. Israel Musisi Opoya.
Trespass - quantum.
Held: The learned trial judge was entitled to hold that conversion had not
been proved because the defendant/appellant had held on to the lorry with
an honest claim of right.
At the time the appellant/defendant seized the lorry it was in running
condition but it was towed from the appellant's premises after it was
cannibalized.  The learned trial judge was therefore entitled to hold that
trespass to the plaintiff's lorry had been proved.
Shs. 20 million general damages for trespass would be reduced to
shs.10 million.
Akisoferi Biteremo Vs. Attorney General.
Special damages as unearned income -whether not proved -
general damages for false imprisonment -quantum.
Held: The plaintiff had established that he had been detained for 14 days
and it was incumbent upon the defence to show that the detention was
lawful.  Since the defence failed to show that the detention was lawful, it
must be presumed that the plaintiff was unlawfully detained.
At the time the plaintiff's vehicle was detained it was in possession of the
plaintiff and the law presumes possession to be lawful unless the contrary
is proved.  The plaintiff's possession was therefore lawful and therefore the
tort of detinue had been established since the plaintiff had demanded for
its return to no avail.
SS.50 and 53 of the Traffic and Road Safety Act require that every motor
vehicle purchased must be transferred into the names of the purchaser.
However in spite of the plaintiff's failure to have the requisite transfer made,
he was still entitled to make his claim in detinue since by virtue of the
purchaser he was entitled to the immediate possession of the motor
vehicle.
Shs. 2.5. Million would be awarded for the unlawful detention as general
damages.
The plaintiff had failed to prove the un earned income as special damages
since he had not shown what business he was doing with the motor
vehicle.
Mbabazi & Co. Ltd Vs. Uganda Railways Corporation.
Special damages - for loss of merchandise - whether money value
of the merchandise as at the date of judgment with a profit elements.
General damages -for breach of contract of bailment quantum.
Held: To establish a contract of bailment, the subject matter must be a
chattel whose custody must have been transferred to the bailee
temporarily for a consideration.  In the instant case the subject matter
was hoes in the custody of the defendant who expected to be paid a
storage charge.  Therefore the contract of bailment was established and
the defendants breached this contract when they failed to return the hoes
to the plaintiff.
The special damages awardable would be the replacement market value of
the hoes as at the time of judgment.
The general damages for the plaintiff's loss occasioned by the defendant
would be shs.5,000,000/= (five million).
Nannyanzi Agenesi Vs. Uganda Metal Products & Enameling
Co. Ltd.
Plaintiff's thumb crushing and being amputated and permanent
disability assessed at 30% in what general damages may be
awarded
Held: The ordering of the plaintiff to continue to operate a defective
machine was clearly without reasonable care and was a negligent act
on the part of the defendant.
It was the duty of the defendant to take reasonable care to provide and
maintain a proper functional condition of the machine so as not to
subject its employee to unnecessary risk.
Since the plaintiff has no choice but to obey the instructions of the
Engineer to continue operating the machine she could not be said to
have been contributorily negligent nor having voluntarily assumed the risk.
The Factories Act cast upon a statutory duty the defendant to prevent
the inquiry sustained by the plaintiff by providing a safe drilling machine.
Because the plaintiff's hand grip was reduced by about 60% and her
permanent incapacity was assessed at 30% but she is still in the
employ of the defendant with a monthly pay of 50/= an award of 70,000/=
general damages would be adequate compensation.
Alex Olwor Vs. Registered Trustees of Arua Catholic Diocese
& another.
Loss of profit -foreseability of loss - whether loss of profit was
foreseeable at the time parties concluded the contract.
Held: S.5 Sale of Goods Act requires a contract of sale of goods of the
amount of or above shs. 200 to be writing.  The suit contract was a validity
enforceable contract as it fulfilled the requirements of the sale of Goods Act.
Where the agent does not indicate in a contract that he is contracting
personality but as an agent, then he is personally liable to the contract.  In
the instant case the principal ratified the contract by making part payment
in pursuance thereof.  Therefore both the agent and the principal were liable.
It is a rule of law and practice that special damages must not only be
pleaded but proved strictly.  Though a receipt of Ushs 540,000/= was
tendered in evidence, the amount pleaded was Ush 810,300/=.  The plaintiff
was precluded from recovering the lesser amount of Ush 540,000/= evidence
for which had been adduced because that proved amount was not pleaded.
A plaintiff will recover damages for loss of profit as damages foreseeable by
the parties at the time they made their contract, as the probable result of
the breach.  In the instant case there was no evidence that the defendant
had knowledge of the plaintiff's nature of business.  It was not mentioned in
evidence that the plaintiff was a regular or casual Timber Trade.  Therefore
the defendant could not foresee loss of profit as the natural consequence of
the breach of the contract.
Suit allowed for the payment of the balance on the contract price and
Ush 100,000/= as compensation for delayed payment and costs.
ELECTIONS
Mpanga Kaggwa Vs. Zzimula Mugwanya & 2 others.
Rules 5(6) Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules
1996 -Registry for filing petitions-whether filing petition in High
Court Registry other than the provided district registry renders the
petition incompetent fatally.
Held: R5(6) Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules, 1996
mandatorily provides that the election petition shall be filed in the district
registry respective of the constituency in which the petitioned election is
held, where such a registry exists.  In the instant case the registry for filing
was Mpigi and not the High Court at Kampala.  Therefore the petition was
wrongly filed in a wrong registry.
A suit filed in a wrong registry is incompetent and the court to which it is
filed has no jurisdiction to transfer the same and can only strike it off the
register.
Petition struck off register with costs.
Mugambwa G.W. Vs. Kisembo Muleju G.W.
S.15(3(,Parliamentary Elections Statute 1996-whether because
decision of the High Court is final-therefore no appeal may lay
therefrom.
Held: The High Court is not amendable to the writ of certiorari because it is
not an inferior tribunal.
S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act provides that the award of costs was at the
discretion of court and therefore the decision of the High Court not to award
costs was not an error on the face of the record.
S.15(3) Parliamentary Elections Statutes 1996 provides that the orders of
the High Court on appeal in determining complaints emanating from the
Electoral Commission shall be final.  Therefore the refusal to award costs
was not appealable since the Court had in its discretion, exercised under
s.27(1) Civil Procedure Act, decided not to award any costs.  Therefore, the
respondent had no right to appeal.
Application allowed no order as to costs.
Gulyetonda Jesse Vs. Henry Muganwa Kajura & others.
Filing thereof -r5(6) Parliamentary Election (Election Petitions)
Rules -whether filing in wrong registry was fatal.
Held: An advocate who neglects to renew his certificate does not get
de-registered but his name continues on the roll of advocates.  It would be
an injury to hold that the absence of a certificate had the effect of invalidating
all proceedings taken in the suit, whereas the litigants would find it almost
impossible to investigate the existence of the certificate before handing
down their instructions.  Therefore, lack of an advocate's practicing
certificate does not invalidate proceedings and the petition was validly before
court.
S.2(4) of the Commissioner for Oaths (Advocates Act) provides that where
an Advocate Commissioner for Oaths ceases to practice as an Advocate
then such commissioner shall cease to be commissioner for Oaths.  Since
the Advocate who commissioned the affidavit had never been de-registered
as an Advocate, inspite of his lack of a practicing certificate he validly
continued to act as Commissioner for Oaths and the affidavit he
commissioned could not be impeached merely because of lack of a
practicing certificate.
R5(6) of the Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions) Rules 1996
provides mandatorily that where a constituency to which a petition relates is
within a district registry of the High Court then the petition must be
presented in that District Registry.  In the instant case the presentation of
the petition at Kampala instead of Masindi where the relevant constituency
had its district registry, was fatal and on that account the petition was
incompetent.
Petition struck off the court record with costs for having been in wrong
registry.
Gulyetonda Jesse Vs. Henry Muganwa Kajura
r27 Parliamentary Election (Election Petitions) Rules-whether costs
must be distributed by court.
Held: It is not true that in election petitions a petitioner has no personal
interest in the matter.  In the instant case the petitioner personally wanted
the petitions as it was in the present petition.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Ngirabakunzi Kwera Stella Vs. Ntabgoba
Appeals-time, r.19 Parliamentary Elections (Election Petitions)
Rules 1996-application to enlarge time within which to file memo
of appeal-whether death of wife of counsel was a special
circumstance enjoining court to extend time.
Zziwa Margaret Vs. Catherine Nabagesera
Appeals from interlocutory orders of the High Court-whether
maintainable, S.96(1) Parliamentary Elections (Interim Provisions)
Statute 1996.
Held: S.96(1) of the Parliamentary Elections Statute 1996 does not confer
upon the court of appeal jurisdiction to entertain appeals emanating from the
orders of the High Court which it passes while trying election petitions.
Preliminary objection upheld and application dismissed with costs.
Muyonga Samuel Wamatsembe Vs. Muloki Mutanje.
Limitation S.96(3) Parliamentary Elections (Interim Provisions)
Statute, 1996-whether petition time barred because filed 30 days
after the results were issued in the instrument, S.17(1) (a)
Interpretation Decree.
Held: S.16 Interpretation decree requires that every statutory instrument
must be published in the Gazette.  And S.17(1)(a) provides that where a
statutory instrument does not itself provide for the date of commencement,
then the date of its publication is the date of commencement.  In this appeal,
the Statutory Instrument in which the results of the election were challenged,
was published in the Gazette on the 7th of July 1996 and therefore the
petition filed on 2nd August 1996 was filed in time.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
J.P. Balidawa Vs. J.W. Ziritwawula & anor
Proceedings fixed for hearing after 90 days c/s 143(2) Local
Government Act-whether proceedings untenable-whether it is
incumbent upon the petitioner to fix hearing date.
Held: It was incumbent upon the petitioner or his counsel to apply for an
early hearing date.  He neglected to do so and applied for the hearing 11
days from the expiry of the hearing period of 90 days as provided for in
S.143 (2) Local Government Act.  The proceedings fixed after the expiry of
90 days were clearly stale and untenable.
O.6 r 2 CPR requires that where a litigant pleads fraud, inter alia, such
pleading should respondent forged the names of the persons whom he
alleged nominated him.  No particulars of the forgery were stated.  The
pleading were therefore defective.
Objection upheld.  Petition dismissed with costs.
Sebugwawo Julius Vs. Electoral Commission & anor
Appeal against ruling of Electoral Commission Art 64 (5)
Constitutional of Uganda- whether by petition or appeal to the
High Court.
Citation of non-existent Law-whether petition wrongly before court
and fatally defective.
Held: Articles 139(3) (b) & 140 ( c) (d) do not exist in the Constitution of
Uganda though the petitioner had purported to have filed this petition under
their provisions.  This means that the petition was brought under a non-
existing law and since no amendment was applied for to correct what
counsel for the petitioner called a typing error, the petition was untenable
and would be struck off because it was not properly before court.
In the instant case what was infringed was not only procedural but also
substantive Law therefore Art 126 (2) (e) constitution would not properly be
called in aid to save the petition.
Defaulters of procedure and substantive Law should not be allowed to run to
S.101 CPA asking court to invoke its inherent power where the matter or
proceeding has been improperly brought to court.
Preliminary objection upheld petition struck out with costs.
EMPLOYMENT
Obonyo Vs. Chillington Tool Co. Ltd
Plaintiff suspected to be in racked of stealing stores and dismissed
whether breach of contract of employment - whether wrongful dismissal.
Held: Where an employee is guilty of sufficient misconduct in his
capacity as employee he may be dismissed summarily without notice
and before the expiry of the fixed period employment.  If the employee
does anything which is incompatible with the due or faithful discharge
of his duty to his employer he may be dismissed without notice.
A dismissed servant is entitled recover any arrears which had been
accrued due by the time of dismissal even though they were in
respect of a period of after he had been guilty of misconduct.
Johnson Samson  Senseko Kulubya Vs. Uganda
Transport Co. (1975) Ltd.
Remuneration - whether terminal benefits is ex-gratia and un-
enforceable.
Held: Since by Decree 11/75 Government become trustee to the
assets and liabilities of UTC which assets and was entitled to
compensation for his shares by the defendant company.
All evidence pointed to the fact that the plaintiff was General Manager
and was regarded as such and was entitled to his terminal benefits
in that capacity.
That since the defendant company had allowed the plaintiff to stay in
the house until payment, terminal benefits, the defendant was now
stopped from evicting him before the payment, terminal benefits.
David B.Kayondo Vs. The Co-operative Bank.
Contract - terms of contract -secretary -bye - laws of co-operative
Bank not find secretary who is not member of the bank.
Held: The plaintiff was not a member of the defendant's contract for an
employer has an inherent right to dismiss an employee.
Re-instatement can be ordered in very special circumstances which
had not been shown in this case.
The plaintiff would be entitled to payment in lieu of proper notice and
leave.  No payment for period after dismissal.
Mary Mugenyi Vs. Coffee Marketing Board.
Contract-summary dismissal -whether the appellant was lawfully
dismissed from employment of the defendant.
Held: The plaintiff had been lawfully dismissed as par article 28(9) of the
terms of employment.  She had failed to account for the money she is
alleged to have received on behalf of her employer and was therefore
guilty as per Art 28(19).
Ladislaus Mukasa Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank.
Unlawful dismissal - whether proved where dismissed bank
employee advanced himself money and repaid it.
Held: Where an employee illicitly takes money behind the back of his
employer and appropriates it for his own use even temporarily when he
is aware that had his employer to know he would disapprove, the
establishes dishonest conduct.  In the instant case the conduct of the
plaintiff undermined the high degree of trust and responsibility expected
of any banking official and contravened the terms under which he was
engaged.  The defendant rightly dismissed the plaintiff.
Had court to hold that the dismissal was unlawful shs.3m= would have
been awarded as general damages.
Peace Kyamureku Vs. Uganda National Examinations Board.
Summary dismissal -fairness and justice - whether the summary
dismissal was unfair and unjust.
Held: The plaintiff had vacated office within the meaning or Regulation 9(3)
and her summary dismissal was proper and justified because it was
accordance with her terms of service.
Suit dismissed.
Moses Bulenzi Vs. U.C.B
Wrongful dismissal - authority to dismiss - whether the plaintiff was
wrongful dismissal because the person dismissing him had no
power to do so.
Wrongful dismissal-general damages-quantum-whether equivalent to
agree period of notice.
Held: The dismissal was clearly wrongful since the plaintiff was a Manager
and could only be dismissed by the Board of the plaintiff bank as provided
for in the Personnel Policies Manual of the defendant bank.
The plaintiff since his contract of service provided for one months notice
for termination by either party, the general damages for wrongful dismissal
was equivalent to his one month's salary in lieu or notice.
The law does not allow a dismissed servant to claim general damages for
injured feelings and embarrassment for dismissal nor can a dismissed
servant claim general damages for the inconvenience of securing
alternative employment.
Wilson Nuwemugizi Vs. National & water sewerage corporation.
Voluntary retirement - acceptance of emoluments and other
terminal benefits -whether evidence that the plaintiff has accepted
voluntary retirement.
Termination-whether plaintiff was terminated from the service of defendant.
Held: The learned trial Judge misdirected himself on the evidence when he
held that the plaintiff/appellant had accepted voluntary retirement.  The
acceptance of the emoluments as suggested in the letter the defendant
did not mean that the plaintiff had accepted to retire voluntarily.  There
was evidence that the plaintiff wanted the contrary situation but the
Managing Director showed him that he could not change the decision of
the Board of the defendant.
Moreover, the terms of service of the defendant stipulated that where a
given situation was not adequately covered by the Terms of Service
Regulations, recourse should be had to the Government standing Orders.
It happens that the terms of service of the defendant did not provide the
procedure for voluntary retirement and therefore resort must be had to the
Government Standing Orders, 1968 chapter one, regulation one, which
provides that an officer cannot voluntarily retire until he applied for the
purpose and acceptance therefore given.  In the instant case the appellant
never applied for voluntary retirement.  Therefore the trial Judge
misdirected himself on the law when he held that the appellant had
voluntarily retired.
The defendant/respondent never pleaded in its Written Statement of
Defence that the plaintiff/appellant had had his contract of service
terminated.  However, the same was framed as an issue for trial and the
plaintiff never protested.  Evidence thereafter was led and the issue was
resolved on the evidence.  Therefore since the plaintiff never objected to
the issue being framed at all nor evidence being led to prove the issue the
irregularity of lack of pleading had been cured.  The learned trial Judge
was entitled to hold that the plaintiff's contract of employment had been
terminated.
Prof. Syed Huq Vs. Islamic University In Uganda.
Employment S.13 Employment Decree-foreign employment
contract-enforceability-whether contract was foreign and whether it
was unenforceable.
Held: An Advocate that practices without a valid practicing certificate after
the grace period, practices illegally and is liable to prosecution as provided
by S.14(1) Advocates Act.  And all proceedings taken such counsel and
documents signed by him are invalid, because to say otherwise would
amount to a perpetuation of an illegality.
However, in this case, the issue of the competence of the appeal could not
be raised as a preliminary objection without the leave of the court according
to the provisions of r10(b) RSC.  Therefore the lack of a practicing certificate
by counsel who extracted the decree, would not interfere with the
competence of the appeal.
Where two parties to a contract have agree to contract, then there is
contract which non of the parties may deny.  In the instant case the
respondent's WSD admitted that the appellant was appointed Rector by the
Governing Council of the respondent.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself when he held that the appointment was null and void
due to lack of quorum by the appointing council.
However, S.13 of the Employment Decree provides that a foreign contract
of employment shall not be enforced unless it has been approved of attested
in accordance with the Employment Decree.  In the instant case since the
appellant was not a Ugandan and the respondent was a corporation that
belonged to a foreign body, the contract the subject of the suit was a foreign
contract and the contract was unenforceable due to lack of it having been
approved or attested in accordance with the Employment Decree.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
EVIDENCE
Uganda Vs. Juma Babuma Masudi Isabirye.
Alibi - accused persons allege that at the time of the killing of the
deceased they were all sleeping in their homes.
Held: Where the accused sets up a defence of alibi he does not
assume responsibility of proving it.  It is incumbent on the prosecution
to destroy or disprove it by adducing evidence placing him at the scene
Where the accused are jointly charged the prosecution must either
prove common intention as provided under Sec. 22 of the Penal Code
Act or each accused in a principal offender under sec. 21 of the PC.
In law for an act to amount to an attempt some actus reus must have
been done by the accused.  The text to apply is the common law
principle of proximity as it was reiterated in the case of Everest Mugabi
Vs. Uganda (1976) HCB 124. The prosecution must prove both an overt
act sufficiently proximate to the intended offence.
As regards attempted murder, an over act and positive intention to
cause the death must be established. Republic Vs. Luseru Wandera
s/o Wandera (1948) 5 EACA 101.
In a deciding whether common intention exists the court is guided by
both evidence and conduct to the accused. Common intention may be
inferred from presence, conduct and omission by anyone of the a
accused to disassociate himself from attack.  Actual participation is
not essential.
It is for the prosecution to established the guilt of the accused beyond
reasonable doubt.  The grave discrepancies and inconsistencies in the
evidence of the prosecution witness especially that of P.W 3, Nuru
Mutesi and P.W.4 which were unresolved and the minor numerous
deliberate lies on the part of the prosecution witnesses coupled with the
failure to produce the first report of the names of the accused and the
inordinate delay to record statements from the chief witnesses.
it would be unsafe to base a conviction on the prosecution evidence.
Ben Byabashaija & Anor Vs. Attorney General.
Secondary evidence -plaintiff seeking to tender in a photocopy
where he original is said to be with the defendant - whether such
evidence is admissible.
Held: Evidence by a photocopy would be admitted since the original
was in the possession of the defendant.  It was therefore not necessary
either to annex the document on the plaint nor to list it.
The defendant would not be given leave to call evidence since in his
written statement of defence there was no specific denial.
The defendant's amended written statement of defence was improperly
filed since it was filed late after six months which required either leave
of court or consent by the plaintiff.
Special damages are not awardable when not pleaded.
Damages awardable are assessed at the market value at the date of
judgment, or the properties confiscated.
Sh. 50,000 general damages for each plaintiff to be awarded for detinue.
Eriya Milling Project Vs. Wade Adams Construction Ltd.
Documentary evidence - company entering into an oral contract
and acting upon it documentary evidence to oral contract should be annulled.
Held: The signature on the invoice that constituted the alleged contract
had not been proved and the alleged signatory had not been called to
testify.  Therefore, this is not the contract that falls under s.90 the
Evidence Act which precludes oral contracts from contradicting
documentary contracts.
The alleged agent of the defendant company could not have either
actual or ostensible authority of the company to bind it because the
defendant company had never introduced the alleged agent to the
plaintiff as holding the said position.  Therefore, the question of estoppel
did not arise.
HIMACO Ltd. Vs. Republic Motors.
Patrol evidence rule - plaintiff paying money against a proforma
invoice for the purchase of a motor vehicle whether patrol evidence
were admissible to show that the delivery, of the vehicle was
dependent on availability of foreign exchange.
Held: For a condition precedent to exist both parties to the contract
must understand it and agree to it at the time of concluding the contract
Since the plaintiff stated in court that he would not have parted with his
money if he had been informed of the requirement of foreign exchange
for the importation of the motor vehicle, it cannot be said that there was
a condition precedent to the contract.
The proforma invoice and receipt were the only documents incorporating
the contract since the invoice stated that the plaintiff was paying for a
fully registered motor vehicle.  Therefore the parol evidence to state that
the contract was precedent upon availability of foreign exchange was
inadmissible.
For the defendant to sit back without initiating the process of obtaining
foreign exchange early enough, there plea of frustration for inability to
acquire foreign exchange would not avail him.
Christopher Kayoboke Vs. Amos Agaba Joseph Byamugisha
and Baryaruha.
Estoppel - whether the plaintiff was estoppel from complaining
against the manner in which the company was run because he
himself had been party to such behavior.
Held: Since Dr. Byamugisha was defendant number 2 and was as a
result likely to give evidence in this suit, it would not be proper for
Dr. Byamugisha to act in person for the there 2 defendants as their  counsel.
The plaintiff had two causes of action properly brought before court I.e.
a personal action by which he sought courts protection of his pecuniary
interest is the company and a derivative action by which he sought
court's protection of the good of the company generally against waste
by the directors.  Therefore court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
The question of whether the plaintiff was estopped from complaining
against the manner of running the company because it was a long
established mode to which he himself was party, would be a question
to be determined at the trial.
Ogola Richard Vs. Uganda
Circumstantial evidence-whether the trial Magistrate's conviction of the
accused was based on an irresistible conclusion of the guilt of the
accused from the circumstantial evidence available.
Hearsay evidence - whether the trial magistrate relied on hearsay
evidence in convicting the accused.
Held: The offence of theft was minor and cognate to that of
embezzlement as both belonged to the same family.  Theft is minor in
a sense that the gravity of punishment therefore prescribed is minor to
that of embezzlement and the two offences are cognate because both
offences involve a fraudulent taking away of someone's property.
It is not mandatory that the items stated in the charge sheet in an
offence of theft must all be proved in order to convict the accused.
The prosecution need to prove that some of more of the items in the
charge sheet were stolen by the appellant.
The trial magistrate failed to exclude hearsay evidence from his
judgment before finding the appellant guilty of theft since the said
hearsay evidence was incriminating to the appellant, it did occasion of
justice, and was fatal to the conviction.
The conduct of the accused in running away from the scene of the
crime was circumstantial evidence pointing to the guilt of the accused
but it required corroboration.  The only would be corroborative evidence
connecting the appellant with the theft was that one by a person who
was not called to testify.  Therefore there was a break in the chain of
the circumstantial evidence and would not properly be relied upon to
irresistibly point to the guilt of the accused.
It was not proper for the trial Magistrate to require the accused to
challenge the evidence of the prosecution that some thefts occurred.
This tended to put the burden of proof on the accused and a conviction
based on the weakness of the defence instead of the strength of the
prosecution case would not stand.
American Express International Banking Corporation Vs.
Atulkumar Summant Patel.
Additional evidence - the evidence sought to be adduced could
have been adduced during the hearing of the original suit whether
there is special reason to justify adducing such additional
evidence.
Held: Rule 29 of the Court of Appeal Rules empowers the Supreme
Court to take additional evidence under certain conditions.  This
discretion is to be exercised for sufficient reason.  The evidence sought
to be added was originally known to the applicants advisers and it could
have been adduced and proved during the hearing of the original suit.
It was not based on some new statute or judicial decision.  There was
no special reason to allow the evidence to be adduced.
Lutaaya Vs. Attorney General
Hearsay, statements by persons not called as witnesses in
admissible as hearsay.
Held: The evidence in respect of the car was hearsay and therefore in
admissible.
there was no complaint which led to the arrest which was therefore
wrongful.
Awards for general damages for wrongful arrest, malicious prosecution
and false imprisonment are inconsistent because each case is taken
on its own facts.
Barugare Vs. Attorney General.
Photocopies attached to plaint, and originals not produced at the
hearing - whether this is secondary evidence and in admissible.
Held: Court is not bound and restricted to counsel's agreed issues.
The photocopies were secondary evidence and inadmissible under s.63
of the evidence act.
For a master to liable the servant must be sufficiently identified as such,
and the relationship cannot be presumed.
A bill of lading made to order of 2 persons does not establish sole
ownership of either.
Sheikh Ali Senyonga & 7 others Vs. Sheikh Hussein Rajab
Kakooza and 6 others.
Burden of proof - claim that a party is unqualified - party alleges he
is qualified burden on party to prove qualification.
Elections for officers of Uganda Muslim supreme council were
disputed on grounds that the meeting was irregular were unequal-
unqualified. The incumbents declined to hand over offices where sought
relief from court.
Held: The council was registered as a company and subject to company
law.  It was a private company because membership was restricted
according to religious criteria.
The Constitution of the Council should be interpreted to give reasonable
business efficacy.
The elected chairman met the requirement of the Degree as he had an
equivalent of a B.A. in Dawa obtained from Libya.  The Deputy Mufti did
not need any specific academic qualifications but had to be of good
character, fluent in Arabic, a practicing Muslim and Ahlisunnah Wal-
Jama'h.  He needed some experience in Sharia matters.
The burden of proving qualifications lay on the person who alleges he
had the same.
Apudhan L'Omodoi Vs. Attorney General & Wakabi.
Evidence -conduct - driver causes an accident and disappears
inference of responsibility for the collision.
Hearsay-instructions to driver given by person not called as witness-
evidence of instructions hearsay, and inadmissible.
Held: The defendant was liable as per the principles of vicarious
liability for the driver was acting in the course of his duties.
The plaintiff's driver was not contributory negligent for he kept to the left
side of the road and there was no cause for him to reduce speed.
A driver owes a duty of care to other road users.
Sam Osingida Vs. David Opolot
Evidence -judicial notice state of insurgency in eastern Uganda-
court took judicial notice.
Held: Court took judicial notice of the state of insurgency in the area
and of the regulations.
The soldier was acting in the course of his duties and government was
vicariously liable.
To determine the quantum of lost dependence, the annual income of
the deceased which used to be spent on the infants would be multiplied
by the number of years that the dependency would have continued.
It would have continued for 25 years.
Proved funeral expenses incurred by the deceased's brother as special
damages are allowed:
Award of exemplary damages was prohibited by S.33(2) of the Law
Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act.
The award would be paid to the public Trustee for the benefit of the
infants.
Struggle (u) Ltd Vs. Pan African Insurance Co. Ltd.
Relevancy of facts - whether evidence to prove that the defendant
company does not exist would be admissible where the pertinent
issue before evidence to prove non existence of the dependant
company was irrelevant.
Held: The issue whether the defendant company has ceased to exist is
not a fact in issue as it was not pleaded.  Therefore evidence to prove
its non-existence was not admissible.
Kalisit Sebugwawo Vs. Uganda.
Dying declaration -whether repetition of same dying declaration by
different witnesses was evidence by accuracy or consistency.
Held: The repetition of a dying declaration by different witnesses is not
corroboration but since the learned trial Judge base his conclusion of
the truthfulness of the dying declaration on the fact that the identification
circumstances of the appellant by the deceased were good and looking
at other evidence on the record, they dying declaration had been
corroborated.
In spite of the fact the fact that no weapon was produced in court there
was ample evidence from the witnesses to show that a spear was.
Kanyolo Patrick & others Vs. Uganda.
Evidence of co-accused -whether safely relied on.
Held: The evidence on record as a whole was enough to favourably
identify the accused.
The learned trial Judge properly cautioned himself before accepting
the evidence of co-accused and accomplice by having this evidence
corroborated in material particulars.
Okumu & sons Vs. Attorney General.
Hearsay evidence - whether evidence hearsay for failure to call the
authors of the documents relied upon.
Held: Where there is an offer by one party and acceptance of the offer by
the other then there is a contract.  In the instant case though informal,
there was an offer by the plaintiff to let the vehicle for here at an agreed
rate, and an acceptance by the Army to hire it at that rate.  There was
a valid contract of hire.
The plaintiff had the onus to prove that the frustration of the contract was
self induced.  The plaintiff had to prove that the suit lorry had broken
down due to non-servicing by the defendant and that it was the defendant
who had cannibalized the lorry to render it a Scrap.  But the plaintiff when
he failed or refused to call the witness who had authorized the letters to
the effect that the defendant had admitted liability in this respect,
rendered his evidence hearsay and valueless in as far as proving that the
defendant was liable for the disrepair of the lorry.  Therefore, the plaintiff
had not proved that the frustration of the contract of hire was self induced.
Management Training & Advisory Center Vs. Patrick Kakuku Ikanza
Proof - whether the evidence merely established a plausible
conjecture and not reasonable inference.
Held: The letters the defendant wrote to the plaintiff in reply stating that
he had pledged the machine, established a plausible conjecture that the
machine belonged to the plaintiff.  Plausible conjecture has no legal
value in establishing a fact in issue.  A reasonable inference from primary
facts has legal value but they would be reasonable inference had been
destroyed by the co-existing fact that the respondent had been blamed
for going to Nairobi without permission.  Therefore the appeal would not
succeed since the appellant had failed to establish its case.
Yeko Mukasa Vs. Attorney General.
Hearsay evidence -ordinary course of business - whether state-
statements made by the driver concerning the cause of the accident
should be admissible.
Held: The driver of a Motor Vehicle is enjoined by law to make a report
of any accident.  In the instant case if the driver made the report to the
police, the defendant could produce it to controvert the allegations of the
plaintiff.  Moreover a fact can be proved by the testimony of a single
witness as it was in this case and in absence of any explanation as to
how and why the accident happened, it must be assumed that the
defendant's motor vehicle was being driven in total disregard to other road
users.
The burden of proving that the plaintiff was negligent and that he
contributed to the accident lies squarely on the defendant.  In the instant
case no such evidence was adduced and there is no other evidence on
which such inference can be made.
The plaintiff's arm was broken and his chest injured and his permanent
disability assessed at 35%.  Therefore sh. 2 million general damages
would be awarded.
Uganda Vs. Mukasa Deogratius.
Public document - whether must be proved in court by evidence.
Held: A birth certificate as per S.72(a) (ii) and (iii) of the Evidence Act is
a public document and therefore it was not necessary to call the
Assistant Registrar General of Births and Deaths to prove its authenticity
and the authenticity of the document would not be vitiated by the fact
that the document was prepared after the commission of the offence
since the particulars appearing on the document were obtained from the
complainant's hospital of birth.
Intoxication may provide a defence by enabling the accused to prove
temporary insanity or by indicating that the accused was incapable of
forming the intention necessary to constitute the offence.  In the instant
case the accused in his won evidence stated that he was not so drank
as to be incapable of forming the intention necessary to constitute the
offence.
The accused by his conduct admitted the offence when he told PW3
that he was not had been told by PW2 that the accused had defiled the
complainant and yet PW3 being a paternal uncle to the complainant
was rightly concerned.  This coupled with the other evidence on record
proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was guilty as
charged.
Uganda Vs. Christopher Kizito
Corroboration - whether complainant's distress condition was
corroborative of unlawful sexual assault.
Held: There was evidence that the complainant was distressed which
evidence was not challenged.  The distress condition corroborated the
evidence of PW1, the complainant, this is because in sexual offences
the distressed condition of the complainant is capable of amounting to
corroboration of the complainant's evidence.  This, couple with the other
evidence on record, and the fact that the defendant's alibi was rejected,
shows that the prosecution had proved the case against the accused
beyond reasonable doubt.
Musisi Dirisa & 3 ors Vs. Sietico (u) Ltd.
Burden of proof -shifting the evidential burden of proof had shifted to
the defendant.
Held: The evidence burden does not shift to the defendant unless there
is cogent and credible evidence produced by the plaintiff on the issue.
In this case the mere claim that the plaintiffs were fare paying passengers
who sustained injuries due to the defendant's negligence, did not
accession the shifting of the evidential burden to the defendant so as to
necessitate her to produce the police accident reports to disprove the
testimony of the plaintiffs.
The trial judge was right in holding that the plaintiffs had abandoned their
pleading in as far as the particulars to injuries were concerned because
there different testimonies at the trial were at variance with their pleading
in the plaint.  This offended against O.6 r6 CPR as it constituted a
departure.
The learned trial judge was correct to have rejected the evidence of the
expert doctor who testified for the plaintiffs because the doctor had only
made a casual examination of the appellants but not a detailed medical
examination.  A doctor or any expert witness must provide a scientific
base for his opinion before his findings can be accepted by court.  This
scientific base was lacking.  The appeal would be dismissed.
J.K Patel Vs. Spear Motors Ltd.
Burden of proof whether burden of proof shifted to the defendant.
Held: The learned trial judge misdirected himself when he held that there
was no definite valid and enforceable contract merely by looking at the
documents tendered and the parties oral testimony.  The parties conduct
definitely showed that an offer on definite terms had been made by one
party and accepted by the other.  There was a valid enforceable contract.
The plaintiff had testified that he had been contracted by the defendant
company to build an assembly plant.  There plaintiff showed that he had
been part paid for this work.  The burden of proof thereby shifted to the
defendant to disprove this allegation.  But the defendant in his testimony
claimed that it had part paid more than the plaintiff had shown.  But
since the defendant's part payment had not been pleaded in his written
statement of defence, its evidence of part payment would be inadmissible.
Therefore the defendant had not discharged its burden of proof and would
have judgment against it.
The parties evidence at the trial amply showed that the defendant's
general manager was a key witness in this case.  But since the
defendant refused to call him as a witness, an adverse inference would
be drawn against the defendant.
The defendant's evidence of a set off, when he claimed that the plaintiff's
four years occupation of the defendant's home was upon an
understanding that the rent would act as a set off and the plaintiff's wife's
air ticket given by the defendant, such evidence was admissible even if
the defendant had not pleaded it in its WSD because the plaintiff at the
trial never objected to it nor did the plaintiff cross examine the
defendant's witness on it.
Rent would be assessed at the market rate for the purpose of the set off.
Court had the discretion to award interest and in this case court would
award interest at the official Bank of Uganda rates.
The trial judge misdirected himself when he failed to award costs to the
successful party.  Though the judge has a discretion not to award costs
to the successful party or at all his discretion must be exercised
judiciously and the reasons given in his judgment for his refusal to award
costs to the successful party.
Dirisa Musisi & ors Vs. Sietco (u) Ltd & onor.
Expert medical evidence whether admissible when expert never
treated the accident nor support by medical notes.
Held: The first defendant was clearly negligent because he drove the
gender in such a way as to afford no opportunity to the second defendant
to avoid knocking the first defendant's grader.
The plaintiffs failure to produce bus tickets to prove that they were fare
paying passengers in the bust in which they allege to have been injured
coupled with their failure to prove that they were immediately treated for
the injuries alleged sustained, together with their failure to produce a
Police Traffic Accident Report to indicate that they had infact been
injured at the material time in the said accident, would exonerate the
defendants from the alleged breach of the duty of care owed to the
plaintiffs.
The expert medical evidence was inadmissible for being hearsay because
the witness never treated the plaintiffs immediately after the accident,
and was not guided by medical notes made at the time of the treatment
but the witness heard what he was told by the plaintiff almost after 4
years of the accident.
Had the plaintiffs succeeded PW1 for the fractured arm would have been
awarded sh.500,000=; PW2 for the amputated arm would have been
awarded sh.300,000/= and PW3 for the lost eye ball and injured thumb
would have been awarded sh.2,000,000/=.
Administrator General Vs. Mrs Norah Nakiyaga & ors Adm.cause.
Whether valid when not arrested.
Held: It had been proved or admitted that the first will had been signed
by the deceased though not attested.  It was invalid for the reason that
it was not attested as required by S.50(1) ( c) of the Succession Act.
The second Will could not be relied upon as its execution was not
proved by one of the attesting witnesses as required by the mandatory
provision of ss.6 and 67 of the Evidence Act.
Stephen Kasozi & ors Vs. Peoples Transport Services Ltd.
Expert opinion - whether the failure to call the doctor who made the
medical report rendered such report inadmissible in evidence.
Held: So long as counsel acting for the party in a case and his
instructions have not been terminated he has full control over the
conduct of the trial and has apparent authority to compromise all
matters connected with the action.
The plaintiffs did not show court that they were fare paying passengers.
Therefore, the defendant has no contractual relation with the plaintiffs.
This meant that the plaintiffs were mere trespassers and the defendant
had no duty of care towards them.
The doctor that made the report should have been called as witness
failure of which made his report in admissible.
Uganda Electricity Board Vs. GM Musoke
Judicial notice -whether court may take judicial notice of a custom that
has not been proved in evidence.
Held: Under ss.7,8 of the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act a
cause of action is provided by which dependants of the deceased may
claim compensation for the loss suffered as a result of his death.
Though Section 8 of the Act provides for the members of the family and
not dependants, nevertheless, the intention is to provide for members of
the family who were dependants of the deceased who had suffered
pecuniary loss as a result of his death.  The plaintiff would claim to have
suffered pecuniary loss if he had lost dependency on the deceased.  In
the present case general damages should not have been awarded to the
deceased's brothers and sisters because they were not his dependants.
It cannot be said that any service carried out by a child for the benefit of
his family has a pecuniary value capable of being compensated as
pecuniary loss.  This is because the small household work done by a
child in company of his brothers and sisters is such as all children in all
families willingly and helpfully do as a discipline of family life in its
numerous activities.  No materialistic view should be made of such and
a monetary value upon a domestic services a kin of an employee would
forsake a proper sense of proportion in judging of the normal pattern of
daily life in a family which pivots around the voluntary and combined
efforts of all family members.  In the present case the respondent failed
to establish that he lost any services of a pecuniary value.
The learned Trial Judge erred in law when he held that there existed a
custom that children in African societies who were educated by their
parents were required to support their parents and families on completion
of school.  He was supposed to have first required evidence from the
respondent/plaintiff to establish the existence of the custom and it
should not have been court itself to take judicial notice of such a custom.
Though court has power to9 take judicial notice of notorious facts, in the
present case it was not shown that the practice where children provided
financial support to their parents was notorious, prevalent or common to
all children.  The plaintiff should have proved to court, that he has lost
a reasonable probability of pecuniary advantage as evidence by custom
and not a mere fanciful probability would not speculate whether his
deceased son would have successfully completed his studies and been
in a position to assist his parents.  The trial judge erred to have held the
contrary and awarded damages for a pecuniary loss that wasn't
ascertainable or proved.
In Uganda general damages are not awarded for bereavement but for loss
of expectation of life i.e., putting a money value on the prospective
balance of happiness in years that the deceased might have lived if he
had not died, calculated subject to the normal risks and uncertainties.
And these damages should be moderate.  The learned trial judge erred
when he applied wrong principles and took into account wrong factors
and he arrived at a wholly erroneous estimate of the damages suffered.
The amount of damages awarded should not have been shs.5.5 million
but 1m.
H.G. Gandesha Vs. Anor Vs. G.J. Lutaya.
Affidavit in reply - whether failure by the respondent to reply by
affidavit or otherwise means that facts stand unchallenged.
Held: The facts as deponed to in the affidavit of the applicant were not
intrinsically incredible and therefore since they were not answered, they
stood unchallenged.
Fam International Ltd Vs. Ahmed Farah Vs. Mohamed EL-Faith.
Standard of proof -fraud -whether trial judge erred in failing to apply
the correct standard of proof of fraud.
Held: Paragraph 4 of the written statement of defence gave the appellants
sufficient particulars of what fraudulent acts the respondent was alleging
against them, namely the backdating of the incorporation of the first
appellant, with intent to defraud the respondent.
The fraudulent acts complained of were imputable on the second plaintiff/
appellant because he stood to gain from them.
In fraud cases the standard of proof is more than a mere balance of
probability though less than proof beyond reasonable doubt.  The learned
trial judge was alive to this provision of the law when he said that he was
satisfied by the evidence which was more than a balance of probabilities.
Therefore the trial judge applied the correct standard of proof of fraud as
required.
The main ground upon which a court can go behind the certificate of
incorporation is fraud and once fraud is alleged the court is entitled to
extend its enquiry to matters precedent and incidental to registration.
The learned trial judge was therefore correct in going behind the
certificate of incorporation, because a certificate of incorporation may
be impeached on the grounds of fraud.
The learned trial judge erred in making a winding up order of the first
appellant because there was no such application properly before the
court as provided by ss 218 and 224 of the Companies Act.
The failure to gazette and entry of the change of name were two
irregularities in procedure which would not vitiate the change of name
property made.  The trial judge was correct in holding so.
It is always better to frame issues at the beginning of the hearing before
evidence is led so that evidence that is led is guided by the framed issues.
A prayer was not an assertion nor a material statement which one party
must allege or the other must deny to constitute an issue.  The trial judge
was right in holding that the issue as to the appellant's holding out as a
shareholder in the respondent's company was a won issue because, it
only appeared as a prayer.
the respondent could not claim his company's property by an action in
his own name as this would offend against the rule of corporate
personality, since the company that owned the property had its own
independent existence.  The trial judge was correct in refusing the prayer
in the counter claim and was also correct in not granting the order for the
recovery of the property in favour or the plaintiffs because they had not
made that prayer.
Uganda Vs. Emmanuel Byakatonda
Proof of age-expert opinion -whether doctors opinion as to the age
of the complainant was preferable.
Corroboration-whether complainant's evidence corroborated.
Held: The Prosecution had proved that the accused had been sexually
intercourse by the accused, and that the victim was below eighteen
years.  Therefore the offence of defilement had been proved.
The accused will be sentenced to 14 years imprisonment.
E. Kangye Vs. Bauana.
Standard of proof of fraud - whether higher than in ordinary cases.
Locus in quo-whether irregularly conducted.
Witnesses' oath-whether irregularly sworn in court must be re-sworn at
the locus in quo.
Held: The terms, decree and order, are mutually exclusive.  However,
whether the memorandum of appeal is a pleading so as to entitle the
appellant to seek amendment thereof under O.6 r 18 was not necessary
to decide since the amendment if allowed so that the term "order" is
substituted for "decree" no miscarriage of justice would arise, the
amendment would be allowed.
The standard of proof required to prove fraud in civil cases was higher
than in ordinary cases.  The learned trial magistrate directed himself
as no miscarriage of justice resulted.
The trial magistrate precisely followed the observations he made at the
locus in quo and properly himself as to the evidential value of observations
as they conformed to the descriptive evidence of the boundaries of the
suit land as given by the parties and their witnesses both in court and at
the locus in quo.
When a witness is sworn in court and he is called upon to give evidence
at the locus in quo it is not necessary to have the witness take another
oath since he continues to be on oath right from court to the locus in quo
Therefore the trial magistrate did not misdirect himself when he did not
require the witness at the locus in quo to take a fresh oath when they
had already taken one in court.
Senyongo and another Vs. Uganda Railways Corporation.
Expert opinion -whether evidence of the doctor who made the
report but did not examine the plaintiffs is admissible.
Held: The principle of res ipsa loquitur means that the happening of an
accident was by itself reasonable evidence of the defendant's negligence.
For the plaintiff to rely on this principle he must have pleaded it and led
evidence to establish it.
The plaintiff's being lawfully on the defendant's carriage creates a duty to
carry him safely and it was necessary for the plaintiff to prove that he
was such a lawful passenger by evidence of receipts as a fair paying
passenger.  In the instant case the plaintiff had not proved that they were
lawfully on the defendant's carriage for their failure to show that they
were fair paying passengers.
medical reports must be proved by the persons making them and when
the medical report is made by a person that did not examine the plaintiff,
his evidence must be of little value like in the instant case.
Uganda Vs. Mugyenyi Geoffrey & another.
Confession -whether admissible when repudiated - whether corroborated
rated.
Blood group-whether the similarity of the blood group of the accused and
the soiled pillow were corroboration of the repudiated confession.
Held: There was no evidence that the deceased had had any injury
leading to bleeding or vomiting blood.  The sample of blood from the
accused revealed that it was similar in group with the blood stain on the
pillow at the scene of the murder.  Since the blood did not come from the
deceased, it came from the accused.  Even though the accused had
repudiated his confession in which he had confessed to have robbed and
murdered the deceased, who in her struggle bit the accused's finger, the
similarity in the blood group corroborated the confession.
Strangulation and suffocation are not mutually exclusive terms because
strangulation invariably suffocation since it involves the blocking of the
flow of blood as well as blocking the trachea or respiration, by pressing
the neck.  Therefore the accused could not take benefit of the alleged
doubt as to the cause of death since the postmortem Report as proved
showed that the deceased died of acute pulmonary edema.  This
necessarily included strangulation or suffocation.
If some assistance or encouragement is voluntarily done with the
knowledge of the circumstances constituting the offence, that is sufficient
to sustain the conviction and it is irrelevant that the assistance was not
given with the motive of encouraging the crime.  In the present case
though there seemed to be no satisfactory evidence that A2 was at the
scene of the crime, the sharing in the loot fully knowing the
circumstances under which the money had been obtained amounted to
assisting or encouraging the crime.  Therefore A2 took part in the
commission of the offence.
Since the accused caused the death of the deceased by suffocation this
was evidence of malice aforethought because the act of suffocating
another means that the person so acting is fully aware of the
consequence of suffocation, death.
It was not necessary to prove all the items listed in the indictment so as
to prove a charge of theft but some of the items proved stolen as listed
suffices.
Ebuneiri Waisswa Kafuko, Deceased.
Affidavit - whether false.
Held: Since the respondent's affidavit was intrinsically false for being
contradictory, court would be inclined to believe the applicant's case that
the respondent was not furnishing accounts and order him to do so.
Since the applicants were successful they would have the costs of the
application.
Patrick Akol Vs. Uganda.
Witness - child of tender years - whether a witness who was 14
years old was necessarily a Child of tender years.
Corroboration -evidence of a child of tender years-whether is inadmissible
without corroboration.
Medical evidence-whether corroborated other evidence.
Admissibility-evidence of child of tender years-whether inadmissible
without corroboration.
Held: While ordinarily a child of apparent age of 14 years was a child of
tender years it still remains a matter of the good sense of the court to
decide whether a particular witness was a child of tender years.  In the
instant case the learned trial judge found that Bonny who 14 years was a
reasonably mature person and therefore the learned trial judge was
entitled to admit Bonny's evidence could rely on Bonny's evidence.
Judith who was 13 years old was a child of tender years and it was
invariably necessary to administer a voire dire to her.  Since the trial court
failed to administer a voire dire to her, her evidence was the kind of
evidence not on oath.
The unsworn evidence of a child of tender years is risky to act upon with
out corroboration but the corroboration is not a requirement of the law.
It is for the court to weight the reliability of the evidence of the particular
unsworn witness.
The medical evidence other than providing the rapture of the hymen did
not connect the appellant to the defilement.
The evidence of Judith and Bonny was intrinsically honest and reliable
and of such quality that the court was entitled to act upon it.  Therefore,
the trial judge was correct to convict the accused. Appeal dismissed.
Uganda Vs. Sebunya Sekaala
Corroboration - whether the witness's evidence required corroborate-
ion, the witness being a Child of tender years.
Held: There is no law requiring proof of age by birth certificate and it was
enough that the parents of the complaint stated what the age of the
complainant was.
