Although it was unsafe to convict on uncorroborated evidence of a child of
tender years, in the instant case the child's evidence was been amply
corroborated and moreover the child's evidence was so truthful and did
not require corroboration.
National Insurance Corporation Vs. National Union of Clerical,
Commercial, Professional & Technical Employees.
Cross examination - denial of opportunity to cross examine -
whether breached natural justice.
Held: 8(1) of the Trades Disputes (Arbitration and Settlement) Act allows
the applicant to apply to the Industrial Court to interpret its award within
28 days from the date of the award.  Therefore notwithstanding S.11 of the
same Act that requires gazetting, the applicant's application to interpret
the Industrial court's award before it was gazetted was proper since it was
done within 28 days as required by S.8(1) of the Act.
the Industrial Court was empowered like any ordinary court to review its
own decisions while exercising its powers of interpretation under S.11 of
the Act.
The failure by the Industrial Court not to allow cross examination of the
witness on a new piece of evidence was not proper and it was a breach of
natural justice.  But, it did not occasion a miscarriage of justice since the
applicant's complaint was merely the procedure by which the respondent
had applied to Industrial Court for the interpretation of the award instead
of applying to the High Court for certiorari.
Petelonia Mpirirwe Vs. Oliver Ninsabimaana.
Paternity -physical features - whether evidence of similar physical
features to prove paternity was admissible.
Held: The evidence that the deceased paid shs.100,000/= as a fine for
cohabiting with the defendant was no evidence of payment of bride which
was an essential pre-requisite for a valid marriage.  Therefore, the
defendant to the grant of letters of Administration.
The evidence of similarity in physical features between a child and the
alleged parent is admissible to prove paternity even it the evidence is not
conclusive.  The failure by the defendant to adduce evidence of genetically,
biological and physical features similar to those of the deceased made
court fail to presume that the alleged twins were fathered by the deceased.
The controlling authority after having allocated the plot to the deceased,
the plot was no longer available for re-allocated plot devolved on the
estate of the deceased for the administration by the Administrator of the
deceased's estate.
The plaintiff was entitled to the grant of the letters of Administration since
she was the rightful widow of the deceased and her application had not
been contested by the beneficiaries.
Blasio Sengendo & anor Vs. Uganda.
Admission - whether alleged admissions were properly admitted.
Held: Although the charge sheet showed that the appellants had been
charged under S.257 (c ) the correct subsection should have been (b)
since the embezzlement with which they were charged concerned a
limited liability company.
Embezzlement is committed by an employee when he steals
property of the employer before the employer acquires either actual or
constructive possession of that property.  In the present case, the
property alleged to have been stolen was already in the custody of the
employer and therefore the offence of embezzlement was not committed.
The offence of theft was committed when the spares were taken out of the
shop even if they were intercepted at the gate but he issue is whether it
were the appellants who stole the spares.  The fraudulent intent was
indicated by the stranger who ran away when he was intercepted with the
spares.  His running away was evidence that he fraudulently intended to
deprive the owner of the property permanently.
An admission is a statement made by the accused, though not amounting
to a confession but contains gravely incriminating facts against the maker.
In the instant case the alleged apologies were not unequivocal as they
were open to different interpretations, one such interpretation being that
they were sorry for a theft to be committed against the company without
their preventing it.
When the trial Magistrate ruled out the possibility that PW3 was not a
credible witness in light of the contradictions in his evidence and should
have admitted his evidence with caution.
It is trial law that invariably circumstantial evidence must be narrowly
examined to avoid a possibility of a fabrication by ruling out co-existing
circumstances reasonably capable of explaining the situation, before
inferring the guilt of the accused.  In the instant case there were several
contradictions in the prosecution case which were not explained away
and his cast doubt on the guilt of the accused.  The circumstantial
evidence was not water tight.
Counsel holding a watching brief has no right to address court in
opposition to a prosecutor although as an officer of court he may inform
court on matters that can assist court while the interest of justice demand.
A trial magistrate has a discretion under S.98 of the Magistrates Court
Act to decide whether or not to recall a witness.  The trial magistrate was
entitled to refuse the recall of the witness and this did not indicate bias on
plot of the magistrate.
The inference of bias must be as to what a reasonable man would think
given the set of circumstances.  It the reasonable man would thing that
the Magistrate did favour one side unfairly at the expense of another than
bias is proved.  In the instant case there was no evidence of a real
likelihood of bias on the part of the Magistrate.
It is not a correct statement of the law that court is at liberty to cancel
bail at any stage.  Evidence in favour of cancellation of bail must be
evidence on oath and the court must decide judiciously that it is justified
in the present case the trial Magistrate erred when she cancelled the
accused's bail on mere speculative information from prosecution.
Appeal allowed.
Ruhini Damji Sidpra Vs. Vijendra Damji Sidpra
Burden of proof, Evidence Acc, ss.100,101,102 on who burden of
proof was.
Held: Both the plaintiff's and defendant's evidence is in agreement that the
plaintiff is entitled to 10% of the shares in the deceased's estate while
the defendant holds power of attorney from 7 other family members and is
entitled to more than 80% of the shares in the estate.
S.201 Succession Act (as amended by Decree 22/72) provides that in a
situation like the one at hand the person entitled to the greatest proportion
of the deceased's estate would be granted the administration of the
deceased's estate.  Accordingly the defendant is entitled to be granted
the letters of administration of the estate.
From the evidence on record, it's quiet clear that apart from merely
alleging that the defendant has mismanaged and wasted the deceased's
estate the plaintiff produced no evidence to support her claims.  Under
sections 100, 101, 102 of the Evidence Act (Cap.43) whoever alleges a
fact is supposed to prove it, and the standard of proof in civil cases is
simply on a balance of probabilities.  In this case the plaintiff alleged and
made no attempt to prove the allegations.  The defendant is accordingly
under no obligation to dispel such allegations.  The plaintiff has thus
shown no circumstances to compel court to refuse to grant letters of
administration to the defendant.
The evidence on record shows that the plaintiff is not a resident of Uganda
and is on bad terms with most of the family members.  It would therefore
be very difficult to justify joint letters of administration between her and the
defendant.  The request thus cannot be granted.
Case dismissed with costs.
Kwerimba Vs. Uganda.
Identification - whether appellant properly identified by victim at
3.00 am using a simple light and grass torch.
Held: There was overwhelming evidence against the appellant.  PW1
knew the appellant well, although the attack occurred at 3:00am there
was ample light first form the tadoba and later from the lighted grass torch
to enable PW1 identify the appellant.
The appellant accepts he was traced at his home only.  His claim that the
injury on his shoulder was inflicted by his arresters is clearly invented
story intended to cover up the incriminating injury inflicted by PW1 which
injury fully corroborated PW1 evidence about the identity of the attacker.
There is no evidence to support appellant's claim that PW1's properties
found by PW2 hardly 3 hours after robbery were planted on the appellant
at Butenga Police post.
Accordingly the trial Judge was justified in convicting the appellant.
Appeal dismissed.
Mohammed Kasoma Vs. Uganda.
Un corroborated evidence of a single witness whether convicted
based on this proper.
Held: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and gave the following
reasons for its orders.  There is no substance to the applicant's complaint
that the learned Judge did not take his defense of alibi into consideration.
Despite certain alleged drawbacks to the complainant's evidence, the
learned Judge found that the testimony of the complainant was reliable
and rejected the defense.  Having examined the evidence again we found
that they could be no doubt at all on that point.  There defence is
accordingly rejected.
The learned Judge having warned himself properly of the need for
corroboration, went on to state that if he were satisfied that the
complainant was truthful he could still convict on her uncorroborated
evidence.  It is apparent that the complainant was an exceptionally
persuasive witness her whole narrative was consistent.  The medical
evidence supported her story we could well understand that with or without
corroboration the complainant's evidence must be accepted in favour of
the appellant's alibi.  Consequently this ground of appeal fails.
The appellant a man of 49 years of age cannot be excused for playing
this dangerous and disgraceful trick on a girl of 14 years who knew the
appellant's wife and so trusted the appellant.
Accordingly, thee is no reason to interfere with the sentence imposed.
In any case it was not manifestly excessive.
Appeal dismissed.
Sam Buteera Vs. Uganda.
Identification evidence -whether identification of accused sufficient.
Uncorroborated evidence of a single witness-whether conviction based on
this proper.
Held: The victim knew the appellant well, she had seen him at her home
before the incident.  Even if she was in a coffee plantation she saw him
coming to attack her with the help to lantern.  He even talked to her after
sexually assaulting her.  The learned trial Judge therefore rightly directed
herself and the assessors on the law relating to uncorroborated evidence
of a complainant in sexual offence.  The circumstances under which the
offence was committed were such as to render aspects of the case in
relation to the fact of defilement such as the medical evidence and
distressed condition in which the victim was found by her grandmother.
Appellant was therefore properly convicted.
S.123 Penal Code does not provide for corporal punishment for defilement
S.108 Trial on Indictment Decree is inapplicable as it gives the High Court
power to impose corporal punishment to persons under the age of 16
years.  The order of corporal punishment against the appellant was
therefore illegal and is accordingly set aside.
Appeal against conviction fails.
Appeal against sentence succeeds only to the extent that the order for
corporal punishment is set aside.
Uganda Vs. Tandema Phillipo.
Circumstantial evidence - whether there was enough circumstantial
for a charge of murder c/s 183 of the Penal Code Act.
Held: The burden of proving the accused's guilt is on the prosecution and
that burden does not shift to the accused except in a few statutory case-
Woolmington Vs. DPP (1935) AC 462.
There was satisfactory evidence to prove that the first element of murder,
that is a human being by the names of Cecilia Otoda alias Cecilia
Achandere is dead.  The prosecution also proved beyond reasonable
doubt that the cause of the deceased's death was unlawful.
As to whether the accused caused death of the deceased, the evidence
available is circumstantial.  The law dealing with circumstantial evidence
was stated in Simon Musoke Vs. R (1958) EA 715.  the principle is that
where prosecution case is founded on circumstantial evidence, that
evidence must show that the accused is guilty and there are no existing
factors that tend to weaken or destroy the inference of his guilt.  In this
statement to the police, which was admitted by, consent of both sides
the accused admitted having killed his wife with his bare hands.  The
accused himself confirmed in court that he had had a quarrel with his wife.
The circumstantial evidence available therefore leads to the inference that
the accused killed his wife.
The evidence available however does not prove beyond reasonable doubt
that the accused killed his wife with malice aforethought.  The conflicting
prosecution evidence as to how the deceased met her death makes the
situation more uncertain.  Further more there was evidence from both
sides that before the incident the accused was so drunk and might not
have been capable of informing the necessary intention to kill his wife.
Accordingly the accused is acquitted of murder but convicted of
manslaughter c/s 182 Penal code Act and S.86 T.I.D.
Alfred Bumbo  Vs. Uganda.
Witness - police witness absence of police evidence was fatal to
the prosecution evidence.
Held: The evidence of eye-witness did not clearly put the first appellant on
the scene of the crime.  His alibi therefore should be truthful and raised a
doubt in the prosecution case.  He was entitled to the benefit of doubt.
His appeal must therefore succeed.
Once an accused person has been positively identified during the
commission of a crime then his claim that he was elsewhere must fail.
In the instant case 2nd and 4th appellants were clearly identified as
being part of the gang that killed the deceased.  The trial Judge correctly
rejected their alibis.
The absence of any evidence of arrest or any evidence from the police
investigating officer did not weaken the prosecution's case because other
evidence was available to provide prosecution's case because other
evidence was available prosecution's case beyond reasonable doubt.
Appeal allowed for appellant number one and dismissed for appellants(2)
and (4).
B.A.T.(U) Ltd Vs. Selestino Mushongere.
Admissibility - photographs - whether photographers were  in
admissible without calling the photographer as a witness.
Held: A person is guilty of contributory negligence if he ought reasonably
to have fore seen that if he did not act as a reasonable prudent man he
might be hurt and in his reckoning he must take into account a possibility
of others being careless.  In the instant case the deceased acted
reasonably in the circumstances by standing at the bust stage where he
was waiting or Public Transport and the appellant was wholly liable for the
accident when its vehicle was driven in such a way as to detour onto the
bus stage thus knocking the deceased dead.
The learned trial Judge was not wrong in holding that the normal life
expectancy for a person in the deceased's occupation was 55 years the
deceased having been a business man.  However the Trial Judge should
have discounted the deceased's working life expectancy by five years from
20 to 15 to allow for imponderables so as to come to a more realistic
position representing what would have been the remaining working life of
the deceased.
The contention by the defendant/appellant that the deceased did not
operate a lodge and restaurant in Namataba Trading Centre was rightly
rejected by the learned Judge because firstly the photographs were
inadmissible in evidence when the photographer had not been called as
a witness and secondly three plaintiff witnesses credibly testified as to
the existence  of a lodge in the area.
The evidence relating to the deceased's income was unsatisfactory and
exaggerated and the evidence of how much the deceased was giving to
the widow to maintain the family appeared exaggerated in view of the
known sources of income and therefore the learned trial Judge should
have found that the deceased's income was Uhs.10,000/= per day and not
20,000/= and that the deceased spent Ush.50,000/=- on his family per
day Uhs.50,000/= should have been multiplied by 15 years being the
deceased's working life expectancy and the resultant Ush.27 million
should have been the figure to award to the dependants.
The contention of the defendants/appellants that Mugisha one of the three
dependants was not going to school and therefore dependency had not
been proved was rightly rejected by the trial Judge since the evidence
whether or not Mugisha was going to school did not go to the root of the
matter which was whether dependants were entitled to share in the
damages awarded for the loss of dependency.  The learned trial Judge
however erred in not apportioning the damages to the beneficiaries.
Appeal allowed in part and file remitted back to trial Court for apportioned
of damages.
Shokatali Abdullah Dhala Vs. Sandrudin Merrali.
Documentary evidence -questioned documents -whether the
submission of questioned documents together with specimens
indicating to the handwriting expert that the questioned documents
were forgeries was a correct procedure - whether this act adversely
affected the probative value of the expert evidence on the hand-
writing of the appellant.
Held: Looking at the plaintiff's/appellant's travel documents including his
passport there was no evidence that the plaintiff/appellant have ever been
to Uganda since he left in 1973 to 1992 when he returned.  Therefore, the
learned trial Judge misdirected himself when he found that it is the
plaintiff/appellant who had signed the documents in question.
The correct procedure of leading with questioned documents is that if a
questioned document cannot be distinguished by other conditions than
those in the writing itself, the questioned writing should be submitted
together with the genuine writing in the handwriting expert without any
information as to which document, or writing is suspected and no outside
facts bearing on the question of genuineness should be given until after a
definite opinion has been given.  In the instant case the plaintiff pointed
out the questioned writing to the witness and this was not proper.
however, the failure to follow the correct procedure in this case did not
affect the probative value of the expert evidence of the circumstance of
this case.
Appeal allowed.
Uganda Vs. Ikikye Zakaria
Evidence of a complaint in sexual offence - whether the evidence
was well corroborated to warrant a conviction of defilement.
Held: The evidence of PW2 and the medical report coupled with common
sense were indeed in agreement that PW1 was far below the age of 18
years.  Though the best way to prove age is a certified birth certificate, the
foregoing have been held to be a conclusive method of proof of age - R Vs.
Recorder of Grimshy Ex-parte Bursar [1951] ALL ER 889.
From the victim testimony and the medial examination report, the
prosecution proved sexual intercourse with the victim beyond reasonable
doubt.  Since it had earlier been proved that PW1, the victim is below 18
years, the sexual intercourse was therefore unlawful by virtue of the
provisions of S.123 Penal Code Act.
From the evidence on record, the testimony of PW1 is corroborated in
every aspect.  Although the corroborating evidence is circulated it is trite
law that circumstantial evidence is good as direct evidence provided that
it irresistibly points to the guilt of the accused and is incompatible with
his innocence; Charles Benon Bitwire Vs. Uganda, Court of Appeal
Criminal Appeal No. 23/85.
Having believed the evidence of the prosecution witness, the alibi put up
by the accused is rejected and the accused is found to have been at the
scene of the crime and defiled PW1 on 5th April 1993.  the accused is
therefore found guilty of the offence of defilement c/s 123 (1) Penal Code
and is accordingly convicted.
John  Baptist Kibuka Vs. Uganda.
Child of tender years s.38(3) trial on indictment decree - whether
issue of tender years arises at the time of trial or when the
incident happened.
Omission to call complainant - whether trial judge failed to sufficiently
evaluate the evidence in the case.
Held: The procedure to be followed by a trial Court which is faced with a
child of tender years as a witness is set out in S.38 (3) Trial on
Indictments Decree.  The most recent decided case to which the trial
judge referred to is Mukasa Deogratius Vs. Uganda, Criminal Appeal
No.21/93 (unreported) where "a child of tender years" has been defined as
any age, or apparent age, of under 14 years, in the absence of any
special circumstances.  In the instant case, PW4 was not a child of
tender years because he was 14 years old when he gave evidence.
There were no special circumstances, which justified him to be regarded
as a child of tender years. It was therefore not necessary for the learned
trial Judge to decide whether PW4 should give sworn or unsworn evidence.
it was self evident from his judgment that the learned trial Judge made a
careful and comprehensive evaluation of all the evidence in the case
before coming to the conclusion he did.  He considered the prosecution
evidence, the most important aspects of which came from P.W.4, an
eyewitness, and the medical evidence.  He also considered the appellant's
alibi, which he found, rightly so in our view, did not create a whole, the
trial Judge, in our view, correctly found that all ingredients of the offence
with which the appellant was charged had been proved to the required
standard.
There was no useful purpose of calling the victim since as the prosecution
State Attorney put it she could not comprehend the proceedings and also
in view of the fact that the evidence of the other witness was sufficient to
prove the case against the appellant to the required standard.
S. 123 (1) of the Penal Code provides for death as the maximum sentence
for the offence of defilement.  Although we are unable to say that the
sentence of 25 years in the instant case is illegal, we are satisfied that it
was manifestly harsh and excessive.  Considering the circumstances of
the case a sentence of 16 years imprisonment would be appropriate.
Regarding Corporal punishment following the decision in the case of
Bambi Vs. Uganda Criminal Appeal No. 33/94, corporal punishment is
neither provided for under S.123(1) Penal Code nor S.108 Trial on
Indictment Decree.  It follows therefore that the order for corporal
punishment was illegal.  The order for police supervision was also illegal,
as the offence of defilement is not one to which S.123 Trial Indictments
Decree, which provides for police supervision applies.
Appeal against conviction dismissed.
Appeal against sentence partly succeeds.
The sentence of 25 years imprisonment, the orders for corporal
punishment and police supervision are set aside.
Abeit Alex & anor Vs. Uganda.
Circumstantial - evidence -whether trial judge erred in relying on
convict the accused where there was no eye witness to the crime
whether there was missing link between the murder weapon.
Held: Although the blood stained panga was neither examined for blood
grouping nor compared with that of the deceased, it was the first
appellant who, when asked where the murder weapon was, showed the
search party where he had hidden the panga.  There was ample evidence
to show that the cut wounds on the deceased were inflicted by the panga.
Even without the appellant's confessions, the circumstantial evidence
sufficiently connected the panga with the offence.
The learned trial Judge correctly directed himself to the law relating to
circumstantial evidence as laid out in Simon Musoke Vs. R (1958) E.A 715.
His holding that the discovery of the panga, gun and ammunition was
sufficient to prove that the gun was robbed from the deceased is therefore
unassailable, and thus was very strong circumstantial evidence against
the first appellant to support the conviction for robbery and even for murder
had it been charged as a separate count.
Regarding the confessions, the statements gave details of the plan to kill
the deceased and the motive for killing.  Both objectives were achieved
by killing the deceased and stilling his gun.  The police officer who
recorded the confessions could not have known all these details because
he was not the investigating officer.  Moreover the alleged assaults and
torture took place at the time of the appellant's arrest and the appellants
did not claimed that the torture had induced them to make or sign the
confessions.  The confessions were therefore made voluntarily and were
rightly admitted in evidence.
The learned trial Judge correctly directed himself and the assessors along
the principles relating to repudiated or retracted confessions as was
summarized in the case of Tuwamoi Vs. Uganda [1967] EA 84.  The
confessions of both the first and second appellants were sufficient to
sustain the conviction of robbery against them and the appellants were
accordingly properly convicted of the offence of robbery.  Their appeal
against the conviction is therefore dismissed.
The conviction on the alternative account of murder was irregular as the
appellants had been found guilty on the main count of robbery, although
the error did not occasion any miscarriage of justice since the appellants
were rightly convicted and sentenced on the main count to robbery.
Ratilal Nanchand Sheth Vs. Dr.C.L.K.Ssali.
Affidavits -what amounts to falsity in order to vitiate an affidavit.
Held: It is not in dispute that inconsistencies in affidavits however minor
cannot be ignored since a sworn affidavit is not a document to be treated
lightly.  In the instant case however, the inconsistency is so innocent,
frivolous and not so serious so as to amount to a spurious and deceitful
statement.  It does not therefore vitiate the affidavit and accordingly the
objection is overruled.
The first respondent could not move the A.G. Commissioner of the
Registration since the first respondent is not the registered Proprietor of
the property caveated.  Consequently the notice issued by the Ag.
Commissioner to the applicant had no legal basis and consequence.
The applicant has no protectable interest, proprietary or compensatory
and therefore had no right to caveat property in which he had no interest.
Since this application is based on no interest at all, it is accordingly
dismissed.
Steven Mugume & Fred Mutumba Vs. Uganda.
Procedure followed at locus in quo -whether irregularities in
procedure at locus in quo vitiated the trial.
Held: It cannot be said that no miscarriage of justice could have occurred
when the appellants were convicted of simple robbery.  It was most
important that witnesses give their evidence regularly in open court,
wherever it is constituted, for all to hear and see, that witnesses are
cross-examined and tested and that no suspicion is encouraged that the
judge favoured one side or the other by listening to stories off record.
To take into account information off record is to invite evil insinuations
against the Bench, the effect of which is often very difficult to refute.
Under the circumstances, the appeals are allowed to the extent that the
convictions are quashed, sentences set aside.  A retrial  before another
Judge and different assessors on the charge of simple robbery c/s 273
and 273(1)(b) is ordered.
Mukasa Deogratuis Vs. Uganda.
Child of tender years - admissibility - whether evidence of child
tender years validly admitted u/s 38(3) Trial on indictments
decree.
Public document-birth certificate-whether birth certificate was a Public
document as per S.72 (a) (ii) and (iii) Evidence Act and did not require
the author to prove in court-whether age of complainant was proved to be
below 18 years.
Conduct of accused immediately after the act he is accused of - whether
relevant.
Held: The complaint's evidence was properly under S.38 (3) Trial on
Indictments Decree because though the witness was a child of tender
years, the section allows admission of the witness's testimony as long as
the witness through the conduct of a voir dire shows court that she is of
sufficient intelligence to justify the reception of her evidence.  The court
record showed that the learned trial Judge conducted a voir dire and came
to the conclusion that though the complainant did not understand the
nature of an oath she had sufficient intelligence to justify the reception of
her testimony.
The age of the complainant though some witnesses said that she was
thirteen and others eleven at the date of the alleged defilement, there was
no materials contradiction since they were all agreed that the complainant
was below 18 years at the time she was defiled. (The Supreme Court did
not impeach the finding of the trial Judge that a birth certificate was a
public document and therefore did not require its author to attend court to
prove it).
The accused's beating the prosecution witness who confronted him
whishing to find out the truth about the allegation that the accused had
defiled the complainant was evidence of guilt.  It is trite law that the
conduct of an accused person.  Subsequent to the offence may be taken
against him in considering his guilt or otherwise of that offence.
The offence committed carried a maximum death sentence, therefore the
sentence of 14 years imprisonment was not manifestly excessive, nor was
it improper or based on wrong principles.
Appeal dismissed.
Sentence of 14 years confirmed.
Uganda Vs. Oloya David.
Evidence of a complainant in a sexual offence whether evidence
was well corroborated to warrant a conviction of rape.
Held: The injuries found on the victim were inconsistent with a consented
sexual intercourse as alleged by the accused.  Furthermore, according to
PW3, she met the victim coming from the direction of the alarm and she
was crying.  That evidence of disposition by the victim was evidence of her
consistency as to her lack of consent to the sexual intercourse.
Although there was no corroboration to the testimony of sexual
intercourse.  Accordingly, the accused is found to have had unlawful
sexual intercourse with the victim without her consent.  He is therefore
found guilty as charged and convicted accordingly.
Uganda Vs. Francis Ssengendo.
Evidence of a complainant in a sexual offence -whether her
evidence was well corroborated to justify a corruption of defilement.
Held: There was no dispute that the complainant was under 18 years. She
told court that she was 14 years.  Therefore she was 12 years at the time
when she was defiled.  The medical evidence corroborated her statement.
The prosecution has therefore proved beyond reasonable doubt that the
complainant was under 18 years.
According to the complainant PW3 the accused chased her, caught her,
pushed her down and squeezed her neck to prevent her from making an
alarm.  He inserted his penis into her vagina and had intercourse with her
for about 10 minutes.  This piece of evidence was not challenged in cross-
examination.  It is conclusive evidence that there was penetration which
for the purpose of the offence of defilement is required to be proved.
The medical report corroborated PW3's evidence on the fact of her
defilement.  The prosecution has thus proved the act of defilement beyond
reasonable doubt.
As to whether PW3 correctly identified the accused as the person who
defiled her, there was sufficient day light to enable correct identification.
Secondly, PW3 told court that she knew the accused by appearance.
Pw3's apparently accurate description of the accused to Sserunkuuma,
secretary for finance RC. 1 Namulanda confirms that she correctly
identified the accused because it was after her description that PW4 and
one katende went to the home of PW6 and had the accused arrested.
The prosecution has therefore proved beyond reasonable doubt that the
accused defiled PW3.  Accordingly the accused is found guilty of the
offence of defilement and is convicted as charged.
Uganda Vs. Happy Godfrey Willy Asiimwe.
Dying declaration of the deceased whether there was enough
evidence to corroborate to justify a conviction of murder.
Held: From the medical evidence and the evidence of PW2, PW3 and
PW5 who saw the body of the deceased and buried him the prosecution
has proved beyond reasonable doubt that the deceased is dead.
As to whether the deceased died as a result of malice aforethought; it
should be noted that malice aforethought could be inferred from the nature
of the weapon used and how it was used and the part of the body aimed
at.  From the medical evidence on record, it was stated that a sharp
instrument caused the cut on the right neck of the deceased.  Since the
neck is a vulnerable part of the body, the assailant must have intended to
cause death.
On whether or not the death was unlawful, it is settled law in our criminal
law that every homicide case is unlawful unless it was accidental or
excusable.  In this case it was not shown anywhere that death was
caused by accident or was excusable.
It is generally very unsafe to base a conviction solely on the dying
declaration of a deceased person made in the absence of the accused of
the accused and not subject to cross-examination unless there is
satisfactory corroboration.  Considering the fact that the prosecution is
solely relying on the dying declaration made by the deceased around
4.00am, there is no doubt that there was a possibility of mistaken identity
of his assailant.  This fortified by the inconsistencies and discrepancies
in the prosecution evidence, which go to support the alibi.  Considering
the whole evidence on record, the prosecution failed to negative the alibi
raised by the accused.  The defense of self-defense was also not
negative by the prosecution.  Accordingly, the accused is therefore not
found guilty of murder C/s 183 and 184 Penal Code Act and is therefore
acquitted.
In re Gurdas Ram Desor.
Documentary evidence -uncertified photocopies of probate and will
whether have probative value.
Held: Failure by the applicant to have the alleged will and grant of probate
certified, as true copies of the original rendered the documents of no
probative value and the application on that ground would fail.
Further s.233(1) (d) which provides that probate may be annulled when
it has become useless and inoperative was not applicable to the
situation because in the case instant the executrix had already obtained
the grant of probate before her demise.  This therefore meant that upon
her demise the grant was part and parcel of her estate administrable by
personal representative.  Annulling the probate at that point would render
the testator intestate, which was untenable in law as it amounted to
disrespecting the will of the deceased.
Application dismissed.
Godfrey Mwesigwa Vs. Semuliki High School, Bundibugyo.
Expert witness - experience-whether a doctor with 8 years' experience-
was not an expert.
Held: The defendant's driver owed a duty of care to the plaintiff because
he was a fare paying passenger.
When a plaintiff boards a motor vehicle as a fare paying passenger, even
a vehicle not meant ordinarily for carrying passengers, such a plaintiff
does not necessarily consent to being injured.  Therefore the plea of
violent non fit injuria would fail.
The defendant having admitted in their WSD that the driver of the motor
vehicle was theirs, they had the burden of proof to prove that the driver
was not acting in the course of his employment when he caused the
accident.  They had not discharged this burden because they called no
evidence.
A person with only 8 years experience would not qualify to be an expert.
The claim for Ush 30,000/= for money paid to nurses would not be allowed
as it offended public policy because it was not allowed to give money to
nurses for any service in a government hospital.
40% permanent disability for a plaintiff who was right handed but suffered
a broken left arm, which healed completely with some resultant weakness
therein, such assessment was highly exaggerated.  It would have been no
more than 20% and Ush 5 million general damages would be awarded.
The claim for money maintaining two attendants in hospital would be
disallowed because there was no proved requirement for 2 attendants.
Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Herbert Turyakira Vs. Uganda.
Corroboration in sexual offences evidence of child of tender years
offences requires corroboration and whether evidence that
requires corroboration can not be corroborated by other evidence
which in itself requires corroboration.
Burden of proof-weakness of defence case-whether conviction based on
weakness of the accused's case tenable.
Held: The learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in holding that the alleged
victim's evidence had been corroborated by PW2's evidence yet PW2
was a child and therefore her evidence required to be corroborated.
Evidence that requires corroboration cannot be corroborated by evidence,
which also requires corroboration.
It is true that a court can convict on uncorroborated evidence in sexual
offences and on the uncorroborated evidence of a child of tender years,
after court has warned itself of the danger of relying upon such
uncorroborated evidence, if court is satisfied that though the evidence
is uncorroborated, it is truthful.  However in the case instant, the
prosecution witness having contradicted herself in cross-examination as
to the identity of the accused and in absence of an identification parade,
it was clearly unsafe to rely on such evidence to convicted the accused.
The prosecution throughout the trial had the burden to prove beyond
reasonable doubt the guilt of the accused and court would not rely on the
weakness of the defence case.
Appeal allowed.
Betty Tibaleka, Hon.Jaberi Bidandi Ssali, Charles, Gafabusa
Asiimwe Vs. Dr.Vicent Karuhanga.
Burden of proof s.102 evidence Act allegation that the defendant
had failed or refused to tender a true inventory of accounts of the
state - whether burden of proof was on the plaintiff who alleged
that the defendant had failed on refused.
Held: S.233 (1) Succession Act provides that court may revoke the grant
where it is proved that the defendant has willfully and without reasonable
cause omitted to exhibit an inventory or account of the assets and
liabilities of the estate within 6 months.  In the instant case apart from
merely alleging in the plaint that the defendant had breached his statutory
duty as executor by failing to exhibit an inventory of the assets and
liabilities of the estate, the plaintiff had therefore failed to discharge her
burden of proof under S.102 of the Evidence Act that he who alleged must
prove the truth of his allegation.
Revocation of grant is only based on breach of statutory duties as outlined
in S.233 (1)(e) and nothing else.  Breach of fiduciary duties is not ground
for the revocation of a grant.  Therefore the plaintiff's evidence, which
showed that the defendant was no longer visiting the children and therefore
breaching his fiduciary duties an executor, was no basis for the revocation
of the grant.
Case dismissed with costs.
PC Tito Mukisa Vs. Uganda.
Identification evidence -single witness-whether circumstances
existed to help witness clearly identify the accused.
Held: Since it was at night when the incident occurred, the circumstances
for a proper identification of the accused while he pointed a gun at the
deceased as alleged by the prosecution, did not exist.  Therefore the
learned trial judge should have warned himself of the danger of relying on
only one identification witness in such difficult circumstances.
Though, in an indictment for murder, motive for the murder is irrelevant in
law, it is relevant and available if a particular motive to kill made it likely
that an accused in fact did commit the offence.  In the instant case the
prosecution did not show the motive why the appellant would want to kill
the deceased.  Therefore, the appellant's defence of accident was sound.
Appeal allowed, conviction quashed.
Sentence set aside.
Nkwine Jackson Vs. Uganda.
Witness -contradiction in prosecution evidence whether major.
Held: S.8 Penal Code Act provides that a person is not criminally liable
in respect of an offence relating to property if his act or omission is done
in exercise of an honest claim of right.  In the instant case what was at
stake was a dispute over land which dispute could only be settled by a
Civil Court.  Therefore, without the settlement of the issue of ownership
of the land in question, the accused could not be found liable for
malicious damage to property since he claimed that the land was his.
The contradictions between the prosecution witnesses as to what nature
of crops were destroyed by the appellants' cows were not minor and had
to be explained before finding the accused guilty because the
contradictions went to the root as to what garden was destroyed.
Appeal allowed.
Henry Kayondo Vs. Uganda.
Admissibility -advocates client communications s.124 evidence
Act-whether communication was absolutely privileged and not
admissible.
Held: The definition section 15 of the official Secrets Acts regarding what
an official document is, was inclusive and therefore extensive.  This
means the documents relating to the case could not be official documents
as per S.15 of the official Secrets Act.  It was a question of evidence and
this evidence could only be deduced at the trial.  Therefore the learned
trial Chief Magistrate was entitled to overrule the preliminary objection.
An alternate charge need not be minor and cognate.
The communication between Advocate and client is absolutely privileged
as per S.124 Evidence Act.  However where an offence is suspected to
having been committed the communication is no longer privileged.
There was no provision in law providing for preliminary objection as to
whether a charge disclosed an offence or not.  Therefore, the preliminary
objection raised by the appellant was misconceived.
Appeal dismissed.
Sheik Katerega & anor Vs. UEB
Burdens of proof course of employment -whether plaintiff has the
burden to prove that defendants servant was acting in the course
of his employment.
Held: In an action found in negligence particulars thereof must be given of
the alleged negligence, showing in what respects the defendant was
negligent.  Though in the instant case the pleadings did not follow the
conventional itemization of the particulars, nevertheless, the pleadings
out particulars, nevertheless, the pleadings set out clearly what the
plaintiffs were alleging against the defendant.
He who affirms must prove the truth of his affirmations.  Since the
plaintiffs alleged that Lugolobi was acting in the course of his employment,
it was incumbent upon them to prove the allegation.  Yet the plaintiffs did
not even produce Lugolobi as a witness to testify as to whether he was
acting on his own frolic or not.
To make an employer liable for the act of a person alleged to his servant
the act must be one of the class of acts which the person was authorized
or employed to do, even if the act is done wrongly or negligently or
wantonly.  In the instant case it was not sufficient to show court that
Lugolobi was an employee of UEB but it was incumbent upon the
plaintiff's to show that the class of duties of the servant of the defendant
were the duties the doing of which resulted from the tortuous damage to
the plaintiffs.
Manasseh Kamugisha Vs. Uganda Prefabricated Building
Industry.
Documentary-exclusion there of by oral evidence whether oral
evidence is admissible to contradict the terms of a contract in
writing.
Held: The law is that a written contract cannot be varied by a verbal
agreement of the parties.  However, where a party by his voluntary
concession leads the other party on the faith of that concession to the
detriment of the other party.  In the instant case, when the plaintiff
subsequently conceded to terms outside the prior written agreement and
led the bank and the defendant to act on the concession, the plaintiff was
estopped from retracting there from.  Therefore the defendant was not in
breach of contract.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Eliot Mugizi Vs. Uganda.
Documentary evidence -opinion as to handwriting s.45 of the
evidence Act -whether a document authored by a doctor may not
tendered in evidence by another doctor because he is not
acquainted with the author's signature.
Held: S.45 of the Evidence Act provides that evidence of a witness
acquainted with the handwriting and signature of the author of a document
is admissible.  In the instant case the trial magistrate erred when he allowed
the testimony of a doctor to testify on the medical notes prepared by
another doctor not in court without court having satisfied itself that the
witness was acquainted with the handwriting or signature of the author of
the medical notes.
However, the witnesses who testified against the accused satisfied court
that the accused was guilty of the assault, although there was no evidence to
establish the gravity of the injury.  Therefore grievous harm had not been
proved but common assault was proved
appeal allowed in part, and sentence reduced from 12 to 6 months
imprisonment.
HMB Kayondo Vs. Somani Amirali
Admissions - proof - whether admitted facts heed not be proved.
Held: It is a rule of pleading that an averment not expressly or implicitly
traversed is deemed to have been admitted.  It is a rule of evidence that a
fact admitted need not be proved.  The plaintiff in Para 5 of the pliant had
pleaded that he gave notice of dishonour to the defendant.  The defendant
in his WDS did not traverse either explicitly or implicitly that plea.
Therefore the defendant had admitted that the plaintiff gave him notice of
dishonour of the cheque as required by S.48, the Bills of Exchange Act.
A company duly registered is a legal entity distinct from the subscribers or
those who formed it.  This is the rule of incorporation.  Therefore the
dishonoured cheques on the account of Uganda Consumer Suppliers Ltd
belonged to the Company.  However the defendant being managing director
thereof would not be allowed to use incorporation as a cloak for fraud.
Therefore, the veil of incorporation would be lifted by court so that the
defendant is found personally liable for the dishonoured bills.
S.30(1) Bills of Exchange Act provides that every party whose signature
appears on a bill is a prima facie deemed to have become a party thereto
for value.  Since the defendant admitted having drawn the cheques, the
burden of proof lay on him to prove that the plaintiff has passed no
consideration to the defendant to the defendant for the cheques.
The defendant fail in this.
Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Walakira Lawrence Vs. Uganda.
Unsworn statement veracity - whether unsown statement is no
evidence.
Held: There was no evidence that the accused ever handed the money
meant to purchase the beer for sale.  The complainant withdrew it himself
from his bank and paid to purchase the beer.  Therefore the conviction was
not supported by evidence.
It is the constitutional right of an accused person to make an unsworn
statement and this should not lead the accused person to be penalized.
Appeal allowed.
Conviction quashed and appellant released.
Mafujja Leus Vs. Uganda
Witness -cross examination -whether failure to cross examine
the witness means that the accused did not dispute the testimony
of witness.
Held: Where a person to avail himself of an opportunity to cross-examine a
witness testifying against him on the essential particulars of the evidence
adduced, it must follow that that person against whom testimony has been
given believes the testimony.  Therefore, in the instant case, even if the
extra judicial statement was excluded, sufficient evidence a bound on which
the trial Magistrate correctly found a conviction.
A sentence of 5 years for a conviction of embezzlement was not excessive
and harsh.
Appeal dismissed.
Christopher Lubaale Vs. Uganda.
Accomplice evidence -corroboration-whether a legal or practical
requirement.
Held: Where an arrest had been made or authorized according to S.68
MCA, police is at liberty to search the place of dwelling or business of the
arrested person or person authorized to be arrested, it police has reason to
believe that material evidence may be obtained threat.  In the instant case,
the appellant's dwelling house was searched after the arrest.  Therefore, the
search did not require a warrant.
The requirement for corroboration for accomplice evidence is requirement
of prudence not one of law.  However in the instant case corroboration was
found in the fact that property recently stolen was found at the home of the
appellant.
Where a person is found in possession of property recently stolen, that
person may be either a thief or may be guilty of receiving stolen property.
In the instant case, property stolen on 24th March 1993 was found at the
appellant's home on 27th March 1993.  the accused's explanation was not
satisfactory to the trial court and the court was entitled to convict the
accused of the theft.
Waiswa Richard & 3 Ors Vs. Uganda
The sentence of 18 months was not excessive.
Expert opinion -medical evidence - whether a medical officers is
qualified to examined and testify.
Held: Although appellant number one did not physically assault the
complainant, he had a common intention with the other 3 to unlawfully
assault the complainant and his intention was readily inferable from his
conduct.  There was no need to prove express agreement between him and
his co-accused.
Although the phrase medical officer is not well known in the medical
profession, considering the training of the witness and his experience of 5
years practice, he was a witness equivalent to a medical assistant and thus
qualified to examine the victims in this single case of assault. The trial court
was correct in basing her finding the evidence of the medical officer.
The sentencing 2 months imprisonment was not excessive.
Appellant number four did not participate in the assault as there was no
such evidence.
Appeal dismissed for appellants number one, two or three.
Uganda Vs. Richard Mutumba.
Admissibility - evidence in another case whether wrongly admitted-
whether therefore trial a nullity.
Burden of proof - whether accused had the burden to produce evidence of
the creditors he alleged paid.
Circumstantial evidence-co-existing circumstances whether appellant
correctly convicted on circumstantial evidence.
Held:The admission of evidence of a witness not before court is wrong in law
because it deprives the opposite party the opportunity to cross examine the
witness on the evidence and to test her credibility.  In the instant case the
trial court misdirected itself when it admitted evidence of a witness from a
previous trial.
However, the wrong admission of evidence dos not necessarily render the
trial a nullity unless the admitted evidence was the foundation of the
conviction.  In the instant case the evidence wrongly admitted was
inconsequential in the finding by court of the appellant's guilt.
Where a person is found not guilty of forgery, it does not ipso facto mean
that therefore he is not guilty of uttering a false document.  In the present
case the trial court found that though the chepues were forged there was no
evidence that the cheques were forged by the appellant.  Court was still
entitled to find whether it was the appellant guilty of uttering the forged
cheques.
A person utters a false document when he tenders the same for payment
knowing it to be forged or false and with intent to defraud.  In the present
case the issue was whether the appellant knew that the cheques were
forged and whether he uttered them with intent to defraud.The trial court held
that the appellant must have known that the cheques were forged since he
was an accounts clerk in the Ministry of Internal Affairs and must know
about the process of clearing cheques.  This finding was based on
conjecture and hypothesis.  Therefore, the trial court misdirected itself on
finding was based on conjecture and hypothesis.  Therefore, the trial court
misdirected itself on finding that the appellant knew that the cheques were
forgery as this circumstantial evidence co-existed with other evidence on
record that showed that the cheques were given to the appellant by third
party.
Certain exceptions apart, the burden of proof in criminal proceedings is
thought out on the prosecution.  Therefore, the learned trial Chief Magistrate
misdirected himself when he held that the accused had the burden to prove
that the money was withdrawn to pay the said third party's creditors.
Appeal allowed. Conviction set aside.
Uganda Vs. Tereza Onziru & another.
Dying declaration -corroborated - whether the fleeing of the accused
from the village corroborated the dying declaration.
Held: It is unsafe to convict on uncorroborated dying declaration.  In the
instant case by fleeing from the home where the deceased met his death,
the two accused by that act, corroborated the dying declaration that
pointed out the onus two accused as the assailants of the deceased.
Where two or more persons jointly assail a person, causing his death and
there is no evidence as to who dealt the death blow, prosecution must first
establish existence of a common intention before the accused are jointly
convicted of the murder.  In the instant case there was no evidence of the
existence of common intention between the two accused to murder the
deceased.  Therefore, each individual would be liable individually for her
respective contribution in the assault of the deceased.
The defence of defending is not available where the accused uses force
unproportional to the attack on the person being defended.  In the instant
case A2 used a knife and stabbed the accused in the back allegedly in
defence of her sister who had only been struck with a piece of wood by
the deceased.  Certainly the stabbing was exceedingly unproportional to
the act of the deceased and therefore the defence of defending a person
was not available to A2, who had been accurately identified by the deceased
in his dying declaration.
Use of a deadly weapon per se does not automatically attract inference of
malice aforethought.  In the instant case only one death blow was struck,
though with a deadly-weapon-a knife.  Since there was evidence of a fight
prior to the death blow, malice aforethought had not been proved and
therefore the accused was guilty of manslaughter c/s 182 Penal Code Act.
Accused A2 convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 5 years
imprisonment. A1 acquitted.
Abbey Semakula Vs. Eldad R. Rubarenzya.
Affidavit disappearance there in - whether affidavit of service defective where
the deponent swears in an affidavit dated 23/194 that he effected service on
Held: The allegation that the respective Commissioners of Oaths did not have
have valid practicing certificates at the time they commissioned the affidavits,
was not substantiated or proved either by an affidavit of counsel alleging the
same or by any other evidence.  Therefore, the learned Chief Magistrate was
correct in law in not considering the same.
Costs are never taken into account in computing the sum in a decree.
Therefore since the decretal award did not exceed Ush 5,000,000/= the
learned Chief Magistrate did not exceed his jurisdiction.
The discrepancies in the affidavits of service as to their dates in which it
appeared that the dates of deponing preceded the dates of service were
clearly typographical errors, which could be ignored.  Therefore this did not
render the affidavits incurably defective.
However, the ambiguities and discrepancies in the process servers' affidavits
of service and reply tended to show that there was no effective service and
that is why the defendant did not appear to defend the suit.
Appeal allowed.
Uganda Vs. Mukalazi Michael
Contradictions I prosecution evidence whether fatal.
Held: By way of common sense by her appearance it was obvious that
complainant was a tiny little girdle very far below the age of 18.  the fact was
not challenged by the defence.  Therefore, this coupled by medical evidence
as to the victim's age was proof that the victim was below the age of 18.
Major contradictions in prosecution evidence should be resolved in favor of
the accused.  In the instant case the contradictions in the prosecution
evidence were minor and would be disregarded.
Accused convicted as charged.
Herbal International & others Vs. Ibrahim Alarakhia.
Oral evidence - whether counsel may adduce oral evidence in
addition to evidence by affidavits of his clients.
Uganda Vs. Ocero George.
Confession - repudiated confession -whether must invariable by
corroborated.
Held: While court must cautiously deal with confession that is repudiated in
this case the confession was detailed enough in material particulars and
corroborated the victim's unsworn evidence that it is the accused who
defiled her.
S.11 Penal Code presumes everybody sane and the accused who sets up
the defence of insanity must rebut the presumption.  In the instant case, the
accused could not be believed when he alleged that he had had a mental
blackout.
The accused had no shown court that the alleged insanity was due to
intoxication as per S.13(2)(6) Penal Code.  Therefore the defense of
intoxication was not available.  Therefore the defense of intoxication was not
available.  S.13(4) of the Penal Code provides that an accused may set up
a defense of intoxication contending that due to intoxication he could not
form the necessary intent to commit the offence.  In the instant defilement
as an offence did not require mens rea for its commission.
Accused convicted as charged.
Prince J.D.C.Mpuga Rukidi Vs. Prince Solomon Iguru & others.
Will - unattested will-whether valid u/s66 Evidence Act.
Admissibility -secondary evidence- whether photocopy was validly
admitted when no evidence of comparison with the original was
led.
Held: The learned trial Judge's admission in evidence of the photocopied
Will could not be impeached because there was evidence before court that
the original will was lost.  Secondly, the will was photocopied which is the
kind of mechanical method that insures accuracy of the copy; there was
evidence that tended to prove that the signature on the will was that of the
testator and the contents of the Will had not been seriously challenged by
the adverse party.
S.13(2) (b) Interpretation Decree provides that when any enactment repeals
another, unless a contrary intention appears, the repeal does not affect
anything previously duly done in pursuance of the repealed enactment.
Therefore when the late King named the Will unattested, such a mode of
making Wills was permissible under S.50(2) Succession Act which
provision allowed Africans to make unattested Wills.  Though the exemption
was repealed by Decree 22/72 Succession Act (Amendment) Decree the
repeal did not affect the act already performed by the late King, the act of
nominating the respondent by a Will unattested.
Moreover, even if the document nominating the respondent as heir was to
be found wanting as a Will, the document could be relied upon as evidence
of nomination of the respondent as heir because paragraph 2 schedule 3 of
the 1962 Constitution under which the nomination was done did not provide
any specific mode by which nominations of successors to the throne of
Bunyoro Kitara could be made.
O.13 r 3 gives discretion to court to frame issues from among or all the
allegations made on oath, allegations made in the pleadings and contents
of documents from the parties.  This rule does not mean that when court is
framing the issues it should look at all the allegations.  It is own discretion
to choose from among the allegations or all of them.  This further means
that court may frame the issues at any stage of the proceedings before
judgment.  Therefore, the learned trial Judge in framing only one issued did
not err since he had the discretion to do and in his opinion, it was enough
to decide whether or not the respondent was qualified to be heir to the
throne of Bunyoro Kitara.  And once this was answered in the affirmative
there was no further need to decided on the other allegations.
S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act provides that the court has the discretion in
determining who may be awarded costs though the costs should follow the
the event.  The instant case involved members of the same family, a family
whose importance went beyond its borders.  Therefore, for the sake of
peace and harmony in the family and community of the Kingdom, to assist
in the process of reconciliation, no costs should have been awarded!
The order awarding costs would be set aside.
The granting of a declaration is a discretionary remedy and the court should
not easily grant a declaration that would serve no useful purpose or seriously
prejudice the security of the state or affect the confidence between the
parties. Had the appellant succeeded, the court would have had to consider
whether to grant the declaration or not in view of the possible repercussions.
Appeal, save as to costs, dismissed.
Mparo Ltd Vs. Attorney General
Valuation report by expert - whether the bills therein not special
damages proved because the figures were mere guess work.
Held: The defendant's prayer to dismiss the plaintiff's suit was not tenable
because liability had already been admitted as per O.11 r6.
Since counsel for the defendant did not cross examine the expert witness
as to the valuation report made by him the witness evidence stood
unchallenged and counsel for the defendant was precluded from impeaching
the evidence from the bar.  The witness's evidence had been accepted by
court as the truth.
Any estimate expertly arrived at cannot be said to be an act of guesswork
as long as the witness expertise is not denied.  Therefore, the evidence as
to the estimates of the value of repairs was a valid estimate and would be
awarded as special damages.
Special damages may be expenditure to be incurred or expenditure already
incurred.  Therefore, even if the plaintiff had not expended the sum claimed
as special damages it was proved as the sum expendable in effecting the
repairs which liability the defendant had admitted.
Interest is awarded by court at its discretion.  In commercial transactions
the rationale is to compensate the litigant for what he would probably earn
if his money were not withheld, like in this case.  Therefore interest would be
awarded on rent arrears and costs of repairs at 22% p.a.
Suit allowed.
Uganda Vs. Police Constable Alfred Ogwang.
Lies by accused - adverse inference - whether adverse inference
may be formed against the accused.
Burden of proof-witnesses-whether prosecution deliberately avoided
tendering some witnesses for cross-examination by the accused-whether
therefore adverse inference may be formed against the prosecution-whether
it was the accused who had the burden of proof to call the witnesses.
Held: Infringement of S.78 TID amounts to adducing evidence to the
evidence already stated in the summary of facts.  In the instant case the
summary of evidence warned the accused that a gun would be tendered in
evidence and the gun was actually tendered in evidence albeit the number
thereof was different.  Therefore this did not amount to new evidence as
such as to mean that S.78 TID had been infringed upon.
The weird story of the accused in defense was indicating of a person who
only wanted to derail the course of justice.  It was clear that it is the
accused who had shot and killed all the deceased.
The prosecution had discretion in choosing what witnesses to bring to prove
its case.  Since the accused wished to rely on the defense of insanity by
intoxication it was a incumbent upon him to prove so.
the accused would not rely on the non-production of particular witnesses by
the prosecution since this by itself was no evidence of a motive deliberate to
hide the truth from the court.
According to the evidence from the witnesses the accused was not so drunk
as not to know what he was doing.  Since the accused was annoyed and
yet was able to go back to the barracks, to collect his gun and go and shoot
the deceased persons and then return to the barracks, it was not reasonable
suppose that the accused was so drunk that he did not know what he was
to doing.  Therefore had failed to rebut the presumption that he intended the
consequences of his acts.
The defense of provocation would be rejected because the accused had
more than sufficient time to cool down and moreover what happened, his
denial of entry into some canteen could not mount to provocation.
Accused convicted as charged.
Uganda Vs. Stephen Mulengera
Identification evidence - whether identification of accused sufficient
whether identification parade necessary.
Held: It is not a requirement to establish sexual intercourse that the hymen
must be proved ruptured.  Any slight penetration is sufficient to establish
intercourse.  In the instant case the edematous vagina was proof of
forcible penile entry therein could not point to the accused as the culprit in
the defilement.
The complainant at the trial told court that she did not report the defilement
to her aunt PW2 and yet PW2 told court that the defendant had told her that
it was the accused who had defiled her.  These contradictions show that the
person who defiled the complainant was not properly identified. Since the
complainant, being a child of tender years her evidence was not on oath and
which evidence was not corroborated as required by S.38(3) TID and S.12
Oaths Act, the prosecution failed to prove their case.
Not guilty as charged.
Wamala William Vs. Uganda
Corroboration -whether it is necessary to corroborate evidence
given by relatives.
Held: The trial judge was of the view that the Panga, which loomed
large in the testimony of the key eye witness could have been used.
So, his theory as to the use of the Panga was not far fetched as to
appear fanciful.  Therefore conviction was not based on fanciful
theories or attractive reasoning but on evidence adduced before him.
A person who inflicts a heavy blow on another person causing
grievous harm has intention to kill and therefore since the appellant
inflicted upon the deceased to a deep cut he intended to kill him.
The fact that all witnesses where relatives did not call for the
corroboration of their evidence.
Bogere Patrick Vs. Wanzira Joshua.
Onus of proving lack of reasonable and probable cause and
malicious prosecution - whether malice could be imputed.
Held: Since the prosecution acted upon the facts as narrated by the
defendant, there had been reasonable and probable cause to have set
the law in motion.
Sine the defendant did not know the plaintiff till his arrest malice could
not be impute upon the defendant.  Case considered: Herniman Vs.
Smith (1939) 1 AER 1.
Andrea Isingoma Vs. Uganda.
Admission of evidence of child tender years - whether fatal to the
trial.
Held: The admission of the evidence of the child of tender years was
irregular since the trial judge held neither a voui dire nor warned himself
but in the light of other corroborative evidence on record this
irregularity was not fatal.
The admission of the post mortem report from a Doctor other than the
one who performed it was not fatal since the appellant was
represented and his counsel cross-examine the Doctor.
Common intent in the murder of the deceased was established by the
confession of the appellant implicating the co-accused in the murder
and their being found together at a home eating from which home
the stolen bicycle and blood stained clothes were found.
The vouire dire had proved that the confession was voluntary and
correctly admitted and corroborating it was not lawful necessary,
though there was ample evidence to corroborate it.
Where the appellant was found in possession of recently stolen
property belonging to the deceased, it was corroborative of the fact
that the appellant was guilty of the murder of the deceased.
Alitabala Eria Vs. Kakaire Vincent
Documentary evidence - proof of hand writing by person other
than expart or person acquainted with the hand writing in question
whether trial court could challenge the will on its won motion -
whether the will had been proved whether legatee can claim under
an unproved will.
Held: The respondent/legatee could not claim under a will that had not
been granted probate.
The trial Magistrate directed himself correctly when he sought to
challenge the propriety of the will on his own motion since the parties
were unrepresented but he erred in basing his finding solely on
independent opinion of a handwriting expert or a person acquainted
with the handwriting in question.
To be an attesting witness one must subscribe his signature on the
will and merely not to se the will be executed and since two so called
attesting witnesses could not even identify the will in question, the
will had not been proved.
Bamweyana Lulenti Vs. Segujja Hamisi
Documentary evidence -proving document by proof of signature.
Held: The defendant was party to agreement since he acknowledge
that the signature thereon was his.
The defendant had failed to persuade court to the view that he was
coerced into signing the agreement because the agreement was
signed in December 1987 and did not report to the authorities that he
was coerced fact into signing an agreement nor did he mention this
fact in his affidavit while applying for leave to appear and defend.
The singing of a contractual document implied consent, therefore the
defendant was bound by it since he had failed to prove that his signing
was under a misapprehension as to the essential nature of the
document.
Kanalusasi George Vs. Uganda
Conviction based on speculation and conjecture and on evidence
adduced - whether such conviction may stand.
Held: The admission by the appellant of killing the deceased did not
weaken his plea of not guilty and therefore the prosecution still had to
discharge its burden to prove that the killing was with malice
aforethought.
Since the prosecution did not adduce evidence to contradict the
appellant's defence of self-defence the appellant's account should have
been accepted.
Donozio Kiiza Vs. Uganda.
Wrong date of the incident given - whether such discrepancy
material.
Held: The inconsistency in the date of the incident was not of serious
consequence since it did not prejudice the appellant in his defence.
That taking into account that the identification circumstances were
poor the trial judge erred in relying on such a single, identification
witness.
The learned trial judge erred is not addressing himself to the need to
establish a common intention between the appellant and the gang in
which he was seen.
Kalyowa Moses & 3 others Vs. Uganda.
Circumstantial evidence - whether of sufficient weight  on which
to base conviction recent possession - appellants found in
possession of property recently stolen whether proof that they
had stolen property - confession by co-accused -whether corroborated-
rated - accomplice evidence -how much weight to attach thereto-
sentencing.
Held: The circumstantial evidence that would otherwise implicate the
first appellant as outline by the learned trial judge fell short of
irresistibly pointing to the guilt of the first appellant and to no other
reasonable hypothesis.
A confession by a co-accused can only be used to lend credence and
strength to other evidence already on record against the co-accused
which only falls short by a very narrow margin of the standard of
proof necessary for a conviction.
The admission of the theft of the property by the appellants and the
blaming of the first appellant for the murder amounted to accomplice
evidence which evidence was of the weakest kind and could only be
used to lend assurance to the evidence against the appellant.
It was necessary for the Supreme Court and or legislature to resolve
whether sentence may be passed on more than one counts where
at least one of the counts is a capital conviction.
Nyendwoha Lucy Vs. Nyendwoha Robert & another.
Admission -whether witness's statement was admission of factor
law.
Held: For a husband or wife of an intestate to be disentitled to the
grant on grounds of separation the matrimonial relationship must have
ceased to exist and this does not mere physical separation for one
reason or other as it is with the instant case.
Court acts on two basic principles in deciding to whom to grant letters
of administration namely the interest of the person who is truly entitled
to the grant prevails over other interests and court takes into account
the interests of the beneficiaries.  Since the widow was entitled to 15%
comparatively greatest proportion of the estate and she had the
children of the intestate to care for as the beneficiary grant of the
letters should go to her.
Uganda Vs. Kiiza Ephraim & another
Prima facie case - where at the close of the prosecution case the
evidence hangs on a mere case made out.
Held: A submission of no case to answer may be properly upheld
where the evidence as presented to court, any reasonable court cannot
call upon the accused to stand defence.
A Prima facie case cannot be made out where at the close of the
prosecution case evidence hangs on a mere possibility, or is
uncoordinated irreconcilable and full of violent contradictions.
Uganda Vs. Kasujja Emmanuel
Conflicts in the evidence of the prosecution - whether minor and
negligible.
Held: Accused was identified properly by the prosecution witness
because there was candle light, the daughter of the deceased shouted
his name and the accused never escaped from the scene of the crime.
The discrepancies within the evidence of the prosecution were minor
and explainable.
The fact that the accused used a fatal implement and the manner he
used it by cutting several times, it left no doubt that he intended to kill
the deceased and this established malice aforethought.
Uganda Vs. Byansi Simpson & another.
Unmarked exhibits police custody - whether admissible.
Held: The admitted evidence contained absolutely nothing to connect
the accused with the offence in the remotest way since no mention is
made of any of them in the summary of evidence.
The exhibits tendered were not marked as required by law and
therefore it was difficult to say whether the exhibits were partly the
stolen goods.
A submission of no case to answer is properly made and upheld
where there is no evidence to prove an essential element of the offence
and or when the evidence adduced has been discredited. In this case
the prosecution evidence was utterly insufficient to place the accused
on their defence.
Boona Majidu Vs. Uganda.
Evidence -contradictions in the case of the prosecutions -whether
minor and negligible.
Held: Inspite of the inconsistencies in the evidence of the prosecution
the witnesses were credible and given the fact that the witnesses were
testifying to facts that had happened more than two years back the
inconsistencies were explainable.  Therefore the prosecution evidence
would be believed.
The trial court must satisfy itself before making a conviction based on
identity that the identification was not erroneous.  The two prosecution
witnesses had known the appellant before and the candle light and
moon light in the kraal helped the prosecution witnesses to identify
the appellant properly.
Specioza Nabasumba Vs. Uganda.
Guilty knowledge -whether refused to accept the keeping of stolen
property in the appellants house and passing it on to another for
custody was evidence of guilty knowledge.
Held: The evidence being wholly circumstantial it did not prove the
charge beyond reasonable doubt since there were other probable
explanations.
Johnson Samson Senseko Kulubya Vs. Uganda Transport
Unseated shareholder's certificate - whether valid evidence of
ownership e.g. shares.
Held: Since by Decree 11/75 Government became trustee to the
assets and liabilities of the UTC which assets and liabilities it vested
in the defendant company, the plaintiff was entitled to compensation
for his shares by the defendant company.
All evidence pointed to the fact that the plaintiff was General Manager
and was regarded as such and was entitled to his terminal benefits in
that capacity.
That since the defendant company had allowed the plaintiff to stay in
the house until payment, terminal benefits, the defendant was now
stopped from evicting him before the payment, terminal benefits.
Uganda Vs. Sulaiman Ndamagye
Whether circumstantial evidence sufficient upon which to base a
conviction for murder.
Held: The facts and the circumstances looked at together are
incompatible with innocence of the accused and irresistibility point to
the causing the deceased's death with malice aforethought.
Wagama Amosi & 2 others Vs. Uganda.
Identification of moonlight - whether identification circumstances
favorable.
Held: Though a conviction can be founded on the dying declaration
courts have almost invariably always insisted on need to corroborate
the dying declaration.  This is more so in the instant case where the
identification circumstances were poor and therefore the deceased
could have been mistaken in his identification.
Business, however multiple could not amount to maim or dangerous
harm and therefore such injury could not be classified as grievous
bodily harm.
It is a settled law that mere presence at the time of the commission
of the crime does not make a person a party to the crime without
participation in some way.
Theft was a minor and cognate offence to robber and therefore an
accused could be convicted thereof when not charged therewith.
Uganda Vs. Paddy Kalenzi
Alibi - whether prosecution disproved it.
Held: Since the victims were arrested at the instigation of the accused
and the allegations made by the accused to the soldiers that the
deceased were guerillas, the  accused was fully aware of the
consequences of such allegations.
It was not necessary that the accused should make a prior arrangement
with the soldiers.  It was enough that the accused had a common
intention with the assailants and the accused's action especially in
point out the deceased to the assailants would help the inference that
the accused had a common intention with the assailants in murdering
or exposing the deceased to the danger of being murdered.
Yeko Mukasa Vs. Attorney General
Hearsay evidence -ordinary course of business-whether statements
made by the driver concerning the cause of the accident should be
admissible.
Held: The driver of a Motor Vehicle is enjoined by law to make a report
of any accident.  In the instant case if the driver made the report to the
police, the defendant could produce it to controvert the allegations of the
plaintiff.  Moreover a fact can be proved by the testimony of a single
witness as it was in this case and in absence of any explanation as to
how and why the accident happened, it must be assumed that the
defendant's motor vehicle was being driven in total disregard of other
road users.
The burden of proving that the plaintiff was negligent and that he
contributed to the accident lies squarely on the defendant.  In the instant
case no such evidence was adduced and there is no other evidence on
which such inference cab be made.
The plaintiff's arm was broken and his chest injured and his permanent
disability assessed at 35%.  Therefore sh. 2 million general damages
would be awarded.
Uganda Vs. Mukasa Deogratius
Public document-whether must be proved in court by evidence.
Held: A birth certificate as per S.72(a) (ii) and (iii) of the Evidence Act is
a public document and therefore it was not necessary to call the
