Assistant Registrar General of Births and Deaths to prove its authenticity
and the authenticity of the document would not be vitiated by the fact
that the document was prepared after the commission of the offence
since the particulars appearing on the document were obtained from the
complainant's hospital of birth.
Intoxication may provide a defence by enabling the accused to prove
temporary insanity or by indicating that the accused was incapable of
forming the intention necessary to constitute the offence.  In the instant
case the accused in his won evidence stated that he was not so drank
as to be incapable of forming the intention necessary to constitute the
offence.
The accused by his conduct admitted the offence when he told PW3
that he was not had been told by PW2 that the accused had defiled the
complainant and yet PW3 being a paternal uncle to the complainant
was rightly concerned.  This coupled with the other evidence on record
proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was guilty as
charged.
Uganda Vs. Kizito Christopher
Corroboration -whether complainant's distress condition was
corroborative of unlawful sexual assault.
Held: There was evidence that the complainant was distressed which
evidence was not challenged.  The distress condition corroborated the
evidence of PW1, the complainant, this is because in sexual offences
the distressed condition of the complainant is capable of amounting to
corroboration of the complainant's evidence.  This, couple with the other
evidence on record, and the fact that the defendant's alibi was rejected,
shows that the prosecution had proved the case against the accused
beyond reasonable doubt.
Musisi Dirisa & 3 others Vs. Sietico (u) Ltd.
Burden of proof -shifting the evidential burden of proof - whether
burden of proof and shifted to the defendant.
Expert opinion-whether doctor's opinion may be rejected for being
superficial.
Held: The evidence burden does not shift to the defendant unless there
is cogent and credible evidence produced by the plaintiff on the issue.
In this case the mere claim that the plaintiffs were fare paying passengers
who sustained injuries due to the defendant's negligence, did not
accession the shifting of the evidential burden to the defendant so as to
necessitate her to produce the police accident reports to disprove the
testimony of the plaintiffs.
The trial judge was right in holding that the plaintiffs had abandoned their
pleading in as far as the particulars to injuries were concerned because
there different testimonies at the trial were at variance with their pleading
in the plaint.  This offended against O.6 r6 CPR as it constituted a
departure.
The learned trial judge was correct to have rejected the evidence of the
expert doctor who testified for the plaintiffs because the doctor had only
made a casual examination of the appellants but not a detailed medical
examination.  A doctor or any expert witness must provide a scientific
base for his opinion before his findings can be accepted by court.  This
scientific base was lacking.  The appeal would be dismissed.
Uganda Commercial Bank Vs. Highway Car Dealers Ltd
Admissions s.56 Evidence Act - pleading O.8 r3 - whether the
accident abstract report was admitted by the defendant when it
did not deny it in it's written statement of defence.
Summary
The Plaintiff Bank sued the defendant in negligence claiming the
replacement value of its motor vehicle.  The plaintiff attached the police
accident abstract report but did not refer to it in its pleadings.  The
defendant in its Written Statement Defense did not deny the contents of
the police abstract report.  When the case came up for hearing counsel
for the plaintiff Mr. Angeret applied to put in the police accident abstract
report contending the defendant had admitted the same since it had not
denied it.
Held: O.8 r3 provides that a pleading that does not deny allegations of
fact specifically or by necessary implication is taken to have admitted
these allegations of fact.  However since the plaintiff merely annexed the
documents to the plaint but did not refer to them, then the defendant was
not obliged to specifically deny issues of fact that were not pleaded.
G.M Combined Ltd Vs. Uganda Development Bank & 4 ors.
Affidavit - submission from the bar - whether may negate affidavit
evidence on oath.
Held: It is true that submission from the bar may not negate what is stated
on oath.  Nevertheless the allegation by Professor Sempebwa to the effect
that his affidavit contained a typographical omission would be believed
because, it was the only logical conclusion when the whole of his affidavit
is read together with the evidence that court never found any record where
Sempebwa had acted for the plaintiff company.
The drawing of an agreement for a given set of parties by an advocate
does not necessarily turn the advocate into a witness in a subsequent
dispute, because, it is the parties to the agreement that are the most
relevant witness since it is them hat know what they agreed upon and
why.  Therefore the fact that Sempebwa may have drawn an agreement of
sale of some properties of the plaintiff, did not necessarily turn him into a
witness and therefore would not be disqualified under r8 of the Advocates
(Professional Conduction) Regulations in the present matter.
A party seeking to disqualify an advocate under r.3 of the Advocates
(Professional Conduct) Regulations on grounds that the said advocate is
seized with knowledge of some fact prejudicial to his former client which
facts came to his knowledge by virtue of him having acted for his former
client, must show which specific facts are feared that might be used to
the prejudice of the party seeking the disqualification of the advocate.
In this the applicant advocate had failed and therefore no disqualification
of the said advocates would be ordered.  Application dismissed.
Fred Kainamura & ors Vs. Attorney General & ors.
Assault - medical evidence -whether every assault must be proved
by medical evidence.
Held: S.23 of the Criminal Procedure Code empowers police to arrest
suspects without a warrant where the police upon reasonable grounds
suspect a parson to have committed a cognizable offence.  In the instant
case the police arrested the plaintiffs on mere suspicion without
reasonable grounds.  Therefore, the arrest was unlawful.
The power of police to detain at their police station a person suspected of
commission of a cognizable offence for 24 hours before being taken to
court is confined to persons who are arrested on reasonable and probable
cause, it does not cover persons arrested by police without reasonable
cause as it was in this case.  Therefore the detention of the plaintiffs at
the various police stations before taking them to court was unlawful.
A detention on court's order is not unlawful.  Therefore, the period of five
months of remand of the plaintiffs by court was not unlawful detention.
It is not a requirement of the law that every allegation of assault must be
proved by medical evidence.  In the instant case the plaintiffs had amply
proved that they were assaulted and tortured while in police detention.
Ush 150,000/= would be advanced as general damages for false arrest,
detention and assault to each of the plaintiffs.
The first plaintiff was detained in police cells for 10 days since he claimed
to have lost Ush 500,000/= per week, he would be awarded Ush 500,000/=
multiplied by 10 days divided by seven days i.e. Ush 411,440/=.
Bosa & Co. Advocates Vs. Vero Nassanga & ors.
Burden of proof - proof of undue influence - whether by party
alleging the same.
Held: In deciding upon the capacity of a testator to make a Will it is the
soundness mind and not the particular state of the bodily health that is to
be considered.  In the instant case, the deceased's mental power could
have been reduced below the ordinary standard by his illness, yet he was
seized with the requisite intelligence to understand and appreciate the
testamentary act he had undertaken and accomplished.
Undue influence or duress is when the testator is induced to make
disposition, which he did, not really intend to make even where force is
not used or threatened.  When pressure of whatever nature is exerted on
the testator as to overpower his own volition without convincing his
judgment.  The defendant had not proved that the testator's widow had
brought such pressure upon the testator.  It was not enough for them to
show that the widow had power to unduly press the testator.  It must
positively be shown that she exercised power or pressure.
Moreover the burden of proof of the existence of undue influence lay on
the party alleging the same.  The defendant had not discharged it.
Thirdly the defendant were supposed to have pleaded particulars of
respective acts of undue influence complained of, with necessary dates
which they did not.  This is because undue influence must be positively
proved and not merely assumed.
Where the testator or those interested in the residue have been the cause
of the litigation, for instance where in the Will the testator used that were
difficult to understand and required construction by the courts for such
litigation will be paid out of the estate.  In the case before us, the
defendants were the sources of the litigation when they put forward
arguments that the testator's Will was made under undue influence,
without attempting reasonably to prove their allegations.  Therefore the
two defendants should be ordered to pay the costs of the whole action.
suit allowed defendant to pay costs of suit.
Silas Majyambere Vs. Cargolux (u)  & ors.
Burden of proof -the right to begin -O.16 r3ss.100, & 101 Evidence
Act -whether where the plaintiff sued for breach of contract and the
defendant alleged lack of title, the defendant was enjoined to
begin first and prove lack of title.
Held: According to O.16 r3, where there are issues the burden of proving
some of which lies not on the plaintiff but the defendant, the plaintiff still
required to begin his case but in so doing the plaintiff has an option to
elect not to lead evidence on some of those other issues to be proved that
the defendant so that the plaintiff only replies thereto. This rule does not
take away the plaintiff's obligation to prove his case under ss.100 and 101
Evidence Act.
Plaintiff ordered to begin his case.
Zita Jackson Vs. Uganda.
Corroboration in sexual offences-whether lack thereof is a material
irregularity.
Distressed condition of complainant-whether corroborative of alleged
defilement.
Held: Failure by a trial judge to record his note of summing up to the
assessors is contrary to s.81(1) TID and this can lead to the quashing of a
conviction if injustice results therefrom.  In the present case the failure to
make the record did not in itself cause injustice since the assessors in their
opinions gave the salient features of the evidence which meant that they
were properly directed.
S.64(2) requires the trial judge to draw up a memorandum of agreed facts
and in the instant case the trial judge failed to comply with this provision of
the law.  However, since the contested medical report was after being
admitted, signed by both counsel for the prosecution and accused and the
trial judge, the report became part of the record of the court.
It is rule of practice for the trial judge to record submissions of counsel and
when counsel's submissions raise issues of law and fact and the trial judge
does not consider the issues in his judgment, then such an omission is
relevant to the merits of an appeal.  However, in the instant case since the
submissions of counsel were made and closed in the morning and
judgment delivered 3 hours later, it means that the submissions were fresh
in the mind of the judge when he was writing the judgment.  Therefore the
omission to record the submissions did not occasion a miscarriage of
justice.
It is a rule of practice for courts to require corroboration of the evidence
against the accused in sexual offences.  In the instant case the distressed
condition of the complainant was corroborative of the sexual assault upon
her.
Seven years imprisonment were neither illegal nor excessive.
Corporal punishment was not provided for the offence of defilement and the
sentence for corporal punishment was illegal and would be set aside.
Appeal dismissed except as to orders for corporal punishment.
Uganda Revenue Authority Vs. Stephen Mabosi.
Documentary evidence Ss.90,91 Evidence Act-exclusion thereof by
oral testimony-whether may be allowed.
Cross-examination-failure to cross examine on a material
proposition by an adverse party-whether thereby testimony
admitted as true.
Held: When, as provided by s.90 of the Evidence act, the terms of a
contract or other disposition of property, have been reduced to the form of a
document, no other evidence is admissible to exclude or add onto what is
contained in the document.  The document speaks alone and by itself.
Therefore, the appellant was estopped from claiming that in the seizure
notice.  The only admissible evidence was the seizure notice.  The learned
trial judge was correct in rejecting the appellant's evidence that derogated
from the seizure notice.
Moreover, an omission or neglect to challenge the evidence in chief of a
material proposition by cross-examination would lead to the inference that
the evidence as given is accepted,.  In the instance case the appellant never
cross-examine the respondent on the number of trips involved in ferrying the
impounded goods.  Therefore, the respondent's testimony was unchallenged.
However, the award of 40% interest, being far above the bank interest was
excessive and would call for the intervention of the appellate court.  Instead
30% would be ordered.
Appeal dismissed except as to rate of interest.  Respondent awarded 80%
of the taxed costs of the appeal.
Grindlays Bank (U) Ltd & Kampala Bottlers Ltd Vs. Uganda
Bottlers Ltd.
Estoppel - S.113 Evidence Act.
Held: The receivers were validly appointed by the bank pursuant to the
powers conferred upon the Bank by the debenture.  The document of
appointment having been written by on of the receivers with authority of the
bank, the receivers were thus appointed in writing.  The relevant document
concerning the appointment need not include "appointment" in its body.
The Mortgage Decree was not applicable to the debenture as it was not
registered with the register of titles but only with the company registry.
S.113 Evidence Act provides that a person is estopped from complaining
against the act of another, which act has been done with the acquiescence
of that person.  In the instant case, the Managing Director of the respondent
was present in the meeting where the bank appointed the receivers and in
fact handed over to the receivers the keys and cash and books of account
of the respondent.  He never protested against the appointment of the
Directors then.  The respondents were therefore estopped from challenging
the validity of the appointment.
Since the appointment of the receivers was valid, so was their transfer of the
suit property to the appellants in appeal No.16/95.
S.184 gives fraud as the only basis upon which title may be impeached.
Since by the time the respondents filed the suit the appellants in appeal
No.16/95 were already registered sufficient to impeach the appellant's title.
Appeals allowed with costs.
Uganda Vs. Pattni Manish.
Admissibility-Police statement recorded by policeman deceased at
the date of trial-whether statement admissible under S.30 Ev. Act.
Held: Where a charge does not set out the particulars of the offence, such
charge is defective.  However, since in this case the accused appeared to
understand the substance of the charge, the defect would not be fatal.
S.30(b) Evidence Act does not permit the admissibility of a statement of a
deceased police officer because such is not one of the instances police
officer because such is not one other instances provided for under the
subsection.  This is because the accused has a right to cross-examine his
accuser.
Embezzlement is committed by an employee of the complainant company
when such employee interrupts in transits the movement of money or
reliable article from a third party to the complainant, and the employee
converts the same to his use before the money or valuable reaches his
embezzled had already been paid to the agent of the complainant. Therefore
it was not possible to embezzle what was already in the custody of the
complainant.  The possible offence could have been theft but not
embezzlement.
Appeal dismissed.
Mitoto Samy Oketch Vs. Uganda
Handwriting-expert opinion-whether evidence of handwriting by a non expert
is inadmissible.
Cross examination-failure to cross examine on evidence in chief-whether
thereby testimony stands unchallenged.
Held: The licensing officer was not a handwriting expert nor did he present
to be one.  However, his conclusion was a common sense view from his
routine matching and observation of signatures in the exercise of his duties
as a licensing officer.  Moreover, the trial court based its conviction of the
appellant on his failure or refusal to challenge the testimony through cross-
examination.
Because there was no aspiration, an essential ingredient in the offence of
theft was not proved. However, the learned trial Magistrate was correct in
finding the appellant guilty of attempted theft because the act of fraudulently
transferring the ownership of the vehicle amounted to an overt act of theft in
terms of S.369(1) Penal Code Act.
Though 2 years imprisonment sentence was the maximum allowable for the
offence of attempted theft, the trial Magistrate was entitled to impose it
because the appellant never struck court as being repentant and the
appellant had grossly abused his position of trust in the company by
committing the offence.
Appeal dismissed.
Luwero Green Acres Ltd Vs. Marubeni Corporation.
Affidavit-summary procedure-whether court may rely on affidavit
sworn in support of application for leave to appear and defend after
the application had been granted.
Held: The law is that if the court grants leave to the defendant to defend the
suit the affidavit sworn in support of the application for leave to appear and
defend the suit forms part of the record but it is never evidence in support of
the defence which has to be adduced before court in the ordinary manner.
In the instant case the learned 1st appellate judge based his judgment and
conclusion on the affidavit sworn in support for the application to defend the
suit, and this was irregular because the contents of the affidavit were never
introduced in the evidence in court during the hearing after leave had been
granted.
The 1st appellate court is duty bound to reconsider and revaluate the
evidence and come to its own conclusion.  Had the 1st appellant judge
carried out this duty, and not relied on the affidavit in the interlocutory
application in the lower court for leave to defend, he would have come to the
conclusion that there was an oral contract between the parties to the suit
which the respondent had breached when it refused to pay Ug. Shs. 4.5m
the balance of the contract amount.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Musoke Sanyu Lwanga Vs. Yakobo Ntate Mayanja.
Burden of proof Ss.100, 101 & 105 Evidence Act-delivery of notice
to remove caveat S.210A(1)(2) Registration of Titles Act-whether
burden of proof on person who claims did not receive the notice.
Held: O.6 r2 CPR requires that where an action is based on fraud, the
particulars must be set out in the pleadings and proved in court strictly.
therefore, in an action involving fraud, proceedings by affidavit is not possible.
Therefore, the learned trial Judge misdirected himself when he proceeded to
entertain a matter where fraud was pleaded basing on affidavits.
Where a notice to remove a caveat is set by the registrar, under S.149(1)
RTA, it is required by S.205 of the RTA that a memorandum, being a copy
of the notice and when it was sent, be made.  In the instant case no such
memorandum existed and therefore there was no proof that the notice was
sent as alleged.
Moreover, even if there was no affidavit from M/s Mulira and Co. Advocates
deponing that they never received the notice, the affidavit was not necessary
because the burden of proof as required by SS.100, 101, 102 and 105 of the
Evidence Act, was on the person alleging that the notice was sent to prove
that actually the notice was sent.
Moreover, a caveat instituted for the beneficiary under a will does lapse after
the expiration of 60 days under S.149(1) of the RTA, the operation of the
caveat must be determined before this removal. Therefore, the learned Judge
misdirected himself when he found that failure by the said Magala Efulaimu
to apply to court for the delay of the registration of the respondent as
proprietor was a ground to remove the caveat.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Mugenyi & Co. Advocates Vs. Attorney General.
Estoppel-pleading-whether failure to plead estoppel meant that it
could not raised.
Held: S.4(1) Companies Act requires at least 2 shareholders to form a
private limited liability company.  The 2 government ministers signed as
shareholders and thus fulfilled the requirements of the Act and it was not
competent to inquire as to whether or not the two ministers were
Shareholders.  Therefore the company was duly incorporated and the
learned trial judge erred when he held otherwise.
In order to lift the veil of incorporation personality so as to find that in fact
there was no company but a government extension, one must allege fraud
on the part of government.  In the instant case there was no fraud or
illegality alleged in the pleadings against government.  Therefore, the veil of
incorporation would remain uplifted and UTC 1975 would be dealt with as an
independent company separate from its owner the government and the
appellant must proceed to recover his fees in liquidation and not against
government.
Unless estoppels is a fact in issue at the trial, it cannot be raised when not
pleaded.  The defendant must plead estoppel and the plaintiff must reply in
order for it to be considered at the trial.  The learned trial judge erred to
have based his judgment on estoppel when the same had not been
pleaded and was not a fact in issue at the trial.
Appeal dismissed in part.  Appellant ordered to recover against the company
in liquidation.
Hotel International Ltd Vs. The Administrator of the Estate of
the Late Robert Kavuma.
Evidence Act Ss 100, 102 & 105-burden of proof-whether defendant
had burden to deny inflicting damages to the suit premises.
Held: The learned trial judge erred in fact when he held that there was the
respondent's caveat on the suit land as a notice of the respondent's
unregistered interest.  This is because the evidence was to the effect that
the Registrar of Titles though she had received the application to register a
caveat she had not done so.  S.51 RTA provides that no unregistered
instruments is effectual.  Therefore his unregistered interest was not
protected and was thus available legally for appropriation to the appellant
who had no notice thereof.
No fraud could be imputed on the appellant since he had no knowledge of
the existence of the respondent's unregistered interest.
The learned trial Principal Judge erred when he sighted the burden of proof
by requiring the appellant/defendant to deny whether or not he had inflicted
damage on the suit premises for purposes of assessing mesne profits.
This was contrary to the requirements of SS.100, 105 Evidence Act that
required the person alleging to prove the truth of his allegations.
The learned trial Judge erred when he awarded interest when the same had
not been prayed for.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Patel B.K. Vs. H.R.Patel
Witness-contradiction by the witness of a document witnessed by
self-whether such witness not credible.
Held: The transfer deed bore both names of the respondent & the appellant
as tenants in common, both having purchased equal shares of the same
property, jointly.  The transfer deed having been witnessed by DW2 who a
lawyer, the witness could not be called credible when he contradicted the
document he had attested to by saying that the appellant never paid his
part of the purchase price.  S.209(1) RAT allows parties to modify the
contents of the transfer deed to show the actual situation.  Since no
modification was done, the transfer deed was final to confer the title to the
respondent and S.51 RAT presumed very person whose name appear in the
registered (instrument) transfer as transferee to be owner and only proof of
fraud could render such presumption ineffectual.  In the instant case no
such fraud was proved.  Therefore the learned trial judge was correct in
holding that the respondent was a 5% tenant in common.
Appeal dismissed.
Tororo District Administration Vs. Andalapo Industries Ltd.
Affidavit in reply-lack thereof-whether matters deponed previously
stand unchallenged.
Held: Though it is mandatory that a notice of motion under O.48 r3 must
state the grounds of the application the irregularity caused by non
compliance is curable if the grounds of the application or appeal are set out
in the accompanying affidavit as was the case in the instant.
Even if it were true that the appellant did not comply with the O.44 r7 by
bringing this appeal under O.46 r7, this by itself would not lead appeal being
struck out because rules of procedure are formulated for purposes of giving
effect to the rights of the parties and where no injustice has been caused to
any of the parties a mere irregularity in relation to rules of procedure should
not be allowed to vitiate the proceedings.
Ordinarily failure to file an affidavit in reply would mean the contents of the
affidavit of the applicant are taken as unchallenged and truthful.  However,
this general rule is subject to whether the contents pass the test of evidence
hat is cogent and of probative value.
A District Registrar proceeding under O.44 r6 may take formal steps
preliminary to the trial and handle applications interlocutory, and fix the case
for hearing.  In the instant case by the learned Registrar entertaining an
application for leave to appear and defend and dismissing the same,
exceeded his jurisdiction and his orders must be set aside.
However, looking at the merits of the application to appear and defend the
suit under summary procedure, the applicant/respondent failed to show by
affidavit that it had triable issues of fact or law.  An applicant in such a
matter must show that there is a question which ought to be tried.  Such
defence when raised should be stated with sufficient particularity as to
appear genuine.  General or vague statements denying liability will not
suffice.  In the instant case it is not enough to state that there were
irregularities in the contract the subject of the suit.  It was incumbent upon
the applicant for leave to appear and defend to state with sufficient
particularity the nature of the irregularities in the contract.
Application for unconditional leave dismissed. Each party to bear own costs.
Musoke Sanyu Lwanga Vs. Sam Galiwango
Admissibility -unproved will S.187 Succession Act-whether will not
admissible in evidence.
Held: S.233(1),(2)(b)( c) Succession Act provides that a grant may be revoked
where it was obtained fraudulently by making a false statement.  In the
instant case there was ample evidence on record to show that the deceased
left a Will which fact the respondent was privy to.  By making a false
allegation to the effect that the deceased left no Will, which allegation was
the basis of the grant of Letters of Administration to the respondent, it
means that the grant was obtained by fraud and should be revoked.
S.187 Succession Act precludes a claimant to take benefit of the provisions
of an unproved Will but the section does render inadmissible in evidence a
Will that has not yet been proved by grant of probate.  Therefore the trial
court misdirected itself when it refused to admit in evidence the alleged Will
for purposes of proving its existence.
It is not necessary to appeal against an interlocutory ruling separate from
the final decision.  Therefore, it was not necessary for the appellant to have
pleaded against the trial judge's upholding of the objection to tender in
evidence the Will.  It was enough that this was incorporated in the
memorandum of appeal against the whole final decision of the trial court.
Therefore, the appeal against the introductory order could not be caught by
time before the final decision on the matter is made.
Under S.32 Judicature Act, the High Court has unlimited jurisdiction to inter
alia take any step to rectify any wrong findings on the face of the record
which comes to its attention.  In the instant case even if there was no
appeal against the grant of the lower court, the High Court could have
interfered against the grant on grounds that the grant was based on a
fraudulent misrepresentation of an essential fact and that the Chief
Magistrate had no jurisdiction to make a grant where the estate was above
Moreover, court countenance an illegality and leave it standing.
Appeal allowed.  Grounds to affirm decision dismissed.
Barclays Bank of Uganda Vs. Godfrey Mubuse.
Trade usage Bank charging compound interest unilaterally whether
this was a trade usage requiring no notice to customer.
Held: Court will hold that a trade usage exists and will take judicial notice
thereof where it is shown that the accounts being dealt with are mercantile
accounts. In the present case the accounts were not mercantile and
therefore, the plaintiff bank did not have the legal basis to charge compound
interest when it was not originally agreed between the parties.
Suit allowed.  Defendant ordered to pay simple interest and costs.
Tusiime Twebaze Drake Vs. Uganda.
Identification -whether sufficiently done without an identification
parade.
Held: The object of an identification parade is to make sure that the ability of
the witness to recognize the suspect is tested.  However, the identification
parade is not the only such test.  The correctness or otherwise of
indent faction by witness, of the accused will depend on the circumstances,
such as the length of time, the distance, the light, the familiarity of the
witness with the accused.  If the quality of these is good, the danger of
distance identity is reduced. In the instance case the evidence adduced
by the prosecution and not contradicted by the appellant clearly showed that
the complainant and other prosecution witnesses who were involved in the
alleged motor vehicle purchase transaction office hours.  The circumstances
of identification could not come not have been better.  The learned trial
magistrate was correct to come to the conclusion she came to.
It is not necessary for the convicting court to always state that the
prosecuting has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The elements of the offence of uttering a false document and those of forging
a document are different.  Therefore it is possible as it was in the case
instant to convict a person of uttering a false document while acquitting him
of forging the same.  Moreover, there was no requirement that to prove of a
handwriting expert.  The appellant had been seen by witnesses that
testified seeing him uttering the false documents.
The sentence of 3 years was not excessive.  The trial court took into
account the fact that the appellant was a graduate who should have used
his education to do better things.
Appeal dismissed.
Uganda Co-operative Transport Union Ltd Vs. Roko
Construction Ltd.
Examination of witnesses S.136(1) Evidence Act-refusal of
opportunity to cross-examine witness-whether trial flawed.
Held: Art 28(1) Constitution of Uganda provides that a person has a right to
a fair and public hearing before an impartial tribunal and the failure by the
trial Judge to afford an opportunity to the appellant to cross-examine and
challenge the evidence of accounts presented by the respondent meant that
the trial was neither fair nor public.
Secondly, S.136(1) Evidence Act mandatorily provides for the opportunity
to a party to challenge evidence adversely given by the other party at the
trial.
Appeal allowed.  Judgment set aside.  Retrial ordered.
Matsanga Deo Vs. Uganda
Identification-whether circumstances afforded a proper identification
of accused.
Former statement of the witness S.155 Evidence Act-corroboration
whether because the witness did not mention his assailant in this
statement at police, may not mention accused in Court.
Witness-failure to call certain witnesses-whether therefore adverse
inference may be drawn.
Held: The essential ingredients of the offence of attempted murder are that
the assailant intended to maim or disfigure the complaint and that the
intention was to be carried out with the weapon and that the assailant started
to execute the said intentions.  In the present case there was cogent
evidence that the appellant had been properly identified by the complainant
is the one that shot at his car while he drove it.  Therefore the Chief
Magistrate had been correct to put the accused to his defence and
eventually to convict him of the same.
The essential ingredients of the offence of malicious damage to property are
the damage is inflicted willfully and unlawfully by the accused.  Since the
complainant's car was damaged by the shots aimed at it by the appellant
who had been properly identified, the learned Chief Magistrate was correct
to find that the offence was proved.
The conditions for a proper unmistaken identification existed because the
appellant was known to his assailant; the distance between the two was a
mere 30 meters when the appellant fired the shots at the complainant; and it
was a clear day at 2:19 pm in broad day light.
It is not a requirement of the law that the trial Magistrate must record his
reasons for rejecting or allowing a submission of no case to answer.
Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate did not commit an error of law
in failing to record his reasons for rejecting the appellant's submission of no
case to answer.  Moreover, this failure to record his reasons did not
occasion a failure of justice.
S. 155 of the Evidence Act provides that statements made y the witness
immediately after the occurrence of an event are relevant to corroborate the
truth or otherwise of his latest statements in Court. In the present case the
fact that the complainant did not mention his assailants name in his
immediate statement at Police was not necessarily corroborative of the fact
that the complainant did not know his assailant, because the complainant
explained in his latest statement that he feared for his life since his
assailant was still at large.
The prosecution must produce all witnesses necessary to establish the truth
of a case.  If it fails to do so where the evidence is barely inadequate, the
Court is entitled to draw the inference that the evidence of the uncalled
witness would have tended to be adverse to the prosecution case.  In the
prosecution case.  In the case instant the prosecution proved all the
essential ingredients of the offences charged.  Therefore, the prosecution
evidence was adequate.
The learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in law in not recording the
proceedings in locus in quo.  However, a visit at a locus in quo is only
necessary to corroborate the evidence already on record.  In the instant case
since the evidence already recorded in open court was sufficient to establish
the guilt of the appellant, no miscarriage of justice was occasioned by the
procedural failure to record the proceedings of the locus in quo since the
visit thereto was superfluous.
The learned trial judge erred in not taking into account the period of remand
spent by the appellant prior to his conviction and sentence as this is now
constitutionally mandatory as per Article 23 (8) of the Constitution of the
Republic of Uganda 1995.
The sentences therefore would be reduced by 6 months.
Appeal against conviction dismissed.Appeal against sentence allowed in part.
Okello Eric & anor Vs. Wade Adams Ltd
Expert opinion-documentary evidence - whether failure to annex
expert documentary evidence means that document may not be
relied upon.
Held: O.7 r 14(2) provides that no reliance in Court shall be allowed on a
document not mentioned in the plaint or annexed there to.  In the present
case since the expert was giving oral evidence it was sufficient without
relying on the document.
It is true that African children, who are educated, often at considerable
sacrifice, by their parents, are expected to make contribution to the welfare
of their parents in return.  However such a custom is not static and the
changes may result in the parents not necessarily expecting contribution
to their welfare from their educated children.  Therefore Ush. 5 million would
be awarded for the loss of life.
Ush. 1,500,000/= would be awarded as general damages for the swollen
tibia where permanent disability was calculated at 10%.

Okello Florence Joyce Vs. Uganda
Burden of proof-whether shifted to the accused.
Held: S.142(1) (b) MCA empowers the High Court on appeal or revision, with
discretion to set aside a judgment and conviction by a trial Magistrate
relied on evidence not wholly recorded by him where it appears that the
accused was thereby prejudiced, and may order a retrial.  However, this
power is discretionary and the learned appellate Judge was correct in not
disturbing the holding of the trial sentence on the record before her, which
was sufficient.
The appellant was not correct to argue that the learned appellate Judge erred
in upholding the shifting of the burden of proof to accused by the trial court
because this was not the case according to the facts on record.
The learned appellant Judge exercise the powers of the first appellate court
duly and correctly by subjecting the evidence on record from the trial court
to exhaustive scrutiny and came to the conclusion that the trial court was
correct in convicting the appellant.
Appeal dismissed.
Tefem (U) Ltd Vs. Tropical Bank Ltd.
Ss.7 and 8 evidence (Bankers Books) Act - whether application to
access bank account may be granted.
Held: It is permissible to file an application for an order of an access to a
Bank account, ex parte, without summoning the bankers or the defendants
where it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that access to the account is
essential  to the valuation of the assets of a joint venture.
Application allowed.
Nile Safaris Ltd Vs. Hot Ice Ltd & Grahamed Denis
Burden of proof of inevitable accident-whether on defendant.
Held: the trial Judge was correct in finding that failure to use the fire
extinguisher if any existed, was not the cause of fire, nor the class of the
driving permit of the driver.  Therefore the appellant had failed to proved
negligence on the part of the respondent.
The burden of proof of inevitable accident is on the defendant pleading the
same.  However, the defendant only needs to plead inevitable accident
where the plaintiff has established a prima facie case of negligence.  In the
present case the appellant failed to establish a prima facie case of
negligence and therefore the respondents were not bound to plead nor prove
inevitable accident.
Costs followed the event unless a successful party proves to court to its
satisfaction that special reasons do exist to warrant him getting the costs
from the successful party.  In the present case the appellant had not
discharged the burden of proof that special circumstances exist to warrant
that appellant be awarded the costs from the successful party.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Kisugu Quarries Ltd Vs. Administration General
Burden of proof-fact within special knowledge of a party, S.105
evidence-whether party has burden to prove.
Held: S.105 Evidence Act provides that the burden of proof is on that party
that has special knowledge of a fact in issue to prove it.  S.2 of the Land
Transfer Act required the non-African who wished to take a lease of Mailo
land to obtain the consent of the Minister, the burden of proof was on the
appellant which is the one that had the duty to seek Ministerial consent, to
prove that in fact the consent was granted because this would be a fact
within its knowledge.  The evidence on record seeking to prove Ministerial
consent was just speculation and conjecture.
Appeal dismissed with costs.

Hon. Ssali Bidandi Vs. The Attorney General.
Notice of defect in title - whether the expropriated properties Act
acted prospectively to invalidate future dealings in expropriated
properties.
Held: Although the Registrar of Titles has powers to rectify errors, the
sublease had been terminated by re-entry therefore, there was no error
to correct.
The plaintiff was therefore a bonafide purchaser for value without notice
of any other person's interest.
The expropriated properties Act 1982 was intended to act prospectively-
to retrieve properties which had fallen into wrong hands.
Gokaldas Tanna Vs. Rosemary Muyinza & DAPCB
Sale of mortgaged property -whether the sale and transfer of the
suit property to the appellant was nullified by the provisions of s.I
of the expropriated properties Act, 1982.
Held: the suit property in the instant case had been owned by a
Departed Asian prior to 1972.  The suit property was subsequently
vested in the second respondent.  The transaction that aimed at
transferring ownership of the suit property from the DAPCB to the
appellant was made void by S.1 (2) (a) of the Expropriated Property
Shabani Matovu Vs. Sikindar Hussein Esmail & 5 others.
Action for compensation for improvements on the premises -
whether against the person repossessing or against the custodian
Board - whether action for compensation not maintainable because
the improvements did not benefit the defendant - whether action
for compensation cannot succeed according to law.
Held: The compensation of the valuation was to be done by a Board of
Valuers appointed by the Minister as required by S.12 of the Expropriated
Properties Act and S.2(1) of the Properties and Business (Acquisition)
Decree no 11 of 1975.  Since the plaintiff had not had his claimed
compensation valued as such his claim must fail.
S.14 of the Expropriated Properties Act required that the claim for
compensation must be placed before the Custodian Board's validation

appeal against the decision of the validation committee.  Therefore the

Stephen Kalani Vs. Satwant Kaur
Repossession -vesting of property - whether the suit property
vested in government where it is alleged that the expropriated
defendant had surrendered her lease.

Held: S.I.(2) of the Expropriated Properties Act nullified all dealings in

Asians Decree.  Since the alleged instrument of surrender was registered
after the coming into force of the Assets Departed Asians Decree, the
registration of the alleged surrender of the lease was null and void.
Under S.14 of the Expropriated Properties Act the person aggrieved by
the decision of the Minister regarding the granting of a certificate of
repossession can certificate but should not file an ordinary suit
Suit dismissed with costs.
United Assurance Co. Ltd Vs. Attorney General.
Expropriated properties Act s.I(a) (b) ( c) -whether only shares of
Asians were expropriated and not the companies in which Asians
had shares.
Held: Company property belongs to the company and not the shareholders.
Since the suit property belonged to the company, it was not expropriated.
What was expropriated were shares of the Asians in the company.
Therefore the suit property registered in the names of the company was not
managed under the provisions of the Expropriated properties Act.
Therefore, the learned trial judge erred when he ruled that the suit was not
maintainable.  The suit was properly brought to contest the constitutional
propriety of the compulsory acquisition.
The management of a private company is in the board of directors who under
S.177 of the company's Act can manage the affairs of the company under
regulation 80 of Table A of the Act.  The management includes instructing
counsel to file proceedings in the name of the company.  In the present
case board of directors of the appellant company consisted of a single
director and it is in this director who instructed counsel and no resolution
was required to evidence the instructions to counsel to file the suit.
The learned trial judge misdirected himself in law and fact when he ruled that
the case had no substantial constitutional issues requiring the interpretation
of the Constitutional Court.
Appeal allowed.
Chris Akena Onapa Vs. Mohammed Hussein Rashid Punjani
Expired lease-application for renewal -whether the departed Asian
whose lease expired and applied for renewal immediately before
he was deported from Uganda became a tenant at wit of the
controlling authority - whether such Deported Asian had any
interest to vest in government under the expropriated properties
Act.
Held: Ss.1(2)(b) of the Expropriated Properties Act allows for repossession
any property, which at the time it was expropriated had a valid subsisting
lease.  In the instant case, since no renewal of the lease had been effected
by the controlling authority in favour of the respondent at the time the
respondent became departed Asian the suit property was not expropriated
and was not governed by the Expropriated Properties Act.  The suit
property was still vested in the controlling authority, which had validly
executed a lease in favor of the appellant.
The respondent was not a tenant at will since he had not fulfilled the
conditions for the renewal of the lease.
Appeal allowed.
Mbwali Aida Vs. Aruindbhai Popat.
Departed Asian S.35-Assets of Departed Asians Decree-whether
a departed Asian who before his departure made arrangements for
the proper care of his property was not a departed Asian.
Abandoned property-Assets of Departed Asians Decree S.35 -
whether because the departed Asian before his departure made
arrangements for the proper care of his property was not abandoned.
Transfer of property of departed Asian - S.I Assets of Departed
Asians Decree - whether departed Asian validly transferred property
to the plaintiff.
Vesting of property in government - S.I(2) (9) Expropriated
Properties Act-whether suit property did not vest in government
because previously transferred by departed Asian.
Repossession Certificate-impeachment thereof by ordinary suit-
whether therefore repossession certificate not validly impeached-
whether therefore repressor entitled to repossess.
Held: S.1 of the Assets of Departed Asians Decree applies only to the

management of such property in Uganda.  In the instant case, the suit
property was granted by the departing Asians to his wife for her upkeep and

property lawfully granted to the plaintiff by the departing Asian.
Since the suit property was lawfully granted to the plaintiff by the departing
Asian before his departure S.1(2)(9) of the Expropriated Properties Act did

Since the property was never lawfully vested in government, it was never the

minister was issued in vain since there was no property to repossess, the
departing Asian having granted the same to his wife intervolves.
S.2 (1) (9) of the Hindu Marriage and Divorce Act recognizes polygamous
marriage celebrated before the coming into force of the Act.  In the instant
case the marriage was celebrated in 1940 and yet the Act came into force
in 1961.  Therefore, the issue of the marriage being polygamous did not by
itself affect the validity of the marriage between the plaintiff and Tailor.
S.3(1)(d) of the Hindu Marriage and Divorce Act provides that a girl below
the age of 18 may marry provided she gets the consent of her guardian.
In this case there was sufficient evidence to prove that the requisite consent
had been granted.
S.9(2)(9) of the Hindu Marriage and Divorce Act entitled either spouse to
the marriage to apply for divorce where if the other has changed her or his
religion. The section is permissive, and since the parties elected to continue
as husband and wife inspite of the plaintiff's change of her religion to Islam,

A Hindu Marriage may be celebrated in any other place other than the
temple.

S.1(2) (a) Expropriated Properties Act-whether the transfer by the
Custodian Board of the suit property to the respondent was
nullified by S.1(2) (a) of the Act.
Held: In a sale of immovable property, upon payment of a deposit, property
passes to the purchaser who acquires an equitable interest in the property
and the vendor becomes a trustee who holds the property in trust for the
purchaser.  The legal title remains with vendor until the final payment when
the legal title remains with vendor until the final payment when the legal title
passes to the purchaser.  Therefore, the 1st respondent was a lawful
purchaser of the suit property who acquired an equitable interest in the
same when he paid the deposit to the appellants.
Where an agent does not disclose the principal for whom he acts, such an
agent acts for himself.  Such an agent is liable for all the liabilities that may
occur in the transaction but also may take full benefit of the contract.  In the
instant case, though the 1st respondent, when he paid the deposit to the
appellants, claimed to be acting as broker for another buyer, because the
first respondent failed or refused to disclose the actual purchaser for whom
he claimed to the working, the law would recognize him as the purchaser of
the suit premises.
In order that a person may be found guilty of fraud, the alleged fraud must be
visited on the person alleged to have committed the same.  In the instant
case the 1st respondent.  Therefore the trial Principal Judge was entitled to
hold that the 1st respondent was a bonafide purchaser who had in turn
passed clean title to the 2nd respondent.
S.1(2)(a) of the Expropriated Properties Act nullified dealings in property
expropriated by government after the Expropriation Decrees 29/72 and 27/73
which dealing could include the transfer of the property to the purchaser by
by the Custodian Board as was the fact in the instant case.  However, since
the purchaser had acquired his equitable interest far before the Expropriation
Decrees, his equitable interest was not subject of the Expropriated
Properties Act.  The Custodian Board was entitled to effect a transfer in
favor of the 1st respondent because the 1st respondent was the owner of
property in law since property passed to him before the law prohibiting
transfer and sales of such property was promulgated.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Poojara Dinesh Vs. Vacu-Lug (U) Ltd.
Appeal to the High Court S.14 Expropriated Properties Act -
whether a defendant claiming a setoff for developments on the suit
property in a suit for rent arrears, could only claim the set off by
of appeal against the Order of the Minister under S.14 Expropriated
Properties Act-that therefore the set off as claimed herein is
unnecessary or scandalous and should be struck off.
Held: S.14 of the Expropriated Properties Act relate to a situation where the
Minister has made a decision concerning the expropriated property which
decision has aggrieved the party.  Such a party can appeal the decision of
the minister to the High Court.  In the instant case the minister had made no
decision to appeal from.  The defendant was entitled to claim a set off in its
WSD.
Moreover, there was nothing unnecessary or scandalous about the pleading.
Preliminary objection overruled.  Case to proceed.
Popat Arvindbhai Vs. Aida Mbwali
Abandoned property Decree 27/73-whether because Departed
Asian left the country after making proper arrangement for the
management of his property, the property was not abandoned-that
therefore property did not fall under S.1(2)(a) Expropriated
Properties Act for repossession.
Held: S.1(1), (2) & (3) OF Decree 27/73 prohibited transfer by a departing
Asian of his property after 6th October 1972 after such Asians had their stay
permits cancelled.  Therefore, the purported transfer of the suit property by
the Departing Asian to his wife the respondent herein was null and void by
virtue of S.1(2) (a) of the Expropriated Properties Act and therefore the suit
property was available for repossession.  This was irrespective of whether or
not the respondent was the wife of the departed Asian.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Pyrari Shunji Ganyi & 3 ors Vs. Coffee Development Authority
Whether property was expropriated where by the time the Asian
left had sold the same but not paid in full, S.1 (1) ( c) Expropriated
Properties Act.
Held: Once a transfer is executed there is a binding contract inter-parties
and the time to register the transfer is not of essence.  In the instant case
the sale of the property and execution of transfer were concluded before the
expulsion Decrees came into force.  Therefore the appellants did not have
the property to be expropriated as the property had passed to the purchasers
and in the same vein the appellants could not repossess the property, as
they had no interest therein.
Appeal dismissed with costs.

Divorce -whether the fraudulent statement by the respondent as to

Adoption - Uganda mother deceased and fathers where about

Adoption - whether petitioners resident in Uganda.

the controlling authority after having allocated the plot to the deceased,

In re(An Infant)
Adoption - resident in Uganda S.4(5) Adoption Act - whether
appellants who own permanent house Uganda where they stay
when on leave, are regarded non Ugandan residents for purposes
of s.4(5) Adoption because they work abroad.
Held: S. 4(5) of Adoption Act did not define residence specifically to provide

Adoption petitions should be liberally considered in favour of the infant

Consent by parents or guardians where at least one of the parties is a minor
