parent's was not guilty of assaulting the child complainant.
Held: It is the right of the defence to move court on a motion of no case to
answer.  Where the defence choose not to make the submission of no case
to answer, it does not preclude the trial court in pursuance of S.126(1) of
Magistrates Courts Act to rule that there is a case to answer or not.
Therefore the learned trial magistrate was entitled in the instant case to rule
on own motion that there was a case to answer.
And whereas according to the evidence on record after the prosecution
evidence, there might have been no case to answer, where nevertheless the
trial court rules that there is a case to answer, where there upon the defence
presents its evidence which only affords to strengthen the prosecution case,
the trial court is entitled to act on the evidence as a whole including that of
the defence to convict the accused.  In the instant case the prosecution
evidence had not made out a prima facie case on the original charge of the
offence of attempted murder.  However when the trial court ruled that there
was a case to answer, and indeed the appellants presented the evidence
which showed that they had indeed burned the complainant, the court was
entitled to treat the evidence as a whole and find that in fact an indictable
offence had been committed.
The defence of accident was not available to the appellants because the
prosecution had proved that the complainant was burn deliberately by the
appellants, who intended to extract information from the complainant about
the whereabouts of the lost money.
Even if the defence of accident was to be considered, and say that the
complainant was burnt by the stove as she ran away from being chastised
by her parent, the evidence still would indicate that the running away was
induced by the appellants' deliberate act of endangering their victim in such
a way that she had to run away and in so doing fell in the danger of being
burnt. Still the appellants would be liable for inflicting the consequent injuries.
An attempt to commit is an act done with intent to commit the crime, and
forming part of a series of acts which would constitute its actual commission
If it were not interrupted.  Therefore to support a charge of attempted murder
the prosecution must prove the full intent to murder, i.e. with malice
aforethought, which intent to murder, while being prosecuted, is interrupted
before the death results.  In the present case the complainant's hands and
legs were burnt by the appellants who left her to go with the injuries.
It cannot be said that the appellants had formed the intention to kill the
complainant but were interrupted in their efforts to do so.  Therefore the trial
magistrate was entitled to find that attempted murder had not been proved.
However, S.130(1)(a) Magistrate Courts Act provides that where, during trial,
it appears to court that the evidence discloses an offence than the offence
originally charged, if no injustice may be caused to the accused, the court
may make an order for the alteration of the charge by way of its amendment.
Therefore the learned trial Chief Magistrate erred in convicting the appellants
of an offence with which they were not charged without having first called
for the amendment of the charge and inviting the appellants to plead thereto.
This was so because the offence of doing an act likely to cause grievous
harm c/s 209(a) Penal Code act was not minor and cognate to the offence
of attempted murder originally charged.
However, the trial was not a nullity because the appellants were not
prejudiced in preparing their defence.  A trial court is empowered to convict
a person of a minor and cognate offence because the major offence
originally charged ipso facto gives notice of the minor offence.  In the instant
case the trial court should have convicted the appellants with the offence of
assault occasioning actual bodily harm c/s 228 Penal Code Act because
the evidence on record disclosed such an offence.
S.331(2)(1) Criminal Procedure Code permits an appellate court to quash a
conviction and substitute it with the one the lower court should have passed.
In the present case the nature of the injuries disclosed the offence of assault
occasioning actual bodily harm therefore the appellants' conviction of doing
an act likely to cause grievous harm would be substituted with committing
an assault occasioning actual bodily harm c/s 228 Penal Code Act.
There was no evidence on record put before sentences.  Since 5 years was
the maximum sentence for the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily
harm, a sentence of 18 months will be substituted from the date of remand.
Appeal against sentence, and conviction for doing an act likely to cause
grievous harm, allowed and substituted with conviction of assault
occasioning actual bodily harm and sentence of 18 months.
In Re Maria Naluggya An Infant
Legal guardianship Act 139(1) Constitution, ss 16 35, 41, Judicature
Statute S.4 Children's Statute-welfare principle -whether application
may be granted-whether welfare principle satisfied.
Held: S.4 of the Children's Statute provides that whenever the state, a court
or local authority or any person determines any question with respect to a
child, the child's welfare shall be of paramount consideration.  In the instant
case the child was an orphan and the applicant was the brother of the
mother of the infant and had the means to meet the welfare requirements for
the infant.
Application allowed.
In Re: Jane Nakintu & 2 others.
Children-guardian-welfare principle, S.4 Children's Statute, O.29 r4
CPR.
Held: Guardian means a person having parental responsibility for a child.
S.4 of the Children's Statutes provides that whenever any question in respect
of a child arises, the welfare of the child shall be of paramount consideration.
In the present case the welfare of the infants would be served by letting
them remain in the care and guardianship of the applicant who was already
in loco parents.
Application allowed.
Rukundo Sarapio Vs. Attorney General
Constitutional Petition against a judgment - whether statute barred
S.4(5) Government Proceedings Act.
Constitutional Petition against a judgment - whether Attorney
General not a party.
Held: R.4(1) of the Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Enforcement
Procedures) Rules, 1996, provides that a petition shall be lodged within 30
days after the breach of the constitution complained of.  This petition
offended against the said rule because it was presented more than 30 days
from the date of judgment complained of.
Art 119 of the Constitution sets out the functions of the Attorney General
and particularly Clause 4 (c ) provides that the Attorney General represents
Government in courts or any other legal proceedings where government is
party.  The Attorney General could not be a party to a petition against a
judgment to which Government was not a party.
Moreover, the petition sought to challenge the exercise of the judicial
functions of courts.  S.4(5) Government Proceedings Act bars any action
against Government in respect of an act or omission done by a person in
discharge of a judicial function.  The petition was untenable.
However, Art 137(3) of the Constitution, notwithstanding the rule of locus
standi, allows any person who alleges that any law or act is inconsistent
with the constitution to file a petition for a declaration to that effect.
Therefore the petitioner had a cause of action in that sense but no more.
Petition struck out with costs.
Nuwagaba Joy Vs. Emmanuel Kakuramatsi
Customary Marriage -dowry-absence of dowry-whether Customary
Marriage not proved-whether parents may waive payment of dowry.
Customary Marriage-non-registration of a Customary Marriage,
S.5 (1) Registration of Customary Marriage, Decree-whether
marriage unenforceable.
Held: Dowry is an essential aspect pf a valid customary marriage. However
the parents of the girl have the option to waive the payment of the dowry as
it was in this case.
Non registration of a customary marriage does not render it void because
S.19 of the Customary Marriages Registration Decree does not say so but
penalizes the parties to a fine of Ugandan shillings 500/- for failure to register
it.  Therefore, the failure of the intestate to register the marriage before his
demise did not render the marriage void.
Letters of Administration should be granted ordinarily to a person who has
the highest percentage of benefit from the estate.  In the case instant the
Widow/plaintiff together with her children were entitled to the biggest part of
the estate. Moreover, letters of Administration should ordinarily also be
granted to widow or widower as first choice.
Application for letters of Administration granted to widow with costs against
the defendant.
In Re Kangume Perez, An Infant
Children-guardianship-whether mother of an infant better qualified
to be appointed guardian of the infant.
Held: Although the Judicature Statute 1996 did not provide specific power to
the High Court for appointment of guardians, unlike the Judicature Act, 1967,
repealed, Ss.16 and 35 of the Statute read together empower the High Court
to Grant any remedy as it deems fit in respect of an application properly
brought before it.  In the instant cause, the Children Statute Ss.3,4,5,6,7,8
and 9 provide for the welfare of the child and impose the duty on the parents
as natural guardians.  Therefore, the application being brought by the mother
of the infant, the mother was naturally qualified to be the legal guardian of
the infant.
Application allowed.
INTERNATIONAL LAW
Bitwire Emmanuel Vs. The Representative of the Zaire
Represented by its Embassy
Vienna Conventions, Art 30 (1) -Diplomatic property-whether
attached property was diplomatic property and was therefore
immune from attachment.
Vienna Convention - Diplomatic staff-whether the persons found at
the attached premises were not members of the diplomatic staff
and therefore the premises were liable for attachment in execution.
Held: For the premises to be said to be immune from attachment in
execution as per the provisions of Art 30 (1) of the Vienna Conventions, it
must be shown that the premises house the mission or are the private
residence of a Diplomatic agent but not the kind of staff like the accountant
and his relatives as it were in this case.  Therefore, the premises were liable
for attachment.
Application dismissed. Each party to bear its own costs due to importance
of the point of law raised by the applicant.
LABOUR LAW
Ateker Ejalu Vs. Uganda Railways Workers Union & Uganda
Railways Corporation.
Trade Unions - suit against Trade union - whether maintainable.
Held: The appellant could proceed to appeal as of right against the ruling
and order of the trial judge because O.6 r 29 under which the trial judge
struck out the plaintiff's proceedings provides that such appeals shall be
as of right and not by leave of court.
The learned trial judge correctly interpreted S.19(1) (b) of the Trade
Union Decree which bars any suit against a registered Trade Union in
respondent was a registered Trade Union and the defamatory letter was
written and published by its officer on its behalf.  It follows that the
appellant had no cause of action against the first respondent.
It is true a Trade Union can be liable in cases where it is proved to have
acted outside its scope as a Trade Union but in the instant case the
defamatory letter was written for purposes of security for the officials of
the Union and since protecting the lives of Union officials is a legitimate
function of a trade Union, the Union could not be said to have acted
outside its scope.
The learned trial judge correctly held that the Union as registered was a
separate legal entity from the second respondent which could not be
held to be vicariously liable for the acts of the first respondent.
The learned trial judge was correct in not requiring first to hear evidence
before striking out the appellants pleadings against the first and second
respondents since the pleadings did not disclose a cause of action
against them.
National Insurance Corporation Vs. National Union of Clerical,
Commercial, Professional and Technical Employees.
Industrial court's award-interpretation - whether application to
interpreter Industrial Court's award not gazetted before the app-
location -ss.5,8,11 of the Trades Disputes (Arbitration and
settlement) Act.
Held: 8(1) of the Trades Disputes (Arbitration and Settlement) Act allows
the applicant to apply to the Industrial Court to interpret its award within
28 days from the date of the award.  Therefore notwithstanding S.11 of the
same Act that requires gazetting, the applicant's application to interpret
the Industrial court's award before it was gazetted was proper since it was
done within 28 days as required by S.8(1) of the Act.
the Industrial Court was empowered like any ordinary court to review its
own decisions while exercising its powers of interpretation under S.11 of
the Act.
The failure by the Industrial Court not to allow cross examination of the
witness on a new piece of evidence was not proper and it was a breach of
natural justice.  But, it did not occasion a miscarriage of justice since the
applicant's complaint was merely the procedure by which the respondent
had applied to Industrial Court for the interpretation of the award instead
of applying to the High Court for certiorari.
Uganda Bankers' (Employers) Association Vs. National Union of
Clerical, Commercial, Professional & Technical Employers.
Industrial Court's 4(2) (c ) Trader disputes (Arbitration and
settlement) Act -quorum of Industrial Court - whether independent
panelist must invariably always sit on the industrial court.
Held: S.4 The Trade Disputes (Arbitration & Settlement) Act establishes the
Industrial court and provides for its composition.  It does not state that the
independent panelist must sit on all cases that arise before the court.
The alleged error of law for purposes of certiorari, must be apparent on the
face of the record, must be self-evident.  The Court's regret that some
information was unavailable did not constitute an error of law apparent on the
face of the record because it is not the duty of court to look for evidence.
Therefore the writs for certiorari and prohibition are refused.
Application dismissed with costs.
LAND LAW
Bidandi  Ssali  Vs. The Attorney General.
Registration Land without any encumbrance at the time of the
purchase and the Registrar of titles re-installing a sublease upon
the plaintiff's Land reporting to rectify the title -whether plaintiff
bonafide purchaser for value without notice of defect in title.
Held: Although the Registrar of Title has powers to rectify errors, the
sublease had been terminated by re-entry therefore, there was no error
to correct.
The plaintiff was therefore a bonafide purchaser for value without notice
of nay other person's interest.
The expropriated properties Act 1982 was intended to act retrospectively
to retrieve properties which had fallen into wrong hands.
Christopher Katongole Vs. Yusufu Ssewanyana.
Trespass - whether trespass proved where respondent a Kibanja
holder on registered land had been compensated but resists eviction.
Held: The respondent was right to resist eviction because the proper
procedure of compensating him had not been followed.  Regulation 9
of the Land Reform Regulations 1976 sets out the manner of calculating
compensation which procedure had not been followed.  Regulation 10
requires the approval of the sub-county Land Committee which although
it does not yet exist recourse should have been had to the Uganda Land
Commission.
Bulaimu Matovu & others Vs. The Attorney General.
Public Land-whether the plaintiff are entitled to an injunction against
eviction by government from public Land.
Held: The application for an order that the plaintiffs remain on their
Bibanja until final disposal of the suit was on unsustainable on grounds
that the Government Proceedings Act precluded orders for recovery of
land against Government.  The plaintiffs were entitled to an order for
compensation only, only for the developments upon their Bibanja.
Haji Sulaiman Lule Vs. Zamu Nalumansi Nalongo Ernest,
Ndiwalana Kakembo.
Cancellation of name from certificate of title rein statement of name
an certificate of title.
Held: The word 'Transfer' is a very wide term and there is no technical
meaning to it.  But in simple terms it means the vesting of property from
one individual or group of individuals to another.  S.90(1) of RTA Cap.
205 gives powers to a proprietor of a lease or mortgage or of any
estate right or interest to transfer such interest using the forms in 7th
schedule of the Act.  The law requires that consideration for such
transfer to be stated concisely.
It is not dispute that on 21/9/1983 the first defendant became the
Registered proprietor of the suit property and under s.5 of RTA that is
conclusive evidence that she is the rightful owner thereof unless it can
shown that the title was obtained by fraud or other unlawful mean.
Court does not go beyond the fact of registration and Olinda De Souza
Figuerireda Vs. Kassamali Nanui (1962) EA 576 followed.
Allegations of fraud must be strictly proved; although the standard of
proof is not beyond reasonable doubt but something more than a mere
balance of probabilities is required.  (Passel V Makanyi (1957) EA 314
followed.
Although signing and sealing of documents are essential to constitute
a valid dead, strictly speaking attestation is not necessary but it has
become the invariable practice for parties to agreement has been
signed, sealed in the presence of a witness who himself signs.
Burden is on the plaintiff who want court to declare that he never signed
the transfer form to prove that his signature was forged.  There was no
evidence adduced by the plaintiff to prove that the signature on the
transfer form was forged. On the evidence available before court, the
plaintiff transferred the suit property to the first defendant.
The first defendant admitted that no consent to transfer was given to
her as required under s.225 ( c) (1) PLA.  The PLA is silent as to what
happens if the necessary consent is not obtained.  But court have held
that if that failure to get the necessary consent renders the transaction
illegal. Bamwite Vs. Babirye Nangobi (1977) HCB 41; Nakayima Vs.
Wadimba (1974) HCB 170.
The provision of the above section are mandatory and ought to be
complied with and to hold otherwise would defeat the purpose for which
the section was enacted.
There is no evidence direct or circumstantial which shows that the first
defendant procured the title by fraud.
Extrinsic evidence is not admissible to construe a document which
is plan and unambiguous and the intention of the parties must be
gathered from the language of the document itself.
The first and second defendant acquired no title to the suit premises
and the second defendant's name must be cancelled from the Register
book.
No evidence was adduced during the trial to prove what damages the
plaintiff suffered. He seemed more concerned with reinstatement of his
name on the Register book rather than proof of the damages.
Judgment will be entered in favour of the plaintiff against the defendants
and in the terms of s.185 RTA, the Registrar of Titles is directed to
cancel the name of the second defendant from the register book and
re-instate it with that of the plaintiff.
Bunjo Amos Vs. Barclays Bank of Uganda Ltd.
Foreclosure of mortgage before the expiry of the loan period but
were mortgagor is in arrears of installments-whether premature and
unlawful.
Held: The application for a temporary injunction would be allowed
because the applicant would suffer irreparable damage if his dwelling
house was sold before the expiry of the agreed 24 months, and
The applicant would be more greatly inconvenienced than the defendant
Bank if the property in question is auctioned prematurely, and
The applicant has a probability of succeeding in the main suit where
he seeks a declaration that the purported fore closure is premature and
unlawful.
Garuga Properties Ltd Vs. Kampala City Council.
Customary Tenant - whether such tenant has priority to the grant
of a lease over other applicants.
Held: A person holding customary tenure in respect of the Land to be
alienated must be considered for a lease if he applies.  Therefore the
plaintiff/applicant had made a prima facie since the balance of
convenience favoured him as a customary tenant whether applicants
who were not customary tenants.
There was a probability of his being entitled to the relief asked for by him.
The comparative convenience which was likely to issue from withholding
the injunction was greater than that which was likely to arise from
granting it.
Boniface Oryema Vs. Uganda Supreme Council.
Tenancy contract-eviction of tenant while tenancy still subsisted -
whether breach of contract.
Held: Since judgment was entered in favour of the plaintiff under O.9 r.6
of the Civil Procedure Rules and since such judgment was not
contested and set aside, the interlocutory judgment upheld the
plaintiff's claim to the compensation for his house hold property
detained and for wrongful eviction.
Special damages shall be computed by a factor of 3/5 of the value
of the detained goods at the current prices of the new such pieces.
An advocate without instructions cannot consent to filing a WSD out of
time and this also meant that there was no WSD filed.
Since thee was no WSD the defendant would not be heard.
Adam Vassiliadis Vs. Libyan Arab (u) Bank.
Land transfer Act - whether "Musoke" the name of the registered
proprietor, was conclusive evidence that he was an African.
Held: Neither parties had adduced evidence to prove whether or not
Musoke' was an African, the position was thereby left open and no
order of specific performance would necessarily follow since this in
effect would be to enforce an illegal contract if it turned out that Musoke
was not in fact an African.  It would follow that the remission of the suit
to the High Court for the assessment of damages would only be if the
applicant's transfer was registrable.  In the circumstances the best
thing to do is to refer the matter to the Registrar of Titles to ascertain
the status of Musoke.
J.W.R.Kazzora Vs. M.L.S Rukuba.
Registration of tittles -caveat-whether this necessarily precludes
sale subsequent.
Held: A caveat that merely stated that the caveator had an interest in
the material property did not necessary preclude a sale subsequent
since the caveat itself was not evidence of sale.
The registration of the transfer on various dates was not evidence of
fraud because it was only the transfer registered subsequent to the
expiry of the notice to the caveator that was valid and moreover since
fraud had not been pleaded in the trial court it could not be a ground of
appeal in the Supreme Court.
The respondent was a bona fide purchaser for value notwithstanding
that he was aware of the existence of the plaintiff's/appellant's caveat
because the alleged sale to the appellant which the caveat was
registered to protect was not shown to exist.  There was no evidence
about the sale to support the caveat.
A document dully addressed to the sender is presumed received at the
time which the document would be delivered in the ordinary course of
the post.  In the instant case, the trial judge found that the appellant
was served with the notice under consideration on 12/10/87 and that
therefore the notice expired on 12/12/87, but because the plaintiff
claimed that he took delivery of the said notice on 16/12/87, even then
the said notice should have expired on 16/2/88.  The appellant then had
until 14/1/88 within which to obtain an order from the court extending
the caveat but did not do so.
By the 15th May 1989, the appellant's application to extend his caveat
had already been disposed of and moreover the existence of the
application in court to extend the caveat did not preclude the effecting
of a transfer because there does not exist in Uganda any pendency
legal rule to the effect that transfers or other dealings in land should not
be registered before a suit contesting such a transfer or dealing cannot
lodge the same caveat as already removed.
The second caveat was in exactly the same terms as the first but the
appellant submitted that the second caveat was different from the first
one in that it was lodged on the basis of the suit he had filed, as a
chose in action, to be protected.  However, even the first caveat sought
exactly the same thing to protect a chose in action namely, the
benefit of the verbal agreement for sale of land.  This was tantamount to
renewing the same caveat which is contrary to the provisions of S.149(3)
of the RTA which states that as caveator cannot lodge the same caveat
as already removed.
Had there been evidence of sale, prior to that one between the
respondent and the administrator, then the subsequent transaction
would have been vitiated by mistake.  But no evidence was adduced to
support it.
It is established that a party relying on fraud must specifically plead it
and that particulars of the alleged fraud must be stated on the face of
the pleading.  In the instant case frauds was not specifically pleaded,
nor was fraudulent intent pleaded or the facts set out in the plaint such
as to create fraud.  Therefore the appellant was not entitled to rely on
fraud because it was different from the original case.
The Standard of proof of fraud is that it must be strictly proved although
not beyond reasonable doubt but something more than a mere balance
of probability is required.
Non-compliance with O.18 r7 which requires that a partly extracting an
order should submit it to the other party for approval, was not fatal
because it was not the order extracted that was the removal of the
appellant's caveat but the caveat had merely lapsed.
The Principle of law is that the first person to register land takes better
title than a person to whom the land was first sold but failed to register
it provided that there was no fraud in the registration.  And in the instant
case there was no fraud proved against the respondent.
Uganda Vs. Sam Salongo Sepuya
Right of way-whether the existence of right of way on the Land
constitutes an encumbrance on it.
Held: Mens rea was an essential element to prove forcible entry and the
appellant honestly believed that he had the authority of RCs and the
water Board to dig and lay pipes on a land he considered was a public
right of way, which therefore constituted an easement and an
encumbrance on the title of who ever claimed ownership.
Sole Electric (u) Ltd Vs.Town clerk K.K.& Nakibuka Enterprises
Tenant whether there was a subsisting tenancy between the
applicant, the owner of the premises, who had bought from the
City Council and the respondent.
Grindlays Bank (u) Ltd Vs. Edward Boazi.
Mortgage-whether receiver validly appointed where Bank gives

Held: A receiver of mortgaged property must be appointed in writing as
required by the Mortgage Decree Ss.2,3 and 5(4).  Therefore thee was

Notice of sale did not amount to a demand for money as required S.116

Chukwuma F.Obidegwu Vs. Daniel B.Ssemakadde.
Leases - where there is an actual demise of a term of three years
and the lessee is not given possession thereof -whether there was
breach of contract.
Held: The defendant's pleadings did not deny the existence of the lease
agreement because they just denied generally the grounds of the claim
of the plaintiff, without being specifics as to whether the alleged lease
agreement existed or not.
The defendant's failure to deliver possession of the said demise was a

demise of a term the lessor impliedly contracts to give the lease

Since the lessor at the commencement of the term agreed to deliver

the tenant into effective possession, and occupation of a tenantable
house by the 1st August 1991.
Charles Kassaja Stokes Vs. Registrar of Titles.
Re-entry -notice to leases, Others pinned on premises Land

Held: There was no re-entry within ss.102(b) and 113 of the RTA, for

The Registrar had already furnished reasons and the application was

Uganda Blanket Manufacturers Ltd Vs. Chief Registrar of Title.
Recovery of Land in suit-directing Registrar to cancel certificate of

Roza Mueangula Vs. Roza Nabirye H.
Laws inquo-procedure -parties and witnesses to be present,

The procedure at the locus in quo is that parties and witnesses should

A certificate of title is conclusive proof of title, but may be impeached

Frank Rwakijanju Vs. Prince Patrick Kaboyo.
Specific performance -sale of performance by taking act of
necessary.

Inspection of the land and introduction did not amount to taking

Hardship to third patties not prior to the contract, in this case squatters,

Acknowledgement of payment in writing did not constitute a written

Francis Butagira Vs. Deborah Namukasa.
Lack of consent to transfer title - whether makes the transaction
void or violable.
Public Land Act-whether lack of consent to transfer is enforceable by

Controlling authority - whether lessor was the controlling authority.
Re-entry-Relief forfeiture-whether a lessee may not pray for relief

the appellant had acted high handedly is an extraneous matter when
considering prayer for relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent.
The Period of seven years during which the appellant failed/refused to
pay rent was a period long enough to show the appellant's callous
disregard of his obligations as a lessee.  Though he assumed there
was no lessor there was no evidence that he had tried to find who the
lessor could be nor did he pay the rent upon the discovery that the
respondent was the lessor.  This was however not enough to be the
basis of the refusal to grant relief against forfeiture.
Equity would intervene to grant relief against forfeiture where the lessee
would suffer serious personal consequences if he lost the land.
The fact that the property to be lost was very valuable was not in itself
evidence of serious personal consequences.
Bona vacancia is where there was no one claiming an interest in the
property.  It is when a person dies intestate without leaving anybody
to claim an interest in the property, in which case such property would
belong to the state.  In the instant case the respondent was executrix
of the will of the original freeholder and according to S.143 of Succession
Act her acquisition of the title to the property was deemed to have
issued at the demise of the testator.  Therefore, the appellant could not
claim that at the time he sub-let the property it was bona vacantia.
In the head lease operating between the appellant and the respondent
the appellant covenanted with the respondent not to sublet the property
without the consent of the lessor.  Therefore the appellant breached the
covenant against subletting and there was no excuse in doing so.
The appellant could not under S.24 of the Judicature Act be aided under
s.32 of the Public Lands Act which deals with relief against forfeiture
for breach of covenant if the controlling authority has re-entered the
Land.
The Learned Trial Judge erred in depriving the respondent who was the
successful party of her costs without good cause.  It was not only the
respondent who acted unreasonably before the institution of the
proceedings but also the appellant.  It could therefore not be said that
it is only the respondent who was guilty of misconduct or whose
conduct might have been averted.  Secondly the respondent was
entitled to re-enter the premises upon the appellant's breach of
covenants in the lease and the appellant cannot complain that it is
the conduct of the respondent that led to this litigation.  This means
that the trial Judge exercised his discretion on wrong principles in
refusing to award the respondent her costs and this Court was therefore
entitled to interfere.
Since the appellant's suit against the respondent was not based on
trespass but on breach of covenant for quiet enjoyment, the point
whether a tenant can sue his landlord  in trespass need not be decided
the instant case.
Somali Democratic Republic Vs. Anoop Sunderial Treon
Registration of transfer -whether non registration of transfer renders
the contract of sale of Land incomplete and violable.
Mense profits - whether moneys for non use of the premises may
accrue from the purchaser of the premises under a voidable contract.
Trespass-whether proved when the defendant is in possession of the
suit premises under voidable contract of sale of the premises.
Held: The part played by the Attorney General on behalf of the
appellant in the negotiations which would otherwise have been private
between the purchaser and vendor and the fact that the appellant and
the President of Uganda had reached an agreement that the appellant
would have full use of the property in question, without first seeking the
view of the owner of the property in the matter, was evidence of duress
by a third party.
Duress does not deprive the person affected of all choice but leaves
such a person to choose between evils.  A person under duress intends
what he does though unwillingly.  The contract procured by duress, a
voidable contract at the discretion of the party to the dress.  Therefore,
since the evidence on record shows that the respondent's predecessor
was under fear for her life when she entered into the purchase deal, the
said sale was voidable at her instance.
The learned Trial Judge erred when he held that the sale contract was
incomplete due to lack of registration.  It is trite law that an
unregistered instrument operates as a contract interpreter and can
confer a right to specific performance.
Since the sale contract was not void but voidable the occupation of the
premises by the appellant was under a perfect legal contract until it was
avoided.  A voidable contract is valid until it is set aside.  Therefore
there was no question of wrongful possession and this was not a case
of trespass.  The purported return of half of the purchase moneys was
not evidence of avoidance of the contract mense profits would not under
a voidable contract until the contract was avoidable by being set aside
in an action.
Mustaq Bhegani Vs. Attorney General.
Whether validity repossessed -whether repossession validity
cancelled.
Held: The defence had failed to prove that the property ever vested in
Government.
The plaintiff must be the owner of the property since it never vested in
Government.
Sarah Karim VS. Chief Registrar of Titles.
Impeachment of good title-registered property for valuable consider-
consideration and without notice of defect in title -whether title possible and
impeachable. Notice of caveat not given.
Held: From the letter of the respondent to the applicant as well as the
affidavit of the applicant in support of the application it was clear that
when the applicant purchased the land in question, there was no caveat
on the Register against its transfer.
At Law Grindlay Bank, in absence of a caveat visible on record, had a
good title to pass to Sarah Larim the applicant.  The applicant was bona
fide purchaser for valuable consideration whose title in the land in
question must be protected.
Christopher Sebuliba Vs. Attorney General.
Holding over -tenancy, expires and tenant continues in occupation
liable to pay rent.
Held: This was a case of holding over and the appellant was entitled to
be paid rent.  The rent should reflect the market rental.
The Defence Ministry was liable for the acts of the army men.  This
made Government vicariously liable, and the proper defendant was the
Attorney General.
An eviction order against Government or its officers is prohibited by
S.15 of the Government Proceedings Act.
However, the protection afforded Government can be waived (per PLATT,
JSC) (Monetary view).
Ismail Jaffer Allibhi & others Vs. The Chief Registrar of Titles.
Registration of Titles concealing of certificate of Title.
Held: The application is proper and it does not offend section 185 of the
Registration of Titles Act.  Thought the words "any proceedings" in
Section 185 of the RTA are not defined by the said Act, a careful
perusal and interpretation clearly shows that the words do not apply to
court proceedings alone.
Livingstone Sewanyana Martin Aliker
Grant of lease-minute of approval on application form offer made
and certificate subsequently issued- grant made when minute made.
Held: The leases was granted when the application form was minuted
as approved.  At the time, the respondent's lease had not expired, and
therefore the suit land was not available for leasing.
Land committees have the duties to inspect the land applied for and
determine whether it is occupied, disputed or some person has a
legitimate interest in it.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Sheikh Mohamed Lubowa Vs. Kitara Enterprises Ltd.
Trespass to Land-elements-entry without permission of owner.
Held: Trespass to land is constituted where entry onto the land by the
defendant was without the consent of the owner.  Where there is a valid
sale agreement, there is no trespass.
Where the initial  entry is unlawful in that there was no consent, a
subsequent sale agreement legalizes it.
There was no valid sale agreement for want of consideration.
Appeal allowed.
David Sejjaka Nalima Vs. Rebecca Musoke
Bonafide purchase of for value - purchaser without notice of fraud
and without intent to wrongfully acquire Bonafide purchase -
acquires good title irrespective of the renders of the renders
defective title.
Held: A later Statute on a specific matter modified an earlier general
statute.  The RTA was enacted in 1922, later than the succession Act
which was enacted in 1906.  The former deals with the specific matter
of the registered land, whereas the latter is on the general matter of
succession to moveable and immovable property.  The RTA therefore
modified the Succession Act.
A bonafide purchaser for value is one without notice of fraud.  The
appellant was not one because he had the imputed fraud from his
advocate and avoided discovering who the rightful owner was.
Yakobo Mayanja Vs. Sanyu Musoke
Caveat-application under s.149(1) and 197 RTA to show cause why
caveat should not be removed - whether may be allowed.
Bona fide purchaser-whether applicant was not a bonafide purchaser
because of his failure to ascertain that the suit land had dispute by
perusing court files and inquiring from RCS.
Notice to caveator-whether delivery to be evidenced by receipts.
Held: The statutory notice to the caveator, the respondent had validity
been given and no receipts were required to evidence it and therefore
the respondent's caveat had lapsed.  This meant that the applicant had
purchased as a bona fide purchaser for value and without notice.
The applicant was not supposed to have inquired from RCs or even
court to ascertain himself that there was no dispute on the property.
It was enough for him to have searched on the register of land.
Okello-Okello Vs. Uganda National Examination Board.
Certificate of title-whether ground existed to impeach it.
General damages for inconvenience and disturbance upon the plaintiff's
lands-whether awardable.
Held: O.6 r 2 mandatorily requires the particularization of fraud in any
pleading thereof.  The allegation that the instruments effecting the
re-entry by the land commission were unlawful does not mean that it is
fraudulent.  It was enough for the appellant/plaintiff to produce the
certificate of Title and then the onus of proof of fraud was upon the
defendant/respondent to show that the certificate was fraudulently
obtained, therefore the learned Trial Judge erred in refusing to strike out
the pleadings in the WSD which alleged fraud without the particulars
thereof.
The Court has a discretion under O.13 r 5(2) to strike out wrongly framed
issues but in the instant case it was the learned trial judge that had
inadvertently wrongly framed the issues she should have proceeded
under O.13 r. 5(1) to amend the wrongly framed issues.
The certificate of Title to the suit property was issued in the names of
the appellant/plaintiff.  It was therefore incumbent upon the respondent
to adduce evidence to show that the issuance of the certificate of Title
was tainted with fraud.  This evidence was not tendered.  Therefore as
s.56 of the Registration of Title Act deems such certificate as a
conclusive proof thereof, the learned trial judge should have found in
favour of the appellant/plaintiff.
Sh.50,000/= general damages awarded by the trial judge immediately
after the currency reform could not be said to be in adequate on grounds
of inflation and moreover the appellant had not shown which principles
the learned trial judge had violated in the assessment of the damages
nor had he shown the extent and convenience the ground of the
damages prayed for.
Sepuya Kyamulesire Vs. Justus Bikanculika.
Fraud - whether defendant had fraudulently brought the plaintiff's
Land under the operation of the Registration of Titles Act.
Held: Fraud must be strictly proved and the plaintiff must show that the
defendant dishonestly dealt with the plaintiff's land as to have it included
in his lease.  However, the evidence on record proves that the defendant
passed through all the procedure to validly acquire the lease and the
plaintiff was not unaware of what was going on.  The plaintiff's action
would be dismissed.
Had the plaintiff succeeded he would have no award for special damages
since these had not been proved let alone needed.  Sh. 200,000/= would
have been awarded as general damages for trespass.
Popular African Traders Ltd Vs. Uganda Red Cross Society.
Transfer of title - whether the vendor plaintiff had good title to pass
to the purchaser.
Transfer of title-whether there was a valid transfer of title where no
necessary consents were obtained, no stamp duty paid no transfer deed
made.
Consent to transfer, payment of stamp duty and transfer deed-whether
all these are necessary conditions for a valid transfer of title.
Held: Because of lack of consent to transfer the suit land from the
controlling authority, coupled with lack of payment of stamp duty and the
absence of a transfer deed, the plaintiffs did not pass good title to the
defendants and were thereby in breach of the Sale Agreement.
Lawrence Mussitwa Kyazze Vs. Eunice Busingye
Damage and menses profits against government officer -whether
order to pay the same in tenable.
Held: Under Common Law rules of pleading and practice, in suits for
recovery of possession a person found in possession of the suit Land is
the proper defendant.  The appellant was the one in physical possession
and was properly sued.  It was upon him to claim indemnity from those
that put him in possession by serving upon them third party notice.
S.15(1) (b) prohibits orders of recovery of land against a government
officer such as the appellant, if the effect of the order would be the same
as an order against Government.  The appellant was in possession in his
official capacity as a Government officer.  The order to recovery against
him was therefore misconceived and a declaration of ownership of the
respondent would be substituted instead.
S.15(1)(b) constituted a restriction on the rights of citizens and would
thereby be construed narrowly.  Accordingly to imply that the order for
the payment of damages and mesne profits is veiled under what is
expressly prohibited under S.15(1)(b) would not be tenable. Therefore
these orders would not be interfered with.
James Semusabwa Vs. Rebecca Mulira
Leases - specific performance -whether an action to recover Land
brought outside the limitation period may be entertained for
purposes of specific performance.
Leases-Limitation- whether the plaintiff's cause of action was time barred-
whether an order of specific performance may still be made outside the
limitation period.
Held: S.4 (1) (a) of the Limitation Act provides that an action for specific
performance is not to be held to be time barred with brought outside the
limitation period.  This instant case sought an order for specific
performance.  Therefore it was not time barred even if it was that brought
outside the period of limitation.
Moreover the cause of action against the defendant arose at the time
she refused to execute a transfer in favour of the plaintiff in breach of the
terms of the agreement of sale in 1990 and not in 1977 when the
agreement was made.  Therefore the action was not time barred.
Edward Musisi Vs. Grindlays Bank (u) Ltd & another.
Mortgage-whether sale invalid because not recognized by mortgage
due to the paucity of the price.
Auction-whether sale invalid because valuation of the suit was done
after the sale.
Bona fide purchase-whether purchaser was guilty of fraud-whether
standard of proof of fraud not considered.
Caveats - whether caveator entitled to be heard even if his alleged caveat
was after the sale was complete.
Held: Although the 1st respondent's bank attempted to avoid the sale,
since it did not countermand its instructions of sale from the court brokers
before the auction, and since the sale was carried out as per the
mortgage deed the sale was valid.
The second respondent was a bona fide purchaser because he bought
the property at an auction and it had not been shown that before the
hummer fell he knew that the auctioneer had no power to sell or that
there was some impropriety affecting or relating to the ownership.  A
bona fide purchaser is one that honestly intends to purchase the
property in question and does not intend to acquire it wrongfully.  Such
was the second respondent.
The standard of proof in fraud cases although not beyond reasonable
doubt or more than a mere balance of probability is required in proof of
fraud.  It was necessary for the learned trial judge to indicate that he
had this in mind when he was considering the evidence.  However, this
omission did not cause injustice as he nevertheless found that fraud had
not been committed.
SS.149 and 150 require that no dealing in land should be done when
there is in force a caveat prohibiting the same.  Therefore, the learned
trial judge misdirected himself to without first having proceedings for the
removal of the caveat.  This breached the rule of nature justice as it
sought to condemn unheard the caveators.
The damages in negligence are assessed as at the date of the cause of
action and not the date of judgment.  Therefore the trial judge property
directed himself to the law and facts when he assessed the appellant's
loss basing himself on the value of his land at the date when the bank
negligently caused his loss.
David mucosa & anor Vs. Christine Nakalanzi and another
Limitation -whether suit filed outside the limitation period - whether
the suit should proceed because limitation was on issue to be
tried.
Held: As per 26 of the Limitation Act, the cause of action arose when the
deceased discovered the alleged fraud and put a caveat on the land.
Therefore, the action was with the limitation period.  Moreover, the issue
of limitation was a triable issue necessitating a full trial.  Therefore, the
preliminary objection would be overruled and the case should proceed to
full trial.
Ronald Kayaba Vs. Hussein Ali Ahmed
License-whether plaintiff respondent who had a temporary occupation-
license (T.O.L) from Town Council was a licensee or tenant.
Grant leases by Municipal Council- whether equality and constitutional
guarantees are a fetter on the power-whether the council acted ultra-vires.
License-whether the plaintiff's license was a bare one.
Customary tenancy-whether a licensee is a customary tenant-whether
such licensee can sublet his premises.
Fraud-whether plaintiff had proved that the defendant was guilty of fraud-
whether the requisite high standard of proof of fraud was attained.
Held: The plaintiff was not a bare licensee because the council by
conduct had led the plaintiff to believe that his renewal of his T.O.L was
permanent.  This meant that the plaintiff's license was coupled with a
proprietary interest which was protected by equity and the principle of
estoppel would operate to prevent revocation of a right which one party
has led the other to suppose it was permanent.  Moreover Art.13 of the
Constitution disallowed expropriation of any ones proprietary interest
without compensation.  Therefore the municipal council acted ulter-vires
when they made a grant of a lease to the defendant on the plaintiff's
premises, he occupied under a T.O.L. without due regard to
compensation.
The law requires a higher standard of proof of fraud than in ordinary Civil
cases.  The learned trial judge, had he in the instant case applied the
requisite standard of proof to the facts it cannot be said that the evidence
would be sufficient to prove fraud.  Therefore the learned trial judge
misdirected himself on the standard of proof of fraud and thereby arrived
at a wrong conclusion of a finding on fraud.
A third party Notice under O.1 r14 issues where the defendant claims to
be entitled to contribution or indemnity from the Third party.  In the
instant case the defendant never claimed anything from the municipal
council but it is only the plaintiff who claimed that the council had acted
ultra vires or arbitrarily.  Therefore it is the plaintiff under O.1 r3 CPR who
should have joined the council as a co-defendant.  Therefore the learned
trial judge misdirected himself to have held that it was the defendant to
apply for court's leave to issue a third party notice.
Francis Nansio Vs. Nuwa Walakira
Leases-limitation -whether a suit for vacant possession and
specific performance could be brought 10years after the cause of
action-whether the contract for the sale of Land was unenforceable
for limitation.
Held: The learned single judge misdirected himself when he rejected the
defence of limitation on grounds that it had not been pleaded.  The trial
judge should have afforded the parties an adjournment so that the
plaintiff cold reply to the contention by the defendant that the plaintiff's
could reply to the contention by the defendant that the plaintiff's action
was time barred instead of rejecting the defence that it had taken court
and the other party by surprise.
The appeal against the preliminary objection that the plaintiff was time
bared could not lie as a right without leave of court but an appellate court
in order that it is not bettered from its duty to give effect to the statute of
limitation, would entertain the ground of appeal against the preliminary
objection.  Moreover s.78(1) empowered an appellate court to entertain
an appeal from a decree that is defective, erroneously given, or is
irregular as long as it was set forth in the memorandum of appeal.
The plaintiff's action was for breach of contract and S.4(1) of the
Limitation Act required such action to be brought before the expiry of six
years from the date of the cause of action.  In the instant case the action
was commenced almost nine years from the date of accrual of the
cause of action.  However, S.4(6) exempts equitable claims like the
claim for specific performance from the application of the six years
limitation period and a party will take advantage of this exemption when
he is not guilty of laches.  In the instant case the plaintiff/respondent
was not guilty of unreasonable delay since he pursued his rights under
the contract as soon as the first opportunity presented itself.
Paul Kisekka Saku Vs. Seventh day Church.
Transfer of a kibanja -whether failure to give notice to prescribed
authority renders such transfer unlawful and void.
Held: Since the appellant's acquisition of the kibanja did not constitute
a creation of a new customary interest on public land, the transfer of the
a new customary interest from Nandaula to the appellant was governed
by S.4 (1) of the Land Reform Decree which requires that the transfer
should be preceded by a three months notice of the intended transfer to
the prescribed authority.  Since there was no such notice, the transfer
was unlawful and void.
S.16 of the Land Reform Decree defines Prescribed Authority as
including the Uganda Land Commission.  This includes the Local chiefs
and the land committees.
Charles Lwanga Vs. Xaverio Ddamulira
Bonafide purchaser -whether respondent was bonafide purchaser.
Held: The respondent could not be said to be a bona fide purchaser when
he knew that the appellant was in possession of the suit house and did
not inquire from him as to the position.  Possession was notice to the
respondent upon which he should have made the necessary inquiries.
When time is not of the essence to the contract it is necessary to
stipulate clearly when time will become of essence to the contract.  In
the instant case the Landlord's stipulation as to the period or the last
installment was necessary to bring the period of payment to an end,
when time became of essence.
Ibrahim Bachu & others Vs. Foods & Beverages Ltd.
Improvements on land by defendant - whether done for the convenience-
of the defendant and therefore not compensentable.
Held: The defendant carried out extensive improvement on the suit
premises which were found incomplete at time they were occupied by
the defendant.  Since these improvements would benefit whoever was
the rightful owner since they enhanced the value of the property, the
defendant would be entitled to a set off even though the plaintiffs were
entitled to vacant possession and mesne profits.
Since the defendants were informed of the plaintiffs claim of the premises
immediately they came back from exile in 1986 and the defendants
never cared to investigate their claim; the plaintiffs were entitled to
general damages of shs.1,000,000 for the inconvenience they had
suffered for non possession of their premises.
Turn Sidpra & another Vs. Uganda Rehabilitation Development
foundation.
Powers of attorney - whether a done of powers of attorney may
sue as a plaintiff with regard to an executed tenancy.
Powers of Attorney-whether application for leave to proceed with suit in
thereto does not indicate capacity.
Held: Powers of Attorney had to be strictly interpreted.  In this case
particular power did not confer upon the plaintiffs to institute legal
proceedings in their names.  Moreover the powers were defective for the
failure of the witness thereto give his particulars.  However, the
proceedings were not thereby invalid because the subject matter of the
suit was the duty to the court to adjudicate on the dispute relating to the
contract and so give effect to the wishes of the parties.
The application for leave of court for an action to continue in the name of
the living plaintiff after the death of the other, is supposed to be by
Chamber summons under O.21 r12 but because the defendant had not
objected to the application and since both plaintiffs were joint parties to
the tenancy agreement, the subject matter of the suit, the Oral
application would be allowed.
Francis Luswa Luyimbazi Vs. DAPCB.
Re-entry suit property recovered by suit - whether this constituted
effective re-entry.
Re-entry-Breach of covenant-failure to pay rent.
Cancellation of encumbrance on certificate-available if report recovered
by suit.
Held: The plaintiff by the court order effective re-entered the premises,
which was justified for breach of covenant.
The plaintiff was entitled to an order under S.185 of the RTA for
cancellation of encumbrances of tenancy on the certificate.
Chief Registrar to remove the encumbrances.
Abdul Karim Vs. L.T.Kabarebe & Mrs. Bakitari.
Certificate of titles-whether impeachable.
Bonafide purchaser-whether defendant was bonafide purchaser.
Trespass-damages for trespass.
Held: A certificate of Titles issued under the Registration of Titles Act is
conclusive evidence that the parson named in such title is proprietor
seized of the interest in the title.  The plaintiff had an impeccable lease
granted by the Uganda Land Commission and therefore the defendants
were merely trespassers.
The first defendant could not be said to be bonafide purchaser because
there was no slightest suggestion or evidence that the 2nd defendant
purported to pass any interest to him through any instrument since no
interest in land passes until it is registered.
Special damages for the destroyed onions would be shs.2,000,000 (two
million).
Namugo Ltd Vs. Tri-Star International Ltd.
Caveat - consent to transfer not given subsequent to agreement
for sublease-whether sufficient cause for subleases to lodge caveat.
Consent to transfer-whether lack thereof renders the contract for a
sublease unenforceable.
Held: The affidavit in reply by Kagoro was valid because he had a general
power of attorney to transact business on behalf of the company and he
was thereby no stranger to the affairs of the company and he could
validly depone to matters regarding the company whether as director
or agent therefore.
It was the applicant who had the obligation to obtain the requisite consent
and therefore their failure to obtain the consent could render the
agreement for a sublease unenforceable as between the applicant and
respondent.  The agreement for the sublease was a valid contract inter-
parties and it conferred a right to the respondent to sue for specific
performance or damages and the respondent's caveat was valid to
prevent any dealing in the land before the respondent was able either to
claim for specific performance or damages.
Barclays Bank of Uganda Vs. Livingstone Katende Luutu.
Mortgages-whether Bank may sell mortgage's Land a court order-
whether courts jurisdiction is expressly ousted by s.9 of the
mortgages Decree.
Held: The Bank did not require leave of court to realize its security since
by the terms of the mortgage the mortgagor irrevocably expressly
consented to the Sale without recourse to court in event of failure to
repay the loan.  This power conformed to S.9 of the mortgage Decree.
The trial Judge erred with he held that S.9 of the mortgage Decree which
allowed the mortgagee to sell without recourse to court ousted the
jurisdiction of court and was thereby a violation of the principle of natural
justice which guaranteed the right to be heard.
The trial judge should have known that there can be no principle of
natural justice which outshines an express legislative provision such as
s.9 of the mortgage Decree.  The sale without recourse to court having
been agreed by the parties it was sanctioned by S.9 of the mortgage
Decree.
Twaha Kabuye Vs. Livingstone Jjuko.
Customary tenure-whether customary acquisition invalid for failure
to get permission from prescribed authority.
Leases -fraud-whether proved-standard and burden of proof fraud.
Held: The plaintiff was in illegal occupation of the Kibenja because he
had not followed the provisions of S.4(1) of the Land Reform Decree
which requires that any transfer or of a customary interest must inform in
writing the prescribed authority 3 months in advance of his intention to
transfer his customary interest.  In the instant case the plaintiff only was
introduced verbally to the local chiefs which did not satisfy the provisions
of S.4(10 of the Land Reform Decree.  Therefore the plaintiff's customary
interest was not legally protected.
Fraud must be proved by something more than the mere balance of
probabilities and the plaintiff has the onus to prove fraud.  In the instant
case it cannot be said that the plaintiff had any land deprived of him by
fraud.
Gomba Marines & Contractors Ltd Vs. Margaret Kiwana.
Relief against forfeiture-whether application tenable where re-entry
was peaceful without ordering court, where third parties have
acquired interest in the suit land.
Re-entry-whether relief against forfeiture time barred because application
brought 6 months late.
Held: The application for relief against forfeiture will not be granted
because first of all it was brought under the wrong law because S.24(4)
of the Judicature Act confers upon court powers to grant relief against
forfeiture where the re-entry has been effected by court order, and yet in
the instant case the re-entry was peaceful.  Secondly, relief against
forfeiture is an equitable remedy and yet one of the maxims of equity
had been breached by the delay in bringing the application, which was
brought after the expiry of 6 months.
Ruth Sirimuzawo Vs. Paulo Mukasa & others.
Registered land - whether a person not being a personal represent-
representative may deal in one land of the intestate-whether such person
can bring an action for recovery of the land of the intestate.
Bonafide purchaser-whether defendant was bonafide purchaser.
Fraud-whether defendant's title was vitiated by fraud.
Held: A personal representative of the deceased must be appointed by
law to administer the estate of the deceased.  Such administration can
not be merely assumed as per the Provisions of the Succession Act as
amended.  And any person dealing in land registered in the names of the
intestate must be a personal representative of the intestate as appointed
by law.  It is only such person who can bring an action in court regarding
the land. The plaintiff did not have locus to bring this suit she was not an
administrator of the estate of the deceased as provided by S.143 of the
Registration of Titles Act and S.179 of the Succession Act.
The plaintiff cannot be a customary heir to the estate of the deceased
because no last funeral rites were made and therefore the plaintiff has
never been recognized as the heir of the deceased.
The plaintiff was not the legal heir because she was not as near in
relationship to the deceased as another living sister of the deceased as
required by S.3 of the Succession (Amendment) Decree.
No proof had been furnished that the defendants refrained from making
inquiries which an honest purchaser would have made.  The official in
the land registry acted upon the certificate of succession, though
fraudulent to effect the disputed transfers.  The defendants were not
guilty of fraud but were bonafide purchasers.  Suit discussed.
Hajati Zirabwa & another Vs. Yakobo Ntate
Limitation -whether recovery of land time barred.
Held: The action was brought after the expiry of 12 years since the
defendant acquired the land.  Since this is an action for recovery of land,
the action must have arisen at the date the defendant acquired the land.
The plaint was therefore time barred and must be rejected.
Yosia Ofumbi Vs. Nagongera Farmers & another.
Customary tenure -whether the growing of seasoned crops by the
plaintiff on the suit land constituted the plaintiff as a customary
tenant.
Lease-fraud-whether established where lease granted without customary
tenant being heard.
Held: There was undisputed evidence that the plaintiff used to grow
seasoned crops on one part of the suit and which thereby established
his unsufructory rights.  S.24(1) of the Public Lands Act recognizes
such tenancy as customary tenancy.
Since the defendant had had a dispute over the suit land in the RC courts
but went ahead and processed a title over the land thought the 2nd
defendant Land Commission without first suit solving the dispute, means
that the first defendant had knowledge of the existence of the plaintiff's
unregistered interest in the disputed land but knowingly and wrongfully
defeated the plaintiff's interest by registration and this constituted fraud
on the part of the 1st defendant.
The fact that the plaintiff had not been heard in defence of his customary
interest before the 1st defendant could take a lease of the dispute land,
constituted a breach of the principle of natural justice, the right to be
heard.  The plaintiff was therefore entitled to a redemacation of the
disputed land for the rectification of the register or he could elect to be
compensated.
Aram Katumba Vs. Uganda Telecommunication Corporation.
Limitation -trespass-whether because 14years have elapsed
since the alleged cause of action therefore the suit was time
barred.
Leases - transfer of title - whether initiated by lack of consent since the
company transferee was Non-African.
Leases - Consent to transfer - whether consent given after transfer had
no legal effect.
Leases-Bonafide purchaser-whether purchaser was bonafide purchaser
since fraud had neither been pleaded nor proved.
Held: The action in trespass was not time barred because trespass was
a containing tort for which the injured party can sue from the date of
cessation of the wrong and in this case the wrong had not ceased.
The belated granting of consent to the transfer of lease from the Mailo
owner to the non-African company had no legal effect and could not
validate the transfer retrospectively.  The transfer retrospectively.  The
transfer had been made in breach of the provisions of S.2 of the Land
Transfer Act which invariably requires consent of the Minister prior to
transfer of Land to a non-African.  Moreover, it could not be said that the
transfer had been made contingent on the Minister's consent.  It was
clear the parties had intended a final transfer which was void for lack of
consent.
However, since the plaintiff was a third party who acquired title from the
Uganda Mixed Farm Ltd his title could only be impeached by proof of
fraud.  But the defendant had neither pleaded nor proved fraud.  Therefore
the plaintiff was a bonafide purchaser for value without notice of nay
defect in the Title of his predecessor and not privy to any fraudulent act.
The plaintiff's action against the defendant in trespass had therefore been
proved since his title under S.189 of the RTA prevailed against the title
of the reversionary under S.61 of the RTA.  The defendant claimed under
the title of the reversionary tile the plaintiff claimed as the holder of the
legal title.
The damages awardable for the trespass are to be calculated as the
market value of the land unlawfully occupied by the defendant and
Shs.400,000/= per acre was a fair market rate to that effect.
Eriyasafu Mudumba Vs. Wilberforce Kaluse
Trespass-limitation -whether trespass was a continuing act.
Held: The evidence from the witnesses proved that the land in dispute
clearly belonged to the defendant/respondent.
The case of Florence Joyce Mutesi Vs. Andereya Kinyamule (1976) HCB
64 was not binding as a precedent as it was based on conflict decisions
namely that the issue of the limitation does not affect customary tenure
and yet at the same time providing that S.6 of the Limitation Act affected
customary tenure.
Since the plea that the defendant was encroaching on the plaintiff's land
was a case of trespass and trespass is a continuing tort, the time started
to run when the encroachment is said to have began, I.e. in 1984, and
was still continuing at the time of the suit.
Petelonia Mpirirwe Vs. Oliver Ninsabimaana.
Lease offer-death of offeree-whether thereby the plot and reverted to
the controlling authority - whether thereby the plot was available
for re-allocation.
Held: The evidence that the deceased paid shs.100,000/= as a fine for
cohabiting with the defendant was no evidence of payment of bride price
which was an essential pre-requisite for a valid marriage.  Therefore, the
defendant was not the widow of the deceased and was not entitled to the
grant of Letters of Administration.
The evidence of similarity in physical features between a child and the
alleged parent is admissible to prove paternity even if the evidence is not
conclusive.  The failure by the defendant to adduce evidence of genetical,
biological and physical features similar to those of the deceased made
court fail to presume that the alleged twins were fathered by the deceased.
the controlling authority after having allocated the plot to the deceased,
the plot was no longer available for re-allocation merely because the
offer had demised.  The allocated plot devolved on the estate of the
deceased for the administration by the Administrator of the deceased's
estate.
The plaintiff was entitled to the grant of the letters of Administration since
she was the rightful widow of the deceased and her application had not
been contested by the beneficiaries. Case allowed.
Resity Nantongo Vs. David Kayondo.
Equitable owner-lessee-whether lease had priority of protection of
her interest against the equitable owner.
Held: The plaintiff /respondent had not even attempted to challenge the
existence of the lease of the appellant herein.  The lease therefore
sidestepped the issue as to who of the parties had purchased the land.
The lessee had legal title as lessee and yet the respondent/plaintiff had
no title at all but could only claim in equity.
The plaintiff respondent had failed to show such a case as would be the
basis upon which court should interfere with an admitted legal rights of the
lease in favour of merely alleged equitable right of the purchaser without
transfer.  Therefore, the learned trial judge erred in granting the order for
an interim injunction when the applicant had not shown substantial
grounds for denoting the existence of the respondent/appellant's legal
right to the lease in the suit property.  Therefore the interim injunction
would be discharge. Appeal allowed.
Famous Cycle Agency Ltd & ors Vs. Manshulular
Certificate of title s.58 RTA -adverse claims for rent by different
landlords - whether the defendant with a certificate of title was the
entitled to the rent.
Held: o.31 R 2(a), (b) and ( c) provides that a litigant that claims no
interest in the subject matter so the suit but is merely concerned with
court's directions as to which of the various claimants he should make the
required satisfaction, then the proper procedure is by interpleader.
Therefore, in the instant case since the tenants/plaintiffs were interested
in knowing as to whom to pay rent, they should have bought the suit by
way of interpleader.
S.58 of the Registration of Titles Act provides that a Certificate of Title is
conclusive evidence of ownership.  In the instant case it was the first
defendant who had a Certificate of Title in his names and was therefore
the owner of the suit property to whom rent must be paid.
Uganda Commercial Bank Vs. Kyagambiddwa Growers Ltd.
Action for affection s.184 RTA objector proceedings whether a
respondent in objector proceeding under O.19r55 CPR may rely on
fraud to impeach the registered title of the objector.
Held: Allegations of fraud were only appropriate in an action for ejectment
under S.184 of the Registration of Titles Act.  The instant proceedings
were merely objector proceedings in which it was not possible to
registered propriator. objector's title.
Objector's action allowed and costs against respondent bank.
Sara Nakabate Serubugo Vs. Robina Nakidali
Fraud -cancellation of certificate of title s.184 RTA-whether a
cancellation certificate of title may be ordered due to fraud.
Held: Although the plaintiff did not explicitly plead non est factum, it was
clear that her claim was based thereto as she pleaded that she had
signed documents presented to her by her daughter who had informed her
that the purpose of the documents was to help her daughter the defendant
to collect the plaintiff's certificate of title from Mukono Land office on her
behalf.  Therefore, the plaintiff had successfully pleaded non est factum.
While locally there is no standard form precedents for pleadings,
particularly the pleading of fraud, and resort is often had to English
precedents, particulars of fraud may nevertheless be found sufficiently
given in any pleading even if a particular format has not been adhered to.
In the instant case the plea that the defendant had informed the plaintiff
that she should sign the documents she had given her to enable the
the defendant collect the certificate of title from Mukono Land Office,
whereas, the plaintiff was in effect signing a transfer and consent from of
her land in favour of the defendant, was sufficient particulars of fraud given,
though not pleaded in a standard form.
S.184 Registration of Titles Act empowers court to order the cancellation
of a Certificate of Title where fraud had been sufficiently proved and
cancellation of the Certificate of Title would be ordered.
Nazarali Hassanali Sayani Vs. Edward Mperese Nsubuga.
Expropriated properties -appropriation whether the property of the
plaintiff was appropriated-whether re-entry by a lessor amounts to
appropriation -whether expropriated properties Act applied to
dealings after the coming into force of the Act.
Expropriated Properties Act-Certificate of repossession and letter, of
repossession - whether they mean the same thing.
Registered Land - bonafide purchase s.189 RTA - whether defendant was
a bonafide purchaser.
Held: Since the plaintiff's land before the re-entry by the landlord, had not
been taken over or appropriated the plaintiff did not have a cause of action
under S.1(a), (b), ( ) of the Expropriated Properties Act. His suit was
misconceived.  The re-entry was lawful and was not precluded by the Act
since the re-entry took place after the coming into force of the Act.
The letter of repossession was of no consequence since it was not
provided for in law.  The Expropriated Properties (Repossession and
Disposal Regulations) empowered only the Ministry of Finance to issue a
Certificate of Repossession. A letter of repossession by a Minister of
State for Finance was not provided for in law.
The defendant's proprietary interest could not be defeated because he
was a bonafide purchaser for value without notice of any defect in title.
He was protected by S.189 of the Registration of Title Act.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Joyce Kasule Kweguya Vs. Apollo Matovu & 3 others.
Customary right in land - long possession and use-whether
plaintiff had possessed and used the suit land so long and whether
this was evidence of title.
Caveat-S.149 (2) Registration Titles Act - beneficiary under a will- whether
caveator was a beneficiary under a will-whether caveator was a beneficiary
under a will - whether therefore caveat could not lapse without a court
order.
Held: Though the deceased died intestate, he died testate to the extent
that the will did not define the property it purported to devise to the
beneficiaries.
No trust was created because the will never defined the property the
subject of the trust.  Since no trust was created the first defendant was
free to make a statutory declaration of the loss of the duplicate Certificate
of Title pursuant to S.67 RTA.  This section allowed any person to make
a statutory declaration.  Case dismissed with costs.
Norah Kawooya Vs. Ahmed Kawooya
Joint tenancy -s.51 registration of titles Act - whether interest in
land was effectively transferred where transfer instrument was not
registered.
Joint tenancy-whether a joint tenant can effectively pass her interest in
land by transfer to another joint tenant.
Held: It was not disputed that the land was jointly acquired by both the
plaintiff and the defendant in 1983.  Both were joint tenants and the
plaintiff's interest in the suit property was a joint tenancy.
From the evidence on record it has been shown that the plaintiff
contributed more than 50% of the developments on the suit property and
the defendant adduced no evidence in rebuttal.  The defendant advanced
no evidence in rebuttal adduced no evidence in rebuttal.  The defendant no
evidence in rebuttal to show how the developments were carried out by
him and from what source.
The defendant advanced no evidence to prove that the plaintiff executed
the alleged transfer of the suit property.  Further there is no evidence to
shoe that the alleged transfer was registered as required by S.51
Registration of Titles Act.  Be that as it may, the plaintiff's interest in the
suit property could not have been passed to the defendant by way of
execution of a transfer of her interest.  Accordingly the plaintiff never
divested herself of her interest in the suit property.
The defendant shall pay Ush 31, 000,000/= to the plaintiff if he wishes to
take over her moiety and retain the suit property.  Alternatively the suit
property shall be sold and the proceeds be shared equally by the parties.
Ratilal Nanchand Sheth Vs. C.L.K Ssali.
Removal of caveat S.149(2) R.T.A S.2 R.T.A
Whether person with repossession certificate falls within the
description of persons entitled to remove caveat under the Act.
S.1(2) Expropriated Properties Act - Whether person who bought
property formerly belonging to the expelled Asian has better title than the
Asian himself.
Held: It is not in dispute that inconsistencies in affidavits however minor
cannot be ignored since a sworn affidavit is not a document to be treated
lightly.  In the instant case however, the inconsistency is so innocent,
frivolous and not so serious so as to amount to a spurious and deceitful
statement.  It does not therefore vitiate the affidavit and accordingly the
objection is overruled.
The first respondent could not move the A.G. Commissioner of the
Registration since the first respondent is not the registered Proprietor of
the property caveated.  Consequently the notice issued by the Ag.
Commissioner to the applicant had no legal basis and consequence.
The applicant has no protectable interest, proprietary or compensatory
and therefore had no right to caveat property in which he had no interest.
Since this application is based on no interest at all, it is accordingly
dismissed.
Stephen Kalani Vs. Satwant Kaur
Surrender of lease -registration there of s.107 RTA - whether the
registered surrender of lease was nullified by s.1(2) of the Expro-
priated properties Act.
Held: S.I.(2) of the Expropriated Properties Act nullified all dealings in
properties that vested in Government under S.4 of the Assets of Departed
Asians Decree.  Since the alleged instrument of surrender was registered
after the coming into force of the Assets Departed Asians Decree, the
registration of the alleged surrender of the lease was null and void.
Under S.14 of the Expropriated Properties Act the person aggrieved by
the decision of the Minister regarding the granting of a certificate of
repossession can certificate but should not file an ordinary suit
Suit dismissed with costs.
Mangalita Namirembe Vs. Kalamatu Tebukola
Rates -ownership of kibanja -whether in absence of evidence to the
contrary, the payer of local government rates for the kibanja is the
owner thereof.
Held: The matter in controversy was a debt of Ush 200,000/= old currency
which had been reduced to Ush 2000/= by the Currency Reform Statute of
1987.  therefore the debt Ush 2000/=, the RC Courts had pecuniary
jurisdiction to entertain the suit as per S.4 RC Judicial Powers Statute.
Since there was no contract, if the appellant mistakenly was paid part of the
money required to be paid to her by the clan elders' meeting, it was money
received for no consideration, received under a mistake of fact and was
recoverable.
In absence of evidence to the contrary a payer of rates in whose names
receipts appear, is the owner of the property and the Chief Magistrate erred
in ignoring the appellant's receipts to prove her ownership of the property in
absence of evidence to the contrary.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Mukasa Lubansa & others Vs. Combined Building Company.
Leases-re-entry s.102(b) -relief against forfeiture s.24 judicature
Act-whether relief against forfeiture may not be granted because
third parties had acquired interest in the property.
Held: A Company is a legal entity separate from its shareholders. Therefore
the departure of the shareholders of the defendant company did not affect
its capacity to own the property in its names under Decree 27/73.
The law is that relief against forfeiture cannot be granted where the parties
have altered their positions.  In the instant case the land had been leased to
a third party.  Therefore the prayer for relief against forfeiture would not
succeed.
