Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff and relief against forfeiture refused.
Famous Cycle Agencies Ltd & 4 others Vs. Mansukhalal
Ramji Karia & others.
Title to property s.56 RTA-whether therefore owner.
Held: O.15 r (1) CPR provides that court, has discretion for sufficient cause
shown to grant adjournment.  The discretion is judicially reasonably
exercised upon proper material, thus considering the party's conduct in the
case and the opportunity he had in getting ready and the truth & sufficiency
of the reason alleged by him for not being ready.  In the instant case the trial
judge was correct in refusing the adjournment because the reason given for
the adjournment, that the second respondent had withdrawn from the case,
was not a surprise to the plaintiffs/appellants.  This fact had been known by
counsel for a long time.
O.22 rr 1 (3)+7 provide to the effect that a defendant's withdrawal can only
be by leave or court upon application by chamber summons.  Therefore the
trial Judge in accepting the withdrawal of the 2nd respondent's defence
without a formal application.  However, this did not occasion a miscarriage
of justice.
A certificate of title is conclusive evidence that the registered person in the
owner therefore, except upon proof of fraud, as per the provisions of SS.56
and 184 RTA. Therefore, the learned trial Judge was correct in finding that
the first respondent was the true landlord or the appellants.
The learned trial Judge erred when he found that rent payable to the first
respondent was from 1st July 1991 instead of from 15th December 1992.
Appeal dismissed except for amount of rent payable.
Mukasa Lubansa & 3 others Vs. Combined Building Co. Ltd.
Leases-relief against forfeiture-whether application therefore not
tenable because third parties had taken interest in the property.
Held: Relief against forfeiture cannot be granted where the parties have
altered their positions.  In the instant case the landlord leased the property
to a third party.  Therefore, the landlord had effectively reentered.
Suit allowed. An order for forfeiture and cancellation of lease granted.
John William Kihuku & 2 others Vs. Personal Representative
of RT.REV.Eric Sabiti.
Fraud - obtaining registration of land already offered to another
person -whether evidence of fraud.
Held: Where a person procures registration to defeat an unregistered
interest on the part of another person of which he is proved to have
knowledge then such person is guilty of fraud.  Therefore the defendant was
guilty of fraud in the instant case when she procured registration of the piece
of land over which the plaintiffs were known customary tenants, in
possession of an offer to lease the same land.
However, since the issue of fraud had arisen in an earlier suit between the
same parties and the same issue was litigated upon on its merits and
concluded in favour of the defendants where fraud was found not to have
been proved, then the present suit was res judicata and not maintainable.
Even if it could be said that the trial magistrate court before which the
parties first litigated was not a competent court for purposes of res judicata
because the Magistrate court had no powers to cancel a certificate of title,
it should be known that the matter went to the High Court on appeal, the
court possessed of the competent jurisdiction.  The High Court on appeal
held that fraud had not been proved.  Therefore, it would still be held that
case was res judicata and maintainable.
There was no evidence on balance of probabilities that the plaintiffs were
disable to file the suit within 12 years because of harassment by
government functionaries.  Therefore the plea of disability would not hold.
Case dismissed with costs.
Resty Nantongo Vs. David Kayondo
Interests-legal and equitable interests - whether leasehold super
ceded on equitable purchase.
Held: The leasehold interest being legal superceded the equitable which the
plaintiff had obtained when he purchases the property without transferring it.
Therefore, the learned trial judge erred in granting an injunction to defeat an
admitted right in favour of an alleged equity.
Appeal allowed.  Interim injunction discharged.
Charles Kabunga Vs. Christopher Baryaruha & others
Recovery of land against registered proprietor s.185 Registration of
titles Act -Application by notice of motion -consequential order-
whether the correct procedure is by originating summons.
Recovery of land against a registered proprietor - whether it is an action in
rem or personal.
Held: An Advocate is not allowed to depone to matters that are not purely
formal but contentious as per r 8 of the Advocates (Professional Conduct)
Regulations 1977. when counsel deponded to the value of the land he was
deponing to a contentious matters since this was not a formal fact in his
knowledge.  Therefore his affidavit was materially defective and would not be
relied upon in court.
The procedure of originating summons applies to questions that arise
between the executors, administrators or trustees on one hand and creditor,
devisee or next of kin who sets up a claim on the other.  In the instant case
the applicant's claim does not fall in that category of questions because the
applicant is a person who has obtained judgment for the recovery of
interest in land against a registered proprietor under S.185 RTA.  The
application by notice of motion was properly brought by notice of motion.
Application allowed.  Registrar to cancel the relevant certificates of title and
transfer the same to the applicant.
Ajiri Namagembe Vs. Attorney General
Tenancy agreement - breach of user clause where occupants
operated a nursery School in the premises the tenancy in respect
of which was for residence -whether failure by land to terminate
the tenancy meant that she had waived her right.
Tenancy - vacation of premises-whether tenant/defendant was in breach of
tenancy agreement when he vacated the demised premises without properly
handing them over to the landlord-quantum of damages for breach.
Tenancy-disrepair of demised premises-whether tenant was liable for the
despairing of the demised premises-quantum of damages therefore.
Held: Since the plaintiff landlord knew that the tenant was operating a
nursery school within the premises and never terminated the tenancy, she
must have waived her right and acquiesced to the change of user of the
premises.  She would therefore recover nominal damages only.
The tenant was in breach of tenancy agreement when it abandoned the
demised premises without handing them over properly to the landlord.  The
plaintiff would therefore be awarded Ush.150,000/= per month for one year
as rental income lost.  The claim for three years would be rejected because
the plaintiff was bound to mitigate her losses.
The tenant was liable for the disrepair of the demised premises and Ush
2,036,5000/= proved by the valuer would be awarded to the plaintiff.
Ush. 10,000/= would be awarded for breach of contract of tenancy.
Suit allowed.
Maria Kevina Sentamu Vs. Kikondo Kyeterekera.
Registered land -jurisdiction-whether an L.C Court has jurisdiction
to try a case involving land registered under the RTA.
Held: Since the subject matter of the suit concerned land registered under
the Registration of Titles Act, the L.C. court did not have jurisdiction for
purposes of res judicata.
preliminary objectives dismissed.
Chris Akena Onapa Vs. Mohammed Hussein Rashid Punjani.
Lease -expired lease-application for renewal -whether lessee
whose lease expires and applies for renewal is a tenant at will-
whether such expired leasee has any interest in the property
whose lease has expired.
Lease-Urban Authorities - non fulfillment of development conditions-whether
thereby no lease grantable.
SS.1(2)(b) of The Expropriated Properties Act allows for repossession any
property, which at the time it was expropriated had a valid subsisting lease.
In the instant case, since no renewal of the lease had been effected by the
controlling authority in favor of the respondent at the time the respondent
became departed Asian the suit property was not expropriated and was not
governed by the Expropriated Properties Act.  The suit property was still
vested in the Controlling Authorities, which had validly executed a lease in
favor of the appellant.
The respondent was not a tenant at will since he had not fulfilled the
conditions for the renewal of the lease.
Appeal allowed.
Isreal Kabwa Vs. Martin Banoba Musiga.
Registration -whether appellant obtained registration by fraud-
whether appellant was a bonafide purchaser for value.
Held: A beneficiary of the estate of the intestate has locus to sue in his own
name to protect the estate of the intestate for the own benefit without first
having letters of Administration.  Therefore the respondent being heir to the
estate of his father had locus to bring this suit without having first sought
letters of Administration.
Moreover the belated grant of the letters of Administration validated all the
intermediate actions related to the estate including the filling of the suit.
The trial Judge was entitled to frame fraud as an issue and to decide the
same as proved against the appellant even though the respondent's
pleadings had given no particulars thereof because the respondents led
evidence at the trial to prove fraud without any objection from the appellant
and the appellant submitted on the same.  Therefore the appellant was
never prejudiced by the Judge's approach.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Sharif Osman Vs. Haji Haruna Mulangwa
Mesne profits -recovery thereof -whether delay in enforcement of
specific performance disentitled purchaser from recovery mesne
profits.
Held: A vendor of real property retains a lien in the property for the unpaid
balance of the purchase money.  However, in the instant case the
agreement of the parties provided a specific time when the purchaser would
take possession.  Since the agreement was prepared by counsel for the
appellant the clause providing for taking possession would strictly be
construed against the vendor/appellant so that it is taken that delivery of
possession was not contingent upon completion of purchase price; since
upon payment of the deposit property passed to the purchaser.
The principle at Common Law is that in absence of a contrary intention time
is of essence of a contract even though the parties have not expressly
provided it.  In the case instant however, it took two years for the appellant/
vendor to claim to rescind the contract.  This was evidence that time of
payment of the purchase price was not of essence to the contract and
therefore the respondent/purchaser was not in breach of the contract for
failure to pay the balance by the agreed date.
If the appellant/vendor had successfully rescinded the contract he would not
be entitled to keep the deposit.
The respondent/purchaser was not entitled to mesne profits and general
damages because he had in ordinarily delayed in enforcing specific
performance.
Appeal dismissed except as to general damages.
Busiro Coffee Farmers & Dealers Ltd Vs. Tom Kayongo & 2ors.
Leases-bonafide purchaser-whether plaintiff was bonafide
purchaser when he leased suit property from the lessor whose
re-entry was challenged.
Trespass-whether proved against defendants who were in
occupation by the time plaintiff acquired interest in the suit property.
Mesne profits -quantum.
Held: Without proof of fraud the register should be treated as a notice to the
whole world that the person whose names appear therein is the lawful owner.
The plaintiff having acquired his lessee from the lesser without any proved
fraud he was a bonafide purchaser and was entitled to bring this action in
trespass against the defendants.
Once the lease has been determined the parson who remains in possession
becomes a trespasser.  An action in trespass can be maintained by a
person who is entitled to possession.  The plaintiff, being the registered
lessee was entitled to file this action in trespass against the defendants.
Where a defendant remains in wrongful possession he is liable to pay
mesne profits to the person entitled to possession.  In the instant case the
defendant's wrongful possession started in November 1990 when they
refused to give vacant possession to the plaintiff.
Since the defendants did not challenge the figure of Shs. 500,000/= claimed
by the plaintiff as mesne profits per month, and the period of trespass was
60 months, then, the plaintiff was entitled to Shs.30 million which would be
reduced to Shs. 25 million to cater for imponderables.
The defendants had failed to prove the claim for special damages put forward
as a counterclaim.
Suit allowed.
Kalani Stephen Vs. Satwart Kaur
Leases-surrender of lease by lessee to landlord-whether surrender
takes effect upon registration only-s.107 RTA.
Held: In law the effect of a surrender is that the lease merges in the
Landlord's reversion and it is extinguished.  Since there is no time limit for
the registration of a lease, the learned trial judge erred in holding that the
surrender could only take effect upon registration in 1977 because, the
surrender was effective upon execution in 1972 inter-parties.  The
respondent was bound by the effect of her surrender of the lease, which is
to the effect that the property had no encumbrance and third parties were
free to take out leases on the same.  This is because unregistered
instruments are binding inter-parties and the respondent was bound by her
instrument of surrender she executed.
Appeal allowed.
Allibhai Ismail Jaffer & 2 ors Vs. Nandlal Harjivan Karia & anor
Purchase of land-passing of property-whether upon payment of
deposit or completion of payment.
Legal interest and equitable interest-whether must pass
concurrently to purchaser.
Bonafide purchaser-fraud-whether the respondents were not
bonafide purchasers because guilty of fraud.
Held: In a sale of immovable property, upon payment of a deposit, property
passes to the purchaser who acquires an equitable interest in the property
and the vendor becomes a trustee who holds the property in trust for the
purchaser.  The legal title remains with vendor until the final payment when
the legal title remains with vendor until the final payment when the legal title
passes to the purchaser.  Therefore, the 1st respondent was a lawful
purchaser of the suit property who acquired an equitable interest in the
same when he paid the deposit to the appellants.
Where an agent does not disclose the principal for whom he acts, such an
agent acts for himself.  Such an agent is liable for all the liabilities that may
occur in the transaction but also may take full benefit of the contract.  In the
instant case, though the 1st respondent, when he paid the deposit to the
appellants, claimed to be acting as broker for another buyer, because the
first respondent failed or refused to disclose the actual purchaser for whom
he claimed to the working, the law would recognize him as the purchaser of
the suit premises.
In order that a person may be found guilty of fraud, the alleged fraud must be
visited on the person alleged to have committed the same.  In the instant
case the 1st respondent.  Therefore the trial Principal Judge was entitled to
hold that the 1st respondent was a bonafide purchaser who had in turn
passed clean title to the 2nd respondent.
S.1(2)(a) of the Expropriated Properties Act nullified dealings in property
expropriated by government after the Expropriation Decrees 29/72 and 27/73
which dealing could include the transfer of the property to the purchaser by
by the Custodian Board as was the fact in the instant case.  However, since
the purchaser had acquired his equitable interest far before the Expropriation
Decrees, his equitable interest was not subject of the Expropriated
Properties Act.  The Custodian Board was entitled to effect a transfer in
favor of the 1st respondent because the 1st respondent was the owner of
property in law since property passed to him before the law prohibiting
transfer and sales of such property was promulgated.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Mulindwa Edward V. Sarha Kalanda
Caveat-S.149(1) Registration of Titles Act- whether caveator
sufficiently has disclosed in affidavit that she has an interest
whether or equitable to protect- whether  failure to do so may render
caveat removable.
Held: The rights of husband and wife regarding matrimonial property are
personal inter se and these rights do not affect third parties.  Therefore, the
applicant's right over the property he had purchased could not be legally
encumbered by the spouse's claim for a matrimonial home over the same
property.
S.148 RTA empowers any person who has a legal or equitable interest or
estate in land accruing under an unregistered instrument to lodge a caveat
to protect such interest or estate against third parties.  The section also
requires the caveator to disclose the nature of his interest in the land.  In the
instant case the caveator/respondent did not disclose that she had either a
legal or equitable interest capable of being registered as a charge on the
land, when her husband was still alive.  This is because the matters
deponed to in her affidavit in support of the caveat were not sufficient to
disclose the nature of her interest and whether such interest was
protectable in law.
Application allowed.  Caveat vacated with costs.
Uganda Commercial Bank Vs. Mrs Bushuyu
Equitable mortgage S.138 Registration of Title Act-non-registration
thereof-whether not enforceable.
Held: S.138 enjoins an equitable mortgagee to invariably register a caveat
on the mortgaged property.  In the subjudice case, when the borrowing
company deposited the certificate of title with the plaintiff, the plaintiff
became an equitable mortgage, but was enjoined to register a caveat on the
suit property, failing which the equitable mortgage would not be enforced by
foreclosure.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Makerere University Vs. St. Mark Education Centre & anor.
Bona fide purchaser-purchase outside register-whether thereby no
title conferred-whether S.189 Registration of Titles Act irrelevant.
Held: The fraud committed by the predecessor in title of the defendants
could not be visited on the defendants as there was no evidence to suggest
that the defendants were party to or knew about the fraud.  However, the
fraud as committed was outside the  register since the alleged block and
plot never existed on the mailo register.  Therefore the defendants received
no title from the alleged original mailo owner and were therefore not
protected by S.189 of the Registration of Titles Act.
Suit allowed with costs.
Omari Mohamed Capt. Vs. Attorney General.
Mesne profits-quantum.
Held: Because of the re-entry the substratum of the contract was non-
existent.  And yet the defendant had represented to the plaintiff that he had
suit property available for sale and because of this representation, the plaintiff
had paid money to the defendant, and yet the representation was false.
Therefore, the defendant is liable for misrepresentation and the breach of
contract.
The defendant would pay to the plaintiff the market value of the property as
at the date of judgment as special damages plus shs.650,000/= per month
from date of breach as mesne profit.
Shs. 2 million would be paid as general damages.
Suit allowed with costs.
Grindlays Bank (U) Ltd & Kampala Bottlers Ltd Vs. Uganda
Bottlers Ltd.
Transfer of title-invalid transfer thereof-whether thereby title
impeachable.
Held: The receivers were validly appointed by the bank pursuant to the
powers conferred upon the Bank by the debenture.  The document of
appointment having been written by on of the receivers with authority of the
bank, the receivers were thus appointed in writing.  The relevant document
concerning the appointment need not include "appointment" in its body.
The Mortgage Decree was not applicable to the debenture as it was not
registered with the register of titles but only with the company registry.
S.113 Evidence Act provides that a person is estopped from complaining
against the act of another, which act has been done with the acquiescence
of that person.  In the instant case, the Managing Director of the respondent
was present in the meeting where the bank appointed the receivers and in
fact handed over to the receivers the keys and cash and books of account
of the respondent.  He never protested against the appointment of the
Directors then.  The respondents were therefore estopped from challenging
the validity of the appointment.
Since the appointment of the receivers was valid, so was their transfer of the
suit property to the appellants in appeal No.16/95.
S.184 gives fraud as the only basis upon which title may be impeached.
Since by the time the respondents filed the suit the appellants in appeal
No.16/95 were already registered sufficient to impeach the appellant's title.
Appeals allowed with costs.
Nakadde Imelda Ndiwalungi Vs. Nsereko Roy Busuulwa
Caveats-extension thereof S.149 RTA-whether caveat had expired-
whether caveat cannot therefore be extended.
Caveats-expiration thereof-time of service of notice to show cause-
whether reckoned from date of posting.
Held: When notice is sent by post, the date of reckoning of time is the date
of receipt of the notice in ordinary post business and not the date of posting.
Since in the instant case the applicant claimed to have received the notice
on 25th October after it was sent by post on 10th October, the date claimed
to have been received would be the date taken from which to reckon time
of 60 days of the notice.
From 25th October the 60 days expired on the 24th of December which was
a Sunday.  In accordance with S.34(1) Interpretation Decree, the last day
being a Sunday, the expiry day was the next non excluded, day which was
27th December.  This application having been filed on 28th December,
means that the caveats had expired and there was nothing to extend.
Application dismissed with costs.
Wakida Edward Vs. Adeodata Kekitiinwa & 3 others.
Leases-Expired lease-whether controlling authority may re-allocate
the same without notice to the lessee.
Leases-development conditions-whether presence of building
materials on suit property was fulfillment of development conditions.
Recovery of land under S.184(e)-whether the plaintiff may recover
land because his certificate of title is prior in time to that of the
defendant.
Relief against forfeiture-whether a lease whose lease had expired
may apply for relief against forfeiture.
Held:  When time has not been made of essence of the contract, one party
cannot avoid the contract on grounds of unreasonable delay by the other
until notice has been served, making time of essence.  When the offer for
the lease was made to the plaintiff on 26 November 1987, it stipulated that
the plaintiff must accept the same within one month by paying all fees
including premium.  The plaintiff accepted the offer 6 months later when he
paid the fees which was accepted by the 3rd defendant Uganda Land
Commission.  Even then the lease agreement was only ready in January
1989 and the certificate of title in November 1989.  This meant that the
parties had not regarded time as being the essence to the contract.  And
third defendant (ULC) could only make time of essence by giving notice to
the plaintiff, which was never done.  Therefore the ULC was in breach of the
lease agreement.
S.51 of the Registration of Titles Act provides that only when an instrument
is registered that it is effectively able to pass estate of interest in land.  In
the present case the plaintiff became the registered lessee of the suit
property not in 1987 when the offer was made but in November 1989 when
the plaintiff was registered as lessee and granted a certificate of title.
Therefore, the 5 year period began to run from November 1989 and not 1987.
Therefore, when the plaintiff's lease was re-allocated in 1993 it had not
expired because it was due to expire in November 1994.
Rule 2 of the Public Lands Miscellaneous Regulations define reasonable
development as being at least one third of the projected development.  In the
instant case, though the covenant in lease required the plaintiff to erect as
shs. 12m building on the suit land within 5 years, the fact that the plaintiff
had ferried building materials on the site as he awaited the approval of his
building plans from KCC, would amount to reasonable development
disentitling the controlling authority from claiming breach of the
development covenant in the lease by the plaintiff.
S.184(e) Registration of Titles Act provides that a person can bring an action
to recover land where that person has a certificate of title prior in time as
against the other person from whom recovery is claimed.
Moreover, it was against public policy to deprive a lessee of his property
without notice and without any blame on his part with regard to the lease
covenants.
The subsequent lease granted to the 1st defendant was unenforceable
because it was granted illegally in breach of public policy, and the 1st
defendant was privy to the illegality because she knew the property had
been previously leased to the plaintiff which fact should have given notice to
her to act prudently.
Suit allowed with costs.
Trespass-damages therefore-quantum.
Rugambwa Gabriel & anor Vs. Ezironi Bwambale & anor.
Expired lease-sale of land-whether contract of sale land on an
expired lease is void-whether land was public land when sold.
Register proprietor-unregistered holder-whether registered
proprietor's interest may be defeated by unregistered possessor
because registered proprietor paid no consideration.
Fraud-notice-whether possession was notice to registered proprietor
of the plaintiff's unregistered interest.
Specific performance-part performance-whether remedy grantable.
Held: It is not essential that at the time of the contract of sale, that the
vendor's title to the property be perfect, provided the vendor can perfect it
when time comes.  In the instant, it is true the lease had expired at the
date of the contract of sale of the suit land in time perfected his title when
he had his initial period of the lease renewed and back-dated.
Moreover, even where a lease has expired the "lessee" remains with some
interest in the land till the same is dealt with by the controlling authority.
Therefore, it is not true that at the time of the contract of sale the suit land
was public land.
S.145 of the RTA would only be helpful to the transferee if such transferee
had paid some consideration to the transferor.  In the instant case the
second defendant was transferee by gift and no consideration moved from
him to the 1st defendant.  Therefore, the second defendant's title, thought
registered, would not operate so as to defeat the unregistered interest of
the plaintiffs.
Moreover, since the plaintiffs were in possession this was sufficient notice
to the second defendant of the unregistered interest belonging to the
plaintiffs.  Therefore, the defendant was not a bonafide purchaser without
notice.
Since there was part performance, remedy of specific performance granted.
Suit allowed with costs.  Second defendant's title cancelled.
Musoke Sanyu Lwanga Vs. Yakobo Ntate Mayanja
Caveat-notice of removal thereof S.149(1)(2) Registration of Titles
Act-whether duly delivered when no memo to that effect under
S.205 Registration of Titles Act.
Caveat on behalf of beneficiary under will, RTA-whether removable
under S.149(1), RTA.
Held: O.6 r2 CPR requires that where an action is based on fraud, the
particulars must be set out in the pleadings and proved in court strictly.
therefore, in an action involving fraud, proceedings by affidavit is not possible.
Therefore, the learned trial Judge misdirected himself when he proceeded to
entertain a matter where fraud was pleaded basing on affidavits.
Where a notice to remove a caveat is set by the registrar, under S.149(1)
RTA, it is required by S.205 of the RTA that a memorandum, being a copy
of the notice and when it was sent, be made.  In the instant case no such
memorandum existed and therefore there was no proof that the notice was
sent as alleged.
Moreover, even if there was no affidavit from M/s Mulira and Co. Advocates
deponing that they never received the notice, the affidavit was not necessary
because the burden of proof as required by SS.100, 101, 102 and 105 of the
Evidence Act, was on the person alleging that the notice was sent to prove
that actually the notice was sent.
Moreover, a caveat instituted for the beneficiary under a will does lapse after
the expiration of 60 days under S.149(1) of the RTA, the operation of the
caveat must be determined before this removal.  Therefore, the learned Judge
misdirected himself when he found that failure by the said Magala Efulaimu
to apply to court for the delay of the registration of the respondent as
proprietor was a ground to remove the caveat.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Paramount Insurance Co. Ltd Vs. Joyce Nagganda.
Power of attorney-equitable mortgage-whether power of attorney
to borrow money from a bank includes power to take goods on
credit against security of the mortgage.
Held: A power of attorney is a document which is strictly construed by the
courts according to well recognized rules.  The authority conferred by the
power of attorney must be adhered to strictly, and nothing done outside the
reasonable scope of the power may make the principal liable.  In the present
case, the power authorized the donee to borrow money from a bank and not
to pledge the property as security for goods taken on credit.  Therefore, the
principal was not liable.
Question determined. Principal not liable.
Hotel International Ltd Vs. The Administrator of the Estate of
the Late Robert Kavuma.
Unregistered instrument S.51-caveat-unregistered caveat -whether
effectual-whether fraud proved where caveat unregistered.
Held: The learned trial judge erred in fact when he held that there was the
respondent's caveat on the suit land as a notice of the respondent's
unregistered interest.  This is because the evidence was to the effect that
the Registrar of Titles though she had received the application to register a
caveat she had not done so.  S.51 RTA provides that no unregistered
instruments is effectual.  Therefore his unregistered interest was not
protected and was thus available legally for appropriation to the appellant
who had no notice thereof.
No fraud could be imputed on the appellant since he had no knowledge of
the existence of the respondent's unregistered interest.
The learned trial Principal Judge erred when he sighted the burden of proof
by requiring the appellant/defendant to deny whether or not he had inflicted
damage on the suit premises for purposes of assessing mesne profits.
This was contrary to the requirements of SS.100, 105 Evidence Act that
required the person alleging to prove the truth of his allegations.
The learned trial Judge erred when he awarded interest when the same had
not been prayed for.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Patel B.K. Vs. Patel H.R.
Tenancy in common-payment of purchase price by one party-
whether the other party may be de-registered for his failure to pay
his contribution-whether de-registration is only upon of fraud,
S.51 RTA.
Fraud-whether proved.
Transfer deed S.42(4) RTA -whether may be contradicted.
Power of attorney S.154(1) RTA-non registration thereof-whether
invalidates the same.
Limitation-accounting for rent paid-whether only limited to only 6
years by S.18 Limitation Act.
Held: The transfer deed bore both names of the respondent & the appellant
as tenants in common, both having purchased equal shares of the same
property, jointly.  The transfer deed having been witnessed by DW2 who a
lawyer, the witness could not be called credible when he contradicted the
document he had attested to by saying that the appellant never paid his
part of the purchase price.  S.209(1) RAT allows parties to modify the
contents of the transfer deed to show the actual situation.  Since no
modification was done, the transfer deed was final to confer the title to the
respondent and S.51 RAT presumed very person whose name appear in the
registered (instrument) transfer as transferee to be owner and only proof of
fraud could render such presumption ineffectual.  In the instant case no
such fraud was proved.  Therefore the learned trial judge was correct in
holding that the respondent was a 5% tenant in common.
Appeal dismissed.
Uganda Posts & Telecommunications Vs. Abraham Kitumba.
Bonafide purchaser-notice-s.61 Registration of Titles Act-adverse
possession-whether this amounted to notice of unregistered interest.
Kibanja-tenure-whether government cannot occupy land by way of
a kibanja.
Held: The issue of stay of suit should be pleaded in the written statement of
defence or be raised as a preliminary point of law before calling evidence.
The appellant having allowed the respondent's witnesses to testify and
conclude their case, could not any more raise the issue of the pending suit
under S.6 Civil Procedure Act.
However, if a person purchases an estate which he knows to be in the
occupation of another other than the vendor, such person is bound by all the
equities which the parties in such occupation may have in the land.  In the
instant case the respondent acquired the suit land when the appellant was
in occupation.  Therefore, this was notice of the claim the appellant might
have over the suit property.  Therefore, the respondent was not a bonafide
purchaser without notice.
There is no law that government cannot own land by Kibanja tenure system.
Therefore, even if the appellant's interest was unregistered, it could lawfully
own and hold land by way of Kibanja.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Nalukwago Joeria Vs. Administrator General.
Lease offer-kibanja-whether the offer of a lease precludes kibanja
holding by a third party.
Held: S.221 Magistrate's Court Act provides that no court shall try another
case when the same case between these parties is still pending before
another court.  In this instant case the section precludes the case filed by
the Administrator General before the Chief Magistrate's Court at Mengo,
when another case was still pending before the Rubaga LCIII Court.
The LC Court has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction to try cases involving
unregistered land.
Appeal allowed.  Case at Mengo stayed pending appeal from Rubaga LCIII
Court.
Rungaranga Edward Vs. Mbarara Municipal Council & 2 ors
Leases-fraud-whether appellant's application for and acquisition of
a development plot was evidence of fraud.
Leases-forfeiture-development conditions-whether lease was sub-
substantially developed-whether therefore lease should not forfeit the
same.
Certificate of title S.56 Registration of Title Act-whether impeachable
S.69 Registration of Titles Act.
Mesne profits-trespass-whether proved against appellant who was
allocated semi-developed premises on an expired lease.
Held: The appellant to have applied for the suit land stating that there was
no building there on except stones and sand, repeating the same in court,
whereas there was evidence of guilty knowledge and fraud.
The Local Administrations & Urban Authorities Decree 1971 dissolved all
district, Town and Municipal Councils and their functions were vested in a
committee appointed by the Minister by statutory order for a period of two
years.  The last such statutory order appointed the committee whose
existence expired on 13th September 1980, such that by May 1981 when
the committee purported to grant the suit lease to the appellant it had no
such power to do so.  Therefore the appellant did not obtain a valid lease
because the committee that purported to do so had expired.
It was inequitable for the 1st respondent to revoke the 2nd and 3rd
respondents' lease without adequate hearing, when the two respondents had
by letter explained that their failure to complete the building was due to the
onset of the 1979 Nyerere-Amin war, and the subsequent failure to find
materials.  And moreover, the building had been substantially completed
excepting the water system, and a temporary occupation permit had been
given.
Though S.56, Registration of Titles Act provides that a registered proprietor
named in the certificate of title is conclusively the owner of the property,
S.69 of the same Act provides for those instances such as the present one
where the Registrar of Titles may upon proof of fraud or mistake, cancel
such certificate and re-issue the same in the name of the person deprived of
the land by the said fraud or mistake.  In the instant, it was not sufficient for
the appellant to wave the certificate of title to the court as ultimate proof of
ownership.  Therefore the learned trial judge was correct to go behind the
certificate of registration and to find that the respondents had been deprived
of their property by fraud, inspite of the existence of the certificate of title in
the names of the appellant.
The learned trial judge erred to have awarded damages as mesne profits
against the appellant because the appellant was not a trespasser at the
time he occupied the suit property, it having been on a lease which had
been on a lease which had been granted him by the 1st respondent.
Appeal dismissed except as regards the decree to pay mesne profits.
Administration General Vs. Registrar of Title & anor.
Cancellation of Certificate of Title, S.185 Registration of Title Act-
application therefore after criminal proceedings - whether application
not tenable.
Held: S.185 RTA empowers the High Court to order the Registrar of Titles to
cancel a certificate of title of the person registered as proprietor, where in
any proceeding for the recovery of land, court has ordered that such land be
recovered from the person registered as proprietor. However, the proceedings
envisaged by S.185 RTA is that kin of proceeding that finally determines the
rights of the parties.  In this case the criminal proceedings under which the
2nd respondent was convicted of procuring registration by false pretences,
was not that kind of proceeding envisaged by S. 185 RTA because it did not
determine the rights of the parties.  Because other than finding the 2nd
respondent guilty and punishing him accordingly, the proceeding did not
determine who to be registered as a lawful substitute.
Application dismissed with costs.
Kayongo Tom & ors Vs. M/S Busiro Coffee Farmers & Dealers Ltd
Leases-re-entry, SS.102 (2) and 113 Registration of Titles Act -
whether there was no effective re-entry because no physical
possession thereof taken whether thereby subsequent lease
ineffective.
Mesne profits-decree therefore-whether improperly made because
plaint did not claim loss.
Held: SS. 102(2)(b) and 113 Registration of Titles Act provide that re-entry is
re-taking possession of the land by the lessor.  The learned trial Judge erred
to have found that the lessor had effectively re-entered when the lessor had
not taken possession of the land.  Therefore the subsequent purported lease
of the property was ineffective because the one prior to it was still
subsisting undermined.
The appellants were entitled to resist the claims of the respondent over the
property because the respondent had no effective lease to claim.
The learned trial Judge erred to have awarded mesne profits to the
respondent when no loss was pleaded in the plaint to sustain the award of
mesne profits.
Appeal allowed with costs.
Omara Atubo Ruth Vs. Uganda Land Commission
Leases - mistake in granting a lease-unenforceable-whether lessor
not liable.
Certificate of Title S.56 RTA - impeachment thereof -whether only
by Court action.
Held: A Contract can only be made on account of mistake if the mistake
of the defendant excusable or where the plaintiff must have known of the
defendants' mistake at the execution of the contract.  And where the
defendant cannot rely on any of the excuses and the mistake is merely the
result of his own carelessness, he cannot avoid performance of the contract
by merely pleading mistake.  In the present case the defendant pleaded
mistake but did not give evidence to show that the plaintiff contributed
thereto.  Therefore the mistake was solely by the defendant and therefore
the lease was not void.
S.56 of the Registration of Titles Act provides that a Certificate of Title is
conclusive evidence that the person named therein is the proprietor and
S.184 Registration of Titles Act provides that impeachment of a Certificate
of Title as in this present case must be based on proof of fraud against the
registered proprietor in a Court action.  Therefore the Registrar of Titles had
no power to cancel the plaintiff's Certificate of Title without an Order of Court.
Therefore the plaintiff was entitled to compensation from the defendant to the
tune of the open market value of the suit Land plus her expenditure on the
site of the Land as Special Damages.
Since the plaintiff suffered inconvenience and mental anguish as a result of
the cancellation of her Certificate of Title she was entitled to Ush. 6 million
as General Damages.
Suit allowed with costs.
Kisugu Quarries Ltd Vs. Administrator General
Transfer of land to a non-African, S.2 Land Transfer Act-whether
validly effect-whether Ministerial consent got.
Held: S.105 Evidence Act provides that the burden of proof is on that party
that has special knowledge of a fact in issue to prove it.  S.2 of the Land
Transfer Act required the non-African who wished to take a lease of Mailo
land to obtain the consent of the Minister, the burden of proof was on the
appellant which is the one that had the duty to seek Ministerial consent, to
prove that in fact the consent was granted because this would be a fact
within its knowledge.  The evidence on record seeking to prove Ministerial
consent was just speculation and conjecture.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Pyrari Shunji Ganyi & 3 ors Vs. Coffee Development Authority
Sale of land and execution of transfer-deferment of payment of
purchase price-whether sale ineffectual.
Held: Once a transfer is executed there is a binding contract inter-partes
and the time to register the transfer is not of essence.  In the instant case
the sale of the property and execution of transfer were concluded before the
expulsion Decrees came into force.  Therefore the appellants did not have
the property to be expropriated as the property had passed to the purchasers
and in the same vein the appellants could not repossess the property, as
they had no interest therein.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Mitwalo Magyengo Vs. Medadi Mutyaba
Trespass by squatter-whether proved.
Held: S.74 (1) Civil Procedure Act precludes second appeals against findings
of fact made by the High Court acting as an appellate court.  Therefore the
grounds of appeal against findings of fact by the High Court would not be
entertained.
According to the evidence on record it was not clear whether the cultivation
by the appellant covered new grounds or only grounds previously cultivated
by the appellant before the respondent purchases the land.  Since the
evidence did not delineate the land previously occupied and cultivated by the
appellant, he could not be called a trespasser and the order for damages
awarded against him for trespass is set aside.
However though the appellant could not be called a trespasser he had failed
to prove that he was a customary tenant or Kibanja holder.  The evidence
clearly showed that the appellant was either a squatter or licensee.
Therefore the order granting the respondent a permanent injunction against
the appellant would be up held.
Appeal allowed just in part and respondent and appellant to share costs in
halves.
Sir John Bagaire Vs. Ausi Matovu
Bonafide purchaser-whether appellant was bonafide purchaser
without notice of fraud.
Held: Bias means real likelihood of an operative prejudice whether conscious
or unconscious and to find bias the appeal court does not look at the mind of
the presiding Judge or Chairperson of a tribunal and does not consider
whether or not the Judge or tribunal Chairman was really likely or did indeed
favour one party at the expense of the other but the appeal court must look
impression which could be formed by right minded persons in the
circumstances of the case that there was a real likelihood or bias.  In the
present case the allegations by counsel for the appellant that the trial Judge
because of bias, refused to grant counsel's interlocutory applications, are
not proved by the record of the proceedings.  Therefore, no bias or likelihood
of bias had been proved against the trial Judge.
The trial Judge was according to the evidence available entitled to hold that
the appellant was not a bonafide purchaser because the appellant had not
discharged the burden of proving his plea that he purchased the Land from
the respondent.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
LOCAL ADMINISTRATION
Nabuyonga Taxi & Omnibus Co. Ltd Vs. Mbale Municipal
Council.
Tenders-Local Government (Resistance Councils) Statute S.43(1)-
whether Municipal Councils had no authority to award a tender
except the Local Government Tender Board.
Held: S.43(1) Local Governments (Resistance Councils) Statute provides
that only a Local Government Tender Board has authority to award tenders but
not the respective Local Government.  Therefore, the purported assurance
by the (Municipal Council) defendant that it would award the contract to the
plaintiff was illegal, and the resultant contract was unenforceable.
Suit dismissed with costs.
SPORTS LAW
Moses Ali & Others Vs. Francis Nyangweso & Others
Uganda Olympic Committee-membership thereof-whether certain
associations were not qualified to be members thereof because they were
not Internationally Federated and or did not exercise specific and real
sporting activities -whether therefore they were not National Associations.
Held: According to Art. 33 of the Olympic Centre, a National Association to
be recognized by Uganda Olympic Committee and accepted as a member
the association must exercises specific and real sporting activity, be
affiliated to its international federation recognized by I.O.C and conduct its
activities according to the Rules and Regulations set by the Olympic
Charter.  In the instant case the Archery Association, the Uganda Amateur
Swimming Association and the Uganda Canoeing Association were not
qualified members since they either did not carry out real sporting activity or
were not Internationally Federated.
However since the quorum of the General Assembly was 6 and 14 members
attended even if 3 disputed associations were discounted the 11 members
were more than necessary quorum.  Therefore the proceedings at which
the defendants were elected could not be impeached.
Case dismissed with costs.
STATUTORY INTERPRETATION
Shaban Birumba & another Vs. Uganda
Implied repeal - whether ss.31 and 32 of the Fire Airms Act
impliedly repealed ss.272 and 173 of the Penal Code Act.
Held: Since the investigation of the case did not include proof that the
pistol was such a weapon capable of causing death, aggravated robbery
the pistol was a deadly weapon.  Therefore the case fell within the
ambit of s.273 (1) (b) of the Penal Code I.e. robbery.
An limitation fire arm, or one unloaded, or otherwise incapable of
discharging any shot cannot be deadly weapon within the meaning of
s.273 (2) of the Penal Code.  It is at best a dangerous weapon
according to s.31 (5) of the Fire Arms Act.
That Penal provisions must be interpreted strictly and where there is
any doubt as to the meaning of a given provision the doubt must be
resolved in favour of the accused.
Uganda Motors Ltd Vs. Wavah Holdings Ltd.
Statutes of General application - whether still application in the
High Court of Uganda.
Held: The reference to Acts of General Application was deleted from the
1967 Judicature Act.  Such Acts consequently do not apply to Uganda,
a fortiori, the material fire prevention (Metropolis) Act 1774 (U.K)
The trial Judge was right to rely on the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur.
The onus was on the defendant to show that the fire was caused by an
external cause or did not originate on its premises or under its
management, else, negligence for the cause of the fire would be
presumed on the defendant.
David Kayondo Vs. The Co-operative Bank (u) Ltd.
Jurisdiction of the High Court - whether the cooperative societies
Act ousted the original jurisdiction of the High Court.
Held: O.13 r 5 clearly requires the trial judge to frame the issues to be
determined right at the beginning of the trial.  The prime duty to frame
the relevant issued lies on the court trying the case although the
Advocates in the case also ought to comply with the requirement.
The appellant was an officer of the respondent bank because
s.87 of the Co-operative Societies Act defined officer to include
Chairman, Secretary and Treasurer.
Dispute though not defined by the Act, it is not a term of Art and it must
therefore be given its ordinary meaning of a controversy or quarrel.
S.73(1) of the Co-operative Societies Act did not oust the Jurisdiction of
the High Court in disputes concerning the Co-operative Societies or its
members past and present.  The is because the Constitution of Uganda
gives the High Court unlimited oringal Jurisdiction in all matters subject
to any written law.  The written law to oust such Jurisdiction it must
expessly state so, which was not the case with S.73(1) of the
Co-operative Societies Act.
Uganda Blanket Manufacturers (1973) Ltd Vs. Attorney General
Winding up-whether a minister can wind up a statutory organ
without statutory provisions.
Held: Decree 22 of 1974 provided that the Minister of Industry shall
control the management of the appellant company through the Board of
Directors, therefore for the Minister to purport to have wound up the
Board which was a statutory body so that he could control the
management of the company directly was illegal.  A statutory body can
only be wound up by a statutory provision.
An action to enforce the company's rights was properly commenced in
the company's name because a new group had assumed the control of
the company which was allowing it to be run on an ultra-vires basis.
And moreover neither the Ministry, nor the Board of Directors nor the
general meeting could have commenced these proceedings in the
circumstances.
The conduct of the Minister did not occasion the award of exemplary
damages because the Minister merely misconceived his task.  He
though he was operating a Government owned Company by virtue of
Decree 2 of 1974 and though he was preserving Government property
and looking to the wider interests of the textile industry.
Matendegyere & others Vs. Y.Kasikura & others.
Third appeals - whether s.74 of the civil procedure Act and it's
marginal note precluded a third appeal.
Held: S.74 of the Civil Procedure Act provides the grounds upon which
second appeals may be lodged.  Ss. 75 and 76 of the Act state that no
appeal shall lie except on grounds expressed in S.74.  This logically
means that the legislature never intended third appeals because no
provisions therefore were made.  This invariably means that the Supreme
Court has no jurisdiction to entertain a third appeal.
Attorney General Vs. Silver Springs Hotel Ltd & others.
Specific legislation -not repealed by general legislation without
clearly saying so.
Subsequent legislation does not repeal previous legislation if the
two are not inconstant and the two serve different purposes.
Judicature Act, 1967, s.36 - did not repeal s.15 of Government
proceedings Act, 1959.
Held: The Cardinal rules of Statutory interpretation in this matter were -
a specific legislation is not repealed by a general legislation which does
not specifically so state and where no necessary implication can be
drawn.
Subsequent legislation does not repeal an earlier legislation without
explicitly stating so and where no necessary implications can be drawn.
Where the two statutes are consistent, no intention of repeal should be
drawn.
Government is not bound by statutes which do not clearly say so.
S.36 of the Judicature Act, 1967 did not repeal S.15 of the Government
Proceedings Act.
An injunction (temporary or permanent) cannot lie against Government
under the laws of Uganda.  The rationale is that the Government
machinery should not be brought to a halt, and it should not be
subjected to embarrassment.
An amicus curiae is invited by Court and he should be a person without
interest in the case.  Mr. Kayondo was not invited, and was an
interested party who therefore did not qualify.
David Sejjaka Nalima Vs. Rebecca Musoke.
Chronology of statutes - later statute on specific matter repeals or
modifies earlier general statute s.189 of RTA - modified s.233 of
succession Act.
Held: A later Statute on a specific matter modified an earlier general
statute.  The RTA was enacted in 1922, later than the succession Act
which was registered land, whereas the latter is on the general matter
of succession to moveable and immovable property.  The RTA therefore
modified the Succession Act.
A bonafide purchaser for value is one without notice of fraud.  The
appellant was not one because he had the imputed fraud from his
advocate and avoided discovering who the rightful owner was.
Edward Frederick Sempebwa Vs. Attorney General
Fundamental right to property - whether suspended by implication.
Held: It was not settled whether the court that makes the reference of
matters to the Constitutional Court should as well act as the
constitutional court to decide on the substantive matters thereby
referred.  The view of the Court was that the Court is not necessarily
the same court as the one that finally determines the Constitutional
questions in substance.
There is no laid down procedure as to how the questions framed by the
court for reference may be brought before the constitutional court.
Neither of the respondents did not contest the method used, I.e. the
notice of motion however.
On or about the 26th day of January 1986 an armed group known as the
National Resistance Army entered Kampala the capital of city of
Uganda and by force of arms took its control and seized the reigns of
power.  Therefore, this amounted in law to a successful revolution
through extra-constitutional means, and that the proclamation (LN 1/86)
establishes a new legal order, in accordance with which the validity of
laws in Uganda has to be determined.
The authorities that made the successful revolution set up conditions for
the basis of the new legal order, and spelt these conditions in Legal
Notice No.1 of 1986 and the saved provisions of the 1967 constitution.
Once this was done, the authorities were precluded from departing from
these conditions and any subsequent legislation by them was to be in
conformity therewith, I.e. within this legislative framework.  Therefore the
validity or otherwise of Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 must be viewed within
the perimeters of the legal order accordance with the place.
Since Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 was a proclamation and not a decree
promulgated by the National Resistance Council as required by Legal
Notice No.1 of 1986, and since the proclamation was not signed by the
President of Uganda but by the Chairman of the National Resistance
Council who was also President of Uganda but by the Chairman of the
National Resistance who was also president of Uganda meant that the
Legal Notice was made not in accordance with the rules already laid
down.
Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 would be declared invalid because it was not
made in accordance with the Legal legislation framework put in place by
the revolution.  The court's pronouncement of invalidation would be
necessary to avoid uncertainty in legislation and cause government to
follow the rule of law in exercising legislative powers and others and
that the situation not prejudice the security of the state and that the
situation would easily be corrected retrospectively by the state putting
in place the right legislation in accordance with the law.
Shah's case set a precedent and defined a judgment debt/decree to be
properly protected by the constitution and this precedent would be
followed since the court in the instant case is of co-ordinate jurisdiction
with the court in Shah's case which was a court of first instance on the
issue of judgment debt being properly protected by the constitution and
the modern practice demands that a judge of first instance should as
a matter of judicial comity follow the decision of another judge of first
instance of the court is that the decision in Shah's case was correct
and should apply to the instant case.
Since the applicant's judgment debt is properly protected by the
constitution, Para 12(2) of the Legal Notice No.6 of 1986 conflicted with
and infringed upon the constitutional rights of the applicant and
consequently that paragraph cannot be valid unless Article 8 (2) (c ) and
13 of the constitution are repealed or modified by paragraph 13 of
Legal Notice No.6 of 1986.  But paragraph 13 does not expressly repeal
the said articles, let alone its being retrospective.  The cardinal
principles of Statutory Interpretation require that legislation that infringe
upon constitutional right must expressly state so.
J.W.R.Kazzora Vs. M.S.L.Rukuba.
Law applicable -whether English Rules of supreme court do not
apply to Uganda.
Held: The decision of a taxing officer with regard to quantum of costs is
final and court may only interfere with it in exceptional circumstances
such as when the quantum allowed for instructions fees is so manifestly
high as to reflect the application of a wrong principle and to amount to
an injustice to one party.  In the instant case the value of the subject
matter was only seventy million, the hearing lasted only two days, the
appeal raised difficult issued but not of exceptional nature.  Therefore
taking into account all the circumstances of the case, it is judged that
the fee of 15 million as instructions fees was excessive as to reflect an
application of a wrong principle and would thereby be reduced to sh.10M.
The English Rules of Procedure do not apply in the taxation of costs in
Uganda Courts.  However, the English rules are similar to the Uganda
Rules of the Supreme Court and the cases decided on them provide a
persuasive guide to the principles governing taxation of costs in the
Supreme Court of Uganda.
The income of counsel was an extraneous matter which could not be
properly taken into consideration in assessing the instructions fee.
Clearly taxation of costs was at the entire discretion of the taxing officer
which discretion is to be excersized judicially in accordance with the
law and rules of the court but the actual estimation of the costs was not
mathematical but was based entirely on the opinion and experience of
the taxing officer.  Therefore the registrar taxing officer was right in
holding that taxation was a matter of opinion based on experience.
The value of the subject matter was the value at the material time that
the matter comes into question, in this case at the time of taxation.
Therefore the Registrar was justified in basing his taxation of instruction
fee on the value as indicated in the valuation Report submitted by the
respondent.
Costs follow the event and the court awarded the respondent full costs
despite the fact that the applicant succeeded on two grounds.  The
Registrar had no power to alter the order of Court.
Paul Kisekka Vs. Seventh Day Adventist Church.
Land Reform Decree public Land -whether since prescribed
authority was not defined, there was no need to give notice to
prescribed authority to have a transfer of public land.
Held: Since the appellant's acquisition of the Kibanja did not constitute
a creation of a new customary interest on public land, the transfer of the
customary interest from Nandaula to the appellant was governed by s.4
(1) of the Land Reform Decree which requires that the transfer should be
preceded by a three months notice of the intended transfer to the
prescribed authority.  Since there was no such notice, the transfer was
unlawful and void.
S.16 the Land Reform Decree defines Prescribed Authority as including
the Uganda Land Commission.  This includes the Local Chiefs and the
land committees.
Appeal Dismissed.
Registered Trustees of Kampala Institute Vs. Departed Asians
Custodian Board.
Expropriated properties Act 9/82 s.I (1) ( c) -ejusdem generis Rule-
whether the words in any other way appropriated ---should be
interpreted to mean appropriated as by different Decrees relating
to appropriation by the military government - whether the interpre-
tation should be ejusdem generis -whether the Act applied to
property illegally expropriated by the military regime.
Remedial Statute-mischief Rule-whether the Expropriated Properties Act
was a remedial Statute requiring liberal interpretation - whether Statute
to be construed in light of the mischief it was meant to prevent-whether
when thus interpreted it applied to property not covered by the Decrees
made consequent upon the expropriation by the military regime.
Held: The Ejusdem Ceneris rule did not apply because paragraphs (a) (b)
and ( c) of section 1 (1) of the Expropriated Properties Act were each
distinct, clear and spoke for itself.  The wording in 1(1) (c ) grammatically
construed themselves, i.e. "in other way appropriated in (a) and (b) or not.
Therefore, the Act must be given a liberal interpretation, to avoid the
perpetuation of the mischief intended to be redressed by the Act.  And
such interpretation is that the Expropriated Properties act 1982 applied to
properties unlawfully acquired but not covered by any Military Decree,
such as the appellant's property in this appeal.
The 1982, Expropriated Property Act, was a remedial Statute which
sought to remedy the mischief of the expropriation of property from lawful
owners.
Therefore, the Act must be given a liberal interpretation, to avoid the
perpetuation of the mischief intended to be redressed by the Act.  And
such interpretation is that the Expropriated Properties Act 1982 applied to
properties unlawfully acquired or acquired but not covered by any
Military Decree, such as the appellant's property in this appeal.
The learned Chief Justice Makika's interpretation of S.1(1) ( c) of the
Expropriated Properties Act 1982 in Gandesha's case was not necessary
for his decision in that case.  Therefore his interpretation is not a
precedent to be followed because it was obiter dictum.  The learned trail
judge erred in following a decision a precedent which was not binding.
Appeal allowed.
Kameke Growers Cooperative Society Ltd & others Vs. North
Bukedi Cooperative Union.
Quester of jurisdiction of court s.72 co-operative societies statute
8/91 - whether the provision that "parties shall refer their disputes
described in s.72 to arbitration -whether this operates to oust the
original jurisdiction of court.
Held: The law on ouster of original jurisdiction of the High Court is to the
effect that a statute purporting to do so must say so explicitly.  S. 72 of
the Co-operative Societies Act did not expressly provide that Art 83(1) of
the Constitution (1967) and S.3 Judicature Act 1967 were not to apply to
the situation provided in that section.  Therefore the learned trial Judge
erred in holding that S.72 of the statute above ousted the original
jurisdiction of the High Court.
Jan Mohamed Ltd Vs. Kemisa Sejya.
Literal rule-s.5(1) expropriated properties Act - whether the
provision as to "minister of Finance" in s.5(1) expropriated
properties Act interpreted literally could lead to unintended
meaning.
Surbodinate legislation-ultra vires rule-whether insistence on a particular
form of repossession made by the minister tended to deny the right of
repossession created by statute.
Held: The literal interpretation of the "Minister responsible for Finance"
would absurdly lead to the conclusion that the Minister himself and not
his deputy or Minister of state should deal with the thousands of
applications from former owners of expropriated properties.  The meaning
therefore would be modified to avoid the absurdity and conclude that the
certificate of repossession was properly and legally signed even if it was
by a deputy or Minister of State for Finance.
The regulations made by the Minister for Finance under the power
conferred upon him by S.15 (a) (b) of the Expropriated Properties Act
prescribing the forms of application for repossession could not be strictly
interpreted as to deny the right granted by statute for repossession.
Therefore the objection that the repossession certificate did not satisfy
the prescribed form would be overruled since the right to repossess was
already granted by the statute.
Objection overruled.
Henry Kayondo Vs. Uganda
Official secrets Act s.3(4) (a) "official" -whether communication
between officials of the movement secretariat was not "official"
as provided by the official secrets Act.
Held: The definition section 15 of the Official Secrets Acts regarding what
an official document is, was inclusive and therefore extensive.  This
means the documents relating to the case could or could not be official
documents as per S.15 of the Official Secrets Act.  It was a question of
evidence and this evidence could only be deduced at the trial.  Therefore
the learned trial Chief Magistrate was entitled to overrule the preliminary
objection.
An alternate charge need not be minor and cognate.
The communication between Advocate and client is absolutely privileged
as per s.124 Evidence Act.  However where an offence is suspected of
having been committed the communication is no longer privileged.
There was no provision in law providing for preliminary objection as to
whether a charge disclosed an offence or not. Therefore, preliminary
objection raised by the appellant was misconceived.
Appeal dismissed.
In re (an infant)
Resident -s.4(5) Adoption Act-whether included constructive
residence.
Held: S.I.(2) of the Expropriated Properties Act nullified all dealings in
properties that vested in Government under S.4 of the Assets of Departed
Asians Decree.  Since the alleged instrument of surrender was registered
after the coming into force of the Assets Departed Asians Decree, the
registration of the alleged surrender of the lease was null and void.
Under S.14 of the Expropriated Properties Act the person aggrieved by
the decision of the Minister regarding the granting of a certificate of
repossession can certificate but should not file an ordinary suit
Suit dismissed with costs.
Prince J.DC Mpuga Rukidi Vs. Prince Solomon Iguru & others.
S.50(2) Succession Act -whether the exemption of non-attest-
ation of wills made by Africans affected a will made prior to 1972
when the exemption was repealed-whether a contrary intention
on the part of the testor had been proved.
Interpretation of the Constitution -whether the Interpretation Decree does
not only apply to the interpretation of the Constitution.
Held: The learned trial Judge's admission in evidence of the photocopied
Will could not be impeached because there was evidence before court that
the original will was lost.  Secondly, the will was photocopied which is the
kind of mechanical method that insures accuracy of the copy; there was
evidence that tended to prove that the signature on the will was that of the
testator and the contents of the Will had not been seriously challenged by
the adverse party.
S.13(2) (b) Interpretation Decree provides that when any enactment repeals
another, unless a contrary intention appears, the repeal does not affect
anything previously duly done in pursuance of the repealed enactment.
Therefore when the late King named the Will unattested, such a mode of
making Wills was permissible under S.50(2) Succession Act which
provision allowed Africans to make unattested Wills.  Though the exemption
was repealed by Decree 22/72 Succession Act (Amendment) Decree the
repeal did not affect the act already performed by the late King, the act of
nominating the respondent by a Will unattested.
Moreover, even if the document nominating the respondent as heir was to
be found wanting as a Will, the document could be relied upon as evidence
of nomination of the respondent as heir because paragraph 2 schedule 3 of
the 1962 Constitution under which the nomination was done did not provide
any specific mode by which nominations of successors to the throne of
Bunyoro Kitara could be made.
O.13 r 3 gives discretion to court to frame issues from among or all the
allegations made on oath, allegations made in the pleadings and contents
of documents from the parties.  This rule does not mean that when court is
framing the issues it should look at all the allegations.  It is own discretion
to choose from among the allegations or all of them.  This further means
that court may frame the issues at any stage of the proceedings before
judgment.  Therefore, the learned trial Judge in framing only one issued did
not err since he had the discretion to do and in his opinion, it was enough
to decide whether or not the respondent was qualified to be heir to the
throne of Bunyoro Kitara.  And once this was answered in the affirmative
there was no further need to decided on the other allegations.
S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act provides that the court has the discretion in
determining who may be awarded costs though the costs should follow the
the event.  The instant case involved members of the same family, a family
whose importance went beyond its borders.  Therefore, for the sake of
peace and harmony in the family and community of the Kingdom, to assist
in the process of reconciliation, no costs should have been awarded!
The order awarding costs would be set aside.
The granting of a declaration is a discretionary remedy and the court should
not easily grant a declaration that would serve no useful purpose or seriously
prejudice the security of the state or affect the confidence between the
parties. Had the appellant succeeded, the court would have had to consider
whether to grant the declaration or not in view of the possible repercussions.
Appeal, save as to costs, dismissed.
Mugambwa G.W. Vs. Kisembo Muleju G.W.
S.15(3) Parliamentary Elections Statute 1996 whether the provision that the
"decision of the High Court shall be final" means that the decision was not
appealable.
Held: The High Court is not amenable to the writ of certiorari because it is
not an inferior tribunal.
S.27(1) Civil Procedure Act provides that the award of costs was at the
discretion of court and therefore the decision of the High Court not to award
costs was not an error on the face of the record.
S. 15(3) Parliamentary Elections Statute 1996 provides that the orders of
the High Court on appeal in determining complaints emanating from the
Electorate Commission shall be final.  Therefore the refusal to award costs
was not appealable since the Court had in its discretion, exercised under
s.27(1) Civil Procedure Act, decided not to award any costs.  Therefore, the
respondent had no right of appeal.
Application allowed no order as to costs.
Mugyenyi Ponsiano Vs. Asiimwe Jacob & 2 others.
Notification of election results-whether notification is a statutory instrument
as defined by S.14 Interpretation Decree.
Statutory instrument-notification of election results under S.90(3) of the
Parliamentary Elections (Interim Provisions) Statute - whether notification
amounted to a statutory instrument.
Held: Statutory Instruments comprise of only legal instruments that
constitute subordinate legislation.  A notification of election results by the
Electoral Commission is not a legislative but administrative act.  The
notification is not valid from the date it is made by the Electoral Commission
but on the date it is published in the gazette.  Therefore S.17 Interpretation
Decree which provides that a statutory instrument is valid from the date it is
published does not apply to a notification because a notification cannot be
published independently outside the gazette.  Therefore the proper date of
reckoning of the 30 days of filing the petition was from the date the
notification in the gazette on 5th July 1996 and therefore the petition filed on
30th August was filed in time.
Once an Advocate has been appointed Commissioner for Oaths, he starts
acting under the Commissioner for Oaths (Advocates) Act.  This act does
not require a commissioner to have a valid practicing certificate.
Moreover, since the issue of an Advocate commissioning an affidavit without
a valid practicing certificate is not canvassed by written law then the
provisions of S.16 of the Judicature Statute apply to the effect that common
law must govern the situation as the law applicable.  Under common law an
Advocate practicing without a valid practicing certificate only loses the legal
opportunity to recover his costs but the documents executed by him must
remain valid.
Preliminary objections all overruled with costs.
Irumba Richard Vs. Irumba Florence
"Law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act," S.3(2)
Judicature Act - law applicable to divorce proceedings, S.4(2) Divorce Act.
Held: "Law in force immediately before the commencement of the Judicature
Act, 1967, for purposes of S.4(2) Divorce act, was the law applicable in the
High Court of Justice in England, in 1950, and that was the Matrimonial
Courses Act (1950), which provided that a Divorce petition could only be filed
after at least 3 years of the marriage sought to be annulled, except with leave
of court.  However, the learned appellate Judge was correct to have held that
the 3 years rule could only be applied subject to the peculiar conditions in
Uganda and for that matter to have held that the 3 year rule could not apply.
Written Law, an expression that appears in S.3(2)(a) of the Judicature Act
1967, means the Constitutional Instruments, and any other legislative
enactments or legislative instruments having effect in Uganda.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Wamatsembe Samuel Muyonga Vs. Muloki Mutanje
Election Petitions-Limitation, S.96(3) Parliamentary Elections (Interim
Provisions) Statute, 1996-whether petition time barred because filed 30 days
after the results were issued in the instrument, S.17(1)(a) Interpretation
Decree.
Held: S.16 Interpretation Decree requires that every statutory instrument
must be published in the Gazette.  And S.17(1)(a) provides that where a
statutory instrument does not of itself provide for the date of commencement.
In this appeal, the Statutory Instrument in the Gazette on the 7th of July
1996 and therefore the petition filed on 2nd August 1996 was filed in time.
Appeal dismissed with costs.

Obiter dictum-whether precedent was not binding because it was obiter
dictum.

and ( c) of section 1 (1) of the Expropriated Properties Act were each
distinct, clear and spoke for itself.  The wording in 1(1) (c ) grammatically
construed themselves, i.e. "in other way appropriated in (a) and (b) or not.
Therefore, the Act must be given a liberal interpretation, to avoid the
perpetuation of the mischief intended to be redressed by the Act.  And
such interpretation is that the Expropriated Properties act 1982 applied to
properties unlawfully acquired but not covered by any Military Decree,

owners.
Therefore, the Act must be given a liberal interpretation, to avoid the

SUCCESSION
Alttabal Eria Vs. Kakaire Vincent
Will leaving land to step brothers of appellant whether will
purportedly made by mother of respondent enough evidence that
the disputed land was bequeathed him -whether legatee could
claim under a will that has not been granted probate.
Held: The respondent/legatee could not claim under a will that had not
been granted probate.
The trial Magistrate directed himself correctly when he sought to
challenge the propriety of the will on his own motion since the parties
were unrepresented opinion of the handwriting in the will without seeking
the aid of a handwriting expert or a person acquainted with the
handwriting in question.
To be an attesting witness one must subscribe his signature on the
will and merely not to see the will be executed and since two so called
attesting witnesses could not even identify the will in question, the will
had not been proved.
Nyendwoha Lucy Vs. Nyendwoha Robert & another.
Intestate succession - whether widow was separated from the
intestate at the time of his decease-Revocation of letters of
administration -whether these may be revoked for just cause .
Held: For a husband or wife of an intestate to be disentitled to the grant
on grounds of separation the matrimonial relationship must have
ceased to exist and this does not included mere physical separation for
one reason or other as it is with the instant case.
Court acts on two basic principles in deciding to whom to grant letters
of administration namely the interest of the person who is truly entitled
to the grant prevails over other interests and court takes into account the
interests of the beneficiaries.  Since the widow was entitled to 15%,
the children of the intestate to care for as the beneficiaries grant of the
letters should go to her.
Erinesti Babumba & 2 others Vs. Nakasi Kizito.
Grant of letters of Administration -whether a woman who mother-
ered Children of the deceased but was neither wife nor cohabited
with the deceased was entitled to letters of administration.
Held: A grant of letters of administration to any person other than the
executor of the will or a widow or a widower of the deceased cannot be
made before the Administrator General has declined to administer the
estate himself or 14 clear days notice of the application for the grant
has been made.  In the instant case since the Administrator General
gave a certificate of no objection this was evidence of such decline.
The Widow or widower takes precedence over all persons applying for
letters of administration.  But since there was no evidence to prove that
the caveator was married to the deceased in any way, she would not
be given the letters of administration.
Hadija Nakibuka Vs. Attorney General
Dependants-proof of dependants' practice is that dependants
should be seen in Court.
Held: In accident cases a sketch plan, accident abstract or postmortem
report, or at least affidavits should be adduced in evidence.
To prove existence of dependants, it is now settled practice to produce
them in court.
Florence Kemitungo Vs. Yolamu Katuramu
Administration letters of administration a widow is a fit and proper
person to be arranged administration.
Held: There was credible evidence that dowry was paid.  The plaintiff
was therefore the widow of the deceased.
following Re- Kibiego, (1972) E.A. 179, a widow is a fit and proper
person to be granted administration, as the person entitled to the
greatest share of the estate under s.28 of the Succession Act.
The plaintiff was looking after the extra-marital children and was a
proper person to look after them, but to allay the defendant's fears,
administration should be granted jointly to the plaintiff and the defendant.
Ruth Sirimuzawo Vs. Paulo Mukasa & others.
Personal representative -whether one plaintiff was the personal
representative to the intestates.
Customary heir-whether the plaintiff was not customary heir because
last funeral rights for the intestate took place.
Succession -Legal heir -whether plaintiff was not legal heir because she
was less nearer in degree of relationship to the intestate than one of the
defendants.

law to administer the estate of the deceased.  Such administration can
not be merely assumed as per the Provisions of the Succession Act as
