No proof had been furnished that the defendants refrianed from making
inquiries which an honest purchaser would have made.  The official in the
land registry acted upon the certificate of succession, though fraudulent
to effect the disputed transfers.  The defendants were not guilty of fraud
but were bonafide purchaser. Suit discussed.
Gladys Ella Felster Omella Vs. Nicholas Etieng & Enoka Odeke
Administration of Estates-whether it is contrary to customary law
for a wife to administer the estate of her deceased husband without
the consent of the deceased's clan.
Grant, Letters of Administration -whether the existence of children
of the deceased not being children of the applicant wives violated
the application-whether therefore member of the clan to be added
as co-administrator.
Held: S.201 of the Succession Act and S.6 of the Administrator General's
Act do not bar a widow from applying for a grant of letters of
Administration to the estate of her deceased husband and nor was such
an application contrary to customary law.
While the widow of the intestate is the proper person who should apply
for letters of administration to the estate of her deceased husband, in the
instant case there were other children of the deceased not begotten from
the applicant wives.  This fact causes doubt as to whether the estate

Ruhini Damji Sidpra Vs. Vijendra Damji Sidpra.
Letters of Administration -entitlement to administration of a
deceased's estate, s.201 Succession Act (as amended by Decree
Held: Both the plaintiff's and defendant's evidence is in agreement that the
plaintiff is entitled to 10% of the shares in the deceased's estate while
the defendant holds power of attorney from 7 other family members and is
entitled to more than 80% of the shares in the estate.
S.201 Succession Act (as amended by Decree 22/72) provides that in a
situation like the one at hand the person entitled to the greatest proportion
of the deceased's estate would be granted the administration of the
deceased's estate.  Accordingly the defendant is entitled to be granted
the letters of administration of the estate.
From the evidence on record, it's quiet clear that apart from merely
alleging that the defendant has mismanaged and wasted the deceased's
estate the plaintiff produced no evidence to support her claims.  Under
sections 100, 101, 102 of the Evidence Act (Cap.43) whoever alleges a
fact is supposed to prove it, and the standard of proof in civil cases is
simply on a balance of probabilities.  In this case the plaintiff alleged and
made no attempt to prove the allegations.  The defendant is accordingly
under no obligation to dispel such allegations.  The plaintiff has thus
shown no circumstances to compel court to refuse to grant letters of
administration to the defendant.
The evidence on record shows that the plaintiff is not a resident of Uganda
and is on bad terms with most of the family members.  It would therefore
be very difficult to justify joint letters of administration between her and the
defendant.  The request thus cannot be granted.
Case dismissed with costs.
Mboijana James Vs. Mboijana Prophine
Administration of estate-whether wife separated from the intestate

Kakire Joyce & another Vs. Charles Mpanga Kaggwa.
Probate-revocation of probate - whether probate may be surrende-
red back to Court before it is revoked.

surrendering probate before it was revoked, it was a lacuna made
possible by the fact that a human legislator could not provide for every
possible human failure.  Therefore court was empowered by the
Judicature Act in such circumstances to look at the provisions of the
Common Law.  And the common law provides that once process issued
to the defendant to an action of Probate, the defendant or plaintiff,
whoever has the grant must surrender it to the Registrar.
The misquotation of the date was clearly a pure error there being no
other document to which that date might refer and therefore the court
was prepared to accept as fact that the Probate being referred to was
that dated 30/4/1987.
Steven Musoke (on behalf of the beneficiaries to the estate

Residential holding - minors-minors entitled to remain in residential

Heir enjoys special position.

The heir is entitled to a special position and should be respected.

Legal representative-and administration, executor and personal

Letters of Administration is a public document and presumed genuine

Esero Bukenya Vs. Administrator General
Estate of deceased-disputed property-whether part of the estate.

Will - whether valid when not attested.

Letters of administration -caveat - whether defendants were entitled

Wills -devise-whether absolute or conditional when made in case

Wills-devise-whether absolute or conditional when made in case the

Assessment of income Tax -whether the learned trial judge

Instruction fees-defending appeal and prosecuting cross-appeal in the

Cost of transport is not part of the professional fee but an out-of-pocket

Receipts must be produced to support items under disbursement other-

Assessment of income tax -whether assessment of income tax

the award of shs.12 million as instruction fee was excessively and

Since no evidence had been led before the appellate court to prove that

Uganda Vs. Mucoori Francis
Failure to pay graduated tax c/s 69(3) Local Administration Act, 1967-
whether proved.
Held: The plea to all the two counts was omnibus and irregular.  A plea must
be for each count separately.
The plea was equivocal because the accused pleaded that he had not paid
the graduated tax, as charged, but in the same breach pleaded he was
unable to pay.  The section creating the offence requires that a person to be
guilty under the section must have failed to pay the tax without lawful
excuse.  Therefore, although the accused pleaded guilty he at the same
time sought to say that his failure was due to lawful excuse.  Therefore the
was equivocal and should not have been the basis of the conviction.
The trial Magistrate must convict the accused person instead of merely
recommending conviction as it was in this case.  Therefore, the accused
person was not convicted and the sentence was a nullity.
Proceedings set aside.  No retrial ordered because has served the illegal
sentence.

The onus was on the defendant to show that the fire was caused by

General damages-trespass-whether awardable when not pleaded.
Held: The evidence showed that the respondent's lorry at the time it was
detained by the appellants was in Running condition but when it was
released to the police it could not run and was missing some parts.
This was proof of a trespass to the Chattel on the balance of probabilities.
Trespass is a remedy affording compensation for injury to  Chattel.
This is upon proof that the defendant has interfered with the plaintiff's
possession of the Chattel and trespass remedies any damage thus
caused.  Trespass is actionable per se without proof of damage
therefore it was not necessary to plead general damages.
The award of shs.20,000,000/= was on the high as damages for
trespass. Shs.10,000,000/= would surface.
Mukasa Yeko Vs. Attorney General
Traffic accident report-whether failure to produce a traffic accident
report implies that the accident never occurred.
Held: The driver of a Motor Vehicle is enjoined by law to make a report
of any accident.  In the instant case if the driver made the report to the
police, the defendant could produce it to controvert the allegations of the
plaintiff. Moreover a fact can be proved by the testimony of a single
witness as it was in this case and in absence of any explanation as to
how and why the accident happened, it must be assumed that the
defendant's Motor Vehicle was being driven in total disregard of other
road users.
The burden of proving that the plaintiff was negligent and the he
contributed to the accident lies squarely on the defendant.  In the instant
case no such evidence was adduced and there is no other evidence on
which such inference can be made.
The plaintiff's arm was broken and his chest injured and his permanent
disability assessed at 35%.  Therefore sh. 2million general damages
would be awarded.
Babigumira Blaze Vs. Besigye Hannis.
Defamation -whether proved where words complained of imputed the
commission of criminal offence by the plaintiff.
Qualified Privilege - whether defence available where the words
complained of were published to superiors of the plaintiff.
Justification-whether defence available where defendant has not
discharged the burden of proving the truth of the allegations.
Punitive damages - whether awardable and quantum for defamation.
General Damages - whether awardable and quantum for defamation
where words complained of were published to only two superiors of the
plaintiff.
Held: The words complained of were defamatory of the plaintiff because
they imputed commission of criminal offences by the plaintiff.  It was not
necessary for the plaintiff to show that in fact because of the words
complained of he was now shunned or that he has been reprimanded by
his superiors.  The allegations by the defendant were actionable perse
without proof of damage since they imputed that the plaintiff was an
embezzler who interfered with court process.  These were offence under
the laws of Uganda and could make the plaintiff liable to criminal
prosecution.
The defence of qualified privilege was not available to the defendant
because for this defence to succeed there must co-exist two
corresponding interests, the person making the communication must
have an interest in making the communication and the person receiving
the communication must have an interest in receiving it.  Although the
Chief Justice must have had an interest in knowing about the conduct
of his officer, the defendant did not have a corresponding interest in
making the Chief Justice know since he was not motivated by patriotism
to save government funds but by malicious blackmail.  Therefore, even if
the occasion was to be held to be qualified, it was destroyed by
malicious blackmail.
The defendant if justification means that the defendant is contending that
the words complained of were true.  The burden of proof is on the
defendant to prove beyond a mere balance of pre respondence of evidence
that in fact these words were true.  In the instant case the defence of
justification would fail because the defendant had not established that the
words were true in substance with the degree of strictness which the law
requires.
The defendant's allegations were unfounded and malicious and his
persistent repetition of the allegations in court without sub standing them
called for some award of punitive damages and in the circumstances
shs.80,000/= would meet the ends of justice.
In actions for libel the plaintiff is entitled to damages for injured feelings
and reputation, annoyance and irritation.  This is inferred as a natural
and the conduct of the defendant.  The quantum of general damages will
be affected by the plaintiff's reputation, absence of an apology and the
extent of the publication.  In the instant case the libel was circulated to
only a limited number of people and therefore its effect was limited.
Considering that the plaintiff was a judicial officer with a long unblemished
record shs.400,000= would be awarded as general damages.
Interfreight Forwarders (U) Ltd Vs. East African Development
Bank.
Inevitable accident -whether defense available where defendant
ferried plaintiff's motor Vehicle which was crushed in an accident.
Common carrier-strict liability-whether the defendant was a common
carrier and therefore strictly liable without proof of negligence.
Damages for injury top goods-whether calculated as replacement value
at the time so judgment.
Held: Inevitable accident is a proper defence to a charge in negligence
whereby the defendant must show that what happened could not have
been avoided by the exercise of care and skill.  In the instant case the
defendant/appellant gave a plausible explanation of the causes and
effect of the accident as being the rough, old road, the on coming
speeding bus and the perforce sudden braking which led to the plaintiff's
car on the carrier to be thrown off.  This evidence was not rebutted.
It proved that what happened was beyond the control of the defendant
exercising due care and skill.
A common carrier is under a Common Law strictly liable for loss or
injury to goods, in damages, because of a warranty to ensure safe
delivery of the goods entrusted to him.  However, the defendant could not
be held to be a common carrier because the plaintiff did not plead that
the defendant was a common carrier, nor did the plaintiff at the hearing
lead evidence to show that the defendant was a common carrier nor was
the issues.  Therefore the learned principle judge misdirected himself
when he held that the defendant was in the alternative a common carrier
and thereby strictly liable in damages for injury to the plaintiff's volvo.
It is not specified as to the currency for the satisfaction of the obligations
under the contract, like in the instant case, damages would be awarded
in the currency which most truly expressed the plaintiff's loss, I.e., the
currency that nearly as possible compensates the plaintiff in accordance
with the principle of restitution in integrum.  The learned trial principle
judge was justified in awarding damages in currency in which the item
injured was to be replaced.  Secondly, it was foreseeable on the part of
the defendant that since the injured care was purchased from abroad, it
was a foreign currency needed to be awarded.
The award of replacement value was justified because the principle of the
Law is that in cases of destruction of goods the measure of damages is
the market value of the goods destroyed at the date of judgment, this is
the principle of restitution in intergrum.
Although interest had not been pleaded, it had prayed for at the hearing
by the plaintiff.  Therefore court was justified in awarding the interests
and the amount of 36% did not appear to be excessive.
The decree as appearing on record was defective for being not in
agreement with the judgment as required by the mandatory provisions of
O.18 r 7 but since this defect was caused by the Registrar, it should not
have been the subject of appeal in the Supreme Court but in the High
Court as provided for under O.46 r8.
Byabalema Matiya & 2 others Vs. Uganda Transport Co. Ltd.
General damages - for amputed leg above the knee - whether
same as amputed below the knee.
Held: The trial judge erred when he based his assessment of damages
on cases decided 10 years ago because due to the drastic devaluation
the shilling has suffered, the awards made 10 years ago were of little
guidance in assessing damages.  The court ought to assess damages
taking into consideration the current value of money in terms of what
goods and services it can purchase at present.  Therefore court ought to
follow the most recent decisions as a guide.
It is trial law that when considering leg injuries where amputation has
been effected, its important to bear in mind.  The distinction between an
injury which involves an amputation below the knee and one which
involves amputation above the knee.  As a rule there is greater disability
where amputation takes place in the thigh and larger sums are awarded
in those circumstances.  Therefore, since the appellants disability was
assessed at 60% the award of shs.4m would be raised to shs.9m as
general damages.
The trial judge erred when he dismissed the claim for the 3rd appellant
on grounds that she had not proved her case.  This is because liability
was not in issue since the respondent had admitted 80% liability and the
case was merely for assessment of damages.  Once liability is
admitted it is not proper for the trial judge to reverse that admission
unless there are valid grounds for doing so.
Departed Asians Property Custodian Board Vs. Bukenya Issa.
Detainee - trespass to goods -whether count may rely on a claim
for damages for trespass to grant a claim for the value of the goods
in detainee.
Conversion-trespass to goods-whether court may use the claim for
damages for trespass as the claim for the value of the goods in
conversion.
Held: There was no claim in the body of the plaint that the plaintiff made
a business loss.  Accordingly the prayer for loss of business was not
supported by any allegation of that nature and no particulars of the loss
were given.  Therefore, the learned trial judge erred in making the award
for lost income.
Although the plaintiff had prayed for general damages for trespass to his
goods, the trespass claim consists in the unlawful possession of the
goods by seizure, removal or damages there to which actions were not
alleged in the plaint nor proved in evidence.  Therefore the plaintiff's
prayer for damages for trespass could not be a basis for the award of the
value of the goods claimed detained or converted by the appellant/
defendant.
Management Training & Advisory Centre Vs. Patrick Kakuku I.
Conversion -whether established.
Held: The letters the defendant wrote to the plaintiff in reply stating that
he had pledged the machine, established a plausible conjecture that the
machine belonged to the plaintiff.  Plausible conjecture has no legal
value in establishing a fact in issue.  A reasonable inference had been
destroyed by the co-existing fact that the respondent had been blamed
for going to Nairobi without permission.  Therefore the appeal would not
succeed since the appellant had failed to establish its case.
Consultant Gas Engineering Vs. Michael Bitature & another
Strict liability -non-natural user of the premises- whether the
stocking of volatile inflammable gas in high quantities was a non-
natural user of the premises - whether defendants liable therefore
by for the subsequent escape of fire that started in the defendant's
premises.
Held: A person must so use his own property as not to injure that others.
If one brings on one's land a dangerous thing, one must keep it under
control or suffer the  consequences.  One keeps such a thing at his
own peril.  In the instant case, the appellants kept a highly flammable gas
in large quantities in their premises at their own peril.
The respondent's claim was also sustainable on account of negligence.
The appellant admittedly did nothing to repair the dangerously naked
electric wires when they had a dangerous gas on their premises.  It was
foreseeable that their omission to take care could result in such a
catastrophe.
The trial judge erred in awarding special damages on articles that had
not been proved to belong to the respondents.
Esso Standard Ltd Vs. Semu Amanu Opio.
Detainee-damages for detainee -whether assessed as at date of the
detainee.
Held: The learned trial judge was entitled to reach the decision that the
appellant company was in breach of its contract with the respondent for
failure to give the respondent the agreed notice before the termination of
contract.
The learned trial judge erred in law when he awarded exemplary
damages for breach of contract because firstly, this had not been
pleaded by the respondent/plaintiff, secondly, an award for exemplary
damages may not be awarded for breach of a tort of trespass and since
no tort of trespass had been proved as committed by the appellant, in
this case the award for exemplary damages was improper and would be
set aside.
The tort of detinue is a continuing tort and damages therefore are
assessed as at the date of judgment as equivalent to the value of the
chattel in issue as at the date of judgment.  Therefore, the damages to
be awarded to the respondent of his detained chattels would be the value
of the chattels as at the date of judgment.
The glaring mistake in the Currency Reform Statute would be corrected
by court by mere application of logic since the only conversion rate
application of logic since the only conversion rate applicable to s.1 (a) is
that in S.(b)) and the courts have since taken that view.
Since detinue was a continuing tort, damages awardable therefore were
to be assessed as at the date of judgment and therefore the Currency
Reform Statute did not apply to the prayer of damages for detinue.
Since it was the learned judge's mistake to ward exemplary damages,
no party should pay costs of setting the award aside.
The learned trial judge erred when he failed to allow counsel to address
court after each had closed their case.
Appeal allowed in part.
Dirisa Musisi & 5 others Vs. SIETCO (U) Ltd & another.
Negligence -whether proved where plaintiffs produced no receipts
of the suit bus in which they traveled.
Held: the first defendant was clearly negligent because he drove the
grader in such a way as to afford no opportunity to the second defendant
to avoid knocking the first defendant's grader.
The plaintiff failure to produce bus tickets to prove that they were fare
paying passengers in the bus in which they allege to have been injured
coupled with their failure to prove that they were immediately treated for
the injuries alleged sustained, together with their failure to produce a
Police Traffic Accident Report to indicate that they had infact been
injured at the material time in the said accident, would exonerate the
defendants from the alleged breach of the duty of care owed to the
plaintiffs.
The expert medical evidence was inadmissible for being hearsay
because the witness never treated the plaintiffs immediately after the
accident and was not guided by medical notes made at the time of the
treatment but the witness heard what he was told by the plaintiff almost
after 4 years of the accident.
Had the plaintiffs succeeded PW1 for the fractured arm would have been
awarded sh. 500.000=; PW2 for the amputated arm would have been
awarded sh. 3,000,000/= and PW3 for the lost eye ball and injured
thumb would have been awarded sh. 2,000,000/=.
Daniel Oboth Vs. The New Vision News Paper.
Defamation -punitive damages whether awardable.
Held: Since the defendants had published the article only once and had
not refused to apologize since they were not asked to do so, there was
no ground upon which the defendants could have punitive damages
awarded against them.
The humble beginnings of the plaintiff cannot be a basis for calculating
the quantum of general damages awarded in defamation cases but the
actual status of the plaintiff at the date of the publication.  The learned
trial judge therefore erred in taking into account the humble beginnings
of the plaintiff and the award for general damages would be increased
The fourth and fifth grounds of appeal were defective for being
argumentative.
Appeal allowed in part.
Ateker Ejalu Vs. Uganda Railways Workers Union & Uganda
Railways Corporation.
Vicarious liability -whether the employer Uganda Railways could
be vicariously liable for the acts of the employees Trade union.
Held: the appellant could proceed to appeal as of right against the ruling
and order of the trial judge because O.6 r 29 under which the trial judge
struck out the plaintiff's proceedings provides that such appeals shall be
as of right and not by leave of court.
The learned trial judge correctly interpreted S.19(1) (b) of the Trade
Union Decree which bars any suit against a registered Trade Union in
respondent was a registered Trade Union and the defamatory letter was
written and published by its officer on its behalf.  It follows that the
appellant had no cause of action against the first respondent.
It is true a Trade Union can be liable in cases where it is proved to have
acted outside its scope as a Trade Union but in the instant case the
defamatory letter was written for purposes of security for the officials of
the Union and since protecting the lives of Union officials is a legitimate
function of a trade Union, the Union could not be said to have acted
outside its scope.
The learned trial judge correctly held that the Union as registered was a
separate legal entity from the second respondent which could not be
held to be vicariously liable for the acts of the first respondent.
The learned trial judge was correct in not requiring first to hear evidence
before striking out the appellants pleadings against the first and second
respondents since the pleadings did not disclose a cause of action
against them.
National Insurance Corporation Vs. National Union of Clerical,
Commercial, Professional and Technical Employees.
Industrial court's award-interpretation - whether application to
interpreter Industrial Court's award not gazetted before the app-
location -ss.5,8,11 of the Trades Disputes (Arbitration and
settlement) Act.
Uganda Bankers' (Employers) Association Vs. National Union of
Clerical, Commercial, Professional & Technical Employers.
Industrial Court's 4(2) (c ) Trader disputes (Arbitration and
settlement) Act -quorum of Industrial Court - whether independent
panelist must invariably always sit on the industrial court.
Held: In principle an appellate court would not interfere with the findings
of the lower court on the issue of damages except where the court has
not properly appraised the evidence in assessing the damages and
thereby made a wholly erroneous estimate of the damages.  In the
instant case the trial judge found the appellant's injuries to have healed
fairly well and the appellant lost neither his job nor his income.  It has
no been shown by the appellant that the trial judge erred in principle in
principle in his assessment of general damages.  Therefore the
appellant Court would not interfere in the award of shs.800,000/= by the
lower court.
Ntege Mayambala Vs. Christopher Mwanje.
Negligence - duty of care whether counsel has a duty to care to a
party that is not his client.
Held: Displinary proceedings before the Law Council were of a criminal
nature which meant that the burden of proof must be on the prosecution
and the proof must be proof beyond reasonable doubt.  This was an
aspect of the case which the prosecution or the committee overlooked
and thereby arrived at a wrong decision.
The Committee erred when they believed that the appellant as lawyer
owed the complainant a duty to protect him when the complainant was
not his client in the transaction itself.
The subsequent finding based on this belief that a lawyer acting for a
seller of land had an obligation to a buyer to ensure that his client's title
was good right up to the moment of the transfer and that the breach of
that obligation would have the effect of rendering the lawyer personally
liable to the purchaser who was not his client was thereby wrong in law.
The appellant did not owe any duty of care to the complainant other than
the duty to draw up a sale agreement that would transfer whatever title
the Seller had to the complainant.
Francis Otile Vs. Uganda Motors.
Negligence, damage to Vehicle-whether defendant driving on the
wrong side of the road made him liable.
Held: Skid marks on the road are evident on a wet surface.  Since the
scene of the accident was tarmac and dry skid marks were evidence of
high speed and abrupt breaking.  The skid marks shown crossing the
road from the defendants left hard side, a side he was not supposed to
be driving on.  It has been long settled that a person who is not driving
on the left had side will usually be held negligent if he meets suddenly
and collides with another vehicle on the road.  Therefore the defendant's
driver was guilty of negligence in causing the said accident.
A part from telling court that on the defendant's Lorry were boxes
labeled "Uganda Motors Ltd" no evidence whatsoever was led to
establish that the driver was using the lorry at the defendant's request
express or implied on his instructions or was doing so in the performance
pf the task or duty thereby delegated to him by the defendant.  The fact
that neither the driver nor the turn boy or the defendant's lorry testified as
to what they were doing or where they were going at the material time
would tend not to make their master liable for their negligence.
Special damages had not been proved.
the valuation report of the damage should have been by the Police
inspector of Motor vehicles and not a private firm.
Uganda Electricity Board Vs. G.M Musoke.
Dependants under s.7 law reform (misc.prov.) Act - whether
brothers and sisters of the deceased are defendants.
General damages for loss of services to the family-whether awardable -
whether a pecuniary value may be attached to the services of a child to
his parents.
General damages for loss of expectation of life-how much should be
awarded to the estate of a child who dies at 14 years of age and was in
primary four.
General damages for bereavement-whether same as damages for loss of
expectation of life.
Held: Under ss.7,8 of the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act a
cause of action is provided by which dependants of the deceased may
claim compensation for the loss suffered as a result of his death.
Though Section 8 of the Act provides for the members of the family and
not dependants, nevertheless, the intention is to provide for members of
the family who were dependants of the deceased who had suffered
pecuniary loss as a result of his death.  The plaintiff would claim to have
suffered pecuniary loss if he had lost dependency on the deceased.  In
the present case general damages should not have been awarded to the
deceased's brothers and sisters because they were not his dependants.
It cannot be said that any service carried out by a child for the benefit of
his family has a pecuniary value capable of being compensated as
pecuniary loss.  This is because the small household work done by a
child in company of his brothers and sisters is such as all children in all
families willingly and helpfully do as a discipline of family life in its
numerous activities.  No materialistic view should be made of such and
a monetary value upon a domestic services a kin of an employee would
forsake a proper sense of proportion in judging of the normal pattern of
daily life in a family which pivots around the voluntary and combined
efforts of all family members.  In the present case the respondent failed
to establish that he lost any services of a pecuniary value.
The learned Trial Judge erred in law when he held that there existed a
custom that children in African societies who were educated by their
parents were required to support their parents and families on completion
of school.  He was supposed to have first required evidence from the
respondent/plaintiff to establish the existence of the custom and it
should not have been court itself to take judicial notice of such a custom.
Though court has power to9 take judicial notice of notorious facts, in the
present case it was not shown that the practice where children provided
financial support to their parents was notorious, prevalent or common to
all children.  The plaintiff should have proved to court, that he has lost
a reasonable probability of pecuniary advantage as evidence by custom
and not a mere fanciful probability would not speculate whether his
deceased son would have successfully completed his studies and been
in a position to assist his parents.  The trial judge erred to have held the
contrary and awarded damages for a pecuniary loss that wasn't
ascertainable or proved.
In Uganda general damages are not awarded for bereavement but for loss
of expectation of life i.e., putting a money value on the prospective
balance of happiness in years that the deceased might have lived if he
had not died, calculated subject to the normal risks and uncertainties.
And these damages should be moderate.  The learned trial judge erred
when he applied wrong principles and took into account wrong factors
and he arrived at a wholly erroneous estimate of the damages suffered.
The amount of damages awarded should not have been shs.5.5 million
but 1m.
Francis Babuzalirwa Vs. Mohammed's Garage.
Detainee -whether proved.
Held: The plaintiff's action in detinue had been established because he
had proved that he was the owner of the tractor and was still owner
thereof at the time of the action.  He was therefore entitled to its
immediate possession and yet the defendant had refused to hand over
possession of the tractor to the plaintiff, wrongfully.  This is because an
action in detinue was a proprietary action.
The plaintiff's evidence that the market value of the tractor at the date of
judgment as being Shs. 5,000,000/= was not challenged.  The plaintiff
was entitled to this value and Shs. 1,500,000/= would be awarded as
general damages for the tractor's detention.
Sentongo & another Vs. Uganda Railway Corp.
Negligence -res ipa loquitur - whether established when not
pleaded.
Held: The principle of res ipsa loquitur means that the happening of an
accident was by itself reasonable evidence of the defendant's negligence.
For the plaintiff to rely on this principle he must have pleaded it and led
evidence to establish it.
The plaintiff's being lawfully on the defendant's carriage creates a duty to
carry him safely and it was necessary for the plaintiff to prove that he
was such a lawful passenger by evidence of receipts as a fare paying
passenger.  In the instant case the plaintiffs had not proved that they
were lawfully on the defendant's carriage for their failure to show that they
were fare paying passengers.
Medical reports must be proved by the persons making them and when
the medical report is made by a person that did not examine the
plaintiff, his evidence must be of little value like in the instant case.
Dr. Willy Kaberuka Vs. Attorney General.
Malicious Prosecution - whether established.
Damages-whether the plaintiff has suffered damage after being
maliciously prosecuted.
Held: Under O.13 r 3 CPR court may amend or frame issues additional
at any time before passing a decree to enable the parties controversy to
be determined.  Therefore, an additional issue whether the plaintiff was
prosecuted by the defendant would be framed.
The plaintiff received criminal summons and was formally charged before
the traffic court Magistrate and released on bail and continued reporting
to court until the proceedings were determined.  Therefore the plaintiff
was prosecuted and the proceedings entered in his favour.
The record of the lower court showed that no traffic police officers
testified to show ho9w the plaintiff was connected with the motor
accident.  Therefore there was no evidence or any facts in which a
reasonable inference could be made that the plaintiff was in any way
party to the offence. Nor did the police honestly believe in the guilt of the
plaintiff.  Since there was no reasonable or probable cause for
prosecuting the plaintiff, the prosecution was malicious.
Whether the plaintiff suffered damage from the prosecution is an
inference as a natural and foreseeable consequence of the defendant's
conduct.  This, coupled with the plaintiff's status in society, shows that
the plaintiff suffered some damage and Shs. 3million would be awarded
as damages for malicious prosecution.
Eriysafu Mudumba Vs. Wilberforce Kuluse.
Trespass to the land -limitation -whether trespass was a
continuing tort for purposes of limitation.
Held: The evidence from the witnesses proved that the land in dispute
clearly belonged to the defendant/respondent.
The case of Florence Joyce Mutesi Vs. Andereya Kinyamule (1976) HCB
64 was not binding as a precedent as it was based on conflicting
decisions namely that the issue to the limitation does not affect
customary tenure and yet at the same time providing that S.6 of the
Limitation Act affected customary tenure.
Since the plea that the defendant was encroaching on the plaintiff's land
was a case of trespass and trespass is a continuing tort, the time started
to run when the encroachment is said to have began, I.e. 1984, and was
still continuing at the time of the suit.  Appeal Dismissed.
Foods & Beverages Ltd Vs. Israel Musisi Opoya
Conversion - whether established - whether appellant held the
respondent's lorry under an honest claim of right.
Trespass-damage to chattel-whether proved.
Held: The learned trial judge was entitled to hold that conversion had not
been proved because the defendant/appellant had held on to the lorry with
an honest claim of right.
At the time the appellant/defendant seized the lorry it was in running
condition but it was towed form the appellant's premises after it was
cannibalized.  The learned trial judge was therefore entitled to hold that
trespass to the plaintiff's lorry had been proved.
The learned trial judge was entitled to award general damages for
trespass even if the damages had not been pleaded because trespass is
actionable parse without proof of damage.
Shs.20 million general damages for trespass would be reduced to
shs.10 million.
Akisoferi Biteremo Vs. Attorney General
False imprisonment -whether established -general damages for
false imprisonment -quantum.
Dentinue-whether proved.
Held: The plaintiff had established that he had been detained for 14 days
and it was incumbent upon the defence to show that the detention was
lawful.  Since the defence failed to shoe that the detention was lawful, it
must be presumed that the plaintiff was unlawfully detained.
At the time the plaintiff's vehicle was detained it was in possession of the
plaintiff and the law presumes possession to be lawful unless the contrary
is proved. The plaintiff's possession was therefore lawful and therefore the
tort of detinue had been established sine the plaintiff had demanded for
its return to no avail.
SS 50 and 53 (2) of the Traffic and Road Safety Act require that every
motor vehicle purchased must be transferred into the names of the
purchaser.  However in spite of the plaintiff's failure to have the requisite
transfer made, he was still entitled to make his claim in detinue since by
virtue of the purchase he was entitled to the immediate possession of the
motor vehicle.
Shs. 2.5 million would be awarded for the unlawful detention as general
damages.
The plaintiff had failed to prove the un earned income as special damages
since he had not shown what business he was doing with the motor
vehicle.
Eriab Wavamuno Vs. Teddy Ssezi Cheeye
Defamation-whether proved where no witnesses testified as to the
attitude of the reasonable thinking members of society towards the
plaintiff offer he was allegedly defamed.
Damages-exemplary damages-quantum
Held: Libel consists of publication of words to at least one person other
than the plaintiff.  The plaintiff having called no witness to testify as to
what they thought of the words complained of, the liable had not been
proved wholly, because not all the ingredients of defamation had been
proved.
Had the plaintiff proved his case would have been awarded shs.3,000,000=
(one million) as exemplary damages.
Had the plaintiff proved his case he would have been awarded
shs.1,000,000/= (one million) as exemplary damages.
Fred Kainamura & others Vs. Attorney General
Unlawful arrest -reasonable and probable cause for the arrest
whether the police had reasonable and probable cause for the
arrest of the plaintiff's s.23 Criminal Procedure Code.
False imprisonment-reasonable and probable cause for detention -
whether police had reasonable and probable cause for detention of the
plaintiffs.
False imprisonment - remand by court - whether because the initial arrest
and detention of the plaintiffs was unlawful therefore the subsequent
remand by court constituted false imprisonment.
Damages - unlawful arrest, false imprisonment and assault-quantum.
Damages-quantum where the plaintiffs were cattle traders.
Held: S. 23 of the Criminal Procedure Code empowers police to arrest
suspects without a warrant where the police upon reasonable grounds
suspect a  person to have committed a cognizable offence.  In the instant
case the police arrested the plaintiffs on mere suspicion without
reasonable grounds.  Therefore, the arrest was unlawful.
The power of police to detain at their police station a person suspected of
commission of a cognizable offence for 24 hours before being taken to
court is confined to persons who are arrested on reasonable and probable
cause, it does not cover persons arrested by police without reasonable
cause as it was in this case.  Therefore the detention of the plaintiffs at
the various police stations before taking them to court was unlawful.
A detention on court's order is not unlawful.  Therefore, the period of five
months of remand of the plaintiffs by court was not unlawful detention.
It is not a requirement of the law that every allegation of assault must be
proved by medical evidence.  In the instant case the plaintiffs had amply
proved that they were assaulted and tortured while in police detention.
Ush 150,000/= would be advanced as general damages for false arrest,
detention and assault to each of the plaintiffs.
The first plaintiff was detained in police cells for 10 days since he claimed
to have lost Ush 500,000/= per week, he would be awarded Ush 500,000/=
multiplied by 10 days divided by seven days i.e. Ush 411,440/=.
George Paul Emenyu & another Vs. Attorney General.
Negligence -Reasonable care - whether negligence proved where
defendant's motor Vehicle moved from lane and damage plaintiff's
motor Vehicle in the other lane.
Negligence contributory negligence-whether plaintiff was contributory
negligent.
Damages-Quantum - Replacement value of damaged motor vehicle and
lost income from operating taxi.
Held: The sale agreement established that the plaintiff was the owner of
the suit motor vehicle since it was common knowledge that vehicles are
sold but the transfers thereof take time much later.
If a motor vehicle swerves to the wrong side of the road and causes an
accident, the driver must explain how his position on the wrong side was
consistent with reasonable care on his part.  In the case instant, the
defendant failed to discharge this burden and the logical conclusion is that
he failed in his duty of care to other road users and was thereby liable in
negligence.
A person is guilty of contributory negligence if he ought reasonably to
have foreseen that if he did not act as reasonable prudent man he might
hurt himself and he must take into account that others may be careless.
In the instant case the first plaintiff who was the driver swerved further left
from his lane to avoid the defendant's motor vehicle, which came wobbling
towards his side of the road.  Therefore the plaintiffs driver acted prudently
to avoid the accident.
Shs.8, million would be paid by the defendant as replacement value of the
motor vehicle damaged beyond repair.  Further shs.42 million would be
paid as lost income for none use of the plaintiff's mini-bus for four years.
suit allowed.
Justine Kabushenga Vs. Haji Abdu Katende
Damages special damages repair charges could be compensatable
as special damages where no documentary proof was furnished.
Damages -unearned income - whether this was awardable-whether had
been strictly proved as special damages Justina Kabushenga, the
plaintiff, operated a transport business with her pick up.
Held: The plaintiff was a witness of truth, when regard is had to her
impressive demeanor.  Moreover there was no other evidence on record to
contradict her testimony. Therefore the plaintiff had successfully proved
her claim for special damages.
Suit allowed.
Gabriel Njaukana Vs. Attorney General
Fatal accidents - limitation s.2(1) civil procedure and limitation
(misc.prov.) Act - whether disability for purposes of proceeding
with action outside the limitation period was proved.
Held: When the order allowing the plaintiff to proceed exparte was
reversed, it put both parties in their original position, logically meaning
that the order allowing the plaintiff to proceed outside the limitation period
was reversed too. Therefore the preliminary objection as to limitation was
properly raised.
The plaintiff had not proved that he was prevented by disability to institute
the suit in time because the disability claimed occurred outside the
limitation.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Sarah Kanabo Vs. Ngabo Newspaper.
Defamation -damages -whether it is the plaintiff's social status that
is paramount in the measure of general damages or the gravity of
the allegation or a combination of both.
Defamation-apology-whether lack of an apology is a factor in the
assessment of the quantum of damages.
Held: The learned trial judge should not have looked at the status of the
plaintiff in isolation from the gravity of the allegations made by the
defendant against her.  The allegation that the plaintiff was guilty of the
heinous crime of murder was so serious that coupling it with the plaintiff's
status the learned trial Judge should have awarded the plaintiff a higher
quantum of damages.
Further the fact that the defendants/respondents instead of an apology
they sought to justify the allegations but failed, should have been a factor
to the take into account while assessing the quantum of damages.
Ush, 2, 250, 060 would be awarded as general damages for defamation to
the appellant plaintiff.
Hassan Mukasa  Vs. U.E.B
Damages -quantum -where plaintiff is 21years, a porter, is Electro
shocked while on duty and 30% to 40% disability is assessed.
Held: The plaintiff was entitled to Ush 16 million since he was a young
man, a porter who needed all his energy but had been rendered almost
helpless by the accident.
Steven Masaba Vs. Uganda Railways Corporation.
Damages - amputation of both legs above knee-quantum.
negligence - contributory negligence-whether plaintiff who traveled
standing on the running board of the locomotive instead of sitting inside
was contributory negligent.
Workmen compensation - amputation of both legs above knee - quantum
of damages.
Workmen compensation - employer's negligence-whether employer
negligent.
Held: The employer has a duty to provide a safe system of work and
proper supervision to his unskilled employees. The employer is bound to
maintain a reasonable safe place for work.  In the instant case the point
of accident was a curve with tall grass on either side of the railways
which obstructed visibility.  The driver had difficulty in seeing signals given
to him by points men.  The defendant had a duty to see that the defendant
was vicariously liable for the negligence of its employees for failure to
provide a safe environment of work.
The plaintiff was contributory negligent when he chose to travel on a
locomotive in such a dangerous fashion.  His contribution would be 30%.
The plaintiff was entitled to Ush 15m/= as general damages for injuries he
sustained in the accident for which the defendant was vicariously liable at
70%.  Therefore the plaintiff should be awarded Ush 10, 500,000/= as
general damages.
suit allowed with costs against defendant.
Yosefu Kashongorize Vs. China Sichuan Corporation
Destruction of property by defendant - damages for destruction of
eucalyptus forest - quantum.
Held: It is practice that any advocate has to seek adjournment of his case,
he must brief a colleague to hold a brief and seek adjournment on his
behalf.  Application for adjournment by letter is not accepted mode of
applying for adjournment.
There is enough evidence on record to prove that 3936 tress belonging to
the plaintiff were uprooted by the defendant.  Considering the fact the
young trees and old stumps were uprooted with no chance of young trees
sprouting from the cut stumps, an estimated price of Ush. 5, 000/= per
tree would be adequate compensation.
Regarding the soil, which was removed, this item was not proved on the
balance of probabilities.  It was not enough to write down the particulars.
The onus of proof was on the plaintiff to prove by calling quantity surveyors
to tell how much soil had been removed and the value thereof.  The claim
for soil, stones, murram therefore fails.
Judgment is accordingly given in favour of the plaintiff and the defendant
is ordered to pay Ush.19, 640, 000/= special damages plus costs of the
suit.
Yekoyakimu Mwene Habyene Vs. Attorney General.
False imprisonment -survival of causes of action - whether false
imprisonment may survive as a cause of action for the estate of the
deceased.
Damages - special and general damages for travel and subsistence,
expenses and for fear and distress-whether recoverable by a parent whose
son is unlawfully imprisoned.
Held: Since the plaintiff's son was dead the father was entitled to continue
the proceedings on behalf of the son's estate.  Even though the plaintiff's
pleadings were affected by bonafide mistake, since the plaintiff was not
represented, it was unnecessary for court not to be stifled by
technicalities and to let substantive justice take its cause.
The plaintiff could not maintain a cause of action on his own behalf for
damages for travel and subsistence expenses incurred by him while
seeking the release of his son.  This is because Art. 15 of the Constitution
provided only for a cause of action for unlawful imprisonment to be brought
by the person imprisoned or for his estate in case of his death.
Appeal allowed - file re-submitted to the trial court for assessment
damages.
B.A.T (U) Ltd Vs. Selestino Mushongere
Negligence -contributory negligence -whether deceased was
contributory negligent.
Fatal accidents-life expectancy whether life expectancy in Uganda is 55yr.
Fetal accidents - income of deceased-whether sufficient proved.
Fatal accidents-dependency - whether proved.
Held: A person is guilty of contributory negligence if he ought reasonably
to have fore seen that if he did not act as a reasonable prudent man he
might be hurt and in his reckoning he must take into account a possibility
of others being careless.  In the instant case the deceased acted
reasonably in the circumstances by standing at the bust stage where he
was waiting or Public Transport and the appellant was wholly liable for the
accident when its vehicle was driven in such a way as to detour onto the
bus stage thus knocking the deceased dead.
The learned trial Judge was not wrong in holding that the normal life
expectancy for a person in the deceased's occupation was 55 years the
deceased having been a business man.  However the Trial Judge should
have discounted the deceased's working life expectancy by five years from
20 to 15 to allow for imponderables so as to come to a more realistic
position representing what would have been the remaining working life of
the deceased.
The contention by the defendant/appellant that the deceased did not
operate a lodge and restaurant in Namataba Trading Centre was rightly
rejected by the learned Judge because firstly the photographs were
inadmissible in evidence when the photographer had not been called as
a witness and secondly three plaintiff witnesses credibly testified as to
the existence  of a lodge in the area.
The evidence relating to the deceased's income was unsatisfactory and
exaggerated and the evidence of how much the deceased was giving to
the widow to maintain the family appeared exaggerated in view of the
known sources of income and therefore the learned trial Judge should
have found that the deceased's income was Uhs.10,000/= per day and not
20,000/= and that the deceased spent Ush.50,000/=- on his family per
day Uhs.50,000/= should have been multiplied by 15 years being the
deceased's working life expectancy and the resultant Ush.27 million
should have been the figure to award to the dependants.
The contention of the defendants/appellants that Mugisha one of the three
dependants was not going to school and therefore dependency had not
been proved was rightly rejected by the trial Judge since the evidence
whether or not Mugisha was going to school did not go to the root of the
matter which was whether dependants were entitled to share in the
damages awarded for the loss of dependency.  The learned trial Judge
however erred in not apportioning the damages to the beneficiaries.
Appeal allowed in part and file remitted back to trial Court for apportioned
of damages.
Hadija Nakibuuka Vs. Attorney General
Fatal accidents -law Reform (miscellaneous provisions) Act
dependency proved where plaintiff alleges that she was the widow
of the deceased having married the deceased when she was 11 yrs.
Fatal accidents-dependency - whether proved when alleged dependants
are not produced in court.
Held: An issue as par O.13 r1 (1) CPR is a material proposition of law or
fact affirmed by the one party and denied by the other.  Since the
defendant/respondent in his Written Statement of Defence denied that the
accident happened when the same had been arrested as have happened
by the plaintiff/appellant, it was an issue to be determined by court
whether or not the accident happened.  The failure to have framed it as an
issued did not mean it was not an issue to be determined by Court.  And
the learned trial Judge was correct in judging that the plaintiff/appellant
had not proved that the accident happened.
The trial Judge was correct to find that the plaintiff failed to prove that she
had been married to that deceased because according to her evidence
she had got married to the deceased in 1966 when she was 11 years old,
which was not possible.
The failure by the plaintiff/appellant to produce the alleged dependants of
the deceased in Court meant that there was no sufficient evidence before
Court for a conclusion that the alleged dependants existed and so to their
particulars, which are essential in determining the quantities of damages.
This should invariably be the case unless there is sufficient explanation
regarding failure to produce the alleged dependants in Court, which was
not given in the instant case.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Mityaba Leonard Sebatya Vs. Attorney General
Vicarious liability -course of employment - whether soldiers who
make gun salutes are acting in the course of their employment as
army officers - whether therefore the Attorney General is not liable
for their acts.
Damages for amputation of leg through the knee and incapacity assessed
at 65% - quantum - whether Ush 4 million damages were adequate.
Held: The learned trial Judge erred in holding that the soldiers were not
acting in the course of their duty with the respondent.  The soldiers were
on the ceremonial duty of burying their colleague which is a normal duty
and the gun salute was the incidental duty to the burial and the
respondent was liable for the subsequent injury resulting from the
negligent performance of that duty.
The learned trial Judge erred in assessing the damages awarded at only
Ushs. 4million.  The plaintiff was 15 years when he was injured; his leg
was amputated through the knee, he was to move on clutches through-
out his life, and his permanent incapacity was 65%.  The award should
have been Ush.10 Million.
Appeal allowed and Ush. 10 million awarded as damages.
Teddy Ssezi Cheeye & 2 others Vs. Emmanuel Tumusiime
Mutebile & 2 others.
Defamation - libel -whether proved - whether failure to call independent-
dent witness as to the effect of the alleged libel meant that the
libel had not been proved -whether the facts of the case did not
disclose a legal innuendo.
Defamation - company defamation-whether a corporation could not be
defamed -whether a corporation cannot maintain a cause of action in libel.
Defamation - publication - whether publication was not proved.
Held: The Judge in libel disputes acts as the jury by finding by himself
whether or not the words complained of were in their ordinary and natural
meaning defamatory of the plaintiff and he makes this finding without
calling for the aid of private witnesses whether for or against the plaintiff or
against the plaintiff or defendant.  It is only when the words  complained
are a legal innuendo where certain facts are known to specific persons,
that the Judge may call in the aid of witnesses who are among the
specific persons who know the specific facts.  In the instant case, since
the plaintiffs complained that the inference from the ordinary and natural
meaning of the words complained of were defamatory of them, the trial
Judge was entitled to formulate his own conclusion without the aid of
witnesses.
A trading corporation or company may maintain an action in respect of
imputation of corruption or any other wrongful conduct if such imputation
is calculated to injure it in its trading character.  In the instant case since
it was alleged that the third plaintiff company was dealing in underhand
and corrupt practices, its trading character was concerned and therefore
rightly brought an action on its behalf for damages.
A libel in a newspaper is prima facie evidence of publication.  Since the
defendants did not rebut this presumption, the learned trial Judge was
entitled to find that the defendants had indeed published the libel
complained of.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Professor Syed Sufderal Huq Vs. Attorney General
Unlawful arrest -whether plaintiff was unlawfully arrested, by the
defendant, detained and eventually deported-whether plaintiff still
unity after losing his job.
Negligence-whether accident in which the plaintiff got injured was caused
by the negligence of the defendant's servants.
Held: The basis for an action of unlawful arrest and detention is the mere
imprisonment itself.  The plaintiff has to prove that he was arrested and
imprisoned by the defendant and the burden shifts to the defendant to
justify the action taken.  In order for an arrest to be lawful, the person
arrested should be informed of the reasons for so doing unless the
circumstances are such that he either knows or he creates a situation
which makes it practically impossible for him to be informed.  The
evidence in this case clearly shows that the plaintiff was not told why he
was being arrested.  In failing to give the plaintiff reasons for their conduct,
the police acted illegally in arresting and detaining him.
The contention by the defense that the plaintiff lost his diplomatic
immunity status upon his dismissal cannot stand because the immunity
accorded to the plaintiff arose from duties owed by the Uganda
Government to the Organization of Islamic Conference and the agreement
they had entered into.  The Uganda Government had the obligation to
accord the plaintiff his immunity until he left the country or give him
reasonable notice to leave the country.  The government did neither of
these.  Accordingly, the arrest, detention and subsequent deportation of
the plaintiff were unlawful and it was done in flagrant violation of his
diplomatic status.
The law imposes a duty on a person driving a vehicle on a road to use
reasonable care to avoid colliding with other road users.  In the absence
of a police accident report coupled with the fact that the vehicle
overturned several times shows that it must have been driven in a
negligent manner.  The evidence available shows that the defendant's driver
did not take reasonable care to avoid the accident.  He is accordingly
liable for the accident and subsequent injuries suffered by the plaintiff.
The plaintiff has also succeeded in proving that he was illegally arrested,
detained and deported, he also suffered injuries as a result of an accident
caused by negligent driving of the defendant's agents.  For all this he is
entitled to be compensated; damages both general and exemplary are
accordingly awarded.
Richard Kaijuka Vs. Teddy Ssezi Cheeye & others.
Defamation whether articles printed were defamation of the plaintiff.
Defamation whether the articles were fair comment made without malice-
whether plea of justification is sustainable.
Defamation-damages-whether the plaintiff is entitled to aggravated and
general damages.
Held: For a plea of fair comment to succeed, the onus is on the defendant
to prove that each and every statement or fact complained about is true
and that the comment on the facts so prove was bonafide comment on a
matter of public interest.  Should the defense fail to prove any of the facts,
the plea will not be available to him although in the instant case the
defendant maintained that his aim was to educate the public on politics,
economy and other issues including malpractices of leaders, it is clear
that his statements about the plaintiff were a mis-statement, ever
bonafide.  The defendant's desire to expose underhand dealings ought to
have been supported with truly stated facts.
The language used in the publication was unjust and virulent.  The words
bore meaning and were capable of being defamatory to the plaintiff.  The
plea of justification is accordingly unsustainable.
As a result of the defendant's conduct, the plaintiff suffered both general
and aggravated damages and they are both accordingly awarded to tune
Godfrey Mwesigwa Vs. Semuliki High School Bundibugyo.
Negligence -duty of care to fare paying passenger-whether no
duty owed to a passenger who boarded a lorry which he knew was
not to transport passengers.
Negligence-volenti non fit injuria-whether because plaintiff accepted to
travel on lorry full of timber he voluntarily assumed the risk.
Vicarious liability-Course of employment-whether burden of proof that the
defendant's driver was acting in the course of his employment or otherwise
was on the defendant.
Damages-Disability-whether assessment of 40% disability for a right
handed plaintiff who suffered a broken and healed though weakened left
arm, occasional post traumatic backaches and headaches, and facial
disfiguring through scars - whether assessment at 40% disability was
exaggerated.
Damages - Public Policy-whether a claim for money paid to a nurse in a
government hospital for drugs would be disallowed because it offended
Public Policy.
Held: The defendant's driver owed a duty of care to the plaintiff because
he was a fare paying passenger.
When a plaintiff boards a motor vehicle as a fare paying passenger, even
a vehicle not meant ordinarily for carrying passengers, such a plaintiff
does not necessarily consent to being injured.  Therefore the plea of
volenti non fit injuria would fail.
The defendant having admitted in their WSD that the driver of the motor
vehicle was theirs, they had the burden of proof to prove that the driver
was not acting in the course of his employment when he caused the
accident.  They had not discharged this burden because they called no
evidence.
A person with only 8 years experience would not qualify to be an expert.
The claim for ush 30,000/= for money paid to nurses would not be allowed
as it offended public policy because it was not allowed to give money to
nurses for any service in a government hospital.
40% permanent disability for a plaintiff who was right handed but suffered
a broken left arm, which healed completely with some resultant weakness
therein, such assessment was highly exaggerated.  It would have been no
more than 20% and Ush 5 million general damages would be awarded.
The claim for money maintaining two attendants in hospital would be
disallowed because there was no proved requirement for 2 attendants.
Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Abednego Absolom Ongom Vs. Amos Kaheru.
Negligence -duty to take care-whether failure to avoid excessive
spared, keep a good work out, and observe traffic rules was a
breach of the duty to take care -whether therefore defendant's
driver was negligent.
Vicarious liability-master/servant-whether master servant relationship
established.
Damages-cost of private medical treatment, loss of sitting allowance as
chairman of Board, Cost of transport to and from hospital, cost of new
replacement of vehicle, general damages for personal injuries inflicted in
the accident.
Held: Where a defendant does not appear, having filed a Written Statement
of Defence and the trial proceeds ex parte, remedies cannot be granted to
the plaintiff just as prayed unless they are sufficiently supported by the
pleadings.
As per s.26(2) of the Sale of Goods Act, the transfer of title and payment
of purchase price in a contract of sale are not concurrent conditions.
Therefore the defendant having bought the car and having obtained
possession of it with the consent of the vendor, he had become its owner
even though he had not paid all the installments.
Negligence is failure to observe the duty of care.  The duty of care is
owed to persons so placed that they may reasonably be expected  to be
injured by the omission to take such care.  In the instant case the facts
of the case clearly show that the defendant's driver attempted to overtake
the plaintiff at a place where it was not safe to do so.  He was therefore
negligent.
Even though the defendant in his WSD attempted to plead contributory
negligence he failed because no particulars there were provided.
Moreover, the burden of proof of contributory negligence lay on the
defendant, who failed to discharge the burden when he failed to come to
court and testify.
The plaintiff had proved as special damages, the cost of private medical
treatment Ush.1,240,000/=; loss of sitting allowances Ush 180,000/=.
The plaintiff had failed to prove the claim for the cost of transport to and
from hospital for himself and his wife who visited him regularly.  This is
because no evidence had been led to the effect.
In case of destruction of goods the measure of damages is taken to be the
market value of the goods destroyed at the time and place of destruction.
Therefore the plaintiff's claim for a replacement value of a new car would
fail since his damaged car was old.
The plaintiff's disability assessed at 60% was quite an exaggeration
because the plaintiff suffered Potts fracture, which healed nicely.
However, the plaintiff was in plaster of Paris for four months and had
screws in his body and suffered posttraumatic arthritis.  He would
therefore be awarded Ush. 5 million general damages.
Case allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Tom Mukalazi Vs. Davis Kisule
Negligence - duty of care-whether proved where plaintiff was a fare
paying passenger in defendant's motor Vehicle and was injured
in an accident.
Vicarious liability - lack of authority-whether the plea that the defendant's
driver had no authority to transport passengers thereby absolved the
defendant from liability.
Contributory negligence-pleading -whether lack of pleading of contributory
negligence meant that the defendant would not raise it at the trial.
General damages-amputated arm at the wrist - quantum.
Held: A driver that drives a motor vehicle is presumed to be driving it with
the authority of the owner or employer.  This is a presumption of fact,
which can be rebutted by evidence.  However since the defence called no
evidence at all, this presumption remained that the driver was authorized
to drive the motor vehicle and therefore the defendant was liable.
Contributory negligence or particulars were not pleaded in the defendant's
written statement of defence and therefore the defendant could not rely on
it at the trial.
Because the plaintiff suffered an amputation of the arm at the wrist, and
his permanent disability was assessed at 70% when he was only 26
years old Ush 9 million would be awarded as general damages.
In absence of the evidence of the employer, special damages for lost
income from employment would not be awarded.
Suit allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Christopher Kisembo Vs. G.W. Byaruhanga & anor
Negligence-collision on the right hand side -whether therefore
negligence established against defendant.
Negligence-contributory negligence-plaintiff's driver convicted of having a
bad tyre-whether contributory negligence established.
Vicarious liability-scope of employment-whether vicarious liability proved
where defendant's driver had competed his task and was on his way
home.
Damages -quantum where value of repairs higher than replacement value.
Damages-lost income-whether from date of damage till judgment.
Damages mitigation of damages-whether plaintiff must mitigate his
damages.
Held: It is trite law that in Uganda vehicles must be driven on the left-hand
side of the road.  The fact that the fist defendant's vehicle knocked that of
the plaintiff on the left hand side of the Mbarara Fort Portal road, in
absence of an explanation or excuse from the first defendant, this was
sufficient to constitute negligence on the part of the first defendant.
Driving a vehicle in dangerous mechanical condition such as having a bad
tyre cannot per se constitute negligence on the part of the driver unless
it is shown by evidence that it was the mechanical condition that of
necessity caused or contributed to the accident.  In the instant case even
if the driver of the plaintiff was convicted of driving a vehicle in a dangerous
mechanical condition because of a bad tyre, it was not shown that he
had negligently failed to control the vehicle because of a bad tyre.
Therefore contributory negligence was not proved.
The first defendant was within the scope of his employment when he
caused the accident while returning home after dropping the veterinary
surgeon to the farm of the second defendant.  Returning home did not
alter the essence of the first engagement, that of dropping a surgeon at
the farm.
The oral application to amend the plaint would be refused because it was
inordinately late and would necessitate fresh investigations on the part of
the defendants to make a rebuttal.
Where the value of repairs is higher than the replacement value, court
would only award the replacement value.
A plaintiff is enjoined to mitigate his damages. Thus court would compute
damages for lost income from the date of collision to the period when with
due diligence the repairs ought to have been completed.  In the present
case it would be the period when the vehicle ought to have been replaced.
Ush 1, 00,000/= would therefore be awarded because the plaintiff had
testified that by the date of the accident he had already made money to
to buy another vehicle.
Suit allowed with costs.
Regina Nalukwago Vs. Dr. Phillip Byaruhanga & 2 others.
Negligence - reipsa laquitur - whether plea available where lorry
over turned along a tarmac road.
Vicarious liability-course of employment-whether lorry not driven in course
of employment because driver not known.
Vicarious liability-frolic of driver-whether owner of lorry not liable because
driver on own frolic-because driver not authorized to carry passengers.
General damages-quantum where plaintiff suffered loss of part of the
right maximally and part of molar borne inter-alia.
Held: It is a presumption of fact that where a vehicle is being driven by
someone other than the owner, the driver is the agent or servant of the
owner.  The owner has the onus to rebut the presumption by proving
otherwise.  In instant case the third defendant, owner of the vehicle failed
to rebut this presumption.
Res ipsa loquitor is a plea to effect that the mere fact of the accident
having happened should tell its own story and raise the inference of
negligence so as to establish a prima facie case.  If a driver is exercising
reasonable care, it is not usual for vehicles to overturn.  In the instant
case the plea of res ipsa loquitor was rightly made because the defendant
failed to explain why the lorry overturned.
A driver owes a duty of care towards everyone whom he knowingly
accepts as a passenger or in whose presence on the lorry he acquiesces
even though his master has forbidden him to take passengers.  Therefore
the happening of the accident was a breach of the duty of care.
A master is only liable where his servant can be said to be doing an act,
the doing of which he is guilty of negligence in the course of his
employment.  In the instant case there was nothing on the lorry by way
of notice to warn the public that the driver was prohibited to carry
passengers.  Therefore the master was liable for the negligence of the
driver because the people who boarded the lorry reasonably believed
that the driver was authorized to carry them.
Ush. 10 million would be awarded in general damages.
Suit allowed.
Raymond Katabakya Vs. Attorney General
Negligence -respsa laquitor - whether plea established where
defendant's driver lost control of the lorry which crushed
defendant's leg.
General damages-amputation above the knee-quantum.
Held: The plea of res ipas loquitor was rightly raised since the lorry
which crushed the plaintiff's leg was under the sole control of the
defendant's driver and the defendant had offered no explanation to show
that there was no negligence.  Therefore negligence on part of the
defendant's driver was presumed.
Uhs. 5 million would be awarded as general damages for an amputation
above the knee and permanent disability at 40%.
A plaintiff is precluded from leading evidence to prove a higher amount
of special damages than pleaded.  Therefore only the pleaded amount
would be awarded.
Suit allowed with costs.
Vincent Okello Vs. Attorney General
Detinue-confiscation of plaintiff's motor vehicle-whether detinue
proved.
Detinue-general damages thereof-quantum.
Exemplary damages-confiscation of plaintiff's motor vehicle-whether
exemplary damages awardable.
Held: Evidence must correspond to the pleadings.  The omission to plead
that the soldiers who confiscated the plaintiff's motor vehicle were acting
in the course of their employment meant that the plaintiff was precluded
from pleading evidence to prove what he did not plead. However, since the
defendant's witness in his evidence conceded this fact, it was proved that
the soldiers were acting in the course of their employment.
The quantum of damages in detinue is the value of the suit article as at
the date of judgment.  Ush 5 million would be awarded since this was
the value of the car at the date of judgment.
Exemplary damages are awarded inter alia where the conduct complained
of is oppressive, arbitrary, high handed, or unconstitutional. In the instant
case it was not unusual for soldiers in a war situation to commandeer a
plaintiff's motor vehicle for their use.  Moreover, the confiscation was not
done in any humiliating way.  Therefore the claim for exemplary damage
would fail.
Suit allowed with costs.
Sheik Kateregga & anor Vs. UEB
Course of employment - burden of proof -whether plaintiff has the
burden to prove that defendant's servants was acting in the course
of his employment.
Vicarious liability-course of employment-whether a UEB employee who
negligently causes damage to the plaintiff's house through dangerous
power connection may not be working in the course of his employment.
Held: In an action founded in negligence particulars thereof must be given
of the alleged negligence, showing in what respects the defendant was
negligent.  Though in the instant case the pleadings did not follow the
conventional itemization of the particulars, nevertheless, the pleadings
set out clearly what the plaintiff were alleging against the defendant.
He who affirms must prove the truth of his affirmations.  Since the
plaintiffs alleged that Lugoloobi was acting in the course of this
employment, it was incumbent upon them to prove the allegation.  Yet
the plaintiffs did not even produce Lugoloobi as a witness to testify as to
whether he was acting on his own frolic or not.
To make an employer liable for the act of a person alleged to be his
servant the act must be one of the class of acts which the person was
authorized or employed to do, even if the act is done wrongly or
negligently or wantonly.  In the instant case it was not sufficient to show
court that Lugoloobi was an employee of UEB but it was incumbent upon
the plaintiff's to show that the class of duties of the servant of the
defendant were the duties the doing of which resulted from the tortuous
damage to the plaintiffs.
Suit dismissed with costs.
Joseph Segirinya Vs. Attorney General
Detinue-smuggled goods-whether detinue proved where goods
were detained on suspicion that they were smuggled goods-
damages for detinue.
Held: Since the suspicion that the goods were smuggled goods was cleared
by the High Court in the order for revision against the Chief Magistrate's
order for repatriation of the goods filed by the DPP, at least from August
1991, the date of the High Court order, the Attorney General was liable in
the detinue by detaining the plaintiffs merchandise to December 1991 when
the goods were eventually released to the plaintiff.
Since the cigarettes were merchantable goods, the plaintiff was entitled to
their costs, and reasonably foreseeable profit as special damages.
Ush 2 million would be awarded as general for inconvenience due to the
detinue.
Jeffrey Thompson & anor Vs. Teddy Ssezi Cheeye & another.
Defamation -fair comment-whether defence proved where
defendant published an article to the effect that the plaintiff and his
company were bribing world bank officials.
Held: The defence of fair comment applies where the defendant's publication
is an honest expression of opinion but not to a statement of false facts.
The defendant had failed to prove the truth of his allegations.  Therefore the
defence of fair comment could not succeed.
Ushs 6 million general damages awarded for first plaintiff and Ush 2 million
general damages awarded to second plaintiff,  Ush 2 million awarded as
punitive damages.
Suit allowed with costs.
Benedict Tugumikiriza Vs. UEB
Damages - Electro shock causing extensive bodily burns and a
strong likelihood of impotence-quantum.
Held: Ush.16 million would be awarded as general damages for pain, and
suffering and loss of amenities due to the serenity of the injuries.
Suit allowed Ush 16m awarded as general damages.
Richard Kawuka Vs. Oboth Okumu
Defamation -slander-whether proved where plaintiff did not produce
the witness who heard the words complained of whether plaintiff
could rely on newspaper reports.
Held: In case of slander the law imposes on the plaintiff the burden to prove
that the words complained of were uttered by the defendant.  In the instant
case the defendant admitted having addressed the seminar but denied
having spoken the words complained of.  Therefore it was incumbent upon
the plaintiff to prove that actually the defendant spoke those words.
However, the plaintiff was his only witness and he himself admitted not
having attended the seminar at which the words complained of were
alleged to have been uttered.
Moreover, the newspaper report could not be used to prove that the words
complained of were spoken by the defendant, without the testimony in court
the newspaper reporter.
Suit dismissed with costs.
David Kironde Vs. Mukono District Administration & A.G
Vicarious liability -LDU )local defence forces) - whether Attorney
General is liable for their tortuous acts - whether LDU were servants
of the Attorney General.
Course of duty-LDU shooting plaintiff-whether acted in course of duty or
was on own frolic.
General damages - quantum for loss of an eye
Exemplary damages-LDU shooting plaintiff whether exemplary damages
awardable -quantum.
Held: It is a notorious fact that LDUs are trained and armed by the
government.  LDUs are an integral part of government machinery for the
maintenance of law and order in the country.  Therefore, even if there is no
statute defining the status of LDUs they are servants of government.
an LDU's duty is to maintain law and order and his duty involves stopping
and interrogating people.  That is why the LDU is armed.  Therefore even if
the act of hitting the plaintiff was wanton and unjustified it was nevertheless
the wrongful way of doing the authorized act.  Therefore the Attorney
General was liable for the tortuous act the LDU since the LDU was acting
in the course of his employment.
Ush 5 million would be awardable as general damages for the injury that
involved loss of an eye.
Exemplary damages are awardable where the act complained is done by a
government servant oppressively, arbitrary or unconstitutionally.  This was
the case when the LDU hit the plaintiff and made him lose his eye.
