Ush 1 million would be awardable as exemplary damages.
Suit allowed with costs to the defendant.
Martin Edeku Vs. Attorney General
Wrongful arrest, false imprisonment, and unlawful assault and
torture-damages -quantum.
Held: Ush 3,500,000/= would be awarded as general damages to the plaintiff
against the defendant for the abuse of the plaintiffs fundamental human
rights.
Suit allowed with costs.
BAT (u) 1984 Ltd Vs. Selestino Mushongore.
Fatal accidents -life expectancy - whether life expectancy in
Uganda has fallen below 50 years due to AIDS.
Fatal accidents-deceased's income-whether same as spent on family.
Fatal accidents-damages-whether damages must be a proportion by court
between dependents.
Held: Contributory negligence should be pleaded and particulars thereof
given.  In the instant case the defendant neither contributory negligence in
defence nor did court frame it as an issue. However, contributory negligence
arose but of the evidence and the learned trial judge was entitled to find that
the deceased who was knocked by the appellant's vehicle at the bus stage
had not acted unreasonably and was thereby not guilty of contributory
negligence.
The United Nations Development Program (UNDP)'s alleged indicators with
regard to life expectancy due to AIDS pandemic, had not been prove in
court as no evidence had been led.  Therefore the trial Judge should not
have used 20 as the multiplier but 15 due to imponderables in life.
The photographs were not admissible in evidence because the photogra-
pher was not called as a witness.  Therefore, the trial Court was entitled to
reject them.
The learned trial Judge erred when he held that the deceased's income
being Ush 20,000/= per day, therefore he  spent all the 20,000/=  per day
on his family.  The trial court should have found that the deceased spent shs
5000/= per day on his family.  This should have been multiplied by 15 years
being his remaining working life expectancy and multiplied by 365 days.
This should have been taxed to Ush 20 million.  This Ush 20 million should
have been apportioned to the tree dependants.
Appeal allowed only in part.  File ordered back to trial court to apportion the
award between to the three dependants.
Sulaim Kabugo Vs. Attorney General
Negligence -damages -quantum where plaintiff suffered chronic
partial intestinal obstruction and sustained ugly scars of the
abdomen and left knee and permanent disability assessed at 30%.
Held: The plaintiff had abdominal injuries and as a result would require
hospitalization from time to time and his disability degree was 30%.
Therefore, Ush 6 million would be awarded as general damages.
Suit allowed.
John Nagenda Vs. The Editor of the Monitor Newspaper & anor.
Defamation -justification -whether defense available where
defendant only pleads that the words complained of were true
infact and in substance.
Defamation -apology-whether a defendant that tenders an apology can rely
on the plea of justification.
Held: A defendant that offers an apology is precluded from raising the
defence of justification.  However in the instant case the alleged apology by
the defendant was the correction published later that the words complained
of were not uttered to the surveyor's wife but to DW1.  this is substance did
not amount to an apology.
Even  if an issue is specifically raised in the pleadings or framed for the
decision of the trial Court, if evidence is lead during the trial of the case on
the unpleaded issue and parties canvas the issue or one of the parties does
canvas the issue in the trial Court, unless the party complaining about the
irregular procedure was prejudiced by the irregularity, an appeal court will
not interfere.  In the instant case though justification was neither pleaded nor
made an issue for the determination of court, nevertheless the parties did
canvass the issue which was left to Court to determine.
Therefore the learned trial judge did not err in law or fact when he allowed
the defence of justification.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Glorious Transport Co.(1977) LTD Vs. Attorney General
Detinue -damages -quantum where soldiers removed motor lorry
from plaintiff and never returned it to him.
Held: In an action detinue the value of the property is assessed replacement
value of the detained article as at the time to judgment.  In the assistant
case, an expert automobile assessor assessment was that the new vehicle
of the same made as the suit vehicle had a life span 9 - 15 years.  The suit
vehicle being eight years old at the time a judgment, had a replacement
value a Sh.42 million.  This would be awarded as lost income as there was
no courtesy evidence.
Suit allowed with costs.
James Kabateraine Vs. Charles Oundo & anor.
Trespass, detinue and conversion -damages-whether punitive
damages may be awarded against court bailiff selling judgment
debtor's property after astray has been agreed.
Held: The sale was in flagrant violation of Rule 9(2) of the Court Bailiff's
Rules 1987 which requires that any sale at a price below the value of the
attached property must have the approval of court.  The bailiff having sold the
tractor valued at Ush 8 million at only Ush 3 million without the approval of
court violated the law and the sale was wrongful.
R 13 of the Court Bailiff's Rules, 1987 enjoins the bailiff not to sell the
property in execution on credit.  The bailiff violated this rule when he sold
the property of the judgment debtor/plaintiff on credit, by post-dated
cheque.
The execution was wrongful when it was levied after the stay had been
agreed between the parties.
The whole execution was irregular and would be set aside for having violated
the rules of court. This would still be so even if only one rule has been
violated.
A wrongful execution is a trespass and the plaintiff is entitled to an order of
restoration.  Therefore the defendant would be ordered to return to the
plaintiff his tractor or its value as at the date of judgment.
Ush 10 million would be awarded as general damages in trespass, detinue
and conversion.
Ush 2 million would be awarded as punitive damages.
Suit allowed with costs.
Joseph Kyalimpa Vs. Uganda Revenue Authority
Damages-damages to motor vehicle-quantum.
Damages-inconveniences-general damages therefore - whether general
damages for inconveniences awardable when damages for lost earnings
have been awarded.
Damages-damages to motor vehicle- replacement value - whether same as
market value.
Damages -punitive damages-whether payable where defendant has not
acted maliciously.
Held: Where an article has been destroyed the measure is the value of the
article in the market for its replacement.  In the instant case since the
plaintiff bought his motor vehicle at Ush 9 million ten years before it was
later destroyed by the defendant's servants Uhs 4.5 million would be
adequate in making good the loss caused by the defendant.
Since there was evidence that the plaintiff used his motor vehicle for profit
and counsel for the defendant had accepted to pay uhs 30,600/= per day
and yet counsel for the plaintiff had asked for Ush 40, 000/= court would
take into account the fact of imponderables like the falling sick of the driver
of the motor vehicle or for any other reason the motor vehicles failing to be
on the road and award Ush 30,600/= as lost earnings per day till payment
in full.
Only Ush 200,000/= nominal damages would be awarded as punitive
damages since the defendants servants acted foolishly and not maliciously.
Since the plaintiff had been awarded lost earnings he would be awarded
damages for inconveniences because the daily income awarded put into
account all he would have earned using the motor vehicle including pleasure
drives.
Case allowed and plaintiff awarded costs, punitive damages lost earnings and
replacement value of his damaged motor vehicle.
Benedict Musisi Vs. Attorney General
Unlawful arrest and imprisonment false imprisonment was defamatory-
- whether plaintiff may recover damages therefore.
Detinue -unlawful arrest and false imprisonment-whether defendant who is
liable for unlawful arrest and false imprisonment is also liable in detinue for
property consequently lost as a result of the detention.
Detinue-special damages therefore-whether general damages may be
awarded where specific damages for detinue have not been proved.
Special damages-detnue-whether general damages may be awarded where
special damages for detnue have not been proved.
Loss of earnings-specific damages-whether general damages may be
awarded in lieu of the failed proof of specific damages for loss of earnings.
False imprisonment-general damages therefore - quantum.
Held: There was no basis in law for false imprisonment and unlawful arrest
to constitute defamation. Therefore the claim for damages in defamation
was rightly dropped by the plaintiff.
The goods that were in the plaintiff's shop were taken by the soldiers or got
lost as a result of the unlawful action of the soldiers of detaining the
plaintiff. In either case the defendant was vicariously liable in detinue for the
In an action in detinue the damages awardable to the plaintiff is value of the
goods as at the date of judgment.  In the instant case since the plaintiff
had failed to show to court the prices of the merchandise he lost, Ush 15
million would be awarded as general damages in lieu of the special
damages claimed in detinue.
Loss of earnings should have been claimed as special damages.  However
the plaintiff had not specifically proved with credible evidence, documentary
or otherwise that he actually earned Ush 10,000 as he claimed.
Nonetheless, the plaintiff would be awarded Ush 5 million as general
damages in lieu of the claim for loss of earnings.
The detention for more than one year in undignified conditions of the
plaintiff by the defendant's servants without any charge, was unlawful
malicious and unfair and Ush 6 million would be awarded to the plaintiff as
general damages.
Suit allowed and the plaintiff awarded ush 15 million for his lost property,
Ush 6m for unlawful arrest and detention and Ush 5m as lost earnings.
Dr. Lukwago Ndawula & ars Vs. Salim Lumago & anor.
Negligence - whether proved against the first defendant whose
motor vehicle collided with the second defendant's stationary lorry
while climbing up hill at about 8.00 pm.
Damages - quantum therefore for various injuries sustained by the plaintiffs.
Held: The first defendant since he was climbing uphill it could not be said
that he drove at excessive speed and therefore negligence against him was
not proved.  It was the second defendant who as negligent by parking his
lorry in such a way as to make it hard for on coming drivers to see it at night
so as to avoid colliding into it.
The plaintiffs would respectively each be awarded the following general
damages - the first plaintiff Ush 3, 000,000 the second plaintiff Ush
3,500,000; the third plaintiff Ush 1,000,000; the fourth plaintiff Ush 1,500,000
the fifth plaintiff Ush 8,500,000.
Suit allowed against second defendant.
Consult Gas Engineers Ltd Vs. Uganda Electricity Board.
Fire -liability therefore where fire in the plaintiff's business premises
is caused by plaintiff's wire shorting.
Damages-destruction of plaintiff's property by fire-quantum of damages
therefore.
Held: Since the defendant's engineer recommended the replacement of the
plaintiff's writing system because it was dangerous but went ahead and
reconnected the electricity supply meant that the defendant was
contributorily negligent.  But since the defendant had not pleaded
contributory negligence in its defence it was wholly liable for the loss
attended by the plaintiff.
Ush 29 million would be paid as value of property destroyed by fire Ush
500,000/= as costs of the valuer's report and Ush 2 million general damages.
Suit allowed.
Amina Musoni Vs. Akamba (u) Ltd & Gaso Transport Services Ltd.
Negligence -whether proved where driver drove at excessive speed
the suit at night with poor head lights and collided with a stationary
lorry -whether the accident was inevitable because of the stationary
lorry which was in the dark with no reflectors or any other form of
warning in the middle road-whether the defence of novas was
available.
Contributory negligence-whether proved where a dimly lit bus collided with a
stationary lorry in the middle of the road with no reflectors at night.
Fatal accidents-life expectancy-deceased 54, business man what was his
working life expectancy.
Fata; accidents-dependency-whether proved where the plaintiff widow gave
conflicting number of children did not know the schools they attended their
ages and did not produce them in court.
Fatal accidents-dependency-whether proved where widow plaintiff could not
establish the income of her deceased husband.
Fatal accidents - damages - quantum.
Held: The transaction by which the first defendant sold the bus to the
second defendant was a normal business transaction.  Therefore the first
defendant could not be held liable for an accident caused by the bus already
sold to the second defendant.  Therefore the first defendant even though a
registered proprietor did not own the bust at the time of the accident and
was therefore wrongly sued.
The defence of novus actus grounded on the alleged sudden seeing and
knocking by the second defendant at the stationary lorry in the middle of the
road at a dark spot was not available to the defendant because the second
defendant's driver was negligent in driving the bust at night with poor head
lights and at excessive speed.  This means, had the second defendant's
driver not been negligent he could have avoided colliding with the lorry.
However, the owner of the lorry having parked the same in the middle of the
road without any sign for on coming traffic to be warned of its presence in
the middle of the road was negligent contributory by 40% and the bus driver
contribution negligent by 60%.
Since the plaintiff was 54 years old, a businessman in private employ, court
would assess his life expectancy at 60 years and his working life
expectancy at 6 years.
Since the plaintiff widow could not tell court consistently and credibly about
the number of children their ages and schools had not produced them in
court she had failed to prove who the dependant relatives were except the
widow.
The inconsistencies by which the plaintiff showed court that her husband
spent more on her family than he earned meant that the plaintiff had failed
to prove to court what her deceased husband's income was.
Had the plaintiff succeeded she would have been awarded Ush 100,000/=
(as she pleaded in the plaint being her late husband's income) multiplied
by 12 months (since the income was monthly) multiplied by 6 (the years of
her deceased husband's working life expectancy).  This would have been
reduced by 30% (being imponderables like death of fall in income and the
fact that the award was limp sum).  This would have been further reduced
by 40% (being the contribution of the third party lorry owner who was not
joined as co-defendant by the plaintiff or defendant).  The figure would have
come to Ush 3,024,000/=.
Suit dismissed.
Terensio Okidi Vs. Attorney General
Wrongful arrests, detention and false imprisonment.
Held: The plaintiff has not proved that he was arrested by the NRA
soldiers and has no complaint against the Police both at Busia and
Kampala or against any specific Government servant or agent.
There are no evidence adduced to lead court to believe that there were
circumstances requiring the army to act as they ought under s.6 of the
Armed Forces Act nor was there any evidence to show any criminal
offence which would have warranted the plaintiff's alleged, but not
produced Police statement.
Government is not vicariously liable to the plaintiff since he has not
proved any case against its agents.
No damages have been proved against the Government suit dismissed
costs to the defendant.
Opika Opoka Vs.1. Munno News Paper 2.The Editor, Munno
Newspaper 3. Munno Publication Ltd.
Libel-whether publisher is only vicariously liable.
Held: since the first and second objections were not raised in the WSD
they were new facts inconsistent with the pleadings and they
constituted a departure from the pleadings.
The Publication of the printed matter to the public makes the publisher
(jointly with the author and printer) personally liable and therefore it was
not necessary for the plaint to plead that the publisher is vicariously
liable.
H.M.B Kayondo SC Vs. The New Vision Printing & Publishing
Corp. An.
Defamation -libel-whether the newspaper article was libelous to
the plaintiff.
Held: This was a contemporaneous Newspaper report of judicial
proceedings and was therefore privileged absolutely unless it was
shown that the report was unfair, inaccurate and malicious, it could not
be called defamatory.
Though the Newspaper Article had some inconsistencies, a report in a
daily Newspaper is not to be judged by the same strict standards of
accuracy as the report of a professional law reporter and therefore the
New Vision reporter is not expected to be able to use exactly the
language used by the learned Principal State Attorney and therefore the
words used were a fair representation of what was said.
The representation having been fair the plaintiff had to prove that it was
malicious which he did not.
Mukasa Sula Vs. Mowrem International Constitution Ltd.
Damages special and general negligence injury to person and
property.
Held: General damages 2,800,000 for loss of motor vehicle.
Special damages 3,707,000/= for loss of fish load.
Bukenya Isa Vs. Departed Asian Property Custodian Board.
Assessment of Damages - general and special for detinue.
Held: Judgment for the plaintiff as prayed for the value of the property
at the date of judgment amounting to shs.14,602,210/= and lost
average income at shs.80,000/= per month.
Rev. Fr. Wasswa Vs. Attorney General
Negligence; Doctrine of res ipsa loquitur when applicable.
Held: This court observed in Edward Tumusiime Vs. Entebbe Municipal
Council C.S.921 of 1987, following Lwanyaga Vs. A.G. C.S.No.69 of
1982 and Hallinel Vs. Vehables (1930) 99 LJ KB 353 that vehicles do
not normally collide or hit other objects without some negligence on the
part of the driver even when driven at high speed.  The doctrine of
res Ipsa Loquitur (the thing speaks for itself) applies to the situation
before court.
The maxim applies whenever it is so improbable that such an accident
would have happened without the negligence of the defendant, that a
reasonable tribunal could find without further evidence, that it was so
caused.
The defendant could have rebutted this presumption by showing either
that there was no negligence on the part to the driver of the motor
vehicle which contributed to the accident, or that there was a probable,
cause of the accident which did not connote negligence on the part of
the driver or that the accident was due to circumstances beyond his
control.
As there is no explanation from the defendant the presumption has not
been rebutted.
It is now trite almost axiomatic that damages for tort or contract are
those which, so far as money can compensate, will give the injured
party reparation for the wrongful act and for all the natural and direct
consequences of the wrongful act.
General damages of 100,000/= are awarded and a decretal sum of
1,216,000 in favour of the plaintiff.
Bogere Patrick Vs. Wanzira Joshua.
Wrongful arrest-whether such had been established.
Held: Since the prosecution acted upon the facts as narrated by the
defendant, thee had been reasonable and probable cause to have set
the law in motion.
Since the defendant did not know the plaintiff till his arrest malice could
not be input upon the defendant.  Case considered; Herniman Vs
Smith (1938) 1 AER 1.
Nanyanzi Agenesi Vs. Uganda Metal Products & Enameling
Co. Ltd.
Negligence -defendant's servant or daring plaintiff to continue
operating defective machine-whether order done without reasonable
care because of subsequent injury.
Held: The ordering of the plaintiff to continue to operate a defective
machine was clearly without reasonable care and was a negligent act
on the part of the defendant. It was the duty of the defendant to take
reasonable care to provide and maintain a proper functional condition of
the machine so as not to subject its employee to unnecessary risk.
The Factories act cast upon a statutory duty the defendant to prevent
the inquiry sustained by the plaintiff by providing a safe drilling machine.
Because the plaintiff's hand grip was reduced by about 60% and her
permanent incapacity was assessed at 30% but she is still in the
employ of the defendant with a monthly pay of 500/= an award of
70.000/= general damages would be adequate compensation.
Charles Lubowa Vs. Kalyango & 3 others.
False imprisonment - whether proved.
Held: Since the arrest was according to S.28(1) of the Criminal
Procedure case where a private person is allowed to make arrests it he
reasonably suspects a commission of a felony, the arrest was lawful.
Since the defendants after effecting the arrest they promptly took the
plaintiff to the police station as per S.28, the criminal procedure code,
the subsequent detention by the police of the plaintiff did not create
liability on the part of the defendants.
Joseph Lukwago Vs. Attorney General.
Detinue-defendant's servants illegally returning the plaintiff's
Vehicle was stolen proved.
Held: Notwithstanding evidence that the chassis number of the was
nobody claiming the vehicle, the defence had not proved that the
vehicle did not belong to the plaintiff.
That since the NRA intelligence officers in illegally taking possession
the plaintiff's vehicle they over acting within the scope of their
employment the defendant was liable in his representative capacity as
Attorney General.
Since the servants of the defendants had acted high handedly, the case
for punitive damages had been proved.
Since the plaintiff had failed to present documentary evidence of other
evidence persuasive as to his having incurred special damage, this
was not proved.
Muwumba Kabire & Patrick Ndugwa Vs. V.H.& Bros.
Negligence-defendant's lorry crushing into plaintiff's premises and
causing damage.
Held: In absence of any guidance as to what general damages are
bought court would not consider them.
Obel Remigio Fr. Vs. Gulu Local Government.
Arrest and assault and 15% disability-quantum.
Exemplary damages-quantum where servants of defendant frog-
matched a catholic priest and assaulted him.
Held: Shs. 5 million would be awarded as general damages for the
unlawful arrest and assault and injuries.
Exemplary damages is essentially a punishment for the high handedness
of the conduct of the defendant or his agent.  It is not compensatory.  In the
instant case shs. 2 million would be awarded.
Suit allowed Shs. 5 million and 2 million general and exemplary damages
respectively awarded.
Musisi Bandito Vs. Attorney General.
Defamation-unlawful arrest and detention-whether this amounts to
defamation.
Damages-unlawful arrest and detention-quantum therefrom.
Detinue-whether proved where servants of defendant -unlawfully
arrested and detained the plaintiff as a consequence of which his
property were lost.
Damages-special damages-failure to prove prices of property lost
and lost earnings-whether court may award general damages in
lieu.
Held: The plaintiff was correct in dropping the claim of defamation arising out
of the illegal arrest and detention because that claim had no basis in law.
The plaintiff would be awarded shs. 6 million for the illegal arrest and
detention.
When goods have been taken from the plaintiff judgment is for the return of
the detained chattel or their market value as at the date of judgment,
together with damages for the detention.  In the present case the plaintiff had
had successfully proved that he lost the items due to the unlawful arrest and
detention by the servants of the defendant and was entitled to the market
value of the goods as at the date of judgment.
The market value of the lost items is claimed as special damages which
must be strictly proved.  In the instant case the plaintiff failed to prove to
court the market value of the items lost.  However, court may in such
circumstances award general damages in lieu of the special damages whose
value is not proved.  In the instant case shs. 15 million would be awarded.
Shs 5 million would be awarded as loss of earning.
Suit allowed with costs.
Mufumu Fred Vs. Uganda Electricity Board.
Damages-special damages-failure to prove thereof-whether general
damages may be granted in lieu thereof.
Held: The plaintiff was a person with established employment for some
length of time and therefore must have reasonably furnished his house with
reasonable domestic equipment.  Shs. 10million would be awarded as
general damages as compensation for the destroyed items.
Suit allowed with costs.
Kamuza Grace Vs. Kibaaya.
Fatal accidents-Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act-
damages for pain and suffering endured by the deceased before his
death-whether awardable to his dependants-quantum for injuries on
the clerical bone and the ankle.
Fatal accidents-Law Reform (Misc.Prov.) Act-deceased aged 76
years-whether dependency not provable because deceased's age
beyond working life expectancy.
Negligence-contributory negligence-clear weather and clear road-
whether defendant thereby liable contributory.
Held: The road being clear in a clear weather and very thin traffic would have
given the defendant's driver opportunity to avoid the accident had he been
mindful enough of other road users.  This was inspite of the folly of the
deceased crossing from one side of the road to the other unmindful of his
satety.Therefore, the defendant would be found 40% contributorily negligent.
In Uganda the working life expectancy is 55 years only and the deceased
being 76 had no more life to expect, having lived beyond his usefulness.
Therefore no damages may be awarded to his dependants for loss of
dependency.
Where a person does not die immediately after the accident his estate is
entitled to claim damages for the pain and suffering inflicted on the deceased.
In the instant case the deceased was hospitalized for one month after having
suffered injuries on his clavicle bone and ankle.  Sh. 200,000/= and shs.
300,000/= would be awarded for the injuries to the clavicle bone and ankle
respectively.  And shs. 57,000/= would be awarded as proved medical
expenses.
Kateregga Sheik & anor Vs. Uganda Electricity Board.
Vicarious liability-course of employment-whether defendant's
servant acted in course of employment when he illegally and
negligently connected electric power to a house that caused
damage to the plaintiff's home.
Held: From the evidence on record there was nothing to show that the
respondent's servant was employed by the respondent as an electricity
technician and that on the fateful day he acted as such on the instructions
of the respondent.  Therefore, the learned trial just was right in holding
that he had no evidence before him to hold that the respondent's servant
made the fatal power connection.
Appeal dismissed.
Kinyera Filda Oyella Vs. Attorney General.
Fatal accidents-dependant-S.3(1)(a) Workmen's Compensation
Act-Girlfriend-whether or not a member of the family and therefore
not a possible dependant.
Fatal accidents-funeral expenses incurred by the aunt of the
deceased-whether not recoverable under S.3(1) (a) Workmen's
Compensation Act.
Held: Under the Law Reform Miscellaneous Provisions Act, the action can
only be brought under S.3 (1) (a) of the Workmen's Compensation Act a
girlfriend cannot be called a member of the family.  Therefore 2nd plaintiff's
action must be dismissed.
To be recoverable, the (funeral) expense must be in respect of the funeral
of the deceased person and must have been incurred by the parties for
whole benefit the action is brought and the action can only be brought for the
benefit of the members of the family.  The funeral expense incurred by the
aunt of the deceased is not recoverable because under S.3 (1)(a)

Shs. 13,608,000/= would be paid as general damages to the 1st plaintiff for
the benefit of the members of the family.  This is because evidence proved
that the deceased spent shs. 60,000/= per month on his family and the life
expectancy being 55 years, the deceased being 25 had 30 years to live
and support his family.  Then 60,000/= x 12 months x 30 years would come
to shs. 21,600,000/=.  That amount has to be scaled down because it is
given as a lump-sum, scaled down by 10%, and further scaled down by 30%
to provide for imponderables.  This would leave shs. 13,608,000/= payable
as general damages, to be apportioned in such a way that the youngest
child takes 50% then 45% the next child and 5% for the mother.

Owiny Kenneth Vs. Attorney General
Malicious prosecution-reasonable and probable cause-whether
proved-whether lack thereof of malice.
Malicious prosecution-general damages-quantum.
Held: To prove the tort of malicious prosecution the plaintiff must prove that
his prosecution by the defendant, was actuated by malice and to prove that
malice the plaintiff may show that the prosecution was not based on
reasonable or probable which he was prosecuted.  In this case the police, as
agents of the defendant, the Attorney General, commenced and continued
the prosecution of the plaintiff on facts that had been previously thoroughly
investigated and dismissed as baseless.  Therefore, the prosecution of the
plaintiff was not based on reasonable or probable cause and this was
evidence of malice.
The plaintiff was entitled to Ug. Shs. 4 million as general damages for
malicious prosecution.
Case allowed with costs.
Kavuma F W Vs. Sembule Investment Bank
Conversion - cheques-whether bank was liable in conversion when
it appropriated the plaintiff's cheques to someone else's use.
Conversion-quantum of damages.
Held: A person is guilty of conversion who without lawful excuse, deprives
another of his goods by giving some other person a lawful title to them.
In the present case, the third party had only defective title to the cheques
as the true owner was the plaintiff.  The defendant dealt with the cheques in
a manner inconsistent with the rights of the plaintiff who was the true owner,
and are therefore prima facie, liable to him for the conversion of the cheques.
S.82(1)(2) Bills of Exchange Act protects a bank from liability in conversion
where the bank has acted in good faith and without negligence and the
cheque in question is a crossed cheque.  In the instant case though the
bank sought to rely on Section 82 Bills of Exchange Act for protection and
pleaded to have acted in good faith and without negligence, the bank did not
lead evidence to show that the cheques in question were crossed.
Secondly, the bank's failure to investigate the particulars of the customer
who purported to be the owner of the cheques was evidence in question
were crossed.
The plea that the plaintiff had ratified the act of the third party cannot stand.
A principal can only ratify the act of a person who is his agent.  In the
instant case the third party never acted for the plaintiff and never said so.
The plead that the plaintiff was a partner of the third party cannot stand
because even if it were true that the third party and the plaintiff were partners
a co-owner can commit conversion in respect of joint property.  However,
neither the third party nor the plaintiff claimed that they were partners.
The alleged indemnification of the defendant by the plaintiff when he agreed
to drop his complaint against the defendant cannot be said to have been
done voluntarily because, the plaintiff had had no legal counsel; the plaintiff
was desperate for accessing even the little balance to offset his debts, so
it was a corrupt bargain and it was unenforceable and moreover the
defendant never performed his part of the bargain.
The measure of damages for conversion of (a chattel) cheques is their face
value.  Therefore, the defendant would pay Ugshs.31 million to the plaintiff
the face value of the cheques.
Case allowed with costs against the defendant.
Arua Motor Dealers Vs. Attorney General
Government proceedings- limitation-whether war a disability -
whether trespass was a continuous tort.
Government proceedings- limitation - whether claim barred by
Legal Notice No.1/86 S.12(2).
Held: S.2(2) Civil Procedure and Limitation (Misc. Prov.) Act bars actions
founded on contract against Government after the expiry of 3 years from the
date the cause of action arose.  However, before it is concluded that a
cause of  action is time barred, it must be shown when the said cause of
action arose. In the present case the plaint did not concisely plead the
terms of the contract nor the date of its execution as required by O.7 r 1(e).
Therefore, it is difficult to conclude that the plaintiff's cause of action had
been accrued.
However, S.23 Limitation act provides that where there is acknowledgement
of the debt the cause of action is revived from the date of acknowledgement.
However, O.7 r 14(1) requires that where a party whishes to sue on a
document must annex the same to the plaint at the date of filing.  In the
instant case the plaintiff while submitting from the bar that it was in
possession of documents showing that government had acknowledge the
date, the documents were never annexed to the plaint.  Therefore, the
alleged acknowledgement and consequent revival of the cause of action was
not proved.
The submission by the plaintiff that there was a war going on in Arua and
this was a disability preventing the plaintiff to file its action in time, would
not succeed because there was no evidence that the whole of Uganda was
engulfed in war.  Courts in many parts of the country were open.
The action in tort was barred by Legal Notice No.1/86.
Objection upheld.  Plaint rejected.
Babita Aisha Vs. Akamba Public Transport Ltd
Negligence - over-speeding-whether negligence established.
Negligence -contributory negligence-whether proved.
Fatal accidents - funeral expenses-failure to attach receipts-
whether damages awardable.
Fatal accidents, Law Reform (Misc. Prov.) Act-damages-quantum-
multiplier applicable.
Held: The fact the skid marks covered 60 meters was evidence that the
defendant's bus was running at very high speed and this was manifest
evidence of negligence.  Moreover the scene of the accident was near a
market where the defendant's driver should have known that it was a busy
place, and thereby taken the necessary caution.
The deceased was knocked a few meters before he was able to cross the
road, at a point which was not a zebra crossing.  This means that the
deceased failed to make sure that he would successfully cross the road
before he ventured to do so.  Therefore, the deceased was guilty of
contributory negligence, which in the circumstances would be assessed at
Funeral expenses as pleaded would be awarded although as special
damages proof thereof is strict.  The failure to attach receipts of expenditure
in proof of funeral expenses was excusable because at the time of
bereavement, it is not possible to attend to details such as asking for
receipts.  Moreover, the items pleaded are such as the ones that must be
available when someone dies.
Although the plaintiff claimed that her husband earned Ugsh.1.5m/=, no
proof was presented and although the plaintiff claimed that the deceased
looked after his family adequately, no evidence was presented as to the lost
benefit likely to be suffered by his family.  However, it is understandable
that a wife may not know quite well the income of her husband.  Therefore
court would follow the precedent in Agnes Nakawooya Sebalamu V. A.G
HCCS 505/96 where court found itself in a similar situation and awarded
Ugsh. 150,000/= as the money spent by the deceased on his family per
month.
Suit allowed with costs.
Ssenynja Pascal Vs. Attorney General.
Negligence-duty of care-whether the defendant was liable for failing
to provide sage means of transport.
Negligence - contributory negligence-whether plaintiff who sat
dangerously on a lorry was contributorily negligent for the resultant
injury.
Damages-loss of an eye-quantum.
Held: Negligence is the failure in the duty of care.  The standard of care is
that foresight and caution expected by the ordinary man in the
circumstances of a particular case.  In the case instant, the defendant
failed to provide safe means of transport by transporting human beings on a
cargo trailer.  Since the defendant knew that his means of transport was not
safe, he should have been cautions enough to at least vicariously liable in
negligence by the resultant damage caused to the plaintiff.
Contributory negligence means that the plaintiff did not take reasonable care
of himself and by reason thereof contributed to his injury.  In the present
case the plaintiff and other students on the lorry sat on their luggage
because there were no seats on the trailer.  There was no evidence that the
plaintiff in any way contributed to his injury.
Shs. 3 million would be awarded as general damages for loss of an eye.
Suit allowed with costs.
Segawa Godfrey Major Vs. Editor Crusader Newspaper & anor
Defamation-Damages, general and aggravated quantum.
Held: Where the defendant does not apologizes after he has written a
defamatory article about the plaintiff, such defendant aggravates the
damages.  Therefore the defendant would pay Ush. 500,000/= as aggravated
damages and Ush. 2 million as general damages for the defamation.
Suit allowed with costs.
Okello Eric & Anor Vs. Wade Adams Ltd.
Negligence - damages - swelling of the tibia and 10% permanent disability-
quantum of damages.
Fatal Accidents SS.7 & 8 Law Reform (misc.prov.) Act - loss of expectation
of life - quantum of damages where deceased was 17 years old at school.
Held: O.7 r.14 (2) provides that no reliance in Court shall be allowed on a
document not mentioned in the plaint or annexed there to. In the present
case since the expert was giving oral evidence it was sufficient without
relying on the document.
It is true that African children, who are educated, often at considerable
sacrifice, by their parents, are expected to make contribution to the welfare
of their parents in return.  However such a custom is not static and the
changes may result in the parents not necessarily expecting contribution to
their welfare from their educated children.
Ush. 1,500,000/= would be awarded as general damages for the swollen
tibia where permanent disability was calculated at 10%.
Suit allowed.
Wayuu Robert & anor Vs. Sugar Corporation of Uganda & anor
Negligence-contributory negligence-burden of proof thereof-whether
invariably on defendant.
Negligence - loss of personal effects and money during an
accident-whether probable and foreseeable loss and compensatable
Negligence-General damages for loss of tooth, cracked tooth,
multiple wounds and pain and shock for one plaintiff and a fractured
right arm resulting in 15% disability, multiple injures, pain and
suffering for the second.
Held: The defendant who sets up the defence of contributory negligence has
the burden of proof to prove that the plaintiff contributed to the negligence
and to what extent.  In the instance case the defendants merely pleaded
contributory negligence but never produced evidence to prove the allegations
of contributory negligence.  Therefore, it is the second defendant's
negligence, which was solely to blame for the accident and the first
defendant was vicariously liable for the negligence of his driver.
It is a notorious fact that victims of accidents in Uganda are stripped of their
properties.  And it is normal and reasonable that an officer traveling from
upcountry to the city would carry along some reasonable amount of money
for some shopping.  All these were foreseeable and probable losses and
compensatable and wee proved.
Ush. 4m/- would be awarded for the fractured right arm of the second plaintiff
whose disability was assessed at 15% and Uhs.2.5 M/- for his bodily injuries
for pain and suffering.
Ush.1.8M/- would be awarded for lost tooth and his damaged tooth and
Ush.1.2M/- for shock, pain and suffering for the first plaintiff.
Suit allowed with costs.
Nile Safaris Ltd Vs. Hot Ice Ltd & Grahamed Denis
Negligence -inevitable accident-whether proved.
Held: The trial Judge was correct in finding that failure to use the fire
extinguisher if any existed, was not the cause of fire, nor the class of the
driving permit of the driver.  Therefore the appellant had failed to prove
negligence on the part of the respondent.
The burden of proof of inevitable accident is on the defendant pleading the
same.  However, the defendant only needs to plead inevitable accident
where the plaintiff has established a prima facie case to negligence.  In the
present case the appellant failed to establish a prima facie case negligence
and therefore the respondents were not bound to plead nor prove inevitable
accident.
Costs followed the event unless a successful party proves to court to its
satisfaction that special reasons do exist to warrant him getting the costs
from the successful party. In the present case the appellant had not
discharged the burden of proof that special circumstances exist to warrant
that appellant be awarded the costs from the successful party.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Deo Kigozi Vs. Uganda Commercial Bank
Negligence-vicarious liability-whether defendant Bank was
vicariously liable for the action of the police whether it is Attorney
General liable.
Held: The plaintiff had shown that the police officers who manned the
investigations of the theft of the defendant's money were delegated by the
defendant and that the defendant controlled and directed the manner in
which the officers did their work.  Therefore, the defendant bank was liable
for the tortuous acts of the police officers seconded to the defendant bank.
The defendant bank was liable for the false arrest, detention and assault of
the plaintiff by the police officers.
Suit allowed.  Ush.500,000/= for false arrest, detention and Ush. 500,000/=
for assault and Ush.86,000/= per day for 89 days for the time the taxi was
detained by the defendant.
TRAFFIC & ROAD SAFETY ACT
Wini Geyonga Rusheyegera Vs. Uganda.
Reckless driving -whether ingredients thereof proved.
Held: The trial Magistrate was fully entitled under section 143 of the
Magistrates' Court Act, 1970 to decide the facts as he did and hold the
appellant guilty of a leasser offence.
Courts have no powers to reduce a sentence below the statutory
minimum sentence.
Where three are more than one count in a charge should carry its own
verdict either of condition or acquittal and each conviction should be
covered by a sentence to be served either concurrently or consecutively.
Akisoferi Biteremo Vs. Attorney General.
Lack of transfer of motor Vehicle-whether vitiates plaintiff's claim.
Held: The plaintiff had established that he had been detained for 14 days
and it was incumbent upon the defence to show that the detention was
lawful.  Since the defence failed to shoe that the detention was lawful, it
must be presumed that the plaintiff was unlawfully detained.
At the time the plaintiff's vehicle was detained it was in possession of the
plaintiff and the law presumes possession to be lawful unless the contrary
is proved. The plaintiff's possession was therefore lawful and therefore the
tort of detinue had been established sine the plaintiff had demanded for
its return to no avail.
SS 50 and 53 (2) of the Traffic and Road Safety Act require that every
motor vehicle purchased must be transferred into the names of the
purchaser.  However in spite of the plaintiff's failure to have the requisite
transfer made, he was still entitled to make his claim in detinue since by
virtue of the purchase he was entitled to the immediate possession of the
motor vehicle.
Shs. 2.5 million would be awarded for the unlawful detention as general
damages.
The plaintiff had failed to prove the un earned income as special damages
since he had not shown what business he was doing with the motor
vehicle.
Abendego Absolom Ongom Vs. Amos Kaheru.
Registered owner -credit purchase-whether therefore new buyer is
not owner of the vehicle because he has not completed payment of
contract price.
Held: Where a defendant does not appear, having filed a Written
Statement of Defence and the trial proceeds ex parte, remedies cannot
be granted to the plaintiff just as prayed unless they are sufficiently
supported by the pleadings.
As per S.26 (2) of the Sale of Goods Act, the transfer of title and payment
of purchase price in a contract of sale are not concurrent conditions.
therefore the defendant having bought the car and having obtained
possession of it with the consent of the vendor, he had become its owner
even though he had not paid all the installments.
Negligence is failure to observe the duty of care.  The duty of care is
owed to persons to place that they may reasonably be expected to be
injured by the omission to take such care.  In the instant case the facts
of the case clearly show that the defendant's driver attempted to overtake
the plaintiff at a place where it was not safe to do so.  He was therefore
negligent.
Even though the defendant in his WSD attempted to plead contributory
negligence he failed because no particulars there were provided.
Moreover, the burden of proof of contributory negligence lay on the
defendant, who failed to discharge the burden when he failed to come to
The plaintiff had proved as special damages, the cost of private medical
treatment ush.1,240,000/=; loss of sitting allowances Uhs.180,000=.
The plaintiff had failed to prove the claim for the cost of transport to and
from hospital for himself and his wife who visited him regularly.  This is
because no evidence had been led to that effect.
In case of destruction of goods the measure of damages is taken to be
the market value of the goods destroyed at the time and place of
destruction.  Therefore the plaintiff's claim for a replacement value of a
new car would fail since his damaged car was old.
The plaintiff's disability assessed at 60% was quite an exaggeration
because the plaintiff suffered potts fracture, which healed nicely.
However, the plaintiff was in plaster of Paris for four months and had
screws in his body and suffered posttraumatic arthritis. He would
therefore be awarded Ush 5 million general damages.
Case allowed with costs to the plaintiff.
Okitoi Epilu Vs. Uganda.
Using a motor vehicle with defective handbrake-driving with unequi-
vocal plea of guilty to the charge-whether sentence excessive.
Held: The Magistrates Courts (Amendment) Act 4/85 amended s.192(d)
and provided that for any fine not exceeding shs.2000/= to be met with
a maximum period of imprisonment not exceeding seven days in
default.  Therefore the default sentence of one month would be set
aside and substituted with 7 days.
Any fine exceeding shs. 2000/= but not exceeding shs.10,000/= carries
a maximum of one month's imprisonment in default.  The sentence of
six months is illegal and should be substituted with one month.

Irumba Richard Vs. Florence Irumba
Written law, S.3(2)(a) Judicature Act.
Held: "Law in force immediately before the commencement of the Judicature
Act, 1967, for purposes of S.4(2) Divorce act, was the law applicable in the
High Court of Justice in England, in 1950, and that was the Matrimonial
Courses Act (1950), which provided that a Divorce petition could only be filed
after at least 3 years of the marriage sought to be annulled, except with leave
of court.  However, the learned appellate Judge was correct to have held that
the 3 years rule could only be applied subject to the peculiar conditions in
Uganda and for that matter to have held that the 3 year rule could not apply.
Written Law, an expression that appears in S.3(2)(a) of the Judicature Act
1967, means the Constitutional Instruments, and any other legislative
enactments or legislative instruments having effect in Uganda.
Appeal dismissed with costs.
Tusiime Twebaze Drake Vs. Uganda
"Beyond reasonable doubt"- whether this must be invariably stated in the
judgment where accused is convicted.
Held: The object of an identification parade is to make sure that the ability of
the witness to recognize the suspect is tested.  However, the identification
parade is not the only such test.  The correctness or otherwise of
indent faction by witness, of the accused will depend on the circumstances,
such as the length of time, the distance, the light, the familiarity of the
witness with the accused.  If the quality of these is good, the danger of
distance identity is reduced. In the instance case the evidence adduced
by the prosecution and not contradicted by the appellant clearly showed that
the complainant and other prosecution witnesses who were involved in the
alleged motor vehicle purchase transaction office hours.  The circumstances
of identification could not come not have been better.  The learned trial
magistrate was correct to come to the conclusion she came to.
It is not necessary for the convicting court to always state that the
prosecuting has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The elements of the offence of uttering a false document and those of forging
a document are different.  Therefore it is possible as it was in the case
instant to convict a person of uttering a false document while acquitting him
of forging the same.  Moreover, there was no requirement that to prove of a
handwriting expert.  The appellant had been seen by witnesses that
testified seeing him uttering the false documents.
The sentence of 3 years was not excessive.  The trial court took into
account the fact that the appellant was a graduate who should have used
his education to do better things.
Appeal dismissed.
